ITID-41111.def: A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary sends a high-rate stream of UDP packets, often to random or fixed destination ports, with the sole aim of consuming available bandwidth and/or forcing the target (or its upstream links/devices) to spend CPU cycles generating ICMP port-unreachable replies until legitimate traffic can no longer get through.
ITID-41111.purpose: Captures a volumetric flood built from raw UDP packets aimed at saturating link bandwidth or a target's packet-processing capacity.
scopeIncludes: Direct (non-reflected) UDP packet floods sent straight at a target IP/port
Random-port UDP floods intended to trigger ICMP unreachable generation
Fixed-port UDP floods against a specific listening service used purely as a bandwidth sink
scopeExcludes: UDP-based reflection/amplification techniques that abuse a third-party service to multiply traffic (see Amplification Attacks)
TCP-based SYN flooding (see SYN Flooding)
Application-layer request floods over UDP-based protocols like DNS or SIP (see their respective leaves)
ITID-41111.severity: High when sustained volume threatens to saturate WAN/ISP-facing bandwidth or exhaust edge device state tables; Medium if absorbed cleanly by existing scrubbing/rate-limiting with no observed service degradation.
ITID-41111.priority: P2 on detection with active mitigation engaged; escalate to P1 if bandwidth saturation is confirmed or customer-facing services are degraded.
ITID-41111.escalation: Escalate to network operations and upstream ISP/scrubbing provider once sustained volume exceeds baseline capacity thresholds or edge devices report packet loss.
indicators: Sharp spike in inbound UDP packets-per-second on border routers/firewalls
Elevated ICMP port-unreachable generation rate from the target
Link utilization graphs showing sudden saturation with no corresponding legitimate traffic growth
NetFlow/sFlow records showing many source IPs (or few spoofed sources) sending small UDP packets to varied or fixed destination ports
vectors: Commodity stresser/booter tooling generating raw UDP floods
Custom or off-the-shelf flooding scripts (e.g. hping3, LOIC-style tools) run from compromised hosts
rootCauses: Insufficient upstream bandwidth or rate-limiting at the network edge
No DDoS scrubbing/black-hole routing agreement in place with the ISP/CDN
Edge firewalls/routers not rate-limiting or filtering high-volume UDP by default
mitreTechniques: T1498.001 Network Denial of Service: Direct Network Flood
controls: Upstream DDoS scrubbing service
Border router/firewall rate-limiting on UDP traffic
BGP black-holing/flowspec for high-volume sources
Anycast/CDN distribution to absorb volumetric traffic
ITID-41111.detection: Strong technical signal from NetFlow/sFlow, SNMP interface counters, and firewall/IPS logs showing packet-rate and bandwidth anomalies in near real time.
ITID-41111.response: Engage upstream scrubbing or rate-limiting immediately on confirmed saturation; capture flow samples for source/pattern analysis; validate service restoration once mitigation is active.
metrics: Peak inbound UDP pps/bps observed
Time to mitigation engagement
Duration of measurable service degradation
detections: Border router UDP pps/bps threshold alerting
NetFlow anomaly detection for volumetric floods
ITID-41111.notes: Differentiate from ICMP Flood by protocol; differentiate from Amplification/Smurf by the absence of a reflecting third party. This is the direct, brute-force sibling in the Volumetric Flooding group.

playbook.name: UDP Flood Attack
playbook.description: High-volume, typically spoofed-source UDP packets are directed at random or fixed ports on the target to saturate inbound bandwidth and exhaust stateful device resources.

steps.title: Confirm volumetric UDP flood via NetFlow/sFlow baseline deviation
steps.desc: Compare current inbound UDP packet/byte rate against the 30-day rolling baseline for the affected prefix or host using flow telemetry.
steps.guidance: Pull NetFlow/sFlow/IPFIX summaries for the last 15-30 minutes and graph pps/bps by destination IP and destination port. A flood typically shows a sharp step-change with wide source-IP dispersion and low port entropy on the destination side (random or single high port).
steps.outcome: Confirmed abnormal UDP pps/bps spike attributable to the affected asset, with source IP/ASN distribution captured for reference.
steps.abort: If the spike correlates with a known legitimate bulk transfer or backup job, stand down and document as false positive.
steps.tool: NetFlow analyzer / sFlow collector (e.g., Kentik, SolarWinds NTA)

steps.title: Engage upstream ISP/scrubbing provider for traffic diversion
steps.desc: Request BGP redirection of affected prefix to DDoS scrubbing service or activate always-on scrubbing if already contracted.
steps.guidance: Notify upstream transit provider(s) and/or cloud DDoS protection (e.g., Cloudflare Magic Transit, AWS Shield Advanced) with attack characteristics; request UDP flood mitigation profile activation.
steps.outcome: Malicious traffic diverted through scrubbing infrastructure; clean traffic returned via GRE/VXLAN tunnel or direct peering.
steps.abort: If scrubbing is unavailable within SLA, proceed to local rate-limiting as interim measure.

steps.title: Validate no reflector/amplifier role and no persistent botnet foothold
steps.desc: Confirm the affected environment is not itself misconfigured to be abused as a UDP reflector and that no compromised internal hosts are participating in the flood.
steps.guidance: Check for open UDP services (DNS, NTP, SNMP) exposed unnecessarily; review internal egress flow logs for hosts sending anomalous outbound UDP consistent with botnet participation.
steps.outcome: Confirmed clean internal posture; any misconfigured exposed services identified for remediation.

steps.title: Remove temporary mitigations and restore normal routing/limits
steps.desc: Roll back BGP diversion and temporary ACLs/rate limits once attack traffic subsides below baseline for a sustained period.
steps.guidance: Monitor for at least 2 hours post-attack-cessation before fully reverting scrubbing diversion to avoid premature exposure to a resurgent flood.
steps.outcome: Traffic restored to normal path with confirmed stable service performance.
steps.abort: If flood resumes, re-engage containment before completing rollback.

steps.title: Document attack profile and update DDoS runbook thresholds
steps.desc: Record attack volume, duration, mitigation effectiveness, and update automated detection thresholds/scrubbing activation triggers accordingly.
steps.guidance: Include timeline, peak pps/bps, mitigation time-to-effect, and any gaps (e.g., delayed scrubbing activation) in the after-action report.
steps.outcome: Updated runbook and detection thresholds; action items assigned for any capacity or automation gaps.

steps.title: Packet-capture sample to characterize flood composition
steps.desc: Capture a short packet sample at the edge to determine source IP spoofing indicators, payload size distribution, and targeted ports.
steps.guidance: Use tcpdump/Wireshark on a SPAN/mirror port for 30-60 seconds. Look for uniform packet sizes (bot-generated), TTL anomalies suggesting spoofing, and whether ports are fixed (service-targeted) or randomized (bandwidth-exhaustion only).
steps.outcome: Documented packet profile (size, TTL distribution, port pattern) supporting classification as UDP flood vs. reflection/amplification.

steps.title: Apply local rate-limiting and ACLs on edge routers/firewalls
steps.desc: Implement UDP rate limiting (e.g., CoPP, policers) and destination-port ACLs on border routers/firewalls to reduce load while scrubbing engages.
steps.guidance: Apply control-plane policing thresholds for UDP and, if ports are fixed, block or rate-limit those specific destination ports at the perimeter.
steps.outcome: Reduced load on downstream infrastructure; service availability partially or fully restored while awaiting scrubbing.
steps.abort: If legitimate UDP services (DNS, VoIP) are impacted, narrow ACL scope immediately.
steps.tool: Router/firewall CLI (Cisco IOS/ASA, Juniper, Palo Alto)

steps.title: Harden exposed UDP services and unnecessary open ports identified
steps.desc: Close or firewall any unnecessarily exposed UDP services discovered during the reflector check, and remove any compromised host from the network for reimaging.
steps.guidance: Apply least-privilege ACLs to any UDP service that does not need to be internet-facing; quarantine and reimage any host confirmed to be participating as a bot.
steps.outcome: No remaining internal exposure that could contribute to a repeat or related attack.

ITID-41112.def: A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary sends a high-rate stream of ICMP packets (typically Echo Request/'ping') directly at a target to consume link bandwidth and force the target or intermediate devices to spend CPU cycles processing and replying to each packet.
ITID-41112.purpose: Captures a volumetric flood built from ICMP Echo Request (or other ICMP type) traffic aimed at saturating bandwidth or exhausting device processing.
scopeIncludes: Direct (non-reflected) ICMP Echo Request floods sent straight at a target IP
High-rate ICMP floods of other types (e.g. Echo Reply, Timestamp) used purely as a bandwidth/processing sink
scopeExcludes: Broadcast-address-spoofed ICMP amplification via intermediary networks (see Smurf Attack)
Oversized/malformed single ICMP packets intended to crash a host (see Oversized Fragmented Packet / Ping of Death-Style Attack)
ITID-41112.severity: High when sustained volume threatens bandwidth saturation or router/firewall CPU exhaustion; Medium if filtered cleanly by existing ICMP rate-limiting.
ITID-41112.priority: P2 on detection with mitigation engaged; escalate to P1 on confirmed link saturation or device CPU exhaustion.
ITID-41112.escalation: Escalate to network operations once ICMP volume exceeds baseline thresholds or edge devices show elevated CPU/interface utilization attributable to ICMP processing.
indicators: Sharp spike in inbound ICMP packets-per-second at the border
Elevated CPU utilization on routers/firewalls correlated with ICMP processing
Link saturation graphs coinciding with ICMP traffic spikes
vectors: Commodity stresser/booter tooling generating raw ICMP floods
Scripted flood tools run from compromised or rented hosts
rootCauses: ICMP not rate-limited at the network edge
Absence of upstream scrubbing for volumetric ICMP traffic
mitreTechniques: T1498.001 Network Denial of Service: Direct Network Flood
controls: Border router/firewall rate-limiting on ICMP
Upstream DDoS scrubbing service
Selective ICMP filtering policies balanced against operational ping/traceroute needs
ITID-41112.detection: Strong technical signal from SNMP interface counters and firewall/IPS logs showing ICMP packet-rate anomalies.
ITID-41112.response: Apply or tighten ICMP rate-limiting immediately; engage upstream scrubbing if bandwidth saturation is confirmed; confirm restoration of normal ICMP baseline.
metrics: Peak inbound ICMP pps observed
Router/firewall CPU utilization during event
Time to mitigation engagement
detections: Border router ICMP pps threshold alerting
ITID-41112.notes: Differentiate from UDP Flood by protocol; differentiate from Smurf Attack by the absence of broadcast-address reflection.

playbook.name: ICMP Flood Attack
playbook.description: A high rate of ICMP Echo Request (ping) or other ICMP messages is sent to the target to consume bandwidth and CPU cycles processing/responding to each packet.

steps.title: Confirm ICMP flood via protocol-breakdown traffic analysis
steps.desc: Analyze flow telemetry to confirm the anomalous traffic is predominantly ICMP (type 8 Echo Request or other types) rather than mixed-protocol volumetric traffic.
steps.guidance: Filter NetFlow/IPFIX by protocol=ICMP and compare pps against baseline. Note ICMP type/code distribution to distinguish simple ping flood from crafted variants.
steps.outcome: Confirmed ICMP-dominant flood with volume and source distribution documented.
steps.abort: If ICMP volume is a small fraction of total anomalous traffic, reclassify as multi-vector flood.

steps.title: Rate-limit or block ICMP at perimeter and upstream
steps.desc: Apply ICMP rate-limiting policers on edge devices and request upstream ACL/rate-limit on ICMP toward the affected prefix.
steps.guidance: Most environments can safely rate-limit ICMP Echo traffic without breaking legitimate operations (path MTU discovery uses ICMP type 3, not type 8) — ensure only Echo Request/Reply are throttled, not all ICMP.
steps.outcome: ICMP flood volume reduced to below saturation threshold at the perimeter.
steps.abort: If blocking all ICMP breaks legitimate monitoring/PMTUD, scope the rate-limit to type 8/0 only.

steps.title: Confirm no directed-broadcast or reflector misconfiguration internally
steps.desc: Verify internal network devices are not configured to allow directed broadcast (which could turn this into a smurf-style amplifier) and that no internal hosts are echoing at scale.
steps.guidance: Check router configs for 'no ip directed-broadcast' equivalent settings and review internal ICMP egress for anomalies.
steps.outcome: Confirmed internal infrastructure is not contributing to or amplifying the attack.

steps.title: Restore normal ICMP policy and validate service performance
steps.desc: Remove temporary rate limits once attack subsides and confirm normal ICMP-dependent functions (PMTUD, monitoring) operate correctly.
steps.guidance: Monitor for 1-2 hours of stable baseline traffic before full rollback.
steps.outcome: Normal ICMP handling restored with no residual service degradation.

steps.title: Update ICMP baseline thresholds and mitigation playback
steps.desc: Record attack characteristics and refine automated ICMP anomaly thresholds for faster future detection.
steps.guidance: Include peak pps, mitigation timeline, and any collateral impact from rate-limiting.
steps.outcome: Updated detection thresholds and documented incident timeline.

steps.title: Determine source spoofing and geographic/ASN distribution
steps.desc: Sample packet captures to assess whether source IPs are spoofed (random, non-routable, or inconsistent with plausible client geography) or from a real distributed botnet.
steps.guidance: Check for source IPs in bogon/reserved ranges (indicates spoofing) and TTL consistency. Cross-reference against threat intel for known botnet C2/reflector lists.
steps.outcome: Documented spoofing assessment informing containment approach (ACL vs. upstream filtering).

steps.title: Activate upstream scrubbing if volume exceeds local mitigation capacity
steps.desc: Engage ISP or cloud DDoS scrubbing provider if local rate-limiting is insufficient to preserve link capacity.
steps.guidance: Provide attack signature (protocol=ICMP, pps, source distribution) to the scrubbing provider for a targeted mitigation profile.
steps.outcome: Attack traffic diverted and scrubbed upstream; local link capacity restored.

steps.title: Remediate any hosts confirmed as flood sources on internal networks
steps.desc: If any internal hosts were found generating or echoing anomalous ICMP as part of the flood, isolate and remediate them.
steps.guidance: Quarantine affected endpoints, run malware scans, and reimage where compromise is confirmed.
steps.outcome: Internal source of the flood, if any, fully remediated.

ITID-41113.def: A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary simultaneously or sequentially combines two or more direct protocol floods (e.g. UDP, ICMP, TCP) against the same target to exceed the capacity or scope of mitigations tuned for any single protocol.
ITID-41113.purpose: Captures a volumetric flood that deliberately blends multiple raw-protocol flood types in the same attack window to defeat single-protocol mitigations.
scopeIncludes: Concurrent UDP+ICMP+TCP floods against one target within the same incident
Sequential shifting between flood protocols during an attack to probe for gaps in mitigation coverage
scopeExcludes: Single-protocol floods (see UDP Flood / ICMP Flood)
Combining volumetric floods with application-layer techniques across the full attack lifecycle (see Combined Volumetric and Application-Layer Multi-Vector DDoS under Hybrid DDoS Attack)
ITID-41113.severity: High by default given the intent to defeat layered mitigation; escalate priority if any single vector achieves partial saturation.
ITID-41113.priority: P1, given the deliberate multi-vector design intended to outpace mitigation response.
ITID-41113.escalation: Escalate to network operations, DDoS mitigation provider, and incident command immediately on confirmation of more than one concurrent flood protocol.
indicators: NetFlow/sFlow showing simultaneous spikes across multiple protocols (UDP, ICMP, TCP SYN)
Mitigation dashboards showing vector counts >1 for a single attack ID
Traffic composition shifting protocol mix mid-attack
vectors: Multi-vector stresser/booter platforms offering combined attack profiles
Botnet C2 issuing sequential or parallel attack-module commands
rootCauses: Mitigation tuned to a single dominant protocol signature
Lack of automated multi-vector detection and correlation across flow sources
mitreTechniques: T1498.001 Network Denial of Service: Direct Network Flood
controls: Multi-vector-aware DDoS scrubbing service
Automated attack-signature correlation across protocols
Border rate-limiting policies covering all common flood protocols
ITID-41113.detection: Strong when flow telemetry is correlated across protocols; weak if monitoring is siloed per protocol and each vector individually stays under threshold.
ITID-41113.response: Treat as a single coordinated incident even when individual vectors appear sub-threshold; engage full-spectrum scrubbing rather than per-protocol filters.
metrics: Number of concurrent flood vectors observed
Time to correlate vectors into a single incident
Peak combined bandwidth/pps across all vectors
ITID-41113.notes: Scoped to combinations of raw network-layer floods only; a mix that also includes application-layer vectors belongs under the Hybrid DDoS Attack leaf instead.

playbook.name: Multi-Vector Volumetric Flood (Combined Protocol Types)
playbook.description: Simultaneous flooding using multiple protocols (e.g., UDP, ICMP, TCP) targets the same infrastructure to overwhelm detection and mitigation systems tuned for a single vector.

steps.title: Break down attack traffic by protocol and vector to build composite profile
steps.desc: Analyze flow telemetry across all protocols simultaneously to identify each concurrent vector (UDP, ICMP, TCP SYN, etc.) and their relative contribution to total volume.
steps.guidance: Generate a protocol-distribution chart over the attack window; multi-vector attacks often show vectors shifting in dominance every few minutes as the attacker adapts to mitigation.
steps.outcome: Documented breakdown of concurrent vectors with timeline showing any vector-shifting behavior.

steps.title: Activate full-spectrum scrubbing covering all identified vectors
steps.desc: Engage upstream/cloud DDoS scrubbing with mitigation profiles covering each concurrent vector rather than a single-protocol filter.
steps.guidance: Provide the scrubbing provider the complete vector breakdown so they enable all relevant mitigation modules (UDP flood, ICMP flood, SYN flood, and L7 WAF rules) concurrently.
steps.outcome: All identified vectors mitigated simultaneously; residual traffic reduced across the board.
steps.abort: If one vector persists after scrubbing activation, escalate that specific vector for targeted tuning.

steps.title: Verify no vector was missed and no internal amplification/compromise contributed
steps.desc: After primary mitigation stabilizes, re-scan traffic for any residual or newly emerging vector, and confirm internal systems are not being abused as reflectors or bots.
steps.guidance: Multi-vector attackers often reintroduce a previously-mitigated vector once others are blocked; maintain heightened monitoring for 24-48 hours.
steps.outcome: Confirmed no residual or resurgent vectors; internal infrastructure integrity confirmed.

steps.title: Phase down mitigations per vector as each normalizes
steps.desc: Incrementally roll back per-vector mitigations only after each shows sustained normal baseline, rather than reverting all controls simultaneously.
steps.guidance: Track each vector independently since one may resolve well before others.
steps.outcome: Full service restoration with no premature exposure to a still-active vector.

steps.title: Document multi-vector timeline and evaluate cross-layer detection gaps
steps.desc: Capture the full attack timeline across vectors and assess whether detection/mitigation tooling correlated vectors quickly enough.
steps.guidance: Recommend investment in unified DDoS detection correlating L3/L4/L7 signals if response was delayed by siloed tooling.
steps.outcome: After-action report with cross-layer detection improvement recommendations.

steps.title: Correlate with DDoS protection platform alerts across all mitigation layers
steps.desc: Cross-check alerts from network-layer scrubbing, WAF, and application monitoring to confirm the attack spans multiple OSI layers.
steps.guidance: Multi-vector campaigns frequently combine an L3/L4 volumetric flood with an L7 application flood as a smokescreen or secondary pressure point — confirm whether application-layer anomalies coincide.
steps.outcome: Full-stack view of concurrent attack vectors across network and application layers.

steps.title: Apply layered local defenses (rate limits, SYN cookies, WAF) as compensating controls
steps.desc: While upstream scrubbing engages, apply local per-vector mitigations (rate limiting UDP/ICMP, enabling SYN cookies, tightening WAF rules) to reduce load on downstream infrastructure.
steps.guidance: Coordinate changes across network and application teams simultaneously to avoid gaps as the attacker pivots between vectors.
steps.outcome: Reduced infrastructure load across all layers pending full scrubbing effectiveness.

steps.title: Close any cross-layer exposure identified across the multiple vectors
steps.desc: Remediate any specific gap identified per-vector (e.g., open reflector service, unpatched L7 endpoint, missing WAF rule) so the same combination cannot be reused.
steps.guidance: Track remediation per vector to ensure none is overlooked given the complexity of a multi-vector campaign.
steps.outcome: All per-vector exposures closed and verified.

ITID-41114.def: A denial-of-service event exhibiting clear volumetric flooding characteristics (bandwidth or packet-rate saturation) where the specific protocol or delivery mechanism has not yet been determined or does not cleanly fit an existing Volumetric Flooding leaf.
ITID-41114.purpose: Intake bucket for volumetric network floods that cannot yet be attributed to a specific protocol category.
scopeIncludes: Initial triage of a suspected volumetric flood before protocol analysis is complete
Volumetric floods using protocols not separately enumerated in this taxonomy branch
scopeExcludes: Any flood already confirmed as UDP, ICMP, or multi-vector (reclassify to the specific leaf once confirmed)
Reflection/amplification or slow-rate attacks, which have their own Tier-4 groups
ITID-41114.severity: Medium-High pending confirmation; reassess once protocol/vector is identified.
ITID-41114.priority: P2 pending triage; adjust once reclassified to a specific leaf.
ITID-41114.escalation: Escalate to network operations for flow capture and protocol identification; reclassify and re-triage once confirmed.
indicators: Bandwidth/pps saturation without a confirmed dominant protocol at initial detection
vectors: Unconfirmed at time of intake
rootCauses: Insufficient initial flow visibility to determine protocol composition
mitreTechniques: T1498.001 Network Denial of Service: Direct Network Flood
controls: Upstream DDoS scrubbing service
Flow-based traffic capture for post-hoc classification
ITID-41114.detection: Depends on available flow telemetry; sufficient to detect volume anomaly but insufficient to classify protocol at time of intake.
ITID-41114.response: Engage general volumetric mitigation immediately; run protocol analysis in parallel to reclassify the incident.
metrics: Count of incidents landing in this catch-all per quarter
Average time to reclassification
ITID-41114.notes: This is a triage/intake bucket; analysts should reclassify to a specific Volumetric Flooding leaf as soon as the protocol is confirmed. A persistently high volume in this bucket signals a flow-visibility gap.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Volumetric Flooding Attack
playbook.description: A high-volume network flood is observed that does not clearly fit a specific UDP, ICMP, or multi-vector classification and requires general volumetric-DoS triage.

steps.title: Establish baseline deviation and gather flow telemetry
steps.desc: Confirm the alert represents a genuine volumetric anomaly by comparing current traffic against historical baseline across all protocols/ports.
steps.guidance: Pull NetFlow/sFlow for the affected destination(s) over the past hour and compare to same-time-of-day/day-of-week baselines.
steps.outcome: Confirmed abnormal traffic volume with initial protocol/port breakdown captured.
steps.abort: If deviation is within normal variance or explained by a legitimate event, close as false positive.

steps.title: Engage upstream scrubbing with general volumetric mitigation profile
steps.desc: Request activation of the provider's general/adaptive DDoS mitigation profile pending more specific vector identification.
steps.guidance: Most cloud scrubbing platforms offer an adaptive/automatic mode suitable for unclassified volumetric attacks.
steps.outcome: Attack traffic diverted and reduced via general mitigation profile.

steps.title: Complete vector classification and close any identified exposure
steps.desc: Once mitigation stabilizes service, complete forensic classification of the attack vector(s) and remediate any contributing internal misconfiguration.
steps.guidance: Reclassify the incident to the specific ITID leaf if a clear technique is identified; document rationale if it remains genuinely unclassified.
steps.outcome: Attack technique documented (or confirmed unclassifiable) and any internal exposure closed.

steps.title: Roll back temporary mitigations and confirm stable baseline
steps.desc: Restore normal traffic handling once attack volume subsides and remains below baseline for a sustained period.
steps.guidance: Monitor for at least 2 hours before full rollback.
steps.outcome: Service restored to normal performance with no residual mitigation-induced impact.

steps.title: Document incident and improve classification tooling
steps.desc: Record why the attack was not immediately classifiable and recommend detection tooling improvements to reduce future triage time.
steps.guidance: Include recommendations for flow-analysis automation or signature libraries that would have sped up classification.
steps.outcome: After-action report with concrete detection tooling improvement items.

steps.title: Attempt vector classification via packet sampling
steps.desc: Capture representative packets to attempt classification into a known volumetric technique for more targeted response.
steps.guidance: If classification succeeds (e.g., clearly UDP or ICMP dominant), pivot to the corresponding specific playbook; otherwise continue general triage.
steps.outcome: Either a refined classification enabling playbook pivot, or confirmation the attack is genuinely mixed/unclear.

steps.title: Apply conservative local rate-limiting across top anomalous flows
steps.desc: Rate-limit the top talkers and top destination ports identified in flow analysis at the network edge as an interim measure.
steps.guidance: Use flow data to identify the highest-volume source ASNs/prefixes or destination ports and apply targeted, reversible rate limits.
steps.outcome: Reduced peak load while broader mitigation and classification continue.
steps.abort: Remove rate limits immediately if legitimate traffic is impacted disproportionately.

steps.title: Confirm no internal hosts or services contributed to or amplified the flood
steps.desc: Review internal egress logs and exposed-service inventory to confirm the organization's own infrastructure did not participate in or amplify the attack.
steps.guidance: Check for any unnecessarily exposed UDP/ICMP services and any internal hosts showing anomalous outbound traffic during the attack window.
steps.outcome: Confirmed clean internal posture or remediation items identified and tracked.

ITID-41121.def: A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary sends a high rate of TCP SYN packets with forged (spoofed) source IP addresses to a target, causing it to allocate connection state for each half-open connection until its backlog/SYN queue is exhausted and legitimate connections are refused.
ITID-41121.purpose: Captures a SYN flood in which the adversary spoofs source IP addresses to exhaust a target's half-open connection table without needing a botnet.
scopeIncludes: SYN floods using randomized or forged source IP addresses from a single or small number of originating hosts
SYN floods relying on IP spoofing rather than distributed real bot sources
scopeExcludes: SYN floods driven by many genuine, non-spoofed bot sources (see Distributed Botnet-Driven SYN Flood)
SYN-ACK reflection techniques abusing third-party hosts (see SYN-ACK Reflection Flood)
ITID-41121.severity: High when the target's SYN backlog is confirmed exhausted and new legitimate connections are being dropped; Medium if SYN cookies/proxying are absorbing the load without service impact.
ITID-41121.priority: P2 on detection; escalate to P1 on confirmed connection-table exhaustion or service unavailability.
ITID-41121.escalation: Escalate to network/security operations immediately if SYN cookies are not enabled or the backlog is confirmed exhausted.
indicators: Sharp rise in half-open (SYN_RECV) connections on the target
High volume of SYN packets from widely varied, often non-routable or unlikely source IPs
No corresponding ACK completion for the majority of observed SYNs
vectors: Raw-socket flooding tools with source IP spoofing (e.g. hping3)
Commodity stresser/booter SYN flood modules
rootCauses: SYN cookies or SYN proxying not enabled on the target/firewall
Ingress/egress filtering (BCP38) not enforced upstream, allowing spoofed traffic to reach the target
Connection backlog queue sized too small for expected peak legitimate load
mitreTechniques: T1498.001 Network Denial of Service: Direct Network Flood
controls: SYN cookies/SYN proxy on load balancers and firewalls
Upstream BCP38 source-address filtering
Connection rate-limiting per source
Upstream DDoS scrubbing service
ITID-41121.detection: Strong technical signal from connection-state tables and firewall/IDS SYN-rate alerting.
ITID-41121.response: Enable/verify SYN cookies immediately; engage upstream filtering or scrubbing if spoofed volume threatens link capacity; validate connection table recovery.
metrics: Peak half-open connection count
SYN cookie activation time
Duration of connection refusals for legitimate clients
ITID-41121.notes: Differentiating axis for this Tier-4 group is delivery mechanism: this leaf is spoofed/single-source, its sibling is genuine distributed bots, and the reflection sibling abuses third-party responders.

playbook.name: Spoofed-Source SYN Flood
playbook.description: TCP SYN packets with forged, randomized source IP addresses are sent at high volume to exhaust the target's connection (half-open) state table.

steps.title: Confirm SYN flood via half-open connection state and SYN-only flow analysis
steps.desc: Check server/firewall connection tables and flow data for a surge in SYN packets with no corresponding completed handshakes (no ACK follow-through).
steps.guidance: Review netstat/ss half-open connection counts on affected hosts and confirm SYN:ACK ratio anomaly in flow telemetry.
steps.outcome: Confirmed SYN flood with connection table near exhaustion documented.

steps.title: Enable SYN cookies and tune backlog on affected hosts
steps.desc: Activate SYN cookie protection on the target servers/load balancers to avoid committing state for unacknowledged connections.
steps.guidance: Enable net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies=1 (Linux) or equivalent on load balancers/firewalls; increase SYN backlog queue size as a secondary buffer.
steps.outcome: Server no longer exhausts connection state table under SYN flood load; legitimate connections continue to complete.

steps.title: Confirm origin infrastructure not exposed to unnecessary direct connectivity
steps.desc: Verify the targeted service sits behind the scrubbing/proxy layer and that direct-to-origin IP access is not still exploitable to bypass mitigation.
steps.guidance: Check for origin IP leakage (e.g., via historical DNS records, TLS certificate transparency) that would let an attacker bypass the CDN/scrubbing layer.
steps.outcome: Confirmed origin is not directly reachable, or origin-IP protection (allowlisting only the CDN/scrubber ranges) is enforced.
steps.tool: Origin firewall allowlist / CT log review

steps.title: Restore standard connection handling and validate performance
steps.desc: Once attack subsides, confirm SYN cookie and backlog settings remain appropriately tuned (rather than fully reverted) for ongoing resilience.
steps.guidance: SYN cookies can generally remain enabled permanently with negligible performance cost; validate no legitimate client connection issues resulted.
steps.outcome: Stable service with hardened SYN handling retained as a permanent improvement.

steps.title: Document attack and confirm BCP38/uRPF coverage improvements with upstream
steps.desc: Record the incident and follow up with upstream providers on anti-spoofing filtering coverage to reduce future spoofed-source attack effectiveness.
steps.guidance: Include correspondence with ISP regarding uRPF deployment status.
steps.outcome: After-action report with anti-spoofing improvement tracking.

steps.title: Verify source-IP spoofing via TTL/bogon analysis
steps.desc: Capture sample SYN packets and analyze TTL consistency and source-IP validity to confirm spoofing rather than a genuine distributed source.
steps.guidance: Spoofed floods typically show implausible TTL variance for claimed source geography and a high proportion of source IPs from unallocated/bogon or unlikely-client ranges.
steps.outcome: Confirmed spoofing assessment informing whether uRPF/BCP38 filtering will be effective.

steps.title: Deploy upstream SYN flood scrubbing and uRPF filtering
steps.desc: Engage upstream/cloud DDoS mitigation with SYN flood-specific proxying (SYN proxy) and request unicast Reverse Path Forwarding filtering to drop obviously spoofed packets.
steps.guidance: Provide attack signature to the scrubbing provider; request BCP38/uRPF enforcement at ISP edge where feasible to reduce spoofed traffic reaching the network.
steps.outcome: Spoofed SYN volume substantially reduced before reaching origin infrastructure.

steps.title: Lock down origin firewall to accept traffic only from scrubbing/CDN ranges
steps.desc: If origin IP exposure was found, apply firewall rules restricting inbound connections to only the known IP ranges of the scrubbing/CDN provider.
steps.guidance: Coordinate the change window with the network team to avoid inadvertently blocking legitimate provider IP range updates.
steps.outcome: Origin no longer directly reachable by attackers bypassing the scrubbing layer.

ITID-41122.def: A denial-of-service attack in which a botnet of compromised, internet-routable hosts each open TCP connections toward a target and either withhold the final ACK or abandon the handshake en masse, exhausting the target's half-open connection capacity through sheer distributed source volume rather than spoofing.
ITID-41122.purpose: Captures a SYN flood generated by a large number of genuine, non-spoofed bot-controlled hosts rather than address spoofing.
scopeIncludes: SYN floods originating from many distinct, real (non-spoofed) source IPs under botnet control
Coordinated SYN flood campaigns issued via botnet C2 commands
scopeExcludes: Spoofed-source SYN floods from a small number of originating hosts (see Spoofed-Source SYN Flood)
Reflection-based SYN-ACK floods (see SYN-ACK Reflection Flood)
The underlying botnet recruitment/infrastructure mechanism, documented under ITID-317xx Botnets
ITID-41122.severity: High given the difficulty of source-based filtering against genuinely distributed real IPs; escalate if geographic/ASN diversity of sources is confirmed.
ITID-41122.priority: P1 on confirmation of distributed botnet sourcing, given limited effectiveness of simple IP blocking.
ITID-41122.escalation: Escalate to network operations and DDoS mitigation provider immediately; consider threat intel correlation against known botnet infrastructure.
indicators: High volume of SYN packets from thousands of distinct, geographically diverse source IPs
Source IPs correlating with known botnet C2 infrastructure or IoT device ranges in threat intel
Half-open connection exhaustion despite source-IP-based rate-limiting attempts
vectors: IoT or general-purpose botnets issuing SYN flood attack commands from infected members
DDoS-for-hire platforms renting access to existing botnets
rootCauses: Reliance on per-source-IP rate-limiting alone, ineffective against high source diversity
No behavioral/anomaly-based DDoS mitigation layer in front of the target
mitreTechniques: T1498.001 Network Denial of Service: Direct Network Flood
controls: Behavioral/anomaly-based DDoS scrubbing service
SYN cookies/SYN proxy on load balancers
Threat intelligence feeds for known botnet source ranges
ITID-41122.detection: Strong when flow telemetry captures source IP diversity and can be correlated with threat intel; weaker with only volumetric thresholds.
ITID-41122.response: Engage upstream scrubbing/anycast absorption rather than manual IP blocking; correlate sources against botnet threat intel to inform longer-term blocklisting.
metrics: Distinct source IP count observed
Peak half-open connections
Time to scrubbing engagement
ITID-41122.notes: This leaf documents the network-layer DoS impact of botnet-driven SYN flooding; the botnet recruitment and C2 mechanism itself is scoped to ITID-31711 (IoT Device Botnet Recruitment) and related ITID-317xx leaves. Cross-reference rather than duplicate.

playbook.name: Distributed Botnet-Driven SYN Flood
playbook.description: A large botnet of real, non-spoofed devices sends SYN packets from genuinely distinct source IPs at high volume, exhausting connection state without relying on spoofing.

steps.title: Confirm SYN flood with genuine (non-spoofed) distributed sourcing
steps.desc: Analyze source IP distribution to confirm a large number of genuinely distinct, geographically plausible source addresses rather than spoofed ranges.
steps.guidance: Cross-reference source IPs against known botnet C2/IoT scanning threat intel feeds and check for TCP three-way-handshake completion attempts (real hosts often complete more of the handshake than spoofed floods).
steps.outcome: Confirmed distributed botnet sourcing with source IP list captured for blocking/reporting.

steps.title: Deploy SYN cookies and connection-rate limiting per source
steps.desc: Enable SYN cookies and apply per-source-IP connection rate limits to blunt the flood without penalizing the full traffic mix.
steps.guidance: Since sources are real IPs, per-IP rate limiting is effective (unlike spoofed floods) — apply granular thresholds at the load balancer/firewall.
steps.outcome: Reduced effective attack volume through per-source throttling while legitimate clients remain largely unaffected.

steps.title: Report botnet nodes and coordinate takedown/abuse notification
steps.desc: Submit abuse reports to hosting providers/ISPs for identified botnet nodes and consider engagement with law enforcement or industry ISAC for large-scale campaigns.
steps.guidance: Include timestamps, source IPs, and attack signature in abuse reports; escalate to ISAC/CERT coordination for widespread or repeat-offender botnets.
steps.outcome: Abuse reports filed; where applicable, coordinated takedown initiated.
steps.tool: Abuse reporting portal (AbuseIPDB, provider abuse contacts)

steps.title: Restore normal connection thresholds and monitor for resurgence
steps.desc: Gradually relax rate-limiting thresholds once attack volume subsides while maintaining heightened monitoring for renewed activity from the same botnet.
steps.guidance: Retain the botnet IP blocklist for an extended monitoring period since botnets frequently resume attacks after brief pauses.
steps.outcome: Service restored to normal with continued blocklist protection against known attacker nodes.

steps.title: Document botnet characteristics and update long-term blocking strategy
steps.desc: Record botnet family, source characteristics, and effectiveness of per-source rate limiting for future reference.
steps.guidance: Recommend subscribing to relevant botnet-tracking threat feeds if this attack revealed a gap in current intel coverage.
steps.outcome: After-action report with threat intel and blocking strategy improvements.

steps.title: Profile botnet behavior and identify C2/family if possible
steps.desc: Analyze connection patterns, user-agent/TLS fingerprints (if any accompanying L7 traffic), and known IOCs to identify the botnet family driving the flood.
steps.guidance: Check request timing regularity, source ASN concentration (hosting providers vs. residential IoT), and any correlation with known botnets (e.g., Mirai variants).
steps.outcome: Botnet family identified or characterized, informing blocklist strategy and law-enforcement/abuse reporting.

steps.title: Push botnet source list to upstream scrubbing and blocklists
steps.desc: Provide the confirmed botnet source IP list to the upstream DDoS scrubbing provider and internal blocklists for immediate filtering.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with the scrubbing provider to apply reputation-based or explicit-list blocking for the identified botnet nodes.
steps.outcome: Confirmed botnet nodes blocked upstream, reducing attack traffic reaching the origin network.

steps.title: Confirm no organization-owned devices are part of the botnet
steps.desc: Check internal device inventory and outbound traffic logs to rule out the possibility that organization-owned IoT or servers are themselves part of the attacking botnet.
steps.guidance: Review egress flow logs for any internal host communicating with known botnet C2 infrastructure or exhibiting scanning/flooding behavior.
steps.outcome: Confirmed no internal devices are compromised botnet members, or any found are isolated and remediated.

ITID-41123.def: A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary spoofs the target's IP address as the source of SYN packets sent to numerous innocent third-party hosts; those hosts each reply with a SYN-ACK directed at the spoofed (target) address, flooding the target with unsolicited SYN-ACK traffic it never requested.
ITID-41123.purpose: Captures a SYN flood delivered via reflection, where spoofed SYN packets sent to third-party hosts cause those hosts to send unsolicited SYN-ACK replies at the true target.
scopeIncludes: SYN packets spoofed with the victim's source IP and sent to third-party reflectors, which respond with SYN-ACK to the victim
Reflection campaigns using large, internet-scanned lists of responsive TCP hosts as unwitting reflectors
scopeExcludes: Direct spoofed SYN floods sent straight at the target (see Spoofed-Source SYN Flood)
Genuine distributed botnet SYN floods with no reflection (see Distributed Botnet-Driven SYN Flood)
ITID-41123.severity: High given the amplification and source-obfuscation characteristics; treat any confirmed reflection campaign as a scrubbing-required event.
ITID-41123.priority: P2 on detection; escalate to P1 on confirmed sustained reflection volume or link saturation.
ITID-41123.escalation: Escalate to network operations and upstream provider for reflection-source filtering; consider reporting reflector ranges to their network owners.
indicators: Inbound flood of unsolicited SYN-ACK packets with no matching prior outbound SYN from the target
Source IPs of the flood corresponding to legitimate, unrelated third-party services rather than obvious botnet hosts
vectors: Internet-wide scanning to build reflector lists of hosts responding to spoofed SYN packets
Booter/stresser services offering SYN-ACK reflection as an attack option
rootCauses: Widespread lack of BCP38 source-address validation across the internet enabling spoofing
Target-side filtering not distinguishing unsolicited SYN-ACK floods from legitimate traffic
mitreTechniques: T1498.002 Network Denial of Service: Reflection Amplification
controls: Upstream DDoS scrubbing service filtering unsolicited SYN-ACK traffic
Stateful firewall rules dropping SYN-ACK with no matching outbound SYN
Industry-wide BCP38 adoption (outside direct organizational control, tracked as a systemic risk)
ITID-41123.detection: Strong technical signal: unsolicited SYN-ACK with no matching connection state is a clean, low-false-positive indicator.
ITID-41123.response: Filter unsolicited SYN-ACK traffic at the firewall/scrubbing layer; engage upstream mitigation for volume; no action needed against reflector hosts themselves beyond optional abuse reporting.
metrics: Peak unsolicited SYN-ACK pps
Number of distinct reflector source IPs observed
Time to filtering engagement
ITID-41123.notes: This is the reflection-based sibling in the SYN Flooding group; its MITRE mapping differs from its direct-flood siblings because it is a reflection/amplification technique.

playbook.name: SYN-ACK Reflection Flood
playbook.description: The attacker spoofs the victim's IP as the source of SYN packets sent to numerous third-party servers, causing those servers' unsolicited SYN-ACK replies to flood the victim.

steps.title: Confirm inbound flood is unsolicited SYN-ACK traffic
steps.desc: Analyze captured traffic to confirm the flood consists of SYN-ACK packets for connections the victim never initiated, arriving from numerous unrelated third-party IPs.
steps.guidance: Correlate destination ports/source IPs against the victim's actual outbound connection log — a reflection flood shows SYN-ACKs with no matching prior outbound SYN from the victim.
steps.outcome: Confirmed SYN-ACK reflection pattern with reflector IP list captured.

steps.title: Apply upstream scrubbing filtering on SYN-ACK-without-prior-SYN pattern
steps.desc: Engage upstream/cloud DDoS mitigation to filter unsolicited SYN-ACK packets before they reach the origin.
steps.guidance: This mitigation is largely stateless-flow-based (drop SYN-ACK packets not matching a tracked outbound SYN) and is typically only feasible at a scrubbing/stateful firewall layer with sufficient capacity.
steps.outcome: Unsolicited SYN-ACK volume substantially reduced before reaching origin infrastructure.

steps.title: Verify victim IP is not being leaked/spoofable in a way enabling repeat abuse
steps.desc: Confirm there is no ongoing IP spoofing occurring from within the victim's own network that could implicate them as a source of spoofed SYNs elsewhere, and assess anti-spoofing posture with upstream.
steps.guidance: Review egress filtering (BCP38) status with the network team; this attack technique relies on spoofing done elsewhere on the internet but reinforces the value of broad anti-spoofing adoption.
steps.outcome: Confirmed the organization's own network correctly filters outbound spoofed traffic.

steps.title: Remove temporary filters and confirm normal TCP handshake completion rates
steps.desc: Roll back interim rate limits once the reflection flood subsides and confirm legitimate connection success rates have returned to baseline.
steps.guidance: Monitor connection success/failure rates for at least 1-2 hours post-mitigation rollback.
steps.outcome: Normal TCP handshake success rates restored.

steps.title: Document reflection attack and advocate for broader anti-spoofing (BCP38) adoption
steps.desc: Record the incident, noting that root-cause mitigation depends on internet-wide anti-spoofing adoption by third parties, and update internal detection playbooks accordingly.
steps.guidance: Include recommendation to participate in industry anti-spoofing initiatives (e.g., MANRS) where applicable.
steps.outcome: After-action report documenting systemic nature of the attack vector.

steps.title: Characterize reflector population (likely legitimate public servers)
steps.desc: Identify the reflecting servers' typical role (e.g., legitimate public web/mail servers) to understand this is third-party infrastructure being abused, not attacker-controlled.
steps.guidance: Reflector IPs are usually widely distributed legitimate servers, meaning source-based blocking will be broad and may need to be temporary/aggressive rather than targeted.
steps.outcome: Documented reflector characteristics informing containment scope.

steps.title: Rate-limit inbound SYN-ACK at perimeter firewall as interim measure
steps.desc: Apply temporary rate limiting on inbound TCP SYN-ACK packets at the perimeter while upstream scrubbing takes effect.
steps.guidance: Ensure this does not block legitimate SYN-ACK replies to the organization's own outbound connections by scoping the rate limit to abnormal volume thresholds rather than blanket blocking.
steps.outcome: Reduced load on downstream infrastructure without breaking legitimate outbound-initiated connections.
steps.abort: If legitimate outbound connections start failing, narrow or remove the rate limit immediately.

steps.title: Notify reflector operators of unwitting participation where feasible
steps.desc: Where reflector servers are identifiable and reachable via abuse contacts, notify their operators that their infrastructure was used to reflect traffic, encouraging anti-spoofing hardening on their side.
steps.guidance: This is a best-effort notification step, not a guaranteed remediation, since reflectors are third-party infrastructure outside direct control.
steps.outcome: Reflector operators notified where feasible; documented for the record.

ITID-41124.def: A denial-of-service event exhibiting clear SYN flooding characteristics (half-open connection exhaustion) where the specific delivery mechanism (spoofed single-source, distributed botnet, or reflection) has not yet been determined.
ITID-41124.purpose: Intake bucket for SYN flooding activity that cannot yet be attributed to a specific delivery mechanism.
scopeIncludes: Initial triage of a suspected SYN flood before source analysis is complete
scopeExcludes: Any SYN flood already confirmed as spoofed-source, botnet-driven, or reflection-based (reclassify to the specific leaf once confirmed)
ITID-41124.severity: Medium-High pending confirmation; reassess once mechanism is identified.
ITID-41124.priority: P2 pending triage; adjust once reclassified.
ITID-41124.escalation: Escalate to network operations for connection-state and source-IP analysis; reclassify once confirmed.
indicators: Half-open connection table growth without confirmed source classification at initial detection
vectors: Unconfirmed at time of intake
rootCauses: Insufficient initial visibility into source-IP patterns to determine delivery mechanism
mitreTechniques: T1498.001 Network Denial of Service: Direct Network Flood
controls: SYN cookies/SYN proxy
Upstream DDoS scrubbing service
ITID-41124.detection: Sufficient to detect the SYN flood pattern but insufficient to classify delivery mechanism at time of intake.
ITID-41124.response: Enable SYN cookies and engage general mitigation immediately; run source-IP analysis in parallel to reclassify.
metrics: Count of incidents landing in this catch-all per quarter
ITID-41124.notes: Triage/intake bucket only; reclassify once the delivery mechanism is confirmed.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General SYN Flooding Attack
playbook.description: An elevated rate of TCP SYN packets is causing connection-state exhaustion but does not clearly match a specific spoofed, botnet, or reflection sub-technique.

steps.title: Confirm SYN flood and gather baseline half-open connection metrics
steps.desc: Confirm elevated SYN rate and half-open connection count against target host/service baselines.
steps.guidance: Check server connection tables, load balancer connection metrics, and flow telemetry for SYN:ACK completion ratio anomalies.
steps.outcome: Confirmed SYN flood condition with severity (connection table utilization %) documented.

steps.title: Enable SYN cookies and increase backlog capacity
steps.desc: Activate SYN cookie protection across affected servers/load balancers as a general-purpose defense regardless of source classification.
steps.guidance: SYN cookies are effective against SYN floods generally, independent of whether sourcing is spoofed or genuine.
steps.outcome: Connection table exhaustion resolved; legitimate handshakes continue to complete.

steps.title: Complete classification and close any confirmed exposure
steps.desc: Finalize sub-technique classification where possible and remediate any related exposure (e.g., anti-spoofing gaps, exposed origin IP).
steps.guidance: Update the incident classification in the case management system with findings.
steps.outcome: Attack technique documented and any identified exposure closed.

steps.title: Roll back temporary controls and confirm stable handshake completion
steps.desc: Restore standard settings (retaining SYN cookies permanently as a hardening measure) once the flood subsides.
steps.guidance: Monitor connection success rates for at least 1-2 hours before declaring full recovery.
steps.outcome: Stable, normal TCP handshake performance confirmed.

steps.title: Document incident and improve source-classification tooling
steps.desc: Record why immediate sub-classification was not possible and recommend tooling/process improvements.
steps.guidance: Include specific gaps in packet capture automation or threat intel enrichment that delayed classification.
steps.outcome: After-action report with concrete improvement items.

steps.title: Attempt sub-technique classification via spoofing and source analysis
steps.desc: Sample packets to determine whether sources appear spoofed, genuinely distributed (botnet), or reflection-pattern, to allow pivot to a more specific playbook if possible.
steps.guidance: If classification succeeds, transition to the corresponding specific SYN flood playbook; otherwise proceed with general mitigation.
steps.outcome: Either successful reclassification or confirmed genuinely mixed/unclear sourcing.

steps.title: Engage upstream DDoS mitigation with general SYN flood profile
steps.desc: Request activation of the provider's standard SYN flood/SYN proxy mitigation profile.
steps.guidance: Most scrubbing providers offer a general SYN-proxy mode effective regardless of spoofing status.
steps.outcome: Reduced SYN volume reaching origin infrastructure.

steps.title: Confirm no internal contribution and validate origin protection
steps.desc: Verify no internal hosts contributed to the flood and confirm the target service's origin is adequately shielded from direct connectivity.
steps.guidance: Check egress logs and origin firewall allowlist configuration.
steps.outcome: Confirmed clean internal posture and hardened origin exposure.

ITID-41131.def: A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary sends small, spoofed UDP queries (commonly the deprecated monlist command) to publicly reachable NTP servers, causing each to send a disproportionately large response to the spoofed victim address, amplifying attack bandwidth well beyond what the adversary directly generates.
ITID-41131.purpose: Captures a reflection/amplification DoS attack that abuses misconfigured NTP servers' monlist (or similar) response to multiply attack traffic toward a target.
scopeIncludes: Spoofed NTP monlist or similar high-amplification-factor query abuse directed at a target via third-party NTP servers
scopeExcludes: Direct floods against an organization's own NTP infrastructure with no spoofed reflection (see Unclassified / General Volumetric Flooding if applicable)
Other reflection protocols such as DNS, memcached, CLDAP/SSDP (see their respective leaves)
ITID-41131.severity: High given NTP's historically very large amplification factor (up to ~500x); treat any confirmed inbound NTP reflection as scrubbing-required.
ITID-41131.priority: P2 on detection; escalate to P1 on confirmed sustained volume or link saturation.
ITID-41131.escalation: Escalate to network operations and upstream scrubbing provider immediately given the high amplification potential.
indicators: Large volume of inbound UDP/123 traffic from many distinct NTP server IPs with no matching outbound NTP query
Response payloads far larger than any legitimate NTP query the organization issued
vectors: Internet-wide scans identifying NTP servers still exposing monlist or other amplifying commands
Booter/stresser services offering NTP amplification as an attack option
rootCauses: Reliance on external NTP servers that remain unpatched/misconfigured (outside organizational control as attack infrastructure, but relevant if the organization operates its own exposed NTP service)
No filtering of unsolicited large inbound UDP/123 responses at the border
mitreTechniques: T1498.002 Network Denial of Service: Reflection Amplification
controls: Upstream DDoS scrubbing service filtering NTP reflection traffic
Border ACLs rate-limiting/dropping unsolicited large UDP/123 responses
If operating own NTP service: disable monlist and restrict to authenticated/internal clients
ITID-41131.detection: Strong technical signal: source port 123 with disproportionate payload size and no matching outbound query is a clean indicator.
ITID-41131.response: Engage upstream scrubbing for volume; filter at border ACL; verify no internally operated NTP servers are exposed as amplifiers.
metrics: Peak inbound NTP reflection bandwidth
Amplification factor observed
Time to filtering/scrubbing engagement
ITID-41131.notes: Differentiating axis for the Amplification Attacks group is reflector protocol; this leaf is scoped specifically to NTP.

playbook.name: NTP Amplification Attack
playbook.description: The attacker spoofs the victim's IP and sends small NTP monlist/get requests to open NTP servers, which respond with disproportionately large replies flooding the victim.

steps.title: Confirm NTP amplification signature (source port 123, oversized responses)
steps.desc: Analyze inbound flood traffic to confirm it originates from UDP source port 123 with response sizes far exceeding typical NTP traffic, indicating monlist/get-based amplification.
steps.guidance: Check packet captures for NTP mode-7 (monlist) or mode-6 control responses; calculate amplification factor (response size / typical query size, often 20-200x for monlist).
steps.outcome: Confirmed NTP amplification with reflector server list and amplification factor documented.

steps.title: Block/rate-limit inbound UDP/123 at perimeter and upstream
steps.desc: Apply ACLs blocking or rate-limiting inbound UDP source port 123 traffic that is not part of legitimate NTP sync with known internal time servers.
steps.guidance: Scope the block to exclude legitimate NTP traffic from the organization's designated upstream time sources.
steps.outcome: Reflected NTP traffic volume reduced at the perimeter.
steps.abort: If internal NTP sync breaks, add explicit allowlist entries for legitimate time server IPs.

steps.title: Disable monlist and restrict NTP query access on any organization-owned NTP servers
steps.desc: If any internal NTP servers were identified as usable reflectors, disable the deprecated monlist command and restrict query/control access to authorized clients only.
steps.guidance: Upgrade ntpd to a version with monlist disabled by default, or add 'disable monitor' in ntp.conf; restrict access using 'restrict default noquery' with explicit allow rules for trusted management/sync sources.
steps.outcome: Organization-owned NTP servers no longer usable as amplification reflectors; confirmed via external open-resolver rescan.

steps.title: Remove temporary ACLs and confirm legitimate NTP sync functioning
steps.desc: Roll back perimeter blocks once attack traffic subsides and validate that legitimate time synchronization continues to function correctly.
steps.guidance: Check system clock drift across critical infrastructure post-recovery to confirm NTP sync was not disrupted.
steps.outcome: Normal NTP operation restored with no clock drift issues.

steps.title: Document incident and audit for other UDP-based amplification exposure
steps.desc: Record the attack and conduct a broader audit for other open/misconfigured UDP services (DNS, SNMP, CLDAP) that could similarly be abused.
steps.guidance: Include results of an external open-resolver/amplifier scan across the organization's public IP space.
steps.outcome: After-action report with a broader amplification-exposure remediation list if additional issues were found.

steps.title: Identify reflector server population and any organization-owned NTP servers among them
steps.desc: Cross-reference the reflector IP list against organization-owned assets and external threat intel/open-resolver lists to determine if any internal NTP servers are being abused.
steps.guidance: Check Shodan/Censys or internal asset inventory for NTP servers matching reflector IPs in the capture.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether any organization-owned NTP servers are contributing to the attack against a third party, or the org is purely the victim.

steps.title: Engage upstream scrubbing with UDP/123 amplification mitigation profile
steps.desc: Request the DDoS scrubbing provider activate NTP amplification-specific filtering (signature/size-based dropping of oversized NTP responses).
steps.guidance: Provide the amplification factor and reflector list gathered during identification to speed mitigation tuning.
steps.outcome: Bulk of amplified traffic scrubbed upstream before reaching the origin network.

steps.title: Rescan public IP space to confirm no remaining open NTP reflectors
steps.desc: Run an external scan of the organization's public IP ranges to confirm no NTP server still responds to monlist or exhibits amplification-capable behavior.
steps.guidance: Use an external scanning tool from outside the corporate network to accurately reflect an attacker's view.
steps.outcome: Confirmed zero remaining exploitable NTP reflectors in the organization's IP space.

ITID-41132.def: A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary sends small, spoofed UDP requests to publicly reachable memcached servers, causing each to return a vastly larger cached-data response to the spoofed victim address, achieving amplification factors that can exceed tens of thousands to one.
ITID-41132.purpose: Captures a reflection/amplification DoS attack that abuses internet-exposed memcached servers, which historically offered the largest known amplification factors.
scopeIncludes: Spoofed UDP requests to internet-exposed memcached instances directed at a target via reflection
Attacks exploiting memcached's lack of default authentication on UDP
scopeExcludes: Direct attacks against an organization's own memcached deployment (an application/infrastructure security concern, not a DoS-reflection leaf)
Other reflection protocols such as NTP, DNS, CLDAP/SSDP (see their respective leaves)
ITID-41132.severity: Critical given memcached's extreme amplification factor; treat any confirmed inbound memcached reflection as an immediate scrubbing-required event.
ITID-41132.priority: P1 given the historically record-setting amplification potential of this vector.
ITID-41132.escalation: Escalate to network operations and upstream scrubbing provider immediately on any confirmed memcached reflection traffic.
indicators: Very large volume of inbound UDP/11211 traffic from many distinct memcached server IPs
Response payloads dramatically larger than any legitimate request the organization issued
vectors: Internet-wide scans identifying UDP-exposed memcached servers with no authentication
Booter/stresser services offering memcached amplification as a premium attack option
rootCauses: Reliance on internet infrastructure containing misconfigured memcached servers (systemic risk, relevant to organizational exposure if self-hosting memcached with UDP enabled)
No filtering of unsolicited inbound UDP/11211 traffic at the border
mitreTechniques: T1498.002 Network Denial of Service: Reflection Amplification
controls: Upstream DDoS scrubbing service filtering memcached reflection traffic
Border ACLs dropping unsolicited inbound UDP/11211
If operating own memcached: disable UDP support and bind to internal interfaces only
ITID-41132.detection: Strong technical signal: source port 11211 with extreme payload-to-request disproportion is a clean, high-confidence indicator.
ITID-41132.response: Engage upstream scrubbing immediately given the scale of potential amplification; filter at border ACL; audit for any internally exposed memcached instances.
metrics: Peak inbound memcached reflection bandwidth
Amplification factor observed
Time to filtering/scrubbing engagement
ITID-41132.notes: Differentiating axis for the Amplification Attacks group is reflector protocol; this leaf is scoped specifically to memcached.

playbook.name: Memcached Amplification Attack
playbook.description: The attacker spoofs the victim's IP and sends small requests to exposed, unauthenticated Memcached UDP servers, which return extremely large responses (amplification factors up to 50,000x) that flood the victim.

steps.title: Confirm Memcached amplification signature (source port 11211)
steps.desc: Analyze inbound flood traffic to confirm UDP source port 11211 with very large response sizes consistent with Memcached amplification.
steps.guidance: Memcached amplification is among the highest-factor amplification techniques observed (tens of thousands to one); confirm via packet capture showing memcached 'get' response payloads.
steps.outcome: Confirmed Memcached amplification with reflector list and estimated amplification factor documented.

steps.title: Block inbound UDP/11211 at perimeter and upstream immediately
steps.desc: Apply an immediate firewall/ACL block on inbound UDP source port 11211, as legitimate Memcached traffic should never traverse the public internet.
steps.guidance: Unlike NTP or DNS, there is essentially no legitimate reason for UDP/11211 to cross the internet perimeter — this can be blocked unconditionally.
steps.outcome: Amplified Memcached traffic dropped at the perimeter with no legitimate service impact.

steps.title: Remediate any exposed Memcached instances (firewall, disable UDP, authentication)
steps.desc: If any organization-owned Memcached servers were found internet-exposed, immediately firewall them to trusted internal networks only, disable the UDP protocol support (memcached -U 0) if UDP is not required, and enable authentication (SASL) where supported.
steps.guidance: Best practice: bind Memcached to localhost/internal interfaces only and disable UDP entirely unless explicitly required by the application architecture.
steps.outcome: Confirmed no Memcached instances remain internet-reachable; verified via external rescan.

steps.title: Restore normal traffic handling and confirm no residual exposure
steps.desc: Remove temporary broad mitigations once attack subsides, retaining the permanent UDP/11211 perimeter block and Memcached hardening.
steps.guidance: The UDP/11211 perimeter block should remain permanent, not just temporary, given no legitimate cross-internet use case.
steps.outcome: Service restored with permanent hardening controls retained.

steps.title: Document incident and mandate Memcached exposure checks in asset/config baselines
steps.desc: Record the incident and add internet-exposed Memcached detection to routine external attack-surface scanning and configuration baseline checks.
steps.guidance: Include this check in recurring external ASM (attack surface management) scans going forward.
steps.outcome: After-action report with a recurring detection control added to prevent recurrence.

steps.title: Identify any organization-owned Memcached instances exposed to the internet
steps.desc: Audit internal asset inventory and run external scans to identify any Memcached servers reachable on UDP/11211 from the internet.
steps.guidance: Memcached should never be exposed to untrusted networks; any internet-reachable instance found is a critical misconfiguration requiring immediate remediation regardless of whether it was used in this specific attack.
steps.outcome: Confirmed presence or absence of internet-exposed Memcached instances within the organization.

steps.title: Engage upstream scrubbing for large-scale volumetric relief
steps.desc: Given the extreme amplification factor possible with Memcached, engage upstream DDoS scrubbing immediately in parallel with local blocking to handle potentially massive traffic volumes.
steps.guidance: Memcached attacks have produced some of the largest recorded DDoS volumes; do not rely on local mitigation alone.
steps.outcome: Bulk of attack traffic absorbed and scrubbed upstream.

steps.title: Rescan public IP space to confirm no remaining exposed Memcached instances
steps.desc: Run an external scan of the organization's public IP ranges to confirm no Memcached instance remains reachable on UDP/11211.
steps.guidance: Use an external scanning tool from outside the corporate network for an attacker's-eye view of exposure.
steps.outcome: Confirmed zero remaining exploitable Memcached reflectors in the organization's IP space.

ITID-41133.def: A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary sends small, spoofed DNS queries (often crafted to return large responses, e.g. ANY or TXT record lookups) to open/misconfigured DNS resolvers, causing each to send an amplified response to the spoofed victim address.
ITID-41133.purpose: Captures a reflection/amplification DoS attack that abuses open DNS resolvers to multiply attack traffic toward a target.
scopeIncludes: Spoofed DNS queries sent to open resolvers as a DDoS amplification vector against a third party
Use of large-response record types (ANY, TXT, DNSSEC-signed zones) to maximize amplification factor
scopeExcludes: Direct high-volume queries against an organization's own authoritative DNS infrastructure with no reflection involved (see Authoritative DNS Server Direct Query Flood under DNS Query Flooding)
Water-torture-style random-subdomain floods against a resolver (see Random Subdomain/NXDOMAIN Flood Attack under DNS Query Flooding)
ITID-41133.severity: High given DNS's substantial amplification factor and ubiquity of exploitable open resolvers; treat confirmed inbound DNS reflection as scrubbing-required.
ITID-41133.priority: P2 on detection; escalate to P1 on confirmed sustained volume or link saturation.
ITID-41133.escalation: Escalate to network operations and upstream scrubbing provider immediately given DNS reflection's prevalence as an attack vector.
indicators: Large volume of inbound UDP/53 traffic from many distinct resolver IPs with no matching outbound query
Response payloads (e.g. ANY/TXT record answers) far larger than the query size that would have produced them
vectors: Internet-wide scans identifying open DNS resolvers usable as amplifiers
Booter/stresser services offering DNS amplification as a standard attack option
rootCauses: Prevalence of open resolvers across the internet (systemic risk; relevant if the organization itself operates an open resolver)
No filtering of unsolicited large inbound UDP/53 responses at the border
mitreTechniques: T1498.002 Network Denial of Service: Reflection Amplification
controls: Upstream DDoS scrubbing service filtering DNS reflection traffic
Border ACLs rate-limiting unsolicited large UDP/53 responses
If operating resolvers: restrict recursion to trusted clients (close open resolver posture)
ITID-41133.detection: Strong technical signal: source port 53 with disproportionate response size and no matching outbound query.
ITID-41133.response: Engage upstream scrubbing for volume; filter at border ACL; audit for any internally operated open resolvers.
metrics: Peak inbound DNS reflection bandwidth
Amplification factor observed
Time to filtering/scrubbing engagement
ITID-41133.notes: Scoped specifically to DNS used as a reflection/amplification vector against a third-party target; distinct from direct query floods against the organization's own DNS infrastructure, which live under DNS Query Flooding.

playbook.name: DNS Amplification Attack (as a DDoS Technique)
playbook.description: The attacker spoofs the victim's IP and sends small DNS queries (often ANY or crafted large-record queries) to open recursive resolvers, which return large responses that flood the victim.

steps.title: Confirm DNS amplification signature (source port 53, oversized responses)
steps.desc: Analyze inbound flood traffic to confirm it consists of UDP source port 53 DNS responses with sizes far exceeding typical query/response ratios.
steps.guidance: Check for large TXT/ANY record responses or crafted zone responses; calculate amplification factor (often 28-70x for standard DNS, higher for crafted large-record zones).
steps.outcome: Confirmed DNS amplification pattern with reflector resolver list and amplification factor documented.

steps.title: Block/rate-limit inbound UDP/53 responses at perimeter and upstream
steps.desc: Apply ACLs rate-limiting or blocking inbound UDP source port 53 traffic not associated with legitimate resolution from the organization's designated resolvers.
steps.guidance: Scope carefully to avoid breaking legitimate DNS resolution; allowlist the organization's actual configured upstream resolvers.
steps.outcome: Reflected DNS traffic volume reduced at the perimeter without breaking legitimate resolution.
steps.abort: If legitimate DNS resolution breaks, add explicit allowlist entries for known-good resolver IPs.

steps.title: Disable open recursion and enable response rate limiting (RRL) on organization DNS servers
steps.desc: If any internal resolvers were found usable as reflectors, restrict recursion to authorized client networks only and enable DNS Response Rate Limiting.
steps.guidance: Configure 'allow-recursion' to trusted networks only (BIND) or equivalent, and enable RRL to cap identical-response rates to any single destination.
steps.outcome: Organization-owned DNS servers no longer usable as open amplification reflectors; confirmed via external open-resolver rescan.

steps.title: Remove temporary ACLs and confirm legitimate DNS resolution functioning
steps.desc: Roll back perimeter blocks once attack subsides and validate legitimate DNS resolution continues correctly for all business services.
steps.guidance: Test resolution from multiple internal and external vantage points post-recovery.
steps.outcome: Normal DNS operation restored with no resolution failures.

steps.title: Document incident and audit for other UDP-based amplification exposure
steps.desc: Record the attack and conduct a broader audit for other open/misconfigured UDP services that could similarly be abused.
steps.guidance: Include results of an external open-resolver/amplifier scan across the organization's full public IP space, covering DNS, NTP, SNMP, and CLDAP.
steps.outcome: After-action report with a broader amplification-exposure remediation list if additional issues were found.

steps.title: Identify any organization-owned DNS resolvers among the reflectors
steps.desc: Cross-reference reflector IPs against organization-owned DNS infrastructure and external open-resolver lists to determine internal exposure.
steps.guidance: Check Shodan/Censys open-resolver project data or run an internal query against known DNS asset inventory.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether any organization-owned DNS resolvers are contributing to the attack against a third party.

steps.title: Engage upstream scrubbing with DNS amplification mitigation profile
steps.desc: Request the DDoS scrubbing provider activate DNS-amplification-specific filtering.
steps.guidance: Provide the amplification factor and reflector list gathered during identification to speed mitigation tuning.
steps.outcome: Bulk of amplified DNS traffic scrubbed upstream before reaching the origin network.

steps.title: Rescan public IP space to confirm no remaining open resolvers
steps.desc: Run an external scan confirming no organization-owned DNS server responds as an open recursive resolver to arbitrary internet clients.
steps.guidance: Use an external scanning tool/service for an attacker's-eye view.
steps.outcome: Confirmed zero remaining exploitable open DNS resolvers in the organization's IP space.
steps.tool: Shodan/Censys / dig from external vantage point

ITID-41134.def: A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary sends small, spoofed queries to internet-exposed CLDAP (Connectionless LDAP, common on Active Directory domain controllers) or SSDP (Simple Service Discovery Protocol, common on consumer routers/IoT devices) services, causing each to send an amplified response to the spoofed victim address.
ITID-41134.purpose: Captures reflection/amplification DoS attacks that abuse CLDAP or SSDP-speaking devices to multiply attack traffic toward a target.
scopeIncludes: Spoofed CLDAP queries against exposed domain controllers used as reflectors
Spoofed SSDP M-SEARCH queries against exposed consumer/IoT devices used as reflectors
scopeExcludes: NTP, memcached, or DNS reflection (see their respective leaves)
Direct exploitation of an organization's own exposed CLDAP service for purposes other than DoS reflection (an infrastructure hardening concern documented elsewhere)
ITID-41134.severity: High given meaningful amplification factors for both protocols (CLDAP notably high); treat confirmed inbound reflection as scrubbing-required.
ITID-41134.priority: P2 on detection; escalate to P1 on confirmed sustained volume or link saturation.
ITID-41134.escalation: Escalate to network operations and upstream scrubbing provider immediately; if the organization operates exposed CLDAP, escalate to identity infrastructure owners to close exposure.
indicators: Large volume of inbound UDP/389 (CLDAP) or UDP/1900 (SSDP) traffic from many distinct source IPs with no matching outbound query
Response payloads far larger than the corresponding query size
vectors: Internet-wide scans identifying exposed CLDAP domain controllers or SSDP-speaking IoT/consumer devices
Booter/stresser services offering CLDAP or SSDP amplification as attack options
rootCauses: Domain controllers with CLDAP inadvertently exposed to the internet
Consumer/IoT devices with SSDP reachable outside the local network (systemic risk; relevant to organizational exposure if such devices sit on internet-facing segments)
mitreTechniques: T1498.002 Network Denial of Service: Reflection Amplification
controls: Upstream DDoS scrubbing service filtering CLDAP/SSDP reflection traffic
Border ACLs dropping unsolicited inbound UDP/389 and UDP/1900
Ensure domain controllers and IoT/consumer devices are not internet-reachable on these ports
