ITID-41134.detection: Strong technical signal: source port 389/1900 with disproportionate response size and no matching outbound query.
ITID-41134.response: Engage upstream scrubbing for volume; filter at border ACL; audit for any internally exposed CLDAP or SSDP services.
metrics: Peak inbound CLDAP/SSDP reflection bandwidth
Amplification factor observed
Time to filtering/scrubbing engagement
ITID-41134.notes: Grouped together as two protocols sharing similar reflector-exposure dynamics (misconfigured internal/consumer infrastructure reachable from the internet); split into separate leaves in a future taxonomy revision if incident volume warrants.

playbook.name: CLDAP/SSDP Amplification Attack
playbook.description: The attacker spoofs the victim's IP and sends small requests to exposed CLDAP (UDP/389) or SSDP (UDP/1900) services, which return amplified responses flooding the victim.

steps.title: Confirm CLDAP/SSDP amplification signature (source port 389 or 1900)
steps.desc: Analyze inbound flood traffic to confirm UDP source port 389 (CLDAP, typically Active Directory domain controllers) or 1900 (SSDP, typically UPnP-enabled devices) with oversized responses.
steps.guidance: CLDAP amplification factors typically range 56-70x; SSDP typically 30x. Confirm via packet capture showing CLDAP searchResponse or SSDP NOTIFY/M-SEARCH response floods.
steps.outcome: Confirmed CLDAP or SSDP amplification with reflector list and amplification factor documented.

steps.title: Block inbound UDP/389 and UDP/1900 at perimeter immediately
steps.desc: Apply an immediate firewall/ACL block on inbound UDP source ports 389 and 1900, as neither CLDAP nor SSDP should legitimately traverse the public internet.
steps.guidance: There is no legitimate business case for CLDAP or SSDP crossing the internet perimeter — block unconditionally at the border.
steps.outcome: Amplified CLDAP/SSDP traffic dropped at the perimeter with no legitimate service impact.

steps.title: Firewall exposed domain controllers/UPnP devices to internal networks only
steps.desc: If any organization-owned domain controller was found exposing CLDAP to the internet, immediately restrict UDP/389 to internal/trusted networks only; disable UPnP/SSDP on any internet-facing devices.
steps.guidance: An internet-exposed domain controller is a critical finding beyond this DoS incident — escalate to the identity/AD team for a full exposure review, as CLDAP exposure can also enable information disclosure.
steps.outcome: Confirmed no CLDAP or SSDP services remain internet-reachable; escalation raised for any domain controller exposure.

steps.title: Restore normal traffic handling with permanent hardening retained
steps.desc: Remove temporary broad mitigations once attack subsides, retaining the permanent UDP/389 and UDP/1900 perimeter blocks.
steps.guidance: These perimeter blocks should remain permanent given no legitimate cross-internet use case for either protocol.
steps.outcome: Service restored with permanent hardening controls retained.

steps.title: Document incident and escalate any domain controller exposure as a separate finding
steps.desc: Record the DoS incident and, if a domain controller was found internet-exposed, ensure a separate, higher-severity exposure investigation is tracked given the broader risk (AD reconnaissance/attack surface).
steps.guidance: Cross-reference with vulnerability management to confirm remediation ticket exists for the exposure finding independent of this DoS incident.
steps.outcome: After-action report plus, where applicable, a linked critical exposure remediation ticket.

steps.title: Identify any organization-owned domain controllers or UPnP devices among reflectors
steps.desc: Cross-reference reflector IPs against organization-owned Active Directory domain controllers (CLDAP) or IoT/consumer devices (SSDP) exposed to the internet.
steps.guidance: CLDAP exposure is particularly severe as it typically indicates an internet-facing domain controller — a critical exposure independent of this specific attack.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether any organization-owned CLDAP or SSDP services are internet-exposed and contributing to amplification.

steps.title: Engage upstream scrubbing for volumetric relief
steps.desc: Engage upstream DDoS scrubbing in parallel with local blocking to absorb attack volume while permanent exposure remediation proceeds.
steps.guidance: Provide the scrubbing provider the confirmed reflector list and amplification factor.
steps.outcome: Bulk of attack traffic absorbed and scrubbed upstream.

steps.title: Rescan public IP space to confirm no remaining exposed CLDAP/SSDP services
steps.desc: Run an external scan confirming no organization-owned service still responds on UDP/389 or UDP/1900 from the internet.
steps.guidance: Use an external scanning tool for an attacker's-eye view of exposure.
steps.outcome: Confirmed zero remaining exploitable CLDAP/SSDP reflectors in the organization's IP space.

ITID-41135.def: A denial-of-service event exhibiting clear reflection/amplification characteristics (unsolicited, disproportionately large inbound responses with no matching outbound query) where the specific reflector protocol has not yet been determined or does not fit an existing Amplification Attacks leaf.
ITID-41135.purpose: Intake bucket for reflection/amplification DoS activity that cannot yet be attributed to a specific reflector protocol.
scopeIncludes: Initial triage of a suspected amplification attack before reflector protocol analysis is complete
Amplification via reflector protocols not separately enumerated in this taxonomy branch (e.g. CharGEN, QOTD, TFTP)
scopeExcludes: Any amplification attack already confirmed as NTP, memcached, DNS, CLDAP, or SSDP (reclassify to the specific leaf once confirmed)
ITID-41135.severity: Medium-High pending confirmation; reassess once reflector protocol is identified.
ITID-41135.priority: P2 pending triage; adjust once reclassified.
ITID-41135.escalation: Escalate to network operations for flow capture and reflector protocol identification; reclassify once confirmed.
indicators: Unsolicited, disproportionately large inbound UDP responses without a confirmed source protocol at initial detection
vectors: Unconfirmed at time of intake
rootCauses: Insufficient initial flow visibility to determine reflector protocol
mitreTechniques: T1498.002 Network Denial of Service: Reflection Amplification
controls: Upstream DDoS scrubbing service
Flow-based traffic capture for post-hoc classification
ITID-41135.detection: Sufficient to detect the amplification pattern but insufficient to classify reflector protocol at time of intake.
ITID-41135.response: Engage general amplification mitigation immediately; run protocol analysis in parallel to reclassify.
metrics: Count of incidents landing in this catch-all per quarter
ITID-41135.notes: Triage/intake bucket only; reclassify once the reflector protocol is confirmed.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Amplification Attack
playbook.description: An amplified reflection-style flood is confirmed but the specific reflector protocol (NTP, DNS, Memcached, CLDAP, SSDP, etc.) has not yet been determined.

steps.title: Confirm amplification pattern via response-size and source-port analysis
steps.desc: Analyze inbound flood traffic for classic amplification indicators: disproportionate response sizes relative to plausible query size, and a consistent UDP source port.
steps.guidance: Identify the dominant source port(s) in the flood (53, 123, 389, 1900, 11211, etc.) to narrow toward a specific protocol classification.
steps.outcome: Confirmed amplification pattern with source port(s) and estimated amplification factor documented.

steps.title: Block/rate-limit identified source ports at perimeter and upstream
steps.desc: Apply ACLs against the identified anomalous UDP source port(s) while preserving legitimate traffic on those ports where feasible.
steps.guidance: For ports with no legitimate cross-internet use (11211, 1900, 389), block unconditionally; for others (53, 123), scope to allowlist legitimate providers.
steps.outcome: Reduced amplified traffic volume at the perimeter.

steps.title: Complete protocol classification and audit organization assets for reflector exposure
steps.desc: Finalize identification of the abused protocol(s) and audit organization-owned infrastructure for any matching exposed services.
steps.guidance: Reclassify the incident to the specific ITID leaf if a clear protocol is identified.
steps.outcome: Attack protocol documented (or confirmed multi-vector) and any internal exposure identified.

steps.title: Roll back temporary mitigations and confirm stable baseline
steps.desc: Restore normal traffic handling once attack volume subsides and remains below baseline for a sustained period.
steps.guidance: Monitor for at least 2 hours before full rollback.
steps.outcome: Service restored to normal performance with no residual mitigation-induced impact.

steps.title: Document incident and improve amplification-protocol classification tooling
steps.desc: Record why immediate protocol classification was not possible and recommend detection tooling improvements.
steps.guidance: Include recommendations for automated protocol-signature libraries covering common amplification vectors.
steps.outcome: After-action report with concrete detection tooling improvement items.

steps.title: Attempt protocol classification via packet payload inspection
steps.desc: Inspect packet payloads to identify the specific protocol/service being abused, enabling pivot to a more specific playbook if possible.
steps.guidance: If classification succeeds, transition to the corresponding specific amplification playbook (DNS, NTP, Memcached, CLDAP/SSDP); otherwise proceed with general mitigation.
steps.outcome: Either successful reclassification or confirmed multi-protocol/unclear reflector usage.

steps.title: Engage upstream scrubbing with general amplification mitigation profile
steps.desc: Request activation of the provider's general amplification/reflection mitigation profile pending full protocol classification.
steps.guidance: Most scrubbing providers can filter based on response-size-to-query ratio heuristics independent of specific protocol.
steps.outcome: Attack traffic volume reduced via general amplification mitigation.

steps.title: Remediate any confirmed internal reflector exposure
steps.desc: Close, firewall, or harden any organization-owned service confirmed as internet-exposed and usable for amplification.
steps.guidance: Apply protocol-specific hardening per the relevant specific playbook once classification completes.
steps.outcome: No remaining internal amplification exposure.

ITID-41141.def: A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary sends ICMP Echo Request packets to a network's broadcast address with the source address spoofed as the victim's IP, causing every host on that broadcast network to send an ICMP Echo Reply to the victim simultaneously, amplifying traffic in proportion to the number of responding hosts.
ITID-41141.purpose: Captures the classic ICMP-based Smurf attack, in which spoofed ping traffic is bounced off a broadcast network to flood a victim.
scopeIncludes: Spoofed ICMP Echo Request sent to a directed broadcast address to elicit mass Echo Reply flooding toward a victim
scopeExcludes: The UDP-based Fraggle variant using echo/chargen services (see Fraggle Attack)
Direct ICMP floods with no broadcast-network reflection (see ICMP Flood Attack under Volumetric Flooding)
ITID-41141.severity: Medium today given widespread disabling of directed broadcast forwarding on modern routers, but High if a legacy/misconfigured network segment is confirmed still forwarding broadcast ICMP.
ITID-41141.priority: P2 on detection; escalate to P1 if the organization's own network is confirmed being used as an unwitting amplifier for a Smurf attack against a third party.
ITID-41141.escalation: Escalate to network operations immediately if internal broadcast-forwarding misconfiguration is implicated, either as victim or as unwitting amplifier network.
indicators: Large volume of inbound ICMP Echo Reply traffic with no matching outbound Echo Request from the victim
Evidence of directed-broadcast ICMP forwarding still enabled on any organization-owned router (if investigating amplifier-network risk)
vectors: Spoofed ICMP Echo Request directed at a subnet broadcast address on a network that still permits directed-broadcast forwarding
rootCauses: Legacy routers/switches configured to forward directed broadcasts (RFC 2644 recommends disabling this by default)
No egress filtering preventing spoofed source addresses from leaving a network that could be misused as an amplifier
mitreTechniques: T1498.002 Network Denial of Service: Reflection Amplification
controls: Disable IP directed-broadcast forwarding on all routers (industry-standard default since the late 1990s)
Border ACLs dropping unsolicited large inbound ICMP Echo Reply volumes
Upstream DDoS scrubbing service
ITID-41141.detection: Strong technical signal, though the underlying vulnerability (broadcast forwarding) is now rare on modern equipment, making genuine Smurf incidents infrequent.
ITID-41141.response: Verify directed-broadcast forwarding is disabled on all organization-owned routers; filter unsolicited ICMP Echo Reply floods at the border if victimized.
metrics: Peak inbound unsolicited ICMP Echo Reply volume
Count of organization routers audited for directed-broadcast forwarding status
ITID-41141.notes: Differentiating axis for the Smurf Attack group is protocol: this leaf is the classic ICMP variant; Fraggle is its UDP sibling.

playbook.name: Classic ICMP Smurf Attack (Broadcast Address Spoofing)
playbook.description: The attacker spoofs the victim's IP and sends ICMP Echo Requests to a network's broadcast address, causing every host on that network to reply to the victim simultaneously.

steps.title: Confirm smurf pattern via broadcast-triggered ICMP Echo Reply flood
steps.desc: Analyze inbound flood traffic to confirm it consists of ICMP Echo Reply packets from numerous hosts within one or a few third-party subnets, consistent with a directed-broadcast amplification.
steps.guidance: A classic smurf flood shows Echo Replies from many sequential/adjacent IPs within the same subnet(s) arriving simultaneously — a signature distinct from a distributed botnet.
steps.outcome: Confirmed smurf attack pattern with amplifying network(s) identified.

steps.title: Block inbound ICMP Echo Reply flood at perimeter and upstream
steps.desc: Apply ACLs to rate-limit or block the inbound ICMP Echo Reply flood from the identified amplifying subnet(s).
steps.guidance: Since smurf floods originate from a limited, identifiable set of subnets, targeted blocking is often more effective than broad ICMP rate limiting.
steps.outcome: Reduced flood volume at the perimeter from the identified amplifying networks.

steps.title: Disable directed broadcast on any organization-owned amplifying networks
steps.desc: If any organization-owned router/network was identified as allowing directed broadcast, disable it immediately (e.g., 'no ip directed-broadcast' on Cisco).
steps.guidance: This is a long-standing, well-known best-practice hardening step; virtually all modern router defaults already disable directed broadcast, so also check for legacy/misconfigured devices.
steps.outcome: Organization-owned network(s) no longer usable as smurf amplifiers; confirmed via test broadcast ping (in a controlled maintenance window).

steps.title: Remove temporary ACLs and confirm normal ICMP handling restored
steps.desc: Roll back perimeter blocks once the flood subsides and confirm normal ICMP-dependent operations function correctly.
steps.guidance: Monitor for 1-2 hours of stable traffic before full rollback.
steps.outcome: Normal ICMP handling restored with no residual service degradation.

steps.title: Document incident and audit organization network edge for directed-broadcast exposure
steps.desc: Record the attack and confirm all organization-owned routers, including legacy devices, have directed broadcast disabled as a baseline configuration standard.
steps.guidance: Add directed-broadcast disablement to the network device configuration baseline/compliance check.
steps.outcome: After-action report with a configuration baseline compliance item added.

steps.title: Identify the amplifying network(s) allowing directed broadcast
steps.desc: Determine the source subnet(s) whose directed-broadcast address was targeted, and check whether any belong to the organization.
steps.guidance: Cross-reference source subnet CIDR against organization-owned network ranges to determine if internal infrastructure is misconfigured to allow directed broadcast.
steps.outcome: Confirmed identity of amplifying network(s) and whether organization-owned infrastructure is involved.

steps.title: Engage upstream scrubbing if volume exceeds local capacity
steps.desc: Engage upstream/cloud DDoS mitigation if the amplified volume exceeds what local ACLs can absorb.
steps.guidance: Provide the amplifying subnet list and attack signature to the scrubbing provider.
steps.outcome: Bulk of attack traffic absorbed and scrubbed upstream.

steps.title: Notify third-party amplifying network operators where feasible
steps.desc: For amplifying subnets not owned by the organization, submit abuse notifications to the responsible network operators encouraging directed-broadcast hardening.
steps.guidance: This is best-effort since third-party networks are outside direct control.
steps.outcome: Abuse notifications sent to identifiable third-party network operators.

ITID-41142.def: A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary sends spoofed UDP packets (typically to the echo or chargen ports) to a network's broadcast address, causing every responding host to send UDP traffic to the spoofed victim address, amplifying attack traffic in the same manner as Smurf but over UDP rather than ICMP.
ITID-41142.purpose: Captures the Fraggle attack, the UDP-based sibling of Smurf, which bounces spoofed echo/chargen traffic off a broadcast network to flood a victim.
scopeIncludes: Spoofed UDP echo/chargen packets sent to a directed broadcast address to elicit mass replies toward a victim
scopeExcludes: The ICMP-based classic Smurf variant (see Classic ICMP Smurf Attack)
Direct UDP floods with no broadcast-network reflection (see UDP Flood Attack under Volumetric Flooding)
ITID-41142.severity: Medium today given the rarity of the legacy echo/chargen services still being enabled, but High if such a service is confirmed still active and reachable on a broadcast segment.
ITID-41142.priority: P2 on detection; escalate to P1 if the organization's own network is confirmed being used as an unwitting amplifier.
ITID-41142.escalation: Escalate to network operations immediately if legacy echo/chargen services or broadcast forwarding are implicated.
indicators: Large volume of inbound UDP traffic on echo (port 7) or chargen (port 19) with no matching outbound request from the victim
Evidence of echo/chargen services still enabled on any organization-owned device (if investigating amplifier-network risk)
vectors: Spoofed UDP echo/chargen requests directed at a subnet broadcast address on a network still forwarding directed broadcasts with legacy services enabled
rootCauses: Legacy echo/chargen services left enabled on network devices/hosts
Directed broadcast forwarding not disabled on routers
mitreTechniques: T1498.002 Network Denial of Service: Reflection Amplification
controls: Disable legacy echo/chargen services on all organization-owned devices
Disable IP directed-broadcast forwarding on all routers
Border ACLs dropping unsolicited inbound UDP/7 and UDP/19 traffic
ITID-41142.detection: Strong technical signal, though genuine Fraggle incidents are now rare given the near-universal deprecation of echo/chargen services.
ITID-41142.response: Verify legacy services and directed-broadcast forwarding are disabled on all organization-owned equipment; filter unsolicited echo/chargen response floods at the border if victimized.
metrics: Peak inbound unsolicited echo/chargen response volume
Count of devices audited for legacy service exposure
ITID-41142.notes: UDP sibling of the classic ICMP Smurf attack; both share the broadcast-reflection mechanism but differ in transport protocol and exploited service.

playbook.name: Fraggle Attack (UDP Variant of Smurf)
playbook.description: The attacker spoofs the victim's IP and sends UDP packets (typically to echo/chargen ports) to a network's broadcast address, causing amplified UDP replies to flood the victim.

steps.title: Confirm fraggle pattern via broadcast-triggered UDP flood on echo/chargen ports
steps.desc: Analyze inbound flood traffic to confirm it consists of UDP packets on echo (7) or chargen (19) ports from numerous hosts within one or a few third-party subnets.
steps.guidance: A fraggle attack mirrors smurf but uses UDP echo/chargen services rather than ICMP; confirm via packet capture showing UDP port 7/19 responses from an adjacent-IP cluster.
steps.outcome: Confirmed fraggle attack pattern with amplifying network(s) and abused UDP service identified.

steps.title: Block inbound UDP/7 and UDP/19 flood at perimeter
steps.desc: Apply ACLs blocking inbound UDP source ports 7 (echo) and 19 (chargen), as these legacy services have no legitimate modern business use.
steps.guidance: This can be blocked unconditionally at the border given no legitimate current use case.
steps.outcome: Amplified fraggle traffic dropped at the perimeter with no legitimate service impact.

steps.title: Disable echo/chargen services and directed broadcast on any organization-owned devices
steps.desc: If any organization-owned hosts were found running echo/chargen services, disable them immediately; disable directed broadcast on any amplifying network.
steps.guidance: These legacy inetd/xinetd services should be disabled organization-wide as a hardening baseline, not just on the identified hosts.
steps.outcome: Organization-owned infrastructure no longer usable as fraggle amplifiers; confirmed via internal service audit.

steps.title: Remove temporary ACLs and confirm no legitimate service impact
steps.desc: Roll back perimeter blocks once the flood subsides, retaining the UDP/7 and UDP/19 blocks permanently.
steps.guidance: These blocks should remain permanent given no legitimate cross-internet use case.
steps.outcome: Normal traffic handling restored with permanent hardening controls retained.

steps.title: Document incident and add legacy-service detection to configuration baselines
steps.desc: Record the attack and ensure echo/chargen/directed-broadcast checks are part of ongoing configuration compliance scanning.
steps.guidance: Add this check to recurring internal vulnerability/compliance scans.
steps.outcome: After-action report with a recurring detection control added to prevent recurrence.

steps.title: Identify the amplifying network(s) and any organization-owned echo/chargen services
steps.desc: Determine the source subnet(s) involved and check whether any organization-owned hosts have echo/chargen services enabled and allow directed broadcast.
steps.guidance: Echo and chargen are legacy services that should not be enabled on modern systems; their presence anywhere is itself a finding.
steps.outcome: Confirmed identity of amplifying network(s) and whether organization-owned infrastructure is involved.

steps.title: Engage upstream scrubbing if volume exceeds local capacity
steps.desc: Engage upstream/cloud DDoS mitigation if amplified volume exceeds local ACL absorption capacity.
steps.guidance: Provide the amplifying subnet list and attack signature to the scrubbing provider.
steps.outcome: Bulk of attack traffic absorbed and scrubbed upstream.

steps.title: Audit organization-wide for legacy echo/chargen/broadcast exposure
steps.desc: Run an internal and external scan across all organization assets to confirm no other systems run echo/chargen or allow directed broadcast.
steps.guidance: These are legacy misconfigurations that may exist on forgotten/unmanaged legacy systems; a full sweep is warranted.
steps.outcome: Confirmed zero remaining echo/chargen services or directed-broadcast-enabled networks organization-wide.

ITID-41143.def: A denial-of-service event exhibiting broadcast-network reflection characteristics where the specific protocol variant (ICMP Smurf or UDP Fraggle) has not yet been determined.
ITID-41143.purpose: Intake bucket for broadcast-reflection DoS activity that cannot yet be attributed to the ICMP (Smurf) or UDP (Fraggle) variant.
scopeIncludes: Initial triage of a suspected broadcast-reflection attack before protocol confirmation is complete
scopeExcludes: Any attack already confirmed as classic ICMP Smurf or UDP Fraggle (reclassify to the specific leaf once confirmed)
ITID-41143.severity: Medium pending confirmation; reassess once protocol variant is identified.
ITID-41143.priority: P2 pending triage; adjust once reclassified.
ITID-41143.escalation: Escalate to network operations for flow capture and protocol identification; reclassify once confirmed.
indicators: Unsolicited inbound flood consistent with broadcast reflection without confirmed protocol at initial detection
vectors: Unconfirmed at time of intake
rootCauses: Insufficient initial flow visibility to determine protocol variant
mitreTechniques: T1498.002 Network Denial of Service: Reflection Amplification
controls: Disable IP directed-broadcast forwarding on all routers
Upstream DDoS scrubbing service
ITID-41143.detection: Sufficient to detect the reflection pattern but insufficient to classify protocol at time of intake.
ITID-41143.response: Engage general reflection mitigation immediately; run protocol analysis in parallel to reclassify.
metrics: Count of incidents landing in this catch-all per quarter
ITID-41143.notes: Triage/intake bucket only; reclassify once the protocol variant is confirmed. Given the rarity of both underlying vulnerabilities on modern networks, sustained volume here should prompt an infrastructure audit.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Smurf-Style Attack
playbook.description: A broadcast-amplified flood is confirmed but the specific protocol variant (classic ICMP smurf vs. UDP fraggle) has not yet been determined.

steps.title: Confirm broadcast-amplification pattern and identify protocol
steps.desc: Analyze inbound flood traffic to confirm a broadcast-triggered amplification pattern (many adjacent-IP sources replying simultaneously) and identify whether the protocol is ICMP or UDP-based.
steps.guidance: Compare packet captures against both classic smurf (ICMP) and fraggle (UDP echo/chargen) signatures to attempt classification.
steps.outcome: Confirmed broadcast-amplification pattern with protocol identified where possible.

steps.title: Block inbound flood traffic from identified amplifying subnet(s)
steps.desc: Apply ACLs targeting the specific amplifying subnets and protocol/port combination identified.
steps.guidance: Targeted blocking based on the identified amplifying subnets is generally more precise than broad protocol-wide rate limiting.
steps.outcome: Reduced flood volume at the perimeter.

steps.title: Disable directed broadcast and any legacy amplifying services on organization-owned networks
steps.desc: If any organization-owned network/device was identified as an amplifier, disable directed broadcast and any legacy echo/chargen services regardless of which protocol was ultimately confirmed.
steps.guidance: Apply the hardening broadly since both smurf and fraggle rely on the same underlying directed-broadcast misconfiguration.
steps.outcome: Organization-owned infrastructure no longer usable as a broadcast amplifier.

steps.title: Remove temporary ACLs and confirm normal traffic handling
steps.desc: Roll back perimeter blocks once the flood subsides and confirm no legitimate service impact.
steps.guidance: Monitor for 1-2 hours of stable traffic before full rollback.
steps.outcome: Normal traffic handling restored with no residual service degradation.

steps.title: Document incident and audit for broadcast-amplification exposure organization-wide
steps.desc: Record the attack and confirm directed-broadcast and legacy echo/chargen checks are part of ongoing configuration compliance scanning.
steps.guidance: Add this check to recurring internal vulnerability/compliance scans if not already covered.
steps.outcome: After-action report with a recurring detection control confirmed or added.

steps.title: Identify the amplifying network(s) involved
steps.desc: Determine the source subnet(s) whose directed-broadcast address was abused, regardless of protocol.
steps.guidance: Cross-reference source subnet CIDR against organization-owned network ranges.
steps.outcome: Confirmed identity of amplifying network(s) and ownership.

steps.title: Engage upstream scrubbing if volume exceeds local capacity
steps.desc: Engage upstream/cloud DDoS mitigation if the amplified volume exceeds local ACL absorption capacity.
steps.guidance: Provide amplifying subnet list and any identified protocol details to the scrubbing provider.
steps.outcome: Bulk of attack traffic absorbed and scrubbed upstream.

steps.title: Complete protocol classification for incident record
steps.desc: Finalize whether the attack was ICMP-based (smurf) or UDP-based (fraggle) for accurate incident classification and reporting.
steps.guidance: Reclassify the incident to the specific ITID leaf if determination succeeds.
steps.outcome: Attack technique documented or confirmed genuinely unclassifiable.

ITID-41151.def: A low-and-slow denial-of-service attack in which an adversary opens many HTTP connections to a target web server and sends partial request headers at a deliberately slow rate (or none at all after the initial line), keeping each connection open just below the server's timeout threshold until the server's maximum concurrent connection limit is exhausted and it can no longer accept new legitimate requests.
ITID-41151.purpose: Captures the Slowloris technique, where an adversary exhausts a web server's connection pool by sending HTTP requests that are never completed.
scopeIncludes: Attacks that open connections and drip-feed incomplete HTTP headers to hold them open indefinitely
Low-bandwidth attacks targeting a web server's connection/thread pool rather than network bandwidth
scopeExcludes: Slow HTTP POST body attacks (see Slow POST (R-U-Dead-Yet) Attack)
Slow consumption of HTTP responses (see Slow Read Attack)
High-volume HTTP request floods that complete requests normally (see HTTP Flood)
ITID-41151.severity: Medium-High: low bandwidth footprint but can fully exhaust a poorly configured web server's connection pool with minimal attacker resources.
ITID-41151.priority: P2 on detection; escalate to P1 if legitimate users are confirmed unable to establish new connections.
ITID-41151.escalation: Escalate to web/application operations to adjust server timeout and connection-limit settings if exhaustion is confirmed.
indicators: Large number of long-lived connections in an incomplete-request state on the web server
Connection count approaching or at the server's configured maximum with minimal bandwidth consumption
Web server logs showing partial/incomplete HTTP headers held open far beyond normal request duration
vectors: Slowloris tool and derivatives issuing many slow-drip HTTP connections from a single or few hosts
rootCauses: Web server not configured with an aggressive enough timeout for incomplete requests
No reverse proxy/load balancer buffering connections ahead of the origin server
Connection pool sized without accounting for slow-rate exhaustion attacks
mitreTechniques: T1499.002 Endpoint Denial of Service: Service Exhaustion Flood
controls: Reverse proxy/load balancer (e.g. nginx, HAProxy) in front of origin to buffer and time out slow connections
Aggressive incomplete-request timeout configuration on the web server
Per-source connection rate-limiting
Web application firewall with slow-request detection
ITID-41151.detection: Strong technical signal from connection-state monitoring and web server access/error logs showing abnormally long incomplete-request durations.
ITID-41151.response: Tighten timeout settings and engage reverse-proxy buffering immediately; block or rate-limit offending source IPs.
metrics: Peak concurrent incomplete-request connections
Time to timeout-configuration remediation
Duration of new-connection refusal for legitimate clients
ITID-41151.notes: Differentiating axis for the Slowloris/slow-rate group is which part of the HTTP transaction is stalled: headers (this leaf), request body (Slow POST), or response consumption (Slow Read).

playbook.name: Slowloris HTTP Header Exhaustion Attack
playbook.description: The attacker opens many HTTP connections and sends partial request headers at a trickle, keeping connections open indefinitely to exhaust the web server's connection pool.

steps.title: Confirm Slowloris pattern via connection-duration and header-completion anomaly
steps.desc: Analyze web server connection tables for an abnormally high count of long-lived connections stuck in a state awaiting header completion.
steps.guidance: Check web server status modules (e.g., Apache mod_status, nginx stub_status) for connections in 'reading' state persisting far longer than typical client latency; correlate with a spike in concurrent connections without a matching spike in completed requests.
steps.outcome: Confirmed Slowloris pattern with count of stuck connections documented.
steps.abort: If long connections correlate with legitimate slow clients (e.g., known high-latency mobile network segment), reassess before treating as attack.

steps.title: Tune reverse proxy/web server timeouts for incomplete request headers
steps.desc: Reduce timeout thresholds for receiving complete request headers so slow/incomplete connections are dropped quickly.
steps.guidance: On Apache, deploy mod_reqtimeout with tight header/body timeout values; on nginx, tune client_header_timeout; on a reverse proxy/load balancer, enable equivalent slow-client protections.
steps.outcome: Connection pool no longer exhausted by slow-trickle connections; legitimate clients unaffected.
steps.abort: If timeouts are set too aggressively and impact legitimate slow-network clients, relax slightly and monitor.
steps.tool: Apache mod_reqtimeout / nginx / load balancer config

steps.title: Deploy a reverse proxy with built-in slow-connection protection if not already present
steps.desc: If the origin web server was directly internet-facing without a hardened reverse proxy, deploy one (e.g., nginx, HAProxy) in front as a permanent architectural mitigation.
steps.guidance: Modern reverse proxies are inherently more resistant to Slowloris due to event-driven connection handling versus thread/process-per-connection models used by vulnerable web servers.
steps.outcome: Origin web server protected by a hardened reverse proxy layer resistant to slow-connection exhaustion.

steps.title: Validate connection pool recovery and normal request completion rates
steps.desc: Confirm the web server connection pool returns to normal utilization and legitimate requests complete at expected latency.
steps.guidance: Monitor active connection count and average request completion time for at least 1-2 hours post-mitigation.
steps.outcome: Normal connection handling and request completion confirmed.

steps.title: Document incident and codify timeout/rate-limit hardening as a standard baseline
steps.desc: Record the attack and ensure the tuned timeout and rate-limit settings are captured in the standard web server/reverse-proxy hardening baseline for all similar deployments.
steps.guidance: Update infrastructure-as-code templates or configuration management baselines to include these settings by default.
steps.outcome: After-action report with hardening settings codified into deployment standards.

steps.title: Sample source IPs and connection headers to confirm attacker behavior
steps.desc: Capture packets or web server logs for a sample of stuck connections to confirm the trickle-header pattern and gather source IP information.
steps.guidance: Slowloris connections typically send a partial header line every 10-30 seconds to avoid server-side idle timeouts, never completing the request.
steps.outcome: Confirmed trickle-header behavior with source IP list captured.

steps.title: Apply per-source connection-rate limiting at the reverse proxy/WAF
steps.desc: Limit the number of concurrent connections permitted per source IP to reduce the effectiveness of a single-source or small-botnet Slowloris attack.
steps.guidance: Configure connection limits per IP at the load balancer, reverse proxy, or WAF layer.
steps.outcome: Reduced ability for a single source to exhaust the full connection pool.

steps.title: Confirm hardened timeout settings retained permanently, not rolled back
steps.desc: Verify the tuned header/connection timeout and per-source rate-limit settings applied during containment remain in place as permanent hardening rather than being reverted along with other temporary measures.
steps.guidance: Distinguish between genuinely temporary emergency measures (e.g., aggressive blanket IP blocks) and the timeout tuning, which should persist.
steps.outcome: Confirmed permanent hardening settings remain active post-incident.

ITID-41152.def: A low-and-slow denial-of-service attack in which an adversary sends a complete HTTP POST header declaring a large Content-Length, then transmits the request body one byte (or a few bytes) at a time over an extended period, holding the server-side request-processing thread or connection open until resources are exhausted.
ITID-41152.purpose: Captures the Slow POST (R-U-Dead-Yet) technique, where an adversary exhausts server resources by sending a legitimate HTTP POST request body at an extremely slow rate.
scopeIncludes: Attacks that declare a large Content-Length and drip-feed the POST body to hold a connection/worker thread open
Attacks targeting form or file-upload endpoints via deliberately slow body transmission
scopeExcludes: Slow HTTP header transmission (see Slowloris HTTP Header Exhaustion Attack)
Slow consumption of HTTP responses (see Slow Read Attack)
Normal-speed POST floods against a resource-intensive endpoint (see POST Flood Targeting Form/Submission Endpoint under HTTP Flood)
ITID-41152.severity: Medium-High: low bandwidth footprint but can exhaust a web server's worker threads or connection pool with minimal attacker resources.
ITID-41152.priority: P2 on detection; escalate to P1 if legitimate form/upload submissions are confirmed failing.
ITID-41152.escalation: Escalate to web/application operations to adjust minimum-throughput and body-timeout settings if exhaustion is confirmed.
indicators: Long-lived POST connections with body transmission far below expected throughput
Worker thread or connection pool saturation correlated with slow-POST connections
Web server logs showing POST requests open far longer than the declared Content-Length should require
vectors: R-U-Dead-Yet (RUDY) tool and derivatives issuing slow-drip POST bodies from a single or few hosts
rootCauses: No minimum-throughput/timeout enforcement on request body transmission
No reverse proxy buffering full requests before forwarding to origin
Worker/thread pool sized without accounting for slow-body exhaustion attacks
mitreTechniques: T1499.002 Endpoint Denial of Service: Service Exhaustion Flood
controls: Reverse proxy/load balancer buffering complete requests before forwarding to origin
Minimum-throughput enforcement (timeout on request body transmission)
Per-source connection rate-limiting
Web application firewall with slow-POST detection
ITID-41152.detection: Strong technical signal from connection-state monitoring and web server logs showing abnormal body-transmission duration relative to declared Content-Length.
ITID-41152.response: Enable minimum-throughput timeouts and reverse-proxy buffering immediately; block or rate-limit offending source IPs.
metrics: Peak concurrent slow-POST connections
Time to timeout-configuration remediation
Duration of form/upload submission failures for legitimate clients
detections: Web server worker/connection pool saturation alerting
ITID-41152.notes: Differentiating axis: this leaf stalls the request body, its Slowloris sibling stalls the headers, and Slow Read stalls response consumption.

playbook.name: Slow POST (R-U-Dead-Yet) Attack
playbook.description: The attacker sends a legitimate-looking HTTP POST with a large declared Content-Length but transmits the body extremely slowly, tying up server resources waiting for completion.

steps.title: Confirm slow-POST pattern via body-transmission-rate anomaly
steps.desc: Analyze web server connection tables for POST requests with large declared Content-Length values but abnormally low body byte-transmission rates, keeping connections open far longer than typical uploads.
steps.guidance: Check for connections in a 'sending body'/reading-request-body state persisting well beyond expected upload duration for the declared size at normal client bandwidth.
steps.outcome: Confirmed slow-POST pattern with count of stuck connections and declared Content-Length values documented.
steps.abort: If slow uploads correlate with a known legitimate large-file-upload feature from low-bandwidth clients, reassess before treating as attack.
steps.tool: Apache mod_status / nginx stub_status / application logs

steps.title: Enforce minimum body-transmission-rate timeouts at web server/reverse proxy
steps.desc: Configure the web server or reverse proxy to close connections where request body data arrives below a minimum acceptable rate.
steps.guidance: On Apache, use mod_reqtimeout body-rate settings; on nginx, tune client_body_timeout; ensure the threshold accommodates legitimate slow-but-valid clients.
steps.outcome: Connections transmitting body data below the minimum rate are terminated promptly, freeing server resources.
steps.abort: If legitimate slow-network clients are impacted, relax the rate threshold and monitor.

steps.title: Validate application-layer upload handling does not itself block on slow input
steps.desc: Review application code/upload handling logic to ensure it does not hold backend resources (e.g., database connections, worker threads) open while waiting on slow client input, independent of web server-level timeout fixes.
steps.guidance: Ensure streaming upload handlers release backend resources or use async I/O rather than blocking a worker thread for the full request duration.
steps.outcome: Confirmed application-layer resource handling is decoupled from raw client transmission speed, or a remediation ticket is filed if not.

steps.title: Validate connection pool recovery and normal upload functionality
steps.desc: Confirm the web server connection pool returns to normal utilization and legitimate large-file uploads still complete successfully under the new timeout/rate settings.
steps.guidance: Test with a representative legitimate large upload from a realistic network condition to confirm no false-positive blocking.
steps.outcome: Normal connection handling confirmed with legitimate uploads unaffected.

steps.title: Document incident and codify body-rate timeout hardening as a standard baseline
steps.desc: Record the attack and ensure the tuned body-rate timeout and size-limit settings are captured in the standard web server hardening baseline.
steps.guidance: Update infrastructure-as-code templates or configuration management baselines to include these settings by default.
steps.outcome: After-action report with hardening settings codified into deployment standards.

steps.title: Sample source IPs and request patterns to confirm attacker behavior
steps.desc: Capture packets or logs for a sample of stuck connections to confirm the deliberately slow body-transmission pattern and gather source IP information.
steps.guidance: R-U-Dead-Yet style attacks typically send body bytes at an extremely low, fixed rate (e.g., one byte every few seconds) to hold the connection open indefinitely.
steps.outcome: Confirmed slow-transmission behavior with source IP list captured.

steps.title: Cap maximum request body size and concurrent uploads per source
steps.desc: Enforce reasonable maximum Content-Length limits and per-source-IP concurrent-connection caps to reduce attack surface.
steps.guidance: Apply limits at the WAF/reverse-proxy layer appropriate to legitimate application upload requirements.
steps.outcome: Reduced ability for a single source to hold multiple oversized slow uploads simultaneously.

steps.title: Confirm hardened body-rate and size-limit settings retained permanently
steps.desc: Verify the tuned body-transmission-rate timeout and content-length caps applied during containment remain in place as permanent hardening.
steps.guidance: Distinguish between temporary emergency measures and the rate/size tuning, which should persist as standard configuration.
steps.outcome: Confirmed permanent hardening settings remain active post-incident.

ITID-41153.def: A low-and-slow denial-of-service attack in which an adversary issues normal, complete HTTP requests but advertises a tiny TCP receive window (or otherwise throttles read speed), forcing the server to hold the response buffer and connection open far longer than a normal client would, exhausting connection/memory resources as more such connections accumulate.
ITID-41153.purpose: Captures the Slow Read technique, where an adversary exhausts server resources by requesting normal content but consuming the response at an artificially slow rate.
scopeIncludes: Attacks manipulating TCP window size or client-side read rate to prolong response delivery unnaturally
Attacks targeting endpoints that generate large responses to maximize the time the server holds the connection open
scopeExcludes: Slow header transmission (see Slowloris HTTP Header Exhaustion Attack)
Slow request body transmission (see Slow POST (R-U-Dead-Yet) Attack)
ITID-41153.severity: Medium-High: low bandwidth footprint but can exhaust server-side connection/memory resources with minimal attacker resources, particularly against endpoints serving large responses.
ITID-41153.priority: P2 on detection; escalate to P1 if legitimate connections are confirmed being refused.
ITID-41153.escalation: Escalate to web/application operations to adjust response-timeout and buffering settings if exhaustion is confirmed.
indicators: Long-lived connections with abnormally small advertised TCP receive windows
Response delivery rate far below expected for the connection type
Connection pool/memory saturation correlated with slow-read connections
vectors: Slow Read attack tools manipulating TCP window size to throttle response consumption from a single or few hosts
rootCauses: No minimum-throughput enforcement on response delivery
No reverse proxy buffering responses independently of client read speed
Server not configured to timeout connections with abnormally small receive windows
mitreTechniques: T1499.002 Endpoint Denial of Service: Service Exhaustion Flood
controls: Reverse proxy/load balancer buffering responses independently of client consumption rate
Minimum-throughput enforcement on response delivery
Per-source connection rate-limiting
Web application firewall with slow-read detection
ITID-41153.detection: Moderate-to-strong: requires TCP-window-level visibility (packet capture or load balancer telemetry) beyond standard HTTP access logs.
ITID-41153.response: Enable minimum-throughput timeouts and reverse-proxy response buffering immediately; block or rate-limit offending source IPs.
metrics: Peak concurrent slow-read connections
Time to timeout-configuration remediation
Duration of new-connection refusal for legitimate clients
detections: Web server connection pool saturation alerting
ITID-41153.notes: Differentiating axis: this leaf stalls response consumption, distinct from its header- and body-stalling siblings.

playbook.name: Slow Read Attack
playbook.description: The attacker sends a normal request but advertises a tiny TCP receive window and reads the server's response extremely slowly, tying up server threads/connections for an extended period.

steps.title: Confirm slow-read pattern via response-transmission stall and small window sizes
steps.desc: Analyze web server connection tables and TCP-level metrics for connections stuck sending a response over an extended period with abnormally small TCP receive windows advertised by the client.
steps.guidance: Check for connections in a 'sending response'/write-blocked state persisting far beyond expected transfer duration; capture TCP window size values from the client side.
steps.outcome: Confirmed slow-read pattern with count of stuck connections and observed window sizes documented.
steps.abort: If small windows correlate with a known legitimate constrained-bandwidth client population, reassess before treating as attack.

steps.title: Enforce minimum outbound-transfer-rate timeouts at web server/reverse proxy
steps.desc: Configure the web server or reverse proxy to close connections where response transmission falls below a minimum acceptable rate for an extended period.
steps.guidance: Many modern reverse proxies (nginx, HAProxy) support explicit slow-client/keepalive write-timeout tuning; ensure buffering is enabled so the origin server can hand off the response quickly and free its own resources even if the client reads slowly.
steps.outcome: Connections transmitting response data below the minimum rate are terminated promptly, freeing server resources.
steps.abort: If legitimate constrained-bandwidth clients are impacted, relax the rate threshold and monitor.

steps.title: Validate origin server architecture decouples backend processing from client read speed
steps.desc: Review the application/web server architecture to confirm backend worker threads or processes are not held for the full duration of a slow client response transfer.
steps.guidance: Ensure a proxy/buffering layer sits between the origin application and internet clients so backend capacity scales independently of client network conditions.
steps.outcome: Confirmed backend resource usage is decoupled from client read speed, or a remediation ticket is filed if not.

steps.title: Validate connection pool recovery and normal response delivery
steps.desc: Confirm the web server/proxy connection pool returns to normal utilization and legitimate slow-network clients still receive complete responses under the new settings.
steps.guidance: Test with a representative legitimate low-bandwidth client scenario to confirm no false-positive blocking.
steps.outcome: Normal connection handling confirmed with legitimate clients unaffected.

steps.title: Document incident and codify slow-read protections as a standard baseline
steps.desc: Record the attack and ensure the tuned rate-timeout and buffering settings are captured in the standard reverse-proxy hardening baseline.
steps.guidance: Update infrastructure-as-code templates or configuration management baselines to include these settings by default.
steps.outcome: After-action report with hardening settings codified into deployment standards.

steps.title: Sample source IPs and TCP window behavior to confirm attacker behavior
steps.desc: Capture packets for a sample of stuck connections to confirm deliberately manipulated small/zero TCP window advertisements and gather source IP information.
steps.guidance: Slow read attacks typically advertise a very small (or near-zero) receive window and read data at a fixed slow rate, sometimes combined with many concurrent connections from a modest number of sources.
steps.outcome: Confirmed manipulated-window behavior with source IP list captured.

steps.title: Cap concurrent connections per source and enable response buffering
steps.desc: Limit concurrent connections per source IP and ensure the reverse proxy buffers full responses from the origin, decoupling origin server resource usage from slow client read rates.
steps.guidance: Response buffering at the proxy layer means the origin server can complete and release its connection quickly, while only the proxy (designed for high-concurrency slow-client handling) manages the slow client.
steps.outcome: Origin server resources no longer tied to slow client read behavior; reduced attack surface per source.

steps.title: Confirm buffering and write-timeout settings retained permanently
steps.desc: Verify the response-buffering configuration and minimum write-rate timeout applied during containment remain in place as permanent hardening.
steps.guidance: Distinguish between temporary emergency measures and the buffering/timeout tuning, which should persist as standard configuration.
steps.outcome: Confirmed permanent hardening settings remain active post-incident.

ITID-41154.def: A denial-of-service event exhibiting slow-rate (low-bandwidth, connection-exhaustion) characteristics where the specific stalled phase of the HTTP transaction (headers, body, or response) has not yet been determined.
ITID-41154.purpose: Intake bucket for slow-rate/low-and-slow DoS activity that cannot yet be attributed to a specific stalling technique.
scopeIncludes: Initial triage of a suspected slow-rate DoS attack before the specific technique is confirmed
scopeExcludes: Any attack already confirmed as Slowloris, Slow POST, or Slow Read (reclassify to the specific leaf once confirmed)
ITID-41154.severity: Medium-High pending confirmation; reassess once technique is identified.
ITID-41154.priority: P2 pending triage; adjust once reclassified.
ITID-41154.escalation: Escalate to web/application operations for connection-state analysis; reclassify once confirmed.
indicators: Connection/thread pool saturation with low bandwidth consumption and unconfirmed stalling technique at initial detection
vectors: Unconfirmed at time of intake
rootCauses: Insufficient initial visibility into which phase of the HTTP transaction is being stalled
mitreTechniques: T1499.002 Endpoint Denial of Service: Service Exhaustion Flood
controls: Reverse proxy/load balancer buffering requests and responses
Aggressive timeout configuration on the web server
ITID-41154.detection: Sufficient to detect the slow-rate pattern but insufficient to classify the specific technique at time of intake.
ITID-41154.response: Tighten timeout settings and engage reverse-proxy buffering immediately; run connection analysis in parallel to reclassify.
metrics: Count of incidents landing in this catch-all per quarter
ITID-41154.notes: Triage/intake bucket only; reclassify once the stalling technique is confirmed.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Slow-Rate DoS Attack
playbook.description: A connection-exhaustion-style attack is confirmed via abnormally long-lived connections but the specific low-and-slow technique (Slowloris, Slow POST, Slow Read) has not yet been determined.

steps.title: Confirm slow-rate connection exhaustion pattern
steps.desc: Analyze web server connection tables for an abnormal count of long-lived connections consuming the connection pool without completing normal request/response cycles at expected speed.
steps.guidance: Check server status modules for connections stuck in reading-header, reading-body, or writing-response states well beyond normal duration.
steps.outcome: Confirmed slow-rate exhaustion pattern with stuck-connection count documented.

steps.title: Apply general timeout hardening across header, body, and write stages
steps.desc: Configure conservative timeouts for header completion, body transmission rate, and response write rate simultaneously to cover all low-and-slow variants pending classification.
steps.guidance: Use mod_reqtimeout (Apache) or equivalent nginx/HAProxy directives covering all three stages.
steps.outcome: Connection pool exhaustion resolved regardless of which specific slow-rate technique is in use.
steps.abort: If legitimate slow-network clients are impacted, relax the most aggressive threshold and monitor.

steps.title: Complete technique classification and apply targeted hardening
steps.desc: Finalize which low-and-slow technique was used and apply the more specific hardening measures from the corresponding playbook.
steps.guidance: Reclassify the incident to the specific ITID leaf if determination succeeds.
steps.outcome: Attack technique documented and technique-specific hardening applied.

steps.title: Validate connection pool recovery and normal request completion rates
steps.desc: Confirm the web server connection pool returns to normal utilization and legitimate requests complete at expected latency.
steps.guidance: Monitor active connection count and average request completion time for at least 1-2 hours post-mitigation.
steps.outcome: Normal connection handling and request completion confirmed.

steps.title: Document incident and improve slow-rate technique classification tooling
steps.desc: Record why immediate sub-classification was not possible and recommend detection tooling improvements to reduce future triage time.
steps.guidance: Include recommendations for connection-state monitoring dashboards that would have sped up classification.
steps.outcome: After-action report with concrete detection tooling improvement items.

steps.title: Attempt sub-technique classification via connection-state analysis
steps.desc: Determine which connection state (incomplete headers, slow body, slow read) dominates the stuck connections to classify as Slowloris, Slow POST, or Slow Read.
steps.guidance: If classification succeeds, pivot to the corresponding specific playbook; otherwise proceed with general mitigation.
steps.outcome: Either successful reclassification or confirmed genuinely mixed/unclear low-and-slow technique.

steps.title: Apply per-source connection-rate limiting
steps.desc: Limit concurrent connections per source IP at the reverse proxy/WAF layer to reduce the effectiveness of the attack regardless of technique.
steps.guidance: Configure connection limits per IP at the load balancer, reverse proxy, or WAF layer.
steps.outcome: Reduced ability for a single source to exhaust the full connection pool.

steps.title: Confirm general timeout hardening retained permanently
steps.desc: Verify the general header/body/write timeout hardening applied during containment remains in place as permanent configuration.
steps.guidance: Distinguish between temporary emergency measures and the general timeout tuning, which should persist regardless of final technique classification.
steps.outcome: Confirmed permanent hardening settings remain active post-incident.

ITID-41211.def: A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary sends a high rate of complete, well-formed HTTP GET requests targeting a specific resource-intensive endpoint (e.g. search, report generation, large media, or database-backed pages) to exhaust backend compute, database, or I/O capacity rather than network bandwidth.
ITID-41211.purpose: Captures an application-layer flood of HTTP GET requests deliberately aimed at an endpoint known to be computationally or I/O expensive to serve.
scopeIncludes: High-rate GET requests against endpoints known to trigger expensive backend processing
Floods that complete the full HTTP request/response cycle, distinguishing them from slow-rate techniques
scopeExcludes: POST-based floods against form/submission endpoints (see POST Flood Targeting Form/Submission Endpoint)
Cache-evasion-specific floods using randomized query strings (see Cache-Busting HTTP Flood)
Low-and-slow connection-exhaustion techniques (see Slowloris Attack group)
ITID-41211.severity: High when the targeted endpoint is confirmed to drive disproportionate backend load (e.g. uncached database queries); Medium if absorbed by caching/CDN with no backend impact.
ITID-41211.priority: P2 on detection; escalate to P1 on confirmed backend resource exhaustion or service degradation.
ITID-41211.escalation: Escalate to application/web operations and WAF/CDN team immediately if backend CPU, database, or I/O saturation is confirmed.
indicators: Sharp rise in GET request rate concentrated on one or a small set of resource-intensive URIs
Backend CPU/database load spiking disproportionately to overall request volume
Web server/application logs showing repeated requests to the same expensive endpoint from many or few sources
vectors: Scripted HTTP clients or botnets targeting known expensive endpoints identified through reconnaissance
Booter/stresser platforms offering targeted Layer-7 HTTP flood modules
rootCauses: Expensive endpoints lacking caching, rate-limiting, or query result limits
No WAF/CDN rule distinguishing normal from abusive request patterns for the specific endpoint
Database queries triggered by user input without cost bounding
mitreTechniques: T1499.003 Endpoint Denial of Service: Application Exhaustion Flood
controls: WAF/CDN rate-limiting scoped to specific high-cost endpoints
Caching layer in front of expensive endpoints
Query result/complexity limits at the application layer
Bot detection/CAPTCHA challenge on suspected abusive traffic
ITID-41211.detection: Strong technical signal from web/application access logs and backend performance monitoring correlated by URI.
ITID-41211.response: Apply endpoint-specific rate-limiting or WAF rules immediately; engage caching if not already in place; monitor backend resource recovery.
metrics: Peak requests-per-second on targeted endpoint
Backend resource utilization during event
Time to rate-limiting engagement
ITID-41211.notes: Differentiating axis for the HTTP Flood group is request method/target and evasion technique; this leaf is the GET/resource-intensive-endpoint variant.

playbook.name: GET Flood Targeting Resource-Intensive Endpoint
playbook.description: A high volume of legitimate-looking HTTP GET requests is directed at a specific resource-intensive endpoint (e.g., search, report generation) to exhaust application/backend capacity.

steps.title: Confirm application-layer flood concentrated on a specific endpoint
steps.desc: Analyze web/application server access logs and APM metrics to confirm an abnormal request-rate spike concentrated on a specific resource-intensive URI path.
steps.guidance: Compare requests-per-second by URI path against baseline; resource-intensive endpoints (search, reporting, export) are common targets since they consume disproportionate backend compute per request.
steps.outcome: Confirmed endpoint-specific GET flood with request rate and targeted URI documented.
steps.abort: If elevated traffic correlates with a legitimate marketing campaign or viral link, stand down and document as false positive.

steps.title: Apply per-endpoint rate limiting and WAF rule for the targeted URI
steps.desc: Deploy a WAF/API gateway rate-limiting rule scoped specifically to the targeted resource-intensive endpoint.
steps.guidance: Scope the rule narrowly to the affected path(s) to avoid impacting unrelated site functionality; set thresholds based on legitimate historical usage patterns for that endpoint.
steps.outcome: Request rate to the targeted endpoint reduced to sustainable levels; overall site availability restored.
steps.abort: If legitimate users report being blocked, relax the threshold or add an allowlist for known-good clients.
steps.tool: WAF / API gateway (Cloudflare, AWS WAF, Akamai)

steps.title: Optimize or cache the targeted resource-intensive endpoint
steps.desc: Work with the application team to add caching, pagination limits, or query optimization to the specific endpoint so it is less resource-intensive per request even under legitimate load.
steps.guidance: Consider adding a CDN/edge cache layer for cacheable responses, or backend query optimization/result caching for the specific report/search operation being targeted.
steps.outcome: Endpoint's per-request resource cost reduced, raising the bar for future flood attempts against it.
steps.tool: Application code review / CDN caching rules

steps.title: Gradually relax rate limits/challenges and confirm normal endpoint performance
steps.desc: Incrementally ease temporary rate limits and challenge requirements once attack traffic subsides, while retaining baseline protective rate limiting permanently.
steps.guidance: Monitor endpoint response time and error rate for at least 1-2 hours as limits are relaxed.
steps.outcome: Endpoint performance restored to normal with permanent baseline rate limiting retained.
steps.abort: If flood resumes, re-tighten limits before completing rollback.

steps.title: Document incident and add the endpoint to ongoing bot-traffic monitoring
steps.desc: Record the attack pattern and ensure the targeted endpoint has dedicated monitoring/alerting for future anomalous request-rate spikes.
steps.guidance: Include specific per-endpoint alert thresholds in the after-action report recommendations.
steps.outcome: After-action report with endpoint-specific monitoring improvement tracked.

steps.title: Analyze source behavior for bot indicators
steps.desc: Examine requesting client behavior (user-agent consistency, request timing regularity, cookie/session handling, JS challenge completion) to distinguish automated flood traffic from a legitimate traffic surge.
steps.guidance: Bot-driven floods typically show missing/generic user-agents, no referrer, perfectly regular request intervals, and no JavaScript execution or cookie persistence.
steps.outcome: Confirmed bot-driven traffic pattern with source IP/ASN and fingerprint characteristics documented.

steps.title: Deploy CAPTCHA or JS challenge on the affected endpoint
steps.desc: Enable a challenge-response mechanism (CAPTCHA or JavaScript proof-of-work) on the targeted endpoint to filter out non-browser automated traffic.
steps.guidance: Use a challenge that most bots cannot pass, while minimizing friction for legitimate users (e.g., invisible/behavioral CAPTCHA where supported).
steps.outcome: Bot traffic to the endpoint substantially reduced while legitimate users continue to access it with minor friction.

steps.title: Validate optimized endpoint performance under representative legitimate load
steps.desc: Load-test the optimized/cached endpoint under a representative legitimate traffic pattern to confirm the eradication-phase performance improvements hold up.
steps.guidance: Use production-representative query parameters and concurrency levels for the test.
steps.outcome: Confirmed the endpoint sustains normal legitimate load with the new optimizations in place.

ITID-41212.def: A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary sends a high rate of complete HTTP POST requests to a form, login, search, or other data-submission endpoint, forcing the backend to process, validate, and often persist each submission until compute, database, or storage capacity is exhausted.
ITID-41212.purpose: Captures an application-layer flood of HTTP POST requests deliberately aimed at a form or data-submission endpoint to exhaust backend processing capacity.
scopeIncludes: High-rate POST requests against form/submission endpoints that trigger backend processing or writes
Floods that complete the full HTTP request/response cycle at normal speed
scopeExcludes: GET-based floods against read-heavy resource-intensive endpoints (see GET Flood Targeting Resource-Intensive Endpoint)
Slow-drip POST body attacks (see Slow POST (R-U-Dead-Yet) Attack)
Credential-stuffing/password-spraying campaigns against login endpoints, which are account-takeover leaves rather than availability leaves (see ITID-122xx/ITID-122xx branch)
ITID-41212.severity: High when the targeted endpoint is confirmed to drive database writes or expensive validation logic; Medium if protected by rate-limiting with no backend impact observed.
ITID-41212.priority: P2 on detection; escalate to P1 on confirmed backend resource exhaustion, database write saturation, or service degradation.
ITID-41212.escalation: Escalate to application/web operations and WAF team immediately if backend write capacity or database connection pool saturation is confirmed.
indicators: Sharp rise in POST request rate concentrated on one or a small set of submission endpoints
Database write/connection pool saturation correlated with the request spike
Application logs showing high volumes of form submissions failing validation or timing out
vectors: Scripted HTTP clients or botnets submitting forms at high rate
Booter/stresser platforms offering targeted Layer-7 POST flood modules
rootCauses: Submission endpoints lacking rate-limiting or CAPTCHA/bot-detection controls
No queuing/backpressure between the web tier and backend database for write-heavy endpoints
Validation logic performing expensive operations before rejecting malformed submissions
mitreTechniques: T1499.003 Endpoint Denial of Service: Application Exhaustion Flood
controls: WAF/CDN rate-limiting scoped to submission endpoints
CAPTCHA/bot-detection challenge on high-frequency submitters
Queuing/backpressure between web tier and database for write-heavy operations
ITID-41212.detection: Strong technical signal from web/application access logs and database performance monitoring correlated by endpoint.
ITID-41212.response: Apply endpoint-specific rate-limiting or CAPTCHA challenges immediately; monitor backend write-capacity recovery.
metrics: Peak requests-per-second on targeted endpoint
Database write/connection pool utilization during event
Time to rate-limiting engagement
ITID-41212.notes: Differentiating axis for the HTTP Flood group is request method/target; this leaf is the POST/submission-endpoint variant. Where the intent is account takeover rather than availability impact, route to the credential-stuffing branch instead.

playbook.name: POST Flood Targeting Form/Submission Endpoint
playbook.description: A high volume of automated HTTP POST submissions is directed at a form or data-submission endpoint (e.g., login, contact form, checkout) to exhaust backend processing or database capacity.

steps.title: Confirm POST flood concentrated on a specific submission endpoint
steps.desc: Analyze application logs for an abnormal spike in POST requests to a specific form/submission endpoint, correlated with backend processing load (database writes, email/notification triggers).
steps.guidance: Compare POST rate by endpoint against baseline and correlate with backend resource metrics (DB connections, queue depth) to confirm downstream impact.
steps.outcome: Confirmed POST flood with targeted endpoint, request rate, and backend impact documented.
steps.abort: If the spike correlates with a legitimate promotional event driving form submissions, stand down and document as false positive.

steps.title: Enforce CSRF token/session validation and per-source rate limiting on the endpoint
steps.desc: Ensure the endpoint strictly validates a session-bound CSRF token obtained from a genuine prior page load, and apply per-source-IP rate limiting on submissions.
steps.guidance: If CSRF validation is not already strict, this alone can eliminate a large share of naive flood traffic; combine with rate limiting for defense in depth.
steps.outcome: Submission rate to the endpoint reduced to sustainable levels; backend load normalized.
steps.abort: If legitimate users are blocked due to session/token issues, review token expiry settings.

steps.title: Harden backend processing path against submission floods
steps.desc: Review and harden the backend handling of the endpoint (e.g., queue-based async processing, database write batching, duplicate-submission detection) so a residual flood cannot exhaust resources.
steps.guidance: Consider moving heavy downstream actions (email sends, notifications) to an asynchronous queue decoupled from the synchronous request path.
steps.outcome: Backend resource exhaustion risk from this endpoint substantially reduced even under residual load.

steps.title: Relax temporary controls and confirm normal submission processing
steps.desc: Incrementally ease temporary rate limits once attack traffic subsides, retaining CAPTCHA/CSRF hardening permanently.
steps.guidance: Monitor submission success rate and backend processing latency for at least 1-2 hours as limits are relaxed.
steps.outcome: Endpoint performance restored to normal with permanent hardening retained.

steps.title: Document incident and review other submission endpoints for similar exposure
steps.desc: Record the attack and audit other form/submission endpoints across the application for the same missing CSRF/rate-limiting/CAPTCHA controls.
steps.guidance: Include an inventory of all public submission endpoints and their current protection status in the after-action report.
steps.outcome: After-action report with a broader endpoint-hardening remediation list if gaps were found elsewhere.

steps.title: Analyze submitted data and source behavior for automation indicators
steps.desc: Examine a sample of submitted form data and request headers for automation signatures (identical/templated field values, missing expected cookies/CSRF tokens, non-browser user-agents).
steps.guidance: Automated floods often reuse identical or programmatically-generated field values and lack a valid session/CSRF token obtained from a prior page load.
steps.outcome: Confirmed automation pattern with source IP/ASN and submission characteristics documented.

steps.title: Deploy CAPTCHA on the submission endpoint
steps.desc: Enable a CAPTCHA or equivalent challenge on the form to filter automated submissions.
steps.guidance: Prefer an invisible/behavioral CAPTCHA to minimize legitimate user friction where the platform supports it.
steps.outcome: Automated submission volume substantially reduced while legitimate users continue to submit successfully.

steps.title: Confirm legitimate submission volume processes correctly end-to-end
steps.desc: Verify that legitimate submissions (including downstream effects like notifications/emails) process correctly end-to-end after the async/queue-based hardening changes.
steps.guidance: Submit a representative test form entry and confirm it flows through the full backend pipeline as expected.
steps.outcome: Confirmed end-to-end submission processing works correctly post-hardening.

ITID-41213.def: A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary appends randomized query strings, headers, or cache-busting parameters to each HTTP request so that CDN or edge caching layers treat every request as unique, forcing each one through to the origin server and defeating the very caching that would otherwise absorb a normal flood.
ITID-41213.purpose: Captures an HTTP flood engineered specifically to defeat CDN/edge caching by randomizing each request so every hit reaches the origin server.
scopeIncludes: Floods using randomized query parameters, cache-control header manipulation, or other techniques specifically intended to bypass CDN/cache layers
Attacks that would otherwise be absorbed by caching if not for the deliberate cache-busting technique
scopeExcludes: Floods against genuinely uncacheable, resource-intensive endpoints where no cache-busting technique is needed (see GET Flood Targeting Resource-Intensive Endpoint)
POST floods against submission endpoints (see POST Flood Targeting Form/Submission Endpoint)
ITID-41213.severity: High: this technique is specifically designed to defeat the organization's primary volumetric defense (CDN caching), so even moderate request volume can reach the origin at full force.
ITID-41213.priority: P1 given the deliberate defeat of caching defenses; escalate immediately on confirmation of cache-hit-ratio collapse.
ITID-41213.escalation: Escalate to CDN provider and application operations immediately once cache-hit ratio is observed collapsing under request volume.
indicators: Sharp, anomalous drop in CDN cache-hit ratio coinciding with a request-volume spike
High volume of requests with distinct, randomized query strings against the same base URI
Origin server load spiking despite CDN being in front of the application
vectors: Scripted HTTP clients or botnets appending random tokens/query parameters to each request
Booter/stresser platforms offering cache-busting as a Layer-7 attack option
rootCauses: CDN/cache configuration keying cache entries on full query string by default rather than normalizing/ignoring irrelevant parameters
No origin-side rate-limiting independent of CDN caching
mitreTechniques: T1499.003 Endpoint Denial of Service: Application Exhaustion Flood
controls: CDN cache-key normalization stripping irrelevant query parameters
Origin-side rate-limiting independent of CDN cache state
WAF rules detecting randomized-parameter request patterns
Bot detection/CAPTCHA challenge on suspected abusive traffic
ITID-41213.detection: Strong technical signal from CDN cache-hit-ratio metrics correlated with origin load; this is often the clearest single indicator in the HTTP Flood group.
ITID-41213.response: Normalize CDN cache keys and apply origin-side rate-limiting immediately; engage CDN provider's Layer-7 mitigation if available.
metrics: Cache-hit ratio during event vs. baseline
Peak origin-server load
Time to cache-key normalization/mitigation
ITID-41213.notes: Differentiating axis for the HTTP Flood group: this leaf's distinguishing feature is the evasion technique (cache-busting) rather than the target endpoint type.

playbook.name: Cache-Busting HTTP Flood (Randomized Query Strings Bypassing CDN Cache)
playbook.description: The attacker appends randomized query-string parameters to otherwise cacheable requests, forcing each request to bypass the CDN cache and hit the origin server directly, exhausting origin capacity.

steps.title: Confirm cache-bypass pattern via CDN cache-hit-ratio drop and origin load spike
steps.desc: Analyze CDN analytics for a sudden drop in cache-hit ratio for a normally highly-cacheable resource, correlated with a spike in origin-server request volume and randomized query strings.
steps.guidance: Check CDN logs for a surge of requests to the same base path with unique/random query parameters (e.g., ?x=<random>) that were never previously cached.
steps.outcome: Confirmed cache-busting flood pattern with affected resource path and origin load impact documented.
steps.abort: If randomized parameters are part of a legitimate new feature (e.g., cache-busting for a real content update), stand down and document as false positive.

steps.title: Configure CDN to normalize/strip cache-busting query parameters
steps.desc: Update CDN cache-key configuration to ignore known-irrelevant query parameters (or strip unrecognized parameters entirely) so requests resolve to the cached object regardless of the injected randomization.
steps.guidance: Most CDNs support cache-key normalization rules (e.g., 'ignore query string' or an explicit allowlist of parameters that affect cache key) — apply this to the affected path.
steps.outcome: Requests once again served from CDN cache, dramatically reducing origin load regardless of continued randomized parameters.
steps.abort: If the application legitimately relies on certain query parameters for varying content, allowlist those specific parameters only.

steps.title: Review and harden cache-key configuration across all cacheable resources
steps.desc: Audit the CDN configuration for other cacheable resources that may be similarly vulnerable to query-string-based cache-busting and apply normalization proactively.
