steps.guidance: This technique is broadly applicable to any cacheable endpoint without a hardened cache-key policy — a full CDN configuration review is warranted.
steps.outcome: Cache-key normalization applied consistently across all cacheable resources, closing the broader exposure class.

steps.title: Confirm cache-hit ratio and origin load return to normal baseline
steps.desc: Monitor CDN cache-hit ratio and origin request volume to confirm they return to and remain at normal baseline levels.
steps.guidance: Retain the cache-key normalization and origin rate-limiting backstop permanently rather than reverting.
steps.outcome: Confirmed sustained normal cache performance and origin load.

steps.title: Document incident and codify cache-key hardening as a CDN configuration standard
steps.desc: Record the attack and add cache-key normalization review to the standard checklist for onboarding any new cacheable endpoint or CDN configuration change.
steps.guidance: Update CDN configuration change-management templates/checklists accordingly.
steps.outcome: After-action report with a configuration standard added to prevent recurrence.

steps.title: Sample requests to characterize the query-string randomization technique
steps.desc: Capture a sample of the flood requests to understand the query-string randomization pattern and source behavior.
steps.guidance: Determine whether randomization uses a fixed parameter name with random values (easier to normalize/strip) or fully randomized parameter names (harder to normalize).
steps.outcome: Documented randomization pattern informing the normalization/caching rule to be deployed.

steps.title: Apply origin-side rate limiting as a backstop
steps.desc: Deploy rate limiting at the origin/WAF layer for the affected path as a defense-in-depth measure in case cache normalization is incomplete or delayed.
steps.guidance: Scope the rate limit to the specific affected path/pattern to avoid unrelated impact.
steps.outcome: Origin protected even if a residual volume of cache-bypassing requests continues to reach it.

steps.title: Validate legitimate content-varying requests still resolve correctly
steps.desc: Confirm that any legitimate use cases relying on query parameters for varying content still function correctly under the new cache-key normalization rules.
steps.guidance: Test each allowlisted parameter scenario explicitly.
steps.outcome: Confirmed no legitimate functionality was broken by the cache-key normalization.

ITID-41214.def: A denial-of-service event exhibiting clear HTTP flood characteristics (high-rate, complete application-layer requests overwhelming a web/application tier) where the specific request method, target endpoint category, or cache-evasion technique has not yet been determined.
ITID-41214.purpose: Intake bucket for HTTP flood activity that cannot yet be attributed to a specific request method, target, or evasion technique.
scopeIncludes: Initial triage of a suspected HTTP flood before method/target/technique analysis is complete
scopeExcludes: Any flood already confirmed as GET/resource-intensive-endpoint, POST/submission-endpoint, or cache-busting (reclassify to the specific leaf once confirmed)
ITID-41214.severity: Medium-High pending confirmation; reassess once specifics are identified.
ITID-41214.priority: P2 pending triage; adjust once reclassified.
ITID-41214.escalation: Escalate to web/application operations for log analysis; reclassify once confirmed.
indicators: Elevated HTTP request rate against the web/application tier without confirmed method/target classification at initial detection
vectors: Unconfirmed at time of intake
rootCauses: Insufficient initial log visibility to determine attack specifics
mitreTechniques: T1499.003 Endpoint Denial of Service: Application Exhaustion Flood
controls: WAF/CDN general rate-limiting
Bot detection/CAPTCHA challenge
ITID-41214.detection: Sufficient to detect the HTTP flood pattern but insufficient to classify specifics at time of intake.
ITID-41214.response: Apply general rate-limiting/bot-detection immediately; run log analysis in parallel to reclassify.
metrics: Count of incidents landing in this catch-all per quarter
ITID-41214.notes: Triage/intake bucket only; reclassify once specifics are confirmed.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General HTTP Flood
playbook.description: An application-layer HTTP flood is confirmed via elevated request rate and resource impact, but the specific technique (targeted GET/POST flood, cache-busting) has not yet been determined.

steps.title: Confirm HTTP flood via request-rate and backend resource impact analysis
steps.desc: Analyze web/application server access logs and APM metrics to confirm an abnormal HTTP request-rate spike correlated with backend resource impact (CPU, database, connection pool).
steps.guidance: Compare requests-per-second across all endpoints against baseline; identify whether the flood is concentrated on specific endpoint(s) or broadly distributed.
steps.outcome: Confirmed HTTP flood condition with impacted endpoints and backend resource impact documented.
steps.abort: If elevated traffic correlates with a legitimate event, stand down and document as false positive.

steps.title: Apply general rate limiting and bot-detection challenge across affected endpoints
steps.desc: Deploy WAF rate limiting and a bot-detection/challenge mechanism across the impacted endpoint(s) pending full technique classification.
steps.guidance: Use adaptive/behavioral bot-management rules where available rather than static thresholds, to handle an unclassified traffic pattern.
steps.outcome: Request rate reduced to sustainable levels and site availability restored.
steps.abort: If legitimate users report being blocked, relax the threshold or add an allowlist for known-good clients.

steps.title: Complete technique classification and apply targeted hardening
steps.desc: Finalize which HTTP flood technique was used and apply the more specific hardening measures from the corresponding playbook.
steps.guidance: Reclassify the incident to the specific ITID leaf if determination succeeds.
steps.outcome: Attack technique documented and technique-specific hardening applied.

steps.title: Relax temporary controls and confirm normal application performance
steps.desc: Incrementally ease temporary rate limits and challenges once attack traffic subsides, retaining baseline protective controls permanently.
steps.guidance: Monitor endpoint response time and error rate for at least 1-2 hours as limits are relaxed.
steps.outcome: Application performance restored to normal with permanent baseline protections retained.

steps.title: Document incident and improve HTTP flood classification tooling
steps.desc: Record why immediate technique classification was not possible and recommend detection tooling improvements.
steps.guidance: Include recommendations for enhanced request-pattern analytics that would have sped up classification.
steps.outcome: After-action report with concrete detection tooling improvement items.

steps.title: Attempt technique classification via method, targeting, and cache-behavior analysis
steps.desc: Determine whether the flood is GET-based, POST-based, or exploiting cache-bypass behavior, to allow pivot to a more specific playbook if possible.
steps.guidance: If classification succeeds, transition to the corresponding specific HTTP flood playbook; otherwise proceed with general mitigation.
steps.outcome: Either successful reclassification or confirmed genuinely mixed/unclear technique.

steps.title: Engage upstream/CDN DDoS mitigation for broader relief
steps.desc: If local WAF mitigation is insufficient, engage the CDN/cloud provider's application-layer DDoS mitigation service.
steps.guidance: Provide the traffic pattern characteristics gathered during identification to speed mitigation tuning.
steps.outcome: Attack traffic further reduced via provider-level mitigation.

steps.title: Confirm technique-specific hardening retained where classification succeeded
steps.desc: Where the attack was reclassified to a specific technique, confirm the corresponding technique-specific hardening measures remain in place post-recovery.
steps.guidance: Cross-check against the specific playbook's hardening recommendations if reclassification occurred.
steps.outcome: Confirmed appropriate hardening retained based on final classification.

ITID-41221.def: A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary repeatedly triggers TLS renegotiation (client-initiated handshake renegotiation within an established session) against a target, exploiting the significant asymmetry between the trivial client-side cost and the far higher server-side cryptographic cost of each renegotiation to exhaust CPU capacity.
ITID-41221.purpose: Captures a DoS attack that abuses the computational cost of TLS renegotiation to exhaust server CPU with minimal attacker bandwidth.
scopeIncludes: Repeated client-initiated TLS renegotiation requests within existing sessions aimed at exhausting server CPU
Tools specifically designed to automate rapid renegotiation cycles against a single connection or many connections
scopeExcludes: High-volume new-connection floods without renegotiation abuse (see SSL/TLS Connection Flood Exhausting Server Compute)
Non-TLS connection exhaustion techniques (see Slowloris Attack group)
ITID-41221.severity: High against servers with TLS renegotiation still enabled and unrestricted, given the extreme client-to-server cost asymmetry (potentially 10x or greater); Low-Medium where renegotiation is disabled or rate-limited.
ITID-41221.priority: P2 on detection; escalate to P1 on confirmed server CPU exhaustion attributable to renegotiation volume.
ITID-41221.escalation: Escalate to web/application operations immediately to disable or rate-limit client-initiated renegotiation if exhaustion is confirmed.
indicators: Server-side CPU spike disproportionate to connection/request volume
TLS/SSL library logs or metrics showing abnormally high renegotiation frequency per connection
A small number of source connections driving outsized CPU load
vectors: THC-SSL-DOS and similar tools automating rapid TLS renegotiation cycles
rootCauses: Client-initiated TLS renegotiation left enabled on the server/load balancer
TLS termination point not rate-limiting renegotiation attempts per connection
mitreTechniques: T1499.002 Endpoint Denial of Service: Service Exhaustion Flood
controls: Disable client-initiated TLS renegotiation at the termination point
Rate-limit renegotiation attempts per connection where renegotiation cannot be fully disabled
TLS termination offload with hardware acceleration or dedicated capacity
ITID-41221.detection: Strong technical signal from TLS/SSL library or load balancer metrics tracking renegotiation frequency, though this requires renegotiation-specific instrumentation beyond generic connection logs.
ITID-41221.response: Disable or rate-limit client-initiated renegotiation immediately; verify server CPU recovery.
metrics: Peak renegotiations-per-second observed
Server CPU utilization during event
Time to renegotiation-disable remediation
ITID-41221.notes: Differentiating axis for the SSL/TLS Exhaustion group: this leaf abuses renegotiation cost asymmetry rather than sheer new-connection volume.

playbook.name: TLS Handshake Renegotiation Exhaustion Attack
playbook.description: The attacker repeatedly triggers TLS renegotiation on established connections, forcing the server to perform computationally expensive cryptographic operations repeatedly and exhaust CPU capacity.

steps.title: Confirm TLS renegotiation exhaustion via handshake-rate and CPU correlation
steps.desc: Analyze TLS termination point (load balancer/reverse proxy) metrics for an abnormal rate of renegotiation handshakes correlated with a CPU utilization spike, disproportionate to the actual application request volume.
steps.guidance: Check load balancer/TLS termination logs for renegotiation event counts per connection; a small number of connections triggering many renegotiations is a strong indicator.
steps.outcome: Confirmed TLS renegotiation exhaustion pattern with source connections and CPU impact documented.
steps.tool: Load balancer TLS metrics / OpenSSL logs

steps.title: Disable or restrict client-initiated TLS renegotiation
steps.desc: Configure the TLS termination point to disable client-initiated renegotiation entirely, or severely rate-limit it per connection.
steps.guidance: Most modern TLS stacks (OpenSSL, nginx) support disabling client-initiated renegotiation (e.g., SSL_OP_NO_RENEGOTIATION) with negligible impact on legitimate traffic, which almost never requires it.
steps.outcome: Renegotiation-based CPU exhaustion eliminated; legitimate TLS connections unaffected.
steps.abort: If a specific legitimate client integration relies on renegotiation (rare, e.g., some mutual-TLS re-auth flows), scope an exception rather than a blanket disable.

steps.title: Audit all TLS termination points for renegotiation hardening
steps.desc: Review all TLS-terminating infrastructure (load balancers, reverse proxies, application servers with direct TLS) organization-wide to confirm client-initiated renegotiation is disabled consistently.
steps.guidance: A single unhardened TLS endpoint elsewhere could be targeted next; apply the fix as a fleet-wide configuration standard.
steps.outcome: Confirmed all TLS termination points have renegotiation hardening applied.

steps.title: Confirm CPU utilization returns to normal and legitimate TLS sessions function correctly
steps.desc: Monitor CPU utilization on the TLS termination tier and confirm legitimate client TLS sessions establish and persist normally under the hardened configuration.
steps.guidance: Test with representative client integrations, particularly any that use less common TLS features.
steps.outcome: Normal CPU utilization and confirmed unaffected legitimate TLS functionality.

steps.title: Document incident and codify renegotiation-disable as a standard TLS hardening baseline
steps.desc: Record the attack and ensure disabling client-initiated renegotiation is part of the standard TLS/load-balancer hardening baseline for all future deployments.
steps.guidance: Update infrastructure-as-code templates or configuration management baselines accordingly.
steps.outcome: After-action report with hardening settings codified into deployment standards.

steps.title: Sample connections to confirm renegotiation-triggering behavior and source
steps.desc: Capture or log-analyze a sample of the offending connections to confirm the client is deliberately and repeatedly initiating renegotiation.
steps.guidance: Legitimate clients essentially never trigger repeated renegotiation on a single connection at high frequency; this behavior alone is a strong attack indicator.
steps.outcome: Confirmed malicious renegotiation behavior with source IP list captured.

steps.title: Block or rate-limit source IPs generating the renegotiation flood
steps.desc: Apply firewall/WAF blocking or rate limiting against the specific source IPs identified as generating the renegotiation flood while the configuration change is validated.
steps.guidance: Use this as an immediate stopgap ahead of the more durable renegotiation-disable configuration change.
steps.outcome: Immediate reduction in CPU load from the offending sources.

steps.title: Remove temporary source IP blocks once configuration hardening is confirmed effective
steps.desc: Roll back the interim source-IP blocking/rate-limiting applied during containment once the renegotiation-disable configuration is confirmed as the durable fix.
steps.guidance: Verify sustained normal CPU levels for at least 1-2 hours before removing the interim blocks.
steps.outcome: Interim blocks removed with no CPU impact recurrence.
steps.abort: If CPU impact recurs, restore the interim blocks and investigate further.

ITID-41222.def: A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary opens a high volume of new SSL/TLS connections, forcing the server to perform a full cryptographic handshake (key exchange, certificate processing) for each, exhausting CPU capacity given the relatively high cost of handshake operations compared to plaintext connection setup.
ITID-41222.purpose: Captures a DoS attack that floods a target with new SSL/TLS connection handshakes to exhaust the server's cryptographic compute capacity.
scopeIncludes: High-rate new TLS connection floods aimed at exhausting handshake-processing CPU capacity
Attacks exploiting the asymmetric cost of TLS handshake (server-side) versus connection initiation (client-side)
scopeExcludes: Renegotiation-abuse attacks within existing sessions (see TLS Handshake Renegotiation Exhaustion Attack)
Plaintext TCP SYN floods with no TLS involvement (see SYN Flooding group)
ITID-41222.severity: High when the volume is sufficient to exhaust TLS termination capacity; Medium if absorbed by dedicated TLS offload/acceleration hardware with headroom.
ITID-41222.priority: P2 on detection; escalate to P1 on confirmed TLS termination CPU exhaustion or new-connection refusal.
ITID-41222.escalation: Escalate to network/web operations and upstream scrubbing provider if TLS termination capacity is confirmed exhausted.
indicators: Sharp rise in new TLS handshake attempts per second
TLS termination point CPU utilization spiking disproportionately to plaintext traffic volume
High rate of incomplete or abandoned handshakes following the initial ClientHello
vectors: Scripted TLS clients or botnets opening high volumes of new connections without completing application-layer requests
Booter/stresser platforms offering TLS handshake flood modules
rootCauses: TLS termination point sized without headroom for handshake-flood scenarios
No rate-limiting on new TLS connection attempts per source
Hardware TLS acceleration not deployed at the termination point
mitreTechniques: T1499.002 Endpoint Denial of Service: Service Exhaustion Flood
controls: Hardware-accelerated TLS termination with adequate headroom
Per-source rate-limiting on new TLS connection attempts
Upstream DDoS scrubbing service with TLS-aware mitigation
TLS session resumption tuning to reduce full-handshake load from legitimate repeat clients
ITID-41222.detection: Strong technical signal from TLS termination point metrics tracking handshake rate and CPU utilization.
ITID-41222.response: Engage upstream scrubbing or rate-limiting immediately; verify TLS termination CPU recovery.
metrics: Peak new-TLS-handshakes-per-second observed
TLS termination CPU utilization during event
Time to mitigation engagement
ITID-41222.notes: Differentiating axis for the SSL/TLS Exhaustion group: this leaf is driven by new-connection volume rather than renegotiation abuse.

playbook.name: SSL/TLS Connection Flood Exhausting Server Compute
playbook.description: The attacker opens a high volume of new TLS connections without renegotiation abuse, relying on the inherent CPU cost of the TLS handshake (key exchange, certificate processing) itself to exhaust server compute capacity.

steps.title: Confirm TLS handshake flood via new-connection-rate and CPU correlation
steps.desc: Analyze TLS termination point metrics for an abnormal rate of new TLS handshake initiations correlated with a CPU utilization spike on the cryptographic processing tier.
steps.guidance: Compare new TLS connections-per-second against baseline; note whether connections are dropped/reset immediately after handshake completion (consistent with a pure compute-exhaustion goal rather than genuine application use).
steps.outcome: Confirmed TLS handshake flood pattern with connection rate and CPU impact documented.
steps.abort: If the connection surge correlates with a legitimate traffic event, stand down and document as false positive.

steps.title: Enable TLS session resumption and offload to hardware/optimized crypto where available
steps.desc: Ensure TLS session resumption (session tickets/IDs) is enabled to reduce full-handshake cost for repeat legitimate clients, and confirm crypto operations are offloaded to hardware acceleration or an optimized TLS library where available.
steps.guidance: This raises the server's effective handshake-processing capacity, buying headroom while other mitigations engage.
steps.outcome: Increased effective handshake capacity, reducing CPU impact per new connection.

steps.title: Scale or right-size TLS termination capacity and review cipher suite efficiency
steps.desc: Assess whether TLS termination capacity should be scaled (horizontally or via dedicated crypto acceleration) and review configured cipher suites/key exchange parameters for computational efficiency without weakening security.
steps.guidance: Prefer modern, computationally efficient cipher suites (e.g., ECDHE with AES-GCM) and appropriately sized key parameters; avoid unnecessarily expensive legacy options still enabled for compatibility.
steps.outcome: TLS termination tier's effective capacity and efficiency improved to better withstand future handshake floods.

steps.title: Confirm CPU utilization and handshake success rate return to normal
steps.desc: Monitor CPU utilization and TLS handshake success/failure rate to confirm they return to and remain at normal baseline levels.
steps.guidance: Retain session resumption and rate-limiting configuration permanently rather than reverting.
steps.outcome: Confirmed sustained normal CPU utilization and handshake performance.

steps.title: Document incident and evaluate TLS termination capacity planning
steps.desc: Record the attack and assess whether TLS termination capacity planning/auto-scaling needs adjustment to better absorb future handshake floods.
steps.guidance: Include capacity headroom recommendations in the after-action report.
steps.outcome: After-action report with capacity planning recommendations tracked.

steps.title: Analyze source distribution and connection lifecycle for attack characteristics
steps.desc: Determine whether connections are largely single-source or distributed, and whether they proceed to any application-layer request or are abandoned immediately post-handshake.
steps.guidance: Connections abandoned immediately after the TLS handshake, with no subsequent application data, strongly indicate a pure resource-exhaustion attack rather than legitimate client behavior.
steps.outcome: Confirmed attack characteristics with source IP/ASN distribution documented.

steps.title: Apply per-source connection-rate limiting and engage upstream DDoS/TLS scrubbing
steps.desc: Limit new-connection rate per source IP at the network/load-balancer layer, and engage upstream/cloud DDoS mitigation with TLS-flood-specific protection if volume exceeds local capacity.
steps.guidance: Cloud DDoS providers increasingly offer TLS-flood-specific mitigation that terminates and filters handshakes before they reach the origin.
steps.outcome: Reduced new-connection rate reaching the origin's TLS termination tier.
steps.tool: Load balancer / upstream DDoS mitigation portal

steps.title: Validate updated cipher suite configuration has no client compatibility regressions
steps.desc: Confirm that any cipher suite or key-exchange parameter changes made during eradication have not broken compatibility with legitimate client populations still using older TLS implementations.
steps.guidance: Check TLS handshake failure rates by client type/version post-change.
steps.outcome: Confirmed no material client compatibility regression from the cipher suite changes.
steps.abort: If compatibility issues are found, adjust the cipher suite policy to a less restrictive but still efficient set.

ITID-41223.def: A denial-of-service event exhibiting clear TLS-layer exhaustion characteristics (disproportionate server-side cryptographic CPU load) where the specific mechanism (renegotiation abuse or handshake flood) has not yet been determined.
ITID-41223.purpose: Intake bucket for SSL/TLS exhaustion DoS activity that cannot yet be attributed to renegotiation abuse or new-connection flooding.
scopeIncludes: Initial triage of a suspected TLS exhaustion attack before mechanism analysis is complete
scopeExcludes: Any attack already confirmed as renegotiation abuse or connection flood (reclassify to the specific leaf once confirmed)
ITID-41223.severity: Medium-High pending confirmation; reassess once mechanism is identified.
ITID-41223.priority: P2 pending triage; adjust once reclassified.
ITID-41223.escalation: Escalate to web/application operations for TLS termination log analysis; reclassify once confirmed.
indicators: TLS termination CPU spike without confirmed mechanism at initial detection
vectors: Unconfirmed at time of intake
rootCauses: Insufficient initial TLS-layer instrumentation to determine mechanism
mitreTechniques: T1499.002 Endpoint Denial of Service: Service Exhaustion Flood
controls: Hardware-accelerated TLS termination
Per-source rate-limiting on TLS connections/renegotiation
ITID-41223.detection: Sufficient to detect the TLS exhaustion pattern but insufficient to classify mechanism at time of intake.
ITID-41223.response: Apply general TLS rate-limiting immediately; run termination-log analysis in parallel to reclassify.
metrics: Count of incidents landing in this catch-all per quarter
ITID-41223.notes: Triage/intake bucket only; reclassify once the mechanism is confirmed.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General SSL/TLS Exhaustion Attack
playbook.description: A TLS-layer resource-exhaustion attack is confirmed via CPU/compute impact on the TLS termination tier, but the specific technique (renegotiation abuse vs. raw handshake flood) has not yet been determined.

steps.title: Confirm TLS-layer resource exhaustion via CPU and handshake/renegotiation metrics
steps.desc: Analyze TLS termination point metrics for CPU exhaustion correlated with abnormal handshake or renegotiation activity.
steps.guidance: Check both new-handshake rate and renegotiation-event rate to determine which (or both) is elevated.
steps.outcome: Confirmed TLS-layer exhaustion condition with contributing factor(s) documented.

steps.title: Disable client-initiated renegotiation and apply connection-rate limiting
steps.desc: Apply both mitigations simultaneously as general-purpose defenses regardless of the precise technique: disable client-initiated renegotiation and rate-limit new connections per source.
steps.guidance: Both measures are low-risk to apply concurrently and cover both known sub-techniques.
steps.outcome: CPU exhaustion on the TLS termination tier resolved or substantially reduced.

steps.title: Complete technique classification and apply targeted hardening
steps.desc: Finalize which TLS exhaustion technique was used and apply the more specific hardening measures from the corresponding playbook.
steps.guidance: Reclassify the incident to the specific ITID leaf if determination succeeds.
steps.outcome: Attack technique documented and technique-specific hardening applied.

steps.title: Confirm CPU utilization and TLS session establishment return to normal
steps.desc: Monitor CPU utilization and TLS session success rate to confirm they return to and remain at normal baseline levels.
steps.guidance: Retain applied hardening measures permanently rather than reverting.
steps.outcome: Confirmed sustained normal CPU utilization and TLS performance.

steps.title: Document incident and improve TLS exhaustion classification tooling
steps.desc: Record why immediate technique classification was not possible and recommend detection tooling improvements.
steps.guidance: Include recommendations for enhanced TLS-layer telemetry that would have sped up classification.
steps.outcome: After-action report with concrete detection tooling improvement items.

steps.title: Attempt technique classification via renegotiation vs. new-handshake analysis
steps.desc: Determine whether the exhaustion is driven primarily by renegotiation abuse on existing connections or by a flood of new handshakes, to allow pivot to a more specific playbook if possible.
steps.guidance: If classification succeeds, transition to the corresponding specific SSL/TLS exhaustion playbook; otherwise proceed with general mitigation.
steps.outcome: Either successful reclassification or confirmed genuinely mixed/unclear technique.

steps.title: Engage upstream DDoS/TLS scrubbing if local mitigation is insufficient
steps.desc: Engage upstream/cloud DDoS mitigation with TLS-flood-specific protection if local mitigation does not resolve the exhaustion.
steps.guidance: Provide the traffic characteristics gathered during identification to speed mitigation tuning.
steps.outcome: Attack traffic further reduced via provider-level mitigation.

steps.title: Confirm technique-specific hardening retained where classification succeeded
steps.desc: Where the attack was reclassified to a specific TLS exhaustion technique, confirm the corresponding technique-specific hardening measures remain in place post-recovery.
steps.guidance: Cross-check against the specific playbook's hardening recommendations if reclassification occurred.
steps.outcome: Confirmed appropriate hardening retained based on final classification.

ITID-41231.def: A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary, holding valid session tokens, API keys, or credentials (legitimately issued, stolen, or self-registered), sends a high rate of authenticated API requests to exhaust backend compute, database, or third-party integration capacity, bypassing controls that assume authenticated traffic is inherently trustworthy.
ITID-41231.purpose: Captures a DoS attack in which an adversary uses valid or stolen authentication credentials/tokens to flood an authenticated API with legitimate-looking calls that exhaust backend resources.
scopeIncludes: High-rate authenticated API calls using valid tokens/keys/sessions intended to exhaust backend resources rather than achieve unauthorized data access
Abuse of self-service API key issuance to generate many keys for distributed authenticated flooding
scopeExcludes: Unauthenticated/anonymous API floods (see Unclassified / General API Request Flooding if no authentication is involved)
Floods targeting algorithmically expensive query logic specifically (see Expensive/Complex Query Endpoint Repeatedly Called)
Credential theft/account takeover as an end in itself, documented under the relevant account-compromise ITID branch
ITID-41231.severity: High: authenticated floods often bypass anonymous-traffic rate-limiting and WAF heuristics, making them disproportionately effective at exhausting backend capacity.
ITID-41231.priority: P2 on detection; escalate to P1 on confirmed backend resource exhaustion or breach of third-party integration rate limits (e.g. payment gateway, SMS provider).
ITID-41231.escalation: Escalate to application operations and identity/API management team immediately to revoke or throttle the abusing tokens/keys.
indicators: Sharp rise in authenticated API call volume from one or a small set of accounts/API keys
Backend resource saturation correlated with a specific token/key rather than broad source diversity
Third-party integration rate-limit errors triggered by internal call volume
vectors: Compromised or self-registered accounts used to generate high-volume authenticated traffic
Automated scripts abusing legitimately issued API keys beyond intended usage patterns
rootCauses: No per-account/per-key rate-limiting independent of IP-based controls
Authenticated traffic implicitly trusted and excluded from WAF/bot-detection scrutiny
API key issuance process lacking abuse monitoring
mitreTechniques: T1499.003 Endpoint Denial of Service: Application Exhaustion Flood
controls: Per-account/per-API-key rate-limiting and quota enforcement
Anomaly detection on authenticated traffic volume, not just anonymous traffic
API key/token revocation and rotation workflow
ITID-41231.detection: Strong technical signal from API gateway logs correlating request volume with authenticated identity (account/key), which is often a cleaner signal than IP-based detection.
ITID-41231.response: Throttle or revoke the abusing tokens/keys immediately; review API key issuance controls; monitor backend resource recovery.
metrics: Peak authenticated requests-per-second from a single identity
Backend resource utilization during event
Time to token/key revocation
ITID-41231.notes: Differentiating axis for the API Request Flooding group is actor/authentication state and query cost; this leaf is the authenticated-identity variant.

playbook.name: Authenticated API Endpoint Flooded to Exhaust Backend Resources
playbook.description: An attacker uses valid or stolen credentials/API keys to send a high volume of requests to an authenticated API endpoint, exhausting backend compute, database, or rate-quota resources.

steps.title: Confirm authenticated API flood via per-account/key request-rate anomaly
steps.desc: Analyze API gateway logs for an abnormal request-rate spike attributable to one or a small number of authenticated accounts/API keys, correlated with backend resource impact.
steps.guidance: Compare requests-per-minute per API key/account against that account's historical baseline and against typical usage across the customer base.
steps.outcome: Confirmed authenticated API flood with offending account(s)/key(s) and backend impact documented.
steps.abort: If the spike correlates with a known legitimate customer batch-processing job, stand down and document as false positive.

steps.title: Revoke or throttle the offending API key/account and enforce per-key rate quotas
steps.desc: Immediately revoke or aggressively throttle the identified API key/account, and ensure per-key rate quotas are enforced at the API gateway going forward.
steps.guidance: If credential compromise is suspected, revoke and force reissuance/rotation rather than simply throttling.
steps.outcome: Flood traffic from the offending key/account eliminated or reduced to sustainable levels.
steps.abort: If revocation impacts a legitimate customer, coordinate with account owner before finalizing.

steps.title: If credential compromise confirmed, rotate keys and investigate compromise vector
steps.desc: For confirmed compromised credentials, force rotation of the affected API key/credentials and investigate how they were obtained (phishing, credential stuffing, code leak).
steps.guidance: Coordinate with the account owner and, if applicable, the broader IAM/identity team to assess whether other credentials from the same source may also be compromised.
steps.outcome: Compromised credentials rotated and compromise vector identified for broader remediation.

steps.title: Restore legitimate account access and confirm normal backend performance
steps.desc: Once remediated, restore legitimate account/API access with new credentials and confirm backend resource utilization returns to normal.
steps.guidance: Communicate with the affected legitimate customer/account owner regarding the incident and new credential issuance.
steps.outcome: Legitimate access restored and backend performance confirmed normal.

steps.title: Document incident and review API rate-quota policy across all endpoints
steps.desc: Record the incident and assess whether per-key/per-account rate quotas are consistently enforced across all authenticated API endpoints.
steps.guidance: Include a review of gateway-wide quota policy consistency in the after-action report.
steps.outcome: After-action report with a broader API quota-hardening remediation list if gaps were found.

steps.title: Determine whether credentials/API key are compromised or the flood is legitimate-account abuse
steps.desc: Investigate the account/key's authentication history, source IP consistency, and any indicators of credential compromise (impossible travel, new device/IP, prior breach exposure).
steps.guidance: Distinguish between a compromised legitimate account being used maliciously versus a legitimate customer's own account misbehaving (e.g., a runaway integration bug) — the remediation differs.
steps.outcome: Determined root cause (compromised credential vs. legitimate-account malfunction) informing the containment approach.

steps.title: Apply backend-side circuit breakers/quotas as defense in depth
steps.desc: Ensure backend services enforce their own resource quotas/circuit breakers independent of the API gateway, so a single account cannot exhaust shared backend capacity even if gateway controls are bypassed.
steps.guidance: Review whether the affected backend service (database, compute cluster) has per-tenant resource isolation or quota enforcement.
steps.outcome: Backend resource exhaustion risk reduced through defense-in-depth controls.

steps.title: Confirm backend circuit breakers/quotas remain enforced post-incident
steps.desc: Verify the backend-side circuit breakers/quotas applied during containment remain in place as a permanent defense-in-depth control.
steps.guidance: Check backend service configuration to confirm settings were not inadvertently reverted.
steps.outcome: Confirmed permanent backend quota enforcement remains active.

ITID-41232.def: A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary identifies and repeatedly calls an API or query endpoint whose underlying implementation has poor algorithmic complexity (e.g. unbounded joins, recursive lookups, unindexed searches, regular-expression denial-of-service patterns) so that a modest request rate produces a disproportionately large backend compute cost, exhausting resources far faster than a naive request-volume flood would.
ITID-41232.purpose: Captures a DoS attack that repeatedly invokes an API endpoint with a known algorithmic-complexity weakness, so a small number of requests causes disproportionate backend compute cost.
scopeIncludes: Requests deliberately crafted to trigger worst-case algorithmic behavior in a specific endpoint (e.g. crafted GraphQL queries, deeply nested filters, catastrophic-backtracking regex inputs)
Low-volume but high-cost-per-request attacks exploiting a known or discovered implementation weakness
scopeExcludes: High-volume floods against endpoints that are simply expensive by design without a specific exploited weakness (see GET Flood Targeting Resource-Intensive Endpoint or Authenticated API Endpoint Flooded)
Exploitation of a vulnerability for purposes other than denial of service, such as remote code execution, which belongs under the relevant exploitation ITID branch
ITID-41232.severity: High: the defining characteristic of this leaf is that request volume is a poor predictor of impact, so traditional volumetric detection and rate-limiting can miss it entirely until backend exhaustion is already underway.
ITID-41232.priority: P1 given the difficulty of detecting and mitigating via conventional rate-based controls.
ITID-41232.escalation: Escalate to application development/engineering immediately, since remediation typically requires a code or query-plan fix rather than a network-layer control.
indicators: Backend CPU/database load spiking disproportionately to request volume or bandwidth
Slow query logs showing repeated execution of a specific costly query pattern or endpoint
A small number of requests correlating with prolonged backend processing time
vectors: Manually or automatically crafted requests targeting a discovered algorithmic-complexity weakness (e.g. GraphQL query depth/complexity abuse, ReDoS payloads, unbounded pagination requests)
rootCauses: Missing query cost limits, depth limits, or complexity analysis on flexible query interfaces (e.g. GraphQL)
Unindexed database queries or unbounded joins triggerable by user input
Regular expressions vulnerable to catastrophic backtracking on attacker-controlled input
mitreTechniques: T1499.004 Endpoint Denial of Service: Application or System Exploitation
controls: Query cost/depth/complexity limits on flexible query interfaces
Database query timeout and resource-governor limits
Static/dynamic analysis for ReDoS-prone regular expressions
Slow query monitoring and alerting
ITID-41232.detection: Weak-to-moderate via volumetric monitoring alone; strong when paired with slow-query logging and per-endpoint cost profiling.
ITID-41232.response: Apply an emergency rate-limit or block on the specific offending request pattern while engineering ships a durable fix (query limits, indexing, regex remediation).
metrics: Backend resource cost per request during event vs. baseline
Time to identify the specific offending query/pattern
Time to durable code/query fix
ITID-41232.notes: Differentiating axis for the API Request Flooding group: this leaf's defining characteristic is exploited algorithmic complexity rather than sheer request volume, which is why it maps to the exploitation sub-technique rather than a pure flood technique.

playbook.name: Expensive/Complex Query Endpoint Repeatedly Called to Exhaust Compute (Algorithmic Complexity Attack)
playbook.description: The attacker repeatedly calls an API/GraphQL endpoint whose underlying query or computation has poor algorithmic complexity (e.g., unbounded joins, nested GraphQL queries, unindexed search), exhausting compute with relatively low request volume.

steps.title: Confirm disproportionate resource cost per request on a specific endpoint
steps.desc: Analyze APM/backend metrics to confirm a relatively modest request volume to a specific endpoint is causing disproportionately high CPU/database load, indicating an algorithmic-complexity issue rather than sheer volume.
steps.guidance: Compare requests-per-second (which may be low/moderate) against backend resource consumption (which is abnormally high) for the specific endpoint — this ratio is the key identification signal distinct from a typical volumetric flood.
steps.outcome: Confirmed algorithmic-complexity attack pattern with the specific endpoint and disproportionate cost-per-request documented.
steps.abort: If the cost is explained by a legitimate but rare complex query from a known internal user, stand down and document as false positive.

steps.title: Block or rate-limit the specific expensive request pattern
steps.desc: Deploy a WAF/API gateway rule blocking or aggressively rate-limiting the specific identified request pattern (e.g., specific GraphQL query shape, parameter combination) rather than the endpoint broadly.
steps.guidance: Where the API gateway/WAF supports request-body inspection, target the specific offending pattern to avoid blocking legitimate, cheaper uses of the same endpoint.
steps.outcome: Expensive request pattern blocked or throttled while legitimate lower-cost use of the endpoint continues.
steps.abort: If the pattern cannot be distinguished from legitimate use, apply a broader endpoint-level rate limit as an interim measure.

steps.title: Fix the underlying algorithmic complexity issue in the endpoint's implementation
steps.desc: Work with the application/database team to fix the root-cause complexity issue — add missing indexes, bound unbounded joins, cap result set sizes, or optimize the specific query logic identified.
steps.guidance: This is the durable fix; the containment-layer blocking/rate-limiting is a stopgap until the underlying inefficiency is resolved.
steps.outcome: Endpoint's worst-case computational cost brought within acceptable bounds regardless of input parameters.

steps.title: Remove temporary blocking and confirm endpoint performs within bounded cost
steps.desc: Once the code fix is deployed and validated, relax temporary pattern-specific blocking while retaining query cost limits permanently.
steps.guidance: Load-test the fixed endpoint with the previously identified expensive pattern to confirm it no longer causes disproportionate resource consumption.
steps.outcome: Endpoint confirmed resilient to the previously exploited pattern with normal performance restored for legitimate use.

steps.title: Document incident and audit other flexible-query endpoints for similar complexity risk
steps.desc: Record the attack and review other GraphQL/search/reporting endpoints across the application for similar unbounded-complexity risk.
steps.guidance: Include recommendations for organization-wide query complexity limiting standards in the after-action report.
steps.outcome: After-action report with a broader algorithmic-complexity remediation list if gaps were found elsewhere.

steps.title: Identify and reproduce the specific expensive query/computation pattern
steps.desc: Capture the exact request parameters (e.g., GraphQL query depth/breadth, search terms, filter combinations) driving the expensive computation, and reproduce the cost in a non-production environment if feasible.
steps.guidance: For GraphQL, check for deeply nested or highly duplicated field selections; for search/filter endpoints, check for parameter combinations forcing full table scans or Cartesian joins.
steps.outcome: Documented specific request pattern responsible for the disproportionate cost, ready for both immediate blocking and permanent code fix.

steps.title: Apply query cost limits/complexity analysis at the API layer
steps.desc: If the endpoint is GraphQL or similarly flexible, deploy a query cost-estimation/complexity-limiting layer that rejects excessively expensive queries before execution.
steps.guidance: For GraphQL specifically, implement query depth limiting, complexity scoring, and/or persisted-query allowlisting.
steps.outcome: Future excessively expensive queries rejected at the API layer before reaching backend compute/database resources.

steps.title: Confirm legitimate complex-but-valid queries still succeed under new cost limits
steps.desc: Verify that legitimate, moderately complex queries that customers rely on still complete successfully under the newly deployed query cost limits.
steps.guidance: Test with representative legitimate queries at the upper end of normal complexity.
steps.outcome: Confirmed no legitimate use case was broken by the new complexity limits.
steps.abort: If legitimate queries are blocked, adjust the cost threshold accordingly.

ITID-41233.def: A denial-of-service attack in which a botnet of many distinct, geographically distributed hosts sends a high rate of API requests to a target, using sheer source diversity to defeat IP-based rate-limiting and exhaust backend capacity.
ITID-41233.purpose: Captures a DoS attack in which a botnet of distributed hosts floods an API with high-volume requests, primarily unauthenticated or using disposable credentials.
scopeIncludes: API floods originating from many distinct, botnet-controlled source IPs
Distributed campaigns coordinated via botnet C2 issuing API-flood attack commands
scopeExcludes: Single-identity authenticated abuse (see Authenticated API Endpoint Flooded)
Algorithmic-complexity exploitation from a small number of sources (see Expensive/Complex Query Endpoint Repeatedly Called)
The underlying botnet recruitment/infrastructure mechanism, documented under ITID-317xx Botnets
ITID-41233.severity: High given the difficulty of source-based filtering against genuinely distributed real IPs; escalate if geographic/ASN diversity of sources is confirmed.
ITID-41233.priority: P1 on confirmation of distributed botnet sourcing, given limited effectiveness of simple IP blocking.
ITID-41233.escalation: Escalate to application operations and DDoS mitigation provider immediately; correlate sources against known botnet threat intel.
indicators: High volume of API requests from thousands of distinct, geographically diverse source IPs
Source IPs correlating with known botnet C2 infrastructure in threat intel
Backend resource exhaustion despite per-source-IP rate-limiting attempts
vectors: IoT or general-purpose botnets issuing API-flood attack commands from infected members
DDoS-for-hire platforms renting access to existing botnets for Layer-7 API targeting
rootCauses: Reliance on per-source-IP rate-limiting alone, ineffective against high source diversity
No behavioral/anomaly-based bot detection layer in front of the API
mitreTechniques: T1499.003 Endpoint Denial of Service: Application Exhaustion Flood
controls: Behavioral/anomaly-based bot detection and mitigation service
API gateway global rate-limiting independent of per-source IP
Threat intelligence feeds for known botnet source ranges
ITID-41233.detection: Strong when API gateway logs capture source IP diversity and can be correlated with threat intel; weaker with only per-IP thresholds.
ITID-41233.response: Engage behavioral bot mitigation rather than manual IP blocking; correlate sources against botnet threat intel to inform longer-term blocklisting.
metrics: Distinct source IP count observed
Peak API requests-per-second
Time to behavioral mitigation engagement
detections: Source IP diversity/entropy alerting on API traffic
ITID-41233.notes: This leaf documents the network/application-layer DoS impact of botnet-driven API flooding; the botnet recruitment and C2 mechanism itself is scoped to ITID-317xx. Cross-reference rather than duplicate.

playbook.name: Distributed Botnet-Driven API Request Flood
playbook.description: A large botnet of genuinely distinct sources sends high-volume requests to one or more API endpoints, exhausting backend capacity without relying on any single compromised credential.

steps.title: Confirm distributed API flood via request-rate and source-diversity analysis
steps.desc: Analyze API gateway logs for an abnormal request-rate spike spread across a large number of genuinely distinct source IPs, rather than concentrated on a single account/key.
steps.guidance: Compare requests-per-second against baseline and examine source IP/ASN diversity; a botnet-driven flood typically shows thousands of distinct low-volume-per-source clients rather than a few high-volume ones.
steps.outcome: Confirmed distributed botnet API flood with source distribution and affected endpoint(s) documented.
steps.abort: If the spike correlates with a legitimate viral event or partner integration surge, stand down and document as false positive.

steps.title: Deploy behavioral bot-management and per-source rate limiting at the API gateway
steps.desc: Enable bot-management rules (behavioral scoring, JA3/TLS fingerprint blocking) and per-source-IP rate limiting at the API gateway/WAF.
steps.guidance: Since sources are genuinely distinct, per-IP rate limiting combined with fingerprint-based bot detection is effective, unlike spoofed network-layer floods.
steps.outcome: Reduced effective attack volume while legitimate clients remain largely unaffected.

steps.title: Report botnet nodes and coordinate takedown/abuse notification
steps.desc: Submit abuse reports to hosting providers/ISPs for identified botnet nodes and consider engagement with law enforcement or industry ISAC for large-scale campaigns.
steps.guidance: Include timestamps, source IPs, and attack signature in abuse reports.
steps.outcome: Abuse reports filed; where applicable, coordinated takedown initiated.

steps.title: Relax rate-limiting thresholds and monitor for resurgence
steps.desc: Gradually relax temporary rate-limiting thresholds once attack volume subsides while maintaining heightened monitoring and the botnet blocklist for an extended period.
steps.guidance: Botnets frequently resume attacks after brief pauses; retain fingerprint-based detection permanently.
steps.outcome: API performance restored to normal with continued blocklist protection against known attacker nodes.

steps.title: Document botnet characteristics and update long-term bot-management strategy
steps.desc: Record botnet family, source characteristics, and effectiveness of behavioral bot-management for future reference.
steps.guidance: Recommend subscribing to relevant botnet-tracking threat feeds if this attack revealed a gap in current intel coverage.
steps.outcome: After-action report with threat intel and bot-management strategy improvements.

steps.title: Profile botnet behavior and identify family/C2 if possible
steps.desc: Analyze request headers, timing patterns, and any accompanying TLS/JA3 fingerprints to characterize the botnet driving the flood.
steps.guidance: Check for known IoT/Mirai-family fingerprints, hosting-provider-concentrated ASNs (rented infrastructure), or residential-proxy characteristics.
steps.outcome: Botnet family/characteristics identified or documented, informing blocklist and reporting strategy.

steps.title: Push confirmed botnet source list to upstream scrubbing/CDN blocklists
steps.desc: Provide the confirmed botnet source IP list and fingerprint signatures to the upstream CDN/DDoS scrubbing provider for immediate filtering.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with the provider to apply reputation-based or explicit-list blocking for the identified botnet nodes.
steps.outcome: Confirmed botnet nodes blocked upstream, reducing attack traffic reaching the API gateway.

steps.title: Review API capacity and auto-scaling posture against large distributed floods
steps.desc: Assess whether the affected API's capacity/auto-scaling configuration is adequate to absorb a similarly-sized distributed flood in the future while mitigation engages.
steps.guidance: Include capacity headroom recommendations in the after-action report.
steps.outcome: Capacity planning recommendations tracked as follow-up items.

ITID-41234.def: A denial-of-service event exhibiting clear API request flooding characteristics (backend exhaustion driven by excessive API call volume) where the specific actor type (authenticated identity, algorithmic-complexity exploitation, or distributed botnet) has not yet been determined.
ITID-41234.purpose: Intake bucket for API request flooding activity that cannot yet be attributed to a specific actor type or exploitation mechanism.
scopeIncludes: Initial triage of a suspected API flood before actor/mechanism analysis is complete
scopeExcludes: Any flood already confirmed as authenticated-identity abuse, algorithmic-complexity exploitation, or botnet-driven (reclassify to the specific leaf once confirmed)
ITID-41234.severity: Medium-High pending confirmation; reassess once mechanism is identified.
ITID-41234.priority: P2 pending triage; adjust once reclassified.
ITID-41234.escalation: Escalate to application operations for API gateway log analysis; reclassify once confirmed.
indicators: Elevated API request rate and backend resource utilization without confirmed actor classification at initial detection
vectors: Unconfirmed at time of intake
rootCauses: Insufficient initial API gateway visibility to determine mechanism
mitreTechniques: T1499.003 Endpoint Denial of Service: Application Exhaustion Flood
controls: API gateway general rate-limiting
Behavioral/anomaly-based bot detection
ITID-41234.detection: Sufficient to detect the API flood pattern but insufficient to classify mechanism at time of intake.
ITID-41234.response: Apply general API rate-limiting immediately; run gateway log analysis in parallel to reclassify.
metrics: Count of incidents landing in this catch-all per quarter
ITID-41234.notes: Triage/intake bucket only; reclassify once the mechanism is confirmed.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General API Request Flooding
playbook.description: An API-layer request flood is confirmed via elevated request rate and backend impact, but the specific technique (authenticated-key abuse, algorithmic-complexity, distributed botnet) has not yet been determined.

steps.title: Confirm API request flood via request-rate and backend resource impact analysis
steps.desc: Analyze API gateway logs and backend metrics to confirm an abnormal request-rate spike correlated with backend resource impact.
steps.guidance: Compare requests-per-second across affected endpoint(s) against baseline; check whether volume is concentrated on few accounts/keys or spread across many sources.
steps.outcome: Confirmed API flood condition with impacted endpoint(s) and backend resource impact documented.
steps.abort: If elevated traffic correlates with a legitimate event, stand down and document as false positive.

steps.title: Apply general rate limiting and bot-management across affected endpoints
steps.desc: Deploy general-purpose per-source rate limiting and bot-management challenges across impacted API endpoint(s) pending full technique classification.
steps.guidance: Use adaptive/behavioral rules where available rather than static thresholds, to handle an unclassified traffic pattern.
steps.outcome: Request rate reduced to sustainable levels and API availability restored.
steps.abort: If legitimate integrations report being blocked, relax the threshold or add an allowlist for known-good clients.

steps.title: Complete technique classification and apply targeted hardening
steps.desc: Finalize which API flooding technique was used and apply the more specific hardening measures from the corresponding playbook.
steps.guidance: Reclassify the incident to the specific ITID leaf if determination succeeds.
steps.outcome: Attack technique documented and technique-specific hardening applied.

steps.title: Relax temporary controls and confirm normal API performance
steps.desc: Incrementally ease temporary rate limits and challenges once attack traffic subsides, retaining baseline protective controls permanently.
steps.guidance: Monitor endpoint response time and error rate for at least 1-2 hours as limits are relaxed.
steps.outcome: API performance restored to normal with permanent baseline protections retained.

steps.title: Document incident and improve API flood classification tooling
steps.desc: Record why immediate technique classification was not possible and recommend detection tooling improvements.
steps.guidance: Include recommendations for enhanced request-pattern analytics that would have sped up classification.
steps.outcome: After-action report with concrete detection tooling improvement items.

steps.title: Attempt technique classification via source and cost-pattern analysis
steps.desc: Determine whether the flood is concentrated on a small number of authenticated keys, driven by disproportionately expensive queries, or spread across a large distributed botnet, to allow pivot to a more specific playbook.
steps.guidance: If classification succeeds, transition to the corresponding specific API flooding playbook; otherwise proceed with general mitigation.
steps.outcome: Either successful reclassification or confirmed genuinely mixed/unclear technique.

steps.title: Engage upstream DDoS/CDN mitigation for broader relief
steps.desc: If local mitigation is insufficient, engage the CDN/cloud provider's application-layer DDoS mitigation service.
steps.guidance: Provide the traffic pattern characteristics gathered during identification to speed mitigation tuning.
steps.outcome: Attack traffic further reduced via provider-level mitigation.

steps.title: Confirm technique-specific hardening retained where classification succeeded
steps.desc: Where the attack was reclassified to a specific API flooding technique, confirm the corresponding technique-specific hardening measures remain in place post-recovery.
steps.guidance: Cross-check against the specific playbook's hardening recommendations if reclassification occurred.
steps.outcome: Confirmed appropriate hardening retained based on final classification.

ITID-41241.def: A denial-of-service attack in which a botnet composed primarily of compromised Internet-of-Things devices (routers, cameras, DVRs, and similar embedded devices) is directed via C2 to generate application-layer request floods (e.g. HTTP) against a target, exploiting the sheer scale and geographic distribution of recruited IoT devices.
ITID-41241.purpose: Captures the network/application-layer denial-of-service impact when an IoT botnet is directed to flood a target at Layer 7, as distinct from the botnet infrastructure itself.
scopeIncludes: Application-layer floods (HTTP or similar) sourced from confirmed IoT botnet members
Attacks attributable to known IoT botnet families (e.g. Mirai and its variants) directed at a target's application tier
scopeExcludes: The IoT botnet recruitment/compromise mechanism itself (see ITID-31711 IoT Device Botnet Recruitment)
Network-layer volumetric floods from an IoT botnet with no application-layer targeting (see Distributed Botnet-Driven SYN Flood or the Unclassified / General Botnet-Based DDoS Attack leaf)
Booter/stresser-mediated attacks where the renter's identity/service model is the differentiating factor (see Rented/Booter-Service DDoS Attack)
ITID-41241.severity: High given the scale typically achievable by IoT botnets and the difficulty of IP-based filtering against thousands of distinct consumer/embedded device addresses.
ITID-41241.priority: P1 on confirmation of IoT botnet sourcing at application layer, given limited effectiveness of simple IP blocking and typical attack scale.
ITID-41241.escalation: Escalate to application operations and DDoS mitigation provider immediately; correlate source IPs against known IoT botnet threat intel.
indicators: Application-layer request flood with source IPs correlating to consumer ISP/broadband and IoT-associated ASN ranges in threat intel
User-agent strings or request patterns consistent with known IoT botnet malware families
Extremely high source IP count relative to request-per-source rate
vectors: Mirai and derivative IoT botnet families issuing HTTP flood attack commands
Compromised routers, cameras, and DVRs recruited via default-credential or unpatched-vulnerability exploitation
rootCauses: Proliferation of unpatched/default-credential IoT devices reachable from the internet (a systemic, largely external risk factor)
No behavioral/anomaly-based bot detection layer distinguishing IoT botnet traffic from legitimate mobile/broadband users
mitreTechniques: T1499.003 Endpoint Denial of Service: Application Exhaustion Flood
controls: Behavioral/anomaly-based bot detection and mitigation service
Threat intelligence feeds for known IoT botnet source ranges/signatures
Upstream DDoS scrubbing service with Layer-7 mitigation
ITID-41241.detection: Strong when combined with threat-intel-enriched source attribution; a raw volumetric view alone cannot distinguish IoT botnet traffic from other distributed sources.
ITID-41241.response: Engage behavioral bot mitigation and threat-intel-informed filtering immediately; correlate with known IoT botnet campaigns for context.
metrics: Distinct source IP count attributed to known IoT botnet ranges
Peak application-layer request rate
Time to behavioral mitigation engagement
detections: IoT botnet threat intel correlation alerting
ITID-41241.notes: This leaf is scoped to the network-layer impact/attack outcome of IoT-botnet-driven application DoS; the underlying malware/recruitment mechanism is documented at ITID-31711 (IoT Device Botnet Recruitment) and related ITID-317xx leaves — cross-reference rather than duplicate.

playbook.name: IoT Botnet-Driven Application Layer DoS
playbook.description: A botnet composed of compromised IoT devices (routers, cameras, DVRs) generates a high volume of application-layer requests to exhaust web/application server capacity.

steps.title: Confirm application-layer flood with IoT-botnet source characteristics
steps.desc: Analyze access logs and threat intel for source IPs consistent with known IoT botnet infrastructure (e.g., residential/consumer ISP ranges, known Mirai-family C2 lists, characteristic device user-agents or lack thereof).
steps.guidance: Check source ASN distribution for concentration in residential/consumer ISP ranges globally, and cross-reference against IoT botnet tracking feeds.
steps.outcome: Confirmed IoT botnet-driven application flood with source characteristics and affected endpoint(s) documented.

steps.title: Deploy IoT-botnet-specific fingerprint blocking and per-source rate limiting
steps.desc: Apply WAF/bot-management rules using known IoT botnet fingerprints (TLS/JA3, HTTP header ordering) combined with per-source-IP rate limiting.
steps.guidance: IoT bot clients often have distinctive, non-browser-standard TLS and HTTP stack fingerprints that can be targeted specifically.
steps.outcome: Reduced effective attack volume through fingerprint-based and per-source throttling.

steps.title: Report botnet nodes to ISPs/CERTs for consumer device remediation outreach
steps.desc: Submit abuse reports identifying the compromised IoT devices to responsible ISPs, encouraging consumer notification and remediation (as ISPs are often best positioned to notify affected device owners).
steps.guidance: Include timestamps, source IPs, and attack signature; engage relevant national CERT/ISAC coordination for widespread campaigns.
steps.outcome: Abuse reports filed; where applicable, ISP-driven consumer remediation outreach initiated.

steps.title: Relax rate-limiting thresholds and monitor for resurgence
steps.desc: Gradually relax temporary rate-limiting thresholds once attack volume subsides while maintaining the botnet blocklist and fingerprint detection for an extended period.
steps.guidance: IoT botnets frequently resume attacks after brief pauses using the same or overlapping device pools.
steps.outcome: Application performance restored to normal with continued blocklist protection.

steps.title: Document botnet characteristics and update long-term IoT-fingerprint detection
steps.desc: Record botnet family, source characteristics, and effectiveness of fingerprint-based blocking for future reference.
steps.guidance: Recommend subscribing to relevant IoT-botnet-tracking threat feeds if this attack revealed a gap in current intel coverage.
steps.outcome: After-action report with threat intel and detection strategy improvements.

steps.title: Identify botnet family and command-and-control indicators
steps.desc: Attempt to identify the specific IoT botnet family (e.g., Mirai variant, Gafgyt) driving the attack based on request patterns and known IOCs.
steps.guidance: Different IoT botnet families have characteristic request-timing and header patterns documented by threat intel vendors.
steps.outcome: Botnet family identified or characterized, informing blocklist strategy and reporting.

steps.title: Push confirmed botnet source list to upstream scrubbing/CDN blocklists
steps.desc: Provide the confirmed IoT botnet source IP list to the upstream CDN/DDoS scrubbing provider for immediate filtering.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with the provider to apply reputation-based or explicit-list blocking for the identified botnet nodes.
steps.outcome: Confirmed botnet nodes blocked upstream, reducing attack traffic reaching the origin.

steps.title: Confirm fingerprint-based detection rules remain active permanently
steps.desc: Verify the IoT-botnet fingerprint-based WAF/bot-management rules deployed during containment remain enabled as permanent protections.
steps.guidance: Check WAF/bot-management configuration to confirm rules were not inadvertently reverted.
steps.outcome: Confirmed permanent fingerprint-based detection remains active.

ITID-41242.def: A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary purchases or rents attack capacity from a commercial 'booter' or 'stresser' service — a platform that packages access to botnet or amplification infrastructure as a paid, self-service product — to launch an attack against a target with minimal technical effort or infrastructure of the adversary's own.
ITID-41242.purpose: Captures denial-of-service attacks launched via a commercial DDoS-for-hire (booter/stresser) service rather than an adversary's own botnet.
scopeIncludes: Attacks attributable to known booter/stresser platform infrastructure or attack signatures
Low-sophistication actors purchasing attack capacity rather than operating their own botnet
scopeExcludes: Attacks from a botnet directly operated by the adversary (see IoT Botnet-Driven Application Layer DoS or the Unclassified / General Botnet-Based DDoS Attack leaf)

The underlying attack technique itself, which should also be documented under the relevant vector-specific leaf if identifiable (e.g. a booter-launched SYN flood is both this leaf and ITID-41121/41122)
ITID-41242.severity: Medium-High: booter services vary widely in attack quality/scale, but their low cost and ease of use make this a common and recurring vector against lower-priority targets.
ITID-41242.priority: P2 on detection; escalate to P1 if sustained/repeated attacks from the same service are confirmed or if scale exceeds typical booter capacity (suggesting escalated service tier or multiple concurrent services).
ITID-41242.escalation: Escalate to DDoS mitigation provider immediately; consider law enforcement referral if the booter service and attacker identity can be attributed.
indicators: Attack traffic signatures matching known booter/stresser platform infrastructure or attack-module fingerprints in threat intel
Attack characteristics (duration, vector selection, scale) consistent with commodity booter service tiers
Correlation with underground forum/marketplace activity referencing the target
vectors: Self-service booter/stresser platforms offering menu-driven selection of flood type, target, and duration for a fee
Booter services often built atop rented or compromised IoT botnet infrastructure
rootCauses: Low barrier to entry for launching attacks via commodity booter services (a threat-landscape factor rather than an organizational control gap)
Insufficient standing DDoS mitigation capacity to absorb even commodity-tier attack volumes
mitreTechniques: T1499.003 Endpoint Denial of Service: Application Exhaustion Flood
controls: Upstream DDoS scrubbing service sized for at least commodity booter-tier volumes
Threat intelligence feeds tracking known booter/stresser infrastructure
Always-on (not purely on-demand) mitigation for high-value targets given the ease of re-attack
ITID-41242.detection: Moderate-to-strong when threat intel maintains current booter infrastructure fingerprints; the underlying traffic otherwise looks like whatever vector the booter service employs (flood/amplification/etc.).
ITID-41242.response: Engage standing or on-demand DDoS mitigation per the specific vector observed; document booter attribution where possible for trend reporting and potential law enforcement referral.
metrics: Count of attacks attributed to known booter services per quarter
Recurrence rate from the same attributed service/actor
Time to mitigation engagement
ITID-41242.notes: Differentiating axis for the Botnet-Based DoS group is delivery/business model: this leaf is defined by the commercial booter service model rather than a specific technical vector, and should typically be tagged alongside whichever vector-specific leaf matches the observed traffic.

playbook.name: Rented/Booter-Service DDoS Attack (DDoS-for-Hire)
playbook.description: The attacker rents a commercial 'booter' or 'stresser' DDoS-for-hire service, which launches a coordinated multi-source application-layer (or blended) attack against the target on the attacker's behalf.

steps.title: Confirm application-layer flood with booter-service infrastructure characteristics
steps.desc: Analyze source IP infrastructure for characteristics common to commercial booter/stresser services (concentration in specific hosting/VPS providers rather than residential IoT, known booter C2/proxy infrastructure lists).
steps.guidance: Booter services frequently use rented VPS/proxy infrastructure or amplification reflectors rather than compromised consumer devices; cross-reference source ranges against known booter infrastructure threat intel.
steps.outcome: Confirmed booter-service-driven attack pattern with source infrastructure characteristics documented.

steps.title: Deploy layered mitigation across all observed vectors from the booter service
steps.desc: Since booter services often launch blended multi-vector attacks, deploy layered defenses (WAF rate limiting, bot management, network-layer scrubbing) covering all observed vectors simultaneously.
steps.guidance: Coordinate network and application teams to apply mitigations concurrently given booter services can pivot between vectors mid-attack.
steps.outcome: Attack traffic reduced across all observed vectors.

steps.title: Preserve evidence and report to law enforcement for booter service takedown
steps.desc: Preserve attack logs/evidence and report the incident to law enforcement (e.g., FBI IC3, national cybercrime units) given booter services are illegal commercial operations subject to takedown efforts.
steps.guidance: Booter/stresser services are frequent targets of coordinated law enforcement takedown operations; timely, detailed reporting supports these efforts.
steps.outcome: Evidence preserved and incident reported to appropriate law enforcement channels.

steps.title: Relax layered mitigations as each vector normalizes
steps.desc: Incrementally roll back per-vector mitigations only after each shows sustained normal baseline, given the blended nature of the attack.
steps.guidance: Track each vector independently since booter attacks may resolve unevenly across vectors.
steps.outcome: Full service restoration with no premature exposure to a still-active vector.

steps.title: Document incident and evaluate DDoS protection contract coverage for blended attacks
steps.desc: Record the incident and assess whether current DDoS protection service coverage adequately handles blended, rapidly-pivoting attack patterns typical of booter services.
steps.guidance: Include contract/SLA review recommendations in the after-action report if gaps were identified.
steps.outcome: After-action report with DDoS protection coverage recommendations tracked.

steps.title: Attempt attribution to a specific known booter service
steps.desc: Compare attack signature (request patterns, timing, targeted ports/protocols) against known booter service signatures tracked by threat intel and law enforcement partners.
steps.guidance: Many booter services have documented, recognizable attack signatures from prior takedown investigations.
steps.outcome: Possible attribution to a specific known booter service, informing law enforcement engagement.
steps.tool: Threat intel platform / law enforcement liaison

steps.title: Engage upstream DDoS scrubbing provider for full-spectrum mitigation
steps.desc: Engage upstream/cloud DDoS scrubbing with a full-spectrum mitigation profile given the likely blended nature of a booter-service attack.
steps.guidance: Provide all observed attack characteristics to the scrubbing provider for comprehensive mitigation tuning.
steps.outcome: Bulk of attack traffic absorbed and scrubbed upstream across all vectors.

steps.title: Confirm all layered defenses restored to permanent baseline configuration
steps.desc: Verify that all layered defenses activated during containment (WAF, bot-management, network scrubbing) settle into their intended permanent baseline configuration rather than an incomplete rollback state.
steps.guidance: Review configuration across all layers for consistency post-incident.
steps.outcome: Confirmed consistent, intentional configuration state across all defensive layers.

ITID-41243.def: A denial-of-service attack in which a botnet's command-and-control infrastructure directs member bots to execute multiple distinct attack vectors (e.g. volumetric flood, SYN flood, and application-layer flood) concurrently or in rapid succession against the same target, coordinated as a single campaign to exceed the coverage of any single mitigation layer.
ITID-41243.purpose: Captures a botnet-coordinated campaign that deliberately combines multiple DoS vectors under unified C2 control to defeat single-vector mitigation.
scopeIncludes: Botnet C2-coordinated campaigns spanning two or more distinct vectors (e.g. UDP flood plus HTTP flood) against one target within the same incident
Campaigns where bot modules are dynamically instructed to shift vectors in response to observed mitigation
scopeExcludes: Single-vector botnet floods (see IoT Botnet-Driven Application Layer DoS)
Non-botnet multi-vector campaigns using other infrastructure (see Combined Volumetric and Application-Layer Multi-Vector DDoS under Hybrid DDoS Attack)
ITID-41243.severity: Critical: the combination of botnet scale with deliberate multi-vector design represents one of the most difficult DoS patterns to mitigate.
ITID-41243.priority: P1, given the deliberate multi-vector, botnet-scale design intended to outpace mitigation response.
ITID-41243.escalation: Escalate to network operations, application operations, DDoS mitigation provider, and incident command immediately on confirmation of coordinated multi-vector botnet activity.
indicators: Mitigation dashboards showing multiple concurrent or rapidly alternating attack vectors from correlated botnet source ranges
C2 traffic or threat intel indicating coordinated multi-module bot tasking
Traffic composition shifting across network and application layers within a single sustained incident
vectors: Full-featured botnets (e.g. Mirai variants with multiple attack modules) tasked to run combined attack profiles
DDoS-for-hire platforms offering multi-vector botnet campaigns as a premium tier
rootCauses: Mitigation architecture siloed by layer (network-layer scrubbing separate from application-layer WAF) without unified correlation
No incident process for treating multi-vector botnet activity as a single coordinated campaign
mitreTechniques: T1498.001 Network Denial of Service: Direct Network Flood
T1499.003 Endpoint Denial of Service: Application Exhaustion Flood
controls: Unified DDoS mitigation platform spanning network and application layers
Cross-layer traffic correlation and single-incident-ID tracking
Threat intelligence feeds for known multi-vector botnet campaigns
ITID-41243.detection: Strong when network and application monitoring are correlated under one incident view; weak if each layer's alerts are triaged independently without cross-referencing.
ITID-41243.response: Treat as a single coordinated incident spanning all mitigation layers; engage full-spectrum (network plus application) mitigation simultaneously rather than sequentially.
metrics: Number of concurrent vectors observed
Time to cross-layer correlation into a single incident
Peak combined impact across all vectors
ITID-41243.notes: Distinguished from the Hybrid DDoS Attack Tier-4 group by the specific attribution to a single coordinated botnet's multi-module tasking, rather than a general multi-vector characterization.

playbook.name: Botnet-Coordinated Multi-Vector DoS Campaign
playbook.description: A sophisticated botnet launches a coordinated campaign combining multiple application-layer (and potentially network-layer) vectors against the target simultaneously or in rapid succession.

steps.title: Break down concurrent botnet-driven vectors to build a composite attack profile
steps.desc: Analyze logs and telemetry across network and application layers to identify each concurrent vector (e.g., HTTP flood, API flood, TLS exhaustion) being driven by the botnet and their relative contribution.
steps.guidance: Multi-vector botnet campaigns often shift vector dominance every few minutes as the botnet operator adapts to mitigation; build a timeline showing vector-shifting behavior.
steps.outcome: Documented breakdown of concurrent vectors with timeline showing any vector-shifting behavior.

steps.title: Activate full-spectrum scrubbing and bot-management covering all identified vectors
steps.desc: Engage upstream/cloud DDoS scrubbing and application-layer bot-management with mitigation profiles covering each concurrent vector rather than a single-protocol filter.
