steps.guidance: Provide the scrubbing provider the complete vector breakdown so they enable all relevant mitigation modules concurrently.
steps.outcome: All identified vectors mitigated simultaneously; residual traffic reduced across the board.
steps.abort: If one vector persists after mitigation activation, escalate that specific vector for targeted tuning.

steps.title: Verify no vector was missed and push confirmed botnet nodes to blocklists
steps.desc: After primary mitigation stabilizes, re-scan traffic for any residual or newly emerging vector, and push all confirmed botnet source IPs to persistent blocklists.
steps.guidance: Multi-vector botnet operators often reintroduce a previously-mitigated vector once others are blocked; maintain heightened monitoring for 24-48 hours.
steps.outcome: Confirmed no residual or resurgent vectors; botnet nodes documented and blocklisted.

steps.title: Phase down mitigations per vector as each normalizes
steps.desc: Incrementally roll back per-vector mitigations only after each shows sustained normal baseline, rather than reverting all controls simultaneously.
steps.guidance: Track each vector independently since one may resolve well before others.
steps.outcome: Full service restoration with no premature exposure to a still-active vector.

steps.title: Document multi-vector campaign timeline and evaluate cross-layer detection gaps
steps.desc: Capture the full attack timeline across vectors and assess whether detection/mitigation tooling correlated vectors quickly enough given the botnet's coordination sophistication.
steps.guidance: Recommend investment in unified DDoS detection correlating L3/L4/L7 signals if response was delayed by siloed tooling.
steps.outcome: After-action report with cross-layer detection improvement recommendations.

steps.title: Profile the coordinating botnet and assess campaign scale/sophistication
steps.desc: Assess the size, geographic distribution, and coordination sophistication of the botnet (e.g., synchronized vector-switching suggests centralized C2 control).
steps.guidance: Cross-reference against threat intel for known large-scale botnet campaigns matching this signature.
steps.outcome: Documented botnet scale and sophistication assessment informing response prioritization and potential law enforcement engagement.

steps.title: Apply layered local defenses as compensating controls while scrubbing engages
steps.desc: While upstream scrubbing engages, apply local per-vector mitigations (rate limiting, WAF rules, connection tuning) to reduce load on downstream infrastructure.
steps.guidance: Coordinate changes across network and application teams simultaneously to avoid gaps as the botnet pivots between vectors.
steps.outcome: Reduced infrastructure load across all layers pending full scrubbing effectiveness.

steps.title: Confirm botnet blocklist and cross-layer detection rules remain active permanently
steps.desc: Verify the confirmed botnet source blocklist and cross-layer detection correlation rules established during the incident remain in place post-recovery.
steps.guidance: Check that blocklist entries and SIEM correlation rules were not inadvertently removed during rollback.
steps.outcome: Confirmed permanent detection and blocking measures remain active.

ITID-41244.def: A denial-of-service event confirmed as botnet-driven where the specific botnet category (IoT, booter-mediated, or coordinated multi-vector) has not yet been determined.
ITID-41244.purpose: Intake bucket for botnet-based DoS activity that cannot yet be attributed to a specific botnet type, delivery model, or vector combination.
scopeIncludes: Initial triage of a confirmed botnet-driven DoS attack before further classification is complete
scopeExcludes: Any attack already confirmed as IoT botnet-driven, booter/stresser-mediated, or coordinated multi-vector (reclassify to the specific leaf once confirmed)
ITID-41244.severity: Medium-High pending confirmation; reassess once botnet category is identified.
ITID-41244.priority: P2 pending triage; adjust once reclassified.
ITID-41244.escalation: Escalate to DDoS mitigation provider for source and infrastructure analysis; reclassify once confirmed.
indicators: Confirmed distributed, non-spoofed source pattern consistent with botnet activity without confirmed subcategory at initial detection
vectors: Unconfirmed at time of intake
rootCauses: Insufficient initial threat-intel correlation to determine botnet subcategory
mitreTechniques: T1499.003 Endpoint Denial of Service: Application Exhaustion Flood
controls: Behavioral/anomaly-based bot detection and mitigation service
Threat intelligence feeds for botnet source attribution
ITID-41244.detection: Sufficient to detect the botnet-driven pattern but insufficient to classify subcategory at time of intake.
ITID-41244.response: Engage general botnet mitigation immediately; run source/infrastructure analysis in parallel to reclassify.
metrics: Count of incidents landing in this catch-all per quarter
ITID-41244.notes: Triage/intake bucket only; reclassify once the botnet subcategory is confirmed.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Botnet-Based DoS Attack
playbook.description: A botnet-driven application-layer attack is confirmed via distributed source characteristics, but the specific botnet type/origin (IoT, booter service, coordinated multi-vector) has not yet been determined.

steps.title: Confirm botnet-driven application flood via distributed source analysis
steps.desc: Analyze access logs for an abnormal request-rate spike spread across a large number of genuinely distinct source IPs consistent with botnet activity.
steps.guidance: Compare source IP/ASN diversity and geographic distribution against baseline traffic patterns.
steps.outcome: Confirmed botnet-driven flood with source distribution and affected endpoint(s) documented.

steps.title: Deploy general bot-management and per-source rate limiting
steps.desc: Apply general-purpose bot-management challenges and per-source-IP rate limiting across impacted endpoint(s) pending full classification.
steps.guidance: Use adaptive/behavioral rules where available.
steps.outcome: Request rate reduced to sustainable levels and service availability restored.

steps.title: Complete botnet-type classification and apply targeted hardening
steps.desc: Finalize the botnet type/origin and apply the more specific hardening/reporting measures from the corresponding playbook.
steps.guidance: Reclassify the incident to the specific ITID leaf if determination succeeds.
steps.outcome: Botnet type documented and technique-specific hardening/reporting applied.

steps.title: Relax temporary controls and confirm normal application performance
steps.desc: Incrementally ease temporary rate limits once attack traffic subsides, retaining baseline protective controls and blocklist permanently.
steps.guidance: Monitor endpoint response time and error rate for at least 1-2 hours as limits are relaxed.
steps.outcome: Application performance restored to normal with permanent baseline protections retained.

steps.title: Document incident and improve botnet-type classification tooling
steps.desc: Record why immediate classification was not possible and recommend detection tooling/threat intel improvements.
steps.guidance: Include recommendations for enhanced source-fingerprinting analytics that would have sped up classification.
steps.outcome: After-action report with concrete detection tooling improvement items.

steps.title: Attempt botnet-type classification via source infrastructure analysis
steps.desc: Determine whether sources are consistent with compromised IoT devices, rented booter-service infrastructure, or a sophisticated multi-vector campaign, to allow pivot to a more specific playbook.
steps.guidance: If classification succeeds, transition to the corresponding specific botnet-based DoS playbook; otherwise proceed with general mitigation.
steps.outcome: Either successful reclassification or confirmed genuinely mixed/unclear botnet type.

steps.title: Push confirmed botnet source list to upstream scrubbing/CDN blocklists
steps.desc: Provide the confirmed botnet source IP list to the upstream CDN/DDoS scrubbing provider for immediate filtering.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with the provider to apply reputation-based or explicit-list blocking.
steps.outcome: Confirmed botnet nodes blocked upstream.

steps.title: Confirm technique-specific hardening retained where classification succeeded
steps.desc: Where the attack was reclassified to a specific botnet type, confirm the corresponding technique-specific hardening/reporting measures remain in place post-recovery.
steps.guidance: Cross-check against the specific playbook's hardening recommendations if reclassification occurred.
steps.outcome: Confirmed appropriate hardening retained based on final classification.

ITID-41311.def: A denial-of-service attack distributed across a botnet of compromised, internet-connected hosts of mixed or general-purpose composition (not specifically IoT-dominant, cloud-hosted, or vector-specialized), coordinated via C2 to overwhelm a target's network or application capacity.
ITID-41311.purpose: Serves as the general classification for a distributed denial-of-service attack confirmed as botnet-sourced but not otherwise specialized by device type, delivery model, or vector mix.
scopeIncludes: General-purpose botnet DDoS campaigns where the compromised host population is mixed (servers, desktops, general devices) rather than IoT-dominant
Botnet DDoS incidents where the specific host-type composition has not been determined but distributed, non-spoofed bot sourcing is confirmed
scopeExcludes: IoT-device-dominant botnet DDoS (see Unclassified / General IoT-Based DDoS Attack under IoT-Based DDoS)
Cloud-compute-sourced DDoS (see Cloud-Based DDoS group)

Vector-specific botnet leaves already documented elsewhere in this taxonomy (e.g. Distributed Botnet-Driven SYN Flood, IoT Botnet-Driven Application Layer DoS) — use those when the vector and host type are both known
ITID-41311.severity: High given the scale typical of botnet-sourced DDoS and the difficulty of simple IP-based filtering against distributed real sources.
ITID-41311.priority: P1 on confirmation of botnet sourcing at DDoS scale, given limited effectiveness of manual IP blocking.
ITID-41311.escalation: Escalate to network operations, application operations, and DDoS mitigation provider immediately on confirmation of botnet-sourced distributed attack traffic.
indicators: Attack traffic from thousands of distinct, geographically diverse source IPs with no evidence of address spoofing
Source IPs correlating with known general-purpose botnet C2 infrastructure in threat intel
Traffic patterns inconsistent with amplification/reflection (i.e., genuine bot-originated requests)
vectors: General-purpose botnets (compromised servers, desktops, mixed device types) issuing DDoS attack commands from infected members
DDoS-for-hire platforms renting access to mixed-composition botnets
rootCauses: Reliance on per-source-IP rate-limiting alone, ineffective against high source diversity
No behavioral/anomaly-based DDoS mitigation layer distinguishing botnet traffic from legitimate distributed users
mitreTechniques: T1498.001 Network Denial of Service: Direct Network Flood
controls: Behavioral/anomaly-based DDoS scrubbing service
Threat intelligence feeds for known botnet source ranges
Upstream BGP black-holing/flowspec for confirmed botnet source ranges at scale
ITID-41311.detection: Strong when flow telemetry captures source IP diversity and can be correlated with threat intel; weaker with only volumetric thresholds alone.
ITID-41311.response: Engage upstream scrubbing/anycast absorption; correlate sources against botnet threat intel; reclassify to a vector-specific or host-type-specific leaf once analysis confirms more detail.
metrics: Distinct source IP count observed
Peak combined attack volume
Time to scrubbing engagement
ITID-41311.notes: This is the general-purpose catch-all for the Botnet-Based DDoS Tier-4 group; vector-specific botnet leaves (SYN flood, application-layer flood) already exist elsewhere and should be used in preference to this leaf when the vector is known. Cross-reference ITID-317xx for the botnet infrastructure mechanism rather than duplicating it here.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Botnet-Based DDoS Attack
playbook.description: A general volumetric or protocol-level DDoS attack originating from a distributed botnet of compromised hosts is degrading or denying service availability.

steps.title: Confirm attack via traffic volume and source diversity analysis
steps.desc: Analyze NetFlow/sFlow, edge router, and load balancer telemetry to distinguish a botnet-driven traffic surge from a legitimate demand spike or internal fault.
steps.guidance: Look for a high count of distinct source IPs (often geographically dispersed), abnormal protocol mix (SYN/UDP/ICMP floods), and correlation with known botnet C2 signatures or ASN reputation feeds. Compare current volume against the service's rolling 30-day baseline.
steps.outcome: Attack confirmed as distributed/botnet-origin with volume, protocol, and source-count metrics captured for the incident record.
steps.abort: If traffic originates from a small number of sources or a single ASN, reclassify as a targeted DoS rather than botnet DDoS and pivot playbooks.

steps.title: Engage upstream DDoS scrubbing / mitigation provider
steps.desc: Activate the organization's DDoS scrubbing service (on-demand or always-on) to reroute traffic through cleaning centers before it reaches origin infrastructure.
steps.guidance: Notify the mitigation provider with attack signature details (protocols, target IPs, approximate volume). Confirm BGP announcement or DNS redirection to scrubbing centers is active.
steps.outcome: Attack traffic is being scrubbed upstream and clean traffic volume to origin returns toward baseline.
steps.abort: If no scrubbing provider is contracted, escalate to ISP/transit provider for emergency rate limiting.

steps.title: Sustain mitigation controls through attack duration
steps.desc: Keep scrubbing, rate limits, and ACLs active and tuned as attack characteristics evolve, until attack traffic sustainably ceases.
steps.guidance: Monitor for attacker pivoting to new ports/protocols/targets and adjust mitigation rules accordingly.
steps.outcome: Attack traffic ceases or is fully absorbed by mitigation with no residual impact on origin infrastructure.

steps.title: Restore normal traffic routing and verify service health
steps.desc: Gradually remove temporary rate limits and confirm service latency, error rates, and throughput return to baseline.
steps.guidance: Roll back scrubbing/rerouting in stages to avoid a rebound surge overwhelming origin if attack traffic resumes.
steps.outcome: All affected services confirmed healthy and operating within normal SLA thresholds.
steps.abort: If attack traffic resumes during rollback, revert to full mitigation posture.

steps.title: Conduct post-incident review and capacity/mitigation assessment
steps.desc: Document attack timeline, mitigation effectiveness, and business impact; assess whether scrubbing capacity, always-on mitigation, or architecture changes are warranted.
steps.guidance: Include recommendations on always-on vs on-demand scrubbing, edge capacity headroom, and runbook gaps identified during response.
steps.outcome: Post-incident report published with actionable follow-up items assigned to owners.

steps.title: Identify targeted services and assess business impact
steps.desc: Determine which public-facing services, IPs, or ports are being targeted and quantify current impact on availability and customer-facing SLAs.
steps.guidance: Check synthetic monitoring and real-user monitoring for latency/error-rate spikes. Map affected IPs to owning applications and business units.
steps.outcome: A documented list of impacted services with severity/priority ranking to guide containment order.

steps.title: Apply rate limiting and ACLs at edge
steps.desc: Implement temporary rate limits, geo-fencing, or ACLs on edge routers/firewalls/WAF for identified attack signatures to reduce load on origin while scrubbing takes effect.
steps.guidance: Use protocol- and port-specific rate limits rather than broad blocks to minimize collateral impact on legitimate users.
steps.outcome: Origin resource utilization (CPU, bandwidth, connection tables) drops to sustainable levels.

steps.title: Validate no secondary compromise resulted from the attack
steps.desc: Confirm the DDoS was not a diversion for a concurrent intrusion attempt by reviewing IDS/IPS and authentication logs during the attack window.
steps.guidance: Cross-check logs for anomalous authentication attempts, new admin accounts, or unexpected configuration changes coinciding with the attack.
steps.outcome: No evidence of concurrent compromise found, or a separate incident opened if evidence is found.

steps.title: Consider BGP blackholing or flowspec for extreme volumetric floods
steps.desc: For attacks exceeding link capacity that scrubbing cannot absorb in time, evaluate remote-triggered blackhole (RTBH) or BGP flowspec rules with upstream transit providers.
steps.guidance: Blackholing sacrifices availability of the targeted IP entirely — weigh against partial degradation. Coordinate with network engineering before announcing.
steps.outcome: A documented decision on blackholing/flowspec use, applied only if warranted.
steps.abort: If blackholing would drop a business-critical service with no alternative path, do not proceed; rely on scrubbing and rate limiting only.

ITID-41321.def: A denial-of-service attack distributed across a botnet composed predominantly of compromised Internet-of-Things devices (routers, cameras, DVRs, and similar embedded consumer/industrial devices), coordinated via C2 to overwhelm a target's network or application capacity, leveraging the scale and poor security posture typical of the IoT device population.
ITID-41321.purpose: Serves as the general classification for a distributed denial-of-service attack sourced predominantly from compromised Internet-of-Things devices.
scopeIncludes: DDoS campaigns confirmed as sourced predominantly from IoT device populations (e.g. Mirai-family botnets and variants)
IoT-botnet DDoS incidents where the specific attack vector (volumetric or application-layer) has not been separately classified
scopeExcludes: Application-layer-specific IoT botnet DoS, which is separately documented at IoT Botnet-Driven Application Layer DoS (ITID-41241) — use that leaf when the vector is confirmed as Layer 7
General mixed-composition botnet DDoS with no IoT dominance (see Unclassified / General Botnet-Based DDoS Attack)
The IoT recruitment/compromise mechanism itself (see ITID-31711 IoT Device Botnet Recruitment)
ITID-41321.severity: High given the very large scale historically achievable by IoT botnets (hundreds of thousands of devices) and the difficulty of IP-based filtering against such a broad, consumer-device-heavy source base.
ITID-41321.priority: P1 on confirmation of IoT-dominant botnet sourcing, given typical attack scale and limited effectiveness of manual IP blocking.
ITID-41321.escalation: Escalate to network operations and DDoS mitigation provider immediately; correlate source IPs against known IoT botnet threat intel and ISP/consumer ASN ranges.
indicators: Attack traffic from an extremely high count of distinct source IPs correlating with consumer broadband and IoT-associated ASN ranges
Traffic/protocol signatures consistent with known IoT botnet malware families (e.g. Mirai and derivatives)
Attack scale (source count, aggregate bandwidth) consistent with historical IoT botnet campaigns
vectors: Mirai and derivative IoT botnet families issuing volumetric or mixed DDoS attack commands
Compromised routers, cameras, and DVRs recruited via default-credential or unpatched-vulnerability exploitation
rootCauses: Proliferation of unpatched/default-credential IoT devices reachable from the internet (a systemic, largely external risk factor)
No threat-intel-informed filtering distinguishing IoT botnet source ranges from legitimate broadband traffic
mitreTechniques: T1498.001 Network Denial of Service: Direct Network Flood
controls: Upstream DDoS scrubbing service sized for high-source-count IoT botnet volumes
Threat intelligence feeds for known IoT botnet source ranges/signatures
Behavioral/anomaly-based mitigation distinguishing IoT botnet traffic patterns
ITID-41321.detection: Strong when combined with threat-intel-enriched source attribution; a raw volumetric view alone cannot reliably distinguish IoT botnet traffic from other distributed sources.
ITID-41321.response: Engage upstream scrubbing and threat-intel-informed filtering immediately; correlate with known IoT botnet campaign activity for context; reclassify to the application-layer-specific leaf if Layer 7 targeting is confirmed.
metrics: Distinct source IP count attributed to known IoT botnet ranges
Peak combined attack volume
Time to scrubbing engagement
detections: IoT botnet threat intel correlation alerting
ITID-41321.notes: General-purpose catch-all for the IoT-Based DDoS Tier-4 group covering network/mixed-vector attacks; the application-layer-specific IoT botnet leaf (ITID-41241) should be used instead once Layer 7 targeting is confirmed. Cross-reference ITID-317xx for the IoT botnet recruitment/infrastructure mechanism rather than duplicating it here.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General IoT-Based DDoS Attack
playbook.description: A DDoS attack driven by a large volume of compromised IoT devices (e.g., Mirai-style botnet) is generating high-volume distributed traffic against organizational services.

steps.title: Fingerprint traffic for IoT botnet characteristics
steps.desc: Analyze source IP ranges, user-agent strings, and protocol behavior to identify signatures consistent with known IoT botnet families (e.g., Mirai variants) versus generic botnet traffic.
steps.guidance: Check threat intel feeds for known IoT botnet C2 infrastructure and compare source ASNs against consumer/IoT-heavy network ranges (residential ISPs, cloud camera vendors).
steps.outcome: Attack confirmed as IoT-botnet-sourced with representative source samples logged.

steps.title: Activate DDoS scrubbing with IoT botnet signature rules
steps.desc: Engage upstream scrubbing provider and supply known IoT botnet signatures/source ranges to accelerate filtering.
steps.guidance: Provide provider with observed protocol mix and any matched threat-intel indicators for faster rule tuning.
steps.outcome: Majority of attack traffic filtered upstream; origin bandwidth utilization normalizes.

steps.title: Maintain mitigation until sustained traffic normalization
steps.desc: Continue scrubbing and rate-limit enforcement, adjusting as the botnet operator potentially rotates source devices or vectors.
steps.guidance: IoT botnets can pivot vectors quickly; monitor continuously rather than assuming a single mitigation pass suffices.
steps.outcome: Attack traffic sustainably eliminated or fully absorbed.

steps.title: Validate service restoration and roll back temporary controls
steps.desc: Confirm affected services are stable and gradually remove emergency rate limits, monitoring for recurrence.
steps.outcome: Services restored to normal operation with no recurrence over a defined monitoring window.
steps.abort: If recurrence detected, reapply full mitigation.

steps.title: Document incident and review inbound traffic filtering posture
steps.desc: Capture attack characteristics, mitigation timeline, and evaluate whether standing amplification-protocol filtering or always-on scrubbing should be adopted.
steps.outcome: Report finalized with follow-up actions tracked.

steps.title: Assess attack vector and volumetric scale
steps.desc: Determine whether the attack is a volumetric flood (UDP/GRE/DNS amplification typical of IoT botnets) or application-layer, and measure peak bandwidth/PPS.
steps.guidance: IoT botnets often generate massive PPS with small packet sizes; ensure monitoring captures packets-per-second, not just bandwidth.
steps.outcome: Attack vector and scale documented to size mitigation response.

steps.title: Deploy protocol-specific rate limiting for amplification vectors
steps.desc: Rate-limit or block UDP-based amplification protocols (DNS, NTP, memcached, CoAP) at the edge if identified as attack vectors.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with network team to avoid blocking legitimate UDP-dependent services.
steps.outcome: Amplification-vector traffic reduced without disrupting legitimate services.

steps.title: Coordinate with upstream ISPs/CERTs on source blocking
steps.desc: Where source IoT devices are traceable to specific ISPs or ranges, report to upstream ISPs or national CERTs for source-side remediation.
steps.guidance: This step reduces attack volume over time rather than providing immediate relief; run in parallel with technical mitigation.
steps.outcome: ISP/CERT notified with indicators; some source suppression may occur.

ITID-41331.def: A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary provisions virtual machines or compute instances from one or more legitimate cloud providers (using stolen payment credentials, free-tier abuse, or compromised cloud accounts) and uses that rented infrastructure directly to generate high-volume attack traffic against a target.
ITID-41331.purpose: Captures a DDoS attack where the adversary's attack traffic originates from compute instances rented from legitimate cloud providers rather than compromised end-user devices.
scopeIncludes: Attack traffic confirmed originating from cloud provider IP ranges under attacker-controlled instances
Use of stolen billing credentials or compromised cloud accounts to provision attack infrastructure at scale
scopeExcludes: Abuse of serverless/function-as-a-service platforms specifically as the traffic-generation mechanism (see Serverless Function Abuse for Distributed Attack Traffic Generation)
Cost-exhaustion attacks targeting the victim's own auto-scaling cloud infrastructure rather than using cloud compute as the attacker's traffic source (see Cloud Auto-Scaling Cost Exhaustion Attack)
Traditional botnet DDoS from compromised consumer/IoT devices (see Botnet-Based DDoS / IoT-Based DDoS groups)
ITID-41331.severity: High: cloud-sourced attack instances typically have far greater per-node bandwidth than compromised consumer devices, allowing significant volume from relatively few instances.
ITID-41331.priority: P2 on detection; escalate to P1 on confirmed sustained volume from cloud provider ranges or link saturation.
ITID-41331.escalation: Escalate to network operations and the source cloud provider's abuse/trust-and-safety team immediately given the high per-node bandwidth typical of this vector.
indicators: High-volume attack traffic sourced from a concentrated set of major cloud provider IP ranges
Fewer distinct source IPs than typical botnet DDoS but disproportionately high per-source bandwidth
Rapid instance provisioning/deprovisioning patterns visible if cloud-side telemetry is available (e.g. via provider abuse reports)
vectors: Attacker-provisioned cloud VMs running flood tools, funded via stolen payment cards or compromised cloud accounts
Cloud account compromise (credential theft, leaked API keys) repurposed for attack infrastructure rather than data theft
rootCauses: Cloud providers' identity/billing verification not catching fraudulent account creation quickly enough to prevent short-lived attack use
No provider-side abuse reporting relationship established in advance for rapid takedown
mitreTechniques: T1498.001 Network Denial of Service: Direct Network Flood
controls: Upstream DDoS scrubbing service
Rapid abuse-reporting relationship with major cloud providers for fast instance takedown
Rate-limiting/blocking of specific cloud provider ranges during active attack if collateral impact to legitimate traffic is acceptable
ITID-41331.detection: Strong technical signal from flow data correlated with cloud provider IP range databases (ASN/IP allocation lookups).
ITID-41331.response: Engage upstream scrubbing immediately; file abuse reports with the source cloud provider(s) for instance takedown; monitor for re-provisioning from the same account/provider.
metrics: Peak attack bandwidth from cloud provider ranges
Time to provider abuse-report submission
Time to source instance takedown by provider
detections: Cloud provider ASN/IP range correlation alerting
ITID-41331.notes: Differentiating axis for the Cloud-Based DDoS group is the specific cloud abuse mechanism; this leaf covers direct rented-compute traffic generation.

playbook.name: DDoS Launched from Rented Cloud Compute Instances
playbook.description: An attacker has rented or hijacked cloud compute instances (across one or more providers) to generate coordinated DDoS traffic against the organization.

steps.title: Confirm cloud-origin attack pattern
steps.desc: Analyze source IP ranges against known cloud provider ASN blocks (AWS, Azure, GCP, DigitalOcean, etc.) to confirm the attack originates from rented compute rather than a botnet of end-user devices.
steps.guidance: Cloud-sourced DDoS typically shows fewer, higher-bandwidth sources with consistent uptime versus the churn seen in consumer botnets. Cross-reference with cloud provider ASN lists.
steps.outcome: Attack confirmed as cloud-instance-origin with source ASN/provider list documented.

steps.title: Engage DDoS scrubbing provider and report abuse to source cloud providers
steps.desc: Activate scrubbing mitigation and simultaneously file abuse reports with the identified cloud providers hosting attacking instances, requesting instance suspension.
steps.guidance: Cloud providers typically respond quickly to abuse reports with clear evidence (timestamps, source IPs, traffic samples) since compromised/abused accounts violate their AUP.
steps.outcome: Scrubbing active; abuse reports filed with each implicated cloud provider.
steps.tool: DDoS scrubbing provider portal, cloud provider abuse contact

steps.title: Monitor for instance suspension and attack cessation
steps.desc: Track abuse-report ticket status and correlate with observed drop in attack traffic as cloud providers suspend abusive instances.
steps.outcome: Attack traffic ceases as source instances are suspended or scrubbing fully absorbs remaining load.
steps.abort: If cloud providers are unresponsive, escalate via provider security/trust & safety escalation channel and continue scrubbing.

steps.title: Restore normal traffic flow and confirm service stability
steps.desc: Roll back temporary filters and confirm affected services meet normal performance baselines.
steps.outcome: Services confirmed stable over a sustained monitoring window.

steps.title: Document incident and review cloud-abuse reporting workflow
steps.desc: Capture attack timeline, provider response times, and effectiveness of abuse reporting; recommend pre-established relationships/escalation contacts with major cloud providers.
steps.outcome: Report finalized with follow-up actions, including any standing abuse-contact list update.

steps.title: Assess targeted service impact and traffic characteristics
steps.desc: Determine attack vector (volumetric, protocol, or application-layer) and quantify impact on targeted services.
steps.guidance: Cloud-origin attacks can sustain high-bandwidth application-layer floods since instances have full network stacks; check for L7 flood patterns (HTTP GET/POST floods).
steps.outcome: Attack vector and impacted services documented.

steps.title: Apply rate limiting and cloud-ASN-aware filtering at edge
steps.desc: Implement temporary rate limits or conditional throttling on traffic from implicated cloud ASNs while preserving legitimate cloud-hosted partner/API traffic.
steps.guidance: Avoid blanket-blocking entire cloud ASNs if legitimate integrations depend on them; use rate limiting rather than hard blocks where feasible.
steps.outcome: Origin load reduced without breaking legitimate cloud-hosted integrations.

ITID-41332.def: A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary invokes serverless functions (e.g. Lambda-style FaaS offerings) at massive parallel scale across one or more cloud providers, using each short-lived function invocation as a distributed source of attack traffic against a target, exploiting the platforms' elastic auto-scaling and per-invocation IP diversity.
ITID-41332.purpose: Captures a DDoS attack where the adversary abuses serverless/function-as-a-service platforms as a distributed, disposable traffic-generation mechanism.
scopeIncludes: Attack traffic generated by mass-invoked serverless functions used as distributed traffic sources
Abuse of free-tier or stolen-credential FaaS access to generate attack traffic at scale with minimal attacker cost
scopeExcludes: Attack traffic from persistent, attacker-provisioned VM instances (see DDoS Launched from Rented Cloud Compute Instances)
Cost-exhaustion attacks targeting the victim's own serverless/auto-scaling infrastructure (see Cloud Auto-Scaling Cost Exhaustion Attack)
ITID-41332.severity: High: serverless invocation at scale can produce very high source-IP diversity with minimal attacker setup, making source-based filtering particularly difficult.
ITID-41332.priority: P1 given the difficulty of mitigating extremely high source diversity generated with minimal attacker effort.
ITID-41332.escalation: Escalate to network operations, DDoS mitigation provider, and the source FaaS platform's abuse team immediately on confirmation of this technique.
indicators: Extremely high count of distinct source IPs, each generating a relatively small, bounded burst of traffic consistent with a single function invocation's lifetime
Source IPs correlating with known FaaS platform egress IP ranges
Attack traffic bursts with a rhythm consistent with function invocation/timeout cycles
vectors: Mass parallel invocation of serverless functions configured to issue outbound requests toward the target, funded via stolen credentials or free-tier abuse across multiple accounts
rootCauses: FaaS platforms' elastic scaling and outbound network access not rate-limited or monitored for abusive outbound request patterns
No provider-side anomaly detection catching mass function invocation used for external attack traffic
mitreTechniques: T1498.001 Network Denial of Service: Direct Network Flood
controls: Upstream DDoS scrubbing service tuned for high source-IP diversity
Rapid abuse-reporting relationship with the source FaaS provider(s)
Behavioral detection distinguishing bursty, short-lived-source attack patterns
ITID-41332.detection: Moderate-to-strong: recognizable once analysts correlate source IP churn and burst rhythm with known FaaS egress ranges, but this is a less mature detection pattern than traditional botnet or cloud-VM DDoS.
ITID-41332.response: Engage upstream scrubbing immediately; file abuse reports with the source FaaS provider(s); monitor for account/technique reuse.
metrics: Distinct source IP count observed
Time to provider abuse-report submission
Peak combined attack volume
detections: FaaS egress IP range correlation alerting
ITID-41332.notes: Differentiating axis for the Cloud-Based DDoS group: this leaf is specifically the serverless-invocation traffic-generation mechanism, distinct from persistent rented VM instances.

playbook.name: Serverless Function Abuse for Distributed Attack Traffic Generation
playbook.description: An attacker has abused serverless/FaaS platforms (e.g., Lambda, Cloud Functions) across many accounts or regions as a distributed traffic generation source for a DDoS-style attack.

steps.title: Correlate attack traffic with serverless platform egress signatures
steps.desc: Analyze source IP ranges and request headers/timing patterns to identify traffic consistent with serverless function invocations at scale (short-lived, high-concurrency, uniform request shape).
steps.guidance: Serverless-sourced traffic often shows very high request-per-second bursts with uniform payloads and origin IPs from major cloud provider function-execution ranges.
steps.outcome: Attack confirmed as serverless-function-origin with representative samples captured.

steps.title: Apply WAF/API gateway rate limiting on identified request patterns
steps.desc: Deploy targeted rate limits or challenge (CAPTCHA/JS challenge) rules on the specific request patterns generated by the serverless abuse.
steps.guidance: Prefer pattern-based throttling over IP-blocking since serverless source IPs rotate frequently across a large pool.
steps.outcome: Malicious request volume reduced without broadly impacting legitimate users.

steps.title: Engage upstream scrubbing if volume exceeds WAF capacity
steps.desc: If the serverless-driven flood exceeds WAF/API gateway absorption capacity, escalate to DDoS scrubbing provider for upstream mitigation.
steps.outcome: Attack volume brought within manageable capacity via combined WAF and scrubbing controls.
steps.abort: If WAF/API gateway controls already fully contain the attack, scrubbing escalation is unnecessary.

steps.title: Confirm service restoration and remove temporary throttles
steps.desc: Verify affected endpoints return to normal latency/error rates before relaxing emergency rate limits.
steps.outcome: Endpoints confirmed stable under normal load.

steps.title: Document incident and evaluate standing bot-mitigation controls
steps.desc: Capture timeline and recommend permanent bot-detection/rate-limiting enhancements for public APIs given the ease of serverless-based abuse.
steps.outcome: Report finalized with prioritized follow-up actions.

steps.title: Determine attack vector and targeted endpoint impact
steps.desc: Identify whether the abuse targets application APIs (L7 flood) or is being used to amplify traffic toward third parties, and assess service impact.
steps.guidance: Check API gateway and WAF logs for the specific endpoints receiving disproportionate load.
steps.outcome: Attack vector and impacted endpoints documented.

steps.title: Report abuse to the source cloud/FaaS provider(s)
steps.desc: File abuse reports with the cloud providers whose serverless platforms are generating the traffic, providing evidence for rapid function/account suspension.
steps.guidance: Include invocation timestamps, target endpoints, and volume evidence to expedite provider trust & safety action.
steps.outcome: Abuse reports filed; providers begin remediation of abusive accounts/functions.

ITID-41333.def: A denial-of-service-adjacent attack (commonly termed 'denial-of-wallet') in which an adversary sends traffic or triggers workload patterns specifically designed to cause a victim's cloud auto-scaling infrastructure to provision excessive additional compute, storage, bandwidth, or third-party API calls, inflating the victim's cloud billing to a damaging or unsustainable level, whether or not availability is meaningfully degraded.
ITID-41333.purpose: Captures an attack that deliberately drives up the victim's own cloud infrastructure costs by triggering excessive auto-scaling, rather than aiming purely at availability impact.
scopeIncludes: Traffic patterns deliberately engineered to maximize auto-scaling trigger events and pay-per-use resource consumption (e.g. serverless invocation costs, egress bandwidth, third-party metered API calls)
Attacks where the primary damage is financial (billing impact) rather than, or in addition to, service unavailability
scopeExcludes: Attacks aimed purely at exhausting fixed-capacity infrastructure with no cost-scaling dimension (see other DDoS/DoS leaves in this taxonomy)
Abuse of the attacker's own rented cloud compute as a traffic source (see DDoS Launched from Rented Cloud Compute Instances / Serverless Function Abuse)
ITID-41333.severity: High when sustained traffic is confirmed driving auto-scaling and measurable billing impact; treat as a business/financial risk in addition to a technical availability risk.
ITID-41333.priority: P2 on detection; escalate to P1 on confirmed significant billing impact or budget-threshold breach.
ITID-41333.escalation: Escalate to cloud infrastructure/FinOps owners and finance stakeholders in addition to standard DDoS escalation, given the direct financial impact dimension.
indicators: Rapid, sustained auto-scaling events (new instances, function invocations, or storage provisioning) disproportionate to genuine business demand
Cloud billing/cost-monitoring alerts triggered by anomalous spend velocity
Traffic patterns targeting metered/pay-per-use services (e.g. serverless functions, third-party API integrations billed per call) rather than fixed-capacity infrastructure
vectors: High-volume or high-frequency requests specifically targeting auto-scaled or metered-cost services
Requests engineered to trigger expensive third-party API calls billed to the victim (e.g. SMS, email, or data-enrichment integrations)
rootCauses: No cost budget alerts or hard spending caps configured on auto-scaling resources
Auto-scaling policies with no upper bound or circuit breaker on scale-out rate
Metered third-party integrations lacking their own rate-limiting or cost governance
mitreTechniques: T1499.003 Endpoint Denial of Service: Application Exhaustion Flood
controls: Cloud budget alerts and hard spending caps
Auto-scaling upper-bound limits and circuit breakers
Rate-limiting on metered third-party integrations
WAF/CDN filtering to reduce illegitimate traffic before it reaches cost-scaling infrastructure
ITID-41333.detection: Moderate: requires cost/billing telemetry integrated with security monitoring, which is less commonly instrumented than pure availability metrics.
ITID-41333.response: Cap or pause auto-scaling immediately upon confirmed abuse; engage standard traffic filtering; notify finance/FinOps stakeholders of billing impact and remediation timeline.
metrics: Anomalous spend attributable to the attack
Time to auto-scaling cap engagement
Time to cost-anomaly detection
ITID-41333.notes: Differentiating axis for the Cloud-Based DDoS group: this leaf's impact is financial (billing) rather than, or in addition to, availability, making it the outlier among its siblings and requiring FinOps stakeholder involvement.

playbook.name: Cloud Auto-Scaling Cost Exhaustion Attack (Denial-of-Wallet)
playbook.description: An attacker is deliberately driving traffic to trigger the organization's cloud auto-scaling to spin up excessive resources, aiming to exhaust budget (denial-of-wallet) rather than directly deny service.

steps.title: Detect abnormal auto-scaling and billing trajectory
steps.desc: Correlate cloud billing anomaly alerts and auto-scaling group activity logs with traffic patterns to confirm a deliberate scaling-cost attack versus organic demand growth.
steps.guidance: Check for a rapid, sustained rise in instance/container count driven by low-value or synthetic-looking requests, paired with a spend-rate spike well above historical norms.
steps.outcome: Attack confirmed as denial-of-wallet via auto-scaling abuse, with cost trajectory and traffic evidence documented.
steps.abort: If scaling growth correlates with a legitimate marketing event or organic traffic, treat as capacity planning, not an incident.
steps.tool: Cloud cost anomaly detection, auto-scaling logs

steps.title: Set or verify hard billing alerts and spend caps
steps.desc: Immediately verify or configure hard spend caps/budget alerts on the affected cloud account/project to prevent unbounded cost escalation while investigation continues.
steps.guidance: Use billing alert thresholds tied to automated notification and, where supported, automated throttling or scale-out ceiling enforcement.
steps.outcome: Spend caps and alerts confirmed active, bounding further financial exposure.

steps.title: Block or challenge confirmed abusive sources
steps.desc: Apply sustained blocking, CAPTCHA, or bot-management challenges against confirmed abusive sources/patterns to eliminate the cost-driving traffic.
steps.outcome: Abusive traffic eliminated; scaling activity and spend return to baseline.

steps.title: Restore normal scaling limits and reconcile costs
steps.desc: Gradually restore auto-scaling ceilings to normal operating levels and reconcile incurred cloud costs for the incident window with finance.
steps.outcome: Scaling limits restored to normal; incident-related cost impact quantified and reported to finance/stakeholders.

steps.title: Document incident and implement standing cost-anomaly guardrails
steps.desc: Capture timeline, financial impact, and recommend permanent per-endpoint rate limiting, cost-anomaly alerting, and scaling ceiling governance to prevent recurrence.
steps.outcome: Report finalized with prioritized guardrail follow-ups assigned.

steps.title: Identify the specific request pattern driving scale-out
steps.desc: Pinpoint which endpoints or request types are triggering scale-out events, distinguishing cheap-to-send but expensive-to-process requests.
steps.guidance: Look for endpoints with disproportionate compute cost per request (e.g., heavy queries, image processing, PDF generation) being hit at high volume.
steps.outcome: Specific abusive request pattern(s) and endpoint(s) identified.

steps.title: Cap auto-scaling maximum instance count and rate-limit abusive endpoints
steps.desc: Temporarily lower the auto-scaling group's maximum instance ceiling and apply rate limiting or a WAF rule against the identified abusive request pattern.
steps.guidance: Balance the scaling cap against maintaining sufficient capacity for legitimate traffic; monitor for user-facing degradation.
steps.outcome: Scale-out growth halted; abusive request volume reduced.
steps.abort: If capping scale-out causes unacceptable legitimate-user impact, prioritize WAF/rate-limit tuning over scaling caps.

ITID-41334.def: A denial-of-service event confirmed as sourced from or targeting cloud infrastructure where the specific mechanism (rented compute, serverless abuse, or cost-exhaustion) has not yet been determined.
ITID-41334.purpose: Intake bucket for cloud-based DDoS activity that cannot yet be attributed to a specific cloud abuse mechanism.
scopeIncludes: Initial triage of a suspected cloud-based DDoS attack before mechanism analysis is complete
scopeExcludes: Any attack already confirmed as rented-compute, serverless-abuse, or cost-exhaustion driven (reclassify to the specific leaf once confirmed)
ITID-41334.severity: Medium-High pending confirmation; reassess once mechanism is identified.
ITID-41334.priority: P2 pending triage; adjust once reclassified.
ITID-41334.escalation: Escalate to network/cloud operations for source and billing analysis; reclassify once confirmed.
indicators: Attack traffic correlated with cloud provider IP ranges without confirmed mechanism at initial detection
vectors: Unconfirmed at time of intake
rootCauses: Insufficient initial visibility to determine cloud abuse mechanism
mitreTechniques: T1498.001 Network Denial of Service: Direct Network Flood
controls: Upstream DDoS scrubbing service
Cloud provider ASN/IP range correlation tooling
ITID-41334.detection: Sufficient to detect cloud-sourced attack traffic but insufficient to classify mechanism at time of intake.
ITID-41334.response: Engage general DDoS mitigation immediately; run source/billing analysis in parallel to reclassify.
metrics: Count of incidents landing in this catch-all per quarter
detections: Cloud provider ASN/IP range correlation alerting
ITID-41334.notes: Triage/intake bucket only; reclassify once the cloud abuse mechanism is confirmed.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Cloud-Based DDoS Attack
playbook.description: A general DDoS attack originating from cloud-hosted infrastructure (rented, hijacked, or serverless) is degrading or denying service availability, not otherwise classified into a more specific cloud-DDoS sub-type.

steps.title: Confirm cloud-hosted origin and attack characteristics
steps.desc: Analyze source IP ranges, ASN ownership, and traffic patterns to confirm the attack is cloud-infrastructure-sourced and characterize volumetric vs application-layer nature.
steps.guidance: Cross-reference source ASNs against known cloud provider ranges; review traffic mix (bandwidth, PPS, request rate) against baseline.
steps.outcome: Attack confirmed as cloud-origin DDoS with vector and scale documented.

steps.title: Engage DDoS scrubbing provider
steps.desc: Activate upstream scrubbing/mitigation to filter attack traffic before it reaches origin infrastructure.
steps.guidance: Provide provider with attack signature and source-ASN details for faster mitigation.
steps.outcome: Attack traffic scrubbed upstream; origin load normalizes.

steps.title: Sustain mitigation until attack traffic ceases
steps.desc: Continue monitoring and adjusting mitigation controls as the attack evolves until traffic returns to baseline.
steps.outcome: Attack traffic eliminated or fully absorbed by mitigation controls.

steps.title: Validate service restoration
steps.desc: Confirm affected services return to normal performance baselines and roll back temporary controls in stages.
steps.outcome: Services confirmed stable over a sustained monitoring window.
steps.abort: If attack resumes, revert to full mitigation posture.

steps.title: Document incident and review mitigation posture
steps.desc: Capture attack timeline, mitigation effectiveness, and recommend any architecture or provider-relationship improvements.
steps.outcome: Report finalized with follow-up items tracked.

steps.title: Assess targeted services and business impact
steps.desc: Identify affected services/endpoints and quantify impact on availability and customer experience.
steps.guidance: Use synthetic monitoring and real-user monitoring to size the impact and prioritize response.
steps.outcome: Impacted services and severity documented.

steps.title: Apply edge rate limiting and report abuse to source cloud providers
steps.desc: Rate-limit identified attack traffic at the edge and file abuse reports with implicated cloud providers to expedite source-side takedown.
steps.outcome: Attack volume reduced through combined edge filtering and provider-side remediation.
steps.tool: Edge firewall, cloud provider abuse contact

ITID-41341.def: A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary combines network-layer volumetric techniques (e.g. UDP/ICMP floods, amplification) with application-layer techniques (e.g. HTTP floods, slow-rate attacks) against the same target within a single campaign, forcing defenders to engage both network-layer scrubbing and application-layer (WAF/bot mitigation) controls simultaneously.
ITID-41341.purpose: Captures a DDoS campaign that deliberately spans both network-layer volumetric flooding and application-layer flooding within a single coordinated attack.
scopeIncludes: Campaigns confirmed combining at least one network-layer vector and at least one application-layer vector against the same target within one incident window
Attacks that shift between layers over the course of the campaign to probe for gaps in layered defenses
scopeExcludes: Single-layer multi-vector attacks confined to network-layer techniques only (see Multi-Vector Volumetric Flood under Volumetric Flooding)

Botnet-attributed multi-vector campaigns where the botnet coordination itself is the differentiating factor (see Botnet-Coordinated Multi-Vector DoS Campaign) — this leaf applies when the differentiating factor is the layer combination regardless of botnet attribution
ITID-41341.severity: Critical: combined-layer attacks are designed specifically to exceed the coverage of any single mitigation control and represent one of the more severe DDoS patterns.
ITID-41341.priority: P1 given the deliberate cross-layer design intended to defeat layered mitigation.
ITID-41341.escalation: Escalate to network operations, application operations, DDoS mitigation provider, and incident command immediately on confirmation of cross-layer vector combination.
indicators: Simultaneous or closely sequential alerts from both network-layer flow monitoring and application-layer (WAF/bot) monitoring against the same target
Mitigation dashboards showing vector types spanning both network and application categories under one attack ID
Traffic composition shifting from network-layer to application-layer emphasis (or vice versa) mid-campaign
vectors: Multi-vector DDoS-for-hire platforms offering combined network- and application-layer attack profiles
Botnet C2 issuing both network-flood and application-flood module commands within one campaign
rootCauses: Mitigation architecture siloed by layer without unified cross-layer incident correlation
Insufficient always-on capacity at either the network scrubbing layer or the application WAF/bot-mitigation layer
mitreTechniques: T1498.001 Network Denial of Service: Direct Network Flood
T1499.003 Endpoint Denial of Service: Application Exhaustion Flood
controls: Unified DDoS mitigation platform spanning network and application layers
Cross-layer traffic correlation and single-incident-ID tracking
Always-on mitigation capacity at both layers for high-value targets
ITID-41341.detection: Strong when network and application monitoring are correlated under one incident view; weak if each layer's alerts are triaged independently.
ITID-41341.response: Treat as a single coordinated incident spanning all mitigation layers; engage full-spectrum (network plus application) mitigation simultaneously rather than sequentially.
metrics: Number of distinct layers/vectors observed
Time to cross-layer correlation into a single incident
Peak combined impact across all layers
ITID-41341.notes: Differentiating axis for the Hybrid DDoS Attack group is what is being combined with the DDoS: here it is network and application layers within the DDoS itself, as opposed to a DDoS paired with extortion (RDoS) or with a concurrent intrusion (smokescreen).

playbook.name: Combined Volumetric and Application-Layer Multi-Vector DDoS
playbook.description: A coordinated multi-vector DDoS attack combining volumetric flooding with application-layer (L7) attacks is targeting the organization simultaneously across multiple layers.

steps.title: Characterize simultaneous attack vectors across layers
steps.desc: Analyze network-layer (volumetric) and application-layer telemetry concurrently to confirm multiple attack vectors are active at the same time.
steps.guidance: Correlate edge router/NetFlow data (volumetric signals) with WAF/APM data (L7 signals: slow POST, HTTP flood, cache-busting requests) on a shared timeline.
steps.outcome: Multi-vector nature confirmed with each vector's characteristics and timeline documented.
steps.abort: If only one layer shows anomalous activity, reclassify as single-vector DDoS.

steps.title: Engage DDoS scrubbing provider for volumetric component
steps.desc: Activate upstream scrubbing to absorb the volumetric portion of the attack.
steps.outcome: Volumetric traffic reduced at the network edge.

steps.title: Sustain and tune multi-layer mitigation as attacker pivots vectors
steps.desc: Continuously monitor for vector-shifting and adjust scrubbing and WAF rules accordingly until all vectors subside.
steps.outcome: All attack vectors eliminated or fully mitigated.

steps.title: Validate full-stack service restoration
steps.desc: Confirm both network-layer and application-layer metrics return to baseline before relaxing controls.
steps.guidance: Roll back network and application mitigations independently, verifying each layer separately.
steps.outcome: Full-stack service health confirmed stable.
steps.abort: If any vector resumes, revert only the relevant layer's mitigation.

steps.title: Document multi-vector incident and cross-team response effectiveness
steps.desc: Capture full timeline across all vectors, evaluate coordination effectiveness between network and application teams, and recommend joint runbook improvements.
steps.outcome: Report finalized with cross-team follow-up actions assigned.

steps.title: Assess cumulative business impact across affected layers
steps.desc: Determine combined impact on network capacity and application responsiveness to prioritize mitigation sequencing.
steps.outcome: Impact prioritization documented, guiding which vector to mitigate first.

steps.title: Deploy WAF rules and bot-management challenges for L7 component
steps.desc: Apply WAF rate limiting, signature-based rules, and challenge mechanisms (CAPTCHA/JS challenge) to mitigate the application-layer flood concurrently.
steps.guidance: L7 mitigation must run in parallel with network-layer scrubbing since the two vectors require different controls.
steps.outcome: Application-layer request volume and error rate reduced.

steps.title: Coordinate response across network and application teams
steps.desc: Establish a joint incident bridge between network engineering and application/security teams to synchronize multi-vector mitigation.
steps.guidance: Multi-vector attacks require tight coordination to avoid mitigation gaps as the attacker shifts between vectors.
steps.outcome: Unified incident bridge established with clear ownership per vector.

ITID-41342.def: A denial-of-service attack, or the credible threat of one, launched or maintained alongside an extortion demand in which the adversary requires payment (typically cryptocurrency) to stop an ongoing attack or to prevent a threatened future attack, distinguishing it from purely technical DDoS incidents by the presence of a financial coercion element.
ITID-41342.purpose: Captures a DDoS attack paired with an extortion demand threatening continued or escalated attack unless a ransom is paid (Ransom DDoS / RDoS).
scopeIncludes: A live DDoS attack accompanied by a ransom demand communicated to the victim (email, message on a landing page, or via a third party)
A demonstration/proof-of-capability attack burst paired with a ransom demand for a threatened larger follow-on attack
scopeExcludes: Pre-attack extortion emails with no attack yet launched, which are scoped separately (see ITID-41711 Pre-Attack Extortion Email Threatening DDoS Unless Paid)
A DDoS attack with no extortion/ransom component (see the relevant technical DDoS leaf)
Recurring scheduled attacks after non-payment, which are scoped separately (see ITID-41731 Recurring Scheduled DDoS Attacks After Ransom Non-Payment)
ITID-41342.severity: High by default given the combined availability and extortion/financial-crime dimensions; escalate further if the ransom note references specific insider knowledge suggesting reconnaissance or prior compromise.
ITID-41342.priority: P1, treated as both an active availability incident and an extortion/financial-crime event.
ITID-41342.escalation: Escalate to incident command, legal, and law enforcement liaison immediately alongside standard DDoS mitigation escalation; do not engage with or pay the ransom without executive and legal sign-off.
indicators: Ransom note or extortion communication referencing an ongoing or imminent DDoS attack
A demonstration attack burst timed closely with the extortion communication
Payment demand denominated in cryptocurrency with a payment deadline tied to attack escalation
vectors: Any of the technical DDoS vectors documented elsewhere in this taxonomy, deployed specifically to lend credibility to the extortion demand
Named or impersonated well-known threat actor branding used to increase perceived credibility of the threat
rootCauses: Insufficient standing DDoS mitigation capacity, increasing the credibility/effectiveness of the extortion threat
No pre-established incident and legal response process for extortion-paired attacks
mitreTechniques: T1498.001 Network Denial of Service: Direct Network Flood
controls: Always-on DDoS mitigation reducing the credibility/effectiveness of the extortion threat
Pre-established legal and law enforcement liaison process for extortion incidents
Organizational policy against ransom payment, communicated in advance to reduce decision-time pressure during an incident
ITID-41342.detection: Strong on the technical attack component; the extortion component is detected via communication channel monitoring (email, web forms) rather than network telemetry.
ITID-41342.response: Engage standard DDoS mitigation for the technical attack; route the extortion communication to legal and law enforcement liaison; do not pay without executive/legal sign-off; preserve all extortion communications as evidence.
metrics: Time from attack/threat to legal and law enforcement notification
Ransom amount demanded
Attack duration/impact relative to ransom deadline
ITID-41342.notes: Differentiating axis for the Hybrid DDoS Attack group: this leaf combines DDoS with financial extortion, as opposed to combining network and application layers or pairing with a concurrent intrusion.

playbook.name: DDoS Combined with Ransomware Extortion Demand (RDoS)
playbook.description: A DDoS attack is accompanied by a ransom/extortion demand threatening continued or escalated attacks unless payment is made.

steps.title: Confirm attack and preserve the extortion communication
steps.desc: Verify the DDoS is active via traffic analysis and preserve the ransom note/email/communication in full (headers, payment details, threat actor branding) as evidence.
steps.guidance: Do not reply to or engage the threat actor. Capture screenshots and original message headers for Legal/Law Enforcement.
steps.outcome: Attack confirmed and extortion communication preserved as evidence with chain of custody maintained.

steps.title: Engage DDoS scrubbing provider immediately
steps.desc: Activate upstream scrubbing/mitigation regardless of ransom demand validity, treating the technical attack as the primary containment priority.
steps.outcome: Attack traffic scrubbed; origin load normalizes.

steps.title: Sustain mitigation through threatened escalation window
steps.desc: Maintain and tune mitigation controls through any deadline stated in the ransom note, anticipating a possible escalation attempt.
steps.outcome: Attack pressure withstood without service impact through the threatened window.

steps.title: Confirm service restoration and monitor for recurrence
steps.desc: Validate services return to baseline and maintain heightened monitoring given the actor's demonstrated willingness to attack.
steps.outcome: Services stable; extended monitoring window established given RDoS recurrence risk.

steps.title: Document incident, Legal/Law Enforcement engagement, and mitigation posture
steps.desc: Capture full timeline including extortion communication handling, Legal/Law Enforcement coordination, and technical mitigation effectiveness.
steps.outcome: Report finalized with follow-up actions including any policy refinement on RDoS response.

steps.title: Assess ransom demand credibility against demonstrated capability
steps.desc: Evaluate whether the actor has demonstrated real attack capability (already-observed traffic) versus an empty threat, and check threat intel for the named actor/brand's track record.
steps.guidance: Cross-reference cryptocurrency wallet addresses and actor branding against known RDoS campaign trackers.
steps.outcome: Credibility assessment documented to inform response posture.

steps.title: Notify Legal and Law Enforcement; do not engage or pay
steps.desc: Escalate the extortion demand to Legal counsel and relevant law enforcement (e.g., FBI/national cyber unit) per organizational ransom policy. Do not communicate with or pay the threat actor.
steps.guidance: Payment does not guarantee attack cessation and may mark the organization as a repeat target; follow established ransomware non-payment policy.
steps.outcome: Legal and Law Enforcement formally notified; no payment or direct engagement made.
steps.abort: If organizational leadership/Legal determine engagement is warranted in a specific case, route all communication through Legal only.

ITID-41343.def: A denial-of-service attack launched concurrently with, or immediately preceding, a separate intrusion or data-exfiltration effort, where the DDoS traffic is intended (or suspected) to serve as a smokescreen that consumes SOC attention, logging capacity, and incident-response resources while the primary breach activity proceeds with reduced scrutiny.
ITID-41343.purpose: Captures a DDoS attack used deliberately as a diversion to draw defender attention and resources away from a concurrent, separate intrusion or data breach.
scopeIncludes: DDoS attacks confirmed or strongly suspected to be timed alongside a separate, concurrent intrusion or exfiltration event
Cases where post-incident analysis reveals unauthorized access or data movement occurring during the window of DDoS-driven SOC distraction
scopeExcludes: A DDoS attack with no evidence of a concurrent intrusion (see the relevant technical DDoS leaf)
A DDoS attack paired with extortion but no separate intrusion (see DDoS Combined with Ransomware Extortion Demand)
ITID-41343.severity: Critical: this pattern indicates the DDoS is not the primary objective but a diversion for a more damaging concurrent compromise, warranting full incident response scope beyond availability restoration alone.
ITID-41343.priority: P1, with mandatory parallel investigation for concurrent intrusion activity regardless of the DDoS's own technical severity.
ITID-41343.escalation: Escalate to incident command and threat hunting/forensics immediately; do not close the incident as resolved once availability is restored without a dedicated concurrent-intrusion investigation.
indicators: Unusual authentication, data-access, or lateral-movement activity occurring during the DDoS attack window
SOC/logging capacity degradation coinciding with the DDoS event, plausibly masking other alerts
Post-incident forensic evidence of access or exfiltration timestamped within the attack window
vectors: Any of the technical DDoS vectors documented elsewhere in this taxonomy, deployed specifically for its diversionary/resource-consumption effect
Coordinated campaigns pairing a hired or self-operated DDoS with a separate intrusion team or toolset
rootCauses: SOC alerting/logging capacity insufficiently resilient to volume spikes, allowing genuine alerts to be missed during a DDoS event
No standing procedure requiring a parallel intrusion investigation whenever a significant DDoS event occurs
mitreTechniques: T1498.001 Network Denial of Service: Direct Network Flood
controls: SOC alerting/logging infrastructure resilient to traffic-volume spikes (out-of-band or rate-independent alerting paths)
Standing procedure to run a parallel intrusion investigation for any significant DDoS event
Upstream DDoS scrubbing to preserve SOC visibility during the attack
ITID-41343.detection: Moderate: the DDoS itself is easily detected, but confirming the smokescreen hypothesis requires deliberate parallel forensic investigation rather than passive monitoring alone.
ITID-41343.response: Engage standard DDoS mitigation while simultaneously initiating a parallel threat-hunting investigation for concurrent intrusion activity; do not close the incident until both tracks are resolved.
metrics: Time to initiate parallel intrusion investigation after DDoS detection
Confirmed vs. suspected smokescreen incidents per year
Outcome of parallel investigation (confirmed intrusion found or ruled out)
ITID-41343.notes: Differentiating axis for the Hybrid DDoS Attack group: this leaf combines DDoS with a separate concurrent intrusion as its true objective, as opposed to combining network/application layers within the DDoS itself or pairing with extortion.

playbook.name: DDoS Used as Smokescreen for Concurrent Data Breach/Intrusion
playbook.description: A DDoS attack is being used to distract security teams and consume monitoring/response resources while a concurrent, separate intrusion or data exfiltration is attempted.

steps.title: Confirm DDoS activity via traffic analysis
steps.desc: Verify and characterize the DDoS attack through standard volumetric/traffic analysis.
steps.outcome: DDoS confirmed with vector and scale documented.

steps.title: Engage DDoS scrubbing provider
steps.desc: Activate upstream scrubbing/mitigation for the DDoS component while the parallel intrusion investigation continues.
steps.outcome: DDoS traffic scrubbed; origin load normalizes.

steps.title: Sustain DDoS mitigation and complete intrusion eradication if applicable
steps.desc: Continue DDoS mitigation to full resolution while completing eradication steps for any confirmed intrusion (credential resets, malware removal, patching exploited vector).
steps.outcome: Both the DDoS and any confirmed intrusion are fully eradicated.

steps.title: Validate service restoration and confirm no residual intrusion footholds
steps.desc: Confirm services are stable and, if an intrusion was found, verify no backdoors, persistence mechanisms, or residual unauthorized access remain.
steps.outcome: Services restored and environment confirmed clean of any intrusion artifacts.

steps.title: Document combined incident and review SOC surge-capacity procedures
steps.desc: Capture the full dual-track timeline, evaluate whether SOC staffing/procedures adequately supported simultaneous DDoS response and intrusion investigation, and recommend improvements.
steps.outcome: Report finalized with follow-up actions on SOC surge-capacity and monitoring coverage during DDoS events.

steps.title: Investigate for a concurrent intrusion in parallel with DDoS response
steps.desc: Assign a separate response track to review authentication logs, endpoint/EDR alerts, IDS/IPS, and privileged-account activity during the DDoS window for signs of an unrelated intrusion or exfiltration attempt.
steps.guidance: Do not let DDoS response consume all security team attention — this step must run concurrently, not after, DDoS mitigation. Look specifically for anomalies that a distracted SOC might otherwise miss: new admin accounts, unusual outbound data transfer, disabled logging, or lateral movement.
steps.outcome: A documented determination of whether a concurrent intrusion is occurring, with any findings escalated as a separate incident.

steps.title: Contain any confirmed concurrent intrusion independently
steps.desc: If the parallel investigation confirms an intrusion, apply standard intrusion-containment actions (isolate affected hosts, disable compromised credentials) without waiting for DDoS resolution.
steps.guidance: Treat the intrusion as its own incident with its own containment timeline, tracked alongside the DDoS response.
steps.outcome: Confirmed intrusion contained independently of DDoS mitigation status.
steps.abort: If no intrusion evidence is found, close this containment track and document the negative finding.

ITID-41344.def: A denial-of-service event confirmed as combining DDoS with another element (a second attack layer, extortion, or a concurrent intrusion) where the specific combination has not yet been determined.
ITID-41344.purpose: Intake bucket for hybrid DDoS activity that cannot yet be attributed to a specific combination pattern.
scopeIncludes: Initial triage of a suspected hybrid DDoS attack before the specific combination pattern is confirmed
scopeExcludes: Any attack already confirmed as cross-layer multi-vector, extortion-paired (RDoS), or intrusion-smokescreen (reclassify to the specific leaf once confirmed)
ITID-41344.severity: High pending confirmation, given the elevated risk profile of any hybrid pattern; reassess once the combination is identified.
ITID-41344.priority: P1 pending triage; maintain until a specific, lower-risk combination is ruled in or a benign explanation is confirmed.
ITID-41344.escalation: Escalate to incident command for full-scope investigation; reclassify once confirmed.
indicators: A DDoS attack with some indication of an additional dimension (communication, timing correlation with other activity) not yet confirmed at initial detection
vectors: Unconfirmed at time of intake
rootCauses: Insufficient initial visibility to determine the specific hybrid combination
mitreTechniques: T1498.001 Network Denial of Service: Direct Network Flood
controls: DDoS Mitigation Activation SOP engagement
Parallel intrusion investigation as a precaution pending clarification
ITID-41344.detection: Sufficient to detect the DDoS and a suspected additional dimension but insufficient to classify the specific combination at time of intake.
ITID-41344.response: Engage general DDoS mitigation immediately and treat as potentially hybrid (parallel intrusion investigation, legal notification readiness) until ruled out; reclassify once confirmed.
metrics: Count of incidents landing in this catch-all per quarter
ITID-41344.notes: Triage/intake bucket only; reclassify once the specific hybrid combination is confirmed. Given the elevated risk profile of this Tier-4 group, err toward treating incidents here as potentially serious until ruled out.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Hybrid DDoS Attack
playbook.description: A DDoS attack combining multiple techniques or vectors in a manner not otherwise classified is degrading or denying service availability.

steps.title: Characterize the hybrid attack's combined vectors
steps.desc: Analyze network and application telemetry to identify which combination of techniques (volumetric, protocol, application-layer, or other) is being used.
steps.guidance: Correlate NetFlow, WAF, and APM data on a shared timeline to build a complete picture of the attack composition.
steps.outcome: Hybrid attack composition documented with each contributing vector characterized.

steps.title: Engage DDoS scrubbing provider for network-layer components
steps.desc: Activate upstream scrubbing to address volumetric/protocol-layer components of the attack.
steps.outcome: Network-layer attack traffic reduced.

steps.title: Sustain and tune mitigation across all identified vectors
steps.desc: Continuously monitor and adjust mitigation as the attacker shifts between vectors until the attack fully subsides.
steps.outcome: All attack vectors eliminated or fully mitigated.

steps.title: Validate service restoration across all layers
steps.desc: Confirm network and application metrics return to baseline before relaxing controls in stages.
steps.outcome: Services confirmed stable across all previously affected layers.
steps.abort: If any vector resumes, revert the relevant layer's mitigation.

steps.title: Document incident and review multi-vector readiness
steps.desc: Capture full timeline and composition of the hybrid attack, and recommend readiness improvements for combined-vector scenarios.
steps.outcome: Report finalized with follow-up actions tracked.

steps.title: Assess business impact across affected services
steps.desc: Determine which services are impacted and to what degree, prioritizing mitigation order.
steps.outcome: Impact assessment documented with prioritized service list.

steps.title: Apply WAF and rate-limiting controls for any application-layer components
steps.desc: Deploy WAF rules, rate limiting, or bot challenges for any application-layer elements identified in the hybrid attack.
steps.outcome: Application-layer impact reduced.

ITID-41411.def: A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary generates a high volume of DNS queries for randomly generated, non-existent subdomains of a target domain, forcing the target's authoritative servers (and any upstream recursive resolvers in the resolution path) to process each unique, uncacheable query and typically return NXDOMAIN responses, exhausting query-processing capacity.
ITID-41411.purpose: Captures a DNS-based DoS technique (commonly 'water torture') that floods a target's DNS infrastructure with queries for random, non-existent subdomains to exhaust resolution capacity.
scopeIncludes: Random-label subdomain query floods against a target domain intended to defeat caching and force full resolution processing for each unique query
Attacks producing a sustained high rate of NXDOMAIN responses from the target's authoritative or recursive infrastructure
scopeExcludes: Direct high-volume repeated queries for existing, valid records against authoritative servers (see Authoritative DNS Server Direct Query Flood)
Queries deliberately structured to bypass resolver caching for existing records rather than using random non-existent labels (see Recursive Resolver Cache-Bypass Query Flood)
DNS used as a reflection/amplification vector against an unrelated third-party victim (see DNS Amplification Attack under Amplification Attacks)
ITID-41411.severity: High: because each query is unique and uncacheable, this technique can exhaust authoritative/recursive capacity at a query rate far lower than would be needed for a generic flood.
ITID-41411.priority: P2 on detection; escalate to P1 on confirmed authoritative or recursive resolver saturation affecting legitimate resolution.
ITID-41411.escalation: Escalate to DNS infrastructure/network operations and, if using a managed DNS provider, to that provider's abuse/support channel immediately on confirmed saturation.
indicators: Sharp spike in DNS query rate for the target domain with a high proportion of distinct, randomized subdomain labels
Elevated NXDOMAIN response rate from authoritative servers
Recursive resolver query queues/caches showing high churn with low cache-hit ratio for the target domain
vectors: Botnet-driven or scripted DNS query generation with randomized subdomain labels targeting a specific domain
Booter/stresser platforms offering DNS water-torture attack modules
rootCauses: Authoritative DNS infrastructure sized without headroom for high-uniqueness query floods
No response-rate-limiting (RRL) or anomaly-based filtering on the authoritative DNS tier
Reliance on a single DNS provider/instance with no secondary or anycast redundancy
mitreTechniques: T1499.002 Endpoint Denial of Service: Service Exhaustion Flood
controls: DNS response-rate-limiting (RRL) on authoritative servers
Anycast-distributed, managed DNS provider with built-in DDoS mitigation
Query-pattern anomaly detection distinguishing randomized-label floods from legitimate traffic
Secondary/redundant DNS provider for failover
ITID-41411.detection: Strong technical signal from DNS query logs showing label randomness and NXDOMAIN response rate.
ITID-41411.response: Engage managed DNS provider's mitigation or enable RRL immediately; verify resolution capacity recovery for legitimate queries.
metrics: Peak query rate observed
NXDOMAIN response rate during event
Time to mitigation engagement
ITID-41411.notes: Differentiating axis for the DNS Query Flooding group is the query target/pattern: this leaf targets non-existent random subdomains specifically to defeat caching.

playbook.name: Random Subdomain/NXDOMAIN Flood Attack
playbook.description: The attacker floods a DNS resolver/authoritative server with queries for random, non-existent subdomains of a target domain, exhausting resolver cache and CPU resources handling NXDOMAIN responses.

steps.title: Confirm NXDOMAIN flood via query-name randomization and response-code analysis
steps.desc: Analyze DNS server query logs for an abnormal spike in queries for random, never-before-seen subdomains of a specific domain, correlated with a surge in NXDOMAIN responses.
