steps.guidance: Check DNS query logs for a high proportion of unique, randomly-generated subdomain labels (e.g., 'a8f3k2.example.com') resulting in NXDOMAIN, distinct from normal query patterns.
steps.outcome: Confirmed random-subdomain/NXDOMAIN flood pattern with targeted domain and query rate documented.

steps.title: Enable DNS Response Rate Limiting (RRL) on authoritative servers
steps.desc: Configure Response Rate Limiting on the authoritative DNS servers for the targeted domain to cap the rate of identical or NXDOMAIN responses sent to any single source.
steps.guidance: RRL is specifically designed to mitigate this attack pattern; tune thresholds to avoid impacting legitimate resolvers making bulk legitimate queries.
steps.outcome: NXDOMAIN response flood volume substantially reduced without impacting legitimate DNS resolution.
steps.abort: If legitimate high-volume resolvers are impacted, add allowlist exceptions for known-good large resolver IPs.
steps.tool: BIND RRL / PowerDNS / commercial DNS provider RRL feature

steps.title: Tune resolver cache and negative-caching behavior for NXDOMAIN resilience
steps.desc: Ensure negative caching (caching of NXDOMAIN responses) is properly configured to reduce repeated authoritative-server load for previously-seen bogus queries, and review resolver resource limits.
steps.guidance: Confirm negative TTL settings are reasonable and that resolver memory/cache limits are sized appropriately for sustained attack conditions.
steps.outcome: Resolver infrastructure more resilient to repeated or sustained NXDOMAIN query patterns.

steps.title: Confirm DNS resolution performance returns to normal and RRL retained
steps.desc: Monitor DNS query success rate and resolver latency to confirm they return to normal baseline, retaining RRL configuration permanently.
steps.guidance: Test resolution from multiple external vantage points to confirm no legitimate resolution impact.
steps.outcome: Normal DNS operation restored with permanent RRL hardening retained.

steps.title: Document incident and confirm RRL coverage across all authoritative DNS infrastructure
steps.desc: Record the attack and audit all authoritative DNS servers for the organization's domains to confirm RRL (or equivalent managed-provider protection) is consistently enabled.
steps.guidance: Include an inventory of all authoritative DNS infrastructure and RRL status in the after-action report.
steps.outcome: After-action report with a broader DNS-hardening remediation list if gaps were found elsewhere.

steps.title: Identify query source pattern (direct or via open resolvers)
steps.desc: Determine whether queries arrive directly from attacker-controlled sources or are being relayed/amplified through open recursive resolvers being abused by the attacker.
steps.guidance: Check source IP diversity and whether sources correspond to known open-resolver infrastructure versus a distributed botnet.
steps.outcome: Documented query-source pattern informing containment approach (direct blocking vs. resolver-side rate limiting).

steps.title: Engage upstream DNS provider/scrubbing for volumetric relief
steps.desc: If using a managed DNS provider, engage their DDoS mitigation capabilities; otherwise engage upstream network-layer scrubbing for the DNS server's IP.
steps.guidance: Many managed DNS providers (Route53, Cloudflare DNS, NS1) have built-in large-scale query-flood mitigation.
steps.outcome: Attack query volume further reduced via provider-level mitigation.

steps.title: Confirm negative-caching and resolver tuning changes did not affect legitimate resolution
steps.desc: Verify that the negative-caching and resolver resource-limit tuning applied during eradication have not introduced any unexpected resolution behavior for legitimate queries.
steps.guidance: Spot-check resolution of a sample of legitimate subdomains and previously-nonexistent-but-now-valid records.
steps.outcome: Confirmed no adverse impact from tuning changes.

ITID-41412.def: A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary sends a high rate of DNS queries to a recursive resolver, each crafted (through randomization, TTL manipulation assumptions, or query variation) to avoid a cache hit, forcing the resolver to perform full iterative resolution against authoritative servers for every query and exhausting the resolver's processing capacity.
ITID-41412.purpose: Captures a DoS attack that floods a recursive DNS resolver with queries deliberately structured to bypass its cache, forcing repeated full resolution work.
scopeIncludes: Query floods against recursive resolvers specifically engineered to defeat cache hits for otherwise-existing, valid records
Attacks primarily impacting resolver-side capacity rather than the authoritative server tier
scopeExcludes: Random non-existent subdomain floods (the water-torture pattern, which also defeats caching but via non-existent labels — see Random Subdomain/NXDOMAIN Flood Attack)
Direct floods against authoritative servers bypassing any recursive resolver (see Authoritative DNS Server Direct Query Flood)
ITID-41412.severity: High: cache-bypass techniques allow attackers to impose disproportionate resolver-side processing cost per query.
ITID-41412.priority: P2 on detection; escalate to P1 on confirmed resolver saturation affecting legitimate resolution for downstream clients.
ITID-41412.escalation: Escalate to DNS infrastructure/network operations immediately on confirmed resolver saturation.
indicators: Sharp spike in recursive resolver query rate with abnormally low cache-hit ratio
Resolver CPU/memory utilization spiking disproportionately to raw query volume
Elevated upstream (resolver-to-authoritative) query rate corresponding to the cache-bypass pattern
vectors: Scripted or botnet-driven query generation using query variation techniques specifically intended to avoid resolver cache hits
rootCauses: Recursive resolver capacity sized without accounting for low-cache-hit-ratio attack scenarios
No query-rate-limiting per source on the recursive resolver tier
Resolver not configured with negative-caching or other cache-efficiency hardening
mitreTechniques: T1499.002 Endpoint Denial of Service: Service Exhaustion Flood
controls: Per-source query rate-limiting on recursive resolvers
Negative-caching and cache-efficiency hardening
Resolver capacity sized with headroom for low-cache-hit-ratio scenarios
Restricting recursive resolution to authorized/internal clients only (closing open-resolver posture also reduces this attack surface)
ITID-41412.detection: Strong technical signal from resolver query logs and cache-hit-ratio metrics.
ITID-41412.response: Apply per-source rate-limiting on the resolver immediately; verify resolver capacity and cache-hit-ratio recovery.
metrics: Resolver cache-hit ratio during event vs. baseline
Resolver CPU/memory utilization during event
Time to rate-limiting engagement
ITID-41412.notes: Differentiating axis for the DNS Query Flooding group: this leaf targets the recursive resolver tier via cache-bypass on otherwise-valid queries, distinct from the random-non-existent-subdomain pattern of water torture.

playbook.name: Recursive Resolver Cache-Bypass Query Flood
playbook.description: The attacker sends queries deliberately crafted to bypass resolver caching (e.g., randomized query names or cache-control-defeating patterns) against a recursive resolver, forcing expensive full recursive lookups for every query.

steps.title: Confirm cache-bypass query flood via cache-hit-ratio drop and CPU correlation
steps.desc: Analyze recursive resolver metrics for a sudden drop in cache-hit ratio correlated with a CPU/resource utilization spike, driven by queries for unique or randomized names that force full recursive resolution.
steps.guidance: Check resolver query logs for a high proportion of unique query names that were never previously cached, distinct from legitimate diverse browsing traffic.
steps.outcome: Confirmed cache-bypass flood pattern with query characteristics and resolver resource impact documented.

steps.title: Restrict recursive query access to authorized client networks only
steps.desc: If the resolver was found to allow recursion from unauthorized/internet sources, immediately restrict recursive access to trusted internal client networks only.
steps.guidance: Configure 'allow-recursion' (BIND) or equivalent to trusted networks only; this alone may fully resolve the attack if the resolver was inappropriately open.
steps.outcome: Attack query volume reaching the resolver eliminated or substantially reduced.
steps.abort: If legitimate external partners require recursive access, add explicit allowlist entries.

steps.title: Scale resolver capacity and tune cache size/negative caching for resilience
steps.desc: Assess whether resolver cache size and compute capacity should be increased, and confirm negative caching is properly configured to reduce repeated lookups.
steps.guidance: Larger cache sizes and appropriate TTL handling reduce the effectiveness of future cache-bypass attempts.
steps.outcome: Resolver infrastructure more resilient to future cache-bypass query patterns.

steps.title: Confirm resolver performance returns to normal and access restrictions retained
steps.desc: Monitor resolver CPU and query latency to confirm return to normal baseline, retaining access-control and rate-limiting hardening permanently.
steps.guidance: Test resolution from authorized internal clients to confirm no legitimate impact.
steps.outcome: Normal resolver operation restored with permanent hardening retained.

steps.title: Document incident and audit all recursive resolvers for open-access exposure
steps.desc: Record the attack and audit all organization-owned recursive resolvers to confirm none are unintentionally open to the internet.
steps.guidance: Include results of an external open-resolver scan across the organization's public IP space.
steps.outcome: After-action report with a broader resolver-exposure remediation list if additional issues were found.

steps.title: Identify source pattern and whether the resolver is an open or restricted-access resolver
steps.desc: Determine the source of the flood queries and confirm whether the affected resolver should be restricting recursive query access to authorized clients only.
steps.guidance: If the resolver is unintentionally open to the internet, this is a critical exposure independent of this specific attack.
steps.outcome: Confirmed source pattern and resolver access-control posture documented.

steps.title: Apply per-source query-rate limiting on the resolver
steps.desc: Configure rate limiting on the number of recursive queries accepted per source IP/client network as defense in depth.
steps.guidance: This protects against a legitimate authorized client being compromised and generating the flood internally.
steps.outcome: Reduced ability for any single source to overwhelm resolver capacity.

steps.title: Confirm authorized external partners retain necessary resolver access
steps.desc: Verify any legitimate external partners requiring recursive access were correctly allowlisted and can resolve successfully after the access restriction was applied.
steps.guidance: Contact known partner integrations to confirm no disruption, if applicable.
steps.outcome: Confirmed no legitimate partner access was broken by the access-control hardening.

ITID-41413.def: A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary sends a high rate of DNS queries directly to a target's authoritative name servers, exhausting query-processing capacity through sheer volume rather than through cache-defeating randomization or third-party reflection.
ITID-41413.purpose: Captures a direct, high-volume query flood aimed straight at an organization's authoritative DNS servers, without a reflection, amplification, or cache-evasion mechanism.
scopeIncludes: High-volume direct query floods against authoritative DNS servers for existing, valid, or repeated record lookups
Attacks where the query pattern does not specifically exploit cache-bypass or amplification mechanics
scopeExcludes: Randomized non-existent subdomain floods (see Random Subdomain/NXDOMAIN Flood Attack)
Cache-bypass floods against recursive resolvers (see Recursive Resolver Cache-Bypass Query Flood)
DNS used as a reflection/amplification vector against a third party (see DNS Amplification Attack under Amplification Attacks)
ITID-41413.severity: High when sustained volume threatens authoritative server capacity or bandwidth; Medium if absorbed cleanly by anycast/managed DNS with headroom.
ITID-41413.priority: P2 on detection; escalate to P1 on confirmed authoritative server saturation affecting resolution for legitimate clients.
ITID-41413.escalation: Escalate to DNS infrastructure/network operations and, if using a managed provider, to that provider's abuse/support channel on confirmed saturation.
indicators: Sharp spike in query rate directed at authoritative name servers from many or few sources
Elevated query-processing latency or timeouts for legitimate resolution requests
Query pattern showing repeated lookups for a small set of existing records rather than randomized labels
vectors: Scripted or botnet-driven direct query floods targeting known authoritative server IPs
Booter/stresser platforms offering DNS flood attack modules
rootCauses: Authoritative DNS infrastructure sized without headroom for direct volumetric floods
No anycast distribution or managed DNS DDoS protection in place
No response-rate-limiting on the authoritative tier
mitreTechniques: T1499.001 Endpoint Denial of Service: OS Exhaustion Flood
controls: Anycast-distributed, managed DNS provider with built-in DDoS mitigation
DNS response-rate-limiting (RRL)
Secondary/redundant DNS provider for failover
ITID-41413.detection: Strong technical signal from authoritative server query logs and latency/timeout metrics.
ITID-41413.response: Engage managed DNS provider's mitigation immediately; verify resolution capacity recovery.
metrics: Peak query rate observed
Authoritative server response latency during event
Time to mitigation engagement
detections: Authoritative DNS server query-rate threshold alerting
ITID-41413.notes: Differentiating axis for the DNS Query Flooding group: this is the direct, non-cache-evasion, non-reflection flood variant, mapped to OS Exhaustion Flood rather than Service Exhaustion Flood since it targets raw server capacity through sheer direct volume.

playbook.name: Authoritative DNS Server Direct Query Flood
playbook.description: The attacker sends a high volume of legitimate-looking DNS queries directly to the target's authoritative name servers, aiming to exhaust their capacity and disrupt resolution of the target's domain(s) for all users.

steps.title: Confirm direct query flood via authoritative-server query-rate anomaly
steps.desc: Analyze authoritative DNS server query logs/metrics for an abnormal spike in query volume directed at the server's public IP, correlated with degraded query response times.
steps.guidance: Compare queries-per-second against baseline and check whether legitimate resolution requests are experiencing increased latency or timeouts.
steps.outcome: Confirmed authoritative-server flood with query rate and resolution impact documented.

steps.title: Enable Response Rate Limiting and engage managed DNS/anycast capacity
steps.desc: Enable RRL on the authoritative servers and, if using anycast or a managed/secondary DNS provider, ensure traffic is distributed across the full anycast network to absorb the flood.
steps.guidance: Anycast DNS deployments inherently distribute flood traffic across multiple points of presence, reducing impact at any single location.
steps.outcome: Flood traffic distributed and rate-limited, reducing impact on any single authoritative server instance.
steps.tool: DNS server RRL / anycast DNS provider console

steps.title: Assess and increase authoritative DNS redundancy/capacity
steps.desc: Evaluate whether the domain's authoritative DNS setup has sufficient redundancy (multiple providers, anycast, geographically distributed servers) to withstand future direct floods.
steps.guidance: A single self-hosted, non-anycast authoritative server is a significant single point of failure for this attack type; recommend migration to a resilient managed/anycast solution if not already in place.
steps.outcome: Documented redundancy assessment with concrete capacity/architecture improvement recommendations.

steps.title: Confirm DNS resolution for the domain returns to normal globally
steps.desc: Verify domain resolution succeeds reliably from multiple global vantage points, confirming full recovery.
steps.guidance: Use external DNS-checking tools from diverse geographic locations.
steps.outcome: Confirmed normal, reliable global resolution of the affected domain(s).

steps.title: Document incident and prioritize DNS redundancy/anycast investment if identified as a gap
steps.desc: Record the attack and, if authoritative DNS redundancy was found lacking, escalate this as a priority infrastructure resilience investment.
steps.guidance: Include a business case for anycast/secondary DNS investment in the after-action report if applicable.
steps.outcome: After-action report with DNS resilience investment recommendation tracked.

steps.title: Analyze query patterns and source distribution
steps.desc: Determine whether queries target a specific record type/name repeatedly or vary randomly, and assess source IP distribution (spoofed vs. genuine).
steps.guidance: Repeated queries for the same record may indicate a simpler flood, while randomized query names combined with this domain suggest a related NXDOMAIN-style technique layered on direct targeting.
steps.outcome: Documented query pattern and source characteristics informing mitigation approach.

steps.title: Engage upstream DDoS mitigation or managed DNS provider's flood protection
steps.desc: Engage the managed DNS provider's built-in DDoS mitigation capabilities, or upstream network-layer scrubbing if self-hosting authoritative DNS.
steps.guidance: Consider adding a secondary managed DNS provider with strong DDoS protection as a redundancy measure if self-hosted authoritative DNS lacks sufficient capacity.
steps.outcome: Attack query volume further reduced via provider-level mitigation.

steps.title: Confirm RRL and anycast/redundancy measures remain in place permanently
steps.desc: Verify the RRL configuration and any anycast/redundancy improvements applied during containment/eradication remain active post-recovery.
steps.guidance: Check configuration across all authoritative server instances for consistency.
steps.outcome: Confirmed permanent hardening remains active across all authoritative DNS infrastructure.

ITID-41414.def: A denial-of-service event exhibiting clear DNS query flooding characteristics (query-processing capacity exhaustion) where the specific pattern (random-subdomain water torture, resolver cache-bypass, or direct authoritative flood) has not yet been determined.
ITID-41414.purpose: Intake bucket for DNS query flooding activity that cannot yet be attributed to a specific target tier or query pattern.
scopeIncludes: Initial triage of a suspected DNS query flood before pattern analysis is complete
scopeExcludes: Any flood already confirmed as water-torture, cache-bypass, or direct authoritative (reclassify to the specific leaf once confirmed)
ITID-41414.severity: Medium-High pending confirmation; reassess once pattern is identified.
ITID-41414.priority: P2 pending triage; adjust once reclassified.
ITID-41414.escalation: Escalate to DNS infrastructure/network operations for query log analysis; reclassify once confirmed.
indicators: Elevated DNS query rate against the organization's DNS infrastructure without confirmed pattern classification at initial detection
vectors: Unconfirmed at time of intake
rootCauses: Insufficient initial query log visibility to determine pattern
mitreTechniques: T1499.002 Endpoint Denial of Service: Service Exhaustion Flood
controls: Anycast-distributed, managed DNS provider with built-in DDoS mitigation
DNS response-rate-limiting (RRL)
ITID-41414.detection: Sufficient to detect the DNS flood pattern but insufficient to classify specifics at time of intake.
ITID-41414.response: Engage managed DNS provider's general mitigation immediately; run query log analysis in parallel to reclassify.
metrics: Count of incidents landing in this catch-all per quarter
ITID-41414.notes: Triage/intake bucket only; reclassify once the specific pattern is confirmed.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General DNS Query Flooding
playbook.description: A DNS-layer flood is confirmed via elevated query rate and resolution impact, but the specific technique (NXDOMAIN/random-subdomain, cache-bypass, direct authoritative flood) has not yet been determined.

steps.title: Confirm DNS query flood via query-rate and resolution-impact analysis
steps.desc: Analyze DNS server logs/metrics for an abnormal query-rate spike correlated with degraded resolution performance (increased latency, timeouts, NXDOMAIN rate).
steps.guidance: Check both resolver-side and authoritative-side metrics depending on which DNS role is affected.
steps.outcome: Confirmed DNS flood condition with affected server role and resolution impact documented.

steps.title: Enable Response Rate Limiting and general query-rate limiting
steps.desc: Apply RRL and general per-source query-rate limiting as a broad-spectrum defense pending full technique classification.
steps.guidance: These general DNS-flood defenses are effective regardless of the specific sub-technique.
steps.outcome: Query flood volume reduced and resolution performance improved.

steps.title: Complete technique classification and apply targeted hardening
steps.desc: Finalize which DNS flooding technique was used and apply the more specific hardening measures from the corresponding playbook.
steps.guidance: Reclassify the incident to the specific ITID leaf if determination succeeds.
steps.outcome: Attack technique documented and technique-specific hardening applied.

steps.title: Confirm DNS resolution performance returns to normal
steps.desc: Monitor DNS query success rate and latency to confirm return to normal baseline, retaining general hardening permanently.
steps.guidance: Test resolution from multiple vantage points to confirm no residual impact.
steps.outcome: Normal DNS operation restored with permanent baseline hardening retained.

steps.title: Document incident and improve DNS flood technique classification tooling
steps.desc: Record why immediate technique classification was not possible and recommend detection tooling improvements.
steps.guidance: Include recommendations for enhanced DNS query-pattern analytics that would have sped up classification.
steps.outcome: After-action report with concrete detection tooling improvement items.

steps.title: Attempt technique classification via query-name and target analysis
steps.desc: Determine whether queries target random/non-existent subdomains, force cache bypass via uniqueness, or are direct floods against authoritative infrastructure, to allow pivot to a more specific playbook.
steps.guidance: If classification succeeds, transition to the corresponding specific DNS flooding playbook; otherwise proceed with general mitigation.
steps.outcome: Either successful reclassification or confirmed genuinely mixed/unclear technique.

steps.title: Engage managed DNS provider/upstream mitigation for additional relief
steps.desc: Engage the managed DNS provider's DDoS mitigation or upstream network-layer scrubbing if local mitigation is insufficient.
steps.guidance: Provide the traffic pattern characteristics gathered during identification to speed mitigation tuning.
steps.outcome: Attack traffic further reduced via provider-level mitigation.

steps.title: Confirm technique-specific hardening retained where classification succeeded
steps.desc: Where the attack was reclassified to a specific DNS flooding technique, confirm the corresponding technique-specific hardening measures remain in place post-recovery.
steps.guidance: Cross-check against the specific playbook's hardening recommendations if reclassification occurred.
steps.outcome: Confirmed appropriate hardening retained based on final classification.

ITID-41421.def: A denial-of-service condition resulting from an adversary announcing unauthorized, more-specific, or otherwise preferred BGP routes for a target organization's IP address space, causing internet traffic destined for the target to be diverted to the adversary's network (or a non-existent path) and effectively blackholed, denying legitimate users the ability to reach the target's services.
ITID-41421.purpose: Captures a denial-of-service outcome caused by an adversary illegitimately announcing (hijacking) BGP routes for the target's address space, diverting or blackholing its traffic.
scopeIncludes: Unauthorized BGP route announcements for a target's prefixes resulting in traffic diversion or blackholing
Both deliberate malicious hijacks and hijacks facilitated by a compromised network operator's infrastructure
scopeExcludes: Unintentional route leaks caused by configuration error rather than deliberate hijack intent (see BGP Route Leak Causing Traffic Misdirection/Overload)
Denial of service caused by disrupting an existing BGP session rather than announcing new unauthorized routes (see BGP Session Reset/Flap Attack)
ITID-41421.severity: Critical: a successful route hijack can cause complete unreachability of the affected address space for the duration of the propagated bad route, regardless of the target's own infrastructure health.
ITID-41421.priority: P1 immediately upon any confirmed unauthorized route announcement for organization-owned prefixes.
ITID-41421.escalation: Escalate to network operations, the organization's upstream transit providers, and regional internet registry/routing security contacts immediately; this typically requires external coordination beyond the organization's own infrastructure to resolve.
indicators: RPKI/route-monitoring alerts showing an unauthorized origin AS announcing the organization's prefixes
Sudden, widespread reachability loss for the affected address space reported from multiple external vantage points
BGP looking-glass or route-collector data showing a conflicting, more-specific announcement from an unexpected AS
vectors: Deliberate malicious route hijack from a rogue or compromised AS
Route hijack facilitated by a compromised internet exchange point or transit provider's infrastructure
rootCauses: Prefixes not covered by RPKI Route Origin Authorizations (ROAs), allowing an unauthorized origin to be accepted by RPKI-validating networks
Reliance on upstream/peer networks that do not enforce strict route filtering or RPKI validation
controls: RPKI Route Origin Authorizations (ROAs) for all organization-owned prefixes
Continuous BGP route-monitoring/hijack-detection service
Upstream transit provider relationships with strict route filtering (MANRS-aligned)
ITID-41421.detection: Strong when a dedicated route-monitoring service is in place; weak-to-none without one, since internal telemetry alone typically cannot see external route propagation.
ITID-41421.response: Engage upstream transit providers and routing security contacts immediately to withdraw/filter the unauthorized announcement; communicate status externally given the reachability impact; conduct post-incident review of RPKI/route-filtering posture.
metrics: Time to hijack detection
Duration of reachability loss
Time to route withdrawal/correction
ITID-41421.notes: This DoS mode does not map cleanly to the standard DoS-specific MITRE techniques since the mechanism is infrastructure/routing compromise rather than a flood; per taxonomy guidance it is mapped to TA0040 Impact paired with T1584.004 Compromise Infrastructure: Server as the closest applicable enabling technique.

playbook.name: BGP Route Hijack Causing Traffic Blackholing
playbook.description: A malicious or erroneous BGP announcement claims ownership of the organization's IP prefix (or a more specific sub-prefix), diverting or blackholing traffic destined for the organization's network.

steps.title: Confirm route hijack via BGP monitoring and route-origin validation
steps.desc: Analyze BGP route monitoring/collector data (e.g., RIPE RIS, RouteViews, commercial BGP monitoring) to confirm an unauthorized AS is announcing the organization's prefix or a more specific sub-prefix.
steps.guidance: Check for a sudden appearance of the organization's prefix (or a more-specific sub-prefix, which wins routing preference) originated by an unexpected AS number not matching the organization's authorized origin AS.
steps.outcome: Confirmed unauthorized route announcement with the offending AS number and announced prefix documented.
steps.abort: If the announcement is from a known, authorized secondary transit/peering arrangement, stand down and document as false positive.
steps.tool: BGP monitoring (RIPE RIS, BGPStream, commercial BGP monitoring service)

steps.title: Re-announce the legitimate, more-specific route to reclaim routing preference
steps.desc: Work with the network engineering team to announce a more-specific (longer-prefix) legitimate route than the hijacker's announcement, where technically feasible, to reclaim BGP path preference.
steps.guidance: BGP path selection prefers more-specific prefixes; if the hijacker announced a /24 within your /22, announcing your own /24 (if not already done) can override the hijack for that portion.
steps.outcome: Legitimate route re-established with routing preference restored for at least the more-specific prefix.

steps.title: Verify and strengthen RPKI Route Origin Validation for the organization's prefixes
steps.desc: Confirm the organization has valid RPKI ROAs (Route Origin Authorizations) published for all owned prefixes, and work with upstream providers to confirm they enforce RPKI-based route origin validation.
steps.guidance: If ROAs were missing or misconfigured, this significantly increases hijack risk; publish/correct ROAs and verify via public RPKI validator tools.
steps.outcome: Valid RPKI ROAs confirmed in place for all organization prefixes, reducing future hijack propagation risk among RPKI-enforcing networks.
steps.tool: RPKI ROA management / public RPKI validator

steps.title: Confirm route withdrawal and full traffic restoration via global monitoring
steps.desc: Monitor BGP route collectors and perform traceroutes from multiple global vantage points to confirm the malicious announcement has been withdrawn and traffic fully restored to legitimate paths.
steps.guidance: Route propagation/withdrawal can take time to fully clear globally; continue monitoring for at least 24-48 hours.
steps.outcome: Confirmed global route table shows only legitimate origin AS for the affected prefix(es).
steps.abort: If the malicious announcement persists after provider filtering requests, escalate further with additional evidence.

steps.title: Document incident and engage industry route-security initiatives
steps.desc: Record the incident timeline and impact, and consider joining or strengthening participation in industry route-security initiatives (e.g., MANRS) to reduce future hijack risk and improve community response.
steps.guidance: Include RPKI ROA coverage status and any provider-response-time gaps in the after-action report.
steps.outcome: After-action report with route-security posture improvements tracked.

steps.title: Assess traffic impact and affected prefix scope
steps.desc: Determine the scope of traffic being blackholed/diverted (which services/prefixes are affected) and the geographic/network extent of the hijack's propagation.
steps.guidance: Use looking-glass servers and traceroute from multiple global vantage points to assess how widely the malicious route has propagated and which regions/networks are affected.
steps.outcome: Documented impact scope informing prioritization and communication with upstream providers.

steps.title: Engage upstream transit providers and IXPs to filter the malicious announcement
steps.desc: Contact all upstream transit providers, peers, and relevant Internet Exchange Points (IXPs) requesting they filter/reject the malicious route announcement.
steps.guidance: Provide the offending AS number, announced prefix, and evidence of hijack (route monitoring data) to expedite provider response; escalate to NOC/abuse contacts with urgency given active traffic impact.
steps.outcome: Upstream providers filter the malicious announcement, restoring normal routing for affected traffic.

steps.title: Establish or refine a BGP route-hijack detection and alerting capability
steps.desc: If detection relied on manual/external notification rather than proactive monitoring, establish continuous automated BGP route monitoring with alerting for future rapid detection.
steps.guidance: Evaluate commercial or open-source BGP monitoring services that provide real-time hijack alerting for the organization's prefixes.
steps.outcome: Proactive BGP monitoring/alerting capability established or confirmed adequate.

ITID-41422.def: A denial-of-service condition resulting from a BGP route leak — the propagation of routes beyond their intended scope, typically due to a configuration error at a network operator (which may or may not be the target organization) — causing traffic destined for the target to be misdirected through an unintended, often under-provisioned path, resulting in congestion, packet loss, or complete unreachability.
ITID-41422.purpose: Captures a denial-of-service outcome caused by an unintentional or improperly filtered BGP route leak that misdirects or overloads traffic paths.
scopeIncludes: Route leaks originating at a third-party network operator (e.g. a customer or peer misconfiguring route redistribution) that cause traffic to the target to traverse an unintended, congested path
Route leaks originating within the organization's own network that cause self-inflicted reachability or congestion issues
scopeExcludes: Deliberate malicious route hijacks (see BGP Route Hijack Causing Traffic Blackholing)
Disruption of an existing BGP session rather than route propagation scope (see BGP Session Reset/Flap Attack)
ITID-41422.severity: High: while typically unintentional (configuration error rather than malicious intent), the availability impact can be as severe as a deliberate hijack, and this taxonomy classifies by impact/outcome rather than intent alone.
ITID-41422.priority: P1 upon confirmed traffic misdirection or overload affecting the organization's reachability, regardless of whether malicious intent is established.
ITID-41422.escalation: Escalate to network operations and affected upstream/peer transit providers immediately to identify and correct the leaking AS's route redistribution policy.
indicators: Route-monitoring alerts showing an unexpected, wider-than-intended propagation of the organization's or a peer's prefixes
Sudden latency increase, packet loss, or congestion on paths correlating with the leaked route's propagation
BGP looking-glass data showing an unusually long or unexpected AS path for traffic destined to the organization
vectors: Not typically an intentional attack vector, but relevant here as a denial-of-service outcome regardless of origin; where deliberate, a malicious actor may exploit a customer/peer network's known filtering weaknesses to induce a leak
rootCauses: Missing or improperly configured route filtering (max-prefix limits, AS-path filtering) at a customer, peer, or the organization's own network edge
No MANRS-aligned route-filtering agreements with upstream/peer networks
controls: Strict route filtering (max-prefix limits, AS-path/prefix filtering) at the organization's own network edge
MANRS-aligned filtering agreements with upstream/peer providers
Continuous BGP route-monitoring service to detect leaks affecting the organization's prefixes
ITID-41422.detection: Strong when a dedicated route-monitoring service is in place; weak-to-none without one.
ITID-41422.response: Engage upstream/peer transit providers and the leaking network operator (directly or via their upstream) to correct the route filtering; verify traffic path and reachability restoration.
metrics: Time to leak detection
Duration of degraded reachability/congestion
Time to route correction
ITID-41422.notes: Differentiating axis for the BGP Hijacking DoS group is the specific BGP manipulation mechanism; this leaf covers route leaks (typically configuration-error-driven) as opposed to deliberate hijacks or session-level disruption. MITRE mapping follows the same rationale as the hijack leaf given the shared infrastructure/routing nature.

playbook.name: BGP Route Leak Causing Traffic Misdirection/Overload
playbook.description: A misconfigured router (often at a peer or customer network) improperly re-announces routes learned from one provider to another, causing the organization's traffic to be misdirected through an unintended, often lower-capacity or higher-latency path, resulting in congestion or outage.

steps.title: Confirm route leak via unexpected AS-path changes and traffic path analysis
steps.desc: Analyze BGP route monitoring data for an unexpected change in the AS-path to the organization's prefix, or unexpected propagation of routes the organization did not intend to be visible via a particular peer/provider.
steps.guidance: Route leaks typically show an unusual AS-path length increase or an unexpected transit relationship appearing (e.g., a customer re-announcing a full-table feed to a peer), distinct from a deliberate hijack by an unrelated malicious AS.
steps.outcome: Confirmed route leak pattern with the leaking AS and affected path(s) documented.
steps.abort: If the path change reflects an intentional, coordinated routing policy change, stand down and document as false positive.

steps.title: Contact the leaking network's operator to withdraw the improper announcement
steps.desc: Identify and directly contact the network operator responsible for the route leak (often identifiable via the AS-path) requesting immediate withdrawal of the improperly re-announced routes.
steps.guidance: Route leaks are usually unintentional misconfigurations rather than malicious acts, so direct operator-to-operator contact is often faster than broad filtering campaigns.
steps.outcome: Leaking operator withdraws the improper announcement, restoring normal routing.

steps.title: Verify IRR/RPKI hygiene and encourage adoption of route-leak prevention mechanisms
steps.desc: Confirm the organization's own IRR route objects and RPKI ROAs are accurate, and, where relevant, engage with the leaking network's operator regarding adoption of route-leak prevention mechanisms (e.g., BGP roles/RFC 9234, prefix filtering based on IRR).
steps.guidance: While the leak originated externally, ensuring the organization's own routing registry data is accurate helps other networks correctly filter and reduces recurrence risk.
steps.outcome: Confirmed accurate IRR/RPKI data for organization prefixes; leak-prevention discussion documented with the responsible operator.

steps.title: Confirm traffic path and performance return to normal
steps.desc: Monitor BGP paths and network performance metrics to confirm traffic returns to the intended path with normal latency/throughput.
steps.guidance: Continue monitoring for recurrence for at least 24-48 hours given route leaks can recur from the same misconfigured source.
steps.outcome: Confirmed normal routing path and performance restored.
steps.abort: If the leak recurs, escalate further with the operator or their upstream provider.

steps.title: Document incident and review peering/transit relationships for leak exposure
steps.desc: Record the incident and review the organization's peering and transit relationships for exposure to similar leaks from other networks.
steps.guidance: Include recommendations for stricter prefix filtering (e.g., max-prefix limits, IRR-based filtering) on peering sessions in the after-action report.
steps.outcome: After-action report with peering hardening recommendations tracked.

steps.title: Assess performance/congestion impact of the misdirected path
steps.desc: Measure latency, packet loss, and throughput along the leaked/misdirected path compared to the intended path to quantify user-facing impact.
steps.guidance: Route leaks often cause congestion on an unintended link rather than a full outage; quantify the degradation to prioritize urgency.
steps.outcome: Documented performance impact informing escalation priority.

steps.title: Apply local BGP filtering/prepending to de-prioritize the leaked path
steps.desc: While awaiting the leaking operator's fix, apply local BGP policy (AS-path prepending, local-preference adjustment, or explicit filtering) to steer traffic away from the degraded path where technically feasible.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with upstream providers if filtering needs to be applied at their edge rather than solely on the organization's own routers.
steps.outcome: Traffic steered away from the congested/leaked path, restoring acceptable performance.

steps.title: Remove any temporary local traffic-steering workarounds once the leak is fully resolved
steps.desc: Roll back any temporary AS-path prepending or local-preference adjustments made during containment once the leaking operator confirms the fix and routing has stabilized.
steps.guidance: Verify with route monitoring data before removing workarounds to avoid re-exposure if the leak recurs.
steps.outcome: Normal routing policy restored without residual workaround configuration.

ITID-41423.def: A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary causes an established BGP session between the target's network and a peer/upstream to reset or repeatedly flap (drop and re-establish), for example via spoofed TCP RST injection against the BGP TCP session or by exhausting router resources handling the session, causing loss of routing information and consequent traffic disruption for the duration of each reset/reconvergence cycle.
ITID-41423.purpose: Captures a denial-of-service technique that disrupts an existing BGP peering session itself, rather than manipulating route announcements.
scopeIncludes: Attacks that inject spoofed TCP RST or other packets to forcibly tear down an established BGP session
Attacks that exhaust router CPU/memory handling BGP session state, causing session instability and repeated flapping
scopeExcludes: Unauthorized route announcements with the session itself remaining stable (see BGP Route Hijack Causing Traffic Blackholing / BGP Route Leak Causing Traffic Misdirection/Overload)
ITID-41423.severity: High: repeated session flapping causes route withdrawal/reconvergence churn that can degrade or interrupt reachability each cycle, and can also destabilize the broader routing table if propagated.
ITID-41423.priority: P1 upon confirmed deliberate session disruption affecting routing stability.
ITID-41423.escalation: Escalate to network operations and the affected peer/upstream transit provider immediately to investigate session-layer disruption and harden session protections.
indicators: BGP session logs showing repeated, abnormal resets/re-establishments outside of planned maintenance
Router CPU/memory utilization spikes correlated with BGP session instability
Routing table churn (rapid withdrawal/re-announcement cycles) correlated with session flap events
vectors: Spoofed TCP RST injection against an identified BGP session's TCP connection
Resource-exhaustion attacks targeting the router's control-plane capacity to handle BGP session state
rootCauses: BGP sessions not protected by TCP MD5/TCP-AO authentication or the Generalized TTL Security Mechanism (GTSM), making session-layer spoofing feasible
Router control-plane resources not adequately protected from external resource-exhaustion attempts
mitreTechniques: T1499.004 Endpoint Denial of Service: Application or System Exploitation
controls: TCP-AO or MD5 authentication on BGP sessions
Generalized TTL Security Mechanism (GTSM) to reject off-path spoofed packets
Control-plane policing/protection on routers to shield BGP process from resource exhaustion
ITID-41423.detection: Strong technical signal from BGP session logs and router control-plane telemetry.
ITID-41423.response: Verify and enable session authentication (TCP-AO/MD5) and GTSM immediately; engage the affected peer/upstream to investigate the source of disruption.
metrics: Count of abnormal session reset/flap events
Duration of routing instability per event
Time to session-hardening remediation
ITID-41423.notes: This leaf does not map cleanly to a specific MITRE DoS technique per taxonomy guidance, since it is a session/control-plane disruption rather than a data-plane flood or a route-announcement manipulation; mapped to TA0040 Impact with an empty technique list.

playbook.name: BGP Session Reset/Flap Attack
playbook.description: The attacker deliberately triggers repeated BGP session resets (flapping) between the organization's routers and peers/providers, typically via TCP-layer attacks against the BGP session, causing route instability and intermittent connectivity loss.

steps.title: Confirm BGP session flapping via router logs and session-state history
steps.desc: Analyze BGP router logs for an abnormal frequency of session establishment/teardown events (flapping) with one or more peers, correlated with intermittent connectivity or reachability issues.
steps.guidance: Check for repeated BGP session state transitions (Established -> Idle -> Established) occurring far more frequently than normal operational baseline.
steps.outcome: Confirmed BGP session flapping pattern with affected peer session(s) and flap frequency documented.
steps.abort: If flapping correlates with a known legitimate maintenance window or physical link issue, stand down and document as an infrastructure/operational issue rather than an attack.

steps.title: Enable BGP session protections (TTL Security/GTSM, MD5/TCP-AO authentication)
steps.desc: Enable BGP TTL Security (Generalized TTL Security Mechanism) and session authentication (MD5 or TCP Authentication Option) on the affected BGP session(s) to reject spoofed/off-path packets targeting the session.
steps.guidance: GTSM rejects packets that do not have the expected TTL for a directly-connected or intentionally-multi-hop peer, effectively blocking most off-path spoofed RST attacks; combine with session authentication for defense in depth.
steps.outcome: BGP session stability restored; spoofed/off-path attack packets rejected.
steps.abort: If enabling authentication requires coordinated change with the peer and causes a temporary outage, coordinate a maintenance window.

steps.title: Audit all BGP sessions for consistent security hardening
steps.desc: Review all BGP peering sessions across the organization's network edge to confirm GTSM, session authentication, and CoPP protections are applied consistently, not just to the affected session.
steps.guidance: A single unhardened session elsewhere could be targeted next; apply the fix as a fleet-wide configuration standard.
steps.outcome: Confirmed all BGP sessions have consistent security hardening applied.

steps.title: Confirm BGP session stability and route table convergence
steps.desc: Monitor BGP session state and route table stability over an extended period to confirm flapping has ceased and routes have fully converged.
steps.guidance: Monitor for at least 24 hours given BGP route dampening/convergence effects can mask brief residual instability.
steps.outcome: Confirmed stable BGP sessions with no further flapping observed.

steps.title: Document incident and codify BGP session hardening as a standard configuration baseline
steps.desc: Record the attack and ensure GTSM, session authentication, and CoPP settings are captured in the standard router configuration baseline for all future BGP peering deployments.
steps.guidance: Update infrastructure-as-code templates or configuration management baselines accordingly.
steps.outcome: After-action report with hardening settings codified into deployment standards.

steps.title: Determine attack vector: TCP RST injection, resource exhaustion, or physical/logical link disruption
steps.desc: Investigate whether the flapping is caused by spoofed TCP RST/attack packets targeting the BGP TCP session, router control-plane resource exhaustion, or an underlying physical/logical link problem being exploited.
steps.guidance: Capture packets on the BGP session's transport if feasible, and check router control-plane CPU/memory utilization during flap events to distinguish an active injection attack from resource exhaustion.
steps.outcome: Identified attack vector informing the appropriate containment measure.

steps.title: Apply control-plane policing to protect BGP process from resource exhaustion
steps.desc: Configure control-plane policing (CoPP) to rate-limit traffic destined to the router's BGP process, protecting it from being overwhelmed if resource exhaustion is contributing to the flapping.
steps.guidance: Ensure CoPP thresholds allow legitimate BGP keepalive/update traffic while limiting excessive or malformed traffic targeting the control plane.
steps.outcome: Router control-plane resources protected, reducing flap frequency caused by resource contention.

steps.title: Confirm peer relationship acknowledges and retains the security hardening changes
steps.desc: Coordinate with the peer to confirm session authentication/GTSM settings are correctly and permanently applied on both ends of the session.
steps.guidance: A mismatch or one-sided rollback of authentication settings could silently reintroduce the vulnerability.
steps.outcome: Confirmed consistent, permanent hardening on both sides of the peering session.

ITID-41424.def: A denial-of-service event confirmed as BGP-routing-related where the specific mechanism (unauthorized route hijack, route leak, or session disruption) has not yet been determined.
ITID-41424.purpose: Intake bucket for BGP-related denial-of-service activity that cannot yet be attributed to a specific manipulation mechanism.
scopeIncludes: Initial triage of a suspected BGP-related availability incident before mechanism analysis is complete
scopeExcludes: Any incident already confirmed as route hijack, route leak, or session-flap (reclassify to the specific leaf once confirmed)
ITID-41424.severity: High pending confirmation, given the potentially severe reachability impact of any BGP-related incident; reassess once mechanism is identified.
ITID-41424.priority: P1 pending triage, given the reachability-impact severity typical of this Tier-4 group.
ITID-41424.escalation: Escalate to network operations and upstream transit providers immediately for route/session analysis; reclassify once confirmed.
indicators: Reachability loss or degradation correlated with routing anomalies, without confirmed mechanism at initial detection
vectors: Unconfirmed at time of intake
rootCauses: Insufficient initial route-monitoring visibility to determine mechanism
controls: Continuous BGP route-monitoring service
Upstream transit provider escalation relationship
ITID-41424.detection: Sufficient to detect the reachability impact but insufficient to classify mechanism at time of intake.
ITID-41424.response: Engage upstream providers and route-monitoring analysis immediately; reclassify once the specific mechanism is confirmed.
metrics: Count of incidents landing in this catch-all per quarter
ITID-41424.notes: Triage/intake bucket only; reclassify once the specific BGP manipulation mechanism is confirmed.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General BGP Hijacking DoS
playbook.description: A BGP-layer routing anomaly causing traffic disruption is confirmed, but the specific mechanism (route hijack, route leak, session flap attack) has not yet been determined.

steps.title: Confirm BGP-layer routing anomaly via route monitoring and connectivity impact
steps.desc: Analyze BGP route monitoring data and connectivity metrics to confirm an abnormal routing event (unexpected origin AS, unexpected AS-path, or session instability) correlated with traffic disruption.
steps.guidance: Check route collector data for the organization's prefixes for any anomalous origin AS, path change, or announcement/withdrawal pattern.
steps.outcome: Confirmed BGP-layer anomaly with affected prefix(es)/session(s) and impact documented.

steps.title: Escalate to upstream providers and network engineering for coordinated investigation
steps.desc: Engage upstream transit providers' NOCs and internal network engineering simultaneously given the provider-dependent nature of most BGP-layer remediation.
steps.guidance: BGP-layer incidents are largely resolved through coordination with external network operators rather than purely internal action; initiate this escalation promptly regardless of final classification.
steps.outcome: Upstream providers and internal network engineering actively engaged in investigation and remediation.

steps.title: Complete mechanism classification and apply targeted remediation
steps.desc: Finalize which BGP-layer mechanism caused the disruption and apply the more specific remediation measures from the corresponding playbook.
steps.guidance: Reclassify the incident to the specific ITID leaf if determination succeeds.
steps.outcome: Mechanism documented and technique-specific remediation applied.

steps.title: Confirm routing stability and connectivity restoration via global monitoring
steps.desc: Monitor BGP route tables and connectivity from multiple vantage points to confirm full restoration of normal routing.
steps.guidance: Continue monitoring for at least 24-48 hours given potential for recurrence.
steps.outcome: Confirmed stable, normal routing restored globally.

steps.title: Document incident and improve BGP anomaly classification and monitoring capability
steps.desc: Record why immediate mechanism classification was not possible and recommend improved BGP monitoring/alerting tooling.
steps.guidance: Include recommendations for continuous automated BGP route monitoring with mechanism-specific alerting.
steps.outcome: After-action report with concrete monitoring tooling improvement items.

steps.title: Attempt mechanism classification via route/session analysis
steps.desc: Determine whether the anomaly is an unauthorized origin AS announcement (hijack), an improperly re-announced route (leak), or repeated session instability (flap attack), to allow pivot to a more specific playbook.
steps.guidance: If classification succeeds, transition to the corresponding specific BGP playbook; otherwise proceed with general escalation.
steps.outcome: Either successful reclassification or confirmed genuinely unclear mechanism requiring broader investigation.

steps.title: Apply general BGP session hardening as a precautionary measure
steps.desc: Verify and, if not already present, apply general BGP session protections (GTSM, session authentication) as a precaution pending full mechanism classification.
steps.guidance: These protections are broadly beneficial regardless of the specific final classification.
steps.outcome: Baseline BGP session hardening confirmed or applied.

steps.title: Confirm technique-specific remediation retained where classification succeeded
steps.desc: Where the incident was reclassified to a specific BGP mechanism, confirm the corresponding technique-specific remediation remains in place post-recovery.
steps.guidance: Cross-check against the specific playbook's remediation recommendations if reclassification occurred.
steps.outcome: Confirmed appropriate remediation retained based on final classification.

ITID-41431.def: A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary sends a high rate of SIP INVITE requests (the message that initiates a call setup) to a target VoIP server or session border controller, forcing it to allocate call-state resources for each attempted session until call-setup capacity is exhausted and legitimate calls can no longer be established.
ITID-41431.purpose: Captures a DoS attack that floods a VoIP/SIP infrastructure with INVITE requests to exhaust call-setup processing capacity.
scopeIncludes: High-rate SIP INVITE floods aimed at exhausting call-setup/session-state capacity on a SIP server or session border controller
Both malformed and well-formed INVITE floods, where the defining characteristic is the message type and volume rather than payload validity
scopeExcludes: SIP REGISTER floods aimed at registration capacity rather than call setup (see SIP REGISTER Flood Attack)
Toll fraud or unauthorized call routing achieved through successfully completed calls, which is a fraud-focused ITID rather than an availability-focused one
ITID-41431.severity: High for organizations dependent on VoIP for business-critical communications; escalate if confirmed call-setup failures are impacting legitimate users.
ITID-41431.priority: P2 on detection; escalate to P1 on confirmed call-setup capacity exhaustion affecting legitimate calls.
ITID-41431.escalation: Escalate to telephony/VoIP operations and the SIP trunk/carrier provider immediately on confirmed exhaustion.
indicators: Sharp spike in SIP INVITE messages per second at the session border controller
Rising call-setup failure rate for legitimate users
Session border controller CPU/session-table utilization spiking disproportionately to legitimate call volume
vectors: Scripted SIP flood tools or botnets targeting known SIP server/SBC endpoints
Booter/stresser platforms offering SIP flood attack modules
rootCauses: SIP infrastructure exposed to the internet without rate-limiting on INVITE messages
No dedicated session border controller with DoS protection in front of the core VoIP infrastructure
SIP trunk provider-side protections not enabled or not requested
mitreTechniques: T1499.002 Endpoint Denial of Service: Service Exhaustion Flood
controls: Session border controller with SIP-aware rate-limiting and DoS protection
Per-source INVITE rate-limiting
SIP trunk provider-side DDoS/flood protection
Restricting SIP signaling to authenticated/known peers where feasible
ITID-41431.detection: Strong technical signal from SBC/SIP server logs tracking INVITE rate and call-setup failure rate.
ITID-41431.response: Apply INVITE rate-limiting at the SBC immediately; engage carrier-side mitigation if available; verify call-setup capacity recovery.
metrics: Peak INVITE messages-per-second observed
Call-setup failure rate during event
Time to rate-limiting engagement
ITID-41431.notes: Differentiating axis for the SIP Flooding group is SIP method: this leaf targets call setup (INVITE), its sibling targets registration (REGISTER).

playbook.name: SIP INVITE Flood Attack (VoIP Call Setup Exhaustion)
playbook.description: The attacker sends a high volume of SIP INVITE requests to the organization's Session Border Controller (SBC)/VoIP infrastructure, exhausting call-setup processing capacity and disrupting legitimate voice service.

steps.title: Confirm SIP INVITE flood via SBC call-setup-rate anomaly
steps.desc: Analyze SBC/SIP proxy logs and metrics for an abnormal spike in INVITE message rate correlated with degraded call setup success rate or SBC CPU/resource utilization.
steps.guidance: Compare INVITE-per-second rate against baseline; check whether INVITEs originate from a small number of sources or are widely distributed.
steps.outcome: Confirmed SIP INVITE flood with request rate and SBC impact documented.
steps.abort: If the spike correlates with a known legitimate call-volume event, stand down and document as false positive.

steps.title: Apply SBC-level rate limiting and per-source INVITE throttling
steps.desc: Configure the SBC to rate-limit INVITE messages per source IP and overall, dropping excess requests before they consume call-processing resources.
steps.guidance: Most enterprise SBCs (e.g., Oracle/Acme Packet, Ribbon, AudioCodes) support granular per-message-type and per-source rate limiting specifically designed for this attack class.
steps.outcome: INVITE flood volume reduced to sustainable levels; legitimate call setup capacity restored.
steps.abort: If legitimate high-volume call center traffic is impacted, add an allowlist for known trunk/carrier source IPs.

steps.title: Verify SBC topology hiding and unnecessary SIP exposure hardening
steps.desc: Confirm the SBC is properly configured for topology hiding and that no internal SIP endpoints/registrars are directly exposed to the internet bypassing the SBC.
steps.guidance: Direct internet exposure of internal SIP infrastructure bypassing the hardened SBC is a common root-cause exposure enabling this and related attacks.
steps.outcome: Confirmed all SIP signaling is properly funneled through the hardened SBC with no bypass exposure.

steps.title: Confirm call setup success rate returns to normal and rate limits retained
steps.desc: Monitor call setup success rate and SBC resource utilization to confirm return to normal baseline, retaining rate-limiting configuration permanently.
steps.guidance: Test with representative legitimate call scenarios to confirm no false-positive blocking.
steps.outcome: Normal voice service restored with permanent hardening retained.

steps.title: Document incident and codify SBC rate-limiting as a standard VoIP security baseline
steps.desc: Record the attack and ensure SBC-level rate-limiting and topology-hiding configuration are part of the standard VoIP infrastructure hardening baseline.
steps.guidance: Update infrastructure-as-code templates or configuration management baselines accordingly.
steps.outcome: After-action report with hardening settings codified into deployment standards.

steps.title: Analyze source and call-parameter patterns for attack characteristics
steps.desc: Examine source IPs, called/calling party numbers, and SIP header patterns in the flood traffic to characterize the attack (e.g., random/invalid destination numbers, malformed headers, missing prior REGISTER).
steps.guidance: Attack INVITEs often target random or sequential destination numbers without a valid prior registration, distinct from legitimate call patterns.
steps.outcome: Documented attack characteristics with source IP list captured.

steps.title: Block or geo-restrict source IPs/trunks not associated with legitimate carriers
steps.desc: Apply firewall/SBC access-control rules restricting SIP signaling to known, authorized carrier/trunk IP ranges where the deployment model allows.
steps.guidance: If the organization only receives legitimate SIP traffic from a defined set of carrier peers, restricting to those ranges can eliminate the bulk of internet-sourced flood traffic.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized source traffic blocked, further reducing attack volume reaching the SBC.
steps.abort: If legitimate remote/mobile SIP clients require broader access, scope restrictions accordingly.

steps.title: Confirm topology-hiding and access restrictions did not disrupt legitimate carrier trunks
steps.desc: Verify all legitimate carrier trunks and remote endpoints continue to function correctly under the hardened SBC configuration.
steps.guidance: Test call setup from each known legitimate trunk/carrier connection.
steps.outcome: Confirmed no legitimate trunk connectivity was broken by the hardening changes.

ITID-41432.def: A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary sends a high rate of SIP REGISTER requests (the message endpoints use to bind their location for incoming calls) to a target VoIP server, forcing it to process registration/authentication attempts for each request until registrar capacity is exhausted, disrupting the ability of legitimate endpoints to register and receive calls.
ITID-41432.purpose: Captures a DoS attack that floods a VoIP/SIP infrastructure with REGISTER requests to exhaust registration/authentication processing capacity.
scopeIncludes: High-rate SIP REGISTER floods aimed at exhausting registrar/authentication processing capacity
Attacks that also function as a byproduct credential-testing vector when REGISTER attempts include password guesses, though the primary classification here is availability impact
scopeExcludes: SIP INVITE floods aimed at call-setup capacity rather than registration (see SIP INVITE Flood Attack)
Credential-stuffing/brute-force campaigns against SIP registration where account compromise, not availability, is the primary objective (see the relevant credential-attack ITID branch)
ITID-41432.severity: High for organizations dependent on SIP endpoint registration for inbound call delivery; escalate if confirmed registration failures are impacting legitimate endpoints.
ITID-41432.priority: P2 on detection; escalate to P1 on confirmed registrar capacity exhaustion affecting legitimate endpoint registration.
ITID-41432.escalation: Escalate to telephony/VoIP operations and the SIP trunk/carrier provider immediately on confirmed exhaustion.
indicators: Sharp spike in SIP REGISTER messages per second at the registrar
Rising registration failure/timeout rate for legitimate endpoints
Registrar CPU/authentication-backend utilization spiking disproportionately to legitimate registration volume
vectors: Scripted SIP flood tools or botnets targeting known SIP registrar endpoints
Booter/stresser platforms offering SIP flood attack modules
rootCauses: SIP registrar exposed to the internet without rate-limiting on REGISTER messages
No account lockout or progressive-delay controls on repeated failed registration attempts
SIP trunk provider-side protections not enabled or not requested
mitreTechniques: T1499.002 Endpoint Denial of Service: Service Exhaustion Flood
controls: Per-source REGISTER rate-limiting at the registrar/SBC
Progressive-delay or lockout controls on repeated failed registration attempts
SIP trunk provider-side DDoS/flood protection
ITID-41432.detection: Strong technical signal from registrar logs tracking REGISTER rate and failure rate.
ITID-41432.response: Apply REGISTER rate-limiting at the registrar/SBC immediately; engage carrier-side mitigation if available; verify registration capacity recovery.
metrics: Peak REGISTER messages-per-second observed
Registration failure rate during event
Time to rate-limiting engagement
ITID-41432.notes: Differentiating axis for the SIP Flooding group is SIP method: this leaf targets registration (REGISTER), its sibling targets call setup (INVITE). Where password-guessing content in the REGISTER attempts suggests account-compromise intent rather than pure availability impact, cross-reference the relevant credential-attack ITID.

playbook.name: SIP REGISTER Flood Attack
playbook.description: The attacker sends a high volume of SIP REGISTER requests to the organization's SIP registrar/SBC, exhausting registration-processing capacity and/or the registration database, disrupting endpoint registration and service.

steps.title: Confirm SIP REGISTER flood via registration-rate anomaly
steps.desc: Analyze SBC/SIP registrar logs and metrics for an abnormal spike in REGISTER message rate correlated with degraded registration success rate or registrar database/resource impact.
steps.guidance: Compare REGISTER-per-second rate against baseline; check whether registration attempts use valid, known extension/account numbers or random/invalid ones.
steps.outcome: Confirmed SIP REGISTER flood with request rate and registrar impact documented.
steps.abort: If the spike correlates with a legitimate mass endpoint reboot/re-registration event, stand down and document as false positive.

steps.title: Apply SBC-level rate limiting and account-lockout thresholds for REGISTER
steps.desc: Configure the SBC/registrar to rate-limit REGISTER messages per source IP and per account, with appropriate account-lockout/backoff thresholds for repeated authentication failures.
steps.guidance: Balance lockout thresholds to prevent legitimate users from being locked out due to a single device's transient registration issues while still blocking sustained brute-force/flood patterns.
steps.outcome: REGISTER flood volume reduced to sustainable levels; registrar capacity restored.
steps.abort: If legitimate users are being locked out, adjust lockout thresholds and communicate with affected users.

steps.title: If credential-targeting confirmed, force password resets for targeted accounts
steps.desc: If the flood was determined to include credential-stuffing/brute-force attempts against valid accounts, force password resets for the targeted accounts and review for any successful unauthorized registrations.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with the identity/IAM team to check for any account compromise resulting from the attack in addition to the DoS impact.
steps.outcome: Targeted accounts secured with new credentials; any successful compromise identified and remediated.

steps.title: Confirm registration success rate returns to normal and rate limits retained
steps.desc: Monitor registration success rate and registrar resource utilization to confirm return to normal baseline, retaining rate-limiting configuration permanently.
steps.guidance: Test with representative legitimate endpoint registration scenarios to confirm no false-positive blocking.
steps.outcome: Normal registration service restored with permanent hardening retained.

steps.title: Document incident and codify registration rate-limiting/lockout as a standard VoIP security baseline
steps.desc: Record the attack and ensure SBC-level registration rate-limiting and account-lockout configuration are part of the standard VoIP infrastructure hardening baseline.
steps.guidance: Update infrastructure-as-code templates or configuration management baselines accordingly.
steps.outcome: After-action report with hardening settings codified into deployment standards.

steps.title: Determine whether flood targets valid accounts (credential stuffing/brute force) or random/invalid accounts (pure resource exhaustion)
steps.desc: Examine the account/extension identifiers used in the flood REGISTER attempts and their authentication success/failure pattern to determine attacker intent.
steps.guidance: A flood using valid account identifiers with varying passwords suggests a credential-stuffing/brute-force objective in addition to DoS; a flood using random/invalid identifiers suggests pure resource-exhaustion intent.
steps.outcome: Determined attacker intent informing whether this incident should also be handled as a credential-attack investigation.

steps.title: Restrict SIP registration to authorized source IP ranges/VPN where feasible
steps.desc: If remote endpoints register from a known, bounded set of networks (e.g., corporate VPN, known remote office IPs), restrict registration access to those ranges.
steps.guidance: For deployments with predominantly on-premises or VPN-connected endpoints, this can eliminate most internet-sourced flood traffic.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized source traffic blocked, further reducing attack volume reaching the registrar.
steps.abort: If legitimate remote/mobile softphone users require broader access, scope restrictions accordingly or rely primarily on rate limiting.

steps.title: Confirm affected legitimate users can register successfully with new credentials
steps.desc: Where password resets were issued, confirm the affected legitimate users/endpoints can re-register successfully with their new credentials.
steps.guidance: Follow up directly with affected users/departments to confirm restored functionality.
steps.outcome: Confirmed all legitimate affected accounts successfully re-registered.

ITID-41433.def: A denial-of-service event exhibiting clear SIP flooding characteristics (VoIP infrastructure capacity exhaustion) where the specific SIP method driving the flood (INVITE or REGISTER) has not yet been determined.
ITID-41433.purpose: Intake bucket for SIP flooding activity that cannot yet be attributed to a specific SIP method.
scopeIncludes: Initial triage of a suspected SIP flood before method analysis is complete
scopeExcludes: Any flood already confirmed as INVITE-based or REGISTER-based (reclassify to the specific leaf once confirmed)
ITID-41433.severity: Medium-High pending confirmation; reassess once method is identified.
ITID-41433.priority: P2 pending triage; adjust once reclassified.
ITID-41433.escalation: Escalate to telephony/VoIP operations for SBC/registrar log analysis; reclassify once confirmed.
indicators: Elevated SIP message rate against VoIP infrastructure without confirmed method classification at initial detection
vectors: Unconfirmed at time of intake
rootCauses: Insufficient initial SIP log visibility to determine method
mitreTechniques: T1499.002 Endpoint Denial of Service: Service Exhaustion Flood
controls: Session border controller with SIP-aware rate-limiting and DoS protection
SIP trunk provider-side DDoS/flood protection
ITID-41433.detection: Sufficient to detect the SIP flood pattern but insufficient to classify the specific method at time of intake.
ITID-41433.response: Apply general SIP rate-limiting at the SBC immediately; run log analysis in parallel to reclassify.
metrics: Count of incidents landing in this catch-all per quarter
detections: SBC SIP message rate threshold alerting
ITID-41433.notes: Triage/intake bucket only; reclassify once the SIP method is confirmed.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General SIP Flooding Attack
playbook.description: A SIP-layer flood is confirmed via abnormal SBC/registrar message rate and resource impact, but the specific message type (INVITE vs. REGISTER) driving the flood has not yet been determined.

steps.title: Confirm SIP-layer flood via SBC message-rate and resource-impact analysis
steps.desc: Analyze SBC logs and metrics for an abnormal SIP message-rate spike correlated with degraded call setup/registration success or SBC resource impact.
steps.guidance: Check message-type breakdown (INVITE, REGISTER, OPTIONS, etc.) to identify which message type dominates the flood.
steps.outcome: Confirmed SIP-layer flood condition with dominant message type(s) and impact documented.

steps.title: Apply general SBC-level rate limiting across all SIP message types
steps.desc: Configure the SBC to rate-limit SIP messages broadly (per source IP and overall) as a general-purpose defense pending full classification.
steps.guidance: Most SBCs support general message-rate limiting independent of specific message type.
steps.outcome: SIP message flood volume reduced to sustainable levels; SBC capacity restored.
steps.abort: If legitimate high-volume traffic is impacted, add an allowlist for known trunk/carrier source IPs.

steps.title: Complete message-type classification and apply targeted hardening
steps.desc: Finalize which SIP message type dominated the flood and apply the more specific hardening measures from the corresponding playbook.
steps.guidance: Reclassify the incident to the specific ITID leaf if determination succeeds.
steps.outcome: Attack technique documented and technique-specific hardening applied.

steps.title: Confirm SIP service performance returns to normal and rate limits retained
steps.desc: Monitor call setup/registration success rates and SBC resource utilization to confirm return to normal baseline, retaining rate-limiting configuration permanently.
steps.guidance: Test with representative legitimate SIP scenarios to confirm no false-positive blocking.
steps.outcome: Normal SIP/voice service restored with permanent hardening retained.

steps.title: Document incident and improve SIP flood message-type classification tooling
steps.desc: Record why immediate message-type classification was not possible and recommend detection tooling improvements.
steps.guidance: Include recommendations for enhanced SBC-level message-type analytics that would have sped up classification.
steps.outcome: After-action report with concrete detection tooling improvement items.

steps.title: Attempt message-type classification to pivot to a specific playbook
steps.desc: Determine whether INVITE or REGISTER messages dominate the flood, to allow pivot to a more specific playbook if possible.
steps.guidance: If classification succeeds, transition to the corresponding specific SIP flooding playbook; otherwise proceed with general mitigation.
steps.outcome: Either successful reclassification or confirmed genuinely mixed/unclear message type.

steps.title: Restrict SIP signaling to authorized source IP ranges where feasible
steps.desc: Apply firewall/SBC access-control rules restricting SIP signaling to known, authorized carrier/trunk/VPN IP ranges where the deployment model allows.
steps.guidance: This general restriction is effective regardless of which specific SIP message type is being flooded.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized source traffic blocked, further reducing attack volume.

steps.title: Confirm technique-specific hardening retained where classification succeeded
steps.desc: Where the attack was reclassified to a specific SIP message type, confirm the corresponding technique-specific hardening measures remain in place post-recovery.
steps.guidance: Cross-check against the specific playbook's hardening recommendations if reclassification occurred.
steps.outcome: Confirmed appropriate hardening retained based on final classification.

ITID-41441.def: A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary sends deliberately malformed IP fragments with overlapping offset values (in the style of the historical Teardrop exploit) to a target host, exploiting flaws in fragment-reassembly logic that cause the target's network stack to crash, hang, or otherwise fail when attempting to reconstruct the invalid fragment set.
ITID-41441.purpose: Captures a denial-of-service attack that exploits how a target OS/network stack handles overlapping, maliciously crafted IP fragments to crash or hang the system.
scopeIncludes: Crafted, overlapping-offset IP fragment sequences sent to trigger a reassembly-logic fault on the target
Attacks targeting legacy or unpatched network stacks still vulnerable to malformed-fragment reassembly flaws
scopeExcludes: High-volume, well-formed fragment floods intended to exhaust reassembly buffer capacity rather than exploit a logic flaw (see Fragmented Packet Reassembly Resource Exhaustion)
Oversized single fragmented packets intended to crash a host via buffer overflow (see Oversized Fragmented Packet (Ping of Death-Style) Attack)
ITID-41441.severity: Low-Medium on fully patched modern operating systems, which are broadly immune to the original Teardrop flaw; High if any legacy or unpatched system is confirmed vulnerable and targeted.
ITID-41441.priority: P2 on detection; escalate to P1 if a legacy/unpatched system is confirmed crashed or destabilized by the attack.
ITID-41441.escalation: Escalate to the affected system's owning team immediately if a crash or instability is confirmed, given the potential for a full outage of that host.
indicators: IDS/IPS alerts on overlapping IP fragment offset patterns
Target host crash, kernel panic, or unresponsive network stack coinciding with receipt of malformed fragments
Packet capture showing fragment offset/length values that produce invalid or overlapping reassembly ranges
vectors: Legacy exploit tools (Teardrop and derivatives) crafting overlapping-offset fragment sequences
Fuzzing tools generating malformed fragment sequences against network-facing hosts
rootCauses: Legacy or unpatched operating systems/network stacks still vulnerable to malformed-fragment reassembly flaws
