No IDS/IPS signature coverage for overlapping-fragment patterns
No firewall-level fragment validation/normalization ahead of endpoints
mitreTechniques: T1499.004 Endpoint Denial of Service: Application or System Exploitation
controls: Firewall/IPS fragment reassembly and validation (normalizing or dropping malformed fragments before they reach endpoints)
OS/network stack patching to current vendor-supported versions
IDS/IPS signatures for known overlapping-fragment exploit patterns
ITID-41441.detection: Strong technical signal via IDS/IPS fragment-anomaly signatures; genuine incidents are now rare given the age and broad remediation of the underlying flaw.
ITID-41441.response: Isolate and restore any crashed/destabilized host immediately; verify patch level; confirm firewall/IPS fragment normalization is in place.
metrics: Count of hosts confirmed vulnerable to legacy fragment-reassembly flaws
Time to host restoration if crashed
IDS/IPS signature hit count
ITID-41441.notes: Differentiating axis for the IP Fragmentation Attacks group: this leaf exploits a reassembly logic flaw (crash-inducing), as distinct from its siblings' focus on buffer exhaustion (volume-based) or oversized-packet exploitation.

playbook.name: Teardrop-Style Overlapping Fragment Attack
playbook.description: The attacker sends deliberately malformed, overlapping IP fragments designed to exploit reassembly logic flaws in the target's TCP/IP stack, potentially causing a crash or resource exhaustion during reassembly.

steps.title: Confirm overlapping-fragment attack via packet capture and fragment-offset analysis
steps.desc: Capture and analyze fragmented packets destined for the affected host to confirm the presence of deliberately overlapping fragment offsets inconsistent with normal fragmentation behavior.
steps.guidance: Normal fragmentation produces non-overlapping, sequential fragment offsets; a teardrop-style attack crafts fragments with overlapping offset/length values designed to confuse reassembly logic.
steps.outcome: Confirmed overlapping-fragment attack pattern with source IP(s) and target host documented.

steps.title: Block source IP(s) generating malformed fragments at the perimeter
steps.desc: Apply firewall/ACL rules blocking the identified source IP(s) sending malformed overlapping fragments.
steps.guidance: Since this is typically a targeted/low-volume exploit attempt rather than a volumetric flood, source-based blocking is usually sufficient and precise.
steps.outcome: Malformed fragment traffic blocked at the perimeter.

steps.title: Verify and apply OS/network stack patches for fragment-reassembly vulnerabilities
steps.desc: Confirm all affected hosts/devices are running fully patched operating systems and network stacks with no known unpatched fragment-reassembly vulnerabilities.
steps.guidance: Review vendor advisories for any outstanding fragment-handling CVEs affecting the specific OS/device versions in use, and apply patches or vendor-recommended mitigations.
steps.outcome: Confirmed all potentially affected systems are patched against known fragment-reassembly vulnerabilities.

steps.title: Confirm affected host/device stability and normal fragment handling
steps.desc: Monitor the previously affected host/device for stability and confirm normal handling of legitimate fragmented traffic (e.g., large UDP-based DNS responses, certain VPN traffic) post-hardening.
steps.guidance: Verify legitimate fragmented traffic is not inadvertently dropped by the new fragment-validation rules.
steps.outcome: Confirmed host/device stability and correct handling of legitimate fragmented traffic.

steps.title: Document incident and confirm fragment-validation hardening applied fleet-wide
steps.desc: Record the attack and audit all perimeter firewalls/IPS and internet-facing hosts for consistent fragment-validation hardening and patch status.
steps.guidance: Include a fleet-wide patch/configuration compliance check in the after-action report.
steps.outcome: After-action report with a broader hardening remediation list if gaps were found elsewhere.

steps.title: Assess target host/device impact (crash, resource exhaustion, or no effect)
steps.desc: Determine whether the targeted host/device (server, firewall, router) exhibited any crash, reboot, high CPU, or memory exhaustion correlated with the attack traffic.
steps.guidance: Modern, patched operating systems and network devices are generally immune to classic teardrop attacks; confirm actual impact versus attempted-but-ineffective attack traffic.
steps.outcome: Documented impact assessment (successful exploitation vs. ineffective attempt) informing response urgency.
steps.abort: If no impact is observed and the target is confirmed patched/immune, document as an unsuccessful attack attempt with lower urgency.

steps.title: Enable firewall/IPS fragment validation and anomaly-based fragment dropping
steps.desc: Configure perimeter firewall/IPS to validate fragment reassembly and drop packets with invalid/overlapping fragment offsets before they reach internal hosts.
steps.guidance: Most modern next-generation firewalls and IPS platforms include built-in fragment validation/anti-evasion features; ensure they are enabled.
steps.outcome: Malformed fragmented packets dropped at the perimeter regardless of source, providing broader protection.

steps.title: Confirm patches applied and no residual vulnerability remains exploitable
steps.desc: Verify via a controlled test or vulnerability scan that the previously vulnerable fragment-reassembly issue is no longer exploitable on the patched systems.
steps.guidance: Use a non-production/lab replica if testing the actual exploit pattern against production systems carries risk.
steps.outcome: Confirmed patched systems are no longer vulnerable to the identified fragment-reassembly issue.

ITID-41442.def: A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary sends a high volume of legitimately structured IP fragments — often deliberately incomplete fragment sets (never sending the final fragment) — forcing the target to allocate and hold reassembly buffer memory for each incomplete set until timeout, exhausting available memory or CPU capacity as buffers accumulate faster than they can be released.
ITID-41442.purpose: Captures a denial-of-service attack that floods a target with well-formed but numerous IP fragments to exhaust its fragment-reassembly buffer capacity.
scopeIncludes: High-volume fragment floods using well-formed (non-malformed) fragments intended to exhaust reassembly buffer/memory capacity through sheer accumulation
Incomplete fragment-set floods that never deliver a final fragment, holding buffers open until timeout
scopeExcludes: Malformed, overlapping-offset fragments intended to exploit a reassembly logic flaw (see Teardrop-Style Overlapping Fragment Attack)
Oversized fragmented packets intended to trigger a buffer overflow on reassembly (see Oversized Fragmented Packet (Ping of Death-Style) Attack)
ITID-41442.severity: Medium-High depending on the target's reassembly buffer sizing and timeout configuration; High if sustained volume is confirmed exhausting available memory.
ITID-41442.priority: P2 on detection; escalate to P1 on confirmed memory/resource exhaustion affecting the target.
ITID-41442.escalation: Escalate to network/system operations immediately if reassembly buffer exhaustion is confirmed impacting the target's stability.
indicators: Sharp rise in fragmented packet volume with a high proportion of incomplete fragment sets
Target host/firewall memory utilization climbing in correlation with fragment volume
Firewall/IPS logs showing fragment reassembly timeout events accumulating
vectors: Scripted fragment-flood tools generating high volumes of incomplete fragment sets
Botnet or booter/stresser platforms offering fragmentation-flood attack modules
rootCauses: Fragment reassembly buffer sized without headroom for high-volume incomplete-set floods
Reassembly timeout set too high, allowing incomplete sets to occupy memory longer than necessary
No firewall-level fragment rate-limiting ahead of endpoints
mitreTechniques: T1499.001 Endpoint Denial of Service: OS Exhaustion Flood
controls: Firewall/IPS fragment rate-limiting and reassembly timeout tuning
Reassembly buffer capacity planning accounting for incomplete-set flood scenarios
Dropping fragments at the perimeter for protocols/services that do not require fragmentation support
ITID-41442.detection: Strong technical signal from firewall/IPS fragment-volume and reassembly-timeout metrics.
ITID-41442.response: Apply fragment rate-limiting and tighten reassembly timeout immediately; verify memory/resource recovery.
metrics: Peak fragmented packet volume observed
Reassembly buffer/memory utilization during event
Time to rate-limiting engagement
ITID-41442.notes: Differentiating axis for the IP Fragmentation Attacks group: this leaf is volume/exhaustion-driven (well-formed fragments accumulating), mapped to OS Exhaustion Flood, as distinct from its logic-flaw-exploiting or buffer-overflow-inducing siblings.

playbook.name: Fragmented Packet Reassembly Resource Exhaustion
playbook.description: The attacker sends a high volume of incomplete or deliberately never-completing IP fragment sets, exhausting the target's reassembly buffer/memory as it waits for fragments that will never arrive.

steps.title: Confirm fragment reassembly exhaustion via incomplete-fragment-set analysis
steps.desc: Analyze packet captures and firewall/host reassembly buffer metrics for a high volume of fragment sets that never complete (missing final fragment or deliberately incomplete), correlated with memory/resource impact.
steps.guidance: Check firewall/IPS or host OS fragment-reassembly queue depth and memory consumption for abnormal growth correlated with a high rate of incomplete fragment sets.
steps.outcome: Confirmed fragment-reassembly exhaustion pattern with resource impact documented.

steps.title: Tune fragment-reassembly timeout and buffer limits on perimeter defenses
steps.desc: Reduce the fragment-reassembly timeout on perimeter firewalls/IPS and hosts so incomplete fragment sets are discarded quickly, freeing buffer memory sooner.
steps.guidance: Balance the timeout reduction against legitimate high-latency network paths that may need slightly longer to deliver all fragments of a legitimate packet.
steps.outcome: Reassembly buffer memory consumption reduced; resource exhaustion resolved.
steps.abort: If legitimate fragmented traffic over high-latency links starts failing, adjust the timeout to a less aggressive value.

steps.title: Consider disabling or minimizing acceptance of fragmented traffic at the perimeter where feasible
steps.desc: Evaluate whether the organization's legitimate traffic requires accepting IP fragments at all; where feasible, configure the perimeter to drop fragmented packets by default and require applications to use appropriately-sized MTU/PMTUD instead.
steps.guidance: This is a stronger, more permanent hardening measure appropriate where fragment traffic has no legitimate business need; validate against known legitimate use cases (e.g., certain UDP-based protocols) before applying broadly.
steps.outcome: Fragment-based resource exhaustion vector substantially reduced for the protected perimeter.
steps.abort: If legitimate fragmented traffic is required, retain fragment acceptance but with hardened timeout/rate-limit settings instead.

steps.title: Confirm reassembly resource utilization returns to normal
steps.desc: Monitor perimeter/host reassembly buffer utilization and memory consumption to confirm return to normal baseline, retaining tuned timeout/rate-limit settings permanently.
steps.guidance: Monitor for at least 1-2 hours of stable operation before considering recovery complete.
steps.outcome: Normal reassembly resource utilization confirmed with permanent hardening retained.

steps.title: Document incident and codify fragment-handling hardening as a standard baseline
steps.desc: Record the attack and ensure the tuned fragment-reassembly timeout and rate-limit settings are captured in the standard perimeter hardening baseline.
steps.guidance: Update infrastructure-as-code templates or configuration management baselines accordingly.
steps.outcome: After-action report with hardening settings codified into deployment standards.

steps.title: Determine source pattern and whether fragmentation is spoofed or genuine
steps.desc: Analyze source IP characteristics and fragment header consistency to determine whether the attack uses spoofed sources or genuine distributed hosts.
steps.guidance: Check TTL consistency and source IP plausibility similar to other spoofed-flood identification approaches.
steps.outcome: Documented source characteristics informing containment approach.

steps.title: Rate-limit fragmented traffic and block source IPs generating the flood
steps.desc: Apply rate limiting specifically on fragmented packet traffic at the perimeter, and block source IPs confirmed as generating the incomplete-fragment flood.
steps.guidance: Many organizations receive very little legitimate fragmented traffic; a conservative rate limit on fragments specifically has low risk of legitimate impact.
steps.outcome: Fragment flood volume reduced; identified source IPs blocked.

steps.title: Confirm legitimate fragmented traffic still processes correctly
steps.desc: Verify that legitimate fragmented traffic (e.g., large DNS responses, certain VPN/tunneling protocols) still reassembles and processes correctly under the tightened timeout/rate-limit settings.
steps.guidance: Test with known legitimate fragmented traffic patterns relevant to the environment.
steps.outcome: Confirmed no legitimate traffic was broken by the hardening changes.

ITID-41443.def: A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary sends a sequence of IP fragments that, when reassembled by the target, produce a packet exceeding the maximum allowed IP packet size (65,535 bytes), exploiting buffer handling flaws in vulnerable network stacks to cause a crash, hang, or reboot.
ITID-41443.purpose: Captures a denial-of-service attack that reassembles fragments into an oversized packet exceeding protocol limits, in the style of the historical Ping of Death, to crash or destabilize a target.
scopeIncludes: Fragment sequences crafted to reassemble into an oversized packet exceeding protocol size limits
Attacks targeting legacy or unpatched network stacks still vulnerable to oversized-reassembly buffer handling flaws
scopeExcludes: Overlapping-offset fragments exploiting reassembly logic rather than size limits (see Teardrop-Style Overlapping Fragment Attack)
Well-formed, correctly sized fragment floods intended purely to exhaust buffer capacity (see Fragmented Packet Reassembly Resource Exhaustion)
ITID-41443.severity: Low-Medium on fully patched modern operating systems, which are broadly immune to the original Ping of Death flaw; High if any legacy or unpatched system is confirmed vulnerable and targeted.
ITID-41443.priority: P2 on detection; escalate to P1 if a legacy/unpatched system is confirmed crashed or destabilized by the attack.
ITID-41443.escalation: Escalate to the affected system's owning team immediately if a crash or instability is confirmed, given the potential for a full outage of that host.
indicators: IDS/IPS alerts on fragment sequences whose cumulative reassembled length exceeds the maximum IP packet size
Target host crash, kernel panic, or reboot coinciding with receipt of an oversized reassembled packet
Packet capture showing fragment offset/length values summing beyond 65,535 bytes
vectors: Legacy exploit tools (Ping of Death and derivatives) crafting oversized-reassembly fragment sequences
Fuzzing tools generating malformed fragment sequences targeting size-limit handling
rootCauses: Legacy or unpatched operating systems/network stacks still vulnerable to oversized-packet buffer handling flaws
No IDS/IPS signature coverage for oversized-reassembly patterns
No firewall-level fragment validation/normalization ahead of endpoints
mitreTechniques: T1499.004 Endpoint Denial of Service: Application or System Exploitation
controls: Firewall/IPS fragment reassembly and validation enforcing maximum packet size
OS/network stack patching to current vendor-supported versions
IDS/IPS signatures for known oversized-reassembly exploit patterns
ITID-41443.detection: Strong technical signal via IDS/IPS fragment-anomaly signatures; genuine incidents are now rare given the age and broad remediation of the underlying flaw.
ITID-41443.response: Isolate and restore any crashed/destabilized host immediately; verify patch level; confirm firewall/IPS fragment size validation is in place.
metrics: Count of hosts confirmed vulnerable to legacy oversized-packet flaws
Time to host restoration if crashed
IDS/IPS signature hit count
ITID-41443.notes: Differentiating axis for the IP Fragmentation Attacks group: this leaf exploits packet-size-limit handling (crash-inducing), as distinct from the overlapping-offset logic flaw exploited by its Teardrop-style sibling.

playbook.name: Oversized Fragmented Packet (Ping of Death-Style) Attack
playbook.description: The attacker sends fragmented packets that, when reassembled, exceed the maximum legal IP packet size, exploiting buffer-handling flaws in the target's network stack to cause a crash, instability, or resource exhaustion.

steps.title: Confirm oversized-reassembly attack via fragment-size and total-length analysis
steps.desc: Analyze captured fragmented packets to confirm the cumulative reassembled size (based on fragment offsets and lengths) exceeds the maximum legal IP packet size (65,535 bytes), consistent with a Ping-of-Death-style attack.
steps.guidance: Calculate the implied total reassembled size from the fragment offset and length of the last fragment; a value exceeding 65,535 bytes confirms the classic Ping-of-Death pattern.
steps.outcome: Confirmed oversized-fragment attack pattern with source IP(s) and target host documented.

steps.title: Block source IP(s) generating oversized fragment sets at the perimeter
steps.desc: Apply firewall/ACL rules blocking the identified source IP(s) sending oversized fragment sets.
steps.guidance: This is typically a targeted/low-volume exploit attempt rather than a volumetric flood, so source-based blocking is usually sufficient.
steps.outcome: Oversized fragment traffic blocked at the perimeter.

steps.title: Verify and apply OS/network stack patches for oversized-packet vulnerabilities
steps.desc: Confirm all affected hosts/devices are running fully patched operating systems and network stacks with no known unpatched oversized-packet/buffer-overflow vulnerabilities related to fragment reassembly.
steps.guidance: Review vendor advisories for any outstanding CVEs affecting the specific OS/device versions in use, and apply patches or vendor-recommended mitigations.
steps.outcome: Confirmed all potentially affected systems are patched against known oversized-packet vulnerabilities.

steps.title: Confirm affected host/device stability and normal legitimate traffic handling
steps.desc: Monitor the previously affected host/device for stability and confirm normal handling of legitimate fragmented traffic post-hardening.
steps.guidance: Verify legitimate fragmented traffic is not inadvertently dropped by the new fragment-size-enforcement rules.
steps.outcome: Confirmed host/device stability and correct handling of legitimate fragmented traffic.

steps.title: Document incident and confirm fragment-size enforcement applied fleet-wide
steps.desc: Record the attack and audit all perimeter firewalls/IPS and internet-facing hosts for consistent fragment-size-enforcement hardening and patch status.
steps.guidance: Include a fleet-wide patch/configuration compliance check in the after-action report.
steps.outcome: After-action report with a broader hardening remediation list if gaps were found elsewhere.

steps.title: Assess target host/device impact (crash, reboot, or no effect)
steps.desc: Determine whether the targeted host/device exhibited any crash, reboot, kernel panic, or instability correlated with the attack traffic.
steps.guidance: Modern, patched operating systems and network devices are generally immune to classic Ping-of-Death attacks; confirm actual impact versus an ineffective attack attempt.
steps.outcome: Documented impact assessment informing response urgency.
steps.abort: If no impact is observed and the target is confirmed patched/immune, document as an unsuccessful attack attempt with lower urgency.

steps.title: Enable firewall/IPS maximum-reassembled-size enforcement
steps.desc: Configure perimeter firewall/IPS to enforce the legal maximum IP packet size during virtual reassembly, dropping any fragment set that would exceed it before it reaches internal hosts.
steps.guidance: Most modern next-generation firewalls and IPS platforms include this validation as part of standard anti-evasion/fragment handling; ensure it is enabled and not just relying on host-side patching.
steps.outcome: Oversized fragmented packets dropped at the perimeter regardless of source, providing broader protection.

steps.title: Confirm patches applied and no residual vulnerability remains exploitable
steps.desc: Verify via a controlled test or vulnerability scan that the previously vulnerable oversized-packet handling issue is no longer exploitable on the patched systems.
steps.guidance: Use a non-production/lab replica if testing the actual exploit pattern against production systems carries risk.
steps.outcome: Confirmed patched systems are no longer vulnerable to the identified oversized-packet issue.

ITID-41444.def: A denial-of-service event exhibiting clear IP fragmentation-based characteristics where the specific mechanism (overlapping-offset logic flaw, reassembly buffer exhaustion, or oversized-packet exploitation) has not yet been determined.
ITID-41444.purpose: Intake bucket for IP fragmentation-based DoS activity that cannot yet be attributed to a specific exploitation mechanism.
scopeIncludes: Initial triage of a suspected IP fragmentation attack before mechanism analysis is complete
scopeExcludes: Any attack already confirmed as Teardrop-style, reassembly-exhaustion, or oversized-packet (reclassify to the specific leaf once confirmed)
ITID-41444.severity: Medium pending confirmation; reassess once mechanism is identified.
ITID-41444.priority: P2 pending triage; adjust once reclassified.
ITID-41444.escalation: Escalate to network operations for packet capture and fragment analysis; reclassify once confirmed.
indicators: IDS/IPS fragmentation anomaly alerts without confirmed mechanism classification at initial detection
vectors: Unconfirmed at time of intake
rootCauses: Insufficient initial packet-capture visibility to determine mechanism
mitreTechniques: T1499.004 Endpoint Denial of Service: Application or System Exploitation
controls: Firewall/IPS fragment reassembly and validation
OS/network stack patching to current vendor-supported versions
ITID-41444.detection: Sufficient to detect the fragmentation anomaly pattern but insufficient to classify mechanism at time of intake.
ITID-41444.response: Apply general fragment validation/rate-limiting immediately; run packet capture analysis in parallel to reclassify.
metrics: Count of incidents landing in this catch-all per quarter
ITID-41444.notes: Triage/intake bucket only; reclassify once the specific fragmentation mechanism is confirmed.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General IP Fragmentation Attack
playbook.description: A fragmentation-based attack against the target's network stack is confirmed via anomalous fragmented packets, but the specific technique (overlapping/teardrop, reassembly exhaustion, oversized/Ping-of-Death) has not yet been determined.

steps.title: Confirm fragmentation-based attack via packet capture analysis
steps.desc: Analyze captured fragmented packets destined for the affected host to confirm anomalous fragmentation characteristics (overlap, incompleteness, or oversized reassembly).
steps.guidance: Compare fragment offsets, lengths, and completeness against normal fragmentation behavior to identify the general nature of the anomaly.
steps.outcome: Confirmed anomalous fragmentation pattern with source IP(s) and target host documented.

steps.title: Block source IP(s) and enable general firewall/IPS fragment validation
steps.desc: Apply firewall/ACL rules blocking the identified source IP(s) and enable general fragment-validation/anti-evasion features on perimeter firewall/IPS.
steps.guidance: General fragment validation covers most known fragmentation-based attack patterns regardless of the specific sub-technique.
steps.outcome: Anomalous fragmented traffic blocked at the perimeter.

steps.title: Complete technique classification and apply targeted hardening/patches
steps.desc: Finalize which fragmentation technique was used and apply the more specific hardening/patching measures from the corresponding playbook.
steps.guidance: Reclassify the incident to the specific ITID leaf if determination succeeds.
steps.outcome: Attack technique documented and technique-specific hardening applied.

steps.title: Confirm affected host/device stability and normal fragment handling
steps.desc: Monitor the previously affected host/device for stability and confirm normal handling of legitimate fragmented traffic post-hardening.
steps.guidance: Verify legitimate fragmented traffic is not inadvertently dropped by the new fragment-handling rules.
steps.outcome: Confirmed host/device stability and correct handling of legitimate fragmented traffic.

steps.title: Document incident and improve fragmentation-attack classification tooling
steps.desc: Record why immediate technique classification was not possible and recommend detection tooling improvements.
steps.guidance: Include recommendations for enhanced packet-capture-based fragment analytics that would have sped up classification.
steps.outcome: After-action report with concrete detection tooling improvement items.

steps.title: Attempt technique classification via fragment characteristics
steps.desc: Determine whether the anomaly is overlapping fragments, incomplete/never-completing fragment sets, or oversized reassembled size, to allow pivot to a more specific playbook.
steps.guidance: If classification succeeds, transition to the corresponding specific IP fragmentation playbook; otherwise proceed with general mitigation.
steps.outcome: Either successful reclassification or confirmed genuinely mixed/unclear technique.

steps.title: Tune general fragment-reassembly timeout and rate limits as a precaution
steps.desc: Apply conservative fragment-reassembly timeout and rate-limiting settings pending full technique classification.
steps.guidance: These general settings provide defense in depth regardless of which specific fragmentation technique is ultimately confirmed.
steps.outcome: Resource impact from the fragmentation anomaly reduced.
steps.abort: If legitimate fragmented traffic is impacted, relax settings and monitor.

steps.title: Confirm technique-specific hardening retained where classification succeeded
steps.desc: Where the attack was reclassified to a specific fragmentation technique, confirm the corresponding technique-specific hardening measures remain in place post-recovery.
steps.guidance: Cross-check against the specific playbook's hardening recommendations if reclassification occurred.
steps.outcome: Confirmed appropriate hardening retained based on final classification.

ITID-41511.def: A resource-depletion attack in which an adversary submits specially crafted strings to an application endpoint that evaluates them against a vulnerable regular expression, forcing the regex engine into exponential/polynomial backtracking that consumes CPU on one or more worker threads/processes until the service becomes unresponsive.
ITID-41511.purpose: Captures denial-of-service caused by an adversary sending crafted input that triggers catastrophic-backtracking behaviour in a vulnerable regular expression, pinning application CPU cores.
scopeIncludes: Crafted payloads submitted to form fields, search boxes, API parameters, or log-parsing pipelines that trigger backtracking
Single-request ReDoS that pins one worker thread indefinitely
Repeated low-volume submission of ReDoS payloads to exhaust a worker pool
scopeExcludes: Volumetric network-layer flooding (Tier-3 Network/Transport Flooding domains)
Cryptomining payload CPU consumption (ITID-41512, a foreign workload rather than an input-triggered algorithmic flaw)
Compression-bomb CPU exhaustion (ITID-41513, decompression cost rather than regex backtracking)
ITID-41511.severity: High if the vulnerable regex sits on an unauthenticated, internet-facing path (e.g., login, search); Medium if authentication or rate limiting reduces exposure.
ITID-41511.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if a single crafted request can pin a worker for minutes or the service is customer-facing and already degraded.
ITID-41511.escalation: Escalate to the owning application team once a specific vulnerable pattern and triggering payload are identified so a hotfix or WAF rule can be deployed.
indicators: A specific worker thread/process pegged at 100% CPU for an abnormal duration
Application logs showing a single long-running request against a known regex-validation endpoint
Response latency spike correlated with a small number of requests rather than high request volume
vectors: Crafted input to a vulnerable regex used for input validation (e.g., email, URL, or password-complexity checks)
Crafted log lines submitted to a regex-based log parser or WAF rule
Malicious payloads in file names or headers parsed by a vulnerable pattern
rootCauses: Use of nested quantifiers or ambiguous alternation in a hand-written regex without complexity review
No timeout/step-limit on regex evaluation
Regex validation performed on untrusted input before any length or character-class pre-filtering
mitreTechniques: T1499.004 Endpoint Denial of Service: Application or System Exploitation
controls: Regex complexity linting/static analysis in CI (e.g., detecting nested quantifiers)
Per-request CPU/time budget or regex-engine step limits
WAF rule blocking known ReDoS payload patterns pending a code fix
ITID-41511.detection: Per-worker CPU and request-duration telemetry give a strong technical signal; APM tracing to the specific endpoint/regex confirms root cause.
ITID-41511.response: Isolate and kill the offending worker/process, identify the vulnerable regex via code or request-log review, and deploy either an input pre-filter or a patched pattern before restoring full traffic.
metrics: Mean time to isolate the offending worker
Number of vulnerable regex patterns remediated per quarter
Recurrence rate of ReDoS findings in code review
ITID-41511.notes: Differentiator within CPU Exhaustion: this leaf is the only one driven by an algorithmic flaw in first-party code triggered by a single crafted input, versus foreign workloads (cryptomining) or decompression cost (compression bombs).

playbook.name: Regular Expression Denial of Service (ReDoS) Exploiting Catastrophic Backtracking
playbook.description: The attacker submits crafted input strings to an application endpoint that trigger catastrophic backtracking in a vulnerable regular expression, causing exponential CPU consumption on a single request thread and exhausting compute capacity.

steps.title: Confirm ReDoS pattern via single-request CPU spike correlation
steps.desc: Analyze APM/backend metrics to confirm one or a small number of specific requests are causing a disproportionate, sustained CPU spike on the worker thread/process handling them, distinct from a broad volumetric flood.
steps.guidance: ReDoS is distinctive in that a very small number of requests (sometimes just one) can pin a CPU core at 100% for an extended duration; identify the specific endpoint and request thread affected.
steps.outcome: Confirmed ReDoS-consistent pattern with the specific endpoint and affected request thread/worker documented.
steps.abort: If the CPU spike is explained by a legitimate heavy computational task, stand down and document as false positive.
steps.tool: APM / profiler (e.g., New Relic, py-spy, async-profiler)

steps.title: Kill the hung request/worker process and block the offending input pattern
steps.desc: Terminate the hung request-processing thread/worker to immediately free the pinned CPU resource, and deploy a WAF rule blocking the specific offending input pattern.
steps.guidance: Killing an individual hung worker in a multi-worker deployment (e.g., a single Node.js/Python worker process) typically has minimal broader impact and immediately restores that resource.
steps.outcome: CPU resource freed immediately; further attempts using the same input pattern blocked at the WAF.

steps.title: Fix the vulnerable regular expression in application code
steps.desc: Rewrite the identified vulnerable regular expression to eliminate catastrophic backtracking potential (e.g., using possessive quantifiers, atomic groups, or a non-backtracking regex engine), and deploy the fix.
steps.guidance: Test the fixed regex against both the original offending input and a broad set of adversarial inputs to confirm the backtracking vulnerability is fully eliminated, not just mitigated for the one observed input.
steps.outcome: Vulnerable regex replaced with a safe equivalent; confirmed no catastrophic backtracking under adversarial input testing.
steps.tool: Code review / regex complexity analysis tooling

steps.title: Remove temporary input blocking and confirm endpoint performs safely under adversarial input
steps.desc: Once the regex fix is deployed and validated, relax the temporary WAF pattern-block while retaining the request-processing timeout permanently as defense in depth.
steps.guidance: Load-test the fixed endpoint with the original offending input and variations to confirm no CPU spike occurs.
steps.outcome: Endpoint confirmed resilient to the previously exploited input pattern with normal performance for legitimate use.

steps.title: Document incident and audit codebase for other ReDoS-vulnerable regular expressions
steps.desc: Record the attack and run a static analysis/regex-complexity scan across the codebase to identify other potentially vulnerable regular expressions before they are exploited.
steps.guidance: Several open-source and commercial static analysis tools can flag regex patterns susceptible to catastrophic backtracking.
steps.outcome: After-action report with a broader ReDoS remediation list if additional vulnerable patterns were found.

steps.title: Capture the offending input and identify the vulnerable regular expression
steps.desc: Capture the exact request payload/input string that triggered the excessive CPU consumption, and use profiling/stack-trace analysis to identify the specific regular expression pattern being evaluated.
steps.guidance: Use CPU profiling tools to capture a stack trace during the hang, which will typically point directly to the regex engine call and the specific pattern/library involved.
steps.outcome: Documented offending input and identified vulnerable regular expression, ready for both immediate blocking and permanent code fix.

steps.title: Apply a request-processing timeout to bound worst-case single-request CPU time
steps.desc: Configure a hard request-processing timeout (or per-request CPU time limit) at the application/web-server layer so no single request can indefinitely consume a worker thread.
steps.guidance: This is an important defense-in-depth measure independent of fixing the specific regex, since other latent ReDoS-vulnerable patterns may exist elsewhere in the codebase.
steps.outcome: Worst-case impact of any single request (including undiscovered ReDoS patterns) bounded to the configured timeout.
steps.tool: Web server / application framework timeout configuration

steps.title: Confirm request-processing timeout retained permanently as defense in depth
steps.desc: Verify the request-processing/CPU-time timeout configured during containment remains in place permanently, independent of the specific regex fix.
steps.guidance: This bounds impact from any other undiscovered ReDoS-vulnerable patterns elsewhere in the codebase.
steps.outcome: Confirmed permanent timeout hardening remains active.

ITID-41512.def: Sustained CPU exhaustion on a host or fleet of hosts caused by an adversary-deployed cryptomining process (T1496 Resource Hijacking) consuming compute resources needed by the legitimate application or service, resulting in degraded performance or outage for the legitimate workload.
ITID-41512.purpose: Captures CPU-based denial of service that is a side effect of an adversary planting an unauthorized cryptomining payload on compromised hosts, degrading the legitimate workload rather than being the attacker's primary objective.
scopeIncludes: Cryptomining binaries or in-browser miners deployed via a prior compromise (webshell, exposed API, supply-chain package) that saturate host CPU
Containerized/serverless cryptomining that starves co-located legitimate workloads
scopeExcludes: The initial-access/exploitation vector that planted the miner (tracked under the relevant Tier-1/Tier-2 intrusion domain)
CPU exhaustion from a single crafted request exploiting an algorithmic flaw (ITID-41511)
Cryptomining with no measurable service-degradation impact (tracked as unauthorized resource use, not DoS)
ITID-41512.severity: Medium-High; escalates with the proportion of fleet CPU consumed and whether the degraded service is customer-facing or safety-relevant.
ITID-41512.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if production capacity is materially degraded or the miner is spreading laterally across the fleet.
ITID-41512.escalation: Escalate immediately to the incident response team as a confirmed compromise (not just a performance issue) once a mining process is identified, since it implies prior unauthorized access.
indicators: Unexplained sustained near-100% CPU utilization on one or more hosts with no corresponding legitimate workload increase
Outbound connections to known mining-pool IPs/domains
Unfamiliar process names or scheduled tasks consuming CPU
vectors: Cryptomining payload dropped via a webshell or RCE on an exposed application
Malicious container image or compromised CI/CD pipeline deploying a miner
Compromised cloud credentials used to spin up mining instances
rootCauses: Unpatched remote-code-execution vulnerability providing initial foothold
Exposed management interfaces or default credentials enabling unauthorized deployment
Lack of egress filtering allowing mining-pool connections to go unnoticed
controls: Egress filtering/DNS blocking of known mining-pool infrastructure
Host-based CPU-anomaly and unauthorized-process detection
Container image scanning and CI/CD pipeline integrity controls
ITID-41512.detection: Strong technical signal from host CPU telemetry combined with network egress monitoring to mining-pool infrastructure.
ITID-41512.response: Isolate affected hosts, terminate the mining process, identify and close the initial-access vector, and rotate any credentials exposed during the compromise.
metrics: Fleet CPU hours lost to unauthorized mining per quarter
Mean time to detect and remove mining payloads
Number of hosts affected per incident
ITID-41512.notes: Differentiator within CPU Exhaustion: the only leaf where the DoS is a byproduct of a foreign, adversary-deployed workload rather than an input exploiting a flaw in the legitimate application.

playbook.name: Cryptomining Payload Consuming Host CPU Resources (Resource Hijacking)
playbook.description: The attacker deploys an unauthorized cryptocurrency-mining process on a compromised host (server, container, or cloud instance), consuming CPU resources and degrading or denying legitimate workloads on that host.

steps.title: Confirm cryptomining process via sustained abnormal CPU utilization and process analysis
steps.desc: Analyze host/container CPU utilization metrics for sustained, abnormally high CPU consumption (often near 100% on multiple cores) not attributable to legitimate workloads, and identify the responsible process.
steps.guidance: Cryptomining processes typically show sustained near-maximum CPU utilization with a distinctive process name/binary (or disguised as a legitimate-sounding process) and often network connections to known mining pool addresses.
steps.outcome: Confirmed unauthorized cryptomining process identified with process details and host/container documented.
steps.abort: If the high CPU usage is attributable to an approved legitimate workload, stand down and document as false positive.
steps.tool: Host/container monitoring (top, EDR, cloud provider CPU metrics)

steps.title: Isolate the affected host/container from the network
steps.desc: Immediately isolate the compromised host or container from the network (or terminate/quarantine the specific container/instance) to halt further resource consumption and prevent lateral movement or further mining pool communication.
steps.guidance: For cloud/container workloads, consider snapshotting the instance/container for forensic analysis before termination, then redeploying from a known-clean image.
steps.outcome: Cryptomining process activity halted; host isolated pending remediation.
steps.abort: If isolation would cause unacceptable business disruption for a production system, coordinate an expedited maintenance window rather than delaying indefinitely.
steps.tool: Network isolation / container orchestration (Kubernetes, cloud console)

steps.title: Remove the cryptomining payload and remediate the initial compromise vector
steps.desc: Remove the malicious payload (or rebuild the host/container from a known-clean image) and remediate the underlying vulnerability, exposed credential, or misconfiguration that enabled initial access.
steps.guidance: Rebuilding from a clean image/snapshot is strongly preferred over attempting in-place removal, given the uncertainty of full payload/persistence-mechanism eradication otherwise.
steps.outcome: Host/container rebuilt clean; initial access vector closed and confirmed remediated.

steps.title: Restore legitimate workloads and confirm normal CPU utilization
steps.desc: Redeploy legitimate workloads to the remediated/rebuilt host or a fresh instance and confirm normal CPU utilization returns.
steps.guidance: Monitor CPU utilization for a sustained period post-recovery to confirm no residual or reintroduced mining activity.
steps.outcome: Normal service operation restored with confirmed clean CPU utilization.

steps.title: Document incident and close the initial access vector organization-wide
steps.desc: Record the full incident, including initial access vector, and ensure the underlying vulnerability/misconfiguration class is remediated across all similarly-configured systems, not just the affected host.
steps.guidance: Include recommendations for improved cloud/container security posture management if the compromise stemmed from a misconfiguration.
steps.outcome: After-action report with organization-wide remediation of the root-cause exposure class.

steps.title: Determine the initial access/compromise vector enabling the unauthorized deployment
steps.desc: Investigate how the cryptomining payload was deployed onto the host (e.g., exploited vulnerability, exposed management interface, compromised credentials, vulnerable container image, supply-chain compromise).
steps.guidance: This incident represents resource hijacking following some form of initial compromise; treat it as part of a broader intrusion investigation, not merely a resource-exhaustion event.
steps.outcome: Identified or narrowed-down initial access vector informing full incident scope and broader remediation.
steps.tool: EDR / host and cloud audit logs

steps.title: Block outbound connections to identified mining pool infrastructure
steps.desc: Apply firewall/proxy rules blocking outbound connections to any identified cryptomining pool domains/IPs, both on the affected host and organization-wide as a precaution.
steps.guidance: Cross-reference against threat intel for known mining pool infrastructure associated with the identified payload.
steps.outcome: Outbound mining pool communication blocked organization-wide, limiting impact of any other undiscovered infected hosts.

steps.title: Scan the broader environment for additional compromised hosts
steps.desc: Search across the environment for other hosts/containers exhibiting the same cryptomining IOCs (process names, mining pool connections, file hashes) to identify the full scope of compromise.
steps.guidance: Cryptomining campaigns frequently compromise multiple hosts via the same vulnerability or exposed service across a fleet.
steps.outcome: Full scope of affected hosts identified and remediated.

ITID-41513.def: A resource-depletion attack in which crafted compressed content (zip bomb, nested archive, or compressed request body) is submitted to a service that automatically decompresses input, causing the decompression routine to consume excessive CPU cycles relative to the small size of the compressed payload.
ITID-41513.purpose: Captures CPU exhaustion caused by an adversary submitting a compression bomb (e.g., a deeply nested or highly compressed archive) that forces the decompression routine to consume disproportionate CPU cycles.
scopeIncludes: Nested/recursive archive payloads submitted to upload or ingestion endpoints
Compressed HTTP request bodies (e.g., gzip) crafted to maximize CPU cost per byte transferred
Malicious compressed attachments processed by mail or content-scanning pipelines
scopeExcludes: Decompression attacks whose primary impact is memory rather than CPU (ITID-41522, Memory Depletion sibling group)
Regex-based algorithmic-complexity attacks (ITID-41511)
Cryptomining CPU consumption (ITID-41512)
ITID-41513.severity: Medium-High if the decompression path is unauthenticated and internet-facing; Medium otherwise.
ITID-41513.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if the affected service is on the critical path for production traffic and cannot shed load.
ITID-41513.escalation: Escalate to the application/platform team to deploy decompression limits (max ratio, max depth, timeout) if repeated occurrences are observed.
indicators: High CPU utilization correlated with a small number of small-sized inbound requests/files
Decompression-library timeouts or crashes in application logs
Upload or ingestion endpoint showing disproportionate processing time relative to payload size
vectors: Recursively nested zip/gzip archives ('zip bomb') submitted via file upload
Highly compressible crafted content sent in a gzip-encoded request body
Malicious compressed email attachments targeting a content-scanning pipeline
rootCauses: No enforced maximum decompression ratio or output size on ingestion endpoints
Decompression performed synchronously on the request-handling thread without a time budget
Third-party libraries used for decompression without hardening configuration
mitreTechniques: T1499.004 Endpoint Denial of Service: Application or System Exploitation
controls: Enforced maximum decompression ratio and output-size limits
Decompression timeouts and worker isolation (separate process/cgroup with CPU caps)
Content-scanning pipeline hardening against nested archives
ITID-41513.detection: CPU telemetry correlated with upload/ingestion endpoint logs gives a clear technical signal; file-size vs. decompressed-size ratio is a strong indicator once instrumented.
ITID-41513.response: Kill the affected decompression worker, block the source of the malicious payload, and confirm decompression limits are enforced before reopening the ingestion path.
metrics: Number of oversized-decompression events blocked per month
Mean time to restore ingestion service after a compression-bomb incident
ITID-41513.notes: Differentiator within CPU Exhaustion: this leaf is specifically about CPU cost of the decompression operation itself; its memory-impact counterpart is filed under Memory Depletion (ITID-41522).

playbook.name: Compression/Decompression Bomb Exhausting CPU
playbook.description: The attacker submits a maliciously crafted, highly compressible file/payload (e.g., a nested-archive or algorithmic decompression bomb) to an endpoint that decompresses it, causing the decompression process to consume disproportionate CPU resources.

steps.title: Confirm decompression-bomb pattern via CPU spike correlated with a specific upload/processing endpoint
steps.desc: Analyze APM/backend metrics to confirm a disproportionate, sustained CPU spike correlated with processing of a specific uploaded file or payload at a decompression-handling endpoint.
steps.guidance: Check for a relatively small input file size correlated with an extremely long or CPU-intensive decompression/processing duration — the classic decompression-bomb signature.
steps.outcome: Confirmed decompression-bomb-consistent pattern with the specific endpoint and offending file/payload identified.
steps.abort: If the CPU spike is explained by a legitimate large, genuinely complex file, stand down and document as false positive.

steps.title: Kill the affected decompression process and quarantine the offending file
steps.desc: Terminate the process consuming excessive CPU on the decompression task, and quarantine/remove the offending uploaded file from storage.
steps.guidance: Ensure the quarantine action does not simply re-trigger decompression during cleanup; isolate the file for forensic reference without reprocessing it.
steps.outcome: CPU resource freed immediately; offending file safely quarantined.

steps.title: Harden the application's decompression handling with resource-bounded processing
steps.desc: Review and harden the application code handling decompression to enforce timeouts, memory limits, and streaming/incremental decompression with early-abort capability rather than unbounded in-memory expansion.
steps.guidance: Ensure decompression occurs in a resource-isolated context (e.g., a sandboxed worker with strict CPU/memory limits) so a malicious payload cannot impact the broader application.
steps.outcome: Decompression handling hardened to bound worst-case resource consumption regardless of input characteristics.

steps.title: Remove temporary restrictions and confirm endpoint handles legitimate files correctly under new limits
steps.desc: Once hardening is deployed and validated, confirm legitimate file uploads/decompression continue to function correctly under the new size/ratio/timeout limits.
steps.guidance: Test with representative legitimate large/complex files at the upper end of normal use.
steps.outcome: Endpoint confirmed resilient to decompression bombs with normal performance for legitimate use.
steps.abort: If legitimate files are blocked, adjust limits accordingly.

steps.title: Document incident and audit other file-processing endpoints for similar exposure
steps.desc: Record the attack and review other endpoints across the application that decompress or process user-supplied files for similar unbounded-resource-consumption risk.
steps.guidance: Include recommendations for organization-wide resource-bounded file-processing standards in the after-action report.
steps.outcome: After-action report with a broader remediation list if gaps were found elsewhere.

steps.title: Analyze the offending file/payload to confirm decompression-bomb characteristics
steps.desc: Examine the captured file/payload (nested archive depth, compression ratio, algorithmic structure) to confirm it is a deliberately crafted decompression bomb rather than a legitimately large file.
steps.guidance: Classic indicators include extreme compression ratios (e.g., a few KB expanding to gigabytes/terabytes) or deeply nested archive structures designed to multiply CPU cost at each layer.
steps.outcome: Confirmed decompression-bomb characteristics documented with compression ratio/nesting depth captured for reference.

steps.title: Apply upload/decompression size and ratio limits as an immediate compensating control
steps.desc: Deploy or tighten limits on maximum decompressed output size, maximum compression ratio, and maximum archive nesting depth accepted by the endpoint.
steps.guidance: Most modern decompression libraries support configurable limits on expanded size and nesting depth specifically to prevent this attack class; ensure they are enabled and appropriately restrictive.
steps.outcome: Future decompression-bomb uploads rejected before consuming significant resources.
steps.abort: If legitimate large/complex files are rejected, adjust limits to accommodate documented legitimate use cases.

steps.title: Confirm resource-isolated decompression handling performs correctly in production
steps.desc: Verify the sandboxed/resource-isolated decompression worker introduced during eradication operates correctly and with acceptable performance under normal production load.
steps.guidance: Monitor decompression task latency and resource isolation boundary enforcement.
steps.outcome: Confirmed resource-isolated decompression handling functions correctly under normal load.

ITID-41514.def: A CPU-exhaustion incident confirmed as an attack against application or host CPU capacity, but not yet classified into a specific mechanism (regex backtracking, resource hijacking, compression bombs) pending further investigation.
ITID-41514.purpose: Serves as the intake bucket for CPU exhaustion attacks that do not yet fit ReDoS, cryptomining, or compression-bomb classifications, so analysts can log and triage before deeper root-cause analysis.
scopeIncludes: Newly observed CPU-exhaustion techniques not yet mapped to an existing sibling leaf
Ambiguous CPU-saturation incidents pending root-cause confirmation
scopeExcludes: Any incident later confirmed as ReDoS (ITID-41511), cryptomining (ITID-41512), or a compression bomb (ITID-41513) — reclassify once confirmed
Volumetric network flooding tracked elsewhere in the Tier-3 taxonomy
ITID-41514.severity: Medium by default pending classification; adjust once the specific mechanism and business impact are confirmed.
ITID-41514.priority: P3 pending triage, escalating per standard severity guidance once root cause is identified.
ITID-41514.escalation: Escalate to the SOC classification lead for prompt re-tagging into a specific sibling leaf once the mechanism is understood; do not leave incidents parked here longer than the triage window.
indicators: Elevated CPU utilization with an unconfirmed cause
Analyst uncertainty about which CPU-exhaustion mechanism applies
vectors: Unclassified/novel CPU-exhaustion technique pending investigation
rootCauses: Root cause not yet determined
mitreTechniques: T1499.004 Endpoint Denial of Service: Application or System Exploitation
controls: Standard CPU/host monitoring and alerting pending classification
ITID-41514.detection: Coverage depends on the eventual root cause; this bucket itself is detected via generic CPU-saturation alerting.
ITID-41514.response: Investigate to determine the specific mechanism and reclassify to the appropriate sibling ITID as soon as possible; apply standard CPU-exhaustion containment in the interim.
metrics: Number of incidents parked in this bucket beyond the triage SLA
Average time to reclassify into a specific sibling leaf
ITID-41514.notes: Catch-all intake leaf; used only during initial triage. Analysts should reclassify into ITID-41511/41512/41513 as soon as the mechanism is confirmed.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General CPU Exhaustion Attack
playbook.description: A CPU resource-exhaustion condition is confirmed via sustained abnormal utilization, but the specific technique (ReDoS, cryptomining/resource hijacking, decompression bomb) has not yet been determined.

steps.title: Confirm CPU exhaustion via sustained abnormal utilization analysis
steps.desc: Analyze host/application CPU utilization metrics to confirm sustained abnormal consumption not attributable to expected legitimate workload.
steps.guidance: Check whether the exhaustion is tied to a specific request/endpoint (suggesting ReDoS or decompression bomb) or a standalone unauthorized process (suggesting cryptomining/resource hijacking).
steps.outcome: Confirmed CPU exhaustion condition with initial characterization documented.
steps.abort: If the high CPU usage is attributable to an approved legitimate workload, stand down and document as false positive.

steps.title: Kill or isolate the resource-consuming process/request as an immediate measure
steps.desc: Terminate the specific hung request/worker or isolate the unauthorized process/host to immediately free CPU resources pending full classification.
steps.guidance: Prioritize immediate resource recovery over full root-cause analysis given active service impact.
steps.outcome: CPU resource freed immediately.

steps.title: Complete technique classification and apply targeted remediation
steps.desc: Finalize which CPU exhaustion technique was the cause and apply the more specific remediation measures from the corresponding playbook.
steps.guidance: Reclassify the incident to the specific ITID leaf if determination succeeds.
steps.outcome: Root cause documented and technique-specific remediation applied.

steps.title: Confirm CPU utilization returns to normal and legitimate workloads unaffected
steps.desc: Monitor CPU utilization to confirm return to normal baseline and confirm legitimate workloads process correctly under any new hardening.
steps.guidance: Monitor for a sustained period post-recovery to confirm no residual or reintroduced issue.
steps.outcome: Normal CPU utilization confirmed with legitimate functionality unaffected.

steps.title: Document incident and improve CPU exhaustion root-cause classification tooling
steps.desc: Record why immediate root-cause classification was not possible and recommend detection/profiling tooling improvements.
steps.guidance: Include recommendations for enhanced per-request and per-process resource attribution that would have sped up classification.
steps.outcome: After-action report with concrete detection tooling improvement items.

steps.title: Attempt technique classification via process and request correlation
steps.desc: Determine whether the exhaustion correlates with a specific application request (ReDoS/decompression bomb) or an independent unauthorized process (cryptomining), to allow pivot to a more specific playbook.
steps.guidance: If classification succeeds, transition to the corresponding specific CPU exhaustion playbook; otherwise proceed with general mitigation.
steps.outcome: Either successful reclassification or confirmed genuinely unclear cause requiring broader investigation.

steps.title: Apply general request-processing timeouts and resource limits as defense in depth
steps.desc: Configure general request-processing timeouts and per-process CPU/memory limits pending full classification, as a broad-spectrum compensating control.
steps.guidance: These general controls provide protection regardless of the specific final classification.
steps.outcome: Worst-case future impact bounded regardless of root cause.

steps.title: Confirm technique-specific remediation retained where classification succeeded
steps.desc: Where the incident was reclassified to a specific CPU exhaustion technique, confirm the corresponding technique-specific remediation remains in place post-recovery.
steps.guidance: Cross-check against the specific playbook's remediation recommendations if reclassification occurred.
steps.outcome: Confirmed appropriate remediation retained based on final classification.

ITID-41521.def: A resource-depletion attack in which an adversary repeatedly submits malformed or edge-case requests that trigger a memory leak (objects, buffers, or connections not properly released) in the target application, causing memory consumption to grow until the process is killed by the OS or becomes unresponsive.
ITID-41521.purpose: Captures denial of service caused by an adversary repeatedly sending malformed requests that trigger a memory leak in application code, gradually exhausting available memory.
scopeIncludes: Repeated submission of malformed requests known to trigger a specific leak in application code
Sustained low-rate requests exploiting an unreleased-resource bug to grow memory usage over hours
Leak triggered via a specific error-handling code path that fails to free allocated memory
scopeExcludes: Single-request decompression/expansion attacks that spike memory instantly (ITID-41522)
Memory growth caused by cache poisoning designed to force large legitimate-looking allocations (ITID-41523)
CPU-only impact with no memory growth (Tier-4 CPU Exhaustion group)
ITID-41521.severity: Medium-High; severity rises with how quickly memory growth leads to an OOM kill or degraded service.
ITID-41521.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if the leak recurs faster than automated restarts can compensate or affects a customer-facing service.
ITID-41521.escalation: Escalate to the owning engineering team with the specific request pattern and stack trace so the leak can be patched; treat as an attack (not just a bug) once repeated crafted requests are confirmed as the trigger.
indicators: Steady upward memory-usage trend correlated with a specific request pattern in access logs
Repeated OOM kills or process restarts on a predictable cadence
Heap-profiling data showing unreleased objects tied to a specific code path
vectors: Malformed API requests repeatedly hitting an error-handling path with a known leak
Long-lived connections deliberately left open to exploit unreleased connection-pool resources
Crafted payloads exercising an edge case in a parsing or serialization library
rootCauses: Unreleased memory/connections in exception-handling or edge-case code paths
Absence of memory-growth alerting tied to request patterns
Third-party library with a known but unpatched leak
mitreTechniques: T1499.004 Endpoint Denial of Service: Application or System Exploitation
controls: Memory-growth-rate alerting with automatic restart/circuit-breaking
Code review and static analysis targeting resource-release in error paths
Rate limiting on request patterns correlated with known leak triggers
ITID-41521.detection: Strong technical signal from memory-usage trend telemetry combined with heap profiling; request-log correlation confirms the trigger.
ITID-41521.response: Restart affected processes to relieve immediate pressure, identify and rate-limit or block the triggering request pattern, and prioritize a code fix for the underlying leak.
metrics: Mean time between OOM restarts during an active incident
Number of confirmed memory-leak vulnerabilities patched per quarter
ITID-41521.notes: Differentiator within Memory Depletion: this leaf is a gradual leak from repeated requests exploiting a code bug, distinct from an instantaneous single-request expansion (ITID-41522) or cache-driven allocation growth (ITID-41523).

playbook.name: Memory Leak Triggered via Repeated Malformed Requests
playbook.description: The attacker sends repeated, specifically-crafted malformed requests that trigger a memory leak in the application (e.g., unreleased allocations on an error path), gradually exhausting available memory until the service degrades or crashes.

steps.title: Confirm gradual memory-leak pattern via memory-utilization trend analysis
steps.desc: Analyze application/host memory utilization metrics for a steady, monotonic increase over time (rather than a sudden spike) correlated with the volume of a specific type of request.
steps.guidance: Memory leaks show a characteristic sawtooth-then-climb or steadily rising memory graph rather than the abrupt spike typical of a single large allocation; correlate the climb rate against request logs for a specific request pattern.
steps.outcome: Confirmed gradual memory-leak pattern with correlated request type and memory growth rate documented.
steps.abort: If the memory growth correlates with an expected legitimate cache-warming or batch-processing behavior, stand down and document as false positive.

steps.title: Block the identified malformed request pattern at the WAF
steps.desc: Deploy a WAF rule blocking the specific malformed request pattern identified as triggering the memory leak.
steps.guidance: Target the specific malformation characteristics (e.g., a specific malformed header, missing field, or edge-case value) rather than blocking the endpoint broadly.
steps.outcome: Further memory-leak-triggering requests blocked while legitimate traffic to the endpoint continues.

steps.title: Fix the underlying memory leak in application code
steps.desc: Work with the application development team to fix the root-cause memory leak (e.g., ensure resources are released on all error/exception paths, fix reference-retention issues) and deploy the fix.
steps.guidance: Validate the fix using heap-profiling tools by re-sending the original offending request repeatedly and confirming memory does not grow.
steps.outcome: Memory leak confirmed fixed; repeated offending requests no longer cause unbounded memory growth.

steps.title: Remove temporary blocking and confirm stable memory utilization under normal load
steps.desc: Once the code fix is deployed and validated, relax the temporary WAF block while monitoring memory utilization under normal production load to confirm long-term stability.
steps.guidance: Monitor for an extended period (e.g., several days) given memory leaks can be slow enough that a short observation window may miss a residual, smaller leak.
steps.outcome: Confirmed stable memory utilization over an extended period post-fix.
steps.abort: If memory growth resumes, restore the temporary restart schedule and investigate further.

steps.title: Document incident and add memory-growth trend alerting
steps.desc: Record the incident and ensure ongoing memory-utilization trend alerting is in place to catch future leaks earlier, before they cause service degradation.
steps.guidance: Include recommendations for proactive heap-profiling in CI/CD or periodic production heap analysis as a preventive measure.
steps.outcome: After-action report with memory-monitoring and preventive-testing improvements tracked.

steps.title: Identify the specific malformed request pattern triggering the leak
steps.desc: Capture and analyze the specific malformed request(s) correlated with memory growth, and use heap-profiling tools to identify the specific code path/allocation responsible.
steps.guidance: Use heap snapshots/diffing tools (e.g., language-specific heap profilers) taken before and after sending a suspected offending request to pinpoint the leaking allocation.
steps.outcome: Documented offending request pattern and identified leaking code path, ready for both immediate blocking and permanent code fix.

steps.title: Restart the affected service/process to reclaim leaked memory as an immediate stopgap
steps.desc: Restart the affected application process/service to immediately reclaim leaked memory and restore normal operation while the permanent fix is developed.
steps.guidance: In a multi-instance/load-balanced deployment, perform a rolling restart to avoid a full service outage; consider whether the leak rate warrants scheduling periodic restarts as a temporary mitigation.
steps.outcome: Memory utilization returns to normal baseline immediately following restart.

steps.title: Confirm legitimate use of the affected endpoint continues functioning normally
steps.desc: Verify legitimate requests to the affected endpoint continue to be processed correctly under the deployed fix.
steps.guidance: Test with representative legitimate request variations, including edge cases near the previously malformed pattern.
steps.outcome: Confirmed no legitimate functionality was broken by the fix.

ITID-41522.def: A resource-depletion attack in which a small, highly compressed payload (zip bomb, gzip bomb, or nested archive) is decompressed into memory in full before size validation, causing the decompression buffer to exhaust available RAM and crash or degrade the target process.
ITID-41522.purpose: Captures denial of service caused by a decompression bomb whose primary impact is memory exhaustion (rather than CPU), where a small compressed payload expands to consume all available memory.
scopeIncludes: Zip/gzip bombs decompressed fully into memory without streaming or size caps
Nested archives designed to maximize decompressed-to-compressed size ratio
Compressed API payloads or file uploads that expand beyond available process memory
scopeExcludes: Decompression attacks whose primary measured impact is CPU cycles rather than memory footprint (ITID-41513)
Gradual memory leaks from repeated malformed requests (ITID-41521)
Cache-driven allocation growth (ITID-41523)
ITID-41522.severity: High if decompression happens fully in memory before any size check on an internet-facing path; Medium if partial mitigations (streaming, size caps) already exist.
ITID-41522.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if the affected process handles production traffic and OOM kills cascade to dependent services.
ITID-41522.escalation: Escalate to the platform/application team to enforce streaming decompression with size caps; treat repeated occurrences as a targeted attack rather than a one-off bug report.
indicators: Sudden, sharp memory-usage spike correlated with a single small inbound file/payload
OOM kill immediately following a decompression operation
Decompressed-size-to-compressed-size ratio far exceeding expected norms
vectors: Zip bomb uploaded via a file-ingestion endpoint
Nested gzip payload submitted as a compressed HTTP request body
Malicious compressed attachment processed by a scanning or indexing pipeline
rootCauses: Decompression performed fully into memory before any size validation
No enforced maximum decompressed-size limit
Third-party decompression library used without hardening/streaming configuration
mitreTechniques: T1499.004 Endpoint Denial of Service: Application or System Exploitation
controls: Streaming decompression with enforced maximum output size
Pre-decompression compressed-size and nesting-depth limits
Isolated decompression workers with memory caps (separate process/cgroup)
ITID-41522.detection: Strong technical signal from sudden memory-spike telemetry tightly correlated with a specific small inbound payload; decompressed-size ratio logging confirms root cause.
ITID-41522.response: Restart the affected process, block the source payload, and enforce decompression size limits before reopening the ingestion path.
metrics: Number of oversized-decompression events blocked per month
Mean time to restore service after a memory-based decompression-bomb incident
ITID-41522.notes: Differentiator within Memory Depletion: instantaneous single-payload memory exhaustion via decompression, as opposed to the gradual leak (ITID-41521) or cache-driven growth (ITID-41523) siblings.

playbook.name: Zip Bomb/Decompression Memory Exhaustion Attack
playbook.description: The attacker submits a maliciously crafted, highly compressible archive (a 'zip bomb') to an endpoint that decompresses it into memory, causing the decompression process to exhaust available memory rather than (or in addition to) CPU.

steps.title: Confirm zip-bomb pattern via memory-utilization spike correlated with a specific upload
steps.desc: Analyze APM/backend metrics to confirm a rapid, disproportionate memory-utilization spike correlated with processing of a specific uploaded archive file, distinct from the gradual growth pattern of a memory leak.
steps.guidance: Check for a relatively small input archive size correlated with an extreme in-memory expansion (e.g., a few KB expanding to gigabytes) causing out-of-memory conditions or swapping.
steps.outcome: Confirmed zip-bomb-consistent pattern with the specific endpoint and offending archive identified.
steps.abort: If the memory spike is explained by a legitimately large file being processed, stand down and document as false positive.
steps.tool: APM / application logs / host memory monitoring

steps.title: Kill the affected decompression process and quarantine the offending archive
steps.desc: Terminate the process consuming excessive memory on the decompression task before it triggers an out-of-memory condition affecting other workloads on the same host, and quarantine the offending archive.
steps.guidance: If the process has already caused broader memory pressure/OOM-killer activity affecting other services, coordinate a broader host-level remediation, not just the single process.
steps.outcome: Memory resource freed immediately; offending archive safely quarantined; other co-located workloads confirmed unaffected or restored.

steps.title: Harden decompression handling with streaming, memory-bounded processing
steps.desc: Review and harden the application code handling archive decompression to use streaming/incremental decompression with hard memory ceilings and early-abort capability, rather than unbounded in-memory expansion.
steps.guidance: Ensure decompression occurs in a resource-isolated context (e.g., a memory-cgroup-limited sandboxed worker) so a malicious archive cannot impact the broader application or co-located workloads.
steps.outcome: Decompression handling hardened to bound worst-case memory consumption regardless of input characteristics.
steps.tool: Application code review / container memory limits

steps.title: Remove temporary restrictions and confirm endpoint handles legitimate archives correctly under new limits
steps.desc: Once hardening is deployed and validated, confirm legitimate archive uploads/decompression continue to function correctly under the new size/nesting limits.
steps.guidance: Test with representative legitimate large/complex archives at the upper end of normal use.
steps.outcome: Endpoint confirmed resilient to zip bombs with normal performance for legitimate use.
steps.abort: If legitimate archives are blocked, adjust limits accordingly.

steps.title: Document incident and audit other file-processing endpoints for similar memory-exhaustion exposure
steps.desc: Record the attack and review other endpoints across the application that decompress or process user-supplied files for similar unbounded-memory-consumption risk.
steps.guidance: Include recommendations for organization-wide memory-bounded file-processing standards in the after-action report.
steps.outcome: After-action report with a broader remediation list if gaps were found elsewhere.

steps.title: Analyze the offending archive to confirm zip-bomb characteristics
steps.desc: Examine the captured archive file (compression ratio, nesting structure) to confirm it is a deliberately crafted zip bomb rather than a legitimately large compressible file.
steps.guidance: Classic indicators include extreme compression ratios or deeply nested archive structures (e.g., '42.zip'-style recursive archives) designed to multiply memory expansion at each layer.
steps.outcome: Confirmed zip-bomb characteristics documented with compression ratio/nesting depth captured for reference.

steps.title: Apply decompressed-size and nesting-depth limits as an immediate compensating control
steps.desc: Deploy or tighten limits on maximum decompressed output size and maximum archive nesting depth accepted by the endpoint, specifically bounding memory rather than just CPU/time.
steps.guidance: Ensure the limit check occurs incrementally during streaming decompression (aborting early once the limit is exceeded) rather than only after full decompression completes, which would defeat the purpose.
steps.outcome: Future zip-bomb uploads rejected before consuming significant memory.
steps.abort: If legitimate large/complex archives are rejected, adjust limits to accommodate documented legitimate use cases.

steps.title: Confirm co-located workloads on the affected host remain stable
steps.desc: Verify that any other workloads co-located on the affected host during the incident have returned to normal stable operation with no lingering resource pressure.
steps.guidance: Check memory utilization and error rates for co-located services over a sustained monitoring window.
steps.outcome: Confirmed all co-located workloads operating normally with no residual impact.

ITID-41523.def: A resource-depletion attack in which an adversary exploits cache-key generation or cache-population logic (e.g., by varying request parameters, headers, or cookies) to force the application or caching layer to allocate and retain an unbounded number of distinct cache entries, exhausting available memory.
ITID-41523.purpose: Captures denial of service in which an adversary manipulates application or CDN caching behavior to force excessive, unbounded memory allocation for cache entries.
scopeIncludes: Cache-key manipulation via varying query parameters, headers, or cookies to force unique cache entries per request
Forcing population of an in-memory cache with a high cardinality of near-duplicate objects
Exploiting unbounded cache growth in application-layer object caches (not just HTTP/CDN caches)
scopeExcludes: Cache poisoning aimed at serving malicious content to other users (a content-integrity/web-attack concern tracked elsewhere)
Simple gradual leaks unrelated to caching logic (ITID-41521)
Decompression-driven memory spikes (ITID-41522)
ITID-41523.severity: Medium-High; severity rises when the cache layer has no eviction policy or size cap and sits in front of a critical service.
ITID-41523.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if cache-layer memory exhaustion causes cascading failures across dependent services.
ITID-41523.escalation: Escalate to the application/platform team to enforce cache-key normalization and eviction limits; coordinate with CDN/edge team if the manipulation occurs at that layer.
indicators: Rapidly growing cache entry count with high key cardinality from a narrow set of source IPs
Memory growth tightly correlated with cache-store metrics rather than general request volume
Low cache hit ratio despite high request volume, indicating forced cache misses/new-key creation
vectors: Requests with randomized or incrementing query parameters/headers designed to bypass cache normalization
Automated tooling generating high-cardinality cookie or session values to force per-user cache entries
Exploiting a caching layer that keys on unsanitized user input
rootCauses: Cache-key generation includes unbounded or attacker-controlled input without normalization
No maximum cache size or eviction policy (e.g., LRU) enforced
Caching layer treats all request variants as cacheable without validation
mitreTechniques: T1499.004 Endpoint Denial of Service: Application or System Exploitation
controls: Cache-key normalization to strip attacker-controllable parameters
Enforced maximum cache size with eviction policy
Rate limiting on requests generating novel cache keys from a single source
ITID-41523.detection: Strong technical signal from cache-store metrics (entry count, key cardinality, hit ratio) correlated with memory-usage telemetry.
ITID-41523.response: Flush or cap the affected cache, identify and normalize the exploited key-generation logic, and rate-limit the offending source pending a permanent fix.
metrics: Cache entry count growth rate during incidents
Cache hit ratio trend
Mean time to restore normal cache behavior
