ITID-41523.notes: Differentiator within Memory Depletion: growth driven specifically by cache-key manipulation, distinct from generic leaks (ITID-41521) or decompression spikes (ITID-41522).

playbook.name: Application Cache Poisoning to Force Excessive Memory Allocation
playbook.description: The attacker deliberately generates a high volume of unique, low-value cache keys (e.g., via randomized request parameters) to force the application's in-memory cache to grow unboundedly, exhausting available memory and evicting legitimate cached data.

steps.title: Confirm cache-poisoning pattern via cache-size growth and key-cardinality analysis
steps.desc: Analyze application cache metrics (size, entry count, eviction rate) for abnormal growth correlated with a high volume of unique, low-repeat-rate cache keys being generated.
steps.guidance: Check cache hit ratio (which will drop as poisoned entries crowd out legitimate cached data) alongside a rapid rise in unique key cardinality driven by a specific request parameter pattern.
steps.outcome: Confirmed cache-poisoning pattern with the offending request parameter/key-generation logic and memory impact documented.
steps.abort: If the key cardinality growth is explained by a legitimate new feature generating genuinely diverse cache keys, stand down and document as false positive.

steps.title: Apply rate limiting and normalize/validate the offending cache-key-driving parameter at the edge
steps.desc: Deploy WAF/edge rules to rate-limit requests using the offending parameter pattern and, where feasible, normalize or strip the parameter before it reaches the caching layer.
steps.guidance: This mirrors CDN cache-key normalization approaches used against cache-busting floods, applied here to the application's internal cache-key generation.
steps.outcome: Rate of new low-value cache-key generation substantially reduced.

steps.title: Fix cache-key generation logic to exclude or normalize attacker-controllable low-value parameters
steps.desc: Work with the application team to fix the cache-key generation logic so it does not directly incorporate unsanitized, attacker-controllable parameters that provide no legitimate caching benefit.
steps.guidance: Review whether the varying parameter actually needs to affect the cached response at all; if not, exclude it from the cache key entirely.
steps.outcome: Cache-key generation logic hardened to prevent recurrence of unbounded key-cardinality growth from this parameter.

steps.title: Confirm cache hit ratio and memory utilization return to normal
steps.desc: Monitor cache hit ratio, entry count, and memory utilization to confirm return to normal baseline, retaining the maximum-size limit and eviction policy permanently.
steps.guidance: Verify legitimate cached data is no longer being prematurely evicted by residual poisoned entries.
steps.outcome: Normal cache performance and hit ratio restored with permanent hardening retained.

steps.title: Document incident and audit other caching layers for similar cache-key exposure
steps.desc: Record the attack and review other application/CDN caching layers for similar unbounded-cache-key-cardinality risk.
steps.guidance: Include recommendations for organization-wide cache-key hygiene standards in the after-action report.
steps.outcome: After-action report with a broader remediation list if gaps were found elsewhere.

steps.title: Identify the specific request parameter(s) driving unbounded cache-key generation
steps.desc: Analyze request logs to identify which request parameter(s) are being varied/randomized by the attacker to force new, low-value cache entries.
steps.guidance: Common vectors include cache keys derived directly from unsanitized query-string parameters, headers, or cookies without normalization.
steps.outcome: Documented specific parameter(s) responsible, ready for both immediate mitigation and permanent code fix.

steps.title: Enforce a maximum cache size/entry-count limit with eviction policy tuning
steps.desc: Confirm the cache layer enforces a hard maximum size/entry-count limit with an appropriate eviction policy (e.g., LRU) so it cannot grow unboundedly regardless of key cardinality.
steps.guidance: If no hard limit was previously configured, this is a critical gap; configure one immediately as defense in depth even after the immediate attack is contained.
steps.outcome: Cache memory consumption bounded regardless of future key-cardinality abuse attempts.

steps.title: Confirm cache-key generation fix has not affected legitimate caching behavior
steps.desc: Verify that the updated cache-key generation logic still correctly caches and serves distinct legitimate variations of the response.
steps.guidance: Test representative legitimate scenarios where the response should legitimately vary.
steps.outcome: Confirmed no legitimate caching behavior was broken by the fix.

ITID-41524.def: A memory-exhaustion incident confirmed as an attack against application or host memory capacity, but not yet classified into a specific mechanism (leak, decompression bomb, cache manipulation) pending further investigation.
ITID-41524.purpose: Serves as the intake bucket for memory-depletion attacks that do not yet fit leak, decompression-bomb, or cache-manipulation classifications.
scopeIncludes: Newly observed memory-exhaustion techniques not yet mapped to an existing sibling leaf
Ambiguous memory-saturation incidents pending root-cause confirmation
scopeExcludes: Any incident later confirmed as a memory leak (ITID-41521), decompression bomb (ITID-41522), or cache manipulation (ITID-41523) — reclassify once confirmed
ITID-41524.severity: Medium by default pending classification; adjust once the specific mechanism and business impact are confirmed.
ITID-41524.priority: P3 pending triage, escalating per standard severity guidance once root cause is identified.
ITID-41524.escalation: Escalate to the SOC classification lead for prompt re-tagging into a specific sibling leaf once the mechanism is understood.
indicators: Elevated memory utilization with an unconfirmed cause
Analyst uncertainty about which memory-exhaustion mechanism applies
vectors: Unclassified/novel memory-exhaustion technique pending investigation
rootCauses: Root cause not yet determined
mitreTechniques: T1499.004 Endpoint Denial of Service: Application or System Exploitation
controls: Standard memory/host monitoring and alerting pending classification
ITID-41524.detection: Coverage depends on the eventual root cause; this bucket itself is detected via generic memory-saturation alerting.
ITID-41524.response: Investigate to determine the specific mechanism and reclassify to the appropriate sibling ITID as soon as possible; apply standard memory-exhaustion containment in the interim.
metrics: Number of incidents parked in this bucket beyond the triage SLA
Average time to reclassify into a specific sibling leaf
ITID-41524.notes: Catch-all intake leaf; used only during initial triage. Analysts should reclassify into ITID-41521/41522/41523 as soon as the mechanism is confirmed.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Memory Depletion Attack
playbook.description: A memory resource-exhaustion condition is confirmed via abnormal utilization, but the specific technique (gradual leak, decompression bomb, cache-key poisoning) has not yet been determined.

steps.title: Confirm memory depletion via utilization trend analysis
steps.desc: Analyze host/application memory utilization metrics to confirm abnormal consumption, characterizing whether the growth is gradual/leak-like or a sudden spike.
steps.guidance: A gradual, steadily-climbing memory graph suggests a leak; a sudden sharp spike correlated with a specific request suggests a decompression bomb or similar single-request cause; growth correlated with cache size suggests cache-key poisoning.
steps.outcome: Confirmed memory depletion condition with growth-pattern characterization documented.
steps.abort: If memory growth is attributable to an approved legitimate workload, stand down and document as false positive.

steps.title: Restart the affected service/process to immediately reclaim memory
steps.desc: Restart the affected application process/service as an immediate stopgap to reclaim consumed memory and restore normal operation pending full classification.
steps.guidance: In a multi-instance/load-balanced deployment, perform a rolling restart to avoid a full service outage.
steps.outcome: Memory utilization returns to normal baseline immediately following restart.

steps.title: Complete technique classification and apply targeted remediation
steps.desc: Finalize which memory depletion technique was the cause and apply the more specific remediation measures from the corresponding playbook.
steps.guidance: Reclassify the incident to the specific ITID leaf if determination succeeds.
steps.outcome: Root cause documented and technique-specific remediation applied.

steps.title: Confirm memory utilization returns to normal and remains stable
steps.desc: Monitor memory utilization over an extended period to confirm return to normal baseline and sustained stability.
steps.guidance: Monitor for at least several days given some memory issues (leaks) require a longer observation window to confirm resolution.
steps.outcome: Confirmed stable, normal memory utilization over an extended period.

steps.title: Document incident and improve memory-depletion root-cause classification tooling
steps.desc: Record why immediate root-cause classification was not possible and recommend detection/profiling tooling improvements.
steps.guidance: Include recommendations for enhanced heap-profiling and cache-metrics visibility that would have sped up classification.
steps.outcome: After-action report with concrete detection tooling improvement items.

steps.title: Attempt technique classification via growth-pattern and correlation analysis
steps.desc: Determine whether the depletion is a gradual leak, a decompression-bomb spike, or cache-key-cardinality growth, to allow pivot to a more specific playbook.
steps.guidance: If classification succeeds, transition to the corresponding specific memory depletion playbook; otherwise proceed with general mitigation.
steps.outcome: Either successful reclassification or confirmed genuinely unclear cause requiring broader investigation.

steps.title: Apply general memory limits/circuit breakers as defense in depth
steps.desc: Configure general per-process/container memory limits pending full classification, as a broad-spectrum compensating control to bound worst-case future impact.
steps.guidance: These general controls provide protection regardless of the specific final classification.
steps.outcome: Worst-case future memory impact bounded regardless of root cause.

steps.title: Confirm technique-specific remediation retained where classification succeeded
steps.desc: Where the incident was reclassified to a specific memory depletion technique, confirm the corresponding technique-specific remediation remains in place post-recovery.
steps.guidance: Cross-check against the specific playbook's remediation recommendations if reclassification occurred.
steps.outcome: Confirmed appropriate remediation retained based on final classification.

ITID-41531.def: A resource-depletion attack in which an adversary establishes a high number of database connections (directly or via an application path that opens one connection per request) and holds them open, exhausting the configured connection-pool limit and causing subsequent legitimate requests to fail or queue indefinitely.
ITID-41531.purpose: Captures denial of service caused by an adversary opening and holding database connections until the connection pool is exhausted, preventing legitimate application requests from obtaining a connection.
scopeIncludes: Directly opening many database connections against an exposed database port
Repeated application requests that each open a new connection without proper pooling/reuse
Deliberately slow or idle-in-transaction connections held open to occupy pool slots
scopeExcludes: Query-volume-driven exhaustion where the pool is saturated by expensive queries rather than raw connection count (ITID-41532)
Lock contention from long-running transactions specifically designed to block other transactions (ITID-41533)
ITID-41531.severity: High if the database is a shared dependency for multiple critical services; Medium if isolated to a single non-critical service.
ITID-41531.priority: P1 if connection exhaustion is actively blocking production transactions; P2 if contained to a non-critical environment.
ITID-41531.escalation: Escalate immediately to database administrators to identify and terminate the offending connections and adjust pool/timeout configuration.
indicators: Connection-pool utilization at or near 100% with application errors indicating pool exhaustion
A small number of source IPs/accounts holding a disproportionate share of open connections
Idle-in-transaction connections with abnormally long duration
vectors: Exposed database port accessible without adequate network segmentation
Application endpoint that opens a new connection per request without pooling
Slow-loris-style connection holding against a database or connection-pooling proxy
rootCauses: No per-source connection limit enforced at the database or proxy layer
Application-level connection pooling misconfigured or absent
Database port exposed beyond the application tier
mitreTechniques: T1499.003 Endpoint Denial of Service: Application Exhaustion Flood
controls: Per-source connection-count limits at the database or pooling-proxy layer
Idle and statement timeouts on database connections
Network segmentation restricting database access to the application tier only
ITID-41531.detection: Strong technical signal from connection-pool utilization metrics and per-source connection-count breakdowns.
ITID-41531.response: Terminate offending connections, apply per-source connection limits, and confirm application connection pooling is correctly configured before restoring full access.
metrics: Connection-pool utilization during incidents
Mean time to restore available connection capacity
Number of source IPs/accounts blocked per incident
ITID-41531.notes: Differentiator within Database Query Flooding: this leaf is about raw connection-slot exhaustion, distinct from query-cost-driven exhaustion (ITID-41532) or lock contention (ITID-41533).

playbook.name: Direct Database Connection Pool Exhaustion Attack
playbook.description: The attacker sends a high volume of requests that each acquire and hold a database connection (e.g., via slow queries or deliberately unclosed connections), exhausting the application's database connection pool and denying database access to legitimate requests.

steps.title: Confirm connection pool exhaustion via pool-utilization and wait-time metrics
steps.desc: Analyze application/database connection pool metrics for near-100% pool utilization correlated with a spike in connection-acquisition wait times or timeouts for new requests.
steps.guidance: Check connection pool dashboards (e.g., via ORM/driver metrics, database proxy stats) for pool saturation correlated with a specific request pattern or source.
steps.outcome: Confirmed connection pool exhaustion with saturation level and correlated request pattern documented.
steps.abort: If pool exhaustion correlates with a legitimate traffic surge and capacity is simply undersized, treat as a capacity issue rather than an attack.

steps.title: Kill long-held/idle-in-transaction database connections and block the offending source
steps.desc: Terminate the identified long-held or idle-in-transaction database connections to immediately free pool capacity, and apply WAF/rate-limiting to block the offending request source/pattern.
steps.guidance: Use database-native session-termination commands (e.g., PostgreSQL pg_terminate_backend, MySQL KILL) targeted at the specific offending sessions rather than a broad restart where possible.
steps.outcome: Connection pool capacity freed immediately; further offending requests blocked.

steps.title: Fix application code paths that fail to release connections promptly
steps.desc: Review and fix the identified application code path(s) that acquire but fail to promptly release database connections, particularly on error/exception paths.
steps.guidance: Ensure connection acquisition uses a pattern that guarantees release (e.g., try-with-resources, context managers, connection pooling middleware with automatic cleanup) regardless of success or failure.
steps.outcome: Confirmed application code reliably releases connections under all code paths, including error conditions.

steps.title: Confirm connection pool utilization returns to normal and remains stable
steps.desc: Monitor connection pool utilization and acquisition wait times to confirm return to normal baseline, retaining timeout hardening permanently.
steps.guidance: Monitor under normal production load for a sustained period to confirm stability.
steps.outcome: Normal database connectivity and performance restored with permanent hardening retained.

steps.title: Document incident and audit other services for similar connection-handling exposure
steps.desc: Record the attack and review other application services/code paths for similar connection-leak or unbounded-hold-time risk.
steps.guidance: Include recommendations for organization-wide connection-pool hygiene standards and monitoring in the after-action report.
steps.outcome: After-action report with a broader remediation list if gaps were found elsewhere.

steps.title: Identify the specific request pattern/source holding connections excessively long
steps.desc: Analyze database session/query logs to identify which requests or sources are holding connections for abnormally long durations, exhausting the pool.
steps.guidance: Check for long-running or slow queries, or application code paths that acquire a connection but fail to release it promptly (e.g., on an unhandled exception path).
steps.outcome: Documented offending request pattern/source and connection-holding behavior.

steps.title: Configure or tighten connection-acquisition and statement timeouts
steps.desc: Configure aggressive connection-acquisition timeouts and per-statement query timeouts at the application/database-proxy layer so no single request can hold a connection indefinitely.
steps.guidance: Ensure timeouts are tuned to accommodate legitimate longest-expected queries while still bounding worst-case connection-holding duration.
steps.outcome: Future connection-holding incidents automatically bounded by enforced timeouts.
steps.abort: If legitimate long-running reporting queries are affected, provide a separate connection pool/timeout profile for those specific use cases.

steps.title: Confirm legitimate long-running queries still complete successfully
steps.desc: Verify that legitimate long-running queries/reports that require extended connection hold times still complete successfully under the new timeout configuration (via the separate profile if one was created).
steps.guidance: Test with representative legitimate long-running query scenarios.
steps.outcome: Confirmed no legitimate use case was broken by the timeout hardening.

ITID-41532.def: A resource-depletion attack in which an adversary crafts input (search terms, filter parameters, sort fields) that forces the application to execute expensive database queries lacking appropriate indexes, consuming disproportionate database CPU and IO and degrading performance for all users of the shared database.
ITID-41532.purpose: Captures denial of service caused by an adversary submitting requests that trigger expensive, unindexed, or full-table-scan database queries, exhausting database CPU/IO capacity.
scopeIncludes: Crafted search/filter/sort parameters that force full-table scans on large tables
Repeated submission of known-expensive query patterns to exhaust database capacity
Exploiting missing or ineffective indexes on user-facing filter/search endpoints
scopeExcludes: Raw connection-count exhaustion unrelated to query cost (ITID-41531)
Deliberate lock-holding transactions designed to block others (ITID-41533)
ITID-41532.severity: High if the affected table underlies multiple critical services; Medium if isolated to a single reporting/analytics path.
ITID-41532.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if database CPU saturation is degrading production transactions.
ITID-41532.escalation: Escalate to the database and application engineering teams to add missing indexes or query-cost limits; treat repeated targeted occurrences as an attack rather than an organic performance issue.
indicators: Database CPU/IO saturation correlated with a specific slow-query pattern in the query log
Query execution plans showing full-table scans on large tables triggered by user input
A small number of source IPs/accounts responsible for a disproportionate share of expensive queries
vectors: Search or filter parameters crafted to bypass indexed columns
Sort-by or pagination parameters forcing expensive re-computation on every request
Automated scripts repeatedly triggering known-expensive report/export queries
rootCauses: Missing indexes on columns exposed to user-controlled filtering/sorting
No query-cost or execution-time limits enforced at the database or application layer
Expensive reporting queries exposed on a user-facing, unauthenticated or lightly-rate-limited endpoint
mitreTechniques: T1499.003 Endpoint Denial of Service: Application Exhaustion Flood
controls: Index coverage review for user-facing filter/search/sort columns
Query-execution-time limits and statement timeouts
Rate limiting on expensive query endpoints
ITID-41532.detection: Strong technical signal from slow-query logs and database CPU/IO telemetry correlated with specific query patterns.
ITID-41532.response: Kill long-running queries, rate-limit or block the offending source, and prioritize adding missing indexes or query-cost guards.
metrics: Number of slow-query incidents per month
Mean time to identify and mitigate the triggering query pattern
Index-coverage remediation count
ITID-41532.notes: Differentiator within Database Query Flooding: this leaf is about query cost/plan inefficiency, distinct from raw connection exhaustion (ITID-41531) or lock contention (ITID-41533).

playbook.name: Unindexed/Full-Table-Scan Query Flood
playbook.description: The attacker repeatedly submits requests that trigger a database query lacking an appropriate index, forcing expensive full-table scans that consume disproportionate database CPU/I/O even at moderate request volume.

steps.title: Confirm full-table-scan pattern via slow-query log and database resource correlation
steps.desc: Analyze database slow-query logs and resource metrics (CPU, I/O) to confirm a specific query is executing full-table scans and consuming disproportionate resources relative to its call frequency.
steps.guidance: Use database query-plan analysis (e.g., EXPLAIN ANALYZE) to confirm the offending query lacks an appropriate index and is performing a sequential/full-table scan.
steps.outcome: Confirmed unindexed full-table-scan query identified with resource impact and calling endpoint documented.
steps.abort: If the query is a known, accepted legitimate reporting query with an approved exception, stand down and document as a known/accepted risk.

steps.title: Rate-limit the specific endpoint driving the expensive query
steps.desc: Deploy WAF/API gateway rate limiting scoped specifically to the endpoint identified as triggering the unindexed query.
steps.guidance: Scope narrowly to avoid impacting unrelated endpoint functionality.
steps.outcome: Query execution rate reduced to sustainable levels; database resource impact reduced.
steps.abort: If legitimate users report being blocked, relax the threshold appropriately.

steps.title: Add the missing index and/or optimize the query
steps.desc: Work with the database/application team to add the appropriate index and/or rewrite the query to eliminate the full-table scan, then deploy and validate the fix.
steps.guidance: Re-run EXPLAIN ANALYZE post-fix to confirm the query now uses an index scan rather than a sequential scan, and benchmark execution time improvement.
steps.outcome: Query execution cost brought within acceptable bounds regardless of call frequency.

steps.title: Remove temporary rate limiting and confirm endpoint performs efficiently under normal load
steps.desc: Once the index/query fix is deployed and validated, relax the temporary endpoint rate limit while retaining the query timeout permanently as defense in depth.
steps.guidance: Load-test the fixed endpoint to confirm database resource consumption is now proportionate to request volume.
steps.outcome: Endpoint confirmed resilient to repeated calls with normal database resource consumption.

steps.title: Document incident and audit schema/query patterns for similar missing-index risk
steps.desc: Record the incident and review other frequently-called queries across the application for similar missing-index or full-table-scan risk.
steps.guidance: Consider adding automated slow-query monitoring/alerting and a query-review step to the development process to catch similar issues before production.
steps.outcome: After-action report with a broader database performance/hardening remediation list if gaps were found elsewhere.

steps.title: Identify the application endpoint/request pattern driving the query
steps.desc: Trace the offending query back to the specific application endpoint and request parameters causing it to be invoked repeatedly.
steps.guidance: Correlate database query logs with application access logs using timestamps and query fingerprints.
steps.outcome: Documented endpoint and request pattern responsible, ready for both immediate mitigation and permanent fix.

steps.title: Apply a query timeout to bound worst-case execution time
steps.desc: Configure a statement-level query timeout so the offending query cannot run indefinitely and consume resources beyond a bounded duration.
steps.guidance: Set the timeout based on the expected legitimate execution time of properly-indexed equivalent queries.
steps.outcome: Worst-case resource impact of any single execution of the query bounded.

steps.title: Confirm query timeout retained permanently as defense in depth
steps.desc: Verify the statement-level query timeout configured during containment remains in place permanently, independent of the specific index fix.
steps.guidance: This bounds impact from any other undiscovered missing-index issues elsewhere in the codebase.
steps.outcome: Confirmed permanent timeout hardening remains active.

ITID-41533.def: A resource-depletion attack in which an adversary opens transactions that acquire and hold locks on rows, tables, or other database objects for an extended period, causing legitimate transactions that need the same locks to queue, time out, or fail — degrading or halting the affected service.
ITID-41533.purpose: Captures denial of service caused by an adversary deliberately initiating long-running transactions that hold locks, blocking legitimate transactions from proceeding.
scopeIncludes: Deliberately holding a transaction open (e.g., via an unclosed session or crafted request) to retain locks on frequently accessed rows/tables
Flooding the database with concurrent transactions targeting the same hot rows to maximize lock contention
Exploiting an application code path known to hold a transaction open longer than necessary
scopeExcludes: Connection-pool exhaustion unrelated to lock contention (ITID-41531)
Query-cost-driven exhaustion from full-table scans without deliberate lock holding (ITID-41532)
ITID-41533.severity: High if the locked rows/tables are on a critical write path (e.g., order processing, authentication); Medium otherwise.
ITID-41533.priority: P1 if production write transactions are blocked; P2 if contained to a lower-impact path.
ITID-41533.escalation: Escalate immediately to database administrators to identify and kill blocking transactions and review application transaction-scoping.
indicators: Rising count of blocked/queued transactions in database lock-monitoring views
A small number of sessions holding locks for abnormally long durations
Application timeouts concentrated on operations touching a specific hot table
vectors: Crafted requests that intentionally leave a transaction open (e.g., via a slow client connection or deliberate delay)
Concurrent automated requests targeting the same hot rows to maximize contention
Exploiting an application bug that fails to commit/rollback promptly
rootCauses: Application transaction scope larger than necessary (locks held across unrelated operations)
No statement/transaction timeout enforced at the database layer
Lack of monitoring/alerting on lock-wait queue depth
mitreTechniques: T1499.003 Endpoint Denial of Service: Application Exhaustion Flood
controls: Transaction and lock-wait timeouts enforced at the database layer
Application-level transaction scope minimization
Lock-wait queue depth monitoring and alerting
ITID-41533.detection: Strong technical signal from database lock-monitoring views showing blocking chains and long-held locks.
ITID-41533.response: Kill blocking sessions/transactions, apply lock and transaction timeouts, and review application code for excessive transaction scope.
metrics: Peak lock-wait queue depth during incidents
Mean time to identify and terminate blocking transactions
ITID-41533.notes: Differentiator within Database Query Flooding: this leaf is specifically about deliberate lock contention, distinct from connection exhaustion (ITID-41531) and query-cost exhaustion (ITID-41532).

playbook.name: Database Lock Contention Attack (Deliberate Long-Running Transaction Flood)
playbook.description: The attacker deliberately initiates a flood of long-running or lock-heavy transactions (e.g., updating widely-referenced rows) to create severe lock contention, causing legitimate transactions to block or time out.

steps.title: Confirm lock contention via blocked-session and lock-wait metrics
steps.desc: Analyze database lock/wait-event metrics for an abnormal spike in blocked sessions and lock-wait time, correlated with one or more sessions holding locks for an extended duration.
steps.guidance: Query the database's lock/blocking-session views (e.g., pg_locks/pg_stat_activity in PostgreSQL, sys.dm_tran_locks in SQL Server) to identify blocking sessions and the duration of held locks.
steps.outcome: Confirmed lock contention pattern with blocking session(s) and affected resource(s)/row(s) documented.
steps.abort: If contention correlates with a known legitimate batch job that should be rescheduled rather than treated as an attack, stand down and document as an operational issue.

steps.title: Kill the blocking transactions/sessions to relieve contention
steps.desc: Terminate the identified blocking database sessions/transactions to immediately relieve lock contention and unblock legitimate waiting transactions.
steps.guidance: Use database-native session-termination commands targeted at the specific blocking sessions; confirm the terminated transactions roll back cleanly without leaving data in an inconsistent state.
steps.outcome: Lock contention relieved; blocked legitimate transactions proceed normally.

steps.title: Review and optimize application transaction design to reduce lock contention risk
steps.desc: Work with the application/database team to review transaction design around the contended resource (e.g., reducing transaction scope, using optimistic concurrency, row-level locking granularity) to reduce future contention risk from both attacks and legitimate load.
steps.guidance: Consider whether the contended row/table design itself (e.g., a single shared counter row) is an architectural bottleneck that should be redesigned (e.g., sharding counters).
steps.outcome: Reduced lock contention risk through improved transaction/schema design.

steps.title: Confirm lock-wait metrics return to normal and remain stable
steps.desc: Monitor lock-wait time and blocked-session counts to confirm return to normal baseline, retaining lock_timeout hardening permanently.
steps.guidance: Monitor under normal production load for a sustained period to confirm stability.
steps.outcome: Normal database transaction performance restored with permanent hardening retained.

steps.title: Document incident and review other high-contention resources for similar exposure
steps.desc: Record the incident and identify other frequently-contended database resources across the application that could be similarly targeted.
steps.guidance: Include recommendations for lock-contention monitoring/alerting in the after-action report.
steps.outcome: After-action report with a broader database resilience remediation list if gaps were found elsewhere.

steps.title: Identify the source and transaction pattern generating the contention
steps.desc: Trace the blocking transactions back to the originating application request/user/source to determine whether this is a deliberate attack versus a legitimate application bug.
steps.guidance: Look for a pattern of the same source repeatedly initiating long-running transactions against high-contention rows/tables, particularly rows with broad read/write dependency (e.g., a shared counter or configuration row).
steps.outcome: Documented source and transaction pattern responsible for the contention.

steps.title: Block the offending source and apply transaction-duration limits
steps.desc: Apply WAF/application-layer blocking against the identified offending source, and configure a maximum transaction duration/lock-wait timeout at the database layer to prevent recurrence.
steps.guidance: Configure lock_timeout (or equivalent) so transactions waiting excessively long for a lock are aborted rather than allowed to cascade into broader contention.
steps.outcome: Further attack attempts blocked; future lock contention automatically bounded by enforced timeouts.

steps.title: Confirm legitimate high-concurrency operations still complete successfully
steps.desc: Verify that legitimate high-concurrency transactions against the previously-contended resource still complete successfully under the new lock_timeout and design changes.
steps.guidance: Test with representative legitimate concurrent-transaction scenarios.
steps.outcome: Confirmed no legitimate use case was broken by the hardening changes.

ITID-41534.def: A database-resource-exhaustion incident confirmed as an attack against database capacity, but not yet classified into a specific mechanism (connection exhaustion, expensive queries, lock contention) pending further investigation.
ITID-41534.purpose: Serves as the intake bucket for database query flooding attacks that do not yet fit connection-exhaustion, query-cost, or lock-contention classifications.
scopeIncludes: Newly observed database-flooding techniques not yet mapped to an existing sibling leaf
Ambiguous database-saturation incidents pending root-cause confirmation
scopeExcludes: Any incident later confirmed as connection-pool exhaustion (ITID-41531), expensive-query flooding (ITID-41532), or lock contention (ITID-41533) — reclassify once confirmed
ITID-41534.severity: Medium by default pending classification; adjust once the specific mechanism and business impact are confirmed.
ITID-41534.priority: P3 pending triage, escalating per standard severity guidance once root cause is identified.
ITID-41534.escalation: Escalate to the SOC classification lead for prompt re-tagging into a specific sibling leaf once the mechanism is understood.
indicators: Elevated database resource utilization with an unconfirmed cause
Analyst uncertainty about which database-flooding mechanism applies
vectors: Unclassified/novel database-flooding technique pending investigation
rootCauses: Root cause not yet determined
mitreTechniques: T1499.003 Endpoint Denial of Service: Application Exhaustion Flood
controls: Standard database resource monitoring and alerting pending classification
ITID-41534.detection: Coverage depends on the eventual root cause; this bucket itself is detected via generic database-saturation alerting.
ITID-41534.response: Investigate to determine the specific mechanism and reclassify to the appropriate sibling ITID as soon as possible; apply standard database-flooding containment in the interim.
metrics: Number of incidents parked in this bucket beyond the triage SLA
Average time to reclassify into a specific sibling leaf
ITID-41534.notes: Catch-all intake leaf; used only during initial triage. Analysts should reclassify into ITID-41531/41532/41533 as soon as the mechanism is confirmed.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Database Query Flooding
playbook.description: A database-layer resource-exhaustion condition is confirmed via abnormal query load/resource impact, but the specific technique (connection pool exhaustion, full-table-scan flood, lock contention) has not yet been determined.

steps.title: Confirm database resource exhaustion via connection/query/lock metric analysis
steps.desc: Analyze database connection pool utilization, query execution metrics, and lock/wait statistics to confirm an abnormal resource-exhaustion condition.
steps.guidance: Check all three dimensions (connections, query cost, locks) to characterize which is the dominant contributing factor.
steps.outcome: Confirmed database resource exhaustion condition with dominant contributing factor(s) documented.
steps.abort: If exhaustion is attributable to an approved legitimate workload/capacity issue, stand down and document as a capacity issue rather than an attack.
steps.tool: Database monitoring (connection pool, slow-query log, lock views)

steps.title: Kill offending sessions/queries and block the identified source
steps.desc: Terminate the specific offending database sessions/queries consuming excessive resources, and apply WAF/rate-limiting against the identified source pending full classification.
steps.guidance: Prioritize immediate resource recovery over full root-cause analysis given active service impact.
steps.outcome: Database resource pressure relieved immediately.

steps.title: Complete technique classification and apply targeted remediation
steps.desc: Finalize which database flooding technique was the cause and apply the more specific remediation measures from the corresponding playbook.
steps.guidance: Reclassify the incident to the specific ITID leaf if determination succeeds.
steps.outcome: Root cause documented and technique-specific remediation applied.

steps.title: Confirm database performance returns to normal and remains stable
steps.desc: Monitor connection pool, query performance, and lock metrics to confirm return to normal baseline, retaining general hardening permanently.
steps.guidance: Monitor under normal production load for a sustained period to confirm stability.
steps.outcome: Normal database performance restored with permanent baseline hardening retained.

steps.title: Document incident and improve database resource-exhaustion classification tooling
steps.desc: Record why immediate technique classification was not possible and recommend detection/monitoring tooling improvements.
steps.guidance: Include recommendations for unified database observability covering connections, query cost, and locks in a single view.
steps.outcome: After-action report with concrete detection tooling improvement items.

steps.title: Attempt technique classification via dominant resource-impact analysis
steps.desc: Determine whether the exhaustion is primarily connection-pool-driven, query-cost-driven (full-table scans), or lock-contention-driven, to allow pivot to a more specific playbook.
steps.guidance: If classification succeeds, transition to the corresponding specific database flooding playbook; otherwise proceed with general mitigation.
steps.outcome: Either successful reclassification or confirmed genuinely mixed/unclear technique.

steps.title: Apply general timeout hardening (connection, query, lock) as defense in depth
steps.desc: Configure general connection-acquisition, statement, and lock-wait timeouts pending full classification, as a broad-spectrum compensating control.
steps.guidance: These general controls provide protection regardless of the specific final classification.
steps.outcome: Worst-case future database resource impact bounded regardless of root cause.
steps.abort: If legitimate long-running operations are affected, provide a separate profile for those use cases.

steps.title: Confirm technique-specific remediation retained where classification succeeded
steps.desc: Where the incident was reclassified to a specific database flooding technique, confirm the corresponding technique-specific remediation remains in place post-recovery.
steps.guidance: Cross-check against the specific playbook's remediation recommendations if reclassification occurred.
steps.outcome: Confirmed appropriate remediation retained based on final classification.

ITID-41541.def: A resource-depletion attack in which an adversary sends requests specifically crafted to generate a high volume of log entries (e.g., repeated authentication failures, malformed requests triggering verbose error logging) until the disk partition hosting logs is filled, causing the application or host to fail.
ITID-41541.purpose: Captures denial of service caused by an adversary triggering excessive log-writing activity to fill available disk space, crashing or degrading the host or service.
scopeIncludes: Repeated malformed or failed requests deliberately generating verbose error/audit log entries
Exploiting a logging configuration that writes excessive detail per request (e.g., full request/response bodies) to accelerate disk fill
Targeting a shared disk partition where log growth impacts co-located services
scopeExcludes: Excessive temporary file writes unrelated to logging (ITID-41542)
Storage-quota exhaustion via legitimate-looking large file uploads (ITID-41543)
ITID-41541.severity: Medium-High if logs share a partition with the application/OS (risk of full host failure); Medium if logs are on an isolated, monitored volume.
ITID-41541.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if disk usage approaches 100% on a partition shared with critical application components.
ITID-41541.escalation: Escalate to the platform/infrastructure team immediately if disk utilization crosses a critical threshold, to rotate/purge logs and block the triggering source.
indicators: Rapid disk-usage growth on the log partition correlated with a spike in a specific log-event type
A small number of source IPs/accounts responsible for a disproportionate share of logged events
Disk-usage alerts approaching capacity on log volumes
vectors: Repeated invalid login attempts generating high-volume authentication failure logs
Malformed requests deliberately crafted to trigger verbose error/stack-trace logging
Automated scanning tools generating high log volume as a side effect
rootCauses: Logs and application/OS files sharing the same disk partition with no isolation
No log rotation, compression, or retention limits enforced
Verbose logging configuration (e.g., full payload logging) enabled in production without volume safeguards
mitreTechniques: T1499.003 Endpoint Denial of Service: Application Exhaustion Flood
controls: Log partition isolation from application/OS storage
Automated log rotation, compression, and retention limits
Disk-usage threshold alerting with automated remediation (e.g., emergency purge)
ITID-41541.detection: Strong technical signal from disk-usage growth telemetry correlated with log-event-type spikes.
ITID-41541.response: Rotate or purge logs to relieve immediate disk pressure, block or rate-limit the triggering source, and confirm log partition isolation and rotation policy going forward.
metrics: Peak disk utilization during incidents
Mean time to restore available disk capacity
Number of incidents caused by log-partition co-location
ITID-41541.notes: Differentiator within Disk I/O Saturation: this leaf is specifically about log-driven disk fill, distinct from temp-file writes (ITID-41542) or storage-quota exhaustion via uploads (ITID-41543).

playbook.name: Log File Flooding to Exhaust Disk Space
playbook.description: The attacker deliberately generates a high volume of events/requests designed to produce excessive log entries, filling disk space allocated to logging and potentially causing the affected system to fail or become unstable when disk space is exhausted.

steps.title: Confirm log-flooding pattern via disk-utilization and log-growth-rate analysis
steps.desc: Analyze disk utilization metrics and log file growth rate to confirm an abnormal, rapid consumption of disk space attributable to a specific log source, correlated with a corresponding spike in the underlying event/request volume.
steps.guidance: Check disk utilization alerts alongside log file sizes and growth rates for the affected partition/volume; identify which specific log stream is growing abnormally.
steps.outcome: Confirmed log-flooding pattern with affected log source, growth rate, and disk impact documented.
steps.abort: If the log growth correlates with a legitimate verbose-debug-logging change or genuine traffic increase, stand down and document as an operational/configuration issue.
steps.tool: Disk utilization monitoring / log management platform

steps.title: Free disk space immediately via log rotation/archival and block the offending source
steps.desc: Trigger immediate log rotation/compression/archival to free disk space, and apply WAF/rate-limiting to block the identified offending request source.
steps.guidance: Prioritize freeing disk space on any partition approaching capacity to avoid a full outage, then address the source.
steps.outcome: Disk space freed to a safe utilization level; further offending requests blocked.

steps.title: Reduce excessive log verbosity/volume for the offending event type where appropriate
steps.desc: Review and adjust logging configuration for the specific offending event type (e.g., rate-limit repeated identical error log entries, reduce verbosity for expected/benign error conditions) to reduce the log-volume amplification per malicious request.
steps.guidance: Ensure security-relevant information is still captured at an appropriate level even while reducing volume (e.g., log a summary/count rather than every individual occurrence for high-frequency repeated events).
steps.outcome: Log volume per malicious/repeated request reduced without losing necessary security visibility.

steps.title: Confirm disk utilization returns to normal and rotation/caps remain enforced
steps.desc: Monitor disk utilization to confirm return to normal baseline, retaining log rotation and disk-usage cap hardening permanently.
steps.guidance: Verify log rotation continues to function correctly on its normal schedule post-incident.
steps.outcome: Normal disk utilization restored with permanent hardening retained.

steps.title: Document incident and audit all systems for consistent log rotation/disk-cap enforcement
steps.desc: Record the attack and audit all organization systems/services for consistent log rotation, retention, and disk-usage cap configuration.
steps.guidance: Include a fleet-wide configuration compliance check in the after-action report.
steps.outcome: After-action report with a broader hardening remediation list if gaps were found elsewhere.

steps.title: Identify the specific request/event pattern driving excessive log generation
steps.desc: Analyze the log content and correlate with application/access logs to identify the specific request pattern or source triggering excessive log entries (e.g., repeated invalid requests each generating a verbose error log entry).
steps.guidance: Look for a high-volume, repetitive pattern of a specific log message/error type correlated with a specific source.
steps.outcome: Documented offending request pattern/source responsible for excessive log generation.

steps.title: Verify and enforce log rotation, retention, and disk-usage caps
steps.desc: Confirm log rotation policies (size/time-based rotation, retention limits, and total disk-usage caps for the logging directory/volume) are properly configured and enforced.
steps.guidance: Ensure the logging subsystem has a hard cap on total disk usage that triggers rotation/deletion of oldest logs well before disk exhaustion, and that this cap was the gap if not previously enforced.
steps.outcome: Disk space consumption for logging bounded going forward regardless of log volume spikes.

steps.title: Confirm reduced-verbosity logging retains necessary security visibility
steps.desc: Verify that the reduced-verbosity logging configuration applied during eradication still captures sufficient detail for security monitoring and future investigations.
steps.guidance: Review a sample of recent log entries for the previously-offending event type to confirm adequate summary-level detail is retained.
steps.outcome: Confirmed logging verbosity reduction did not compromise necessary security visibility.

ITID-41542.def: A resource-depletion attack in which an adversary repeatedly triggers an application code path that writes temporary files (e.g., file-processing, session, or cache-to-disk operations) without adequate cleanup, filling the disk partition and degrading or crashing the affected service.
ITID-41542.purpose: Captures denial of service caused by an adversary triggering excessive temporary-file creation to fill disk space, distinct from log-driven disk fill.
scopeIncludes: Repeated uploads or requests that each generate a temporary file never cleaned up due to an application bug
Exploiting a file-processing pipeline (e.g., image conversion, document rendering) that writes large intermediate temp files per request
Session or cache-to-disk mechanisms accumulating orphaned temporary files
scopeExcludes: Log-file-driven disk exhaustion (ITID-41541)
Storage-quota exhaustion via legitimate large uploads counted against a user quota (ITID-41543)
ITID-41542.severity: Medium-High if the temp directory shares a partition with the application/OS; Medium if isolated and monitored.
ITID-41542.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if disk usage approaches capacity on a partition shared with critical components.
ITID-41542.escalation: Escalate to the owning engineering team to fix temp-file cleanup logic and to platform/infrastructure to relieve immediate disk pressure.
indicators: Rapid growth in temp-directory file count/size correlated with a specific request pattern
Orphaned temp files with no corresponding active session or job
Disk-usage alerts on the temp partition
vectors: Repeated file-upload or conversion requests exploiting a cleanup bug in the processing pipeline
Deliberately abandoned sessions/jobs that leave temp files behind
Automated scripts hammering an endpoint known to generate large temp artifacts
rootCauses: Temporary files not cleaned up on request completion, failure, or timeout
No disk-quota or file-count limit on the temp directory
Temp storage sharing a partition with application/OS files
mitreTechniques: T1499.003 Endpoint Denial of Service: Application Exhaustion Flood
controls: Guaranteed temp-file cleanup on request completion, failure, and timeout (e.g., via a supervised cleanup job)
Temp partition isolation with enforced quota
Rate limiting on endpoints known to generate large temp artifacts
ITID-41542.detection: Strong technical signal from temp-directory size/file-count telemetry correlated with request-pattern logs.
ITID-41542.response: Purge orphaned temp files to relieve immediate pressure, rate-limit or block the triggering source, and fix the underlying cleanup bug.
metrics: Peak temp-directory utilization during incidents
Mean time to restore available disk capacity
ITID-41542.notes: Differentiator within Disk I/O Saturation: this leaf is about temp-file accumulation from processing pipelines, distinct from log growth (ITID-41541) or quota exhaustion via uploads (ITID-41543).

playbook.name: Excessive Temporary File Write Attack
playbook.description: The attacker exploits an application feature that creates temporary files (e.g., file upload processing, report generation, session data) to force the creation of an excessive number or size of temporary files, exhausting disk space on the temp partition.

steps.title: Confirm temp-file-exhaustion pattern via disk-utilization and temp-directory-growth analysis
steps.desc: Analyze disk utilization metrics for the temporary file storage location/partition, confirming abnormal growth in file count or total size correlated with a specific application feature's usage.
steps.guidance: Check disk utilization alerts alongside temp-directory file counts/sizes; identify which application feature (upload processing, report generation, etc.) is responsible for the growth.
steps.outcome: Confirmed temp-file-exhaustion pattern with affected feature, growth rate, and disk impact documented.
steps.abort: If growth correlates with a legitimate batch processing job, stand down and document as an operational/capacity issue.

steps.title: Free disk space immediately by cleaning orphaned/stale temp files and block the offending source
steps.desc: Trigger immediate cleanup of orphaned or stale temporary files to free disk space, and apply WAF/rate-limiting to block the identified offending request source.
steps.guidance: Verify cleanup only removes genuinely orphaned/stale files, not files actively in use by legitimate in-progress operations.
steps.outcome: Disk space freed to a safe utilization level; further offending requests blocked.

steps.title: Implement reliable temp-file cleanup and lifecycle management in application code
steps.desc: Review and fix the application's temp-file lifecycle management to ensure temp files are reliably deleted immediately after use (including on error paths), and implement a scheduled cleanup job as a safety net for any that are orphaned.
steps.guidance: Ensure temp-file creation uses a pattern that guarantees cleanup (e.g., try-finally blocks, context managers) regardless of success or failure of the operation using them.
steps.outcome: Confirmed application reliably cleans up temp files under all code paths, with a scheduled safety-net job also in place.

steps.title: Confirm disk utilization returns to normal and remains stable
steps.desc: Monitor temp-directory disk utilization to confirm return to normal baseline, retaining rate-limiting and lifecycle-management hardening permanently.
steps.guidance: Monitor under normal production load for a sustained period to confirm stability.
steps.outcome: Normal disk utilization restored with permanent hardening retained.

steps.title: Document incident and audit other features for similar temp-file exposure
steps.desc: Record the attack and review other application features that create temporary files for similar unbounded-growth or lifecycle-management risk.
steps.guidance: Include recommendations for organization-wide temp-file hygiene standards and monitoring in the after-action report.
steps.outcome: After-action report with a broader remediation list if gaps were found elsewhere.

steps.title: Identify the specific request pattern/source driving excessive temp-file creation
steps.desc: Analyze application logs to identify the specific request pattern or source repeatedly triggering the temp-file-creating feature.
steps.guidance: Look for a high-volume, repetitive pattern from a specific source triggering the temp-file-creating operation (e.g., repeated file uploads or repeated report-generation requests) without corresponding legitimate need.
steps.outcome: Documented offending request pattern/source responsible for excessive temp-file creation.

steps.title: Apply per-source rate limiting and per-request temp-file size/count caps
steps.desc: Configure the affected feature to enforce per-source rate limiting and reasonable per-request limits on temp-file size and count.
steps.guidance: Ensure limits accommodate legitimate use cases while bounding the worst-case impact of a single malicious source.
steps.outcome: Future temp-file exhaustion attempts bounded by enforced limits.
steps.abort: If legitimate large-file processing is affected, adjust limits accordingly.

steps.title: Confirm scheduled cleanup safety-net job runs correctly
steps.desc: Verify the scheduled temp-file cleanup safety-net job introduced during eradication executes successfully on its schedule and correctly removes orphaned files.
steps.guidance: Check job execution logs over at least one full scheduled cycle.
steps.outcome: Confirmed scheduled cleanup job operates correctly.

ITID-41543.def: A resource-depletion attack in which an adversary (an authenticated user, abused free-tier account, or automated script) repeatedly uploads large but individually valid files to a service, exhausting a shared storage quota or the backing disk/volume capacity and degrading the service for other users.
ITID-41543.purpose: Captures denial of service caused by an adversary repeatedly uploading large legitimate-looking files to exhaust a shared storage quota or backing disk capacity.
scopeIncludes: Repeated large-file uploads via a legitimate upload feature that lacks per-account or per-request size/volume limits
Automated abuse of free-tier or trial accounts to consume shared storage capacity
Exploiting a lack of storage-quota enforcement across many accounts to exhaust a shared backing volume
scopeExcludes: Log-driven disk exhaustion (ITID-41541)
Temp-file accumulation from processing pipelines (ITID-41542)
ITID-41543.severity: Medium-High if the backing storage is shared across many tenants/services; Medium if per-account quotas already contain the impact to a single account.
ITID-41543.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if shared storage capacity is at risk of full exhaustion affecting multiple tenants.
ITID-41543.escalation: Escalate to the platform/storage team to enforce or tighten per-account quotas and to identify and suspend abusing accounts.
indicators: Rapid storage-consumption growth attributable to a small number of accounts
Upload volume from a single account far exceeding typical usage patterns
Storage-capacity alerts approaching threshold on a shared volume
vectors: Automated scripts repeatedly uploading large files via a free or under-limited account tier
Bulk account creation to multiply per-account quota abuse
Exploiting an upload endpoint with no enforced maximum file size or count
rootCauses: No enforced per-account storage quota or upload-rate limit
Shared backing storage without per-tenant isolation or capacity alerting
Free-tier or trial accounts provisioned without abuse controls
mitreTechniques: T1499.003 Endpoint Denial of Service: Application Exhaustion Flood
controls: Enforced per-account storage quotas and upload-rate limits
Abuse detection and automated suspension for anomalous upload volume
Shared storage capacity alerting with headroom thresholds
ITID-41543.detection: Strong technical signal from per-account storage-consumption telemetry and upload-rate anomaly detection.
ITID-41543.response: Suspend or throttle the abusing account(s), enforce/tighten storage quotas, and monitor shared-volume headroom until normal levels are restored.
metrics: Storage consumed by abusing accounts per incident
Mean time to detect and suspend abusive upload activity
ITID-41543.notes: Differentiator within Disk I/O Saturation: this leaf is about quota exhaustion via legitimate-looking uploads across accounts, distinct from log growth (ITID-41541) or temp-file accumulation (ITID-41542).

playbook.name: Storage Quota Exhaustion via Repeated Large Uploads
playbook.description: The attacker (often an authenticated user or abused free-tier account) repeatedly uploads large files to consume the organization's allocated storage quota/capacity, denying storage availability to legitimate users or triggering costly auto-scaling.

steps.title: Confirm storage-exhaustion pattern via quota/capacity-utilization and upload-rate analysis
steps.desc: Analyze storage quota/capacity utilization metrics for abnormal, rapid consumption correlated with a spike in large-file upload activity from a specific account/source.
steps.guidance: Check storage utilization dashboards (cloud storage billing/usage metrics or on-premises capacity monitoring) alongside upload logs for the account/source responsible.
steps.outcome: Confirmed storage-exhaustion pattern with offending account/source, upload volume, and capacity impact documented.
steps.abort: If the upload volume correlates with a legitimate customer's approved large-scale usage, stand down and document as a capacity-planning matter rather than an attack.
steps.tool: Storage/cloud provider usage metrics / upload logs

steps.title: Suspend/throttle the offending account and enforce per-account storage quotas
steps.desc: Immediately suspend or throttle the offending account's upload capability, and ensure per-account storage quotas are enforced (hard-capped) at the application layer.
steps.guidance: If credential compromise is suspected, coordinate with the account owner regarding suspension and credential rotation rather than unilaterally deleting data.
steps.outcome: Further uploads from the offending account halted; per-account quota enforcement confirmed active.
steps.abort: If suspension impacts a legitimate customer, coordinate with the account owner before finalizing.

steps.title: Remove abusive content and reclaim storage capacity
steps.desc: Delete or archive the uploaded content confirmed as abusive/malicious (following appropriate data-retention/legal review processes), reclaiming storage capacity.
steps.guidance: Follow organizational data-handling policy for reviewing and disposing of potentially illicit content; preserve evidence/metadata as needed for any legal/law-enforcement follow-up.
steps.outcome: Storage capacity reclaimed; abusive content appropriately handled per policy.

steps.title: Confirm storage capacity/quota utilization returns to normal and quotas remain enforced
steps.desc: Monitor storage utilization to confirm return to normal baseline, retaining per-account quota and rate-limiting hardening permanently.
steps.guidance: Verify legitimate accounts retain appropriate access to their allocated storage.
steps.outcome: Normal storage capacity restored with permanent hardening retained.

steps.title: Document incident and review account-provisioning/quota policy for abuse resistance
steps.desc: Record the incident and assess whether account-provisioning controls (e.g., free-tier signup verification, default quota levels) need strengthening to reduce future abuse risk.
steps.guidance: Include recommendations for anomaly-based storage-usage alerting to catch similar abuse earlier in the after-action report.
steps.outcome: After-action report with account-provisioning and monitoring improvement recommendations tracked.

steps.title: Determine whether the account is compromised, a legitimate-but-abusive free-tier user, or a malicious signup
steps.desc: Investigate the account's history, authentication pattern, and any indicators of compromise to determine the appropriate response (credential remediation vs. account suspension for terms-of-service abuse).
steps.guidance: Distinguish between a compromised legitimate account being used maliciously versus a threat actor abusing a free-tier signup for storage abuse (e.g., for hosting illicit content or a resource-exhaustion campaign).
steps.outcome: Determined root cause informing the appropriate containment approach.

steps.title: Apply per-source upload-rate limiting at the API/edge layer as defense in depth
steps.desc: Configure upload-rate and size limiting at the API gateway/edge layer independent of application-layer quota enforcement, to reduce the risk of quota-enforcement bugs or gaps being exploited.
steps.guidance: This mirrors general API-flooding containment but specifically scoped to upload/storage-consuming endpoints.
steps.outcome: Additional defense-in-depth layer against upload-based storage abuse.

steps.title: Confirm any legitimately affected account was appropriately restored
steps.desc: Where the offending account was later confirmed as a compromised legitimate customer rather than a malicious signup, verify their access and data were appropriately restored after credential remediation.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with the account owner to confirm satisfactory resolution.
steps.outcome: Confirmed legitimate account access appropriately restored where applicable.

ITID-41544.def: A disk-resource-exhaustion incident confirmed as an attack against disk capacity or I/O throughput, but not yet classified into a specific mechanism (log flooding, temp-file accumulation, storage-quota abuse) pending further investigation.
ITID-41544.purpose: Serves as the intake bucket for disk I/O saturation attacks that do not yet fit log-flooding, temp-file, or storage-quota classifications.
scopeIncludes: Newly observed disk-exhaustion techniques not yet mapped to an existing sibling leaf
Ambiguous disk-saturation incidents pending root-cause confirmation
scopeExcludes: Any incident later confirmed as log flooding (ITID-41541), temp-file accumulation (ITID-41542), or storage-quota abuse (ITID-41543) — reclassify once confirmed
ITID-41544.severity: Medium by default pending classification; adjust once the specific mechanism and business impact are confirmed.
ITID-41544.priority: P3 pending triage, escalating per standard severity guidance once root cause is identified.
ITID-41544.escalation: Escalate to the SOC classification lead for prompt re-tagging into a specific sibling leaf once the mechanism is understood.
indicators: Elevated disk utilization or I/O saturation with an unconfirmed cause
Analyst uncertainty about which disk-exhaustion mechanism applies
vectors: Unclassified/novel disk-exhaustion technique pending investigation
rootCauses: Root cause not yet determined
mitreTechniques: T1499.003 Endpoint Denial of Service: Application Exhaustion Flood
controls: Standard disk/host monitoring and alerting pending classification
ITID-41544.detection: Coverage depends on the eventual root cause; this bucket itself is detected via generic disk-saturation alerting.
ITID-41544.response: Investigate to determine the specific mechanism and reclassify to the appropriate sibling ITID as soon as possible; apply standard disk-exhaustion containment in the interim.
metrics: Number of incidents parked in this bucket beyond the triage SLA
Average time to reclassify into a specific sibling leaf
ITID-41544.notes: Catch-all intake leaf; used only during initial triage. Analysts should reclassify into ITID-41541/41542/41543 as soon as the mechanism is confirmed.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Disk I/O Saturation Attack
playbook.description: A disk I/O or storage-capacity resource-exhaustion condition is confirmed, but the specific technique (log flooding, excessive temp-file writes, storage quota exhaustion via uploads) has not yet been determined.

steps.title: Confirm disk I/O/capacity exhaustion via utilization and growth-source analysis
steps.desc: Analyze disk utilization and I/O metrics to confirm an abnormal resource-exhaustion condition, identifying which directory/partition/storage location is growing or being saturated.
steps.guidance: Check disk utilization alerts alongside per-directory/partition growth rates to localize the source of the exhaustion.
steps.outcome: Confirmed disk resource exhaustion condition with affected location and growth pattern documented.
steps.abort: If exhaustion is attributable to an approved legitimate workload/capacity issue, stand down and document as a capacity issue rather than an attack.

steps.title: Free disk space immediately via cleanup/archival and block the offending source
steps.desc: Trigger immediate cleanup/archival of the identified excessive data to free disk space, and apply blocking/rate-limiting against the identified offending source pending full classification.
steps.guidance: Prioritize freeing disk space on any partition approaching capacity to avoid a full outage.
steps.outcome: Disk space freed to a safe utilization level; further offending activity blocked or reduced.

steps.title: Complete technique classification and apply targeted remediation
steps.desc: Finalize which disk I/O saturation technique was the cause and apply the more specific remediation measures from the corresponding playbook.
steps.guidance: Reclassify the incident to the specific ITID leaf if determination succeeds.
steps.outcome: Root cause documented and technique-specific remediation applied.

steps.title: Confirm disk utilization returns to normal and remains stable
steps.desc: Monitor disk utilization to confirm return to normal baseline and sustained stability, retaining general hardening permanently.
steps.guidance: Monitor under normal production load for a sustained period to confirm stability.
steps.outcome: Normal disk utilization restored with permanent baseline hardening retained.

steps.title: Document incident and improve disk-exhaustion root-cause classification tooling
steps.desc: Record why immediate root-cause classification was not possible and recommend detection/monitoring tooling improvements.
steps.guidance: Include recommendations for per-directory/per-feature disk-usage attribution monitoring that would have sped up classification.
steps.outcome: After-action report with concrete detection tooling improvement items.

steps.title: Attempt technique classification via storage-location and growth-pattern analysis
steps.desc: Determine whether the exhaustion is driven by log growth, temp-file accumulation, or user-uploaded content growth, to allow pivot to a more specific playbook.
steps.guidance: If classification succeeds, transition to the corresponding specific disk I/O saturation playbook; otherwise proceed with general mitigation.
steps.outcome: Either successful reclassification or confirmed genuinely mixed/unclear technique.

steps.title: Apply general disk-usage caps/quotas as defense in depth
steps.desc: Configure or verify general disk-usage caps/quotas for logs, temp files, and user-uploaded content pending full classification, as a broad-spectrum compensating control.
steps.guidance: These general controls provide protection regardless of the specific final classification.
steps.outcome: Worst-case future disk exhaustion impact bounded regardless of root cause.

steps.title: Confirm technique-specific remediation retained where classification succeeded
steps.desc: Where the incident was reclassified to a specific disk I/O saturation technique, confirm the corresponding technique-specific remediation remains in place post-recovery.
steps.guidance: Cross-check against the specific playbook's remediation recommendations if reclassification occurred.
steps.outcome: Confirmed appropriate remediation retained based on final classification.

ITID-41611.def: A denial-of-service incident in which the organization's cloud-hosted services become unavailable or severely degraded because an adversary launched a targeted attack against shared infrastructure of the multi-tenant cloud provider itself (e.g., a control-plane component, shared networking fabric, or a co-tenant causing provider-wide contention), rather than against the organization's workloads directly.
ITID-41611.purpose: Captures denial of service impacting the organization's own workloads as a result of a targeted attack against the shared infrastructure of a multi-tenant cloud service provider the organization depends on.
scopeIncludes: Provider control-plane or shared-fabric outage traced to a confirmed targeted attack (as opposed to accidental provider failure)
Impact inherited by the organization solely because it shares infrastructure with the attacked tenant/component
Provider-communicated security incidents that caused measurable service disruption to the organization
scopeExcludes: Attacks directed specifically at the organization's own load balancer/API gateway within the cloud (ITID-41612)
Cloud identity/authentication service disruption specifically (ITID-41613)
Ordinary provider outages with no attack attribution (an availability/reliability event, not a security incident)
ITID-41611.severity: High given the incident is outside the organization's direct control and may affect multiple critical services simultaneously.
ITID-41611.priority: P1 for the duration of confirmed provider-wide impact; downgrade once provider mitigation restores service.
ITID-41611.escalation: Escalate to executive/business-continuity stakeholders immediately given the incident is outside organizational control; open a case with the cloud provider and activate any documented multi-region/multi-provider failover.
indicators: Provider status-page or security-bulletin confirmation of a targeted attack
Simultaneous impact across unrelated organizational services hosted on the same provider/region
Provider support case correlating the outage with an attack rather than routine failure
vectors: Adversary attack against provider control-plane APIs or shared orchestration systems
Attack against a co-tenant that saturates shared network fabric
Attack against provider-managed DNS or routing infrastructure
rootCauses: Reliance on a single cloud provider/region with no failover
No contractual/technical visibility into provider-side attack status
Business-critical services concentrated on shared (non-dedicated) infrastructure
controls: Multi-region or multi-provider failover architecture for critical services
Cloud provider status/security-bulletin monitoring integration
Documented cloud-provider incident-communication and escalation contacts
ITID-41611.detection: Limited direct technical signal since the root cause lives in provider infrastructure; detection relies on correlating internal service-degradation telemetry with provider status/security bulletins.
ITID-41611.response: Activate failover where available, maintain a provider support case, communicate status to affected business stakeholders, and document the timeline for post-incident review of provider dependency risk.
metrics: Duration of provider-attributed outage
Time to activate failover (where available)
Number of organizational services impacted
ITID-41611.notes: Differentiator within Cloud Service Disruption: this leaf covers provider-side, shared-infrastructure attacks outside organizational control, distinct from attacks against the organization's own gateway (ITID-41612) or identity service (ITID-41613).

playbook.name: Multi-Tenant Cloud Service Provider Outage Caused by Targeted Attack
playbook.description: A targeted attack against the organization's multi-tenant cloud service provider (IaaS/PaaS) has caused an outage affecting the organization's hosted services, with the organization having limited direct control over remediation.

steps.title: Correlate internal service degradation with provider status dashboards
steps.desc: Cross-check internal monitoring alerts against the cloud provider's public and account-specific status/health dashboards to confirm the outage is provider-side and attack-related rather than an internal fault.
steps.guidance: Check the provider's status page, any posted security advisories, and account health dashboard notifications simultaneously with internal APM alerts.
steps.outcome: Outage confirmed as provider-side and attributed (per provider communication) to a targeted attack, with evidence timestamped.
steps.abort: If the provider dashboard shows no incident, treat as an internal fault and pivot to standard internal outage response.
steps.tool: Cloud provider status dashboard, internal APM

steps.title: Open a priority support ticket with the cloud provider
steps.desc: File a priority/severity-1 support ticket with the cloud provider referencing the public incident, requesting status updates and any available mitigation guidance.
steps.guidance: Use the highest support tier available under contract; reference the account ID and affected resource IDs to expedite handling.
steps.outcome: Support ticket opened and acknowledged, with a named escalation contact where available.

steps.title: Monitor provider remediation progress and validate mitigation
steps.desc: Track the provider's incident updates and confirm, once the provider reports the attack mitigated, that the organization's services are actually restored (do not rely solely on provider status page).
steps.guidance: Independently verify via internal monitoring rather than assuming provider status updates fully reflect the organization's specific experience.
steps.outcome: Provider-side attack confirmed resolved and independently verified against internal service health.
steps.tool: Cloud provider status dashboard, internal APM

steps.title: Fail back from secondary provider/region and confirm full service restoration
steps.desc: If failover was exercised, plan and execute a controlled fail-back to primary infrastructure once stability is confirmed; verify all services meet normal baselines.
steps.guidance: Fail back gradually and monitor for regression before fully decommissioning the failover path.
steps.outcome: Services fully restored to primary infrastructure with normal performance confirmed.

steps.title: Document incident and review multi-provider resilience posture
steps.desc: Capture the timeline, provider communication quality, and business impact; evaluate whether additional failover capacity, multi-cloud architecture, or contractual SLA changes are warranted.
steps.outcome: Report finalized with resilience-improvement recommendations tracked to owners.

steps.title: Assess scope of organizational impact
steps.desc: Determine which of the organization's services, regions, or tenants are affected by the provider outage.
steps.guidance: Map affected provider services/regions to internal application dependencies to scope the blast radius.
steps.outcome: Impact scope documented for internal stakeholder communication.

steps.title: Evaluate and execute failover to a secondary provider/region
steps.desc: If a secondary cloud provider, region, or on-premises failover path exists for the affected services, activate it to restore availability while the primary provider resolves the attack.
steps.guidance: Weigh data-consistency and cutover risk against the duration/severity of the outage before failing over.
steps.outcome: Critical services restored via failover where a viable path exists; decision and rationale documented if failover is not exercised.
steps.abort: If no failover path exists or failover risk exceeds outage impact, do not fail over — focus on provider engagement and internal communication instead.

ITID-41612.def: A denial-of-service incident in which an adversary directs a volumetric or application-layer attack specifically at the organization's cloud load balancer, API gateway, or ingress controller, exhausting its request-handling or connection capacity and preventing legitimate traffic from reaching backend services.
ITID-41612.purpose: Captures denial of service caused by an adversary targeting the organization's own cloud load balancer or API gateway resource directly, distinct from a provider-wide infrastructure attack.
scopeIncludes: Application-layer request floods targeting a specific API gateway endpoint
Connection exhaustion against a cloud load balancer's listener/target-group capacity
