steps.desc: Check for a ransom note referencing the demonstration attack, which often follows shortly after.
steps.outcome: Any accompanying ransom communication identified and preserved.

steps.title: Notify Legal and Law Enforcement if a ransom demand is received
steps.desc: If a ransom communication accompanies or follows the demonstration, escalate to Legal counsel and law enforcement per organizational non-payment policy.
steps.outcome: Legal and Law Enforcement notified where applicable; no payment or engagement made.
steps.abort: If no ransom communication is received, this step is not applicable.

ITID-41731.def: A pattern of repeated, scheduled denial-of-service attacks launched against the target at intervals (e.g., daily or weekly) following non-payment of an RDoS ransom demand, intended to sustain pressure and force payment through cumulative business disruption rather than a single decisive attack.
ITID-41731.purpose: Captures the sustained extortion campaign phase in which a threat actor launches recurring, scheduled DDoS attacks against the organization after a ransom deadline passes without payment.
scopeIncludes: Attacks recurring on a predictable or announced schedule following a missed payment deadline
Campaigns where the threat actor explicitly ties each recurrence to continued non-payment
Attacks of broadly consistent volume/duration to the original demonstration, repeated over time
scopeExcludes: The single demonstration attack that preceded the ransom demand (ITID-41721/41722)
Campaigns where volume/duration is deliberately increasing over time to escalate pressure (ITID-41732)
Campaigns spreading across multiple distinct targets within the victim's infrastructure (ITID-41733)
ITID-41731.severity: High given sustained, recurring business disruption across multiple attack windows.
ITID-41731.priority: P1 for the duration of the active recurring campaign.
ITID-41731.escalation: Escalate to executive leadership and network operations to sustain mitigation posture across the campaign's duration; coordinate with law enforcement per organizational policy on extortion reporting.
indicators: Multiple distinct DDoS attack events against the same target(s) at regular intervals
Attack timing correlated with the organization's continued non-payment
Consistent attack signature/infrastructure across recurrences, indicating the same threat actor
vectors: Scheduled volumetric or application-layer attacks launched from consistent botnet/booter infrastructure
Attacks timed to coincide with periods of peak business activity to maximize pressure
rootCauses: Non-payment of the initial ransom demand without adequate sustained mitigation capacity in place
DDoS mitigation not scaled/sustained for a multi-day or multi-week campaign
controls: Sustained DDoS mitigation/scrubbing capacity maintained for the campaign duration
Documented no-payment policy with executive alignment
Law-enforcement/regulatory extortion-reporting process
ITID-41731.detection: Strong technical signal from repeated, correlated attack-event telemetry over time; campaign tracking links recurrences to the same threat actor and demand.
ITID-41731.response: Maintain continuous DDoS mitigation posture, track each recurrence against the campaign timeline, and coordinate with leadership and law enforcement on the no-payment decision.
metrics: Number of recurring attack events in the campaign
Cumulative business downtime across the campaign
Mitigation capacity utilization across recurrences
ITID-41731.notes: Differentiator within Persistent Ransom DoS: recurring but roughly steady-state attacks, distinct from escalating-intensity campaigns (ITID-41732) or multi-target campaigns (ITID-41733).

playbook.name: Recurring Scheduled DDoS Attacks After Ransom Non-Payment
playbook.description: Following the organization's refusal to pay a ransom, the threat actor has begun launching recurring, scheduled DDoS attacks against organizational infrastructure.

steps.title: Confirm the recurring attack pattern and correlate with prior ransom timeline
steps.desc: Analyze traffic telemetry across multiple attack instances to confirm a recurring/scheduled pattern and correlate timing with the prior ransom demand and non-payment decision.
steps.guidance: Look for consistent timing intervals (e.g., daily, specific days of week) and consistent vectors across occurrences, indicating automation on the attacker's side.
steps.outcome: Recurring pattern confirmed with historical occurrence log established.

steps.title: Maintain escalating mitigation response as attacks recur
steps.desc: Given the pattern of recurrence, transition to (or reaffirm) always-on DDoS scrubbing rather than reactive on-demand engagement for each occurrence, scaling capacity if the trend shows escalation.
steps.guidance: Reactive per-incident engagement is inefficient against a known recurring attacker; standing mitigation reduces response latency for each new occurrence.
steps.outcome: Always-on mitigation posture established/reaffirmed and scaled to the observed escalation trend.
steps.abort: If occurrences are de-escalating and infrequent, on-demand engagement may remain sufficient — document the rationale.

steps.title: Mitigate each recurring attack instance promptly under standing posture
steps.desc: Apply the standing mitigation controls to each new occurrence as it happens, minimizing manual intervention and response time.
steps.outcome: Each recurring attack instance is absorbed with minimal to no service impact.

steps.title: Validate service stability between occurrences and reassess standing posture periodically
steps.desc: Confirm services remain stable between attack occurrences and periodically reassess whether standing mitigation levels remain appropriate as the pattern evolves.
steps.outcome: Service stability maintained between occurrences; mitigation posture reassessed on a defined cadence.

steps.title: Document the recurring campaign and long-term mitigation strategy
steps.desc: Capture the full multi-occurrence timeline, cumulative business impact, and recommend a long-term mitigation and Legal/Law Enforcement engagement strategy for the ongoing campaign.
steps.outcome: Report finalized with a long-term strategy documented and follow-up actions tracked.

steps.title: Assess trend in attack scale/duration across occurrences
steps.desc: Compare scale, vector, and duration across successive occurrences to determine whether the actor is escalating, maintaining, or de-escalating pressure.
steps.outcome: Escalation trend documented to inform response scaling.

steps.title: Maintain Legal and Law Enforcement engagement on the ongoing campaign
steps.desc: Provide Legal counsel and law enforcement with updated evidence of each recurring attack instance as part of the ongoing case, reaffirming the non-payment position.
steps.outcome: Legal/Law Enforcement kept updated with a consolidated evidence trail across occurrences.

ITID-41732.def: A pattern of denial-of-service attacks in which each successive attack following a missed ransom deadline is deliberately larger in volume, longer in duration, or more sophisticated in technique than the last, signaling an intentional escalation strategy designed to force payment by demonstrating growing capability and impact.
ITID-41732.purpose: Captures RDoS campaigns in which the threat actor deliberately escalates attack volume, duration, or sophistication over successive attempts to increase pressure following a missed deadline.
scopeIncludes: Measurable, attacker-driven increase in attack volume/duration/technique sophistication across successive attack events tied to the same campaign
Explicit threat-actor communication announcing intent to escalate if payment continues to be withheld
Escalation crossing from a single vector to multi-vector attacks over the campaign
scopeExcludes: Recurring attacks of consistent, non-escalating volume/duration (ITID-41731)
Escalation achieved by spreading to additional distinct targets rather than increasing intensity against the same target (ITID-41733)
ITID-41732.severity: High, escalating to Critical if the trend indicates attack volume/duration will soon exceed current mitigation capacity.
ITID-41732.priority: P1, with capacity-planning review triggered after each escalation to confirm mitigation headroom remains sufficient.
ITID-41732.escalation: Escalate immediately to network operations/DDoS mitigation leadership after any confirmed escalation step to reassess capacity and consider engaging additional scrubbing capacity or provider support.
indicators: Attack volume/duration metrics trending upward across successive events in the same campaign
Introduction of new attack vectors not used in earlier events of the same campaign
Threat-actor communication explicitly warning of intensifying attacks
vectors: Progressive increase in botnet size/bandwidth committed to successive attacks
Addition of application-layer attack vectors after initial volumetric attacks proved insufficient
Multi-vector attacks combining several techniques simultaneously in later campaign stages
rootCauses: Initial mitigation response perceived by the threat actor as insufficient, incentivizing escalation
Mitigation capacity not scaled proactively in anticipation of a continuing campaign
controls: Elastic/scalable DDoS mitigation capacity with rapid capacity-increase procedures
Campaign-level trend tracking with automated capacity-headroom alerting
Multi-vector DDoS protection covering both volumetric and application-layer techniques
ITID-41732.detection: Strong technical signal from trend analysis across successive attack-event telemetry within the same campaign.
ITID-41732.response: Proactively scale mitigation capacity ahead of anticipated further escalation, track the escalation trend for the incident record, and reassess the no-payment decision with leadership as impact grows.
metrics: Rate of volume/duration increase across successive attack events
Mitigation capacity headroom remaining after each escalation
ITID-41732.notes: Differentiator within Persistent Ransom DoS: escalating intensity against the same target over time, distinct from steady-state recurrence (ITID-41731) or lateral spread to new targets (ITID-41733).

playbook.name: Escalating Attack Volume/Duration Following Missed Deadline
playbook.description: After a ransom payment deadline was missed, the threat actor has escalated attack volume and/or duration in an apparent attempt to increase pressure on the organization.

steps.title: Confirm and quantify the escalation relative to prior attack instances
steps.desc: Analyze current attack telemetry against the baseline established by earlier occurrences to quantify the increase in volume/duration/vector sophistication.
steps.outcome: Escalation magnitude documented with side-by-side comparison to prior occurrences.

steps.title: Escalate mitigation response to match the increased attack pressure
steps.desc: Request emergency capacity expansion from the scrubbing provider and tighten edge controls to match the escalated attack scale.
steps.guidance: Engage the provider's emergency escalation contact given the established pattern of a known active campaign.
steps.outcome: Mitigation capacity scaled to absorb the escalated attack with minimal service impact.

steps.title: Sustain expanded mitigation through the escalated attack window
steps.desc: Maintain the expanded mitigation posture until the escalated attack subsides, monitoring for further escalation.
steps.outcome: Escalated attack fully mitigated with minimal service impact.

steps.title: Validate service restoration and reassess standing mitigation capacity for future occurrences
steps.desc: Confirm services return to baseline and reassess whether the expanded mitigation capacity should become the new standing baseline given the demonstrated escalation trend.
steps.outcome: Services restored; standing mitigation capacity reassessed and adjusted as needed.

steps.title: Document the escalation and update the long-term response strategy
steps.desc: Capture the escalation timeline and update the organization's long-term RDoS response strategy to anticipate further escalation.
steps.outcome: Report finalized with updated strategy and follow-up actions tracked.

steps.title: Assess whether existing mitigation capacity can absorb the escalated attack
steps.desc: Determine whether current scrubbing/mitigation capacity is sufficient for the escalated scale or requires emergency expansion.
steps.outcome: Capacity gap identified, if any, to drive an emergency scaling decision.

steps.title: Update Legal and Law Enforcement on the escalation
steps.desc: Provide Legal counsel and law enforcement with evidence of the escalation as part of the ongoing case, reaffirming the non-payment position.
steps.outcome: Legal/Law Enforcement updated with escalation evidence.

ITID-41733.def: A pattern of denial-of-service attacks in which a threat actor, following non-payment, broadens the campaign to strike multiple distinct services, subsidiaries, or business units within the same victim organization, demonstrating breadth of reach and multiplying simultaneous business impact to increase pressure to pay.
ITID-41733.purpose: Captures RDoS campaigns in which the threat actor spreads attacks across multiple distinct targets within the victim's infrastructure (subsidiaries, business units, or separate services) rather than repeating or escalating against a single target.
scopeIncludes: Attacks against multiple distinct, separately identifiable services/domains/subsidiaries within the same overall campaign
Simultaneous or closely sequenced attacks against different parts of the organization's infrastructure
Threat-actor communication indicating intent to expand targeting scope across the organization
scopeExcludes: Repeated attacks against the same single target at consistent intensity (ITID-41731)
Escalating intensity against the same single target (ITID-41732)
ITID-41733.severity: Critical given the campaign has demonstrated capability to disrupt multiple parts of the organization simultaneously.
ITID-41733.priority: P1, with coordinated incident command spanning all affected business units.
ITID-41733.escalation: Escalate immediately to enterprise-level incident command and executive leadership given the multi-target scope requires cross-business-unit coordination.
indicators: DDoS attack events against two or more distinct organizational services/domains within the same campaign timeframe
Attack infrastructure/signature consistent with the same threat actor across the different targets
Threat-actor communication naming multiple targeted business units/subsidiaries
vectors: Parallel attacks launched against multiple distinct public-facing services using shared botnet infrastructure
Sequential targeting of subsidiaries/business units identified via reconnaissance of the organization's structure
rootCauses: Inconsistent DDoS mitigation coverage across different business units/subsidiaries
Lack of centralized visibility into attacks occurring across decentralized organizational infrastructure
controls: Enterprise-wide, centrally coordinated DDoS mitigation coverage across all business units/subsidiaries
Centralized incident visibility/correlation across decentralized infrastructure
Cross-business-unit incident command procedures
ITID-41733.detection: Strong technical signal requires centralized correlation across otherwise siloed monitoring for different business units/subsidiaries.
ITID-41733.response: Stand up enterprise-level incident command, ensure consistent mitigation coverage is applied across all targeted units, and centrally track the full multi-target campaign for attribution and decision-making.
metrics: Number of distinct organizational targets affected by the campaign
Time to achieve centralized visibility across all affected units
ITID-41733.notes: Differentiator within Persistent Ransom DoS: the axis is lateral spread across multiple distinct targets, distinct from repetition (ITID-41731) or escalation (ITID-41732) against a single target.

playbook.name: Multi-Target Persistent RDoS Campaign Across Victim's Infrastructure
playbook.description: A persistent ransom DoS campaign is rotating attacks across multiple distinct targets within the organization's infrastructure (different services, subsidiaries, or regions) rather than repeatedly hitting a single target.

steps.title: Map the pattern of targets across the campaign
steps.desc: Compile a timeline correlating each attack occurrence with its specific target (service, subsidiary, region) to identify the actor's targeting pattern and rotation logic.
steps.outcome: A consolidated target-rotation map documented across all observed occurrences.

steps.title: Extend standing mitigation coverage across all identified at-risk targets
steps.desc: Proactively extend always-on DDoS mitigation to cover the full set of at-risk infrastructure identified, not just previously hit targets.
steps.guidance: A reactive, target-by-target approach will always lag a multi-target rotating campaign; broaden coverage proactively.
steps.outcome: Mitigation coverage extended across all at-risk infrastructure identified.

steps.title: Mitigate each new target occurrence under the extended standing posture
steps.desc: Apply extended mitigation controls to each new target as the campaign rotates, minimizing response latency.
steps.outcome: Each new target occurrence is absorbed with minimal service impact.

steps.title: Validate stability across all business units and reassess coverage
steps.desc: Confirm all business units/subsidiaries remain stable and periodically reassess whether mitigation coverage should be further expanded as the campaign evolves.
steps.outcome: Stability confirmed across all units; coverage reassessed on a defined cadence.

steps.title: Document the multi-target campaign and cross-business-unit coordination effectiveness
steps.desc: Capture the full campaign timeline across all targets and evaluate the effectiveness of centralized tracking and coordination across business units.
steps.outcome: Report finalized with follow-up actions on cross-unit coordination tracked.

steps.title: Identify remaining untargeted critical infrastructure at risk
steps.desc: Using the target-rotation pattern, assess which critical services/subsidiaries have not yet been targeted and may be at risk next.
steps.outcome: A prioritized list of at-risk untargeted infrastructure for proactive mitigation.

steps.title: Coordinate centralized incident tracking and Legal/Law Enforcement engagement across all business units
steps.desc: Establish centralized incident tracking across all affected business units/subsidiaries and provide consolidated evidence to Legal counsel and law enforcement.
steps.guidance: Multi-target campaigns risk being tracked as separate unrelated incidents by different business units; centralize tracking to preserve the full campaign picture.
steps.outcome: Centralized tracking established; Legal/Law Enforcement briefed with the consolidated campaign picture.

ITID-41734.def: A sustained RDoS campaign confirmed as ongoing following non-payment, but not yet classified into a specific pattern (steady recurrence, escalating intensity, multi-target spread) pending further investigation.
ITID-41734.purpose: Serves as the intake bucket for persistent Ransom DoS campaigns that do not yet fit steady-state recurrence, escalation, or multi-target classifications.
scopeIncludes: Newly observed persistent-campaign patterns not yet mapped to an existing sibling leaf
Ambiguous multi-event RDoS campaigns pending classification
scopeExcludes: Any incident later confirmed as steady recurrence (ITID-41731), escalating intensity (ITID-41732), or multi-target spread (ITID-41733) — reclassify once confirmed
ITID-41734.severity: High by default pending classification given the campaign is confirmed ongoing; adjust once the specific pattern is confirmed.
ITID-41734.priority: P1 pending triage, maintained per standard severity guidance once the pattern is identified.
ITID-41734.escalation: Escalate to the SOC classification lead for prompt re-tagging into a specific sibling leaf once the pattern is understood, without delaying active mitigation response.
indicators: Multiple confirmed DDoS attack events tied to the same RDoS campaign with an unconfirmed pattern
Analyst uncertainty about whether the campaign is recurring, escalating, or spreading to new targets
vectors: Unclassified/novel persistent-campaign pattern pending investigation
rootCauses: Root cause/pattern not yet determined
controls: Standard sustained DDoS mitigation posture pending classification
ITID-41734.detection: Coverage depends on the eventual classification; this bucket itself is tracked via generic multi-event campaign correlation.
ITID-41734.response: Maintain active mitigation posture, investigate to determine the specific pattern, and reclassify to the appropriate sibling ITID as soon as possible.
metrics: Number of incidents parked in this bucket beyond the triage SLA
Average time to reclassify into a specific sibling leaf
ITID-41734.notes: Catch-all intake leaf; used only during initial triage. Analysts should reclassify into ITID-41731/41732/41733 as soon as the pattern is confirmed.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Persistent Ransom DoS
playbook.description: A persistent ransom DoS campaign involving repeated or ongoing attacks following ransom non-payment is occurring, not otherwise classified into a more specific sub-type.

steps.title: Confirm the persistent/recurring nature of the campaign
steps.desc: Analyze traffic telemetry across multiple attack instances to confirm a persistent or recurring pattern tied to the ongoing RDoS campaign.
steps.outcome: Persistent campaign pattern confirmed with historical occurrence log established.

steps.title: Establish or reaffirm standing mitigation response for the recurring campaign
steps.desc: Transition to always-on DDoS scrubbing scaled to the observed campaign trend rather than reactive per-incident engagement.
steps.outcome: Standing mitigation posture established and scaled to the observed trend.
steps.abort: If occurrences are de-escalating and infrequent, on-demand engagement may remain sufficient.

steps.title: Mitigate each recurring attack instance under standing posture
steps.desc: Apply standing mitigation controls to each new occurrence, minimizing manual intervention and response time.
steps.outcome: Each recurring attack instance is absorbed with minimal to no service impact.

steps.title: Validate service stability between occurrences and reassess standing posture periodically
steps.desc: Confirm services remain stable between occurrences and periodically reassess whether mitigation levels remain appropriate.
steps.outcome: Service stability maintained; mitigation posture reassessed on a defined cadence.

steps.title: Document the campaign and long-term mitigation strategy
steps.desc: Capture the full multi-occurrence timeline and recommend a long-term mitigation and Legal/Law Enforcement engagement strategy.
steps.outcome: Report finalized with a long-term strategy documented and follow-up actions tracked.

steps.title: Assess trend in attack scale/frequency across occurrences
steps.desc: Compare scale and frequency across successive occurrences to determine whether the actor is escalating, maintaining, or de-escalating pressure.
steps.outcome: Trend documented to inform response scaling.

steps.title: Maintain Legal and Law Enforcement engagement on the ongoing campaign
steps.desc: Provide Legal counsel and law enforcement with updated evidence of each occurrence as part of the ongoing case, reaffirming the non-payment position.
steps.outcome: Legal/Law Enforcement kept updated with a consolidated evidence trail.

ITID-41811.def: A resource-depletion attack in which a co-tenant on shared virtualized infrastructure (whether malicious or an unwitting victim of compromise) deliberately or through abuse consumes a disproportionate share of hypervisor-level CPU, memory, or I/O capacity, causing measurable performance degradation or outage for the organization's own virtual machines sharing that physical host.
ITID-41811.purpose: Captures denial of service caused by another tenant's (or attacker-controlled tenant's) workload on shared virtualized infrastructure consuming a disproportionate share of hypervisor resources, degrading the organization's co-located workloads.
scopeIncludes: A co-tenant VM deliberately driving resource consumption to degrade shared hypervisor capacity
Abuse of insufficient resource isolation/limits between tenants on the same physical host
Noisy-neighbor impact traced to a specific identifiable co-tenant workload
scopeExcludes: Uncontrolled but non-malicious internal VM sprawl consuming hypervisor capacity (ITID-41812)
Hypervisor scheduler overload caused by a malicious guest exploiting scheduling logic itself rather than raw resource consumption (ITID-41813)
ITID-41811.severity: Medium-High; severity depends on whether resource isolation guarantees (reserved capacity) were violated and how business-critical the affected workloads are.
ITID-41811.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if reserved/guaranteed capacity for critical workloads is being violated.
ITID-41811.escalation: Escalate to the cloud/virtualization platform team (internal or provider, depending on hosting model) to enforce resource isolation or migrate affected workloads.
indicators: Host-level hypervisor metrics (CPU steal time, noisy-neighbor indicators) showing resource contention despite normal workload demand
Performance degradation correlated with co-tenant activity spikes rather than the organization's own workload
Provider-reported resource contention alerts for the shared host
vectors: Co-tenant VM deliberately running CPU/IO-intensive workloads to degrade shared capacity
Compromised co-tenant VM used by an external attacker to consume shared resources
Exploiting insufficient hypervisor-level resource quotas/reservations
rootCauses: No enforced per-tenant resource reservation/limits at the hypervisor level
Shared (non-dedicated) hosting model with inadequate isolation guarantees for critical workloads
Lack of visibility into co-tenant resource consumption on shared infrastructure
mitreTechniques: T1499.002 Endpoint Denial of Service: Service Exhaustion Flood
controls: Enforced per-tenant resource reservations/limits (CPU shares, memory limits) at the hypervisor level
Migration to dedicated/isolated hosting for business-critical workloads
Hypervisor-level noisy-neighbor monitoring (e.g., CPU steal time alerting)
ITID-41811.detection: Strong technical signal from hypervisor-level resource-contention metrics (e.g., CPU steal time) where available; more limited if hosted on a public cloud provider with restricted host-level visibility.
ITID-41811.response: Engage the platform/provider to identify and constrain or migrate the contending co-tenant workload, and consider migrating critical workloads to dedicated capacity if recurrence continues.
metrics: CPU steal time / contention metric trend during incidents
Time to identify and constrain the contending co-tenant workload
detections: CPU steal time / noisy-neighbor anomaly alerting
ITID-41811.notes: Differentiator within Hypervisor Exhaustion: this leaf is co-tenant resource-consumption abuse, distinct from internal VM sprawl (ITID-41812) or scheduler-exploitation attacks (ITID-41813).

playbook.name: Noisy-Neighbor VM Resource Exhaustion Attack (Co-Tenant Abuse)
playbook.description: A co-tenant on a shared multi-tenant hypervisor is deliberately or negligently consuming excessive CPU, memory, disk I/O, or network bandwidth, degrading the organization's own VM performance ('noisy neighbor' effect).

steps.title: Correlate VM performance degradation with hypervisor-level utilization anomalies
steps.desc: Review cloud/hypervisor billing and utilization dashboards alongside internal VM performance metrics to confirm degradation stems from host-level resource contention rather than the organization's own workload.
steps.guidance: Look for CPU steal time, noisy I/O wait, or network jitter metrics that indicate contention at the hypervisor/host level rather than within the guest OS itself.
steps.outcome: Noisy-neighbor contention confirmed with host-level contention metrics documented.
steps.abort: If degradation correlates with the organization's own workload spike, redirect to internal capacity investigation.
steps.tool: Cloud provider utilization dashboard, VM performance monitoring

steps.title: Open a support ticket with the cloud/hosting provider reporting host-level contention
steps.desc: Escalate to the provider's support channel with evidence of contention (steal time, latency metrics) and request host rebalancing or migration of the organization's VMs.
steps.outcome: Support ticket opened; provider begins investigation or rebalancing.

steps.title: Verify sustained resolution of host-level contention
steps.desc: Confirm CPU steal time, I/O wait, and network jitter metrics return to normal levels following migration or provider remediation.
steps.outcome: Contention metrics confirmed normalized over a sustained monitoring window.

steps.title: Confirm application performance restoration
steps.desc: Verify affected applications/services return to normal performance baselines.
steps.outcome: Application performance confirmed restored to baseline.

steps.title: Document incident and evaluate dedicated/isolated hosting options
steps.desc: Capture the timeline and evaluate whether dedicated instances, capacity reservations, or single-tenant hosting are warranted for performance-sensitive workloads to prevent recurrence.
steps.outcome: Report finalized with follow-up hosting-architecture recommendations tracked.

steps.title: Assess business impact of the degraded performance
steps.desc: Determine which applications/services are affected and the severity of the performance impact.
steps.outcome: Impact documented to prioritize response urgency.

steps.title: Request or trigger VM migration to a different host/availability zone
steps.desc: Where self-service migration is available, initiate migration of affected VMs to a different underlying host or availability zone to escape the noisy co-tenant.
steps.outcome: Affected VMs relocated away from the contended host; performance improves.
steps.abort: If self-service migration is unavailable, rely on provider-side rebalancing via the support ticket.

ITID-41812.def: A resource-depletion incident in which an excessive, uncontrolled number of virtual machine instances is created within the organization's own virtualization/cloud environment (via compromised credentials, runaway automation, or unmanaged self-service provisioning) exhausting hypervisor host capacity or account-level instance quotas, degrading or blocking legitimate workload provisioning and operation.
ITID-41812.purpose: Captures denial of service caused by uncontrolled, unauthorized proliferation of virtual machine instances within the organization's own environment exhausting hypervisor capacity, whether through automation error or credential abuse.
scopeIncludes: Compromised cloud/IAM credentials used to mass-provision VM instances (e.g., for cryptomining or botnet infrastructure)
Runaway internal automation/scripts repeatedly creating instances without cleanup
Unmanaged self-service provisioning exhausting account-level instance or capacity quotas
scopeExcludes: A co-tenant's workload on shared infrastructure degrading the organization's own VMs (ITID-41811, an external-tenant issue rather than the organization's own sprawl)
Hypervisor scheduler-exploitation attacks (ITID-41813)
ITID-41812.severity: Medium-High; severity rises sharply if the sprawl is attributable to compromised credentials rather than an internal process error, given the security-breach implications.
ITID-41812.priority: P2 for internal process-driven sprawl; P1 if traced to compromised credentials, given the incident is then also a confirmed compromise.
ITID-41812.escalation: Escalate to cloud security/IAM immediately if compromised credentials are suspected as the cause; escalate to platform engineering for runaway-automation cases.
indicators: Rapid, abnormal growth in active VM instance count with no corresponding legitimate provisioning request
Instance creation activity attributable to a single automated process, script, or credential set
Account/hypervisor capacity quota alerts triggered by instance count
vectors: Compromised cloud API credentials used to script mass instance creation
Misconfigured or buggy auto-scaling/automation logic creating instances without bound
Unmanaged developer self-service access with no provisioning guardrails
rootCauses: No enforced maximum instance-count quota or approval workflow for provisioning
Compromised credentials with excessive instance-creation privileges
Automation/auto-scaling logic lacking an upper bound or circuit breaker
mitreTechniques: T1499.002 Endpoint Denial of Service: Service Exhaustion Flood
controls: Enforced instance-count quotas with approval workflows for exceptions
Least-privilege IAM policies limiting instance-creation scope per credential
Automated anomaly detection on instance-creation rate
ITID-41812.detection: Strong technical signal from cloud-provider instance-creation audit logs and quota-utilization telemetry.
ITID-41812.response: Halt further instance creation (quota enforcement or credential revocation), terminate unauthorized instances, and determine whether the root cause is credential compromise or an internal process failure.
metrics: Peak instance count during the incident
Time to halt further unauthorized instance creation
Cost impact of unauthorized instances
ITID-41812.notes: Differentiator within Hypervisor Exhaustion: this leaf is internal/own-environment instance sprawl (credential abuse or automation failure), distinct from external co-tenant noisy-neighbor impact (ITID-41811).

playbook.name: VM Sprawl/Uncontrolled Instance Creation Exhausting Hypervisor Capacity
playbook.description: Uncontrolled or malicious mass creation of virtual machine instances is exhausting hypervisor/cluster capacity, denying resources needed for legitimate workloads.

steps.title: Detect abnormal VM instance creation rate and cluster capacity trajectory
steps.desc: Review cloud/virtualization management console and billing anomaly alerts to confirm an abnormal surge in VM instance creation is depleting available cluster/hypervisor capacity.
steps.guidance: Distinguish between a legitimate scaling event (e.g., approved batch job) and unauthorized/malicious sprawl by checking requester identity, approval records, and instance naming/tagging patterns.
steps.outcome: Instance-creation surge confirmed as anomalous with creation rate and capacity trajectory documented.
steps.abort: If the surge corresponds to an approved, legitimate scaling event, close as non-incident and address via capacity planning.
steps.tool: Cloud/virtualization management console, billing anomaly detection

steps.title: Suspend or restrict the responsible account/credential's instance-creation privileges
steps.desc: Immediately revoke or restrict the identified account/credential's ability to create further instances to halt continued capacity consumption.
steps.guidance: If credentials appear compromised, rotate them and treat as a potential broader compromise requiring separate investigation.
steps.outcome: Further unauthorized instance creation halted.

steps.title: Verify no residual unauthorized instances or automation remain active
steps.desc: Confirm all unauthorized instances are terminated and any runaway automation/pipeline causing the sprawl is disabled or fixed.
steps.outcome: Environment confirmed free of unauthorized instances and runaway automation.

steps.title: Restore legitimate workload capacity and validate service performance
steps.desc: Confirm legitimate workloads have sufficient capacity and are performing normally.
steps.outcome: Legitimate workload performance confirmed restored to baseline.

steps.title: Document incident and implement instance-creation quota/guardrails
steps.desc: Capture the timeline and recommend permanent instance-creation quotas, approval workflows, and anomaly alerting to prevent recurrence.
steps.outcome: Report finalized with guardrail follow-up actions assigned.

steps.title: Identify the source account/credentials driving instance creation
steps.desc: Determine which account, automation pipeline, or credential set is responsible for the mass instance creation.
steps.guidance: Check for compromised API keys/service accounts as a possible root cause alongside insider misuse or runaway automation.
steps.outcome: Responsible account/credential identified.

steps.title: Terminate unauthorized/excess instances and reclaim capacity
steps.desc: Identify and terminate the unauthorized instances (after evidence preservation if malicious intent is suspected) to restore capacity for legitimate workloads.
steps.guidance: Capture instance metadata/logs before termination if the sprawl appears intentional/malicious for follow-up investigation.
steps.outcome: Cluster/hypervisor capacity restored to levels sufficient for legitimate workloads.

ITID-41813.def: A resource-depletion attack in which a guest virtual machine under the adversary's control deliberately crafts its workload pattern to exploit weaknesses in the hypervisor's CPU/IO scheduling algorithm, gaining disproportionate scheduling priority and starving other co-located guest workloads of execution time beyond what raw resource consumption alone would explain.
ITID-41813.purpose: Captures denial of service caused by a malicious guest workload deliberately exploiting hypervisor scheduling logic (rather than simply consuming raw resources) to starve other guests.
scopeIncludes: Workload patterns specifically engineered to exploit scheduler fairness gaps or priority-inversion weaknesses
Exploitation of hypervisor-specific scheduling quirks (e.g., burst-credit mechanisms) to gain outsized effective priority
Confirmed scheduler-level starvation of other guests disproportionate to the offending guest's actual resource allocation
scopeExcludes: Simple high resource consumption by a co-tenant without evidence of scheduler-logic exploitation (ITID-41811)
Uncontrolled instance sprawl (ITID-41812)
ITID-41813.severity: High given this requires deliberate technical sophistication and indicates a knowledgeable, targeted adversary.
ITID-41813.priority: P1 given the sophistication implies a targeted, capable threat actor requiring prompt platform-level response.
ITID-41813.escalation: Escalate immediately to virtualization platform engineering and, where hosted with a third party, to the cloud provider's security team, given this requires hypervisor-level remediation.
indicators: Guest workload starvation disproportionate to the offending guest's measured resource consumption
Hypervisor scheduler logs/metrics showing anomalous priority or credit accumulation by a specific guest
Workload pattern from the offending guest inconsistent with any legitimate application behavior
vectors: Crafted workload timing designed to repeatedly trigger scheduler burst-credit or priority-boost mechanisms
Exploiting a known hypervisor scheduler vulnerability or misconfiguration
rootCauses: Hypervisor scheduler configuration/version with known fairness or priority-inversion weaknesses
Lack of hard resource caps independent of scheduler priority logic
Delayed hypervisor patching against known scheduler-exploitation vulnerabilities
mitreTechniques: T1499.004 Endpoint Denial of Service: Application or System Exploitation
controls: Timely hypervisor patching against known scheduler vulnerabilities
Hard per-guest resource caps independent of scheduler priority mechanisms
Hypervisor-level anomaly detection on scheduling priority/credit metrics
ITID-41813.detection: Requires hypervisor-level telemetry (often only available to the infrastructure/platform owner rather than tenants) to confirm; a strong signal once that telemetry is available.
ITID-41813.response: Isolate or terminate the offending guest, apply hard resource caps, and patch or reconfigure the hypervisor scheduler to close the exploited weakness.
metrics: Time to isolate the offending guest
Guest starvation severity relative to its measured resource consumption
ITID-41813.notes: Differentiator within Hypervisor Exhaustion: the most technically sophisticated leaf in this group, requiring deliberate exploitation of scheduling logic rather than raw resource consumption (ITID-41811) or sprawl (ITID-41812).

playbook.name: Hypervisor Scheduler Overload via Malicious Guest Workload
playbook.description: A malicious guest VM is deliberately generating workload patterns (e.g., excessive context switching, CPU pinning abuse) designed to overload the hypervisor's scheduler and degrade performance for co-located guests.

steps.title: Confirm hypervisor scheduler overload and isolate the offending guest
steps.desc: Review hypervisor-level scheduler metrics (run queue length, context-switch rate, CPU ready time) alongside per-guest resource usage to identify which guest VM is generating the abusive workload pattern.
steps.guidance: Look for a specific guest with abnormal context-switching or scheduling-abuse patterns correlated with degraded performance across co-located guests.
steps.outcome: Offending guest VM identified with scheduler-impact evidence documented.
steps.abort: If no single guest stands out as the cause, investigate hypervisor/host-level fault instead.
steps.tool: Hypervisor management console, host performance monitoring

steps.title: Throttle or isolate the offending guest's resource allocation
steps.desc: Apply CPU/resource limits, scheduling priority reduction, or migrate the offending guest to an isolated host to stop its impact on co-located guests.
steps.outcome: Offending guest's impact on co-located guests eliminated or substantially reduced.

steps.title: Remediate or shut down the offending guest workload
steps.desc: Clean/remediate the compromised guest or shut down/quarantine the offending workload based on the root-cause finding.
steps.outcome: Malicious workload eliminated; scheduler behavior returns to normal.

steps.title: Verify co-located guest performance restoration
steps.desc: Confirm previously affected co-located guests return to normal performance baselines.
steps.outcome: Co-located guest performance confirmed restored.

steps.title: Document incident and review scheduler-abuse detection/isolation controls
steps.desc: Capture the timeline and recommend scheduler-abuse detection rules and resource-isolation policy improvements.
steps.outcome: Report finalized with follow-up actions tracked.

steps.title: Assess impact on co-located guest performance
steps.desc: Determine which co-located guests/applications are affected and the severity of the performance impact.
steps.outcome: Impact documented to prioritize response.

steps.title: Investigate whether the offending guest is compromised or intentionally malicious
steps.desc: Determine whether the offending guest belongs to a legitimate tenant/workload that has been compromised, or represents an internal misuse case, to guide next steps (remediation vs. account action).
steps.outcome: Root cause of the malicious workload determined.

ITID-41814.def: A hypervisor-resource-exhaustion incident confirmed as an attack against virtualization-layer capacity, but not yet classified into a specific mechanism (co-tenant noisy-neighbor abuse, uncontrolled instance sprawl, scheduler exploitation) pending further investigation.
ITID-41814.purpose: Serves as the intake bucket for hypervisor exhaustion attacks that do not yet fit noisy-neighbor, VM-sprawl, or scheduler-exploitation classifications.
scopeIncludes: Newly observed hypervisor-exhaustion techniques not yet mapped to an existing sibling leaf
Ambiguous virtualization-layer resource incidents pending root-cause confirmation
scopeExcludes: Any incident later confirmed as noisy-neighbor abuse (ITID-41811), VM sprawl (ITID-41812), or scheduler exploitation (ITID-41813) — reclassify once confirmed
ITID-41814.severity: Medium by default pending classification; adjust once the specific mechanism and business impact are confirmed.
ITID-41814.priority: P3 pending triage, escalating per standard severity guidance once root cause is identified.
ITID-41814.escalation: Escalate to the SOC classification lead for prompt re-tagging into a specific sibling leaf once the mechanism is understood.
indicators: Elevated hypervisor-level resource contention with an unconfirmed cause
Analyst uncertainty about which hypervisor-exhaustion mechanism applies
vectors: Unclassified/novel hypervisor-exhaustion technique pending investigation
rootCauses: Root cause not yet determined
mitreTechniques: T1499.002 Endpoint Denial of Service: Service Exhaustion Flood
controls: Standard hypervisor/virtualization monitoring and alerting pending classification
ITID-41814.detection: Coverage depends on the eventual root cause; this bucket itself is detected via generic hypervisor-resource-contention alerting.
ITID-41814.response: Investigate to determine the specific mechanism and reclassify to the appropriate sibling ITID as soon as possible; apply standard hypervisor-exhaustion containment in the interim.
metrics: Number of incidents parked in this bucket beyond the triage SLA
Average time to reclassify into a specific sibling leaf
ITID-41814.notes: Catch-all intake leaf; used only during initial triage. Analysts should reclassify into ITID-41811/41812/41813 as soon as the mechanism is confirmed.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Hypervisor Exhaustion Attack
playbook.description: An attack or abuse pattern is exhausting hypervisor/virtualization-cluster resources, denying capacity to legitimate guest workloads, not otherwise classified into a more specific sub-type.

steps.title: Confirm hypervisor-level resource exhaustion via utilization monitoring
steps.desc: Review hypervisor/cluster utilization dashboards and per-guest metrics to confirm resource exhaustion is occurring at the host/cluster level.
steps.outcome: Exhaustion condition confirmed with contributing metrics documented.

steps.title: Apply resource limits or isolate the offending workload
steps.desc: Apply CPU/memory/resource quotas, throttling, or migrate/isolate the offending workload to stop further capacity exhaustion.
steps.outcome: Further resource exhaustion halted.

steps.title: Verify sustained resolution of resource exhaustion
steps.desc: Confirm hypervisor/cluster utilization returns to normal levels and remains stable.
steps.outcome: Utilization confirmed normalized over a sustained monitoring window.

steps.title: Confirm legitimate workload performance restoration
steps.desc: Verify legitimate guest workloads/applications return to normal performance baselines.
steps.outcome: Application performance confirmed restored.

steps.title: Document incident and review capacity governance controls
steps.desc: Capture the timeline and recommend resource quota, isolation, or capacity-monitoring improvements to prevent recurrence.
steps.outcome: Report finalized with follow-up actions tracked.

steps.title: Identify the source workload(s) or account(s) driving exhaustion
steps.desc: Determine which guest VM, tenant, or account is responsible for the excessive resource consumption.
steps.outcome: Responsible workload/account identified.

steps.title: Escalate to cloud/hosting provider if exhaustion is host/cluster-wide
steps.desc: If the exhaustion spans provider-managed infrastructure beyond the organization's direct control, escalate via support ticket for capacity rebalancing.
steps.outcome: Provider engaged where applicable to assist with remediation.
steps.abort: If exhaustion is fully within organization-controlled infrastructure, this step is not applicable.

ITID-41821.def: A resource-depletion attack in which an adversary triggers a high volume of concurrent invocations of a serverless function (e.g., AWS Lambda, Azure Functions), consuming the account's or function's configured concurrency limit and causing legitimate invocations to be throttled or rejected.
ITID-41821.purpose: Captures denial of service caused by an adversary flooding a serverless function with invocations to exhaust its account- or function-level concurrency limit, blocking legitimate invocations.
scopeIncludes: High-volume concurrent invocation of a publicly triggerable serverless function to exhaust concurrency limits
Exploiting an event-source integration (e.g., API Gateway, queue, storage trigger) to indirectly flood function invocations
Impact measured specifically as invocation throttling/rejection rather than billing cost
scopeExcludes: Attacks whose primary measured impact is excessive billing cost rather than availability (ITID-41822)
Attacks specifically exploiting cold-start latency rather than concurrency-limit exhaustion (ITID-41823)
ITID-41821.severity: High if the function is on a critical request path with no reserved concurrency for legitimate traffic; Medium if reserved concurrency isolates critical paths.
ITID-41821.priority: P1 if critical-path function invocations are being throttled; P2 if impact is contained to non-critical functions.
ITID-41821.escalation: Escalate to the platform/serverless engineering team to apply reserved concurrency and rate limiting at the triggering event source.
indicators: Function invocation-concurrency metrics at or near the configured limit
Throttling/rejection errors spiking for legitimate invocation sources
Invocation volume traceable to a narrow set of anomalous source IPs/accounts/event sources
vectors: Direct high-volume calls to a publicly exposed function endpoint (e.g., via API Gateway)
Flooding an upstream event source (queue, storage bucket, HTTP trigger) that fans out to function invocations
Exploiting a function with no per-source rate limiting on its trigger
rootCauses: No reserved concurrency isolating critical functions from account-wide concurrency exhaustion
No rate limiting at the API Gateway/event-source layer in front of the function
Function trigger exposed without authentication or abuse controls
mitreTechniques: T1499.003 Endpoint Denial of Service: Application Exhaustion Flood
controls: Reserved concurrency for business-critical functions
Rate limiting/throttling at the API Gateway or event-source layer
Authentication/authorization on function trigger endpoints
ITID-41821.detection: Strong technical signal from cloud-provider function-concurrency and throttling metrics.
ITID-41821.response: Apply or tighten rate limiting at the trigger layer, reserve concurrency for critical functions, and block the identified abusive source.
metrics: Peak concurrency utilization during incidents
Number of throttled/rejected legitimate invocations
Time to restore normal invocation success rate
ITID-41821.notes: Differentiator within Serverless Function Abuse: this leaf is concurrency-limit exhaustion causing invocation rejection, distinct from cost-driven abuse (ITID-41822) or cold-start-specific exploitation (ITID-41823).

playbook.name: Serverless Function Invocation Flood Exhausting Concurrency Limits
playbook.description: A flood of serverless function invocations is exhausting the organization's account/region concurrency limits, causing throttling or failure of legitimate function-dependent workloads.

steps.title: Confirm concurrency-limit exhaustion via cloud provider metrics
steps.desc: Review serverless platform monitoring (invocation count, concurrent execution count, throttle/error rate) to confirm the account or specific function is hitting concurrency limits due to an invocation flood.
steps.guidance: Check whether throttling errors correlate with a genuine traffic surge or with an abnormal invocation source (unexpected trigger, exposed endpoint, or automation loop).
steps.outcome: Concurrency exhaustion confirmed with invocation source and rate documented.
steps.abort: If the surge correlates with a legitimate traffic event within expected growth, treat as capacity planning rather than an incident.
steps.tool: Cloud provider serverless monitoring (e.g., CloudWatch/Cloud Monitoring)

steps.title: Apply reserved/provisioned concurrency or per-function throttling
steps.desc: Configure reserved concurrency limits on unaffected critical functions to protect them from account-wide exhaustion, and throttle the offending function/trigger.
steps.guidance: Reserved concurrency on critical functions ring-fences their capacity from being starved by the flood affecting other functions.
steps.outcome: Critical functions protected; offending function's invocation rate reduced.

steps.title: Verify sustained normalization of invocation and concurrency levels
steps.desc: Confirm invocation rate and concurrent execution count return to and remain at normal levels.
steps.outcome: Concurrency and invocation metrics confirmed normalized.

steps.title: Restore normal concurrency configuration and validate dependent workloads
steps.desc: Roll back temporary reserved-concurrency/throttling changes where appropriate and confirm all dependent workloads/applications are functioning normally.
steps.outcome: Dependent workloads confirmed restored to normal operation.

steps.title: Document incident and implement standing concurrency-protection guardrails
steps.desc: Capture the timeline and recommend permanent reserved-concurrency allocation, endpoint rate limiting, and invocation-anomaly alerting for critical functions.
steps.outcome: Report finalized with guardrail follow-up actions assigned.

steps.title: Identify the specific function(s) and trigger source causing the flood
steps.desc: Determine which function(s), API endpoints, or event triggers (queue, API Gateway, webhook) are generating the excessive invocation volume.
steps.outcome: Responsible function(s) and trigger source identified.
steps.tool: Serverless platform console, API gateway logs

steps.title: Rate-limit or block the abusive request source at the API gateway/WAF
steps.desc: If the flood originates from an externally exposed endpoint, apply rate limiting, WAF rules, or authentication requirements to block the abusive traffic at the gateway before it reaches the function.
steps.outcome: Abusive invocation traffic blocked upstream of the function layer.

ITID-41822.def: A resource-depletion attack in which an adversary triggers a sustained high volume of serverless function invocations specifically to inflate the organization's usage-based billing (per-invocation and compute-duration charges), where the function itself may continue operating normally for legitimate users while the financial cost accumulates.
ITID-41822.purpose: Captures denial-of-wallet incidents in which an adversary deliberately triggers excessive serverless function invocations to inflate usage-based billing costs, with financial impact as the primary objective rather than availability disruption.
scopeIncludes: Sustained invocation volume calibrated to stay under concurrency/availability-impact thresholds while maximizing billed invocation count or duration
Triggering functions with deliberately long execution duration or expensive downstream calls to maximize per-invocation cost
Automated abuse of a publicly triggerable function with no invocation-volume safeguards
scopeExcludes: Attacks whose primary measured impact is invocation throttling/availability degradation (ITID-41821)
Cold-start-specific exploitation (ITID-41823)
ITID-41822.severity: Medium; driven by financial impact rather than availability, though sustained abuse can still degrade downstream dependencies invoked by the function.
ITID-41822.priority: P2, escalating if billing-anomaly detection shows cost trending to breach a defined budget-alert threshold within the billing cycle.
ITID-41822.escalation: Escalate to finance/platform stakeholders once projected cost impact is quantified; apply invocation-rate limiting to cap further cost accumulation.
indicators: Serverless billing metrics (invocation count, total compute duration) trending sharply above historical baseline
Invocation volume from a narrow set of anomalous sources with no legitimate business driver
Function execution duration abnormally elevated in correlation with the invocation spike
vectors: Automated scripts repeatedly invoking a publicly exposed function endpoint
Crafted input designed to maximize function execution duration or trigger expensive downstream API calls per invocation
Abuse of a function with no per-account or per-source invocation-rate limiting
rootCauses: No invocation-rate limiting or budget-based circuit breaker on publicly exposed functions
No billing-anomaly alerting tied to serverless usage
Function logic with unbounded or attacker-influenceable execution duration
controls: Invocation-rate limiting and budget-based circuit breakers on publicly exposed functions
Billing-anomaly alerting with defined budget thresholds
Maximum execution-duration limits configured per function
ITID-41822.detection: Strong technical signal from serverless billing/usage telemetry correlated with per-source invocation volume and duration.
ITID-41822.response: Apply invocation-rate limiting or disable the abused trigger, engage finance on billing impact, and add budget-based circuit breakers to prevent recurrence.
metrics: Projected/actual billing cost impact per incident
Invocation volume anomaly magnitude
Time to apply rate limiting/circuit breaker
ITID-41822.notes: Differentiator within Serverless Function Abuse: this leaf is a denial-of-wallet/cost-driven abuse, distinct from availability-focused concurrency exhaustion (ITID-41821) or cold-start exploitation (ITID-41823).

playbook.name: Denial-of-Wallet Attack via Excessive Serverless Function Billing
playbook.description: An attacker is deliberately driving high-volume invocations of the organization's serverless functions to inflate billing costs (denial-of-wallet) rather than solely denying availability.

steps.title: Detect abnormal serverless billing/invocation trajectory
steps.desc: Correlate cloud billing anomaly alerts with function invocation and duration metrics to confirm a deliberate cost-driving attack versus organic usage growth.
steps.guidance: Look for sustained high-volume invocations of functions with high per-invocation cost (long duration, high memory allocation, or downstream paid API calls) from a suspicious source pattern.
steps.outcome: Attack confirmed as denial-of-wallet via serverless billing abuse, with cost trajectory and invocation evidence documented.
steps.abort: If the trajectory correlates with a legitimate feature launch or campaign, treat as capacity planning, not an incident.
steps.tool: Cloud billing anomaly detection, serverless monitoring

steps.title: Set or verify hard billing alerts and spend caps
steps.desc: Immediately verify or configure hard spend caps/budget alerts on the affected cloud account/project to bound further financial exposure while investigation continues.
steps.outcome: Spend caps and alerts confirmed active.

steps.title: Block or challenge confirmed abusive sources
steps.desc: Apply sustained blocking or bot-management challenges against confirmed abusive sources to eliminate remaining cost-driving traffic.
steps.outcome: Abusive traffic eliminated; invocation volume and spend return to baseline.

steps.title: Reconcile incurred costs and confirm normal function operation
steps.desc: Reconcile incurred serverless billing costs for the incident window with finance and confirm legitimate invocations continue functioning normally.
steps.outcome: Cost impact quantified and reported; legitimate function operation confirmed unaffected.

steps.title: Document incident and implement standing cost-anomaly guardrails
steps.desc: Capture the timeline, financial impact, and recommend permanent concurrency limits, authentication requirements, and cost-anomaly alerting for public-facing functions.
steps.outcome: Report finalized with prioritized guardrail follow-ups assigned.

steps.title: Identify the specific functions and sources driving cost
steps.desc: Pinpoint which functions and invocation sources (endpoints, triggers, IPs) are responsible for the disproportionate cost.
steps.outcome: Specific abusive functions and sources identified.
steps.tool: Serverless platform console, API gateway logs

steps.title: Apply concurrency limits, rate limiting, and authentication on abused functions/endpoints
steps.desc: Reduce reserved concurrency for the abused function(s), rate-limit the invoking endpoint, and require authentication where the endpoint was previously open.
steps.outcome: Invocation volume and associated cost drop sharply.

ITID-41823.def: A resource-depletion attack in which an adversary deliberately structures invocation patterns (e.g., bursty traffic with unique parameters preventing instance reuse, or exploiting scale-to-zero behavior) to force the serverless platform to repeatedly cold-start new function instances rather than reuse warm ones, degrading response latency and consuming disproportionate initialization resources compared to steady-state invocation.
ITID-41823.purpose: Captures denial of service caused by an adversary deliberately triggering serverless cold starts at scale to exploit the higher latency/resource cost of initializing new function instances, degrading response times or downstream capacity.
scopeIncludes: Invocation patterns deliberately engineered to defeat instance-warm-reuse (e.g., varying container-affinity-relevant parameters)
Exploiting scale-to-zero configurations by sending bursts after idle periods to force mass cold starts
Targeting functions with especially expensive initialization (e.g., heavy dependency loading) to maximize per-cold-start cost
scopeExcludes: Concurrency-limit exhaustion where the mechanism is raw invocation volume rather than defeating warm-instance reuse (ITID-41821)
Billing-cost-focused abuse (ITID-41822)
ITID-41823.severity: Medium-High if the function underlies a latency-sensitive critical path; Medium otherwise.
ITID-41823.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if degraded cold-start latency is materially affecting a customer-facing critical path.
ITID-41823.escalation: Escalate to the platform/serverless engineering team to apply provisioned concurrency or warm-pool strategies for the affected function.
indicators: Elevated cold-start rate and initialization latency metrics correlated with a specific invocation pattern
Burst invocation patterns following idle periods consistent with deliberate scale-to-zero exploitation
Response latency spikes disproportionate to overall invocation volume
vectors: Deliberately varied request parameters designed to prevent instance/container reuse
Timed bursts following induced idle periods to force mass cold starts on a scale-to-zero function
Targeting known heavy-initialization functions specifically for their high per-cold-start cost
rootCauses: Scale-to-zero configuration with no provisioned/warm concurrency for latency-sensitive functions
Function initialization logic with unnecessarily heavy startup cost
No monitoring/alerting specifically on cold-start rate and latency
mitreTechniques: T1499.003 Endpoint Denial of Service: Application Exhaustion Flood
controls: Provisioned/warm concurrency for latency-sensitive functions
Cold-start rate and latency monitoring with dedicated alerting
Optimized function initialization to reduce per-cold-start cost
ITID-41823.detection: Moderate-to-strong technical signal from cold-start-rate and initialization-latency telemetry where the platform exposes it.
ITID-41823.response: Apply provisioned concurrency to stabilize latency, identify and rate-limit the pattern defeating instance reuse, and review function initialization cost.
metrics: Cold-start rate during incidents
Initialization latency trend during incidents
Time to stabilize via provisioned concurrency
ITID-41823.notes: Differentiator within Serverless Function Abuse: this leaf specifically targets the cold-start mechanism, distinct from raw concurrency exhaustion (ITID-41821) or billing-cost abuse (ITID-41822).

playbook.name: Serverless Cold-Start Exhaustion Attack
playbook.description: An attacker is deliberately triggering large numbers of unique, rarely-used function code paths or configurations to force repeated cold starts, degrading latency and exhausting initialization resources.

steps.title: Confirm abnormal cold-start rate via serverless platform metrics
steps.desc: Review serverless platform monitoring for an abnormal spike in cold-start rate/init duration correlated with elevated request latency, and inspect invocation patterns for signs of deliberate cold-start forcing (e.g., unique query parameters routing to distinct execution contexts, container-recycling triggers).
steps.guidance: Cold-start exhaustion attacks are subtler than volumetric floods — focus on init-duration and cold-start-percentage metrics rather than raw request count.
steps.outcome: Cold-start exhaustion pattern confirmed with representative request samples documented.
steps.abort: If cold-start rate rise correlates with a legitimate deployment/version change, treat as operational, not an attack.

steps.title: Enable provisioned concurrency for affected functions
steps.desc: Configure provisioned concurrency (pre-warmed execution environments) for the targeted function(s) to reduce cold-start exposure while the attack pattern is addressed.
steps.outcome: Cold-start rate and associated latency reduced despite continued abusive request pattern.

steps.title: Verify sustained normalization of cold-start rate and latency
steps.desc: Confirm cold-start rate and latency metrics return to and remain at normal levels.
steps.outcome: Metrics confirmed normalized over a sustained monitoring window.

steps.title: Reassess provisioned concurrency sizing and confirm normal application performance
steps.desc: Right-size provisioned concurrency for ongoing steady-state operation and confirm dependent applications perform normally.
steps.outcome: Application performance confirmed restored with appropriately sized standing concurrency.

steps.title: Document incident and evaluate standing cold-start mitigation posture
steps.desc: Capture the timeline and recommend permanent provisioned-concurrency policy and request-normalization controls to prevent recurrence.
steps.outcome: Report finalized with follow-up actions tracked.

steps.title: Assess latency/user-experience impact
steps.desc: Determine the degree of latency degradation experienced by legitimate users due to the elevated cold-start rate.
steps.outcome: Impact documented to prioritize response urgency.

steps.title: Filter or normalize the request pattern forcing new execution contexts
steps.desc: Apply request normalization, caching, or WAF rules at the gateway to reduce the variability being exploited to force fresh cold starts.
steps.outcome: Malicious request pattern's effectiveness at forcing cold starts substantially reduced.

ITID-41824.def: A serverless-function-abuse incident confirmed as having a denial-of-service or resource-depletion character, but not yet classified into a specific mechanism (concurrency exhaustion, denial-of-wallet billing abuse, cold-start exploitation) pending further investigation.
ITID-41824.purpose: Serves as the intake bucket for serverless function abuse (in a DoS context) that does not yet fit concurrency-exhaustion, billing-abuse, or cold-start-exploitation classifications.
scopeIncludes: Newly observed serverless-abuse techniques not yet mapped to an existing sibling leaf
Ambiguous serverless-function incidents pending root-cause confirmation
scopeExcludes: Any incident later confirmed as concurrency exhaustion (ITID-41821), billing/denial-of-wallet abuse (ITID-41822), or cold-start exploitation (ITID-41823) — reclassify once confirmed
ITID-41824.severity: Medium by default pending classification; adjust once the specific mechanism and business impact are confirmed.
ITID-41824.priority: P3 pending triage, escalating per standard severity guidance once root cause is identified.
ITID-41824.escalation: Escalate to the SOC classification lead for prompt re-tagging into a specific sibling leaf once the mechanism is understood.
indicators: Elevated serverless resource/billing anomaly with an unconfirmed cause
Analyst uncertainty about which serverless-abuse mechanism applies
vectors: Unclassified/novel serverless-abuse technique pending investigation
rootCauses: Root cause not yet determined
mitreTechniques: T1499.003 Endpoint Denial of Service: Application Exhaustion Flood
controls: Standard serverless monitoring and alerting pending classification
ITID-41824.detection: Coverage depends on the eventual root cause; this bucket itself is detected via generic serverless usage-anomaly alerting.
ITID-41824.response: Investigate to determine the specific mechanism and reclassify to the appropriate sibling ITID as soon as possible; apply standard containment in the interim.
metrics: Number of incidents parked in this bucket beyond the triage SLA
Average time to reclassify into a specific sibling leaf
ITID-41824.notes: Catch-all intake leaf; used only during initial triage. Analysts should reclassify into ITID-41821/41822/41823 as soon as the mechanism is confirmed.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Serverless Function Abuse (DoS Context)
playbook.description: Abuse of the organization's serverless/FaaS infrastructure is causing denial-of-service impact (availability degradation or resource exhaustion), not otherwise classified into a more specific sub-type.

steps.title: Confirm serverless-layer abuse via platform monitoring
steps.desc: Review serverless platform monitoring (invocation rate, concurrency, error/throttle rate, cost) to confirm abuse is occurring at the function layer and characterize its nature.
steps.outcome: Abuse pattern confirmed with contributing metrics documented.

steps.title: Apply concurrency limits and rate limiting to affected functions
steps.desc: Configure reserved/provisioned concurrency and rate limiting on the affected functions and their triggering endpoints to contain the abuse.
steps.outcome: Abuse impact reduced or eliminated.

steps.title: Verify sustained normalization of function-layer metrics
steps.desc: Confirm invocation, concurrency, and cost metrics return to normal levels and remain stable.
steps.outcome: Metrics confirmed normalized.

steps.title: Confirm dependent application performance restoration
steps.desc: Verify dependent applications/services are functioning normally.
steps.outcome: Application performance confirmed restored.

steps.title: Document incident and review serverless abuse-prevention guardrails
steps.desc: Capture the timeline and recommend concurrency, rate-limiting, and cost-anomaly guardrail improvements.
steps.outcome: Report finalized with follow-up actions tracked.

steps.title: Identify affected functions and business impact
steps.desc: Determine which functions/applications are affected and the severity of impact on availability or cost.
steps.outcome: Impact documented to prioritize response.

steps.title: Set or verify billing alerts if cost impact is present
steps.desc: Verify billing alerts/spend caps are active on the affected account if the abuse carries a cost dimension.
steps.outcome: Cost exposure bounded where applicable.
steps.abort: If no cost dimension is present, this step is not applicable.

ITID-41831.def: A resource-depletion attack in which an adversary exploits a publicly writable or abusable object-storage upload path to deposit a high volume of objects or a large total data volume into a bucket, exhausting the account's storage quota, driving up storage costs, or degrading bucket listing/access performance for legitimate operations.
ITID-41831.purpose: Captures denial of service caused by an adversary deliberately filling an object storage bucket (e.g., S3-style) with a high volume of objects or data to exhaust a storage quota or degrade bucket-level performance.
scopeIncludes: Exploiting a publicly writable object-storage upload endpoint (e.g., a misconfigured pre-signed URL policy or open bucket policy) to mass-upload objects
Automated abuse of a legitimate user-upload feature to exceed intended storage bounds
High object-count uploads specifically degrading bucket listing/enumeration performance
scopeExcludes: Storage abuse whose primary measured impact is egress-bandwidth billing cost (ITID-41832)
Cloud database storage quota exhaustion, a distinct storage layer (ITID-41833)
ITID-41831.severity: Medium-High if the bucket underlies a critical service or shares a quota with other critical workloads; Medium if isolated.
ITID-41831.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if the bucket approaches a hard quota limit that would block legitimate write operations.
ITID-41831.escalation: Escalate to the cloud/platform team to lock down the abused upload path and enforce per-source upload limits.
indicators: Rapid growth in bucket object count or total storage consumption with no corresponding legitimate business activity
Uploads traceable to a narrow set of anomalous source IPs/accounts/pre-signed URLs
Storage-quota utilization alerts approaching threshold
vectors: Abuse of an overly permissive bucket policy or misconfigured pre-signed URL allowing unauthenticated uploads
Automated scripts exploiting a legitimate upload feature with no per-account volume limit
Bulk account creation to multiply per-account upload quota abuse
rootCauses: Bucket policy or pre-signed URL configuration too permissive for the intended use case
No enforced per-account or per-source upload-volume limit
No storage-quota alerting with sufficient headroom to react before exhaustion
mitreTechniques: T1499.003 Endpoint Denial of Service: Application Exhaustion Flood
controls: Tightened bucket policies/pre-signed URL scoping to prevent unauthorized uploads
Per-account/per-source upload-rate and volume limits
Storage-quota threshold alerting with sufficient response headroom
ITID-41831.detection: Strong technical signal from bucket-level object-count and storage-consumption telemetry correlated with upload-source logs.
ITID-41831.response: Lock down the abused upload path, purge unauthorized objects, and enforce per-source upload limits going forward.
metrics: Storage/object-count growth during the incident
Time to lock down the abused upload path
Cost impact of unauthorized storage consumption
ITID-41831.notes: Differentiator within Storage Exhaustion in Cloud Services: this leaf is bucket-fill via upload abuse, distinct from egress-billing abuse (ITID-41832) or database-storage-quota exhaustion (ITID-41833).

playbook.name: Object Storage (S3-Style) Bucket Fill Attack
playbook.description: An attacker (or misconfigured process) is deliberately filling the organization's object storage bucket(s) with large volumes of data to exhaust storage quotas or degrade dependent application performance.

steps.title: Confirm abnormal bucket fill rate via storage utilization monitoring
steps.desc: Review cloud storage utilization/billing dashboards to confirm an abnormal, rapid increase in object count/storage volume in the affected bucket(s), distinguishing it from legitimate data ingestion.
steps.guidance: Check upload source (public write access, exposed pre-signed URLs, compromised credentials) and object naming/content patterns for signs of automated abuse.
steps.outcome: Bucket fill attack confirmed with fill rate, source, and object characteristics documented.
steps.abort: If the fill rate correlates with a legitimate batch data load, treat as operational, not an attack.
steps.tool: Cloud storage console, billing anomaly detection

steps.title: Restrict or revoke the exploited write access immediately
steps.desc: Tighten the bucket policy to remove public/unauthenticated write access, revoke or rotate compromised credentials, or invalidate abused pre-signed URLs.
steps.outcome: Further unauthorized writes halted.
steps.tool: Cloud IAM console, bucket policy configuration

steps.title: Remove the abusive objects and reclaim storage capacity
steps.desc: Identify and delete the malicious/abusive objects (after evidence preservation of samples if intent appears malicious) to reclaim storage capacity for legitimate use.
steps.guidance: Preserve object metadata and a sample of content before bulk deletion if the fill appears deliberately malicious, to support any follow-up investigation.
steps.outcome: Storage capacity reclaimed to levels sufficient for legitimate workloads.

steps.title: Verify dependent application functionality and storage headroom
steps.desc: Confirm applications dependent on the affected bucket function normally and storage utilization/headroom is at healthy levels.
steps.outcome: Application functionality and storage headroom confirmed restored.

steps.title: Document incident and implement standing bucket-access guardrails
steps.desc: Capture the timeline and recommend permanent bucket policy hardening, quota enforcement, and anomaly alerting to prevent recurrence.
steps.outcome: Report finalized with guardrail follow-up actions assigned.

steps.title: Identify the write access path being exploited
steps.desc: Determine whether the bucket allows public/unauthenticated writes, has an overly permissive bucket policy, or is being abused via leaked/compromised credentials or pre-signed URLs.
steps.outcome: Exploited write access path identified.

steps.title: Set or verify hard storage quota and billing alerts
steps.desc: Configure or verify storage quota limits and billing alerts on the affected bucket/account to bound further exposure while cleanup proceeds.
steps.outcome: Storage quota and billing exposure bounded.

ITID-41832.def: A resource-depletion attack in which an adversary generates sustained, high-volume download/read traffic against objects in cloud storage specifically to inflate the organization's usage-based egress-bandwidth billing, with financial cost as the primary impact.
ITID-41832.purpose: Captures denial-of-wallet incidents in which an adversary deliberately drives excessive egress bandwidth from cloud storage to inflate billing costs, distinct from bucket-fill attacks that target storage capacity itself.
scopeIncludes: Automated repeated downloads of large objects from a publicly accessible bucket/container to maximize billed egress
Hotlinking of large stored objects embedded on third-party sites driving unexpected egress traffic
Distributed download requests designed to evade simple per-IP rate limiting on storage access
scopeExcludes: Attacks whose primary measured impact is storage-capacity/quota exhaustion via uploads (ITID-41831)
Cloud database storage quota exhaustion (ITID-41833)
ITID-41832.severity: Medium; driven by financial impact rather than availability, though sustained abuse can still degrade access for legitimate users if bandwidth throttling engages.
ITID-41832.priority: P2, escalating if billing-anomaly detection shows cost trending to breach a defined budget-alert threshold within the billing cycle.
ITID-41832.escalation: Escalate to finance/platform stakeholders once projected cost impact is quantified; apply download-rate limiting or access restrictions on the abused objects.
