indicators: Cloud storage egress-bandwidth billing metrics trending sharply above historical baseline
Download volume for specific objects far exceeding normal demand
A small number of source IPs/accounts responsible for a disproportionate share of egress traffic
vectors: Automated scripts repeatedly downloading large publicly accessible stored objects
Hotlinking of large media/files stored in cloud storage on high-traffic third-party sites
Distributed download requests designed to evade simple per-IP rate limiting
rootCauses: No per-object or per-account download-rate limiting
Large objects served without hotlink protection or signed-URL controls
No billing-anomaly alerting tied to storage egress usage
controls: Download-rate limiting and hotlink protection on high-cost stored objects
Signed URLs/tokenized access for expensive-to-serve content
Billing-anomaly alerting with defined budget thresholds for storage egress
ITID-41832.detection: Strong technical signal from cloud storage billing/egress telemetry correlated with per-object and per-source download volume.
ITID-41832.response: Apply download-rate limiting or hotlink protection to the targeted object(s), engage the provider on abuse mitigation, and reconcile billing impact with finance.
metrics: Projected/actual egress cost impact per incident
Download volume anomaly magnitude
Time to apply rate limiting/hotlink protection
ITID-41832.notes: Differentiator within Storage Exhaustion in Cloud Services: this leaf is a denial-of-wallet/egress-billing abuse, distinct from storage-capacity bucket-fill (ITID-41831) or database-storage-quota exhaustion (ITID-41833).

playbook.name: Cloud Storage Billing/Cost Exhaustion via Egress Bandwidth Abuse
playbook.description: An attacker is deliberately driving high-volume downloads/reads from the organization's cloud storage to inflate egress bandwidth billing costs (denial-of-wallet) rather than directly denying availability.

steps.title: Detect abnormal egress bandwidth/billing trajectory
steps.desc: Correlate cloud billing anomaly alerts with storage access logs to confirm a deliberate cost-driving attack via excessive egress/download volume versus organic usage growth.
steps.guidance: Look for sustained high-volume downloads of large objects from a broad or suspicious source set, with a spend-rate spike well above historical norms.
steps.outcome: Attack confirmed as denial-of-wallet via egress bandwidth abuse, with cost trajectory and access evidence documented.
steps.abort: If egress growth correlates with a legitimate content distribution event, treat as capacity planning, not an incident.
steps.tool: Cloud billing anomaly detection, storage access logs

steps.title: Set or verify hard billing alerts and spend caps
steps.desc: Immediately verify or configure hard spend caps/budget alerts on the affected cloud account to bound further financial exposure while investigation continues.
steps.outcome: Spend caps and alerts confirmed active.

steps.title: Block or challenge confirmed abusive sources
steps.desc: Apply sustained blocking or bot-management challenges against confirmed abusive sources to eliminate remaining cost-driving traffic.
steps.outcome: Abusive traffic eliminated; egress volume and spend return to baseline.

steps.title: Reconcile incurred costs and confirm normal access patterns restored
steps.desc: Reconcile incurred egress bandwidth costs for the incident window with finance and confirm legitimate access to protected objects remains unaffected.
steps.outcome: Cost impact quantified and reported; legitimate access confirmed unaffected.

steps.title: Document incident and implement standing cost-anomaly guardrails
steps.desc: Capture the timeline, financial impact, and recommend permanent access controls, signed-URL policy, and cost-anomaly alerting for high-value storage.
steps.outcome: Report finalized with prioritized guardrail follow-ups assigned.

steps.title: Identify the specific objects and sources driving egress cost
steps.desc: Pinpoint which objects/buckets and source IP ranges or credentials are responsible for the disproportionate egress volume.
steps.outcome: Specific abusive objects and sources identified.

steps.title: Restrict public/unauthenticated read access and rate-limit downloads
steps.desc: Tighten bucket/object access policy to require authentication or signed URLs, and apply download rate limiting or a CDN in front of the storage to absorb/control egress traffic.
steps.outcome: Egress volume from abusive sources drops sharply.

ITID-41833.def: A resource-depletion attack in which an adversary exploits a data-write path (e.g., an abusable API creating database records, an unauthenticated write endpoint, or excessive legitimate-looking record creation) to grow a managed cloud database's storage consumption to its provisioned or account-level quota limit, causing write failures or forced (and potentially costly/disruptive) auto-scaling of storage capacity.
ITID-41833.purpose: Captures denial of service caused by an adversary exhausting a managed cloud database's storage quota, distinct from object-storage bucket fill or egress-billing abuse.
scopeIncludes: Exploiting an application write path to mass-create database records with no volume limit
Abuse of bulk-import or data-ingestion API endpoints to exhaust provisioned database storage
Exhausting storage on managed database services (e.g., managed relational or NoSQL offerings) specifically, as distinct from object storage
scopeExcludes: Object-storage bucket-fill attacks (ITID-41831)
Egress-bandwidth billing abuse (ITID-41832)
Database query-flooding attacks targeting compute/connection capacity rather than storage volume (Tier-4 Database Query Flooding group)
ITID-41833.severity: High if the database underlies a critical service and lacks storage headroom or auto-scaling limits; Medium if storage auto-scales with cost controls in place.
ITID-41833.priority: P1 if write failures are occurring on a critical service due to quota exhaustion; P2 if auto-scaling is absorbing impact but at rising cost.
ITID-41833.escalation: Escalate to the database/platform team to cap further growth, identify and purge abusive records, and enforce write-rate limits on the exploited path.
indicators: Database storage-consumption metrics trending sharply upward with no corresponding legitimate data-growth driver
Record creation traceable to a narrow set of anomalous source IPs/accounts/API keys
Storage-quota utilization alerts approaching threshold, or write failures once the quota is hit
vectors: Automated scripts exploiting an application API to mass-create database records
Abuse of a bulk-import/data-ingestion endpoint with no volume validation
Exploiting an unauthenticated or lightly-protected write endpoint
rootCauses: No per-account or per-source write-volume/rate limiting on record-creation paths
No storage-quota alerting with sufficient headroom to react before exhaustion
Auto-scaling storage configured without cost or growth-rate guardrails
mitreTechniques: T1499.003 Endpoint Denial of Service: Application Exhaustion Flood
controls: Per-account/per-source write-rate and volume limits on record-creation paths
Storage-quota threshold alerting with sufficient response headroom
Auto-scaling storage guardrails with growth-rate anomaly alerting
ITID-41833.detection: Strong technical signal from database storage-consumption telemetry correlated with write-volume logs by source.
ITID-41833.response: Halt further abusive writes (rate-limit or block the source), purge unauthorized records where safe to do so, and enforce write-volume limits going forward.
metrics: Storage growth rate during the incident
Time to halt abusive write activity
Cost impact of forced auto-scaling
ITID-41833.notes: Differentiator within Storage Exhaustion in Cloud Services: this leaf is managed-database storage-quota exhaustion via write abuse, distinct from object-storage bucket fill (ITID-41831) and egress-billing abuse (ITID-41832).

playbook.name: Cloud Database Storage Quota Exhaustion Attack
playbook.description: An attacker is deliberately inserting large volumes of data into the organization's cloud-hosted database(s) to exhaust storage quota, causing write failures or performance degradation for legitimate operations.

steps.title: Confirm abnormal database storage growth via utilization monitoring
steps.desc: Review cloud database storage utilization and growth-rate metrics to confirm an abnormal, rapid increase in storage consumption, distinguishing it from legitimate data growth.
steps.guidance: Check for abnormal insert/write volume concentrated in specific tables/collections and correlate with the source (API endpoint, user account, or exposed write path) responsible.
steps.outcome: Storage exhaustion attack confirmed with growth rate and source documented.
steps.abort: If growth correlates with a legitimate data migration or feature rollout, treat as capacity planning, not an incident.

steps.title: Restrict or rate-limit the exploited write path
steps.desc: Apply rate limiting, input-size validation, or authentication requirements on the exploited endpoint/write path to stop further abusive inserts.
steps.outcome: Further abusive data insertion halted.

steps.title: Remove the abusive data and reclaim storage capacity
steps.desc: Identify and remove the malicious/abusive records (after evidence preservation of samples if intent appears malicious) to reclaim storage capacity for legitimate use.
steps.outcome: Storage capacity reclaimed to levels sufficient for legitimate operations.

steps.title: Verify database performance and dependent application functionality
steps.desc: Confirm database write/read performance and dependent applications function normally with healthy storage headroom.
steps.outcome: Database performance and application functionality confirmed restored.

steps.title: Document incident and implement standing write-path guardrails
steps.desc: Capture the timeline and recommend permanent input validation, rate limiting, and storage-quota anomaly alerting to prevent recurrence.
steps.outcome: Report finalized with guardrail follow-up actions assigned.

steps.title: Identify the exploited write path and responsible source
steps.desc: Determine which API endpoint, application feature, or credential is being used to insert the excessive data.
steps.outcome: Exploited write path and source identified.

steps.title: Set or verify hard storage quota and billing alerts
steps.desc: Configure or verify storage quota limits and billing alerts on the affected database instance/account to bound further exposure while cleanup proceeds.
steps.outcome: Storage quota and billing exposure bounded.

ITID-41834.def: A cloud-storage-resource-exhaustion incident confirmed as an attack against cloud storage capacity or cost, but not yet classified into a specific mechanism (object-storage bucket fill, egress-bandwidth billing abuse, managed database storage-quota exhaustion) pending further investigation.
ITID-41834.purpose: Serves as the intake bucket for cloud storage exhaustion attacks that do not yet fit bucket-fill, egress-billing, or database-quota classifications.
scopeIncludes: Newly observed cloud-storage-exhaustion techniques not yet mapped to an existing sibling leaf
Ambiguous cloud-storage-related incidents pending root-cause confirmation
scopeExcludes: Any incident later confirmed as bucket-fill (ITID-41831), egress-billing abuse (ITID-41832), or database storage-quota exhaustion (ITID-41833) — reclassify once confirmed
ITID-41834.severity: Medium by default pending classification; adjust once the specific mechanism and business impact are confirmed.
ITID-41834.priority: P3 pending triage, escalating per standard severity guidance once root cause is identified.
ITID-41834.escalation: Escalate to the SOC classification lead for prompt re-tagging into a specific sibling leaf once the mechanism is understood.
indicators: Elevated cloud storage consumption/cost with an unconfirmed cause
Analyst uncertainty about which cloud-storage-exhaustion mechanism applies
vectors: Unclassified/novel cloud-storage-exhaustion technique pending investigation
rootCauses: Root cause not yet determined
mitreTechniques: T1499.003 Endpoint Denial of Service: Application Exhaustion Flood
controls: Standard cloud storage monitoring and alerting pending classification
ITID-41834.detection: Coverage depends on the eventual root cause; this bucket itself is detected via generic storage-usage anomaly alerting.
ITID-41834.response: Investigate to determine the specific mechanism and reclassify to the appropriate sibling ITID as soon as possible; apply standard containment in the interim.
metrics: Number of incidents parked in this bucket beyond the triage SLA
Average time to reclassify into a specific sibling leaf
ITID-41834.notes: Catch-all intake leaf; used only during initial triage. Analysts should reclassify into ITID-41831/41832/41833 as soon as the mechanism is confirmed.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Cloud Storage Exhaustion Attack
playbook.description: An attack is exhausting the organization's cloud storage capacity or associated cost/quota limits, not otherwise classified into a more specific sub-type.

steps.title: Confirm abnormal storage consumption via utilization monitoring
steps.desc: Review cloud storage utilization and billing dashboards to confirm abnormal storage consumption or cost trajectory and characterize the pattern.
steps.outcome: Exhaustion pattern confirmed with contributing metrics documented.
steps.abort: If growth correlates with legitimate activity, treat as capacity planning, not an incident.

steps.title: Restrict the exploited access path and set quota/billing alerts
steps.desc: Tighten access controls on the exploited path and configure or verify storage quota and billing alerts to bound further exposure.
steps.outcome: Further abuse halted; exposure bounded.

steps.title: Reclaim consumed capacity and remove abusive data
steps.desc: Identify and remove the abusive data/objects to reclaim capacity for legitimate use.
steps.outcome: Storage capacity reclaimed.

steps.title: Verify dependent application functionality and storage headroom
steps.desc: Confirm dependent applications function normally with healthy storage headroom restored.
steps.outcome: Application functionality and headroom confirmed restored.

steps.title: Document incident and review storage-abuse guardrails
steps.desc: Capture the timeline and recommend access control, quota, and anomaly-alerting improvements to prevent recurrence.
steps.outcome: Report finalized with follow-up actions tracked.

steps.title: Identify the source and exploited access path
steps.desc: Determine which account, credential, or access path is responsible for the abnormal consumption.
steps.outcome: Responsible source/access path identified.

steps.title: Rate-limit or block confirmed abusive sources
steps.desc: Apply rate limiting or blocking against confirmed abusive sources to further contain the exhaustion.
steps.outcome: Abusive traffic contained.

ITID-41911.def: An intentional denial-of-service incident in which an employee, contractor, or other trusted insider with legitimate administrative access deliberately deletes, disables, or corrupts the configuration of a critical service (e.g., removing a load balancer rule, disabling a service, deleting a DNS record) with the intent to cause disruption.
ITID-41911.purpose: Captures denial of service caused by an insider with legitimate access deliberately deleting or disabling the configuration of a critical service to cause an outage.
scopeIncludes: Deliberate deletion/modification of critical infrastructure-as-code, DNS, load-balancer, or service configuration by an insider with legitimate access
Insider action confirmed as intentional (distinguished from an honest operational mistake) via investigation, motive, or admission
Sabotage carried out through legitimate administrative credentials rather than exploiting a technical vulnerability
scopeExcludes: Accidental configuration changes causing an outage with no malicious intent (ITID-41922)
Insider deploying a resource-exhaustion script rather than directly deleting/disabling configuration (ITID-41912)
Departing-employee sabotage specifically timed around an exit event (ITID-41913, a related but temporally distinct pattern warranting separate tracking)
ITID-41911.severity: High-Critical given deliberate sabotage by a trusted insider often targets the highest-impact configuration and can be difficult to distinguish from legitimate change activity until after the fact.
ITID-41911.priority: P1, treated as a confirmed malicious insider incident requiring both technical restoration and HR/legal involvement.
ITID-41911.escalation: Escalate immediately to incident response, HR, and legal/security leadership given the incident involves a trusted insider and may have employment and legal consequences.
indicators: Configuration change/deletion attributable to a specific insider account with no corresponding approved change ticket
Timing or pattern of the change inconsistent with normal operational activity (e.g., after-hours, outside the individual's normal scope)
Change-management/audit logs showing the deletion bypassed standard review process
vectors: Direct deletion of critical configuration via legitimate administrative console/CLI access
Use of legitimate credentials to modify infrastructure-as-code and push a destructive change
Disabling monitoring/alerting immediately before making the destructive change to delay detection
rootCauses: Excessive standing administrative privilege without change-approval gating for critical configuration
No mandatory peer review/approval workflow for high-impact configuration changes
Insufficient monitoring of privileged-account activity against critical infrastructure
controls: Mandatory peer review/approval workflow (four-eyes principle) for changes to critical configuration
Privileged-access monitoring and alerting on critical infrastructure changes
Immutable/versioned configuration with rapid rollback capability
ITID-41911.detection: Strong technical signal from change-management and privileged-access audit logs once correlated with the outage timeline.
ITID-41911.response: Restore the deleted/disabled configuration from a known-good version, suspend the insider's access pending investigation, and engage HR/legal per the organization's insider-threat process.
metrics: Time to identify the responsible account and restore configuration
Mean time to detect unauthorized privileged configuration changes
ITID-41911.notes: Differentiator within Malicious Employee DoS: direct deletion/disabling of configuration, distinct from a deployed resource-exhaustion script (ITID-41912) or exit-timed sabotage (ITID-41913). Because this leaf involves a genuine adversarial actor (an insider acting maliciously), it retains a MITRE mapping — unlike the accidental-configuration sibling group (ITID-4192x).

playbook.name: Deliberate Deletion/Disabling of Critical Service Configuration
playbook.description: A malicious insider has deliberately deleted or disabled critical service configuration (e.g., DNS records, firewall rules, load balancer config) causing a denial of service.

steps.title: Confirm the configuration change and correlate with user activity
steps.desc: Review configuration/change-management logs and cloud/system audit trails to identify the specific deletion/disabling action, its timestamp, and the authenticated identity that performed it.
steps.guidance: Correlate the change timestamp precisely with the onset of the service outage to establish causation, not just correlation.
steps.outcome: Deliberate configuration change identified with responsible identity, timestamp, and exact change documented.
steps.abort: If the change appears to be an approved, accidental, or automated action rather than deliberate insider action, redirect to the Accidental Configuration DoS playbook.
steps.tool: Change management system, cloud/system audit logs

steps.title: Preserve evidence before taking any account action
steps.desc: Capture forensic evidence (audit logs, session records, configuration change history, relevant communications) before disabling or modifying the suspected insider's account access, in coordination with HR/Legal.
steps.guidance: Acting on the account before evidence is preserved risks losing critical audit trail data and undermining any subsequent HR/legal action.
steps.outcome: Evidence preserved with documented chain of custody.

steps.title: Restore the deleted/disabled configuration from backup or known-good state
steps.desc: Restore the affected configuration (DNS, firewall, load balancer, etc.) from a verified backup or documented known-good baseline.
steps.outcome: Configuration restored and validated against the known-good baseline.

steps.title: Verify service restoration and audit for any additional tampering
steps.desc: Confirm the affected service is fully operational and audit related configuration items for any additional unauthorized changes by the same identity.
steps.outcome: Service confirmed restored; no additional unauthorized changes found, or further remediation performed if found.

steps.title: Document incident, HR/Legal outcome, and review change-control and privileged-access safeguards
steps.desc: Capture the full timeline, HR/Legal case outcome, and recommend change-approval workflow, privileged-access segregation, or configuration-change alerting improvements to reduce future insider sabotage risk.
steps.outcome: Report finalized with follow-up actions tracked.

steps.title: Assess indicators of malicious intent
steps.desc: Review the identified user's recent activity, access patterns, and HR context (e.g., recent disciplinary action, resignation) for indicators suggesting deliberate sabotage versus error.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with HR/Legal at this stage before drawing conclusions, since intent determination affects subsequent account-action steps.
steps.outcome: Initial intent assessment documented and shared with HR/Legal.

steps.title: Suspend the suspected insider's access in coordination with HR and Legal
steps.desc: Once evidence is preserved, coordinate with HR and Legal to suspend the individual's access to prevent further damage, following the organization's insider-threat response procedure.
steps.guidance: Do not unilaterally act without HR/Legal coordination given the employment-law and evidentiary implications.
steps.outcome: Access suspended through a formally coordinated process with HR/Legal sign-off.

ITID-41912.def: An intentional denial-of-service incident in which an insider with legitimate access deliberately develops and executes a script, job, or automation specifically engineered to consume excessive CPU, memory, disk, or database resources on internal systems, with the intent to degrade or crash a service.
ITID-41912.purpose: Captures denial of service caused by an insider deliberately writing and executing a script or automation designed to consume system resources and degrade or crash a service.
scopeIncludes: A deliberately authored fork bomb, infinite loop, or resource-exhaustion script executed by an insider on internal infrastructure
Scheduling a malicious job/cron task designed to recur and repeatedly degrade a system
Deliberate misuse of legitimate automation tooling (e.g., a CI/CD pipeline) to run resource-exhaustion workloads
scopeExcludes: Direct deletion/disabling of service configuration (ITID-41911)
An accidental runaway script/loop with no malicious intent (ITID-41931, tracked under API Abuse from Internal Users as a non-malicious pattern)
ITID-41912.severity: High given deliberate technical intent to cause resource exhaustion by someone with insider access and knowledge of the environment.
ITID-41912.priority: P1, treated as a confirmed malicious insider incident requiring both technical containment and HR/legal involvement.
ITID-41912.escalation: Escalate immediately to incident response, HR, and legal/security leadership given the incident involves a trusted insider and confirmed malicious intent.
indicators: Resource-exhaustion pattern traced to a specific script/job attributable to a known insider account
Script content or execution context showing deliberate design to consume resources with no legitimate business purpose
Insider's access/authorship of the script confirmed via code-repository or execution logs
vectors: Direct execution of a resource-exhaustion script on internal servers via legitimate shell access
Malicious job scheduled via legitimate automation/orchestration tooling
Abuse of legitimate CI/CD pipeline execution to run a disguised resource-exhaustion payload
rootCauses: Excessive standing access allowing arbitrary script execution on production/internal systems
No resource-usage anomaly detection tied to individual user/service accounts
Insufficient code-review/approval gating for scheduled jobs and automation changes
controls: Resource-usage anomaly detection attributable to specific user/service accounts
Mandatory review/approval for new scheduled jobs and automation changes
Least-privilege access limiting arbitrary script execution on production systems
ITID-41912.detection: Strong technical signal from resource-usage telemetry correlated with execution/audit logs attributing the activity to a specific account.
ITID-41912.response: Terminate the offending process/job, suspend the insider's access pending investigation, and engage HR/legal per the organization's insider-threat process.
metrics: Time to identify and terminate the offending script/job
Mean time to detect anomalous resource consumption attributable to an insider account
ITID-41912.notes: Differentiator within Malicious Employee DoS: deliberate resource-exhaustion scripting, distinct from direct configuration deletion (ITID-41911) or exit-timed sabotage (ITID-41913).

playbook.name: Insider Deploying Deliberate Resource-Exhaustion Script
playbook.description: A malicious insider has deployed a script or automated process specifically designed to exhaust system, network, or cloud resources and deny service.

steps.title: Identify the resource-exhaustion script and its deployment source
steps.desc: Analyze system/process telemetry and deployment/execution logs to identify the specific script or process responsible for the resource exhaustion and trace it to its deploying identity.
steps.guidance: Look for scripts deployed outside normal change-management/CI-CD processes, or authorized deployments repurposed for exhaustion behavior.
steps.outcome: Malicious script and responsible identity identified with deployment evidence documented.
steps.abort: If the script was deployed as part of an approved process and the exhaustion is unintentional, redirect to the Accidental Configuration DoS playbook.

steps.title: Preserve evidence before taking any account or system action
steps.desc: Capture forensic evidence (the script itself, execution logs, deployment records, relevant communications) before terminating the process or disabling the suspected insider's access.
steps.outcome: Evidence preserved with documented chain of custody.

steps.title: Remove the script and any persistence mechanisms; verify resource levels normalize
steps.desc: Fully remove the malicious script and any scheduled tasks, cron jobs, or automation configured to redeploy it, then confirm system/network resource utilization returns to baseline.
steps.outcome: Script and persistence mechanisms fully removed; resource utilization confirmed normalized.

steps.title: Verify service restoration and audit for additional unauthorized deployments
steps.desc: Confirm affected services are fully operational and audit deployment history for any other unauthorized changes by the same identity.
steps.outcome: Service confirmed restored; no additional unauthorized deployments found, or further remediation performed if found.

steps.title: Document incident, HR/Legal outcome, and review deployment-control safeguards
steps.desc: Capture the full timeline, HR/Legal case outcome, and recommend deployment-pipeline access controls and anomaly-detection improvements.
steps.outcome: Report finalized with follow-up actions tracked.

steps.title: Assess indicators of malicious intent
steps.desc: Review the identified user's recent activity and HR context for indicators suggesting deliberate sabotage.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with HR/Legal at this stage before drawing conclusions.
steps.outcome: Initial intent assessment documented and shared with HR/Legal.

steps.title: Terminate the exhaustion process and suspend access in coordination with HR/Legal
steps.desc: Terminate the running resource-exhaustion process/script and, in coordination with HR and Legal, suspend the identified individual's access.
steps.outcome: Exhaustion process stopped; access suspended through a formally coordinated process with HR/Legal sign-off.

ITID-41913.def: An intentional denial-of-service incident in which an employee, in the period immediately before, during, or shortly after their resignation or termination, deliberately damages, disables, or disrupts systems or services using access retained from their employment, motivated by grievance or retaliation related to their departure.
ITID-41913.purpose: Captures denial of service caused by an employee deliberately sabotaging systems in the window around their departure from the organization, a pattern warranting distinct handling due to its predictable timing and elevated risk window.
scopeIncludes: Sabotage carried out in the window surrounding a known resignation, termination, or role change
Use of access not yet revoked following departure to cause disruption after the employee's last working day
Sabotage explicitly motivated by grievance related to the departure circumstances (e.g., termination, layoff, dispute)
scopeExcludes: Malicious sabotage by an insider with no connection to a departure event (ITID-41911/41912, tracked under the general malicious-employee leaves)
Accidental disruption during offboarding with no malicious intent (an accidental-configuration DoS concern, ITID-4192x)
ITID-41913.severity: High-Critical given the elevated motive and the frequent finding that access was not revoked promptly enough to prevent the sabotage.
ITID-41913.priority: P1, treated as a confirmed malicious insider incident with urgent access-revocation review across all departing/departed personnel.
ITID-41913.escalation: Escalate immediately to incident response, HR, and legal/security leadership; trigger an emergency review of access-revocation status for all recently departed personnel given this incident may indicate a broader offboarding process gap.
indicators: Destructive activity attributed to an account belonging to a recently departed or currently departing employee
Activity occurring after the employee's resignation/termination date but before access revocation completed
Sabotage pattern consistent with knowledge only a departing insider would have (e.g., targeting a system they personally administered)
vectors: Use of retained credentials/access after the employee's last working day due to delayed offboarding
Deliberate destructive action taken during the notice period before departure
Abuse of legitimate access to disable services, delete data, or revoke others' access as a parting act
rootCauses: Offboarding process with a gap between departure and full access revocation
No automated, immediate access revocation triggered by HR termination/resignation events
Standing access to critical systems not reviewed/reduced during an employee's notice period
controls: Automated, immediate access revocation triggered directly by HR termination/resignation events
Heightened access review/monitoring during an employee's notice period
Same-day offboarding checklist covering all systems the departing employee had access to
ITID-41913.detection: Strong technical signal once activity is correlated against HR departure-date records; access-revocation-timing audits are a key detection and prevention tool.
ITID-41913.response: Immediately revoke all remaining access, restore affected systems, and conduct a full review of the offboarding process alongside the HR/legal investigation.
metrics: Time between departure date and full access revocation across all incidents
Number of offboarding-related sabotage incidents per year
ITID-41913.notes: Differentiator within Malicious Employee DoS: distinguished from ITID-41911/41912 by its specific temporal link to a departure event, which drives distinct preventive controls (offboarding speed) rather than general privileged-access controls.

playbook.name: Departing Employee Sabotaging Systems Before Exit
playbook.description: An employee who has resigned or been notified of termination sabotages organizational systems or services before their departure, causing a denial of service.

steps.title: Correlate the service disruption with the departing employee's known access and timeline
steps.desc: Review audit logs and change history for actions by the departing employee's accounts in the period surrounding their resignation/termination notice, correlating with the onset of the disruption.
steps.guidance: Pay particular attention to activity occurring after resignation was announced but before offboarding was completed — a common exposure window.
steps.outcome: Sabotage action identified and attributed to the departing employee's account(s) with supporting evidence.
steps.abort: If no correlation to the departing employee is found, investigate other causes.
steps.tool: IAM/system audit logs, HR offboarding record

steps.title: Preserve evidence before revoking access
steps.desc: Capture forensic evidence of the sabotage action and the employee's account activity before revoking access, in coordination with HR/Legal.
steps.outcome: Evidence preserved with documented chain of custody.

steps.title: Restore or remediate all sabotaged systems/configurations
steps.desc: Restore any deleted/disabled configuration or systems from backup/known-good state and remove any other unauthorized changes identified.
steps.outcome: All sabotaged systems restored and validated against known-good baselines.

steps.title: Verify full service restoration and complete offboarding audit
steps.desc: Confirm all affected services are operational and complete a full offboarding audit to ensure no residual access or persistence mechanisms remain.
steps.outcome: Services confirmed restored; offboarding audit confirms no residual access.

steps.title: Document incident, HR/Legal outcome, and review offboarding procedures
steps.desc: Capture the full timeline, HR/Legal case outcome, and recommend improvements to offboarding timeliness (e.g., immediate access revocation upon resignation notice) and access-review processes.
steps.outcome: Report finalized with follow-up actions on offboarding process improvements tracked.

steps.title: Determine full scope of the departing employee's access and recent activity
steps.desc: Enumerate all systems, accounts, and privileges held by the departing employee and review their full recent activity for any other suspicious actions beyond the confirmed sabotage.
steps.outcome: Full access scope and activity history documented for HR/Legal and IT to act on.

steps.title: Immediately revoke all access for the departing employee across all systems
steps.desc: In coordination with HR and Legal, immediately revoke the departing employee's access across all identified systems to prevent further sabotage.
steps.guidance: Ensure offboarding covers all systems enumerated in the prior step, not just primary directory access, since departing-employee sabotage often exploits secondary/forgotten access.
steps.outcome: All access for the departing employee revoked across every identified system.

ITID-41914.def: A denial-of-service incident confirmed as caused by a malicious insider, but not yet classified into a specific pattern (configuration deletion, resource-exhaustion script, departure-linked sabotage) pending further investigation.
ITID-41914.purpose: Serves as the intake bucket for malicious employee DoS incidents that do not yet fit configuration-deletion, resource-exhaustion-script, or departing-employee classifications.
scopeIncludes: Newly observed malicious-insider DoS patterns not yet mapped to an existing sibling leaf
Ambiguous insider-caused disruption incidents pending confirmation of both malicious intent and specific mechanism
scopeExcludes: Any incident later confirmed as configuration deletion (ITID-41911), resource-exhaustion script (ITID-41912), or departure-linked sabotage (ITID-41913) — reclassify once confirmed
Any incident where intent turns out to be accidental rather than malicious — reclassify under Accidental Configuration DoS (ITID-4192x)
ITID-41914.severity: High by default pending classification given confirmed malicious insider involvement; adjust once the specific mechanism is confirmed.
ITID-41914.priority: P1 pending triage as a confirmed malicious insider incident.
ITID-41914.escalation: Escalate to the SOC classification lead and HR/legal for prompt handling and re-tagging into a specific sibling leaf once the mechanism is understood.
indicators: Disruption confirmed as intentional insider action with an unconfirmed specific mechanism
Analyst uncertainty about which malicious-insider DoS pattern applies
vectors: Unclassified/novel malicious-insider DoS technique pending investigation
rootCauses: Root cause/mechanism not yet determined
controls: Standard insider-threat investigation and containment process pending classification
ITID-41914.detection: Coverage depends on the eventual mechanism; this bucket itself is logged via confirmed-malicious-insider incident intake.
ITID-41914.response: Contain the immediate disruption, suspend the insider's access, engage HR/legal, and reclassify to the appropriate sibling ITID as soon as the mechanism is confirmed.
metrics: Number of incidents parked in this bucket beyond the triage SLA
Average time to reclassify into a specific sibling leaf
ITID-41914.notes: Catch-all intake leaf; used only during initial triage. Analysts should reclassify into ITID-41911/41912/41913 as soon as the mechanism is confirmed.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Malicious Employee DoS
playbook.description: A malicious employee has deliberately caused a denial of service through an action not otherwise classified into a more specific sub-type.

steps.title: Confirm the malicious action and identify the responsible employee
steps.desc: Review relevant audit logs and system telemetry to identify the specific action causing the denial of service and attribute it to the responsible employee's account.
steps.outcome: Malicious action and responsible identity confirmed with supporting evidence.
steps.abort: If evidence points to an unintentional action, redirect to the Accidental Configuration DoS playbook.

steps.title: Preserve evidence before taking any account action
steps.desc: Capture forensic evidence before disabling or modifying the suspected employee's account access, in coordination with HR/Legal.
steps.outcome: Evidence preserved with documented chain of custody.

steps.title: Remediate the impact of the malicious action
steps.desc: Restore any affected configuration, systems, or data from backup/known-good state as required.
steps.outcome: Impacted systems restored and validated.

steps.title: Verify service restoration and audit for additional unauthorized actions
steps.desc: Confirm affected services are fully operational and audit for any other unauthorized actions by the same identity.
steps.outcome: Service confirmed restored; no additional unauthorized actions found, or further remediation performed if found.

steps.title: Document incident, HR/Legal outcome, and review insider-threat safeguards
steps.desc: Capture the full timeline, HR/Legal case outcome, and recommend privileged-access and monitoring improvements to reduce future insider-threat risk.
steps.outcome: Report finalized with follow-up actions tracked.

steps.title: Assess indicators of malicious intent
steps.desc: Review the identified employee's recent activity and HR context for indicators suggesting deliberate sabotage.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with HR/Legal at this stage before drawing conclusions.
steps.outcome: Initial intent assessment documented and shared with HR/Legal.

steps.title: Suspend the employee's access in coordination with HR and Legal
steps.desc: Coordinate with HR and Legal to suspend the individual's access following the organization's insider-threat response procedure.
steps.outcome: Access suspended through a formally coordinated process with HR/Legal sign-off.

ITID-41921.def: A denial-of-service incident in which an authorized administrator, performing a legitimate change, unintentionally misconfigures a firewall rule or network access control list in a way that blocks legitimate traffic to a service, causing an outage; the incident is a human-error operational event, not an adversary attack.
ITID-41921.purpose: Captures denial of service caused by an unintentional firewall or network access-control-list misconfiguration made by an authorized administrator, with no malicious intent.
scopeIncludes: Firewall rule change intended to restrict unwanted traffic that inadvertently also blocks legitimate traffic
Network ACL update applied to the wrong scope (e.g., wrong environment, wrong subnet) causing unintended blocking
Rollout of a security-hardening change without adequate testing that breaks legitimate connectivity
scopeExcludes: Deliberate deletion/disabling of configuration by a malicious insider (ITID-41911)
Accidental faulty code/application-configuration deployment unrelated to firewall/network ACL rules (ITID-41922)
ITID-41921.severity: Medium-High depending on how quickly the misconfiguration is identified and rolled back, and how business-critical the blocked traffic path is.
ITID-41921.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if a production-critical service is fully unreachable.
ITID-41921.escalation: Escalate to the network/platform team to identify and roll back the change; no HR/legal involvement is warranted since this is a confirmed accidental error.
indicators: Outage onset immediately following a recent, identifiable firewall/network ACL change in change-management records
Traffic blocked matching the pattern of the recently applied rule rather than any attack signature
Rollback of the specific change resolving the outage
vectors: No MITRE ATT&CK mapping applies — this is a human-error/operational incident, not an adversary technique.
rootCauses: Insufficient pre-deployment testing/validation of firewall and network ACL changes
Change applied to the wrong scope/environment due to inadequate change-management safeguards
No staged rollout or canary process for network-security changes
controls: Mandatory peer review and staged/canary rollout for firewall and network ACL changes
Pre-deployment connectivity testing against a defined set of critical paths
Automated rollback capability tied to post-change health checks
ITID-41921.detection: Strong technical signal from tight correlation between change-management records and outage onset timing.
ITID-41921.response: Roll back the specific change immediately, verify service restoration, and conduct a blameless post-incident review of the change-management process.
metrics: Mean time to identify and roll back the causal change
Number of accidental network-configuration outages per quarter
ITID-41921.notes: No MITRE ATT&CK mapping applies — this is a human-error/operational incident, not an adversary technique. Differentiator within Accidental Configuration DoS: network/firewall ACL layer specifically, distinct from application code/config deployment errors (ITID-41922) or capacity/auto-scaling misconfiguration (ITID-41923).

playbook.name: Accidental Firewall/Network ACL Misconfiguration Causing Outage
playbook.description: An employee unintentionally misconfigured a firewall rule or network ACL, causing an unintended denial of service for legitimate traffic.

steps.title: Confirm the misconfiguration and correlate with the outage onset
steps.desc: Review firewall/network ACL change history and configuration-management logs to identify the specific change that caused the outage, correlating the change timestamp with the onset of service impact.
steps.guidance: Check change-management records to see whether the change was part of a planned/approved activity that had an unintended side effect.
steps.outcome: Misconfiguration identified with the specific change, timestamp, and responsible party documented.
steps.abort: If evidence suggests the change was deliberate/malicious rather than accidental, escalate to the Malicious Employee DoS playbook instead.

steps.title: Roll back the misconfigured rule/ACL
steps.desc: Revert the firewall rule or network ACL to its last known-good configuration through the standard change-management rollback procedure.
steps.guidance: Use emergency change procedures where the outage severity warrants expedited rollback, but still log the change for audit.
steps.outcome: Misconfigured rule reverted; affected traffic begins flowing normally.
steps.abort: If rollback alone does not resolve the issue, investigate for a compounding secondary cause.

steps.title: Verify no other related misconfigurations remain
steps.desc: Review related firewall rules/ACLs changed in the same maintenance window for any other unintended side effects.
steps.outcome: No additional related misconfigurations found, or further corrections applied.

steps.title: Confirm full service restoration for all affected traffic/services
steps.desc: Verify all previously impacted services and traffic flows have returned to normal operation.
steps.outcome: Service restoration confirmed across all affected traffic/services.

steps.title: Conduct a blameless post-incident review and strengthen change-management guardrails
steps.desc: Hold a blameless post-incident review focused on process and tooling gaps (e.g., lack of pre-deployment validation, insufficient peer review, no staged rollout) rather than individual fault, and recommend change-management or automated-validation improvements.
steps.guidance: Frame the review around systemic prevention (pre-change validation/testing, mandatory peer review, staged rollout with automated rollback) rather than blaming the individual who made the change.
steps.outcome: Report finalized with process-improvement recommendations tracked to owners.

steps.title: Assess scope of impacted traffic/services
steps.desc: Determine which services, users, or network segments are affected by the misconfigured rule.
steps.outcome: Impact scope documented to prioritize remediation.

steps.title: Confirm rollback propagation across all affected devices
steps.desc: Verify the reverted firewall rule/ACL has fully propagated and taken effect across all affected devices, including any HA pairs, regional replicas, or redundant nodes.
steps.guidance: A rollback applied to only one node in a redundant pair can leave partial outage conditions in place; check device sync status explicitly.
steps.outcome: Rollback confirmed fully propagated and effective across all affected devices.
steps.abort: If propagation is incomplete on any device, manually apply the correction to that device.

ITID-41922.def: A denial-of-service incident in which an authorized engineer deploys a code change or application configuration update that contains an unintentional defect, causing the affected service to crash, hang, or reject legitimate requests; the incident is a human-error operational event, not an adversary attack.
ITID-41922.purpose: Captures denial of service caused by an unintentional deployment of faulty application code or configuration by an authorized engineer, with no malicious intent.
scopeIncludes: A deployed code change containing a bug (e.g., an infinite loop, unhandled exception, resource leak) that causes a production outage
An application configuration change (e.g., a feature flag, environment variable, connection string) deployed incorrectly and causing service failure
A deployment that passed testing but failed under production load/data conditions not represented in test
scopeExcludes: Firewall/network ACL misconfiguration (ITID-41921)
Capacity/auto-scaling misconfiguration specifically (ITID-41923)
Deliberate deployment of a resource-exhaustion script by a malicious insider (ITID-41912)
ITID-41922.severity: Medium-High depending on the blast radius of the deployment and how quickly rollback occurs.
ITID-41922.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if the affected service is production-critical and rollback is not immediately available.
ITID-41922.escalation: Escalate to the owning engineering team to execute rollback; no HR/legal involvement is warranted since this is a confirmed accidental error.
indicators: Outage onset immediately following a recent, identifiable deployment in CI/CD or release records
Error signature consistent with a code/configuration defect (e.g., stack traces, crash loops) rather than an attack pattern
Rollback of the specific deployment resolving the outage
vectors: No MITRE ATT&CK mapping applies — this is a human-error/operational incident, not an adversary technique.
rootCauses: Insufficient automated testing coverage for the change (unit, integration, load)
No staged/canary rollout process to catch defects before full production exposure
Production configuration/data conditions not adequately represented in the test environment
mitreTechniques: T1499.004 Endpoint Denial of Service: Application or System Exploitation
controls: Staged/canary deployment with automated health-check gating before full rollout
Expanded automated test coverage including load/production-representative scenarios
Fast, reliable automated rollback capability
ITID-41922.detection: Strong technical signal from tight correlation between deployment records and outage onset timing, combined with crash/error-log signatures.
ITID-41922.response: Roll back the specific deployment immediately, verify service restoration, and conduct a blameless post-incident review to improve testing/rollout safeguards.
metrics: Mean time to identify and roll back the causal deployment
Number of accidental deployment-caused outages per quarter
Percentage of deployments using staged/canary rollout
ITID-41922.notes: No MITRE ATT&CK mapping applies — this is a human-error/operational incident, not an adversary technique. Differentiator within Accidental Configuration DoS: application code/config deployment layer, distinct from network ACL errors (ITID-41921) or capacity/auto-scaling errors (ITID-41923).

playbook.name: Accidental Deployment of Faulty Code/Configuration Change
playbook.description: A deployment of faulty application code or configuration by an internal team unintentionally caused a denial of service or severe performance degradation.

steps.title: Confirm the faulty deployment and correlate with the service degradation
steps.desc: Review deployment/CI-CD pipeline logs and application error rates to identify the specific deployment that introduced the fault, correlating deployment timestamp with the onset of degradation.
steps.outcome: Faulty deployment identified with the specific change, timestamp, and responsible team documented.
steps.abort: If the deployment appears deliberately malicious rather than an honest error, escalate to the Malicious Employee DoS playbook instead.

steps.title: Roll back the faulty deployment
steps.desc: Execute an immediate rollback to the last known-good deployment version through the standard CI-CD rollback procedure.
steps.guidance: Use automated rollback tooling where available to minimize time-to-restore.
steps.outcome: Faulty deployment rolled back; service degradation resolves.
steps.abort: If rollback is not immediately possible, apply a feature flag/circuit breaker to disable the faulty component while a fix is prepared.

steps.title: Verify no residual faulty configuration or data corruption remains
steps.desc: Confirm the rollback fully reverted the faulty change and check for any data written/modified by the faulty deployment that requires correction.
steps.outcome: No residual faulty configuration or data corruption found, or further corrective action applied.

steps.title: Confirm full service restoration and validate before re-attempting deployment
steps.desc: Verify affected services return to normal performance baselines, and validate the corrected deployment in a staging environment before any re-attempt to production.
steps.outcome: Service restoration confirmed; corrected deployment validated in staging before any re-release.

steps.title: Conduct a blameless post-incident review and strengthen deployment guardrails
steps.desc: Hold a blameless post-incident review focused on process gaps (insufficient testing, lack of canary/staged rollout, missing automated rollback triggers) and recommend deployment-pipeline improvements.
steps.guidance: Frame the review around systemic prevention rather than individual fault.
steps.outcome: Report finalized with process-improvement recommendations (e.g., canary deployments, automated health-check rollback) tracked to owners.

steps.title: Assess scope of impacted services and users
steps.desc: Determine which services, features, or user populations are affected by the faulty deployment.
steps.outcome: Impact scope documented to prioritize remediation.

steps.title: Notify affected stakeholders and freeze further deployments to the impacted service
steps.desc: Notify dependent teams and stakeholders of the disruption and status, and freeze further deployments to the affected service until the rollback is confirmed stable.
steps.guidance: A deployment freeze prevents a second team from inadvertently redeploying the faulty change or compounding the incident with an unrelated change during triage.
steps.outcome: Stakeholders informed; deployment freeze in effect for the affected service.
steps.tool: CI-CD deployment console, incident communication channel

ITID-41923.def: A denial-of-service incident in which an authorized engineer misconfigures a resource quota, rate limit, or auto-scaling policy (e.g., setting a scaling ceiling too low, misconfiguring a threshold, or applying an overly restrictive quota) such that the service cannot scale to meet legitimate demand, causing a self-inflicted outage or severe degradation; the incident is a human-error operational event, not an adversary attack.
ITID-41923.purpose: Captures denial of service caused by an unintentional resource-quota or auto-scaling misconfiguration that leaves a service unable to absorb legitimate demand, with no malicious intent.
scopeIncludes: Auto-scaling maximum-instance ceiling set too low for actual demand, causing throttling under normal or promotional traffic
Rate-limit or quota configuration applied too restrictively to legitimate traffic patterns
Scaling-policy metric or threshold misconfigured such that scale-out does not trigger in time
scopeExcludes: Firewall/network ACL misconfiguration (ITID-41921)
Application code/configuration deployment defects unrelated to quota/scaling settings (ITID-41922)
ITID-41923.severity: Medium-High, particularly when the misconfiguration surfaces during a period of unusually high but entirely legitimate demand (e.g., a marketing campaign or seasonal peak).
ITID-41923.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if the throttling is actively blocking a high proportion of legitimate production traffic.
ITID-41923.escalation: Escalate to the platform/SRE team to raise the scaling ceiling or quota immediately; no HR/legal involvement is warranted since this is a confirmed accidental error.
indicators: Throttling/rejection errors correlated with legitimate demand exceeding a configured ceiling rather than any attack signature
Auto-scaling metrics showing the service at its configured maximum with healthy, non-anomalous traffic patterns
Recent change to scaling/quota configuration in change-management records preceding the incident
vectors: No MITRE ATT&CK mapping applies — this is a human-error/operational incident, not an adversary technique.
rootCauses: Scaling ceilings/quotas set based on outdated demand assumptions and not revisited before a known high-demand event
No load-testing or capacity-planning review before major traffic-driving events (launches, promotions)
Scaling-policy thresholds/metrics misconfigured, delaying scale-out response
mitreTechniques: T1499.003 Endpoint Denial of Service: Application Exhaustion Flood
controls: Capacity-planning review and load testing ahead of known high-demand events
Regular review of scaling ceilings/quotas against current demand trends
Alerting when a service is sustained at its configured scaling maximum
ITID-41923.detection: Strong technical signal from auto-scaling/quota utilization metrics showing the service pinned at a configured ceiling under legitimate traffic.
ITID-41923.response: Raise the scaling ceiling or quota immediately to relieve throttling, and conduct a capacity-planning review to prevent recurrence for future demand events.
metrics: Mean time to identify and raise the limiting configuration
Number of self-inflicted throttling incidents per quarter
Percentage of high-demand events preceded by a capacity-planning review
ITID-41923.notes: No MITRE ATT&CK mapping applies — this is a human-error/operational incident, not an adversary technique. Differentiator within Accidental Configuration DoS: resource-quota/auto-scaling layer, distinct from network ACL errors (ITID-41921) or code/config deployment errors (ITID-41922).

playbook.name: Accidental Resource Quota/Auto-Scaling Misconfiguration Causing Self-Inflicted Outage
playbook.description: An internal team unintentionally misconfigured cloud resource quotas or auto-scaling limits (set too low, or a scale-down triggered incorrectly), causing a self-inflicted denial of service under normal load.

steps.title: Confirm the quota/auto-scaling misconfiguration and correlate with the outage onset
steps.desc: Review auto-scaling group configuration history and cloud resource quota change logs to identify the specific change that caused capacity to fall below required levels, correlating the change timestamp with the onset of service impact.
steps.guidance: Check whether a recent quota reduction, scaling-policy change, or scheduled scale-down action coincides with the outage.
steps.outcome: Misconfiguration identified with the specific change, timestamp, and responsible team documented.
steps.abort: If evidence suggests the change was deliberate/malicious, escalate to the Malicious Employee DoS playbook instead.
steps.tool: Cloud auto-scaling console, configuration change logs

steps.title: Correct the quota/auto-scaling configuration to restore adequate capacity
steps.desc: Revert or correct the auto-scaling limits/resource quota to restore sufficient capacity for current demand through the standard change-management procedure, using emergency change authority given the active outage.
steps.outcome: Capacity restored to a level sufficient to handle current demand.

steps.title: Verify no other related quota/scaling misconfigurations remain
steps.desc: Review related auto-scaling groups/quotas changed in the same maintenance window or by the same automation for any other unintended side effects.
steps.outcome: No additional related misconfigurations found, or further corrections applied.

steps.title: Confirm full service restoration under normal load
steps.desc: Verify the affected service handles current and peak-expected load normally with the corrected capacity configuration.
steps.outcome: Service restoration confirmed under normal and peak load conditions.

steps.title: Conduct a blameless post-incident review and strengthen capacity-change guardrails
steps.desc: Hold a blameless post-incident review focused on process gaps (e.g., lack of minimum-capacity floors, insufficient alerting on quota changes, no pre-change capacity-impact review) and recommend guardrail improvements such as minimum-instance floors and change-approval workflows for scaling configuration.
steps.guidance: Frame the review around systemic prevention rather than individual fault.
steps.outcome: Report finalized with process-improvement recommendations tracked to owners.

steps.title: Assess current capacity shortfall against actual demand
steps.desc: Quantify the gap between current provisioned capacity and actual traffic/load demand to size the required correction.
steps.outcome: Capacity shortfall quantified to guide the correction.

steps.title: Apply temporary manual capacity while the quota/scaling fix propagates
steps.desc: If the auto-scaling/quota correction requires time to propagate or take effect, manually provision additional capacity (e.g., manually launched instances) as an interim measure.
steps.guidance: Manual capacity addition provides an immediate buffer while the underlying configuration correction rolls out.
steps.outcome: Interim capacity in place, preventing further degradation while the permanent fix propagates.
steps.abort: If the configuration correction takes effect immediately, manual capacity addition is not necessary.

ITID-41924.def: A denial-of-service incident confirmed as accidental (no malicious intent) and caused by human configuration error, but not yet classified into a specific mechanism (network ACL, deployment defect, capacity/scaling misconfiguration) pending further investigation; a human-error/operational incident, not an adversary technique.
ITID-41924.purpose: Serves as the intake bucket for accidental configuration DoS incidents that do not yet fit network-ACL, deployment-defect, or capacity/scaling-misconfiguration classifications.
scopeIncludes: Newly observed accidental-configuration-error patterns not yet mapped to an existing sibling leaf
Ambiguous self-inflicted outage incidents pending confirmation of both accidental intent and specific mechanism
scopeExcludes: Any incident later confirmed as network ACL misconfiguration (ITID-41921), deployment defect (ITID-41922), or capacity/scaling misconfiguration (ITID-41923) — reclassify once confirmed
Any incident where intent turns out to be malicious — reclassify under Malicious Employee DoS (ITID-4191x)
ITID-41924.severity: Medium by default pending classification; adjust once the specific mechanism and business impact are confirmed.
ITID-41924.priority: P3 pending triage, escalating per standard severity guidance once root cause is identified.
ITID-41924.escalation: Escalate to the SOC classification lead for prompt re-tagging into a specific sibling leaf once the mechanism is understood.
indicators: Self-inflicted outage confirmed as accidental with an unconfirmed specific mechanism
Analyst uncertainty about which accidental-configuration category applies
vectors: No MITRE ATT&CK mapping applies — this is a human-error/operational incident, not an adversary technique.
rootCauses: Root cause/mechanism not yet determined
controls: Standard change-management and rollback process pending classification
ITID-41924.detection: Coverage depends on the eventual mechanism; this bucket itself is logged via change-correlated outage intake.
ITID-41924.response: Roll back the causal change, restore service, and reclassify to the appropriate sibling ITID as soon as the specific mechanism is confirmed.
metrics: Number of incidents parked in this bucket beyond the triage SLA
Average time to reclassify into a specific sibling leaf
ITID-41924.notes: No MITRE ATT&CK mapping applies — this is a human-error/operational incident, not an adversary technique. Catch-all intake leaf; used only during initial triage. Analysts should reclassify into ITID-41921/41922/41923 as soon as the mechanism is confirmed.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Accidental Configuration DoS
playbook.description: An unintentional configuration error by an internal team caused a denial of service, not otherwise classified into a more specific sub-type.

steps.title: Confirm the configuration error and correlate with the outage onset
steps.desc: Review relevant configuration change history to identify the specific change that caused the outage, correlating the change timestamp with the onset of service impact.
steps.outcome: Misconfiguration identified with the specific change, timestamp, and responsible team documented.
steps.abort: If evidence suggests the change was deliberate/malicious, escalate to the Malicious Employee DoS playbook instead.

steps.title: Roll back or correct the misconfiguration
steps.desc: Revert the configuration to its last known-good state through the standard (or emergency) change-management rollback procedure.
steps.outcome: Misconfiguration reverted; affected service begins recovering.
steps.abort: If rollback alone does not resolve the issue, investigate for a compounding secondary cause.

steps.title: Verify no other related misconfigurations remain
steps.desc: Review related configuration items changed in the same window for any other unintended side effects.
steps.outcome: No additional related misconfigurations found, or further corrections applied.

steps.title: Confirm full service restoration
steps.desc: Verify all previously impacted services have returned to normal operation.
steps.outcome: Service restoration confirmed.

steps.title: Conduct a blameless post-incident review and strengthen change-management guardrails
steps.desc: Hold a blameless post-incident review focused on process and tooling gaps rather than individual fault, and recommend change-management improvements.
steps.guidance: Frame the review around systemic prevention rather than individual fault.
steps.outcome: Report finalized with process-improvement recommendations tracked to owners.

steps.title: Assess scope of impacted services/users
steps.desc: Determine which services, users, or systems are affected by the misconfiguration.
steps.outcome: Impact scope documented to prioritize remediation.

steps.title: Notify affected stakeholders and freeze related change activity pending investigation
steps.desc: Notify dependent teams of the disruption and status, and pause any related pending changes in the same system until the root cause is confirmed and corrected.
steps.outcome: Stakeholders informed; related change activity paused pending investigation outcome.

ITID-41931.def: A denial-of-service incident in which an internally developed script, job, or automation — due to a logic defect (e.g., a missing exit condition, retry loop with no backoff) — enters a runaway state and issues an excessive volume of requests against an internal API, degrading or crashing the API for other internal consumers; the incident is a human-error/operational event, not an adversary attack.
ITID-41931.purpose: Captures denial of service caused by an internal script or automation entering a runaway loop and overwhelming an internal API, with no malicious intent behind the original script.
scopeIncludes: A script with a missing loop-termination condition repeatedly calling an internal API
A retry mechanism with no backoff repeatedly hammering an internal API after transient failures
An internal automation/orchestration job stuck in a retry cycle against an internal endpoint
scopeExcludes: A deliberately authored resource-exhaustion script by a malicious insider (ITID-41912)
A bulk operation performed manually by an employee without automation, unaware of rate-limiting impact (ITID-41932)
A third-party integration misconfigured by an internal team (ITID-41933, a distinct root cause involving external vendor tooling)
ITID-41931.severity: Medium-High depending on how central the affected internal API is to other production workflows.
ITID-41931.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if the internal API is a shared dependency causing cascading failures.
ITID-41931.escalation: Escalate to the owning engineering team to identify and kill the runaway script/job; no HR/legal involvement is warranted since this is a confirmed accidental error.
indicators: Internal API request volume spiking from a single internal service/script account with no corresponding legitimate business driver
Repetitive, identical request patterns consistent with a loop rather than varied legitimate usage
Correlation with a recently deployed or scheduled internal automation job
vectors: No MITRE ATT&CK mapping applies — this is a human-error/operational incident, not an adversary technique.
rootCauses: Missing exit/termination condition in a loop calling an internal API
Retry logic with no exponential backoff or maximum retry cap
Insufficient testing of automation/orchestration jobs under failure conditions before production deployment
mitreTechniques: T1499.003 Endpoint Denial of Service: Application Exhaustion Flood
T1499.004 Endpoint Denial of Service: Application or System Exploitation
controls: Mandatory backoff-and-retry-cap standards for internal automation calling internal APIs
Per-caller rate limiting on internal API endpoints
Automated anomaly detection on internal API request volume by calling service/account
ITID-41931.detection: Strong technical signal from internal API request-volume telemetry correlated with the specific calling service/script account.
ITID-41931.response: Identify and terminate the runaway script/job, apply or verify per-caller rate limiting on the internal API, and fix the underlying loop/retry logic.
metrics: Mean time to identify and terminate the runaway job
Number of runaway-automation incidents per quarter
detections: Per-caller internal API request-volume anomaly alerting
ITID-41931.notes: No MITRE ATT&CK mapping applies — this is a human-error/operational incident, not an adversary technique. Differentiator within API Abuse from Internal Users: automated runaway script/loop, distinct from a manual bulk operation (ITID-41932) or a misconfigured third-party integration (ITID-41933).

playbook.name: Internal Script/Automation Runaway Loop Overloading Internal API
playbook.description: An internal script or automation, due to a coding error, entered a runaway loop generating excessive requests against an internal API, causing a denial of service to legitimate internal consumers.

steps.title: Identify the runaway script/automation via API traffic and log analysis
steps.desc: Analyze internal API gateway logs and request telemetry to identify the specific source (script, service account, scheduled job) generating the excessive request volume, and confirm it is an unintentional loop rather than external abuse.
steps.guidance: Look for a single internal source/service account generating a uniform, repetitive request pattern inconsistent with normal usage — often indicative of a missing loop-termination condition or retry-storm bug.
steps.outcome: Runaway script/automation and its owning team identified with supporting request-log evidence.
steps.abort: If the source is external or malicious rather than an internal automation error, redirect to the appropriate DDoS or intrusion playbook.
steps.tool: API gateway logs, internal service monitoring

steps.title: Stop or throttle the runaway script/automation
steps.desc: Terminate the identified script/job/process, or apply rate limiting at the API gateway targeting its service account/source, to immediately relieve load on the internal API.
steps.outcome: Excessive request volume stopped; internal API load returns toward normal.

steps.title: Fix and validate the script/automation before allowing it to resume
steps.desc: Correct the underlying coding error (missing loop-termination condition, missing backoff/retry limits) and validate the fix in a non-production environment before re-enabling.
steps.outcome: Fix validated; automation confirmed safe to re-enable.

steps.title: Confirm internal API restoration and re-enable the corrected automation under monitoring
steps.desc: Verify the internal API and its dependent consumers return to normal operation, then re-enable the corrected automation with heightened monitoring.
steps.outcome: Internal API confirmed restored; corrected automation running normally under monitoring.

steps.title: Conduct a blameless post-incident review and implement rate-limiting/circuit-breaker guardrails
steps.desc: Hold a blameless post-incident review focused on process improvements (mandatory retry/backoff limits, circuit breakers, internal API rate limiting per consumer) rather than individual fault, and track follow-up guardrail work.
steps.guidance: Frame the review around systemic prevention rather than individual fault.
steps.outcome: Report finalized with guardrail follow-up actions tracked to owners.

steps.title: Assess impact on the internal API and its dependent consumers
steps.desc: Determine which internal services/teams depend on the affected API and the severity of degraded availability they are experiencing.
steps.outcome: Impact scope documented to prioritize remediation and stakeholder communication.

steps.title: Notify the owning team of the runaway automation
steps.desc: Inform the team responsible for the script/automation so they can begin root-cause analysis and prevent restart without a fix.
steps.guidance: Frame the notification collaboratively — the goal is a fix, not blame.
steps.outcome: Owning team informed and engaged in remediation.

ITID-41932.def: A denial-of-service incident in which an employee, using legitimate tools and access, manually initiates a bulk data operation (e.g., a large export, mass update, or batch report generation) against an internal or shared API without awareness of the request volume or rate impact, degrading the service for other consumers; the incident is a human-error/operational event, not an adversary attack.
ITID-41932.purpose: Captures denial of service caused by an employee manually performing a bulk operation against an internal or shared API without realizing its rate-limiting impact on other consumers.
scopeIncludes: A manually triggered bulk export/report/update operation issuing a high volume of API calls in a short window
Use of a legitimate admin tool's bulk-action feature without understanding its backend request-volume impact
Ad hoc scripting by a non-engineering employee (e.g., via a spreadsheet macro or low-code tool) generating unexpectedly high API call volume
scopeExcludes: An automated script entering a runaway loop (ITID-41931, a code-logic defect rather than a manually-initiated one-off action)
A third-party integration misconfigured by an internal team (ITID-41933)
ITID-41932.severity: Low-Medium; typically self-limiting once the operation completes or is identified, though impact can be significant if the operation targets a shared production API.
ITID-41932.priority: P2 if actively degrading a shared production API; P3 if impact is contained and the operation can be safely allowed to complete.
ITID-41932.escalation: Escalate to the platform team to apply emergency rate limiting or pause the operation if a shared production API is materially degraded; no HR/legal involvement is warranted since this is a confirmed accidental error.
indicators: API request volume spike attributable to a single known employee account performing a bulk action
Request pattern consistent with a legitimate bulk-operation tool rather than an attack signature
Employee self-reports or is readily identified as the source upon investigation
vectors: No MITRE ATT&CK mapping applies — this is a human-error/operational incident, not an adversary technique.
rootCauses: No rate limiting or throttling on bulk-operation features exposed to end users
Lack of employee awareness/training on the backend impact of bulk actions in admin tools
No pre-flight warning or confirmation step for large-scale bulk operations
mitreTechniques: T1499.003 Endpoint Denial of Service: Application Exhaustion Flood
controls: Rate limiting/throttling built into bulk-operation features in admin tooling
Pre-flight confirmation and impact warning for large-scale bulk actions
Employee training on the operational impact of bulk data operations
ITID-41932.detection: Strong technical signal from API request-volume telemetry correlated with a specific employee account and a recognizable bulk-operation pattern.
ITID-41932.response: Pause or throttle the operation if a shared production API is materially degraded, confirm no lasting impact once the operation completes, and add rate-limiting safeguards to the bulk-operation feature.
metrics: Mean time to identify the responsible employee/operation
Number of bulk-operation-caused degradation incidents per quarter
detections: Per-account internal API request-volume anomaly alerting
ITID-41932.notes: No MITRE ATT&CK mapping applies — this is a human-error/operational incident, not an adversary technique. Differentiator within API Abuse from Internal Users: a manually-initiated one-off bulk action lacking rate-limit awareness, distinct from a code-logic runaway loop (ITID-41931) or a third-party integration misconfiguration (ITID-41933).

playbook.name: Employee Bulk Operation Performed Without Rate Limiting Awareness
playbook.description: An employee performed a legitimate bulk operation (e.g., mass data export, bulk update) against an internal system without awareness of rate-limiting/capacity constraints, unintentionally causing a denial of service.

steps.title: Identify the bulk operation and correlate with the service degradation
steps.desc: Review application/API logs to identify the specific bulk operation, its initiating user, and correlate its execution window with the onset of service degradation.
steps.outcome: Bulk operation and initiating user identified with supporting log evidence.
steps.abort: If the operation appears deliberately designed to cause harm rather than an unaware legitimate task, escalate to the Malicious Employee DoS playbook instead.

steps.title: Pause or throttle the bulk operation
steps.desc: Contact the employee to pause the operation, or apply rate limiting/throttling at the application or API layer targeting the operation's source, to relieve load.
steps.guidance: Approach the employee collaboratively — they were performing a legitimate task without awareness of the system impact.
steps.outcome: Load relieved; affected system begins recovering.

steps.title: Verify system resource levels return to normal and no data corruption resulted from the interrupted operation
steps.desc: Confirm system load returns to baseline and check whether the interrupted bulk operation left any partial/inconsistent data requiring correction.
steps.outcome: System load normalized; any partial-data issues identified and corrected.

steps.title: Confirm full service restoration and reschedule the bulk operation safely
steps.desc: Verify affected services return to normal performance and work with the employee/team to reschedule or restructure the bulk operation (e.g., batched with throttling, off-peak execution) so it can be completed safely.
steps.outcome: Service restoration confirmed; a safe path for completing the legitimate bulk operation is established.

steps.title: Conduct a blameless post-incident review and implement bulk-operation guardrails
steps.desc: Hold a blameless post-incident review focused on process improvements (documented safe bulk-operation procedures, built-in throttling/pagination in admin tools, awareness training) rather than individual fault.
