steps.guidance: Frame the review around systemic prevention and process/tooling gaps rather than blaming the employee.
steps.outcome: Report finalized with guardrail and process-improvement follow-up actions tracked.

steps.title: Assess impact on the affected system and its other consumers
steps.desc: Determine the severity of degraded availability experienced by other users/systems dependent on the affected service.
steps.outcome: Impact scope documented to prioritize remediation.

steps.title: Verify no other concurrent bulk operations are contributing to the load
steps.desc: Check for any other concurrent bulk/batch operations running against the same system that may be compounding the load, in addition to the identified operation.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether the identified operation is the sole contributor or one of several; any additional contributors addressed.

ITID-41933.def: A denial-of-service incident in which an internal team, while configuring or integrating a third-party tool or service (e.g., a webhook, sync job, monitoring agent, or SaaS connector), introduces a misconfiguration (e.g., an overly frequent polling interval, a webhook loop, or missing pagination) that causes the third-party system to generate an excessive volume of requests against internal APIs; the incident is a human-error/operational event, not an adversary attack.
ITID-41933.purpose: Captures denial of service caused by an internal team misconfiguring a third-party integration in a way that generates an excessive volume of API calls against internal systems.
scopeIncludes: Third-party webhook configured to trigger a loop (e.g., an internal system's response triggers another outbound webhook call back to the same system)
SaaS connector or sync job configured with a polling interval far more aggressive than intended
Third-party monitoring/integration agent misconfigured to retry excessively against an internal endpoint after failures
scopeExcludes: An internally authored script/automation runaway loop (ITID-41931)
A manually-initiated bulk operation by an employee (ITID-41932)
ITID-41933.severity: Medium, particularly when the misconfigured integration is difficult to immediately disable (e.g., requires vendor-side changes).
ITID-41933.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if the internal API affected is a shared production dependency and disabling the integration is not immediately possible.
ITID-41933.escalation: Escalate to the owning internal team and the third-party vendor's support channel to correct the configuration or temporarily disable the integration; no HR/legal involvement is warranted since this is a confirmed accidental error.
indicators: Internal API request volume spike attributable to a known third-party integration's service account/API key
Request pattern and timing consistent with the third-party tool's known polling/webhook behavior rather than an attack signature
Correlation with a recent change to the third-party integration's configuration
vectors: No MITRE ATT&CK mapping applies — this is a human-error/operational incident, not an adversary technique.
rootCauses: Third-party integration configured without reviewing or testing its request-volume/polling-frequency impact
No rate limiting applied to API keys/service accounts used by third-party integrations
Webhook configuration allowing an unintended feedback loop between systems
mitreTechniques: T1499.003 Endpoint Denial of Service: Application Exhaustion Flood
T1499.001 Endpoint Denial of Service: OS Exhaustion Flood
controls: Rate limiting applied to API keys/service accounts used by third-party integrations
Mandatory configuration review/testing before enabling a new third-party integration in production
Webhook loop-prevention safeguards (e.g., idempotency checks, call-depth limits)
ITID-41933.detection: Strong technical signal from internal API request-volume telemetry correlated with the specific third-party integration's service account/API key.
ITID-41933.response: Disable or throttle the misconfigured integration, correct the configuration with the vendor if needed, and apply rate limiting to the integration's API key going forward.
metrics: Mean time to identify and disable/correct the misconfigured integration
Number of third-party-integration-caused degradation incidents per quarter
detections: Per-integration internal API request-volume anomaly alerting
ITID-41933.notes: No MITRE ATT&CK mapping applies — this is a human-error/operational incident, not an adversary technique. Differentiator within API Abuse from Internal Users: root cause traced specifically to third-party integration misconfiguration by an internal team, distinct from an internally authored runaway script (ITID-41931) or a manual bulk operation (ITID-41932).

playbook.name: Third-Party Integration Misconfigured by Internal Team Causing API Flood
playbook.description: An internal team misconfigured a third-party integration (e.g., webhook retry settings, sync interval, batch size) causing it to flood an internal or partner API with excessive requests, resulting in a denial of service.

steps.title: Identify the misconfigured integration and its request pattern
steps.desc: Review API gateway/integration logs to identify the specific third-party integration generating excessive requests and the configuration parameter (retry interval, sync frequency, batch size) responsible.
steps.guidance: Check the integration's configuration change history for a recent change coinciding with the onset of the flood.
steps.outcome: Misconfigured integration and responsible configuration parameter identified with supporting log evidence.
steps.abort: If the flood originates from the third party's own systems rather than an internal misconfiguration, redirect to vendor/provider escalation instead.
steps.tool: API gateway logs, integration platform console

steps.title: Correct or disable the misconfigured integration
steps.desc: Revert the integration's configuration to safe parameters, or temporarily disable the integration if an immediate safe configuration cannot be applied.
steps.outcome: Excessive request volume from the integration stopped; API load returns toward normal.

steps.title: Verify sustained normalization of API load and validate the corrected configuration
steps.desc: Confirm API request volume and load return to and remain at normal levels, and validate the corrected integration configuration in a non-production environment before full re-enablement.
steps.outcome: API load confirmed normalized; corrected configuration validated as safe.

steps.title: Re-enable the integration under monitoring and confirm full service restoration
steps.desc: Re-enable the integration with the corrected, safe configuration under heightened monitoring, and confirm the affected API and its consumers return to normal operation.
steps.outcome: Integration operating normally with the corrected configuration; API service restoration confirmed.
steps.tool: Integration platform console, API gateway metrics

steps.title: Conduct a blameless post-incident review and implement integration-configuration guardrails
steps.desc: Hold a blameless post-incident review focused on process improvements (configuration validation/testing for integrations, mandatory rate-limit safety nets, change-review for integration settings) rather than individual fault.
steps.guidance: Frame the review around systemic prevention rather than individual fault.
steps.outcome: Report finalized with guardrail follow-up actions tracked to owners.

steps.title: Assess impact on the affected internal/partner API
steps.desc: Determine the severity of degraded availability experienced by the affected API and its other consumers.
steps.outcome: Impact scope documented to prioritize remediation.

steps.title: Apply rate limiting on the integration's API consumer identity as a safety net
steps.desc: Configure rate limiting at the API gateway for the integration's consumer/service account to prevent recurrence even if the configuration is reintroduced.
steps.outcome: Rate-limiting safety net in place for the integration's traffic.

ITID-41934.def: A denial-of-service incident confirmed as caused by accidental internal API abuse, but not yet classified into a specific mechanism (runaway automation, manual bulk operation, misconfigured third-party integration) pending further investigation; a human-error/operational incident, not an adversary technique.
ITID-41934.purpose: Serves as the intake bucket for internal API abuse (DoS-causing) incidents that do not yet fit runaway-script, manual-bulk-operation, or third-party-integration-misconfiguration classifications.
scopeIncludes: Newly observed internal-API-abuse patterns not yet mapped to an existing sibling leaf
Ambiguous internal API degradation incidents pending confirmation of both accidental origin and specific mechanism
scopeExcludes: Any incident later confirmed as runaway automation (ITID-41931), manual bulk operation (ITID-41932), or third-party integration misconfiguration (ITID-41933) — reclassify once confirmed
Any incident where intent turns out to be malicious — reclassify under Malicious Employee DoS (ITID-4191x)
ITID-41934.severity: Medium by default pending classification; adjust once the specific mechanism and business impact are confirmed.
ITID-41934.priority: P3 pending triage, escalating per standard severity guidance once root cause is identified.
ITID-41934.escalation: Escalate to the SOC classification lead for prompt re-tagging into a specific sibling leaf once the mechanism is understood.
indicators: Internal API degradation confirmed as accidental with an unconfirmed specific mechanism
Analyst uncertainty about which internal-API-abuse category applies
vectors: No MITRE ATT&CK mapping applies — this is a human-error/operational incident, not an adversary technique.
rootCauses: Root cause/mechanism not yet determined
mitreTechniques: T1499.003 Endpoint Denial of Service: Application Exhaustion Flood
controls: Standard internal API governance and rate-limiting review pending classification
ITID-41934.detection: Coverage depends on the eventual mechanism; this bucket itself is logged via internal API request-volume anomaly intake.
ITID-41934.response: Contain the request-volume spike (throttle the identified source), restore normal API performance, and reclassify to the appropriate sibling ITID as soon as the specific mechanism is confirmed.
metrics: Number of incidents parked in this bucket beyond the triage SLA
Average time to reclassify into a specific sibling leaf
detections: Generic internal API request-volume anomaly alerting
ITID-41934.notes: No MITRE ATT&CK mapping applies — this is a human-error/operational incident, not an adversary technique. Catch-all intake leaf; used only during initial triage. Analysts should reclassify into ITID-41931/41932/41933 as soon as the mechanism is confirmed.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Internal API Abuse DoS
playbook.description: Unintentional internal misuse of an API caused a denial of service to legitimate consumers, not otherwise classified into a more specific sub-type.

steps.title: Identify the source of internal API misuse and correlate with the service degradation
steps.desc: Review API gateway/application logs to identify the internal source (user, script, integration) generating excessive or abnormal requests, correlating with the onset of degradation.
steps.outcome: Responsible internal source identified with supporting log evidence.
steps.abort: If evidence suggests deliberate misuse rather than an unaware/accidental cause, escalate to the Malicious Employee DoS playbook instead.

steps.title: Stop or throttle the source of the excessive requests
steps.desc: Pause the responsible process/operation or apply rate limiting at the API gateway targeting its source to relieve load.
steps.outcome: Excessive request volume stopped; API load returns toward normal.

steps.title: Verify sustained normalization of API load
steps.desc: Confirm API request volume and load return to and remain at normal levels.
steps.outcome: API load confirmed normalized.

steps.title: Confirm full service restoration
steps.desc: Verify the affected API and its consumers return to normal operation.
steps.outcome: Service restoration confirmed.

steps.title: Conduct a blameless post-incident review and implement API-usage guardrails
steps.desc: Hold a blameless post-incident review focused on process improvements (rate limiting, usage awareness training, safer tooling defaults) rather than individual fault.
steps.guidance: Frame the review around systemic prevention rather than individual fault.
steps.outcome: Report finalized with guardrail follow-up actions tracked to owners.

steps.title: Assess impact on the affected API and its consumers
steps.desc: Determine the severity of degraded availability experienced by the affected API and dependent consumers.
steps.outcome: Impact scope documented to prioritize remediation.

steps.title: Verify no other internal consumers are contributing similar excessive load
steps.desc: Check whether other internal consumers of the affected API are also generating abnormal load, in addition to the identified source.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether the identified source is the sole contributor; any additional contributors addressed.

ITID-42111.def: Use of a still-active VPN account belonging to a former employee to gain remote entry into the internal network, indicating a failure in the offboarding/deprovisioning process rather than a technical exploit against the VPN itself.
ITID-42111.purpose: Captures unauthorized network access obtained through a VPN credential that should have been deactivated when the employee left the organization.
scopeIncludes: VPN logon using credentials of an employee who separated from the organization
Contractor VPN account left active past engagement end date
Detection of VPN authentication from a departed user's account regardless of who is actually using it
scopeExcludes: VPN access via a currently-employed user's stolen credentials (see credential-theft ITIDs elsewhere in the taxonomy)
Vendor account lifecycle failures (ITID-42143)
Exploitation of a VPN configuration flaw such as split tunneling (ITID-42112)
ITID-42111.severity: High — represents a live, unmonitored path into the internal network under an identity nobody is watching.
ITID-42111.priority: P1 upon any confirmed authentication; P2 if only discovered via periodic account audit with no evidence of use.
ITID-42111.escalation: Escalate immediately to IT security and HR/People teams; disable the account and force a full session/token revocation the moment reuse is suspected.
indicators: VPN authentication event tied to an account flagged as terminated in HR/IAM records
VPN login from a geographic location inconsistent with the departed employee's last known whereabouts
Access-review audit surfacing an enabled account with no matching active HR record
vectors: Former employee retaining and reusing personal knowledge of still-valid credentials
Credential resale or reuse by a third party after departure
Shared/team VPN credentials never individually rotated at offboarding
rootCauses: No automated linkage between HR termination events and IAM/VPN deprovisioning
Offboarding checklist gaps for remote-access-specific accounts
Absence of periodic dormant/stale account reviews
controls: Automated HR-to-IAM deprovisioning workflow
Periodic dormant-account review
MFA on all VPN authentication
Time-bound access certification for remote-access accounts
ITID-42111.detection: Strong when VPN logs are correlated against an authoritative HR/employment-status feed; weak or absent without that integration.
ITID-42111.response: Disable the account, revoke all active sessions/tokens, review all network activity performed under the account since separation, and confirm no persistence was established.
metrics: Mean time from termination to account deactivation
Count of stale/enabled accounts found per access review cycle
Count of confirmed post-termination authentications
ITID-42111.notes: The root cause here is a process failure, not a technical vulnerability in the VPN; response and remediation should target the deprovisioning workflow.

playbook.name: Unauthorized VPN Access via Departed Employee Account Never Revoked
playbook.description: A former employee's VPN credentials remained active after termination and were used (by the ex-employee or a third party who obtained the credentials) to authenticate into the corporate network.

steps.title: Correlate VPN authentication logs against HR termination records
steps.desc: Pull VPN concentrator/IdP authentication logs for the flagged account and cross-reference login timestamps against the HR-reported last-day-of-employment date.
steps.guidance: Check VPN/SSO logs (RADIUS, Azure AD Sign-In logs, or VPN appliance auth log) for any session with a start time after the termination date recorded in HRIS. Note source IP, session duration, and any resources accessed during the session.
steps.outcome: Confirmed timeline of post-termination authentication events, including at least one successful login after the recorded termination date.
steps.abort: If no post-termination logins are found, close as a false positive and verify the alert's timestamp logic.
steps.tool: SIEM / RADIUS logs / Identity Provider sign-in logs

steps.title: Disable the VPN account and revoke active sessions immediately
steps.desc: Disable the departed employee's VPN and directory account and forcibly terminate any active VPN sessions or tokens tied to it.
steps.guidance: Disable in the IdP/AD, revoke VPN client certificates if certificate-based auth is used, and invalidate any active RADIUS/session tokens. Confirm the account can no longer authenticate.
steps.outcome: Account disabled and no further authentication possible; active session terminated.
steps.tool: Active Directory / VPN concentrator admin console

steps.title: Audit and disable all departed employee's residual access
steps.desc: Search for any other lingering credentials, API keys, shared accounts, or SaaS access tied to the departed employee beyond the primary VPN/AD account.
steps.guidance: Check SaaS SSO app assignments, shared mailboxes, service accounts, and any locally-cached credentials that may not be tied to central directory deprovisioning.
steps.outcome: All residual access for the individual fully revoked across the environment.
steps.tool: SSO admin console / SaaS management platform

steps.title: Reconcile active VPN account list against current employee roster
steps.desc: Run a full reconciliation of all currently-enabled VPN accounts against the active employee/contractor roster to catch any other stale accounts.
steps.guidance: Export enabled VPN account list, compare against HRIS active-employee export, flag and disable any mismatches.
steps.outcome: All stale/orphaned VPN accounts identified and disabled; clean reconciliation baseline established.

steps.title: Document incident and update offboarding SLA/monitoring
steps.desc: Produce a post-incident report covering timeline, root cause, and remediation, and recommend a recurring automated audit of VPN accounts against HR status to prevent recurrence.
steps.guidance: Include recommendation for periodic (e.g., weekly) automated reconciliation job and alerting on any VPN login from an account flagged inactive in HRIS.
steps.outcome: Report distributed to IT security, IAM, and HR stakeholders; recurring reconciliation control implemented or scheduled.

steps.title: Determine offboarding process failure point
steps.desc: Trace why the account was not disabled at termination — check whether an offboarding ticket was created, assigned, and closed, and whether VPN/IdP deprovisioning was included in that ticket's task list.
steps.guidance: Review ITSM offboarding ticket history and the deprovisioning checklist used by IT/HR at separation. Identify whether the gap was a missed manual step, a broken automated deprovisioning integration, or an account HR never reported as terminated.
steps.outcome: Root cause of the deprovisioning gap identified (process, tooling, or reporting failure).

steps.title: Block source IP/device associated with unauthorized sessions
steps.desc: If the unauthorized access originated from an identifiable external IP or device fingerprint not belonging to the organization, block it at the firewall/VPN gateway.
steps.guidance: Add temporary deny rule at perimeter firewall or VPN gateway ACL for the offending source IP ranges pending investigation.
steps.outcome: Source of unauthorized access blocked from further connection attempts.
steps.abort: Skip if the source IP is a shared/dynamic consumer ISP range where blocking could be ineffective or impact legitimate users; rely on account disablement instead.

steps.title: Remediate the offboarding process gap
steps.desc: Implement or fix the automated linkage between HR termination events and IT deprovisioning (e.g., HRIS-to-IdP automated deprovisioning trigger) so future departures immediately disable VPN/directory access.
steps.guidance: Work with HR and IT identity teams to close the specific gap identified during investigation — whether that is enabling an existing automation, fixing a broken integration, or adding VPN account disablement to a manual checklist with an enforced SLA.
steps.outcome: Verified automated or enforced process ensures VPN/account disablement occurs within a defined SLA (e.g., same business day) of termination.

steps.title: Assess scope of activity performed during unauthorized sessions
steps.desc: Review all resources, systems, and data accessed during each post-termination VPN session to determine potential data exposure or further compromise.
steps.guidance: Correlate VPN session windows with file server access logs, application logs, and endpoint activity from the associated device if known.
steps.outcome: Documented list of systems/data touched during unauthorized access, feeding severity assessment.

ITID-42112.def: Exploitation of a split-tunnel VPN setup — where only some traffic is routed through the corporate tunnel while the rest goes directly to the internet — to bridge an attacker-controlled or compromised remote device/network into the internal environment, bypassing perimeter inspection.
ITID-42112.purpose: Captures an adversary abusing a split-tunnel VPN configuration to pivot from a compromised remote endpoint into the internal corporate network.
scopeIncludes: Malware on a split-tunnel-connected endpoint pivoting through the VPN adapter into internal subnets
Home/public network traffic bridging into the corporate network via a simultaneously-connected split-tunnel session
Attacker-controlled device on the same local network as a split-tunnel VPN client using it as a relay
scopeExcludes: Access via a legitimately-scoped but overly broad VPN grant (ITID-42113)
Use of a departed employee's VPN account (ITID-42111)
Device-level compromise that precedes the pivot (covered under the relevant device-domain ITIDs)
ITID-42112.severity: High — the internal network is reachable from an uncontrolled, uninspected network segment.
ITID-42112.priority: P1 when active pivot traffic is confirmed; P2 for configuration findings without confirmed exploitation.
ITID-42112.escalation: Escalate to network engineering to disable split tunneling and to SOC to investigate whether internal systems were reached during the exposure window.
indicators: Simultaneous routing of internal VPN traffic and untrusted internet traffic on the same client
Internal connections originating from a VPN client IP shortly after suspicious local-network activity on that client
Endpoint telemetry showing dual network adapters active during a security event
vectors: Compromised home router or IoT device on the same LAN as a split-tunnel VPN client
Malware on the remote endpoint using the split tunnel as a bridge
Public Wi-Fi adjacency exploited while split tunneling is active
rootCauses: Split tunneling enabled for bandwidth/performance reasons without compensating controls
No endpoint firewall rule blocking bridging between tunnel and local interfaces
Lack of network access control validating device posture before granting internal reach
controls: Full-tunnel (force-tunnel) VPN policy for sensitive access tiers
Endpoint host-based firewall blocking interface bridging
Network access control / posture check prior to internal segment access
Segmentation limiting what a VPN session can reach
ITID-42112.detection: Moderate — requires endpoint telemetry showing dual-interface activity correlated with internal network access; VPN concentrator logs alone rarely reveal the bridging.
ITID-42112.response: Terminate the session, disable split tunneling for the affected user/policy group, and audit internal systems reached during the session for signs of compromise.
metrics: Percentage of VPN population still on split-tunnel policy
Count of confirmed pivot events per quarter
detections: Anomalous internal access following remote endpoint alert
ITID-42112.notes: This is a configuration-driven risk; the differentiator from other VPN leaves is that the network path itself, not the credential, is the weakness.

playbook.name: Split-Tunnel VPN Misconfiguration Exploited for Network Pivot
playbook.description: A split-tunnel VPN configuration allowed traffic to bypass corporate inspection, enabling an attacker who compromised the remote endpoint to pivot from the unfiltered internet path into the internal corporate network.

steps.title: Confirm split-tunnel configuration and identify affected VPN profile
steps.desc: Verify which VPN policy/profile has split-tunneling enabled and confirm the endpoint involved in the incident was using that profile.
steps.guidance: Review the VPN client configuration policy, routing table pushed to the client, and confirm which traffic classes (e.g., only corporate subnet routed, all other traffic direct-to-internet) bypass inspection.
steps.outcome: Confirmed split-tunnel policy and affected endpoint identified, with routing scope documented.

steps.title: Isolate the compromised endpoint from the internal network
steps.desc: Immediately terminate the VPN session for the compromised endpoint and quarantine the device from further network access.
steps.guidance: Disable the VPN session/credential, and if the device is centrally managed, push an EDR network-isolation action.
steps.outcome: Compromised endpoint disconnected and unable to reach internal resources.

steps.title: Remediate the compromised endpoint
steps.desc: Perform full malware remediation or reimage of the compromised endpoint before restoring its network access.
steps.guidance: Follow standard endpoint remediation playbook — reimage where trust cannot be re-established through cleaning.
steps.outcome: Endpoint verified clean and reissued current security baseline before VPN access is restored.

steps.title: Restore VPN access under hardened configuration and monitor
steps.desc: Restore the endpoint's and other affected users' VPN access under the new full-tunnel (or compensated) configuration, with heightened monitoring for a defined period.
steps.guidance: Re-enable VPN access, confirm routing enforces intended path, and add temporary heightened alerting on the affected users' traffic.
steps.outcome: Users restored to normal operation with verified secure configuration and monitoring in place.

steps.title: Document incident and update VPN configuration standards
steps.desc: Record root cause, remediation, and update the organization's VPN configuration baseline/standard to prohibit or restrict split-tunneling by default.
steps.guidance: Include recommendation to periodically audit VPN profiles for policy drift back to split-tunnel configurations.
steps.outcome: Updated VPN configuration standard published; periodic audit scheduled.

steps.title: Analyze endpoint compromise vector and pivot activity
steps.desc: Investigate how the remote endpoint was compromised over its unfiltered internet path, and trace any lateral pivot attempts from that endpoint into internal network segments over the VPN tunnel.
steps.guidance: Review EDR telemetry on the endpoint for malware/initial-access indicators, and correlate VPN tunnel traffic/NetFlow for connections from the endpoint to internal hosts beyond expected use.
steps.outcome: Compromise vector confirmed and scope of internal reconnaissance/pivot attempts established.
steps.abort: If endpoint shows no compromise indicators, reclassify as a configuration-risk finding rather than an active incident.

steps.title: Disable split-tunneling on the affected VPN profile
steps.desc: Reconfigure the VPN profile to force full-tunnel routing so all client traffic passes through corporate inspection until the exposure is remediated.
steps.guidance: Push updated VPN client configuration removing split-tunnel routes; force reconnect of affected sessions to apply.
steps.outcome: All traffic from the affected profile now routes through corporate security stack.
steps.abort: If full-tunnel causes unacceptable performance/business impact, apply a scoped exception (e.g., full-tunnel only for internal-resource routes plus explicit deny of split traffic to known-risky categories) with documented compensating control.

steps.title: Review and harden split-tunnel policy usage organization-wide
steps.desc: Assess whether split-tunneling is required for any VPN profile and, where retained for business reasons, add compensating controls (DNS filtering, endpoint firewall, mandatory EDR).
steps.guidance: Work with network and security architecture teams to define an approved split-tunnel exception policy requiring documented business justification and compensating controls.
steps.outcome: Split-tunnel usage reduced to only justified/approved cases with compensating controls in place.

steps.title: Identify other endpoints using the same vulnerable split-tunnel profile
steps.desc: Enumerate all remote users/devices assigned the same split-tunnel VPN profile to determine full exposure.
steps.guidance: Query VPN policy assignment records for all active users on the affected profile.
steps.outcome: Complete list of exposed endpoints for scoping and containment.

ITID-42113.def: Exploitation of a VPN access policy that grants a user or group routable access to network segments beyond what their job function requires, allowing a compromised legitimate session to reach sensitive systems that should have been out of scope.
ITID-42113.purpose: Captures cases where a legitimate VPN grant provides far more internal network reach than the user's role requires, and that excess reach is exploited.
scopeIncludes: A compromised standard-user VPN session reaching server or admin VLANs it was never scoped to touch
VPN group policy that grants 'any-any' internal routing instead of role-based segment access
Contractor VPN profile mirroring a full-access employee profile instead of a scoped one
scopeExcludes: Split-tunnel bridging from an external network (ITID-42112)
Stale/departed-user credential reuse (ITID-42111)
Post-access lateral movement technique details (covered under the Lateral Movement Tier-3 category)
ITID-42113.severity: Medium-High, escalating to High when the reachable segments include sensitive/crown-jewel systems.
ITID-42113.priority: P2 for policy findings identified proactively; P1 when a compromised session is confirmed to have used the excess reach.
ITID-42113.escalation: Escalate to network/identity engineering to tighten VPN routing scope; escalate to SOC/IR if a compromised account is found to have exercised the excess access.
indicators: VPN session reaching network segments with no legitimate business relationship to the user's role
Firewall/NAC logs showing a remote-access IP touching admin or server subnets
Access review flagging a VPN group policy with unusually broad ACLs
vectors: Credential theft or phishing against a user whose VPN grant is over-scoped
Session hijacking of an over-privileged VPN connection
Insider abuse of legitimately broad but unnecessary access
rootCauses: VPN policies built around convenience ('one profile for everyone') rather than least privilege
No periodic review of VPN group-to-segment mappings
Network segmentation not aligned to VPN policy design
controls: Role-based VPN network segment scoping
Least-privilege review of remote-access group policies
Internal segmentation/microsegmentation independent of VPN trust
Conditional access limiting reachable segments by device posture
ITID-42113.detection: Moderate — requires correlating VPN session identity with destination-segment logs; policy-review findings are the more reliable detection path.
ITID-42113.response: Restrict the VPN policy to least-privilege scope, investigate whether the excess reach was exercised maliciously, and remediate the underlying group/ACL design.
metrics: Count of VPN policies reviewed/rescoped per cycle
Number of segments reachable per average VPN profile
ITID-42113.notes: The differentiator here is authorization scope, not the legitimacy of the credential or session itself.

playbook.name: VPN Access Granted with Overly Broad Network Segment Reach
playbook.description: A VPN user or group profile was provisioned with network-layer access to segments far beyond what their role required, and this excess reach was exploited to reach sensitive internal systems.

steps.title: Map the VPN profile's granted network reach against actual usage
steps.desc: Pull the ACL/routing scope assigned to the VPN user or group and compare it against the segments the account actually accessed historically and during the incident.
steps.guidance: Review VPN gateway ACLs/firewall policy bound to the profile, and NetFlow/firewall logs for destination segments accessed during the incident window versus the account's job function.
steps.outcome: Documented gap between provisioned reach and legitimate business need, plus confirmed segments accessed during the incident.
steps.tool: VPN gateway ACL config / NetFlow logs

steps.title: Restrict the VPN profile's network reach to least privilege immediately
steps.desc: Apply an emergency ACL change scoping the affected VPN profile/group down to only the network segments required for its role.
steps.guidance: Update firewall/VPN gateway policy to remove routes/ACL entries for segments outside legitimate need; verify with a test connection that access to sensitive segments is now blocked.
steps.outcome: VPN profile reach reduced to least-privilege scope; access to sensitive segments blocked.
steps.abort: If immediate restriction would break a business-critical dependency, apply a temporary allow-list exception with compensating monitoring while the correct scope is finalized.

steps.title: Rebuild VPN access policy using role-based segmentation
steps.desc: Redesign the VPN group/profile ACL model so network reach is explicitly mapped to role-based need rather than broad defaults.
steps.guidance: Work with network architecture to define role-based VPN groups tied to specific segment ACLs, replacing any broad 'all internal' default group.
steps.outcome: Role-based VPN access model implemented, eliminating overly broad default profiles.

steps.title: Validate legitimate users retain required access under new scoping
steps.desc: Confirm that all legitimate VPN users can still reach the systems required for their job function after the ACL rework.
steps.guidance: Run a user-acceptance check with representative accounts from each role group post-change.
steps.outcome: No legitimate business disruption; access confirmed correctly scoped.

steps.title: Document incident and institute periodic VPN access-scope review
steps.desc: Record findings and establish a recurring (e.g., quarterly) access-scope review process for all VPN profiles against role requirements.
steps.guidance: Assign ownership of the recurring review to network/IAM team; include in access-certification program if one exists.
steps.outcome: Recurring review process established and documented.

steps.title: Determine how the account or its credentials were used to exploit the excess reach
steps.desc: Investigate whether the access was exploited by the legitimate account holder, a compromised credential, or a session hijack, and identify what systems in the over-provisioned segments were touched.
steps.guidance: Cross-reference authentication source/behavior anomalies (impossible travel, unusual hours, unfamiliar device) with activity on the reached segments.
steps.outcome: Determination of insider misuse vs. credential compromise, with full list of systems accessed beyond role scope.

steps.title: Rotate credentials if compromise is suspected
steps.desc: If the investigation indicates credential compromise rather than authorized misuse, force a password/token reset and re-enroll MFA for the affected account.
steps.guidance: Reset credentials via IdP, revoke existing sessions/tokens, and require MFA re-registration.
steps.outcome: Compromised credential invalidated; account secured under new credentials.
steps.abort: Skip if investigation confirms authorized-user misuse rather than compromise; handle via HR/insider-threat process instead.

ITID-42114.def: General/unclassified VPN access exploitation: unauthorized use of, or abuse of a weakness in, remote-access VPN infrastructure that cannot yet be attributed to stale credentials, split-tunnel pivoting, or over-broad access scope.
ITID-42114.purpose: Serves as the intake bucket for VPN access exploitation cases that do not yet fit a more specific sibling leaf.
scopeIncludes: Any confirmed unauthorized VPN access pending root-cause classification
Novel VPN exploitation techniques not yet covered by a dedicated leaf
Initial triage of VPN anomalies before the specific mechanism is confirmed
scopeExcludes: Cases that have been root-caused to a departed-employee credential (ITID-42111)
Cases root-caused to split-tunnel pivoting (ITID-42112)
Cases root-caused to over-broad access scope (ITID-42113)
ITID-42114.severity: Default Medium-High pending triage; reassess once root cause is determined and reclassify to a specific leaf where possible.
ITID-42114.priority: P2 pending triage, escalating to P1 on confirmation of active unauthorized use.
ITID-42114.escalation: Escalate to SOC for triage; reclassify to the appropriate sibling ITID as soon as root cause is established.
indicators: Anomalous VPN authentication or session behavior not yet matched to a known pattern
Alerting from VPN concentrator/IAM tooling requiring manual investigation
vectors: Varies — captured here only until root cause is determined
rootCauses: To be determined via investigation; this leaf exists to avoid forcing premature classification
controls: MFA on VPN
VPN session anomaly monitoring
Standard incident triage workflow
ITID-42114.detection: Varies by underlying cause; general VPN anomaly detection provides the initial signal.
ITID-42114.response: Triage promptly, contain the session if unauthorized use is confirmed, and reclassify the record once root cause is established.
metrics: Count of records held in unclassified status beyond SLA
Time to reclassification
ITID-42114.notes: This is a catch-all/intake leaf; analysts should actively work to reclassify records out of it wherever a specific root cause can be established.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General VPN Access Exploitation
playbook.description: VPN access was exploited through means not matching a more specific known pattern (e.g., stolen credential used without MFA, unusual client fingerprint, or anomalous VPN login behavior), requiring general investigation to determine the exact method.

steps.title: Review VPN authentication and session logs for the flagged account
steps.desc: Pull authentication logs, source IP/geolocation, device fingerprint, and MFA status for the flagged VPN session(s) to characterize the anomaly.
steps.guidance: Look for indicators such as impossible travel, new/unrecognized device, missing or unusual MFA method, or connection from known-malicious infrastructure.
steps.outcome: Anomaly characterized with supporting evidence, narrowing the likely access method.
steps.abort: If logs show fully expected behavior consistent with the account holder's normal pattern, close as false positive.

steps.title: Disable the affected account and terminate active VPN sessions
steps.desc: Immediately disable the compromised VPN/directory account and forcibly terminate any active sessions.
steps.guidance: Disable in IdP/AD and revoke VPN session tokens/certificates.
steps.outcome: Account access halted; no further sessions possible.

steps.title: Reset credentials and enforce/verify MFA
steps.desc: Force a credential reset for the affected account and confirm MFA is properly enrolled and enforced for VPN access.
steps.guidance: Reset password/token, re-enroll MFA if needed, and confirm VPN policy enforces MFA with no bypass exceptions for this account.
steps.outcome: Account secured with strong credentials and enforced MFA.

steps.title: Restore legitimate access and monitor for recurrence
steps.desc: Restore the legitimate user's VPN access under new credentials/MFA and apply heightened monitoring for a defined period.
steps.guidance: Confirm user can authenticate normally; add temporary alerting on the account for anomalous access patterns.
steps.outcome: Legitimate access restored with no further anomalous activity observed during monitoring window.

steps.title: Document incident and close any organization-wide MFA/VPN gaps
steps.desc: Record the confirmed access method and, if a systemic gap was found (e.g., MFA exceptions, weak password policy), recommend organization-wide remediation.
steps.guidance: Escalate systemic findings to IAM/security architecture for policy update.
steps.outcome: Report filed; systemic gaps (if any) tracked for remediation.

steps.title: Determine the specific exploitation technique used
steps.desc: Based on initial findings, drill into the specific method (e.g., credential stuffing, phished credential, missing MFA enforcement, session token theft) so containment can be targeted.
steps.guidance: Interview the account holder if appropriate, check for phishing reports, review MFA enrollment/enforcement status for the account, and check for known-breached-credential matches.
steps.outcome: Root access-method identified and documented.

steps.title: Block identified malicious source infrastructure
steps.desc: Block the source IP(s) or infrastructure used in the unauthorized access at the perimeter firewall/VPN gateway.
steps.guidance: Add temporary deny rules; check threat intel feeds for related infrastructure to block proactively.
steps.outcome: Malicious source blocked from further connection attempts.
steps.abort: Skip if source is shared/dynamic consumer infrastructure where blocking has limited value.

ITID-42121.def: Capture of a wireless network's WPA2/WPA3 authentication handshake (or PMKID) followed by offline dictionary/brute-force cracking to recover the pre-shared key or credentials, enabling subsequent unauthorized network access.
ITID-42121.purpose: Captures an adversary defeating WPA2/WPA3 wireless encryption by capturing an authentication handshake and cracking it offline.
scopeIncludes: Passive or deauthentication-forced handshake capture against a corporate SSID
PMKID capture and offline cracking against WPA2-PSK networks
Successful key recovery followed by unauthorized association to the network
scopeExcludes: WPS PIN brute force, a distinct protocol weakness (ITID-42122)
Segmentation bypass once already associated to a guest network (ITID-42123)
Passive wireless sniffing for reconnaissance purposes without a cracking objective (ITID-42343)
ITID-42121.severity: High — successful cracking grants direct unauthorized network access under the guise of a legitimate wireless client.
ITID-42121.priority: P1 upon confirmed successful key recovery or unauthorized association; P2 for detected capture/deauthentication activity alone.
ITID-42121.escalation: Escalate to network security immediately on detection of deauthentication floods or rogue capture activity; rotate the PSK/certificates if compromise is suspected.
indicators: Burst of 802.11 deauthentication frames preceding a handshake capture
Wireless IDS alert for handshake/PMKID capture tooling signatures
Unauthorized device association using a key not issued through the normal provisioning process
vectors: Deauthentication attack to force a handshake capture
Passive capture near the facility using commodity wireless adversary tooling
PMKID capture without requiring client interaction
rootCauses: Weak/short pre-shared key vulnerable to offline cracking
Reliance on WPA2-PSK instead of enterprise (802.1X) authentication
No wireless intrusion detection covering the facility's RF footprint
controls: WPA3-Enterprise/802.1X authentication instead of shared PSK
Wireless intrusion detection/prevention system (WIDS/WIPS)
Strong, high-entropy PSK rotation policy where PSK must be used
Physical RF footprint minimization
ITID-42121.detection: Strong where WIDS/WIPS is deployed; weak-to-absent without dedicated wireless monitoring, since wired network logs show nothing until after association.
ITID-42121.response: Rotate credentials/keys, identify and remove the unauthorized associated device, and review WIDS coverage gaps that allowed the capture to go undetected.
metrics: Count of deauthentication/handshake-capture alerts per period
Percentage of corporate SSIDs on enterprise (802.1X) authentication
ITID-42121.notes: Differentiates from WPS brute force by targeting the WPA2/WPA3 handshake cryptography itself rather than a separate PIN-based provisioning mechanism.

playbook.name: WPA2/WPA3 Handshake Capture and Offline Cracking
playbook.description: An attacker within radio range captured a WPA2/WPA3 4-way handshake (or PMKID) and attempted or succeeded in offline dictionary/brute-force cracking of the wireless pre-shared key to gain network access.

steps.title: Detect handshake-capture/deauthentication indicators via wireless IDS
steps.desc: Review wireless intrusion detection system (WIDS) or AP controller logs for deauthentication flood activity or repeated association/handshake attempts characteristic of a capture attack, and identify the capturing device if detectable.
steps.guidance: Look for bursts of 802.11 deauth/disassoc frames, PMKID request anomalies, and unusual client MAC addresses probing the SSID.
steps.outcome: Confirmed handshake-capture attempt with timeframe, target SSID, and if possible, attacker device/location fingerprint (signal strength triangulation).
steps.abort: If no deauth/capture pattern is found, verify whether the alert was a false positive (e.g., legitimate client roaming).

steps.title: Rotate the affected wireless network's pre-shared key
steps.desc: Immediately change the PSK for the targeted SSID to invalidate any captured/cracked key.
steps.guidance: Push new PSK to the WLAN controller/AP configuration and redistribute to authorized users via secure channel.
steps.outcome: Old PSK invalidated; any device still using the old key is disconnected.

steps.title: Migrate to WPA3-Enterprise or 802.1X authentication where feasible
steps.desc: Reduce susceptibility to offline PSK cracking by migrating the affected SSID to certificate/RADIUS-based 802.1X authentication (WPA2/3-Enterprise) rather than a shared PSK.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with network team to plan a phased migration; if Enterprise auth is not immediately feasible, at minimum enforce a long, high-entropy PSK and disable WPS/PMKID-vulnerable fast-roaming features.
steps.outcome: SSID authentication hardened against offline handshake-cracking attacks.
steps.abort: If Enterprise migration is not feasible in the short term, document as an accepted risk with compensating controls (long PSK, WIDS monitoring) and a remediation timeline.

steps.title: Redistribute new credentials and verify legitimate device reconnection
steps.desc: Confirm all authorized devices reconnect successfully under the new PSK/authentication method and no service disruption persists.
steps.guidance: Spot-check a sample of authorized devices across affected locations.
steps.outcome: All legitimate devices reconnected; no lingering access issues.

steps.title: Document incident and update wireless security standard
steps.desc: Record findings and update the organization's wireless security baseline to require WPA3/802.1X and periodic WIDS review going forward.
steps.guidance: Include recommendation for periodic penetration testing of wireless infrastructure.
steps.outcome: Updated wireless security standard published.

steps.title: Determine whether the PSK was successfully cracked and used
steps.desc: Check for any subsequent successful wireless association using the SSID's PSK from an unrecognized device following the capture event.
steps.guidance: Cross-reference AP client association logs for new/unknown MAC addresses joining shortly after the capture window, and any downstream network activity from that client.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether the crack succeeded and network access was obtained, with scope of any resulting activity.

steps.title: Disconnect and block any unauthorized client identified on the network
steps.desc: If an unauthorized device successfully associated using the cracked key, forcibly disconnect it and block its MAC/deny it via NAC.
steps.guidance: Use WLAN controller to deauthenticate the rogue client and add a persistent block/deny entry.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized client removed from the network and blocked from reassociating.

ITID-42122.def: Brute-force attack against a wireless access point's WPS (Wi-Fi Protected Setup) PIN, exploiting the mechanism's limited PIN keyspace and weak lockout enforcement to recover the PIN and, from it, the WPA key.
ITID-42122.purpose: Captures exploitation of the WPS PIN mechanism to recover wireless network access independent of WPA2/WPA3 key strength.
scopeIncludes: Online or offline (Pixie Dust-style) brute force of an access point's WPS PIN
Access points with WPS enabled and no effective lockout after failed attempts
Recovery of the WPA passphrase via a cracked WPS PIN
scopeExcludes: Direct handshake capture/cracking against WPA2/WPA3 (ITID-42121)
Guest network segmentation bypass (ITID-42123)
ITID-42122.severity: High — WPS's short PIN keyspace makes this a comparatively fast path to full network key recovery.
ITID-42122.priority: P1 on confirmed PIN recovery/unauthorized association; P2 for detected brute-force attempt activity.
ITID-42122.escalation: Escalate to network security to disable WPS on the affected access point(s) and rotate the WPA key immediately.
indicators: High volume of WPS authentication attempts against a single access point
WIDS alert for known WPS brute-force/Pixie Dust tooling signatures
Unauthorized association shortly after a burst of WPS PIN attempts
vectors: Commodity WPS brute-force tooling run against consumer-grade or misconfigured enterprise access points
Pixie Dust offline attack against vulnerable chipset implementations
rootCauses: WPS left enabled on enterprise-grade access points where it is unnecessary
Access point firmware with weak/absent lockout enforcement after failed WPS attempts
Lack of asset inventory tracking which access points have WPS enabled
controls: Disable WPS on all enterprise access points
Wireless intrusion detection/prevention system
Firmware patching to address known WPS lockout bypass vulnerabilities
ITID-42122.detection: Moderate to strong where WIDS/WIPS is deployed; access point logs alone may show only a burst of authentication failures without RF-layer context.
ITID-42122.response: Disable WPS, rotate the WPA key, and confirm no unauthorized device remains associated.
metrics: Count of access points with WPS still enabled
Count of WPS brute-force alerts per period
ITID-42122.notes: Differentiates from ITID-42121 by targeting the WPS provisioning shortcut rather than the WPA2/WPA3 handshake itself.

playbook.name: WPS PIN Brute Force Exploitation
playbook.description: An attacker exploited an access point's Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS) feature by brute-forcing the 8-digit WPS PIN to recover the wireless PSK and gain unauthorized network access.

steps.title: Detect repeated WPS PIN attempt patterns
steps.desc: Review AP/WLAN controller logs for repeated WPS registration/PIN-entry attempts from a single client, characteristic of tools like Reaver/Bully.
steps.guidance: Look for high-frequency WPS M-message exchange failures/retries from the same MAC address over a short window.
steps.outcome: Confirmed WPS brute-force attempt with source device fingerprint and target AP identified.
steps.abort: If no repeated WPS attempt pattern is found, verify alert accuracy before proceeding.

steps.title: Disable WPS on the affected access point(s) immediately
steps.desc: Turn off the WPS feature on the targeted AP (and any other APs sharing the same configuration profile) to close the immediate attack surface.
steps.guidance: Disable WPS via AP/WLAN controller configuration; verify the setting takes effect (some AP firmware requires a reboot to fully disable WPS).
steps.outcome: WPS disabled and no longer exploitable on affected APs.

steps.title: Audit all access points for WPS enablement and disable organization-wide
steps.desc: Inventory all deployed APs to confirm WPS is disabled everywhere, not just on the targeted device, and update the AP baseline configuration/golden image accordingly.
steps.guidance: Use WLAN controller bulk configuration audit or manual check across all AP models/firmware in use; update provisioning templates.
steps.outcome: WPS confirmed disabled across the entire wireless estate and removed from future AP provisioning defaults.

steps.title: Verify legitimate device reconnection and AP configuration compliance
steps.desc: Confirm authorized devices reconnect under the new PSK and that all APs pass a post-remediation compliance scan for WPS disablement.
steps.guidance: Run a configuration compliance scan against the AP baseline.
steps.outcome: All APs compliant; legitimate users unaffected.

steps.title: Document incident and add WPS check to wireless hardening baseline
steps.desc: Record findings and formally add 'WPS disabled' as a mandatory checklist item in the wireless AP hardening standard and periodic audit.
steps.outcome: Hardening standard updated; periodic audit scheduled.

steps.title: Determine if the WPS PIN/PSK was successfully recovered and used
steps.desc: Check for a successful wireless association immediately following the brute-force attempt sequence, indicating the PIN was cracked and PSK extracted.
steps.guidance: Cross-reference AP association logs for a new client joining right after the WPS attempt burst ends.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether unauthorized network access was achieved via this method.

steps.title: Rotate the wireless PSK and block any unauthorized client
steps.desc: Change the SSID's PSK in case it was recovered, and disconnect/block any client that associated via the exploited WPS path.
steps.guidance: Push new PSK, force reconnection of legitimate clients, and add MAC-deny entries for any confirmed rogue client.
steps.outcome: PSK rotated; rogue client removed and blocked.

ITID-42123.def: Exploitation of an inadequately enforced network segmentation boundary between a guest wireless SSID and the internal corporate network, allowing a device associated to the guest network to reach corporate resources it should have no route to.
ITID-42123.purpose: Captures an adversary breaking out of an intentionally-isolated guest wireless network to reach the internal corporate network.
scopeIncludes: VLAN hopping or routing misconfiguration allowing guest wireless traffic onto corporate subnets
Shared infrastructure (e.g., switch/AP) between guest and corporate SSIDs without effective isolation
Client isolation bypass allowing peer-to-peer or upstream reach from the guest network
scopeExcludes: Cracking the guest or corporate wireless key itself (ITID-42121/ITID-42122)
Firewall rule misconfiguration unrelated to wireless segmentation (ITID-42131-42134)
ITID-42123.severity: High — a network explicitly designed to be untrusted is bridging into the trusted environment.
ITID-42123.priority: P1 upon confirmed traffic crossing from guest to corporate segments; P2 for identified segmentation gaps without confirmed exploitation.
ITID-42123.escalation: Escalate to network engineering to correct VLAN/ACL segmentation immediately; treat any confirmed crossing as a potential precursor to broader intrusion.
indicators: Traffic from guest-SSID-assigned IP ranges observed on internal/corporate subnets
Firewall/switch logs showing inter-VLAN routing where none should exist
Device discovered on the corporate network with a MAC/DHCP lease history tied to the guest SSID
vectors: VLAN hopping (e.g., double tagging) from the guest network
Misconfigured router/firewall ACL permitting guest-to-corporate routing
Shared DNS/DHCP infrastructure inadvertently bridging segments
rootCauses: Guest network built on shared physical infrastructure without proper VLAN enforcement
Firewall rule between guest and corporate VLANs never implemented or later disabled
No periodic segmentation testing validating guest network isolation
controls: Dedicated physical or strongly enforced logical segmentation for guest wireless
Periodic segmentation validation testing
Default-deny firewall policy between guest and corporate VLANs
ITID-42123.detection: Moderate — requires network flow monitoring capable of distinguishing guest-origin traffic reaching corporate segments; often only found via segmentation testing.
ITID-42123.response: Correct the segmentation gap immediately, audit for evidence of prior crossings, and validate no corporate systems were accessed improperly.
metrics: Count of segmentation validation tests passed/failed per cycle
Time to remediate confirmed segmentation gaps
ITID-42123.notes: This leaf is about the segmentation boundary failing, not about compromising the guest network's own wireless key.

playbook.name: Guest Wireless Network Segmentation Bypass to Reach Corporate Network
playbook.description: An attacker connected to the organization's guest wireless network and exploited insufficient network segmentation to reach internal corporate systems that should have been isolated from guest traffic.

steps.title: Confirm guest-to-corporate traffic crossing the segmentation boundary
steps.desc: Review firewall/VLAN routing logs between the guest wireless VLAN and internal corporate VLANs to confirm and characterize traffic that should have been blocked.
steps.guidance: Check firewall logs at the guest VLAN gateway for allowed connections into internal subnets, and inter-VLAN routing/ACL configuration for the gap.
steps.outcome: Confirmed segmentation bypass with source guest client, destination internal system(s), and traffic type documented.
steps.abort: If no cross-VLAN traffic is found, verify whether the alert was triggered by legitimate guest-network-only activity.

steps.title: Block the offending guest client and enforce segmentation at the firewall
steps.desc: Immediately block the guest client's MAC/IP and apply an emergency firewall rule enforcing default-deny between the guest VLAN and internal corporate VLANs.
steps.guidance: Add explicit deny-all rule from guest VLAN to internal VLANs except only truly required internet-bound egress; disconnect the identified client from the guest SSID.
steps.outcome: Guest-to-corporate traffic blocked; offending client disconnected.

steps.title: Rebuild guest network segmentation with verified default-deny policy
steps.desc: Redesign and validate the guest VLAN firewall/ACL configuration to enforce true isolation from all internal corporate segments, with only explicitly required, narrowly-scoped exceptions.
steps.guidance: Conduct a segmentation test (internal pen-test style scan from the guest VLAN) after reconfiguration to confirm no internal reachability remains.
steps.outcome: Verified, tested default-deny segmentation between guest and corporate networks.

steps.title: Restore guest network service and confirm internal systems unaffected
steps.desc: Restore guest wireless service under the corrected segmentation and confirm previously-reached internal systems show no signs of compromise.
steps.guidance: Run integrity checks on affected internal systems before releasing them from heightened monitoring.
steps.outcome: Guest network operational under verified isolation; internal systems confirmed clean.

steps.title: Document incident and institute recurring segmentation validation testing
steps.desc: Record root cause and remediation, and establish periodic (e.g., quarterly) automated segmentation testing between guest and corporate networks.
steps.outcome: Recurring segmentation test scheduled and documented.

steps.title: Assess what internal systems/data were accessed from the guest network
steps.desc: Determine which internal systems the guest client reached and what actions were taken, to gauge impact.
steps.guidance: Correlate with internal system access/authentication logs for connections originating from the guest VLAN IP range.
steps.outcome: Documented scope of internal exposure and any data/systems compromised.

steps.title: Isolate any internal systems reached from the guest network pending review
steps.desc: If internal systems were accessed, place them under heightened monitoring or temporary network isolation pending integrity verification.
steps.guidance: Apply temporary access restrictions or enhanced logging on affected internal hosts.
steps.outcome: Affected internal systems contained pending eradication/verification.
steps.abort: Skip if no internal systems were actually reached beyond the network layer.

ITID-42124.def: General/unclassified exploitation of wireless network infrastructure that cannot yet be attributed to handshake cracking, WPS brute force, or guest-network segmentation bypass.
ITID-42124.purpose: Serves as the intake bucket for wireless network exploitation cases that do not yet fit a more specific sibling leaf.
scopeIncludes: Any confirmed unauthorized wireless access pending root-cause classification
Novel wireless exploitation techniques not yet covered by a dedicated leaf
scopeExcludes: Cases root-caused to handshake capture/cracking (ITID-42121)
Cases root-caused to WPS brute force (ITID-42122)
Cases root-caused to guest segmentation bypass (ITID-42123)
ITID-42124.severity: Default Medium-High pending triage; reassess once root cause is determined.
ITID-42124.priority: P2 pending triage, escalating to P1 on confirmation of active unauthorized use.
ITID-42124.escalation: Escalate to SOC/network security for triage; reclassify once root cause is established.
indicators: WIDS/WIPS alert not yet matched to a known attack pattern
Unexplained unauthorized association to a corporate SSID
vectors: Varies — captured here only until root cause is determined
rootCauses: To be determined via investigation
controls: Wireless intrusion detection/prevention system
Standard incident triage workflow
ITID-42124.detection: Varies by underlying cause; general WIDS/WIPS alerting provides the initial signal.
ITID-42124.response: Triage promptly, contain unauthorized association if confirmed, and reclassify the record once root cause is established.
metrics: Count of records held in unclassified status beyond SLA
Time to reclassification
ITID-42124.notes: This is a catch-all/intake leaf; analysts should actively work to reclassify records out of it wherever a specific root cause can be established.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Wireless Network Exploitation
playbook.description: Wireless network access was exploited through a method not matching a more specific known pattern, requiring general investigation into the wireless attack vector used.

steps.title: Review wireless IDS and AP logs for anomalous activity
steps.desc: Review WIDS alerts, AP association/authentication logs, and RF spectrum anomalies to characterize the nature of the wireless exploitation.
steps.guidance: Look for rogue AP presence, evil-twin SSIDs, unusual authentication failures/successes, or unexpected client behavior.
steps.outcome: Wireless exploitation method characterized with supporting evidence.
steps.abort: If no supporting evidence is found, close as false positive.

steps.title: Disconnect and block the offending device/AP
steps.desc: Remove the identified rogue device or malicious client from the wireless environment and block it from reassociating.
steps.guidance: Use WLAN controller deauthentication and MAC-deny listing; if a rogue/evil-twin AP is involved, physically locate and remove it where possible.
steps.outcome: Malicious wireless presence removed from the environment.

steps.title: Remediate the specific wireless configuration weakness identified
steps.desc: Based on the confirmed technique, close the specific gap (e.g., weak encryption, missing WIDS coverage, unmanaged AP) that enabled the exploitation.
steps.guidance: Tailor remediation to root cause found during identification; escalate to network architecture if a broader design change is needed.
steps.outcome: Root-cause wireless configuration weakness closed.

steps.title: Verify wireless environment integrity and restore normal operation
steps.desc: Confirm the wireless environment is free of rogue devices/configurations and legitimate users are unaffected.
steps.guidance: Run a wireless site survey/audit post-remediation.
steps.outcome: Clean wireless environment confirmed; normal operations restored.

steps.title: Document incident and update wireless monitoring coverage
steps.desc: Record findings and evaluate whether WIDS/WIPS coverage needs expansion to detect similar attacks earlier.
steps.outcome: Report filed; monitoring gaps (if any) tracked for remediation.

steps.title: Determine scope of unauthorized access or data exposure
steps.desc: Assess what network access, if any, was achieved and what systems/data were reached as a result.
steps.guidance: Correlate wireless association logs with downstream internal network/system access logs.
steps.outcome: Documented scope of impact.

steps.title: Rotate affected wireless credentials
steps.desc: Change the PSK or force credential reset for any SSID/account implicated in the exploitation.
steps.guidance: Push updated credentials and redistribute securely to authorized users.
steps.outcome: Previously exposed credentials invalidated.
steps.abort: Skip if no credential exposure is indicated by the investigation.

ITID-42131.def: Exploitation of an inbound firewall rule that is broader than necessary (e.g., overly wide IP/port ranges, 'any' source) to reach an internal service that should not be directly exposed, resulting in unauthorized network access.
ITID-42131.purpose: Captures external unauthorized network access enabled by a firewall rule that permits far more inbound traffic than intended.
scopeIncludes: Rule permitting inbound access from 'any' source to a service intended only for a limited partner or internal range
Overly broad port range opened for a single required port
Successful connection/exploitation attributable to the overly permissive rule
scopeExcludes: A rule left open after a maintenance window that should have been reverted (ITID-42132)
A rule specifically exposing a management interface (ITID-42133)
Exploitation of a vulnerable service reached through a correctly-scoped rule (covered under the relevant vulnerability/exploit ITIDs)
ITID-42131.severity: High — directly exposes internal services to a far larger population of potential attackers than intended.
ITID-42131.priority: P1 upon confirmed connection/exploitation via the rule; P2 for identified overly permissive rules without confirmed exploitation.
ITID-42131.escalation: Escalate to network/firewall engineering to tighten the rule immediately; escalate to IR if traffic indicates active exploitation.
indicators: Inbound connections from unexpected/global source IP ranges hitting an internal service
Firewall rule audit finding source scope far broader than the documented business requirement
Connection attempts from known scanning/attacker infrastructure succeeding where they should have been blocked
vectors: Internet-wide scanning discovering and connecting through the overly broad rule
Targeted reconnaissance identifying the exposed rule via port scanning
Automated exploitation tooling probing exposed services
rootCauses: Firewall change requests approved without least-privilege scoping review
Rule created broadly 'to be safe' during initial setup and never tightened
No periodic firewall rule audit/attestation process
controls: Least-privilege firewall change management process
Periodic firewall rule audit and attestation
Automated rule-scope linting/policy-as-code validation
Network segmentation limiting blast radius of any single exposed rule
ITID-42131.detection: Strong — firewall logs and connection telemetry directly show traffic traversing the overly permissive rule once flagged for review.
ITID-42131.response: Tighten the rule to least-privilege scope immediately, review connection logs for evidence of exploitation, and trace the change-management gap that allowed the rule to exist.
metrics: Count of overly permissive rules identified per audit cycle
Mean time to remediate flagged rules
ITID-42131.notes: The distinguishing factor from ITID-42132 is that the rule was wrong from creation, not left open after a legitimate temporary need.

playbook.name: Overly Permissive Inbound Firewall Rule Exploited
playbook.description: An overly broad inbound firewall rule (e.g., any-any, or a wide port/IP range beyond business need) exposed an internal service to the internet or an untrusted zone, and was exploited to gain unauthorized access.

steps.title: Identify the offending firewall rule and exposed service
steps.desc: Locate the specific inbound rule permitting the unauthorized traffic and identify the internal service/host it exposed.
steps.guidance: Review firewall rule base and change history for rules with broad source (e.g., 0.0.0.0/0) or broad port ranges; correlate with the exploited connection's timestamp and destination.
steps.outcome: Offending rule identified along with the exposed service and when the rule was introduced.

steps.title: Restrict or remove the overly permissive firewall rule immediately
steps.desc: Tighten the rule to the minimum required source/destination/port scope, or disable it entirely if not business-justified.
steps.guidance: Verify with the service/application owner what legitimate access is actually required before finalizing the restricted rule.
steps.outcome: Rule scoped to least privilege or removed; unauthorized access path closed.
steps.abort: If the service has a legitimate broad-access business need, apply compensating controls (WAF, IP allow-listing, additional authentication) rather than full removal.

steps.title: Remediate the exposed host and review firewall change-control process
steps.desc: Clean/rebuild the exposed host as needed based on compromise findings, and review how the overly permissive rule was introduced to prevent recurrence.
steps.guidance: Determine whether the rule resulted from a change-control bypass, a misconfigured template, or lack of periodic review, and address that process gap.
steps.outcome: Host remediated; process gap that allowed the permissive rule identified and addressed.

steps.title: Validate firewall rule base against least-privilege baseline
steps.desc: Run a full firewall rule audit to confirm no other similarly overly permissive rules exist, and restore normal service under the corrected rule.
steps.guidance: Use automated firewall policy analysis tooling if available to flag other broad/any-any rules.
steps.outcome: Firewall rule base confirmed compliant with least-privilege standard.

steps.title: Document incident and implement recurring firewall rule review
steps.desc: Record findings and establish a recurring (e.g., quarterly) firewall rule review/certification process with change-control enforcement for new rules.
steps.outcome: Recurring review process documented and scheduled.

steps.title: Determine exploitation activity against the exposed service
steps.desc: Review logs on the exposed service/host to determine what actions the attacker performed once access was gained (e.g., login attempts, exploitation of a vulnerability, data access).
steps.guidance: Check host/application logs, EDR telemetry, and any subsequent lateral movement or persistence indicators.
steps.outcome: Full picture of attacker activity following exploitation of the exposed rule.

steps.title: Isolate the exposed host pending compromise verification
steps.desc: If the exposed service/host shows signs of compromise, isolate it from the rest of the internal network while eradication proceeds.
steps.guidance: Apply EDR network isolation or a temporary internal firewall segmentation rule.
steps.outcome: Potentially compromised host contained from further lateral spread.
steps.abort: Skip if no compromise indicators are found on the host beyond the exposure itself.

ITID-42132.def: Exploitation of a firewall rule that was legitimately opened to support a temporary maintenance window, migration, or vendor task and was not reverted afterward, leaving an unintended exposure window that an adversary later used.
ITID-42132.purpose: Captures unauthorized access enabled by a firewall rule that was appropriately created for a temporary need but never closed afterward.
scopeIncludes: Rule opened for a scheduled maintenance/change window and left active past its intended expiry
Temporary vendor/contractor access rule never removed after the task concluded
Exploitation occurring any time after the rule's intended close date
scopeExcludes: A rule that was overly broad from the moment it was created (ITID-42131)
A rule specifically exposing a management interface (ITID-42133)
ITID-42132.severity: Medium-High, escalating to High the longer the rule remained open and the more sensitive the exposed service.
ITID-42132.priority: P1 upon confirmed exploitation; P2 upon discovery of an expired-but-still-open rule with no confirmed exploitation.
ITID-42132.escalation: Escalate to change management/network engineering to close the rule immediately and to review the change-management process failure.
indicators: Firewall rule with a documented expiry/maintenance-window date that has passed and remains enabled
Connections to the exposed service occurring well after the associated maintenance ticket was closed
Audit finding a rule with no corresponding active change record
vectors: Opportunistic scanning discovering the still-open rule after the maintenance window
Reconnaissance specifically timed around known/observed maintenance windows
rootCauses: No automated expiry/rollback for temporary firewall changes
Change management process lacking a mandatory close-out/revert step
Maintenance rule changes tracked outside the standard change ticketing system
controls: Automated time-bound (expiring) firewall rules for temporary changes
Mandatory change-management close-out/revert verification
Periodic firewall rule audit and attestation
ITID-42132.detection: Strong once rule-expiry tracking exists; weak without it, since the rule looks legitimate absent a corresponding maintenance record.
ITID-42132.response: Close the rule immediately, review connection logs since the intended expiry date, and add the rule to the audit trail for change-management remediation.
metrics: Count of expired-but-still-open rules found per audit cycle
Average dwell time of temporary rules past their intended close date
ITID-42132.notes: The distinguishing factor from ITID-42131 is process/lifecycle failure on an otherwise appropriately-scoped rule, not an incorrectly broad rule from the start.

playbook.name: Firewall Rule Left Open After Temporary Maintenance Window
playbook.description: A firewall rule opened to support a temporary maintenance or testing window was never closed afterward, leaving an unauthorized access path open that was later exploited.

steps.title: Identify the stale maintenance rule and its original change record
steps.desc: Locate the firewall rule exploited and trace it back to the original change ticket/request to confirm it was intended to be temporary.
steps.guidance: Review firewall change-management records for a ticket referencing the rule with an expected removal/expiration date that was never actioned.
steps.outcome: Confirmed the rule originated from a temporary change that was not reverted, with original ticket and intended expiration documented.

steps.title: Close the stale firewall rule immediately
steps.desc: Remove or disable the temporary rule that was never reverted.
steps.guidance: Confirm with the original requestor/system owner that the maintenance window has long passed and the rule is no longer needed before removal.
steps.outcome: Stale rule removed; unauthorized access path closed.

steps.title: Remediate the exposed system and implement rule-expiration enforcement
steps.desc: Clean/rebuild the exposed system as needed, and implement a technical or process control that automatically expires or flags temporary firewall rules for review at their intended end date.
steps.guidance: Where the firewall platform supports scheduled/time-bound rules, use that feature; otherwise implement a tracked expiration date field in the change-management system with automated reminder/removal workflow.
steps.outcome: System remediated; automated or enforced expiration control implemented for temporary rules.
steps.tool: EDR / firewall management console / change-management system

steps.title: Audit all active firewall rules for other unexpired temporary changes
steps.desc: Sweep the full firewall rule base for other rules originating from maintenance/temporary change tickets that were never closed.
steps.guidance: Cross-reference change-management ticket history against the current live rule set.
steps.outcome: All other stale temporary rules identified and remediated.

steps.title: Document incident and update change-management process for temporary rules
steps.desc: Record findings and formalize a mandatory rule-expiration/review step in the change-management workflow for any temporary firewall change.
steps.outcome: Updated change-management process documented and communicated to network operations.

steps.title: Determine exploitation activity through the stale rule
steps.desc: Review logs to determine what access/activity occurred through the stale rule, and how long it was exposed before exploitation.
steps.guidance: Correlate firewall traffic logs for the rule's source/destination with host/application logs on the affected system.
steps.outcome: Documented exposure window and confirmed scope of exploitation.

steps.title: Assess and isolate the exposed system if compromise indicators are found
steps.desc: If exploitation activity indicates the exposed system was compromised, isolate it pending further investigation.
steps.guidance: Apply EDR isolation or internal segmentation controls.
steps.outcome: Compromised system contained.
steps.abort: Skip if no compromise indicators found beyond the exposure itself.
