ITID-42133.def: Exploitation of a firewall misconfiguration that exposes a management-plane interface (e.g., router/switch admin UI, hypervisor management, out-of-band management) to a network segment or the internet where it should only be reachable from a dedicated, restricted management network.
ITID-42133.purpose: Captures unauthorized access to a network device's or system's administrative management interface caused by a firewall rule that should have kept it internal-only.
scopeIncludes: Router/switch/firewall admin interface reachable from a general user VLAN or the internet
Hypervisor/iLO/iDRAC/BMC management interface exposed outside the dedicated management network
Successful connection attempt or exploitation via the exposed management interface
scopeExcludes: General overly permissive rule exposing a non-management service (ITID-42131)
Rule left open after maintenance that does not involve a management interface (ITID-42132)
ITID-42133.severity: Critical — compromise of a management interface can yield control over the network infrastructure itself.
ITID-42133.priority: P1 immediately upon discovery, regardless of confirmed exploitation.
ITID-42133.escalation: Escalate immediately to network engineering leadership and IR; treat as a potential precursor to full infrastructure compromise until ruled out.
indicators: Connection attempts to management ports/interfaces from outside the designated management network
Firewall/ACL audit finding management VLAN reachable from general-purpose segments
Authentication attempts against device admin interfaces from unexpected sources
vectors: Internet-wide or internal scanning identifying exposed management interfaces
Credential brute force or default-credential exploitation against the exposed interface
Exploitation of known management-plane vulnerabilities once reachable
rootCauses: Management network not properly isolated (out-of-band) from production/user segments
Firewall/ACL rule error exposing the management VLAN
Devices shipped/deployed with management interfaces reachable by default and never restricted
controls: Dedicated out-of-band management network with strict access control
Firewall rule restricting management interfaces to designated jump hosts only
MFA on all management-plane authentication
Periodic exposure scanning for management interfaces
ITID-42133.detection: Strong once dedicated exposure-scanning for management interfaces is in place; otherwise this often goes undetected until actively exploited.
ITID-42133.response: Restrict the interface immediately, rotate credentials on the affected device(s), and treat any confirmed connection as a potential infrastructure-compromise incident requiring full device integrity review.
metrics: Count of management interfaces found exposed per scan cycle
Mean time to remediate exposed management interfaces
ITID-42133.notes: This is the highest-severity of the firewall misconfiguration siblings because it targets the control plane of the network itself, not an end-user service.

playbook.name: Firewall Rule Misconfiguration Exposing Internal Management Interface
playbook.description: A firewall misconfiguration exposed the management interface of an internal device or application (e.g., router admin panel, hypervisor console, application admin UI) to an untrusted network, and it was accessed without authorization.

steps.title: Identify the exposed management interface and the firewall gap allowing reach
steps.desc: Determine which device/application management interface was reachable and trace the specific firewall rule or missing rule that allowed the exposure.
steps.guidance: Review firewall rule base and traffic logs for connections to the management port/interface from an untrusted zone; confirm the interface's intended access scope per network design documentation.
steps.outcome: Exposed interface and the enabling firewall gap identified and documented.
steps.tool: Firewall management console / network design documentation

steps.title: Close the firewall gap exposing the management interface
steps.desc: Restrict the firewall rule so the management interface is reachable only from the designated management network/jump host.
steps.guidance: Apply the correct source restriction (e.g., management VLAN or bastion host IP only) and verify via test connection that broader access is blocked.
steps.outcome: Management interface no longer reachable from untrusted networks.

steps.title: Revert unauthorized configuration changes and harden management-plane access
steps.desc: Restore the device to its verified-clean configuration and implement management-plane hardening (dedicated management VLAN, jump-host-only access, disabled unused management protocols).
steps.guidance: Restore from known-good backup where changes were malicious; disable any insecure management protocols (e.g., unencrypted Telnet/HTTP) in favor of SSH/HTTPS with restricted source.
steps.outcome: Device restored to trusted configuration with hardened management-plane access.

steps.title: Verify device integrity and restore normal operation
steps.desc: Confirm the device is functioning normally under the corrected configuration and access restrictions.
steps.guidance: Run functional verification tests appropriate to the device type.
steps.outcome: Device confirmed operational and secure.

steps.title: Document incident and add management-interface exposure to recurring audit scope
steps.desc: Record findings and add management-interface exposure checks to the recurring firewall/network configuration audit.
steps.outcome: Recurring audit scope updated and documented.

steps.title: Determine whether the management interface was accessed and what actions were taken
steps.desc: Review the device/application's own access and audit logs to determine if login attempts succeeded and what configuration changes, if any, were made.
steps.guidance: Check device authentication logs, configuration change history, and any newly created accounts or altered settings on the exposed device.
steps.outcome: Confirmed access outcome and any unauthorized configuration changes documented.
steps.abort: If logs show no successful authentication or exploitation attempt, downgrade to an exposure finding rather than confirmed compromise.

steps.title: Reset credentials and review configuration on the exposed device
steps.desc: If unauthorized access is confirmed, reset all administrative credentials on the device and review its current configuration for unauthorized changes.
steps.guidance: Compare current running configuration against last-known-good backup to identify any tampering.
steps.outcome: Credentials rotated; unauthorized configuration changes identified for reversal.
steps.abort: Skip credential reset if investigation confirms no successful authentication occurred.
steps.tool: Device admin console / configuration backup system

steps.title: Audit other devices for the same class of management-interface exposure
steps.desc: Scan the environment for other devices/applications whose management interfaces may be similarly exposed due to the same or a related firewall misconfiguration pattern.
steps.guidance: Run an internal exposure scan against known management ports from untrusted zones across the environment.
steps.outcome: All similarly exposed management interfaces identified and remediated.

ITID-42134.def: General/unclassified exploitation of a misconfigured firewall rule that cannot yet be attributed to an overly permissive rule, an expired temporary rule, or exposure of a management interface.
ITID-42134.purpose: Serves as the intake bucket for firewall misconfiguration exploitation cases that do not yet fit a more specific sibling leaf.
scopeIncludes: Any confirmed unauthorized access via a firewall misconfiguration pending root-cause classification
Novel firewall misconfiguration patterns not yet covered by a dedicated leaf
scopeExcludes: Cases root-caused to an overly permissive inbound rule (ITID-42131)
Cases root-caused to an expired maintenance rule (ITID-42132)
Cases root-caused to management interface exposure (ITID-42133)
ITID-42134.severity: Default Medium-High pending triage; reassess once root cause is determined.
ITID-42134.priority: P2 pending triage, escalating to P1 on confirmation of active unauthorized use.
ITID-42134.escalation: Escalate to SOC/network security for triage; reclassify once root cause is established.
indicators: Firewall log anomaly not yet matched to a known misconfiguration pattern
vectors: Varies — captured here only until root cause is determined
rootCauses: To be determined via investigation
controls: Standard incident triage workflow
Periodic firewall rule audit
ITID-42134.detection: Varies by underlying cause; general firewall log review provides the initial signal.
ITID-42134.response: Triage promptly, contain unauthorized access if confirmed, and reclassify the record once root cause is established.
metrics: Count of records held in unclassified status beyond SLA
Time to reclassification
ITID-42134.notes: This is a catch-all/intake leaf; analysts should actively work to reclassify records out of it wherever a specific root cause can be established.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Misconfigured Firewall Rule Exploitation
playbook.description: A firewall misconfiguration not matching a more specific known pattern was exploited to gain unauthorized network access, requiring general investigation to characterize the exact misconfiguration.

steps.title: Identify the exploited firewall rule and traffic pattern
steps.desc: Review firewall logs and rule base to identify the specific rule that permitted the unauthorized traffic and characterize the type of misconfiguration.
steps.guidance: Look for unexpected allow entries, incorrect zone assignments, NAT misconfigurations, or rule-ordering errors that produced unintended permit behavior.
steps.outcome: Offending rule and misconfiguration type documented.
steps.abort: If no misconfiguration is found and traffic was in fact intentionally permitted, close as false positive.

steps.title: Correct the misconfigured firewall rule
steps.desc: Fix the rule to enforce the intended access policy and verify the fix closes the unauthorized path without breaking legitimate traffic.
steps.guidance: Test the corrected rule against both the unauthorized traffic pattern (should now be blocked) and known legitimate use cases (should still pass).
steps.outcome: Rule corrected; unauthorized access path closed.

steps.title: Remediate affected systems and review firewall change process for the root cause
steps.desc: Remediate any compromised system and identify how the misconfiguration was introduced (manual error, template defect, missing peer review) to prevent recurrence.
steps.guidance: Escalate a process fix (e.g., mandatory peer review for firewall changes) if the root cause was procedural.
steps.outcome: Systems remediated; process gap addressed.

steps.title: Audit firewall rule base for similar misconfiguration patterns
steps.desc: Run a broader review of the rule base for other instances of the same class of misconfiguration.
steps.guidance: Use automated firewall policy analysis tooling where available.
steps.outcome: No further instances of the same misconfiguration found, or all identified and corrected.

steps.title: Document incident and reinforce firewall change-control review
steps.desc: Record findings and reinforce or introduce mandatory peer review/testing for firewall rule changes going forward.
steps.outcome: Change-control process reinforced and documented.

steps.title: Assess scope of unauthorized access enabled by the misconfiguration
steps.desc: Determine what systems/data were reachable and accessed as a result of the misconfigured rule.
steps.guidance: Correlate firewall logs with destination host/application logs for the relevant time window.
steps.outcome: Documented scope of exposure and any confirmed unauthorized access.

steps.title: Isolate any system confirmed accessed through the misconfiguration
steps.desc: If a system was reached and shows signs of compromise, isolate it pending further investigation.
steps.guidance: Apply EDR isolation or internal network segmentation.
steps.outcome: Potentially compromised system contained.
steps.abort: Skip if no compromise indicators found.

ITID-42141.def: Compromise or abuse of a third-party vendor's remote access tool (e.g., remote support software, always-on jump box, IoT/OT vendor agent) that maintains standing connectivity into the internal network, giving an adversary who compromises the vendor's infrastructure or the tool itself a persistent path in.
ITID-42141.purpose: Captures the risk created when a vendor's remote access tool maintains a persistent, always-on connection into the network rather than being invoked only when needed.
scopeIncludes: Vendor remote-support agent configured for continuous rather than on-demand connectivity
Compromise of vendor-side infrastructure used to reach the always-on tool
Abuse of the standing connection by a party other than the intended vendor technician
scopeExcludes: A shared vendor VPN credential used by multiple people (ITID-42142)
Vendor access not revoked after contract end (ITID-42143)
ITID-42141.severity: High — a standing connection is a persistent, often under-monitored path into the network independent of any single authentication event.
ITID-42141.priority: P1 upon any confirmed unauthorized activity over the connection; P2 for identified always-on tools without confirmed abuse.
ITID-42141.escalation: Escalate to vendor management and network security to convert the connection to on-demand/just-in-time access, and to IR if abuse is confirmed.
indicators: Vendor remote-access tool showing connectivity outside scheduled/expected support windows
Traffic from the vendor connection to systems unrelated to the vendor's scope of support
Vendor's own security advisory disclosing a compromise of their remote-support platform
vectors: Supply-chain compromise of the vendor's remote-support platform
Credential theft against the vendor's technicians
Abuse of the always-on tunnel by an insider at the vendor
rootCauses: Vendor tool configured for convenience as always-on rather than just-in-time
No monitoring of vendor connection activity against an expected usage baseline
Vendor risk assessment not covering the security posture of their remote-access tooling
controls: Just-in-time/on-demand vendor access provisioning
Monitoring of vendor connection activity against expected support windows
Network segmentation limiting vendor tool reach to only the systems it supports
Vendor security assessment covering remote-access tooling
ITID-42141.detection: Moderate — requires baselining expected vendor activity patterns; without a baseline, standing connections generate little distinguishable signal.
ITID-42141.response: Convert to just-in-time access, investigate all activity over the connection for the review period, and coordinate with the vendor on their own compromise investigation if applicable.
metrics: Count/percentage of vendor connections converted from always-on to just-in-time
Count of anomalous vendor connection activity alerts
detections: Vendor connection activity baseline deviation alert
ITID-42141.notes: The differentiator from sibling leaves is the standing/persistent nature of the connection itself as the risk driver.

playbook.name: Vendor Remote Access Tool with Standing/Always-On Network Access
playbook.description: A third-party vendor's remote access tool was configured with persistent, always-on network access rather than access granted only during authorized support sessions, and this standing access was exploited for unauthorized entry.

steps.title: Identify the vendor remote access tool and its access scope/configuration
steps.desc: Locate the vendor remote-access tool (e.g., remote support agent, always-on tunnel) involved, and document its configured network reach and whether it requires session approval or connects unattended.
steps.guidance: Review the tool's admin console, firewall rules permitting its traffic, and vendor contract/SOW for the intended access model.
steps.outcome: Confirmed the tool was configured for standing access rather than session-based access, with scope documented.
steps.tool: Vendor remote-access tool admin console / firewall config

steps.title: Disable standing access and require session-based approval
steps.desc: Immediately revoke the vendor tool's persistent network access and reconfigure it (or firewall rules) to require explicit, time-boxed approval for each support session.
steps.guidance: Disable the always-on tunnel/agent connectivity at the firewall or tool configuration; implement a break-glass or ticket-triggered access enablement process.
steps.outcome: Standing access removed; vendor access now requires per-session authorization.
steps.abort: If disabling breaks a critical support SLA, apply an interim compensating control (enhanced session logging/alerting) while transitioning to session-based access.
steps.tool: Firewall management console / vendor tool admin console

steps.title: Implement vendor access lifecycle management for remote access tools
steps.desc: Establish a formal process requiring vendor remote-access tools to use time-boxed, ticket-triggered access with automatic expiration, reviewed as part of vendor onboarding and periodic vendor access recertification.
steps.guidance: Work with vendor management and IAM teams to define the standard and apply it to this and other vendor remote-access integrations.
steps.outcome: Formal vendor remote-access lifecycle process implemented, eliminating standing access by default.

steps.title: Validate vendor support capability under the new access model
steps.desc: Confirm the vendor can still perform legitimate support functions under the new session-based, time-boxed access model.
steps.guidance: Run a test support session with the vendor to confirm the approval workflow functions as intended.
steps.outcome: Vendor support confirmed functional under the corrected access model.

steps.title: Document incident and extend review to all vendor standing-access integrations
steps.desc: Record findings and initiate a review of all other third-party vendor remote-access tools for similar standing-access risk.
steps.guidance: Include recommendation for annual vendor access recertification.
steps.outcome: Broader vendor access review initiated and documented.

steps.title: Determine unauthorized activity conducted through the standing access
steps.desc: Review session logs from the remote access tool to identify connections and activity outside of approved support windows or scope.
steps.guidance: Cross-reference tool session logs against the vendor's approved support ticket history to identify any unapproved or unattended session activity.
steps.outcome: Documented unauthorized session activity, timing, and actions taken.
steps.abort: If all sessions correlate to approved support tickets, close as expected vendor activity and address only the standing-access design issue.

steps.title: Rotate vendor credentials/tokens associated with the tool
steps.desc: Reset any credentials, API keys, or tokens the vendor tool used, in case they were compromised.
steps.guidance: Coordinate the rotation with the vendor to avoid unplanned support disruption.
steps.outcome: Vendor credentials invalidated and reissued securely.

steps.title: Coordinate with the vendor relationship manager to validate findings
steps.desc: Engage the internal vendor relationship manager and the vendor's security point of contact to corroborate session activity and determine if the vendor's own credentials/tool were compromised.
steps.guidance: Request the vendor's own audit logs for the tool/account in question and confirm whether the activity originated from their environment or was spoofed.
steps.outcome: Joint understanding established of whether the vendor or an external attacker is responsible for the unauthorized activity.

ITID-42142.def: Unauthorized or unattributable network access resulting from a vendor VPN credential that is shared among multiple individuals at the vendor organization, breaking individual accountability and making it impossible to attribute or fully contain access when misuse or compromise occurs.
ITID-42142.purpose: Captures the accountability and containment failure that results when a single vendor VPN credential is shared across multiple vendor employees.
scopeIncludes: A single vendor VPN account used by more than one vendor employee
Inability to attribute a specific session to an individual due to credential sharing
Compromise of the shared credential exposing access to all who had it, not just the compromised individual
scopeExcludes: A standing always-on vendor connection (ITID-42141)
Access not revoked after contract termination (ITID-42143)
ITID-42142.severity: Medium-High — the direct network risk depends on scope of access, but the accountability failure itself compounds every other vendor-access risk.
ITID-42142.priority: P2 for identified shared-credential arrangements; P1 upon confirmed misuse or compromise where individual attribution is not possible.
ITID-42142.escalation: Escalate to vendor management to move to individually-attributed credentials; escalate to IR if misuse is confirmed and full containment requires disabling the shared account.
indicators: VPN sessions from the same vendor account originating from multiple distinct geographic locations concurrently or in rapid succession
Vendor unable to identify which individual initiated a specific session during an investigation
Vendor contract/onboarding records showing one credential issued for a multi-person team
vectors: Credential theft or leakage from any one of multiple people with access to the shared credential
Insider misuse by a vendor employee who should no longer have access but still knows the shared credential
rootCauses: Vendor onboarding process not enforcing individually-attributed accounts
Cost or administrative convenience driving a single shared account per vendor engagement
No contractual requirement for individual vendor user accountability
controls: Contractual requirement for individually-attributed vendor credentials
MFA tied to individual vendor identities
Vendor access reviews reconciling credentials to named individuals
ITID-42142.detection: Moderate — concurrent-session or impossible-travel analytics can surface sharing, but only if individual attribution is otherwise expected.
ITID-42142.response: Disable the shared credential, reissue individually-attributed accounts, and investigate historical sessions for misuse where attribution is not possible.
metrics: Count of vendor accounts identified as shared per review cycle
Percentage of vendor access individually attributed
detections: Concurrent/impossible-travel session detection on vendor accounts
ITID-42142.notes: The differentiator here is loss of individual accountability, distinct from the standing-connectivity risk in ITID-42141.

playbook.name: Vendor VPN Credential Shared Across Multiple Vendor Employees
playbook.description: A single vendor VPN credential was shared and used by multiple individuals at the vendor organization, breaking individual accountability and enabling unauthorized or unattributable access when the shared credential was misused or leaked.

steps.title: Confirm credential sharing via authentication pattern analysis
steps.desc: Analyze VPN authentication logs for the vendor account to identify simultaneous or geographically inconsistent logins indicating multiple individuals using the same credential.
steps.guidance: Look for concurrent sessions from different source IPs/geolocations or distinct device fingerprints under a single account within overlapping time windows.
steps.outcome: Confirmed credential-sharing pattern with evidence of multiple distinct users/devices.
steps.abort: If login patterns are consistent with a single individual (e.g., VPN client roaming), close as false positive.

steps.title: Disable the shared credential and revoke active sessions
steps.desc: Immediately disable the shared vendor VPN account and terminate any active sessions.
steps.guidance: Disable in IdP/VPN concentrator and revoke any associated certificates/tokens.
steps.outcome: Shared credential invalidated; no further access possible under it.

steps.title: Issue individual, named vendor credentials with MFA
steps.desc: Replace the shared credential model with individually issued, named accounts (one per vendor employee) enforcing MFA, restoring accountability.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with the vendor to identify all individuals requiring access and provision named accounts through the standard vendor onboarding process.
steps.outcome: Shared credential eliminated; each vendor user has individually attributable, MFA-enforced access.

steps.title: Verify vendor support continuity under new individual credentials
steps.desc: Confirm all vendor personnel needing access can authenticate under their new individual credentials without disruption to support operations.
steps.guidance: Coordinate a validation check with the vendor's team lead.
steps.outcome: Vendor support confirmed functional under the corrected credential model.

steps.title: Document incident and update vendor access policy to prohibit shared credentials
steps.desc: Record findings and formally update the vendor access management policy to prohibit shared/generic credentials for all third-party access going forward.
steps.guidance: Include this requirement in future vendor security addenda/contracts.
steps.outcome: Vendor access policy updated and communicated to vendor management team.

steps.title: Determine which sessions were authorized vendor personnel vs. unauthorized use
steps.desc: Coordinate with the vendor relationship manager and the vendor's own management to identify which individuals used the shared credential and whether any session was unauthorized.
steps.guidance: Request the vendor provide a roster of personnel who had access to the shared credential and cross-reference against session timestamps/locations.
steps.outcome: Determination of whether all use was by authorized vendor staff or included unauthorized/unaccounted-for access.

steps.title: Assess and contain any unauthorized activity conducted under the shared credential
steps.desc: If unauthorized access is confirmed, review and contain any systems/data touched during those sessions.
steps.guidance: Correlate session windows attributed to unauthorized use against internal system access logs.
steps.outcome: Scope of unauthorized activity contained and documented.
steps.abort: Skip if all use is confirmed authorized vendor personnel.

steps.title: Add credential-sharing detection to vendor account monitoring
steps.desc: Implement or tune alerting for concurrent/impossible-travel logins on vendor accounts to detect future credential sharing promptly.
steps.guidance: Configure UEBA or SIEM correlation rules specific to vendor account behavior patterns.
steps.outcome: Detection control in place for future credential-sharing attempts.

ITID-42143.def: Use of a vendor VPN or remote-access account that remains active after the underlying contract or engagement has been terminated, mirroring the departed-employee pattern but at the organizational/contractual level rather than the individual employee level.
ITID-42143.purpose: Captures unauthorized network access resulting from a vendor's access not being deprovisioned when their contract ended.
scopeIncludes: Vendor VPN/remote-access account still enabled after contract end date
Access used by the former vendor or a third party who obtained the still-valid credential
Detection via periodic vendor access audit finding an active account with no corresponding active contract
scopeExcludes: A departed individual employee's account (ITID-42111, which covers the organization's own workforce)
A shared credential issue during an active contract (ITID-42142)
A standing-access tool issue during an active contract (ITID-42141)
ITID-42143.severity: High — represents a live, unmonitored path into the network with no ongoing business relationship to justify or oversee it.
ITID-42143.priority: P1 upon any confirmed post-termination authentication; P2 if only discovered via periodic account audit with no evidence of use.
ITID-42143.escalation: Escalate immediately to vendor management and IT security; disable the account and review all activity since contract end.
indicators: VPN/remote-access authentication from a vendor account tied to a contract marked closed/expired in procurement records
Access-review audit surfacing an enabled vendor account with no active contract or statement of work
Vendor unable to confirm the activity as theirs during investigation
vectors: Former vendor personnel retaining and reusing still-valid credentials
Credential resale or leakage after the vendor relationship ends
Compromise of the vendor's own environment used to access the never-revoked account
rootCauses: No automated linkage between contract/procurement lifecycle and vendor account deprovisioning
Vendor offboarding checklist gaps for remote-access-specific accounts
Absence of periodic vendor access certification against active contract status
controls: Automated procurement-to-IAM deprovisioning workflow for vendor accounts
Periodic vendor access certification against active contract status
Time-bound/expiring vendor access grants tied to contract end dates
ITID-42143.detection: Strong when vendor access logs are correlated against an authoritative contract/procurement status feed; weak or absent without that integration.
ITID-42143.response: Disable the account, revoke all active sessions, review all network activity performed under the account since contract end, and confirm no persistence was established.
metrics: Mean time from contract end to vendor account deactivation
Count of stale/enabled vendor accounts found per review cycle
ITID-42143.notes: This is the vendor-organization-level analogue of ITID-42111; the process failure is at the contract lifecycle rather than the HR lifecycle.

playbook.name: Vendor Access Not Revoked After Contract Termination
playbook.description: A third-party vendor's network access remained active after the vendor's contract/engagement ended, and this lingering access was exploited for unauthorized entry into the corporate network.

steps.title: Correlate vendor account activity against contract end date
steps.desc: Pull authentication logs for the vendor's account(s) and compare against the contract/engagement termination date recorded in vendor management records.
steps.guidance: Check VPN/SSO logs for any login after the recorded contract end date; note source, duration, and resources accessed.
steps.outcome: Confirmed timeline of post-termination vendor access.
steps.abort: If no post-termination access is found, close as false positive and verify alert logic.

steps.title: Disable vendor account access immediately
steps.desc: Disable the vendor's VPN/directory/application accounts and revoke any active sessions or API tokens.
steps.guidance: Disable in IdP/VPN concentrator and revoke certificates/tokens; confirm no further authentication is possible.
steps.outcome: Vendor access fully revoked.

steps.title: Implement automated vendor offboarding tied to contract lifecycle
steps.desc: Establish or fix the linkage between vendor contract management and IT deprovisioning so vendor access is automatically disabled at contract end (or extension is explicitly required to keep it active).
steps.guidance: Work with vendor management and IAM teams to close the specific gap identified — an automated trigger, or an enforced manual checklist with SLA and escalation if missed.
steps.outcome: Verified process ensures vendor access is disabled at contract end unless explicitly extended.

steps.title: Reconcile all active vendor accounts against current contract roster
steps.desc: Run a full reconciliation of all enabled vendor accounts against the active vendor contract list to catch other stale accounts.
steps.guidance: Export enabled vendor accounts and compare against vendor management system's active-contract list; disable mismatches.
steps.outcome: All stale vendor accounts identified and disabled.

steps.title: Document incident and update vendor lifecycle management policy
steps.desc: Record findings and recommend periodic (e.g., quarterly) reconciliation of vendor access against contract status.
steps.outcome: Recurring reconciliation process documented and scheduled.

steps.title: Determine offboarding process failure with vendor management
steps.desc: Coordinate with the vendor relationship manager to determine why vendor access deprovisioning did not occur at contract end, and confirm the vendor organization's own involvement or awareness.
steps.guidance: Review the vendor offboarding checklist/process and confirm whether a deprovisioning ticket was ever created; ask the vendor relationship manager to confirm the vendor's contract end date and any extension.
steps.outcome: Root cause of the offboarding gap identified, and vendor coordination established for the response.
steps.tool: Vendor management system / vendor relationship manager

steps.title: Audit and revoke all other residual vendor access
steps.desc: Search for any other lingering access tied to the vendor organization or its personnel beyond the primary account (shared accounts, API keys, SaaS access, physical badges if relevant).
steps.guidance: Check SaaS SSO app assignments, service accounts, and any vendor-specific integrations.
steps.outcome: All residual vendor access fully revoked.
steps.tool: SSO admin console / SaaS management platform

steps.title: Assess scope of activity during unauthorized post-termination access
steps.desc: Review all systems and data accessed during the post-termination sessions.
steps.guidance: Correlate session windows with internal system/file access logs.
steps.outcome: Documented scope of potential exposure.

ITID-42144.def: General/unclassified exploitation of third-party vendor network access that cannot yet be attributed to a standing-access tool, a shared credential, or a post-termination access failure.
ITID-42144.purpose: Serves as the intake bucket for third-party vendor access exploitation cases that do not yet fit a more specific sibling leaf.
scopeIncludes: Any confirmed unauthorized vendor access pending root-cause classification
Novel vendor-access exploitation techniques not yet covered by a dedicated leaf
scopeExcludes: Cases root-caused to standing/always-on vendor tools (ITID-42141)
Cases root-caused to shared vendor credentials (ITID-42142)
Cases root-caused to post-termination access (ITID-42143)
ITID-42144.severity: Default Medium-High pending triage; reassess once root cause is determined.
ITID-42144.priority: P2 pending triage, escalating to P1 on confirmation of active unauthorized use.
ITID-42144.escalation: Escalate to SOC/vendor management for triage; reclassify once root cause is established.
indicators: Anomalous vendor access activity not yet matched to a known pattern
vectors: Varies — captured here only until root cause is determined
rootCauses: To be determined via investigation
controls: Standard incident triage workflow
Vendor access anomaly monitoring
ITID-42144.detection: Varies by underlying cause; general vendor-access anomaly monitoring provides the initial signal.
ITID-42144.response: Triage promptly, contain unauthorized access if confirmed, and reclassify the record once root cause is established.
metrics: Count of records held in unclassified status beyond SLA
Time to reclassification
ITID-42144.notes: This is a catch-all/intake leaf; analysts should actively work to reclassify records out of it wherever a specific root cause can be established.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Third-Party Vendor Access Exploitation
playbook.description: Third-party vendor network access was exploited through a method not matching a more specific known pattern, requiring general investigation to characterize the exact vector.

steps.title: Review vendor account activity and access configuration
steps.desc: Pull authentication and session logs for the vendor account(s) involved and review the vendor's granted access scope to characterize the anomaly.
steps.guidance: Look for unusual login patterns, access beyond scope of engagement, or activity inconsistent with known vendor support windows.
steps.outcome: Anomaly characterized with supporting evidence.
steps.abort: If activity is consistent with expected vendor behavior, close as false positive.

steps.title: Disable the affected vendor account/access path
steps.desc: Immediately disable the vendor account or access mechanism involved and revoke active sessions.
steps.guidance: Disable in IdP/VPN concentrator or relevant access platform; confirm no further access is possible.
steps.outcome: Vendor access path halted.

steps.title: Remediate the specific vendor access weakness identified
steps.desc: Close the specific gap identified (e.g., weak vendor authentication, excessive access scope, missing offboarding trigger) in coordination with vendor management.
steps.guidance: Tailor remediation to root cause found during identification.
steps.outcome: Root-cause vendor access weakness closed.

steps.title: Restore vendor access under corrected controls and monitor
steps.desc: Restore legitimate vendor access under the corrected configuration with heightened monitoring for a defined period.
steps.guidance: Confirm vendor can resume normal support activity; add temporary alerting on the vendor account.
steps.outcome: Vendor access restored with no further anomalous activity during monitoring window.

steps.title: Document incident and review vendor access governance program
steps.desc: Record findings and, if a systemic gap was found in vendor access governance, recommend broader program-level remediation.
steps.outcome: Report filed; systemic gaps tracked for remediation.

steps.title: Coordinate with vendor relationship manager to determine root cause
steps.desc: Engage the vendor relationship manager and vendor security contact to determine the specific access method exploited and whether it originated from the vendor's environment.
steps.guidance: Request vendor-side logs/attestation to corroborate findings.
steps.outcome: Root cause and responsible party (vendor-side compromise vs. internal misconfiguration) identified.

steps.title: Contain any systems reached through the exploited vendor access
steps.desc: If internal systems were accessed as a result, contain them pending further investigation.
steps.guidance: Apply EDR isolation or internal segmentation as appropriate.
steps.outcome: Affected systems contained.
steps.abort: Skip if no internal systems were reached.

ITID-42211.def: General/unclassified use of reused, stolen, or shared credentials to move between hosts or network segments, viewed here from the network-path/topology angle (which segments and routes the reuse traversed) rather than the device-level mechanics of the technique.
ITID-42211.purpose: Provides a network-infrastructure-level classification point for credential reuse observed as part of lateral movement across the network path, cross-referencing the more detailed device-level credential/lateral-movement techniques documented elsewhere.
scopeIncludes: Cross-segment authentication events using a credential already used to authenticate elsewhere in the network in a manner inconsistent with legitimate use
Correlating network flow/segment-traversal data with credential reuse detected at the device layer
Cases where the network path/topology context (e.g., unexpected segment-to-segment reach) is the primary investigative angle
scopeExcludes: Device-level mechanics of RDP-based lateral movement (see the ITID-333xx Lateral Movement family, e.g. Remote Desktop Protocol Access under Attacks Against the Device)
Device-level mechanics of admin share abuse (ITID-333xx family) or Pass-the-Hash (ITID-333xx family)
Departed-employee VPN credential reuse (ITID-42111), which is a remote-access-specific case
ITID-42211.severity: High — credential reuse enabling movement across network segments indicates an active intrusion in progress.
ITID-42211.priority: P1 upon confirmed cross-segment authentication using a reused credential.
ITID-42211.escalation: Escalate immediately to IR; coordinate with the device-level investigation tracked under the corresponding ITID-333xx leaf where applicable.
indicators: Same credential authenticating across network segments with no legitimate business path between them
Network flow logs showing segment traversal immediately following a credential-reuse authentication event
vectors: Credential theft on one host reused to authenticate into a different network segment
Shared local administrator credentials reused across segment boundaries
rootCauses: Flat or under-segmented network topology allowing credential reuse to translate directly into broad reach
Lack of network-layer correlation with identity/credential telemetry
controls: Network segmentation limiting cross-segment reach
Credential reuse detection correlated with network flow data
Unique local administrator passwords (e.g., LAPS-style tooling)
ITID-42211.detection: Moderate — strongest when identity telemetry (device-level) is correlated with network flow/segment data (network-level); weak if the two data sources are not joined.
ITID-42211.response: Contain the credential and the network path used; coordinate with the device-level investigation for full technique attribution (RDP, admin share, or pass-the-hash specifics).
metrics: Count of cross-segment credential reuse events detected per period
Mean time to contain a confirmed cross-segment reuse event
ITID-42211.notes: This is a network-infrastructure-context cross-reference leaf: it exists to capture the network-path angle of credential reuse without re-describing the device-level technique detail already documented under the ITID-333xx Lateral Movement family (RDP Access, Admin Shares Abuse, Pass-the-Hash) and the ITID-32xxx exploit-kit-driven access leaves; use those leaves for technique-specific device mechanics.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Credential Reuse for Lateral Movement (Network Intrusion Context)
playbook.description: An attacker reused a valid credential (obtained via phishing, prior breach, or password reuse across systems) to authenticate to multiple additional hosts across the network, moving laterally beyond the initial point of compromise.

steps.title: Determine full scope of hosts authenticated to using the reused credential
steps.desc: Search authentication logs organization-wide (not just the first-found host) for every system the compromised credential was used against, since lateral movement implies multiple hosts.
steps.guidance: Query centralized authentication logs (AD/Kerberos, RADIUS, application SSO) for all successful and failed logon events tied to the affected account across the full environment and timeframe.
steps.outcome: Complete list of hosts/systems the credential was used against, with timestamps establishing the movement sequence.

steps.title: Disable the compromised account and force credential reset
steps.desc: Immediately disable the affected account, terminate active sessions/tokens, and force a password reset with MFA re-enrollment.
steps.guidance: Disable in AD/IdP, revoke Kerberos tickets (e.g., via krbtgt consideration if domain-wide compromise is suspected), and reset the account's password.
steps.outcome: Compromised credential invalidated across all systems.

steps.title: Remove attacker tooling/persistence from all affected hosts
steps.desc: Clean or reimage each affected host to remove any malware, scheduled tasks, or persistence mechanisms established during the lateral movement.
steps.guidance: Use EDR remediation actions where sufficient; reimage hosts where trust cannot be re-established.
steps.outcome: All affected hosts verified clean of attacker artifacts.

steps.title: Restore affected hosts to service and verify no residual compromise
steps.desc: Confirm all affected hosts are functioning normally and free of attacker artifacts before returning them to production use.
steps.guidance: Run a final EDR sweep and vulnerability scan on each restored host.
steps.outcome: All hosts confirmed clean and restored to normal operation.

steps.title: Document incident and reinforce credential hygiene controls
steps.desc: Record the full lateral movement timeline and recommend organization-wide controls (unique local admin passwords, credential monitoring, phishing-resistant MFA) to prevent recurrence.
steps.outcome: Report filed; recommended controls tracked for implementation.

steps.title: Identify the original credential compromise source
steps.desc: Trace back to how the credential was originally obtained (phishing, credential-stuffing, reused password from an external breach, keylogger) to inform full remediation scope.
steps.guidance: Review email security logs, endpoint telemetry on the initial host, and check the credential against known breach-data feeds.
steps.outcome: Root cause of initial credential compromise identified.
steps.tool: Email security gateway / EDR / threat intel breach feeds

steps.title: Segment or isolate all affected hosts to prevent further lateral spread
steps.desc: Apply network segmentation or EDR isolation to every host identified in the lateral movement scope, not just the initial host.
steps.guidance: Use EDR network-isolation actions or internal firewall/NAC quarantine VLANs for each affected host simultaneously to prevent the attacker from pivoting further while remediation proceeds.
steps.outcome: All identified affected hosts contained from further network communication.

steps.title: Implement unique local administrator passwords across the environment
steps.desc: Deploy a LAPS-equivalent solution to ensure local administrator credentials are unique per host, closing the root cause that allowed a single reused credential to work across multiple systems.
steps.guidance: Deploy Microsoft LAPS (or equivalent for non-Windows systems) organization-wide if not already in place; verify no shared local admin passwords remain.
steps.outcome: Unique local administrator credentials enforced across the environment.

steps.title: Assess actions taken by the attacker on each accessed host
steps.desc: For each host identified in the lateral movement scope, determine what data was accessed, what tools were run, and whether further credentials were harvested.
steps.guidance: Review EDR process execution history and file access logs on each affected host.
steps.outcome: Full activity timeline across all affected hosts documented.

ITID-42221.def: General/unclassified abuse of hidden administrative shares (e.g., C$, ADMIN$, IPC$) for lateral movement, viewed here from the network-path/topology angle rather than the device-level mechanics of share access and remote execution.
ITID-42221.purpose: Provides a network-infrastructure-level classification point for administrative share abuse observed as part of lateral movement across the network path, cross-referencing the detailed device-level admin share technique documented elsewhere.
scopeIncludes: Network-path/segment-traversal context surrounding admin share access observed to cross network boundaries
Correlating SMB traffic flow data across segments with admin share abuse detected at the device layer
scopeExcludes: Device-level mechanics of admin share abuse: hidden share access, PsExec-style remote service creation, and IPC$ null session abuse (see ITID-33320 Admin Shares Abuse family under Attacks Against the Device)
ITID-42221.severity: High — admin share traversal across network segments indicates an active intrusion with elevated access already obtained.
ITID-42221.priority: P1 upon confirmed cross-segment SMB admin share access.
ITID-42221.escalation: Escalate immediately to IR; coordinate with the device-level investigation tracked under ITID-33320 where applicable.
indicators: SMB traffic to admin shares (C$/ADMIN$/IPC$) crossing network segment boundaries with no legitimate administrative path
Network flow logs showing segment traversal coincident with device-level admin share alerts
vectors: Lateral movement tooling using admin shares to cross from a compromised segment into an adjacent one
PsExec-style remote execution reaching hosts across segment boundaries
rootCauses: Flat or under-segmented network topology permitting SMB admin share traffic between segments that should be isolated
SMB not restricted at network boundaries between segments
mitreTechniques: T1021.002 Remote Services: SMB/Windows Admin Shares
controls: Network segmentation restricting SMB (445/tcp) between segments
SMB traffic monitoring at segment boundaries
Disabling unnecessary administrative shares where feasible
ITID-42221.detection: Moderate — strongest when network flow/segment boundary monitoring is correlated with device-level SMB/admin share telemetry.
ITID-42221.response: Contain the network path used for the share traversal; coordinate with the device-level investigation for full technique attribution.
metrics: Count of cross-segment admin share traversal events detected per period
detections: Cross-segment SMB admin share traffic alert
ITID-42221.notes: This is a network-infrastructure-context cross-reference leaf: it exists to capture the network-path angle of admin share abuse without re-describing the device-level technique detail already documented under ITID-33320 (Lateral Movement via C$/ADMIN$, PsExec-style remote service creation, IPC$ null session abuse).

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Admin Share Abuse (Network Intrusion Context)
playbook.description: An attacker used administrative shares (e.g., C$, ADMIN$, IPC$) to move laterally across the network, copying tools and executing commands on remote hosts via SMB.

steps.title: Determine full scope of hosts accessed via administrative shares
steps.desc: Search SMB/file-share access logs and Windows event logs organization-wide for connections to admin shares (C$, ADMIN$, IPC$) from the suspected attacker-controlled account/host, since this technique implies movement across multiple hosts.
steps.guidance: Review Windows Security Event ID 5140/5145 (network share access) and EDR process/file telemetry across the environment for admin-share connections outside normal administrative tooling patterns.
steps.outcome: Complete list of hosts accessed via admin shares, with timestamps establishing the movement sequence.

steps.title: Disable the compromised account and terminate active sessions
steps.desc: Disable the account used to perform the admin-share-based lateral movement and terminate any active sessions/tokens.
steps.guidance: Disable in AD/IdP and revoke active Kerberos tickets/SMB sessions.
steps.outcome: Compromised account access halted.

steps.title: Remove attacker tooling and persistence from all affected hosts
steps.desc: Clean or reimage each affected host to remove tools/payloads deployed via the admin shares.
steps.guidance: Use EDR remediation for lightweight cases; reimage where deeper persistence or rootkit-level compromise is suspected.
steps.outcome: All affected hosts verified clean.

steps.title: Restore affected hosts and verify SMB activity returns to baseline
steps.desc: Confirm all affected hosts are clean and that SMB/admin-share traffic patterns return to normal baseline levels.
steps.guidance: Run a final EDR sweep and monitor SMB traffic for a defined period post-remediation.
steps.outcome: Hosts restored; SMB activity confirmed at normal baseline.

steps.title: Document incident and update monitoring for admin-share abuse
steps.desc: Record the full timeline and recommend enhanced detection rules for anomalous admin-share access patterns going forward.
steps.outcome: Report filed; detection rule enhancements tracked for implementation.

steps.title: Identify files copied/executed via the admin shares
steps.desc: Determine what tools, scripts, or payloads were transferred to or executed on each accessed host via the admin share connections.
steps.guidance: Review EDR file-creation and process-execution telemetry correlating with the admin-share connection timestamps on each host.
steps.outcome: Documented list of attacker tooling deployed via admin shares across all affected hosts.

steps.title: Isolate all affected hosts and restrict SMB admin-share traffic
steps.desc: Apply network segmentation/EDR isolation to all hosts identified in scope, and apply a temporary internal firewall restriction limiting SMB (port 445) traffic to only necessary management sources.
steps.guidance: Use EDR isolation for affected endpoints and host-based firewall or internal segmentation rules to restrict lateral SMB traffic organization-wide during containment.
steps.outcome: Affected hosts contained; SMB lateral movement path restricted.

steps.title: Restrict administrative share usage and enforce unique local admin credentials
steps.desc: Reduce reliance on default admin shares where not operationally required, and deploy unique local administrator passwords (LAPS-equivalent) so a single compromised credential cannot access admin shares across many hosts.
steps.guidance: Evaluate disabling default admin shares on workstations where not needed for management tooling; deploy LAPS across the environment if not already present.
steps.outcome: Admin-share attack surface reduced and local admin credential reuse eliminated.

ITID-42231.def: General/unclassified use of RDP for lateral movement, viewed here from the network-path/topology angle (which segments and routes RDP traffic traversed) rather than the device-level mechanics of the specific RDP technique used.
ITID-42231.purpose: Provides a network-infrastructure-level classification point for RDP-based lateral movement observed across the network path, cross-referencing the detailed device-level RDP technique documented elsewhere.
scopeIncludes: Network-path/segment-traversal context surrounding RDP sessions observed to cross network boundaries that should not permit RDP
Correlating RDP (3389/tcp) flow data across segments with device-level RDP lateral movement alerts
scopeExcludes: Device-level mechanics of RDP lateral movement: stolen local admin credentials, compromised domain accounts, and session hijacking (see ITID-33310 Remote Desktop Protocol Access family under Attacks Against the Device)
Internet-exposed RDP brute force/scanning, a perimeter-facing concern (ITID-43xxx family)
ITID-42231.severity: High — RDP traversal across network segments indicates an active intrusion with credentialed access already obtained.
ITID-42231.priority: P1 upon confirmed cross-segment RDP session establishment outside expected administrative paths.
ITID-42231.escalation: Escalate immediately to IR; coordinate with the device-level investigation tracked under ITID-33310 where applicable.
indicators: RDP (3389/tcp) sessions crossing network segment boundaries with no legitimate administrative jump-host path
Network flow logs showing segment traversal coincident with device-level RDP lateral movement alerts
vectors: RDP used to hop between segments after initial compromise, bypassing intended jump-host chokepoints
Direct workstation-to-server RDP traversal across segments that should require a bastion host
rootCauses: Flat or under-segmented network topology permitting direct RDP between segments that should require a jump host
RDP not restricted at network boundaries to designated bastion/jump infrastructure
mitreTechniques: T1021.001 Remote Services: Remote Desktop Protocol
controls: Network segmentation restricting RDP (3389/tcp) to designated jump/bastion hosts only
RDP traffic monitoring at segment boundaries
Network-level enforcement of jump-host-only administrative access
ITID-42231.detection: Moderate — strongest when network flow/segment boundary monitoring is correlated with device-level RDP telemetry.
ITID-42231.response: Contain the network path used for the RDP traversal; coordinate with the device-level investigation for full technique attribution.
metrics: Count of cross-segment RDP traversal events detected per period outside designated jump-host paths
detections: Cross-segment RDP traffic alert outside jump-host paths
ITID-42231.notes: This is a network-infrastructure-context cross-reference leaf: it exists to capture the network-path angle of RDP-based lateral movement without re-describing the device-level technique detail already documented under ITID-33310.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General RDP Abuse for Lateral Movement (Network Intrusion Context)
playbook.description: An attacker used Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) with a compromised credential to move laterally between hosts across the internal network.

steps.title: Determine full scope of hosts accessed via RDP with the compromised credential
steps.desc: Search RDP/logon logs organization-wide for the compromised account's RDP sessions across all hosts, since lateral movement implies multiple hosts beyond the first found.
steps.guidance: Review Windows Event ID 4624 (Logon Type 10) and RDP gateway/jump-host logs for the account across the full environment and timeframe.
steps.outcome: Complete list of hosts accessed via RDP with the compromised credential, with timestamps establishing the movement sequence.
steps.tool: Windows Event Logs / RDP gateway logs / SIEM

steps.title: Disable the compromised account and terminate active RDP sessions
steps.desc: Disable the account and forcibly terminate any active RDP sessions across all affected hosts.
steps.guidance: Disable in AD/IdP; use remote session management tools or direct host access to terminate active RDP sessions.
steps.outcome: Compromised account access halted across all hosts.
steps.tool: Active Directory / remote session management tools

steps.title: Remove attacker tooling and persistence from all affected hosts
steps.desc: Clean or reimage each affected host to remove tools/payloads deployed during RDP sessions.
steps.guidance: Use EDR remediation for lightweight cases; reimage where deeper persistence is suspected.
steps.outcome: All affected hosts verified clean.

steps.title: Restore affected hosts and verify RDP activity returns to baseline
steps.desc: Confirm all affected hosts are clean and RDP traffic patterns return to normal baseline levels under the hardened configuration.
steps.guidance: Run a final EDR sweep and monitor RDP logon patterns for a defined period post-remediation.
steps.outcome: Hosts restored; RDP activity confirmed at normal, hardened baseline.

steps.title: Document incident and reinforce RDP hardening standard
steps.desc: Record the full timeline and formalize the NLA/MFA/bastion-only RDP requirement in the organization's endpoint hardening baseline.
steps.outcome: Hardening baseline updated and communicated.

steps.title: Assess attacker activity performed during each RDP session
steps.desc: Review what actions were taken during each RDP session on the affected hosts (tools executed, data accessed, further credential harvesting).
steps.guidance: Correlate EDR process execution telemetry with RDP session windows on each host.
steps.outcome: Full activity timeline across all affected hosts documented.

steps.title: Restrict RDP access organization-wide pending remediation
steps.desc: Apply a temporary internal firewall/NAC restriction limiting RDP (port 3389) to only jump-host/bastion sources, and isolate all affected hosts identified in scope.
steps.guidance: Use EDR isolation for affected endpoints and internal segmentation rules to restrict lateral RDP traffic during containment.
steps.outcome: RDP lateral movement path restricted; affected hosts contained.

steps.title: Enforce Network Level Authentication and MFA for all RDP access
steps.desc: Require NLA and MFA for RDP across the environment, and restrict direct RDP access to only jump-host/bastion paths, closing the root cause that allowed unrestricted RDP-based lateral movement.
steps.guidance: Update Group Policy to enforce NLA, integrate MFA at the RDP gateway/bastion, and disable direct RDP exposure between general workstations/servers.
steps.outcome: RDP access hardened with NLA and MFA enforced organization-wide.
steps.tool: Group Policy / RDP gateway / MFA solution

ITID-42241.def: General/unclassified use of a Pass-the-Hash technique for lateral movement, viewed here from the network-path/topology angle rather than the device-level mechanics of hash extraction and reuse.
ITID-42241.purpose: Provides a network-infrastructure-level classification point for Pass-the-Hash activity observed across the network path, cross-referencing the detailed device-level technique documented elsewhere.
scopeIncludes: Network-path/segment-traversal context surrounding authentication using a captured/reused hash observed to cross network boundaries
Correlating network flow data across segments with device-level Pass-the-Hash alerts
scopeExcludes: Device-level mechanics of Pass-the-Hash: LSASS/SAM extraction, workstation-to-workstation reuse, domain controller targeting, and network-capture-derived hashes (see ITID-12720 Pass-the-Hash family under Credential Exploitation, and ITID-33330/ITID-33331 Pass-the-Hash under Attacks Against the Device Lateral Movement)
ITID-42241.severity: High — hash reuse traversal across network segments indicates an active intrusion with captured credential material already in hand.
ITID-42241.priority: P1 upon confirmed cross-segment authentication using a reused hash.
ITID-42241.escalation: Escalate immediately to IR; coordinate with the device-level investigation tracked under ITID-12720/ITID-33330 where applicable.
indicators: NTLM authentication events using a hash already observed elsewhere on the network, crossing segment boundaries with no legitimate path
Network flow logs showing segment traversal coincident with device-level Pass-the-Hash alerts
vectors: Hash captured on one segment reused to authenticate into a different, isolated segment
Shared local administrator hash reused across segment boundaries to expand reach
rootCauses: Flat or under-segmented network topology allowing hash reuse to translate directly into broad cross-segment reach
Shared local administrator credentials/hashes across hosts in different segments
mitreTechniques: T1550.002 Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Hash
controls: Network segmentation limiting cross-segment authentication reach
Unique local administrator passwords (e.g., LAPS-style tooling) to reduce hash-reuse value
NTLM restriction/monitoring at network boundaries
ITID-42241.detection: Moderate — strongest when network flow/segment boundary monitoring is correlated with device-level NTLM/hash-reuse telemetry.
ITID-42241.response: Contain the network path used for the hash-reuse traversal; coordinate with the device-level investigation for full technique attribution.
metrics: Count of cross-segment Pass-the-Hash traversal events detected per period
ITID-42241.notes: This is a network-infrastructure-context cross-reference leaf: it exists to capture the network-path angle of Pass-the-Hash without re-describing the device-level technique detail already documented under ITID-12720 (Credential Exploitation domain) and ITID-33330/ITID-33331 (Attacks Against the Device Lateral Movement domain).

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Pass-the-Hash Attack (Network Intrusion Context)
playbook.description: An attacker extracted a password hash from a compromised host and reused it (without cracking) via NTLM authentication to move laterally and authenticate to additional systems across the network.

steps.title: Determine full scope of hosts authenticated to via the stolen hash
steps.desc: Search NTLM authentication logs organization-wide for the compromised account's use across all hosts, since pass-the-hash implies movement across multiple systems using a single reused hash.
steps.guidance: Review Windows Event ID 4624 (Logon Type 3, NTLM) and domain controller authentication logs for the account across the environment; look for logons without corresponding interactive/console activity, indicative of hash reuse.
steps.outcome: Complete list of hosts authenticated to using the stolen hash, with timestamps establishing the movement sequence.
steps.tool: Windows Event Logs / Domain Controller logs / SIEM

steps.title: Disable the compromised account and force a full credential reset
steps.desc: Disable the account and reset its password (which invalidates the underlying hash), and terminate any active sessions/tickets.
steps.guidance: Disable in AD/IdP, reset password, and revoke active Kerberos tickets. For domain admin-level compromise, evaluate krbtgt account password reset (twice) per Microsoft guidance.
steps.outcome: Stolen hash invalidated; compromised account secured.

steps.title: Remove credential-dumping tooling and persistence from all affected hosts
steps.desc: Clean or reimage each affected host to remove credential-dumping tools and any persistence mechanisms established.
steps.guidance: Reimage hosts where LSASS-level compromise occurred, since trust in the host's credential material cannot be reliably re-established through cleaning alone.
steps.outcome: All affected hosts verified clean of attacker artifacts.

steps.title: Restore affected hosts to service and verify no residual compromise
steps.desc: Confirm all affected hosts are functioning normally and free of attacker artifacts before returning them to production use.
steps.guidance: Run a final EDR sweep and credential-access anomaly check on each restored host.
steps.outcome: All hosts confirmed clean and restored to normal operation.

steps.title: Document incident and reinforce credential-theft mitigations
steps.desc: Record the full lateral movement timeline and recommend organization-wide deployment of Credential Guard, LAPS, and tiered administrative model if not fully in place.
steps.outcome: Report filed; recommended controls tracked for implementation.

steps.title: Identify the source host where the hash was originally extracted
steps.desc: Trace back to the initial host where credential-dumping tooling (e.g., Mimikatz-style LSASS access) was used to extract the hash.
steps.guidance: Review EDR telemetry for LSASS memory access or known credential-dumping tool signatures on the suspected initial host.
steps.outcome: Initial extraction host and tooling identified.

steps.title: Isolate all affected hosts from the network
steps.desc: Apply EDR isolation or network segmentation to every host identified in the lateral movement scope, including the initial extraction host.
steps.guidance: Isolate simultaneously across all affected hosts to prevent further pivoting while remediation proceeds.
steps.outcome: All affected hosts contained from further network communication.

steps.title: Deploy Credential Guard and enforce unique local admin credentials
steps.desc: Enable Windows Defender Credential Guard (or equivalent LSASS protection) across the environment and deploy unique local administrator passwords (LAPS-equivalent) to close the root cause enabling pass-the-hash movement.
steps.guidance: Verify hardware/OS compatibility for Credential Guard deployment; roll out via Group Policy/configuration management alongside LAPS if not already in place.
steps.outcome: Credential Guard and unique local admin credentials enforced, substantially reducing pass-the-hash viability.

steps.title: Assess attacker activity on each affected host
steps.desc: Review actions taken on each host reached via the stolen hash, including further credential harvesting that could extend the attack.
steps.guidance: Correlate EDR process execution and credential-access telemetry across all affected hosts.
steps.outcome: Full activity timeline across all affected hosts documented.

ITID-42311.def: A full TCP connect scan (completing the three-way handshake for each probed port) directed at externally-facing infrastructure to enumerate open ports and reachable services, typically the first visible step in an external reconnaissance campaign.
ITID-42311.purpose: Captures reconnaissance activity using a full TCP three-way handshake to enumerate open ports against the external network perimeter.
scopeIncludes: Full-connect scans against internet-facing IP ranges/hosts
Scans completing the TCP handshake, as opposed to half-open/stealth techniques
Scans that log clearly in perimeter firewall/IDS due to their noisiness
scopeExcludes: Half-open SYN scans designed to avoid full connection logging (ITID-42312)
Distributed low-and-slow scans designed to evade threshold-based detection (ITID-42313)
Internal-network scanning (covered under Network Mapping, ITID-4233x)
ITID-42311.severity: Low-Medium standalone; escalate if followed by targeted exploitation attempts against discovered open ports.
ITID-42311.priority: P3 for isolated scan activity; P2 if scan activity is followed by connection attempts to newly-discovered services.
ITID-42311.escalation: Escalate to P1/IR only if scanning is immediately followed by successful exploitation; otherwise log, block source, and monitor for follow-up activity.
indicators: Sequential or rapid connection attempts across a wide port range from a single source
Perimeter firewall/IDS full-connect scan signature alerts
Source IP matching known scanning infrastructure or threat intelligence feeds
vectors: Commodity scanning tools (e.g., Nmap full-connect mode) run against the organization's public IP ranges
Internet-wide scanning services (e.g., Shodan/Censys-style crawlers) indexing exposed ports
rootCauses: Public attack surface not minimized (unnecessary ports/services exposed)
No rate-limiting or automated blocking of scanning source IPs at the perimeter
mitreTechniques: T1595.001 Active Scanning: Scanning IP Blocks
controls: Perimeter IDS/IPS scan detection and automated source blocking
Attack surface reduction (minimizing exposed ports/services)
Rate limiting on perimeter connection attempts
ITID-42311.detection: Strong — full-connect scans complete handshakes and generate clear, reliable log entries on perimeter devices.
ITID-42311.response: Block or rate-limit the source, log the scan for pattern tracking, and monitor discovered-open-port services for follow-up exploitation attempts.
metrics: Count of full-connect scans detected per period
Percentage of scans followed by exploitation attempts
ITID-42311.notes: This is the noisiest and most easily detected of the port-scanning siblings; the differentiator from ITID-42312/42313 is scan technique/stealth level, not target or intent.

playbook.name: Full TCP Connect Scan Against External Perimeter
playbook.description: An external actor conducted a full TCP connect (three-way handshake completing) scan against the organization's internet-facing perimeter to enumerate open ports and services, a typically lower-severity precursor activity that may indicate a larger attack is being planned.

steps.title: Detect and characterize the scan via perimeter IDS/IPS and flow logs
steps.desc: Review perimeter IDS/IPS alerts and NetFlow/firewall connection logs to confirm a full TCP connect scan pattern and identify the source IP(s), scanned port range, and targeted hosts.
steps.guidance: Look for a high volume of completed TCP handshakes across a broad port range from one or a small number of source IPs within a short window, distinguishing from a legitimate vulnerability scan by an authorized third party.
steps.outcome: Confirmed scan activity with source, scope, and targeted hosts documented.
steps.abort: If the source is a known/authorized scanning service (e.g., contracted vulnerability assessment vendor), close as expected activity.

steps.title: Block the scanning source IP(s) at the perimeter firewall
steps.desc: Add a temporary or permanent deny rule for the confirmed malicious/unauthorized scanning source at the perimeter firewall.
steps.guidance: Verify the block does not impact legitimate business traffic before applying; consider a time-boxed block with review if the source is a shared/dynamic range.
steps.outcome: Scanning source blocked from further reconnaissance against the perimeter.
steps.abort: Skip if the source is confirmed to be an authorized scanning service.

steps.title: Reduce unnecessary exposed attack surface identified by the scan
steps.desc: Review the ports/services the scan found open and close or restrict any that are not business-justified for external exposure.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with system/service owners to confirm business need for each exposed port; disable or firewall-restrict unnecessary services.
steps.outcome: External attack surface reduced to only business-justified exposed services.

steps.title: Maintain heightened monitoring on scanned hosts for a defined follow-up period
steps.desc: Continue elevated monitoring/alerting on the previously scanned hosts and ports beyond immediate containment, given recon often precedes further attack activity.
steps.guidance: Configure a time-boxed heightened-alert rule in the SIEM for the affected hosts.
steps.outcome: Heightened monitoring window completed with no follow-on attack activity observed, or follow-on activity caught and handled.

steps.title: Document scan activity and reinforce perimeter attack-surface reduction
steps.desc: Record the scan details and any attack-surface reductions made, and recommend periodic external attack-surface reviews to catch unnecessary exposure proactively.
steps.outcome: Report filed; periodic external attack-surface review scheduled if not already in place.

steps.title: Check source IP against threat intelligence and prior activity history
steps.desc: Determine whether the scanning source is known-malicious infrastructure, a research/scanning-as-a-service provider (e.g., Shodan/Censys crawler), or previously unseen.
steps.guidance: Query threat intel feeds and internal historical logs for the source IP's reputation and prior interaction with the organization.
steps.outcome: Source classification established to inform response severity.

steps.title: Correlate scan activity with any subsequent exploitation attempts
steps.desc: Because reconnaissance often precedes a larger attack, monitor for and correlate any follow-on connection attempts or exploitation activity against the specific ports/services identified as open during the scan, rather than treating the incident as closed once the scan itself stops.
steps.guidance: Set a monitoring watch on the scanned hosts/ports for a defined follow-up period (e.g., 14-30 days) and correlate any new alerts against the original scan source and discovered open ports.
steps.outcome: Determination of whether the scan was followed by exploitation activity, with heightened monitoring in place regardless.

ITID-42312.def: A stealth/half-open TCP scan (SYN scan) directed at network infrastructure, where the adversary sends a SYN packet and analyzes the response without completing the three-way handshake, reducing the log footprint on many traditional connection-logging systems.
ITID-42312.purpose: Captures reconnaissance activity using half-open (SYN) scanning to enumerate open ports while avoiding full connection logging.
scopeIncludes: SYN/half-open scans against externally-facing or internal infrastructure
Scans specifically chosen to avoid full-connection-based logging or IDS thresholds tuned for connect scans
Detection reliant on IDS/IPS signature or flow-based analysis rather than connection logs
scopeExcludes: Full TCP connect scans (ITID-42311)
Distributed/low-and-slow scans specifically evading rate-based thresholds (ITID-42313)
ITID-42312.severity: Medium — the deliberate use of a stealth technique suggests a more capable/intentional adversary than commodity full-connect scanning.
ITID-42312.priority: P2 for confirmed SYN scan activity; P1 if followed by targeted exploitation.
ITID-42312.escalation: Escalate to SOC for source tracking and blocking; escalate to IR if follow-up exploitation is observed.
indicators: SYN packets without corresponding completed handshakes across a range of ports from a single source
IDS/IPS signature alerts for known SYN scan tooling (e.g., Nmap SYN scan mode)
NetFlow/sFlow anomalies showing high SYN-to-completed-connection ratios from one source
vectors: Nmap or similar tooling run in SYN scan (-sS) mode
Custom scanning tooling designed to minimize the connection-log footprint
rootCauses: IDS/IPS not tuned to detect half-open scan patterns, relying only on full-connection logs
Perimeter devices not configured to log or alert on incomplete TCP handshakes
mitreTechniques: T1595.001 Active Scanning: Scanning IP Blocks
controls: IDS/IPS tuned for half-open/SYN scan detection
NetFlow-based anomaly detection for SYN-heavy traffic patterns
Perimeter connection-state logging beyond completed handshakes only
ITID-42312.detection: Moderate — requires IDS/IPS or flow-based analysis specifically tuned for incomplete handshakes; connection-log-only monitoring will miss this technique.
ITID-42312.response: Block or rate-limit the source and monitor for follow-up exploitation attempts against discovered ports.
metrics: Count of SYN scan detections per period
Percentage of perimeter sensors with half-open scan detection enabled
ITID-42312.notes: Differentiates from ITID-42311 purely on scan technique/stealth level and the detection tooling required to see it.

playbook.name: Stealth SYN/Half-Open Scan
playbook.description: An external actor conducted a stealth SYN (half-open) scan against the organization's perimeter, sending SYN packets without completing the TCP handshake to enumerate open ports while attempting to evade basic connection-logging detection.

steps.title: Detect the half-open scan pattern via IDS/IPS and flow analysis
steps.desc: Review IDS/IPS alerts and firewall/flow logs for a pattern of SYN packets across a broad port range without corresponding completed handshakes or application-layer traffic, characteristic of a SYN scan.
steps.guidance: Since half-open scans may not appear in connection-oriented logs, prioritize IDS/IPS signature detection and raw packet capture/flow data (SYN without SYN-ACK completion or with RST responses) rather than relying solely on standard connection logs.
steps.outcome: Confirmed SYN scan activity with source IP, scope, and targeted hosts documented.
steps.abort: If pattern is consistent with an authorized scanning vendor, close as expected activity.

steps.title: Block the scanning source IP(s) at the perimeter firewall
steps.desc: Add a deny rule for the confirmed malicious/unauthorized scanning source at the perimeter firewall.
steps.guidance: Consider blocking at a broader ASN/range level if the actor is using a rotating pool of addresses within the same infrastructure.
steps.outcome: Scanning source blocked from further reconnaissance.
steps.abort: Skip if source is confirmed authorized.

steps.title: Reduce unnecessary exposed attack surface identified by the scan
steps.desc: Review ports/services found reachable during the scan and close or restrict any not business-justified for external exposure.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with service owners to confirm business need for each exposed port.
steps.outcome: External attack surface reduced.

steps.title: Maintain heightened monitoring on scanned hosts for a defined follow-up period
