steps.title: Verify DAI/DHCP snooping enforcement and monitor for recurrence
steps.desc: Confirm the new switch-level controls are functioning correctly and monitor the segment for any recurrence of ARP anomalies.
steps.guidance: Test DAI enforcement by attempting a controlled ARP spoof in a maintenance window, if safe to do so, and review switch logs for a defined follow-up period.
steps.outcome: Controls confirmed effective; no recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document findings and update switch hardening baseline for DAI/DHCP snooping
steps.desc: Record findings and formalize DAI and DHCP snooping as mandatory items in the network switch hardening baseline for all access-layer switches.
steps.outcome: Hardening baseline updated and communicated to network operations.

steps.title: Assess what traffic was intercepted and what data may have been exposed
steps.desc: Determine the duration of the MITM positioning and what protocols/sessions between the victim hosts and gateway were exposed to interception during that window.
steps.guidance: Correlate the spoofing timeframe with victim host network activity to estimate exposure, prioritizing unencrypted protocol usage.
steps.outcome: Documented estimate of intercepted traffic and data exposure risk.

steps.title: Force credential resets for accounts potentially exposed via the MITM interception
steps.desc: If unencrypted credential or session-token transmission was likely intercepted, force a password/session reset for affected accounts.
steps.guidance: Identify accounts that authenticated over the affected segment during the spoofing window using vulnerable protocols.
steps.outcome: Potentially exposed credentials/sessions invalidated.
steps.abort: Skip if no vulnerable credential/session transmission occurred during the window.

steps.title: Migrate remaining unencrypted protocols on the segment to encrypted equivalents
steps.desc: Reduce the value of any future MITM positioning by eliminating cleartext protocol usage on the segment.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with system/application owners to disable legacy unencrypted protocols in favor of encrypted alternatives.
steps.outcome: Segment no longer transmits sensitive data in cleartext.

ITID-42343.def: Passive capture of wireless network traffic (802.11 management, control, and data frames) for reconnaissance purposes, exploiting the broadcast nature of RF transmission to observe traffic without needing any wired network access or foothold.
ITID-42343.purpose: Captures reconnaissance that captures wireless traffic over the air rather than from a wired network vantage point.
scopeIncludes: Passive capture of 802.11 frames within RF range of the target network
Capture of unencrypted wireless traffic or traffic metadata (SSIDs, client MAC addresses, signal patterns) for reconnaissance
Reconnaissance conducted purely from RF proximity, with no wired network access required
scopeExcludes: Handshake capture specifically for offline key cracking, a distinct objective (ITID-42121)
Wired-network passive capture (ITID-42341)
ARP-spoofing-based on-path interception (ITID-42342)
ITID-42343.severity: Medium — primarily a reconnaissance/intelligence-gathering risk unless paired with follow-on cracking or exploitation.
ITID-42343.priority: P2 for confirmed wireless capture activity in proximity to corporate facilities; P1 if paired with evidence of follow-on exploitation.
ITID-42343.escalation: Escalate to physical/network security if capture activity is detected near a facility; coordinate with WIDS/WIPS response.
indicators: WIDS/WIPS alert for a device operating in monitor/promiscuous wireless mode nearby
Detection of rogue wireless capture hardware in physical security sweeps
Correlation of RF capture activity with subsequent targeted attacks against identified clients/SSIDs
vectors: Commodity wireless adapters in monitor mode running capture tooling within RF range of the facility
Drive-by or park-and-capture reconnaissance against corporate wireless networks
rootCauses: No WIDS/WIPS coverage of the facility's RF footprint
Wireless traffic not fully encrypted end-to-end at the application layer, leaving metadata or content exposed to capture
controls: Wireless intrusion detection/prevention system (WIDS/WIPS)
End-to-end encryption for sensitive traffic independent of wireless-layer encryption
Physical security sweeps for rogue capture hardware
ITID-42343.detection: Moderate — WIDS/WIPS can detect monitor-mode devices and capture-related RF anomalies, but coverage depends entirely on deployment extent.
ITID-42343.response: Investigate the source of the capture activity, assess what wireless traffic may have been exposed, and coordinate physical security response if a device is locatable.
metrics: Count of monitor-mode/capture device detections per period
Percentage of facility RF footprint covered by WIDS/WIPS
ITID-42343.notes: Differentiates from ITID-42121 (handshake capture for cracking) by covering general wireless reconnaissance/metadata capture rather than a cryptographic-attack objective.

playbook.name: Wireless Packet Sniffing for Network Reconnaissance
playbook.description: An actor within radio range passively captured wireless network traffic (management/control frames or, where encryption is weak/absent, data frames) to gather reconnaissance information about the wireless environment and connected clients.

steps.title: Detect wireless sniffing activity, acknowledging detection is inherently harder than wired capture
steps.desc: Because passive wireless capture is largely undetectable by network-based tools, rely on wireless IDS (WIDS) indicators of a monitoring-mode adapter in the area (where detectable via anomalous probe/beacon behavior) or on RF monitoring/spectrum analysis if available, and treat this as a lower-confidence detection than wired equivalents.
steps.guidance: Review WIDS logs for anomalous client behavior (e.g., a device associating briefly then dropping to monitor mode is not directly visible, but surrounding indicators like unusual probe request patterns from unrecognized devices may be present); consult physical security/RF monitoring resources if the organization has them.
steps.outcome: Best-available characterization of the wireless sniffing activity, acknowledging some uncertainty is expected given detection limitations.
steps.abort: If no supporting evidence beyond a general suspicion exists, document as a low-confidence finding and proceed directly to hardening recommendations rather than active containment.
steps.tool: Wireless IDS / RF spectrum monitoring (if available)

steps.title: Increase RF monitoring and physically locate the suspected source if feasible
steps.desc: Where the organization has wireless spectrum analysis or WIDS capability, attempt to triangulate the physical location of the suspected sniffing device for potential removal/investigation.
steps.guidance: Use AP-based signal strength triangulation or a dedicated RF scanning tool to narrow the physical location.
steps.outcome: Physical location of the suspected device narrowed, if feasible.
steps.abort: Skip if the organization lacks RF monitoring/triangulation capability; proceed directly to hardening controls.

steps.title: Harden wireless encryption and management-frame protection organization-wide
steps.desc: Ensure all SSIDs use WPA2/WPA3 with Protected Management Frames (PMF/802.11w) enabled to reduce the value and feasibility of wireless sniffing, and eliminate any remaining open/legacy-encryption SSIDs.
steps.guidance: Enable PMF where supported by client devices; audit all deployed SSIDs for encryption compliance.
steps.outcome: Wireless environment hardened against passive sniffing value extraction.

steps.title: Verify wireless configuration compliance and monitor for recurrence
steps.desc: Confirm all SSIDs pass a post-remediation compliance check for encryption and PMF settings, and maintain heightened WIDS monitoring for a defined follow-up period.
steps.guidance: Run a wireless configuration compliance scan across all APs.
steps.outcome: All APs compliant; heightened monitoring window completed with no further indicators.

steps.title: Document findings and evaluate investment in dedicated WIDS/RF monitoring capability
steps.desc: Record findings, acknowledging the inherent detection limitations of wireless sniffing, and evaluate whether dedicated WIDS/RF monitoring investment is warranted given the organization's risk profile.
steps.outcome: Report filed; WIDS/RF monitoring investment decision documented.

steps.title: Assess wireless encryption posture and potential data exposure
steps.desc: Review the encryption standard in use on the affected SSID(s) to determine whether captured traffic could plausibly be decrypted or otherwise yield useful information (e.g., WPA2/3 protects data frames from casual sniffing, but management/control frames and any WEP/open-network traffic would be readable).
steps.guidance: Confirm current encryption configuration for all SSIDs on the affected AP(s) and identify any weak/legacy configurations.
steps.outcome: Documented exposure risk based on actual encryption posture.

steps.title: Rotate wireless credentials as a precaution if weak encryption exposure is confirmed
steps.desc: If the affected SSID was found to use weak/legacy encryption or an open configuration, rotate the PSK/credentials and correct the encryption configuration.
steps.guidance: Push updated PSK/encryption settings to the WLAN controller.
steps.outcome: Wireless credentials rotated where exposure risk was confirmed.
steps.abort: Skip if the affected SSID already uses strong WPA2/WPA3 encryption protecting data frames.

ITID-42344.def: General/unclassified packet sniffing/traffic capture activity that cannot yet be attributed to passive wired capture, ARP-spoofing-based on-path capture, or wireless capture.
ITID-42344.purpose: Serves as the intake bucket for packet sniffing activity that does not yet fit a more specific sibling leaf.
scopeIncludes: Any confirmed packet sniffing activity pending technique classification
scopeExcludes: Cases root-caused to passive wired capture (ITID-42341)
Cases root-caused to ARP spoofing (ITID-42342)
Cases root-caused to wireless capture (ITID-42343)
ITID-42344.severity: Default Medium pending triage; reassess once technique is determined.
ITID-42344.priority: P2 pending triage, escalating if data harvesting is confirmed.
ITID-42344.escalation: Escalate to SOC for triage; reclassify once the specific technique is established.
indicators: Capture/sniffing activity not yet matched to a specific known technique
vectors: Varies — captured here only until technique is determined
rootCauses: To be determined via investigation
controls: Standard incident triage workflow
ITID-42344.response: Triage promptly and reclassify the record once the specific technique is established.
metrics: Count of records held in unclassified status beyond SLA
Time to reclassification
ITID-42344.notes: This is a catch-all/intake leaf; analysts should actively work to reclassify records out of it wherever a specific technique can be established.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Packet Sniffing
playbook.description: Packet sniffing activity was detected that does not match a more specific known technique (wired passive capture, ARP-spoofing-enabled MITM, or wireless sniffing), requiring general investigation to characterize the vector.

steps.title: Determine the sniffing vector (wired vs. wireless, passive vs. MITM-enabled)
steps.desc: Review available evidence (EDR, switch logs, WIDS) to classify the sniffing activity by vector, since detection approach and containment differ substantially between wired switch-based capture and wireless capture.
steps.guidance: Check for packet-capture tool execution on hosts (EDR), switch port/SPAN misconfigurations, ARP anomalies (DAI logs), and wireless IDS indicators as applicable to narrow down the vector.
steps.outcome: Sniffing vector classified, directing subsequent investigation and containment steps.
steps.abort: If no supporting evidence is found across all vectors, document as a low-confidence finding.
steps.tool: EDR / switch management console / wireless IDS

steps.title: Remove or block the identified capture presence
steps.desc: Disconnect/block the identified device, switch port, or wireless client responsible for the sniffing activity, using the containment method appropriate to the confirmed vector.
steps.guidance: Apply switch port shutdown/NAC quarantine for wired scenarios, or wireless deauthentication/blocking for wireless scenarios.
steps.outcome: Identified capture presence removed or blocked.
steps.abort: Skip if no specific device could be conclusively identified; proceed to broader hardening.
steps.tool: Switch management console / NAC / WLAN controller

steps.title: Harden the affected environment per the confirmed vector
steps.desc: Apply switch-level controls (port security, DAI, DHCP snooping) for wired scenarios, or wireless encryption/PMF hardening for wireless scenarios, based on the confirmed vector.
steps.guidance: Tailor remediation to the specific vector identified during investigation.
steps.outcome: Environment hardened against the confirmed sniffing vector.

steps.title: Verify hardening effectiveness and monitor for recurrence
steps.desc: Confirm the applied controls are functioning and monitor for recurrence for a defined follow-up period.
steps.outcome: Controls confirmed effective; no recurrence observed.

steps.title: Document findings and reinforce relevant hardening baseline
steps.desc: Record findings and update the appropriate (wired or wireless) network hardening baseline based on the confirmed vector.
steps.outcome: Hardening baseline updated as appropriate.

steps.title: Assess potential data exposure based on the identified vector and protocols in use
steps.desc: Determine what sensitive data may have been exposed based on the encryption/protocol posture of the affected segment or wireless network.
steps.guidance: Inventory unencrypted protocols/weak wireless encryption in use during the relevant window.
steps.outcome: Documented exposure risk estimate.

steps.title: Rotate credentials for accounts potentially exposed
steps.desc: If unencrypted credential transmission was likely exposed, force resets for affected accounts.
steps.guidance: Identify accounts active on the affected segment/network during the exposure window.
steps.outcome: Potentially exposed credentials invalidated.
steps.abort: Skip if no credential exposure risk is indicated.

ITID-42411.def: Physical placement of an unauthorized switch, router, or similar network device within the organization's facility and cabling infrastructure, giving the adversary a durable, physically-present foothold that survives credential rotations and many remote remediation efforts.
ITID-42411.purpose: Captures the planting of a physical, adversary-controlled network device to maintain a persistent foothold inside the network.
scopeIncludes: A physically planted switch/router connected to live network infrastructure
A device disguised as legitimate infrastructure (e.g., hidden behind a patch panel) to avoid casual discovery
Persistence maintained specifically through physical presence rather than software/credential-based mechanisms
scopeExcludes: An unauthorized wireless access point bridged to the network (ITID-42412)
Rogue device registration via NAC bypass, a logical-control-evasion mechanism rather than physical placement (ITID-42413)
ITID-42411.severity: Critical — a planted physical device typically survives password rotations and many remote containment actions, requiring physical removal.
ITID-42411.escalation: Escalate immediately to physical security and network engineering; treat as an active, ongoing compromise until the device is physically located and removed.
indicators: Unrecognized device appearing in network inventory/asset discovery (unexpected MAC address, switch port, or CDP/LLDP neighbor)
Physical security sweep discovering unauthorized hardware in wiring closets or patch panels
Unexplained additional switch/hop appearing in traceroute or topology data
vectors: Insider or social-engineered physical access used to install the device during a facility visit
Device planted during a maintenance window or by an impersonated vendor technician
rootCauses: Insufficient physical access control over wiring closets/network infrastructure spaces
No port-level authentication (e.g., 802.1X) preventing unauthorized devices from joining the network
Network asset inventory not reconciled against physical infrastructure regularly
controls: Port-level network access control (802.1X) on all switch ports
Physical access control over wiring closets and network infrastructure spaces
Periodic physical/asset inventory reconciliation against network topology discovery
ITID-42411.detection: Moderate — port-level NAC and CDP/LLDP-based topology monitoring can surface unexpected devices; without them, discovery typically depends on manual physical sweeps.
ITID-42411.response: Physically locate and remove the device, review all traffic that may have traversed it, and audit physical access controls that allowed its placement.
metrics: Count of unauthorized devices found per physical/asset sweep
Percentage of switch ports with 802.1X enforced
ITID-42411.notes: This is the highest-durability persistence mechanism in the Rogue Devices group, since it requires physical intervention to remediate.

playbook.name: Rogue Switch/Router Planted for Persistent Network Foothold
playbook.description: An attacker with physical or logical access planted an unauthorized switch or router on the internal network to establish a persistent foothold, enabling continued access even if the initial compromised host is remediated.

steps.title: Identify the rogue device via NAC/asset-inventory reconciliation
steps.desc: Reconcile the current NAC-connected device inventory and switch CAM tables against the authorized asset inventory to identify the unrecognized switch/router and its physical connection point.
steps.guidance: Cross-reference NAC logs, DHCP lease records, and switch CAM tables against the IT asset management (ITAM) database to find devices/MAC vendor OUIs inconsistent with approved hardware.
steps.outcome: Rogue device identified, along with its physical connection point (switch port/location) and duration of presence on the network.
steps.abort: If the device is confirmed as newly-deployed authorized hardware missing from inventory records, close as an asset-tracking gap rather than a security incident.
steps.tool: NAC / switch CAM tables / IT asset management system

steps.title: Physically or logically disconnect the rogue device from the network
steps.desc: Locate and physically remove the rogue device, or if immediate physical access is not possible, administratively shut down the switch port it is connected to.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with facilities/physical security if the device is in a location requiring escorted access; administratively disable the upstream switch port in the interim.
steps.outcome: Rogue device disconnected from the network.
steps.tool: Switch management console / physical security coordination

steps.title: Preserve and forensically examine the rogue device, then remove entirely
steps.desc: Because the device itself is attacker-controlled hardware, it cannot be 'cleaned' — preserve it for forensic analysis (chain of custody) and physically remove/decommission it entirely rather than attempting to reconfigure and reuse it.
steps.guidance: Follow evidence-handling procedures if pursuing potential legal/HR action; do not return the device to service under any circumstances.
steps.outcome: Rogue device forensically examined (as warranted) and permanently removed from the environment.

steps.title: Verify affected hosts and network integrity, then restore normal operations
steps.desc: Confirm any hosts that connected through the rogue device show no signs of compromise and that the network segment is functioning normally post-removal.
steps.guidance: Run EDR sweeps on affected hosts and verify network connectivity/performance at the affected location.
steps.outcome: Hosts confirmed clean; network segment restored to normal operation.

steps.title: Document incident and institute recurring physical/logical rogue-device sweeps
steps.desc: Record findings and establish a recurring (e.g., monthly) NAC/asset-inventory reconciliation process specifically to catch rogue devices, plus a physical security review of unattended network access points.
steps.outcome: Recurring reconciliation process documented and scheduled.

steps.title: Assess network activity and reach established by the rogue device
steps.desc: Review traffic logs and any routing/switching behavior from the rogue device to determine what network segments it could reach and what activity occurred through it.
steps.guidance: Review NetFlow/firewall logs for traffic sourced from or through the rogue device's IP/MAC, and any devices/hosts that connected to or through it.
steps.outcome: Documented scope of network reach and activity attributable to the rogue device.

steps.title: Isolate and investigate any hosts that connected through the rogue device
steps.desc: Identify and isolate any endpoints that passed traffic through the rogue device, since it may have facilitated additional compromise or interception.
steps.guidance: Apply EDR isolation to affected hosts pending investigation.
steps.outcome: Potentially affected hosts contained pending further investigation.
steps.abort: Skip if no hosts are confirmed to have routed traffic through the rogue device.

steps.title: Implement/strengthen 802.1X port-based network access control
steps.desc: Deploy or strengthen 802.1X authentication on all access-layer switch ports to prevent unauthorized devices from being physically connected and gaining network access in the future.
steps.guidance: Prioritize deployment on switch ports in physically less-controlled areas (conference rooms, unattended offices, common areas).
steps.outcome: 802.1X enforcement in place preventing future rogue device connections at the switch-port level.

ITID-42412.def: Deployment of an unauthorized wireless access point physically connected to the internal wired network, creating a persistent wireless entry point that an adversary (or anyone within RF range) can use to reach internal systems without needing further physical access.
ITID-42412.purpose: Captures the planting of an unauthorized wireless access point that bridges RF-reachable devices into the wired internal network.
scopeIncludes: A rogue AP plugged into an internal network jack, bridging wireless clients to the wired LAN
An AP disguised as legitimate infrastructure or hidden to avoid discovery
Persistent wireless reach into the internal network established via the rogue AP
scopeExcludes: A planted switch/router with no wireless bridging component (ITID-42411)
Guest wireless segmentation bypass using an authorized guest SSID (ITID-42123, a Tier-4 sibling under Unauthorized Network Access rather than persistence)
ITID-42412.severity: Critical — a rogue AP creates an ongoing, remotely-reachable (within RF range) entry point into the internal network.
ITID-42412.escalation: Escalate immediately to network and physical security; disconnect the device and investigate all wired-side traffic since its estimated installation.
indicators: WIDS/WIPS alert for an unrecognized AP broadcasting from within or near the facility
Unrecognized MAC address/device appearing in switch port inventory consistent with an AP
Wireless client traffic reaching internal wired-network resources through an unauthorized SSID
vectors: Insider or social-engineered physical access used to plug in a consumer-grade AP
AP disguised as or substituted for legitimate network equipment
rootCauses: No WIDS/WIPS coverage to detect rogue APs
Insufficient physical access control over network jacks
No port-level network access control preventing unauthorized devices, including APs, from bridging onto the LAN
controls: Wireless intrusion detection/prevention system (WIDS/WIPS) for rogue AP detection
Port-level network access control (802.1X) on all switch ports
Physical access control over network infrastructure spaces
ITID-42412.detection: Strong where WIDS/WIPS is deployed with adequate RF coverage; weak without it.
ITID-42412.response: Disconnect and physically remove the AP, review wired-side and wireless-side traffic for evidence of unauthorized access, and audit physical/port-level controls.
metrics: Count of rogue AP detections per period
Percentage of facility RF footprint covered by WIDS/WIPS
ITID-42412.notes: Differentiates from ITID-42411 by the RF/wireless bridging element, which extends the reachable perimeter beyond the physical cable itself.

playbook.name: Unauthorized Wireless Access Point Bridged to Internal Network
playbook.description: An unauthorized wireless access point was physically connected to an internal switch port, bridging wireless access into the corporate wired network and creating a persistent, unmonitored entry point.

steps.title: Identify the rogue AP via wireless scanning and NAC/switch reconciliation
steps.desc: Use WIDS/rogue-AP detection (comparing observed SSIDs/BSSIDs against the authorized AP inventory) combined with switch CAM table and NAC reconciliation to identify the unauthorized AP and its physical connection point.
steps.guidance: Cross-reference WIDS rogue-AP alerts with switch port MAC address tables to trace the AP back to its physical network connection.
steps.outcome: Rogue AP identified along with its SSID, physical connection point, and duration of presence.
steps.abort: If the AP is confirmed as authorized hardware missing from the WIDS allow-list, close as a configuration/inventory gap rather than a security incident.

steps.title: Physically or logically disconnect the rogue AP
steps.desc: Locate and physically remove the rogue AP, or administratively shut down the switch port it is connected to if immediate physical access is not possible.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with facilities/physical security for physical removal; disable the switch port administratively in the interim.
steps.outcome: Rogue AP disconnected from the internal network.
steps.tool: Switch management console / physical security coordination

steps.title: Remove the rogue AP entirely and forensically examine as warranted
steps.desc: Preserve the rogue AP for forensic examination if pursuing further investigation/action, and permanently remove it from the environment rather than reconfiguring for reuse.
steps.guidance: Follow evidence-handling procedures if warranted.
steps.outcome: Rogue AP permanently removed from the environment.

steps.title: Verify affected clients and network integrity, then restore normal operations
steps.desc: Confirm clients that connected through the rogue AP show no signs of compromise and the network segment is functioning normally post-removal.
steps.guidance: Run EDR sweeps on affected client devices.
steps.outcome: Clients confirmed clean; network segment restored to normal operation.

steps.title: Document incident and institute recurring rogue-AP detection sweeps
steps.desc: Record findings and establish or reinforce a recurring WIDS-based rogue-AP detection process, plus a physical security review of unattended switch ports.
steps.outcome: Recurring detection process documented and scheduled.

steps.title: Assess wireless client activity and internal network reach via the rogue AP
steps.desc: Determine what wireless clients connected to the rogue AP and what internal network segments/resources were reachable through the bridge.
steps.guidance: Review WIDS client-association logs for the rogue AP and correlate with internal network traffic logs for the bridged switch port.
steps.outcome: Documented scope of client activity and internal exposure via the rogue AP.

steps.title: Investigate and contain any clients that connected through the rogue AP
steps.desc: Identify devices that associated with the rogue AP and assess whether they present a compromise risk (e.g., if the AP was used for MITM/credential harvesting).
steps.guidance: Apply EDR isolation or heightened monitoring to affected client devices pending investigation.
steps.outcome: Potentially affected client devices contained pending investigation.
steps.abort: Skip if no clients are confirmed to have connected to the rogue AP.

steps.title: Deploy 802.1X port-based access control to prevent future unauthorized bridging
steps.desc: Implement 802.1X authentication on access-layer switch ports (particularly in physically less-controlled areas) so unauthorized devices, including rogue APs, cannot bridge onto the network by simply being plugged in.
steps.guidance: Prioritize ports in conference rooms, common areas, and other unattended/publicly accessible locations.
steps.outcome: 802.1X enforcement in place preventing future unauthorized AP bridging.

ITID-42413.def: Establishment of persistent network access by a rogue device that circumvents Network Access Control enforcement — for example via MAC address spoofing of an authorized device, exploitation of a NAC agent/policy weakness, or compromise of the NAC system's authorization database — rather than through unmonitored physical infrastructure alone.
ITID-42413.purpose: Captures a rogue device gaining and maintaining network access by defeating or bypassing the network access control (NAC) system meant to prevent unauthorized devices from joining.
scopeIncludes: MAC address spoofing of a known-good device to pass NAC authentication checks
Exploitation of a NAC agent, posture-check, or policy engine weakness to gain a passing status improperly
Compromise of NAC backend/authorization data enabling registration of an unauthorized device
scopeExcludes: A device planted on infrastructure with no NAC control to bypass at all (ITID-42411/ITID-42412, where the gap is physical access control rather than NAC)
ITID-42413.severity: High — defeating the control specifically designed to prevent this class of persistence indicates a more capable, deliberate adversary.
ITID-42413.priority: P1 upon confirmed NAC bypass and device registration.
ITID-42413.escalation: Escalate immediately to network security to investigate the NAC bypass mechanism and to identify/remove the rogue device.
indicators: Duplicate MAC address observed on the network (the spoofed device and the legitimate device active simultaneously or at different times/locations)
NAC system logs showing an authorization decision inconsistent with the device's actual posture/identity
Anomalous device behavior on a segment inconsistent with the profile of the device it is impersonating
vectors: MAC spoofing of an already-authorized device's identity
Exploitation of a known NAC agent or posture-assessment vulnerability
Compromise of NAC administrative credentials to directly register a rogue device
rootCauses: NAC relying solely on MAC address for device identity without stronger authentication (e.g., 802.1X certificates)
Unpatched NAC agent/appliance software
NAC administrative access not sufficiently protected
controls: Certificate-based (802.1X) device authentication rather than MAC-address-only NAC
NAC platform patching and hardening
Monitoring for duplicate MAC addresses on the network
ITID-42413.detection: Moderate — duplicate-MAC detection and NAC log review can surface this, but detection quality depends heavily on the strength of the underlying NAC authentication mechanism.
ITID-42413.response: Remove the rogue device, investigate the specific NAC bypass mechanism used, and harden the NAC authentication method to prevent recurrence.
metrics: Count of NAC bypass incidents detected per period
Percentage of network ports using certificate-based rather than MAC-only NAC
ITID-42413.notes: The differentiator from ITID-42411/ITID-42412 is that a NAC control existed and was specifically defeated, rather than the device simply exploiting an absence of physical/port-level control.

playbook.name: Rogue Device Registered via Compromised Network Access Control (NAC) Bypass
playbook.description: An attacker compromised or bypassed the Network Access Control (NAC) system's authorization mechanism (e.g., MAC spoofing an approved device, exploiting a NAC policy gap, or compromising a NAC administrator account) to register an unauthorized device as trusted on the network.

steps.title: Identify the NAC bypass method and the fraudulently registered device
steps.desc: Review NAC system logs and configuration to determine how the unauthorized device was registered as trusted — MAC spoofing of an approved device, exploitation of a policy exception, or compromise of a NAC administrator/enrollment credential.
steps.guidance: Check NAC registration/enrollment logs for duplicate MAC addresses (indicating spoofing of a legitimate device), unusual enrollment approval patterns, or administrator account activity inconsistent with normal behavior.
steps.outcome: Bypass method identified and the fraudulently registered device documented.

steps.title: Revoke the fraudulent NAC registration and disconnect the device
steps.desc: Immediately revoke the device's trusted NAC registration and disconnect it from the network.
steps.guidance: Remove the device entry from the NAC trusted database and quarantine or administratively shut down its connection point.
steps.outcome: Rogue device's trusted status revoked and disconnected.
steps.tool: NAC admin console / switch management console

steps.title: Preserve and remove the rogue device; audit NAC trusted-device database for other fraudulent entries
steps.desc: Forensically examine the rogue device as warranted and permanently remove it, and audit the full NAC trusted-device registry for other potentially fraudulent registrations using the same technique.
steps.guidance: Cross-check for duplicate MAC addresses or other anomalies across the entire NAC database, not just the device involved in this incident.
steps.outcome: Rogue device removed; NAC database audited and cleaned of other fraudulent entries.
steps.tool: NAC admin console / forensic imaging tools

steps.title: Verify network integrity and restore normal NAC operations
steps.desc: Confirm no other systems were compromised as a result of the rogue device's trusted access, and verify the NAC system is functioning correctly under the hardened configuration.
steps.guidance: Run EDR sweeps on systems the rogue device could have reached and validate NAC enrollment functions correctly for legitimate devices.
steps.outcome: Systems confirmed clean; NAC operations restored and verified secure.

steps.title: Document incident and reinforce NAC administrative access controls
steps.desc: Record findings and recommend stronger administrative access controls (MFA, least-privilege, audit logging) for the NAC system itself, plus periodic review of the trusted-device registry.
steps.outcome: Report filed; NAC administrative hardening tracked for implementation.

steps.title: Assess network access and activity performed by the rogue device under its trusted status
steps.desc: Because the device was trusted by NAC, it may have gained broader access than a typical unauthorized device — review what network segments/resources it reached and what activity occurred.
steps.guidance: Correlate NAC-granted access scope with NetFlow/firewall logs for the device's IP/MAC during its period of trusted registration.
steps.outcome: Documented scope of network access and activity attributable to the rogue device.

steps.title: Secure the compromised NAC administrator account or close the exploited policy gap
steps.desc: If a NAC administrator credential was compromised, disable and reset it; if a policy/enrollment gap was exploited, apply an emergency configuration fix.
steps.guidance: Disable and reset the affected admin account with MFA re-enrollment; correct the specific NAC policy exception or enrollment workflow gap identified.
steps.outcome: NAC system's integrity restored; the specific bypass mechanism closed.
steps.abort: Skip credential reset if the bypass was purely a policy gap with no account compromise involved.

steps.title: Harden NAC enrollment/authorization workflow against the exploited bypass technique
steps.desc: Strengthen the NAC system's device-authentication method (e.g., move from MAC-based authentication to 802.1X certificate-based authentication) to prevent the specific bypass technique from being reused.
steps.guidance: Where feasible, migrate from MAC-authentication-bypass (MAB) fallback to certificate-based 802.1X for all device categories capable of supporting it.
steps.outcome: NAC authorization workflow hardened against the confirmed bypass technique.

ITID-42414.def: General/unclassified rogue device persistence that cannot yet be attributed to a planted wired device, a rogue wireless access point, or a NAC bypass mechanism.
ITID-42414.purpose: Serves as the intake bucket for rogue device persistence cases that do not yet fit a more specific sibling leaf.
scopeIncludes: Any confirmed rogue device persistence pending root-cause classification
scopeExcludes: Cases root-caused to a planted wired device (ITID-42411)
Cases root-caused to a rogue AP (ITID-42412)
Cases root-caused to NAC bypass (ITID-42413)
ITID-42414.severity: Default High pending triage, given the general risk profile of rogue devices; reassess once root cause is determined.
ITID-42414.priority: P1 pending triage given the persistence risk class.
ITID-42414.escalation: Escalate to SOC/network security for triage; reclassify once root cause is established.
indicators: Unrecognized device detected in asset/network inventory not yet matched to a known mechanism
vectors: Varies — captured here only until root cause is determined
rootCauses: To be determined via investigation
controls: Standard incident triage workflow
Network asset inventory reconciliation
ITID-42414.response: Triage promptly, isolate the device if confirmed unauthorized, and reclassify the record once root cause is established.
metrics: Count of records held in unclassified status beyond SLA
Time to reclassification
ITID-42414.notes: This is a catch-all/intake leaf; analysts should actively work to reclassify records out of it wherever a specific root cause can be established.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Rogue Device Persistence
playbook.description: An unauthorized device was found connected to the internal network establishing a persistent foothold through a method not matching a more specific known pattern, requiring general investigation to characterize how it gained and maintained network access.

steps.title: Identify the rogue device via NAC/asset-inventory reconciliation
steps.desc: Reconcile NAC-connected device inventory and switch CAM tables against the authorized asset inventory to identify the unrecognized device and its physical/logical connection point.
steps.guidance: Cross-reference NAC logs, DHCP lease records, and switch CAM tables against the IT asset management database.
steps.outcome: Rogue device identified along with connection point and duration of presence.
steps.abort: If the device is confirmed as authorized hardware missing from inventory records, close as an asset-tracking gap.
steps.tool: NAC / switch CAM tables / IT asset management system

steps.title: Physically or logically disconnect the rogue device
steps.desc: Locate and remove the device, or administratively shut down the switch port it is connected to if immediate physical access is not possible.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with facilities/physical security for physical removal; disable the port administratively in the interim.
steps.outcome: Rogue device disconnected from the network.

steps.title: Preserve and permanently remove the rogue device
steps.desc: Because the device is attacker-controlled hardware, forensically examine it as warranted and permanently remove/decommission it rather than reconfiguring for reuse.
steps.guidance: Follow evidence-handling procedures if pursuing further action.
steps.outcome: Rogue device permanently removed from the environment.

steps.title: Verify affected hosts and network integrity, then restore normal operations
steps.desc: Confirm hosts that interacted with the rogue device show no signs of compromise and the network segment functions normally post-removal.
steps.guidance: Run EDR sweeps on affected hosts.
steps.outcome: Hosts confirmed clean; network segment restored to normal operation.

steps.title: Document incident and institute recurring rogue-device detection sweeps
steps.desc: Record findings and establish or reinforce a recurring NAC/asset-inventory reconciliation process to catch rogue devices proactively.
steps.outcome: Recurring detection process documented and scheduled.

steps.title: Determine how the device gained and maintained network access
steps.desc: Investigate the specific mechanism that allowed the device to connect and persist (e.g., unsecured port, weak NAC policy, disabled port security) to characterize the exact technique.
steps.guidance: Review switch port configuration, NAC policy applied to the connection point, and any authentication logs associated with the device.
steps.outcome: Root-cause access mechanism identified.

steps.title: Isolate any hosts that interacted with the rogue device
steps.desc: Identify and contain any endpoints that communicated with the rogue device, pending investigation for further compromise.
steps.guidance: Apply EDR isolation to affected hosts as needed.
steps.outcome: Potentially affected hosts contained pending investigation.
steps.abort: Skip if no hosts are confirmed to have interacted with the rogue device.

steps.title: Close the specific access-control gap that allowed persistence
steps.desc: Remediate the root-cause mechanism identified (e.g., enable port security/802.1X, correct NAC policy gap) to prevent recurrence of this specific access method.
steps.guidance: Tailor the fix to the specific mechanism identified during investigation.
steps.outcome: Root-cause access-control gap closed.

steps.title: Assess network activity and reach established by the rogue device
steps.desc: Review traffic logs to determine what network segments the device could reach and what activity occurred through it.
steps.guidance: Review NetFlow/firewall logs for traffic sourced from or through the rogue device's IP/MAC.
steps.outcome: Documented scope of network reach and activity.

ITID-42421.def: Modification or replacement of a network switch's or router's firmware to embed adversary-controlled backdoor functionality, surviving reboots, configuration resets, and most standard remediation short of a full firmware re-flash from a trusted source.
ITID-42421.purpose: Captures the most durable form of network infrastructure persistence: a backdoor embedded directly in a device's firmware.
scopeIncludes: Malicious firmware image flashed onto a switch, router, or similar network infrastructure device
Firmware-level implants surviving factory reset or configuration rollback
Supply-chain-compromised firmware shipped with backdoor functionality pre-installed
scopeExcludes: A backdoor account created within the device's normal OS/configuration layer rather than firmware (ITID-42422)
A hidden management interface enabled through configuration rather than firmware modification (ITID-42423)
ITID-42421.severity: Critical — firmware-level compromise represents the deepest and most durable form of network infrastructure persistence.
ITID-42421.priority: P1 immediately upon any suspicion or confirmation.
ITID-42421.escalation: Escalate immediately to network engineering leadership and IR; treat the device as fully compromised and plan for full re-imaging or hardware replacement.
indicators: Firmware hash/checksum mismatch against the vendor's known-good baseline
Unexpected outbound connections originating from the device itself (not through it) to unfamiliar destinations
Device behavior surviving a configuration reset or reboot that should have cleared it
vectors: Supply-chain compromise during manufacturing or distribution
Direct firmware flashing following prior administrative compromise of the device
Exploitation of a firmware update mechanism vulnerability
rootCauses: No firmware integrity verification (signed firmware / secure boot) on network infrastructure devices
Devices sourced through unvetted or insufficiently trusted supply chains
No periodic firmware hash validation against vendor baselines
controls: Secure boot / signed firmware verification on network infrastructure devices
Periodic firmware integrity/hash validation against vendor baselines
Vetted, trusted supply chain for network hardware procurement
ITID-42421.detection: Weak-to-moderate — firmware-level implants are specifically designed to evade standard configuration/log-based monitoring; detection typically requires dedicated firmware integrity tooling.
ITID-42421.response: Isolate the device immediately, treat as fully compromised, re-flash from a verified trusted firmware source or replace the hardware, and investigate the supply-chain/access vector that enabled the modification.
metrics: Percentage of network devices with firmware integrity verification enabled
Count of firmware baseline mismatches found per audit cycle
ITID-42421.notes: This is the deepest/most severe of the Network Backdoors siblings, since firmware-level compromise survives most standard containment actions.

playbook.name: Backdoor Firmware Flashed onto Network Switch/Router
playbook.description: An attacker with elevated access to network infrastructure flashed modified/backdoored firmware onto a switch or router, establishing persistence that survives reboots and standard configuration resets.

steps.title: Verify firmware integrity against known-good baseline hashes
steps.desc: Compare the running firmware version and cryptographic hash on the suspected device against the vendor's official published hash for that firmware version, and against the organization's golden-image baseline.
steps.guidance: Use vendor-provided firmware verification tools or manual hash comparison; check for firmware version reported by the device vs. what change-management records indicate should be installed.
steps.outcome: Confirmed firmware tampering with hash mismatch or unexpected firmware version documented.
steps.abort: If firmware hash matches the expected known-good baseline, close as false positive and investigate the alert source.
steps.tool: Vendor firmware verification tool / configuration management database

steps.title: Remove the compromised device from active network service
steps.desc: Immediately take the backdoored device out of production, rerouting traffic through a known-clean redundant device where available, or isolating the affected network segment if no redundancy exists.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with network operations to execute a controlled failover/isolation to minimize service disruption.
steps.outcome: Backdoored device removed from active traffic path.
steps.abort: If no redundant path exists and removal would cause unacceptable outage, apply compensating monitoring/traffic inspection on the device's links as an interim measure while emergency hardware replacement is arranged.

steps.title: Reflash or replace the compromised device hardware entirely — do not attempt to 'clean' it
steps.desc: Because backdoored firmware can persist through standard resets and even legitimate-looking reflashing in some cases, reimage the device using verified clean firmware from an out-of-band trusted source, or replace the hardware entirely if firmware-level compromise cannot be conclusively ruled out or reversed.
steps.guidance: Obtain firmware directly from the vendor via a verified secure channel; where the compromise involved hardware-level implants or cannot be conclusively remediated via reflash, replace the physical device.
steps.outcome: Device restored to a verified-clean state via reflash with vendor-verified firmware, or physically replaced.
steps.tool: Vendor firmware distribution channel / hardware procurement

steps.title: Verify replacement/reflashed device operation and audit other devices for similar compromise
steps.desc: Confirm the restored device operates correctly under production traffic, and run firmware integrity checks across all other network infrastructure devices with similar access exposure.
steps.guidance: Perform a functional and security validation of the restored device before returning it to full production, and sweep the broader fleet for related compromise.
steps.outcome: Device confirmed operational and secure; no other devices found compromised, or additional compromised devices identified and remediated.
steps.tool: Network configuration management / firmware integrity monitoring

steps.title: Document incident and formalize firmware integrity verification as a standing control
steps.desc: Record the full incident timeline and formalize periodic firmware integrity verification and management-plane access hardening as mandatory controls in the network infrastructure security baseline.
steps.outcome: Security baseline updated and communicated to network operations.

steps.title: Determine how elevated access was obtained to flash the firmware
steps.desc: Investigate how the attacker gained the administrative/console access required to flash firmware — compromised admin credential, exposed management interface, or supply-chain tampering before deployment.
steps.guidance: Review device administrative access logs, management-interface exposure history, and procurement/supply-chain records if tampering prior to deployment is suspected.
steps.outcome: Root cause of the access/compromise vector identified.
steps.tool: Device admin logs / network access logs

steps.title: Rotate all credentials that may have transited or been managed through the compromised device
steps.desc: Reset administrative credentials for the device itself and any credentials for systems whose traffic passed through it during the compromise window.
steps.guidance: Prioritize credentials for other network infrastructure devices managed via the same management network segment.
steps.outcome: Potentially exposed credentials invalidated.

steps.title: Harden network device management-plane access and implement firmware integrity monitoring
steps.desc: Restrict firmware update capability to a dedicated, tightly controlled management process, and implement periodic firmware integrity verification across all network infrastructure devices.
steps.guidance: Implement a management-plane access model requiring multi-person authorization for firmware changes, and deploy automated firmware hash verification against vendor baselines on a recurring schedule.
steps.outcome: Firmware update process hardened; recurring integrity verification in place across network infrastructure.
steps.tool: Network configuration management / firmware integrity monitoring tooling

steps.title: Assess scope of network activity enabled by the backdoored device
steps.desc: Because a compromised network device sits in the traffic path, determine what traffic it could intercept, redirect, or manipulate, and what other systems may have been affected.
steps.guidance: Review the device's role in network topology and correlate its traffic logs (where available) with downstream system activity for signs of interception or manipulation.
steps.outcome: Documented scope of potential network-wide impact from the compromised device.

ITID-42422.def: Creation of an unauthorized local user/administrative account on a switch, router, firewall, or similar network infrastructure device's configuration, giving the adversary durable credentialed access that survives most password rotations of the legitimate administrative accounts.
ITID-42422.purpose: Captures persistence established by creating a hidden or unauthorized administrative account directly on a network infrastructure device.
scopeIncludes: A new local admin/enable-level account added to a network device's configuration without change-management authorization
A backdoor account disguised with a name resembling a legitimate service or vendor account
Persistence surviving rotation of the device's primary administrative credentials because the backdoor account is separate
scopeExcludes: A firmware-embedded backdoor, a deeper persistence layer than a configuration-level account (ITID-42421)
A hidden remote management interface/service enabled rather than a user account created (ITID-42423)
ITID-42422.severity: High — a backdoor account provides durable, credentialed administrative access to core network infrastructure.
ITID-42422.priority: P1 upon confirmed discovery of an unauthorized account.
ITID-42422.escalation: Escalate immediately to network engineering to remove the account and rotate all administrative credentials on the device.
indicators: Device configuration audit revealing a local account not present in the authorized account baseline
Authentication logs showing logons from an account unfamiliar to network administrators
Configuration change history (if available) showing account creation outside an approved change window
vectors: Account creation following prior administrative compromise of the device (e.g., via exposed management interface or weak credentials)
Abuse of a vendor/support account left with standing privileges and repurposed as a backdoor
rootCauses: No configuration baseline/drift detection on network device accounts
No periodic review of local accounts configured on network infrastructure
Weak change-management controls over device configuration changes
controls: Configuration baseline/drift detection for network device local accounts
Periodic local account review on all network infrastructure devices
Centralized AAA (e.g., TACACS+/RADIUS) reducing reliance on local device accounts
ITID-42422.detection: Moderate — strong where configuration management/drift-detection tooling is in place; weak where device configuration is only reviewed ad hoc.
ITID-42422.response: Remove the unauthorized account, rotate all administrative credentials on the device, and investigate the access vector that enabled its creation.
metrics: Count of unauthorized device accounts found per audit cycle
Percentage of network devices under configuration drift monitoring
ITID-42422.notes: Differentiates from ITID-42421 by operating at the configuration/account layer rather than the firmware layer, making it detectable via configuration auditing rather than requiring firmware-integrity tooling.

playbook.name: Backdoor Account Created on Network Infrastructure Device
playbook.description: An attacker with administrative access to a network infrastructure device (switch, router, firewall) created a hidden or unauthorized local administrative account to maintain persistent access independent of the organization's normal credential management.

steps.title: Identify the unauthorized account via device configuration/GPO-equivalent audit review
steps.desc: Review the device's local user/account database against the authorized administrator roster to identify the unauthorized account.
steps.guidance: Pull the device's running configuration or local account list and compare against the organization's approved administrator list and centralized AAA (e.g., TACACS+/RADIUS) records.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized account identified, with creation timestamp and privilege level documented.
steps.abort: If the account matches an approved, documented administrator not yet reflected in the roster, close as a documentation gap.

steps.title: Remove the backdoor account immediately
steps.desc: Delete the unauthorized account from the device and terminate any active sessions associated with it.
steps.guidance: Confirm removal via a subsequent configuration audit.
steps.outcome: Backdoor account removed; no further access possible under it.

steps.title: Revert unauthorized configuration changes and verify device configuration integrity
steps.desc: Restore the device to its last-known-good configuration if unauthorized changes were made under the backdoor account, and verify no other persistence mechanisms remain (e.g., altered ACLs enabling covert access).
steps.guidance: Restore from verified-clean backup where changes were malicious; manually review the full configuration for any subtle persistence mechanisms if a clean backup is not available.
steps.outcome: Device configuration confirmed clean and consistent with intended baseline.
steps.tool: Device admin console / configuration backup system

steps.title: Audit other network devices for similar backdoor accounts
steps.desc: Extend the account audit across all network infrastructure devices to ensure no other backdoor accounts exist using the same technique.
steps.guidance: Run a fleet-wide local-account audit against the approved administrator roster.
steps.outcome: No other backdoor accounts found, or all identified and remediated.

steps.title: Document incident and reinforce centralized administrative account governance
steps.desc: Record findings and formalize centralized AAA with alerting as a mandatory control in the network device hardening baseline.
steps.outcome: Hardening baseline updated and communicated to network operations.

steps.title: Determine how administrative access was obtained to create the backdoor account
steps.desc: Investigate the access vector used to reach the device with sufficient privilege to create the account (compromised legitimate admin credential, exploited management-interface vulnerability, or physical console access).
steps.guidance: Review device access/authentication logs around the account-creation timestamp, and correlate with any known compromised credentials.
steps.outcome: Root cause access vector identified.

steps.title: Reset credentials for all legitimate administrative accounts on the device
steps.desc: Rotate passwords/keys for all other legitimate administrative accounts on the device, in case the same access vector exposed additional credentials.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with the centralized AAA system to force credential rotation.
steps.outcome: Legitimate administrative credentials rotated as a precaution.

steps.title: Harden device administrative account management and enable centralized AAA with alerting
steps.desc: Migrate local account management to centralized AAA (TACACS+/RADIUS) with MFA where supported, and configure alerting for any local account creation on network infrastructure devices going forward.
steps.guidance: Disable or minimize local account usage in favor of centralized authentication; configure SIEM alerting on local-account-creation events on network devices.
steps.outcome: Centralized AAA enforced with alerting on local account creation.

steps.title: Assess whether the backdoor account was used and what configuration changes resulted
steps.desc: Review the device's configuration change history and command logs for activity performed under the backdoor account.
steps.guidance: Compare current running configuration against last-known-good backup to identify any unauthorized changes made via the backdoor account.
steps.outcome: Documented scope of activity/changes made under the backdoor account.
steps.tool: Device command/audit logs / configuration backup system

ITID-42423.def: Enabling of a remote management service or interface on a network infrastructure device (e.g., an undocumented management VLAN, an alternate management protocol, or a non-standard listening port) that is not part of the organization's approved management configuration, giving the adversary a durable remote access path that blends into normal device functionality.
ITID-42423.purpose: Captures persistence established by enabling a hidden or non-standard remote management interface/service on a network device.
scopeIncludes: An additional/non-standard management service (e.g., Telnet, an alternate SSH port, a web management interface) enabled beyond the organization's approved baseline
A management interface bound to an unexpected VLAN or interface not part of the designated management network
Remote access maintained through the hidden interface independent of the device's normal administrative accounts
scopeExcludes: A backdoor local account used through the standard management interface (ITID-42422)
Firmware-level backdoor functionality (ITID-42421)

A legitimate management interface simply exposed due to a firewall misconfiguration rather than deliberately enabled by an adversary (ITID-42133, a device-facing configuration exposure rather than an adversary-created backdoor)
ITID-42423.severity: High — a hidden management interface provides a durable, often-overlooked remote access path into core network infrastructure.
ITID-42423.priority: P1 upon confirmed discovery of an unauthorized management interface.
ITID-42423.escalation: Escalate immediately to network engineering to disable the interface and audit the device for further unauthorized changes.
indicators: Configuration audit revealing an enabled management service/protocol not part of the approved baseline
Port scan of the device (from the authorized management network) revealing an unexpected open management port
Traffic to/from the device on a non-standard management port or VLAN
vectors: Enabling an insecure legacy management protocol (e.g., Telnet) left dormant but present in the device's feature set
Binding a management service to an unexpected interface/VLAN following prior administrative compromise
rootCauses: No configuration baseline/drift detection covering enabled management services
Devices shipped with legacy/insecure management protocols enabled by default and never disabled
No periodic port/service audit of network infrastructure devices
controls: Configuration baseline/drift detection for enabled management services
Disable unused/legacy management protocols by default
Periodic port/service audit of network infrastructure devices from the management network
ITID-42423.detection: Moderate — configuration drift detection and periodic service audits can surface this; passive network monitoring alone may miss infrequently-used hidden interfaces.
ITID-42423.response: Disable the unauthorized interface, audit the device configuration for further changes, and review how the interface was enabled.
metrics: Count of unauthorized management interfaces found per audit cycle
Percentage of network devices with legacy management protocols disabled
ITID-42423.notes: Differentiates from ITID-42422 by hiding in the service/interface layer rather than creating a new account, and from ITID-42133 by being an adversary-established backdoor rather than a firewall-scoping error.

playbook.name: Hidden Remote Management Interface Enabled on Network Device
playbook.description: An attacker enabled a hidden or non-standard remote management interface/service (e.g., an alternate management VTY line, an undocumented web-admin port, or a covert listening service) on a network device to maintain remote access independent of the device's normal management channel.

steps.title: Identify the hidden management interface via configuration and port audit
steps.desc: Review the device's running configuration and perform a port scan against the device to identify any management service/interface enabled beyond the documented, approved management access method.
steps.guidance: Compare the running configuration against the organization's approved device configuration baseline, and run an authenticated port/service scan against the device to catch listening services not reflected in configuration (e.g., a service enabled via an exploited vulnerability rather than standard configuration).
steps.outcome: Hidden management interface identified, with its access method and port/protocol documented.
steps.abort: If the interface matches an approved, documented alternate management method not yet reflected in the baseline, close as a documentation gap.
steps.tool: Device configuration audit / network port scanner

steps.title: Disable the hidden management interface immediately
steps.desc: Remove the configuration enabling the hidden interface/service and confirm via rescan that it is no longer listening.
steps.guidance: Apply the configuration change and verify with a follow-up port scan that the service is no longer reachable.
steps.outcome: Hidden management interface disabled and confirmed closed.
steps.tool: Device admin console / network port scanner

steps.title: Verify device configuration integrity and revert any other unauthorized changes
steps.desc: Review the full device configuration for any other unauthorized changes made in connection with establishing the hidden interface, and restore to a verified-clean baseline if needed.
steps.guidance: Compare against last-known-good configuration backup.
steps.outcome: Device configuration confirmed clean and consistent with intended baseline.

steps.title: Verify device operation and audit fleet for similar hidden interfaces
steps.desc: Confirm the device operates normally post-remediation and extend the audit across the network device fleet for similar hidden management interfaces.
steps.guidance: Run a fleet-wide authenticated port scan against the approved service baseline.
steps.outcome: Device confirmed operational; no other hidden interfaces found, or all identified and remediated.

steps.title: Document incident and formalize recurring configuration/port compliance scanning
steps.desc: Record findings and formalize recurring configuration compliance and port-exposure scanning as a standing control in the network device hardening baseline.
steps.outcome: Hardening baseline updated and communicated to network operations.

steps.title: Determine how the hidden interface was enabled and whether it was used
steps.desc: Investigate the access vector used to enable the hidden interface, and review any available logs for connections made to it.
steps.guidance: Review device configuration change history/timestamps and any connection logs for the hidden interface's port.
steps.outcome: Root cause and any confirmed usage of the hidden interface documented.
steps.tool: Device admin logs / configuration change history

steps.title: Reset administrative credentials on the affected device
steps.desc: Rotate all administrative credentials on the device as a precaution, in case the hidden interface was used to harvest or bypass authentication.
steps.guidance: Coordinate rotation through the centralized AAA system where applicable.
steps.outcome: Administrative credentials rotated.

steps.title: Implement recurring configuration compliance and port-exposure scanning for network devices
steps.desc: Deploy or tune automated configuration compliance checking and periodic authenticated port scanning against all network infrastructure devices to catch future hidden-interface attempts.
steps.guidance: Schedule recurring scans and configuration drift detection covering the full network device fleet.
steps.outcome: Recurring detection capability in place for hidden management interfaces.

ITID-42424.def: General/unclassified network infrastructure backdoor persistence that cannot yet be attributed to firmware-level compromise, a backdoor account, or a hidden management interface.
ITID-42424.purpose: Serves as the intake bucket for network backdoor persistence cases that do not yet fit a more specific sibling leaf.
scopeIncludes: Any confirmed network device backdoor persistence pending root-cause classification
scopeExcludes: Cases root-caused to firmware compromise (ITID-42421)
Cases root-caused to a backdoor account (ITID-42422)
Cases root-caused to a hidden management interface (ITID-42423)
ITID-42424.severity: Default High pending triage, given the general risk profile of network backdoors; reassess once root cause is determined.
ITID-42424.priority: P1 pending triage given the persistence risk class.
ITID-42424.escalation: Escalate to SOC/network security for triage; reclassify once root cause is established.
indicators: Device behavior or configuration anomaly not yet matched to a specific known backdoor mechanism
vectors: Varies — captured here only until root cause is determined
rootCauses: To be determined via investigation
controls: Standard incident triage workflow
Network device configuration baseline monitoring
ITID-42424.response: Triage promptly, isolate the device if confirmed compromised, and reclassify the record once root cause is established.
metrics: Count of records held in unclassified status beyond SLA
Time to reclassification
ITID-42424.notes: This is a catch-all/intake leaf; analysts should actively work to reclassify records out of it wherever a specific root cause can be established.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Network Backdoor
playbook.description: A persistence mechanism was identified on a network infrastructure device that does not match a more specific known pattern (firmware tampering, backdoor account, or hidden management interface), requiring general investigation to characterize the exact backdoor technique.

steps.title: Characterize the backdoor mechanism via firmware, account, and configuration review
steps.desc: Perform a combined review of firmware integrity, local account roster, and running configuration/listening services on the suspected device to determine the specific backdoor technique in use.
steps.guidance: Compare firmware hash against vendor baseline, local accounts against the approved roster, and configuration/open ports against the approved baseline.
steps.outcome: Backdoor mechanism classified (firmware, account, hidden service, or other), directing subsequent containment and eradication steps.
steps.abort: If all checks return clean against baseline, close as false positive.
steps.tool: Device configuration audit / firmware verification tool / network port scanner

steps.title: Remove the device from active service or disable the identified backdoor mechanism
steps.desc: Depending on the confirmed mechanism, either take the device out of production (for firmware-level compromise) or disable the specific account/service (for account or interface-based backdoors).
steps.guidance: Select the containment approach appropriate to the confirmed backdoor type.
steps.outcome: Backdoor access halted.

steps.title: Remediate per the confirmed backdoor type — reflash/replace if firmware-level, otherwise restore clean configuration
steps.desc: Because network hardware cannot always be trusted to be 'clean' after simple remediation, apply the eradication method matching the confirmed mechanism: reflash with vendor-verified firmware or replace hardware for firmware-level compromise; restore verified-clean configuration for account/interface-based backdoors.
steps.guidance: Escalate to hardware replacement if firmware-level compromise cannot be conclusively ruled out or reversed via reflash.
steps.outcome: Device restored to a verified-clean, trusted state.
steps.tool: Vendor firmware distribution channel / device admin console / hardware procurement

steps.title: Verify device operation and audit fleet for similar compromise
steps.desc: Confirm the restored/replaced device operates correctly and extend the audit across the network device fleet for the same backdoor technique.
steps.outcome: Device confirmed operational and secure; fleet-wide audit completed.

steps.title: Document incident and formalize recurring integrity/compliance monitoring as a standing control
steps.desc: Record the full incident timeline and formalize the applicable monitoring controls in the network infrastructure security baseline.
steps.outcome: Security baseline updated and communicated to network operations.

steps.title: Determine how the backdoor was established and whether it was used
steps.desc: Investigate the access vector used to establish the backdoor and review available logs for any confirmed use.
steps.guidance: Review device access/authentication logs and configuration change history around the suspected establishment window.
steps.outcome: Root cause and any confirmed usage documented.

steps.title: Rotate administrative credentials associated with the device
steps.desc: Reset all administrative credentials on the device as a precaution.
steps.guidance: Coordinate rotation through the centralized AAA system where applicable.
steps.outcome: Administrative credentials rotated.

steps.title: Implement recurring integrity and compliance monitoring for network infrastructure devices
steps.desc: Deploy or reinforce recurring firmware integrity verification, account audits, and configuration compliance scanning across the network device fleet to catch similar backdoor techniques earlier.
steps.outcome: Recurring monitoring capability in place across the fleet.
steps.tool: Network configuration management / firmware integrity monitoring

ITID-42431.def: Creation of a malicious scheduled task deployed domain-wide (or across a targeted OU) via Group Policy, giving the adversary a durable, self-reinstating execution mechanism across a large population of hosts from a single point of administrative compromise.
ITID-42431.purpose: Captures persistence achieved at scale by pushing a malicious scheduled task to many domain-joined systems via Group Policy.
scopeIncludes: A malicious Scheduled Task GPO pushed to a domain, site, or organizational unit
Persistence achieved via Group Policy's native scheduled task deployment mechanism
Detection via Group Policy object audit or domain-wide scheduled task inventory
scopeExcludes: A scheduled task created on a single network infrastructure device rather than pushed via domain policy (ITID-42432)
A cron-based equivalent on a Linux-based appliance (ITID-42433)
ITID-42431.severity: Critical — domain-wide GPO-based persistence indicates the adversary already holds domain administrative privileges and can re-establish access across the entire environment.
ITID-42431.escalation: Escalate immediately to IR and domain administration; this typically represents a domain-compromise-level incident requiring full credential rotation, not just task removal.
indicators: Group Policy Object audit revealing an unauthorized Scheduled Task policy
Widespread, simultaneous scheduled task execution across many hosts traced to a common GPO
SYSVOL change history showing GPO modification outside an approved change window
vectors: Abuse of compromised domain administrative credentials to create or modify a GPO
Direct manipulation of SYSVOL scheduled task XML files
rootCauses: Domain administrative credentials compromised through a prior intrusion stage
No GPO change monitoring/alerting
Overly broad delegation of GPO edit rights
mitreTechniques: T1484.001 Domain or Tenant Policy Modification: Group Policy Modification
controls: GPO change monitoring and alerting
Least-privilege delegation of Group Policy edit rights
Tiered administration model limiting domain admin credential exposure
ITID-42431.detection: Strong where GPO/SYSVOL change monitoring is deployed; weak without it, since the resulting task execution can otherwise blend into normal endpoint activity across many hosts.
ITID-42431.response: Remove the malicious GPO immediately, force a full domain administrative credential rotation, and investigate the extent of domain compromise as a top-tier incident.
metrics: Count of unauthorized GPO changes detected per period
Mean time to detect and remove a malicious domain-wide GPO
ITID-42431.notes: The differentiating axis for this group is deployment scale/scope — domain-wide GPO push versus single-device scheduling — reflecting materially different severity and response scope.

playbook.name: Domain-Wide Scheduled Task Deployed via Group Policy
playbook.description: An attacker with domain administrative access created or modified a Group Policy Object (GPO) to deploy a malicious scheduled task across some or all domain-joined systems, establishing broad, self-propagating persistence.

steps.title: Identify the malicious GPO and its scheduled task configuration via GPO audit review
steps.desc: Review Group Policy Objects for unauthorized or recently modified entries containing scheduled task configuration, and identify the scope (OU/domain) of systems targeted.
steps.guidance: Use GPO reporting tools (e.g., Group Policy Management Console reports, or a GPO change-auditing tool) to find recently created/modified GPOs with Scheduled Tasks preferences or Task Scheduler settings, and identify their linked OUs.
steps.outcome: Malicious GPO identified with its scheduled task payload/command and the scope of affected systems documented.
steps.abort: If the GPO/task is confirmed as an approved, documented IT administrative task, close as false positive.
steps.tool: Group Policy Management Console / GPO audit tooling

steps.title: Disable or delete the malicious GPO immediately
steps.desc: Unlink or disable the malicious GPO to prevent it from applying to any further systems, and force a Group Policy update to remove it from already-affected systems where feasible.
steps.guidance: Unlink the GPO from its OU(s) rather than deleting immediately if forensic preservation is needed; force gpupdate across the domain to propagate the removal.
steps.outcome: Malicious GPO no longer applying to any systems.

steps.title: Remove the scheduled task and any deployed payload from all affected systems
steps.desc: Clean or reimage each affected system to remove the malicious scheduled task and any tooling/payload it deployed.
steps.guidance: Use EDR remediation actions or centralized scripted removal for lightweight cases; reimage systems where deeper compromise occurred.
steps.outcome: All affected systems verified clean of the malicious task and payload.

steps.title: Verify all affected systems are clean and Group Policy application returns to baseline
steps.desc: Confirm all affected systems are free of the malicious task and that Group Policy application across the domain reflects only approved GPOs.
steps.guidance: Run a final EDR sweep and Group Policy compliance report across the domain.
steps.outcome: All systems confirmed clean; Group Policy state confirmed compliant.

steps.title: Document incident and reinforce privileged access and GPO governance
steps.desc: Record the full incident timeline and recommend a tiered administrative model and formal GPO change-approval process to prevent recurrence.
steps.outcome: Report filed; governance recommendations tracked for implementation.

steps.title: Determine how domain administrative access was obtained
steps.desc: Investigate how the attacker obtained the domain admin (or GPO-edit-delegated) privileges required to create/modify the GPO.
steps.guidance: Review domain controller authentication logs and privileged account activity around the GPO modification timestamp.
steps.outcome: Root cause of the privileged access compromise identified.

steps.title: Disable the compromised privileged account and reset domain administrative credentials
steps.desc: Disable the account(s) used to create/modify the GPO, and given the domain-admin-level compromise, evaluate a broader credential reset for privileged accounts and the krbtgt account.
steps.guidance: Follow Microsoft's guidance for a suspected domain compromise, including double krbtgt password reset if warranted by the scope of privileged access compromised.
steps.outcome: Compromised privileged access invalidated across the domain.
