steps.desc: Aggregate the total data transferred and identify the recipient email address/external sharing target to assess sensitivity and inform whether legal/law-enforcement engagement is warranted.
steps.guidance: Review DLP content-inspection results where available and correlate with the sender's file-access activity.
steps.outcome: Documented estimate of data volume, sensitivity, and recipient identified.

steps.title: Isolate the source host or disable the compromised/misused account
steps.desc: Depending on the root cause determined, apply EDR network isolation to a compromised host, or disable/restrict the account if insider misuse is confirmed.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with HR/legal before taking action against an employee account if insider-threat activity is suspected.
steps.outcome: Further exfiltration halted.

steps.title: Deploy or tune DLP controls for email and file-sharing exfiltration permanently
steps.desc: Implement or tune DLP policies on the email gateway and file-sharing platform to detect and block future exfiltration of sensitive data via these channels.
steps.guidance: Configure content-inspection rules for sensitive data patterns and external-sharing restrictions on both channels.
steps.outcome: Permanent detection/prevention capability in place for email and file-sharing exfiltration.

steps.title: Determine whether the activity reflects external compromise or insider threat
steps.desc: Investigate whether the transfer was performed by a compromised account/host (external attacker) or a legitimate account holder (potential insider threat) to determine the appropriate response track.
steps.guidance: Review EDR telemetry for malware/account-compromise indicators and correlate with any HR/insider-threat signals for the account holder.
steps.outcome: Root cause determined (external compromise vs. insider activity), directing subsequent response.

ITID-43111.def: The use of DNS queries and responses to carry non-DNS payloads (commands, files, or arbitrary data) by encoding them into subdomain labels, TXT records, or other resource-record fields, exploiting the fact that DNS is near-universally permitted outbound through firewalls.
ITID-43111.purpose: Captures DNS tunneling classified purely as an abuse of the DNS protocol's transport properties, before analysts have determined whether it was used for command-and-control, data exfiltration, or filter evasion.
scopeIncludes: Encoding arbitrary data into DNS query subdomains or TXT/NULL record responses
Use of a DNS tunneling protocol/tool (iodine, dnscat2, DNS2TCP) where analysts have not yet confirmed the operational intent
Anomalous DNS query volume/entropy consistent with tunneling but not yet attributed to a specific campaign
scopeExcludes: DNS tunneling confirmed as the mechanism for command-and-control traffic (ITID-32513, ITID-44221)
DNS tunneling confirmed as the mechanism for data exfiltration using a commodity tool (ITID-34123) or in general (ITID-34124)
Legitimate DNS-based services (e.g. some CDN/anti-spam TXT lookups) with high query entropy but no covert payload
ITID-43111.severity: Medium, pending intent determination; escalate to High if payload content, destination domain, or volume indicates active exfiltration or C2.
ITID-43111.priority: P2 initial triage; re-prioritize once intent is confirmed and the ITID is reclassified to the appropriate exfiltration/C2 leaf.
ITID-43111.escalation: Escalate to Tier 2/3 SOC analysis for payload decoding and domain reputation checks; escalate to IR if confirmed as active data movement.
indicators: High-entropy or unusually long subdomain labels
Sustained high-volume queries to a single authoritative domain
TXT/NULL/CNAME record usage inconsistent with the domain's normal purpose
DNS query patterns with regular beacon-like timing
vectors: Malware embedding a DNS tunneling client
Living-off-the-land use of nslookup/dig scripted to exfiltrate data
Commercial or open-source tunneling tools repurposed for covert channels
rootCauses: DNS egress traffic not inspected or rate-limited at the perimeter
No DNS query-logging or analytics platform in place
Overly permissive DNS resolution allowed direct to internet rather than via a controlled resolver
controls: DNS query logging and analytics (entropy/volume baselining)
Forced use of internal recursive resolvers with egress DNS blocked
DNS firewall/RPZ filtering against known tunneling domains
ITID-43111.detection: Strong where DNS query logging and entropy-based analytics are deployed; weak in environments that only log resolver errors or sample traffic.
ITID-43111.response: Capture and decode representative query samples, identify the destination domain's registrant/reputation, and reclassify the incident once intent is established.
metrics: Count of DNS-tunneling detections pending reclassification
Mean time to intent determination
Percentage of tunneling detections later confirmed as malicious vs. benign anomaly
ITID-43111.notes: This leaf exists to hold protocol-level DNS tunneling observations before intent is known. The taxonomy's detailed exfiltration/C2 breakdowns live under ITID-32513 (covert exfil/C2), ITID-34123 (commodity tool), ITID-34124 (general exfiltration) and ITID-44221 (C2 context) — analysts should reclassify into one of those once the purpose is clear rather than leaving mature incidents here.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General DNS Tunneling (Protocol Exploitation Context)
playbook.description: An internal host is exfiltrating data or maintaining C2 by encoding traffic inside DNS queries/responses to an attacker-controlled authoritative domain.

steps.title: Hunt DNS query logs for tunneling indicators
steps.desc: Review recursive resolver / DNS firewall logs for high-entropy subdomain labels, abnormally long QNAMEs, unusual record types (TXT/NULL/CNAME chains), and high query volume to a small set of second-level domains.
steps.guidance: Filter for QNAME length > 50 chars, Shannon entropy above baseline, and NXDOMAIN rate spikes to a single registered domain. Cross-reference with newly-registered-domain (NRD) threat intel feeds.
steps.outcome: Candidate tunneling domain(s) and source host(s) identified with query samples exported for analysis.
steps.abort: If volume is explained by a legitimate CDN/security-vendor DNS-based service (e.g. SPF lookups, threat-intel DNS feeds), document and close as benign.
steps.tool: DNS resolver logs / DNS firewall (e.g. Infoblox, Cisco Umbrella)

steps.title: Sinkhole or block the tunneling domain
steps.desc: Add the identified C2/exfil domain(s) to the DNS firewall blocklist or redirect to an internal sinkhole to immediately cut the channel.
steps.guidance: Block at the recursive resolver and at perimeter firewall for direct UDP/53 to external authoritative servers bypassing the resolver.
steps.outcome: DNS tunneling traffic to the identified domain(s) stops; sinkhole logs confirm continued beacon attempts from the infected host.

steps.title: Remove tunneling client and persistence mechanisms
steps.desc: Remove the identified tunneling binary/process and any associated scheduled tasks, services, or registry run-keys establishing persistence.
steps.guidance: Use EDR remote remediation or offline forensic removal; re-image if rootkit-level persistence is suspected.
steps.outcome: Host confirmed clean via re-scan; no further outbound DNS anomalies from the host.

steps.title: Restore host to production and monitor
steps.desc: Return the remediated host to normal network access and monitor DNS logs for 14 days for recurrence.
steps.guidance: Add the host to a watchlist in the DNS firewall/SIEM for elevated logging.
steps.outcome: No recurrence of tunneling indicators over the monitoring window.

steps.title: Document root cause and update detection rules
steps.desc: Record initial infection vector, tune DNS analytics thresholds (entropy/length/NXDOMAIN rate) to reduce future detection time, and brief the SOC.
steps.guidance: Update the DNS-tunneling detection use case and add the discovered domain/IOC to threat intel feeds.
steps.outcome: Updated detection rule deployed and after-action report filed.

steps.title: Correlate suspect host with endpoint telemetry
steps.desc: Pivot from the source IP/host identified in DNS logs to EDR process and network telemetry to confirm an active tunneling client process (e.g. iodine, dnscat2, DNSExfiltrator) or malware beaconing.
steps.guidance: Check parent-child process trees, unsigned binaries making direct UDP/53 or DoH calls outside the browser/OS resolver stack, and scheduled task/service persistence.
steps.outcome: Confirmed malicious process and host, or determination that DNS is being proxied through a compromised internal resolver.

steps.title: Isolate the affected host from the network
steps.desc: Quarantine the confirmed host via EDR network isolation to prevent further exfiltration or lateral movement while forensic imaging is arranged.
steps.guidance: Preserve volatile memory/process state before full isolation if forensic capture is planned.
steps.outcome: Host is network-isolated with only EDR management channel active.
steps.abort: If host is business-critical, apply host-based egress ACL to permit only required traffic instead of full isolation, with compensating monitoring.

steps.title: Restrict direct external DNS resolution org-wide
steps.desc: Enforce that all internal hosts resolve only through sanctioned internal resolvers (block outbound UDP/TCP 53 and DoH/DoT to arbitrary external endpoints at the perimeter).
steps.guidance: Coordinate with network team to add firewall rules; validate no legitimate business dependency on direct external DNS is broken.
steps.outcome: Perimeter firewall confirmed blocking direct external DNS resolution except through approved resolvers.

ITID-43121.def: An attacker positioned to observe or predict a DNS query races the legitimate authoritative server by injecting a forged response with a matching transaction ID and source port, exploiting the connectionless, unauthenticated nature of UDP-based DNS.
ITID-43121.purpose: Captures the classic on-path/off-path race condition attack where a forged DNS response is delivered before the legitimate authoritative answer arrives.
scopeIncludes: Off-path transaction-ID and source-port guessing/racing attacks (Kaminsky-class)
On-path attacker on a shared network segment racing the real resolver response
Exploitation of predictable/insufficiently randomized query IDs or source ports
scopeExcludes: Spoofing achieved by compromising the resolver or router itself (ITID-43122)
Spoofing whose defining feature is the redirection outcome rather than the racing mechanism (ITID-43123)
Cache poisoning that persists a forged record for later victims (ITID-43131)
ITID-43121.severity: High — a successful race can redirect any client resolving through the targeted resolver in real time.
ITID-43121.priority: P1 if confirmed against a production resolver; P2 during triage of a suspected single occurrence.
ITID-43121.escalation: Escalate immediately to network engineering to validate resolver source-port/transaction-ID randomization and to IR if redirected traffic reached a malicious destination.
indicators: Duplicate DNS responses for the same query with differing answer data
Resolver logs showing a rejected/late-arriving authoritative response after an earlier one was accepted
Unexpected TTL or answer changes for a domain with no legitimate registrar change
vectors: UDP source-port and transaction-ID prediction against a non-randomizing resolver
On-path positioning via a compromised network segment to win the race deterministically
rootCauses: Resolver software with weak or absent query-ID/source-port randomization
No DNSSEC validation enforced on the resolution path
Resolver reachable from untrusted network segments
controls: DNSSEC validation on all recursive resolvers
Query-ID and source-port randomization patching/configuration
Network segmentation limiting on-path positioning
ITID-43121.detection: Moderate — requires resolver-side logging of duplicate/conflicting responses, which many deployments do not retain.
ITID-43121.response: Validate resolver patch level and randomization settings, capture packet evidence of the race if available, and rotate any credentials/sessions exposed via redirected traffic.
metrics: Confirmed DNS response race events per quarter
Resolvers validated for DNSSEC/randomization compliance
ITID-43121.notes: Differentiated from sibling leaves by mechanism: this is specifically the race-condition/prediction attack against an in-flight query, not resolver compromise or cache persistence.

playbook.name: DNS Response Spoofing via On-Path Attacker (Race-the-Real-Response)
playbook.description: An on-path attacker races a forged DNS response to a client's query ahead of the legitimate authoritative/resolver reply, redirecting the client to a malicious IP.

steps.title: Identify duplicate/conflicting DNS responses for a query
steps.desc: Analyze packet captures or resolver logs for a single query transaction ID receiving two responses with differing answer records, or clients resolving a known-good domain to an unexpected IP.
steps.guidance: Look for mismatched TTL/answer sections arriving in rapid succession, and unexpected ARP entries suggesting the attacker sits on-path (ARP cache manipulation, rogue switch port).
steps.outcome: Confirmed spoofed response instance with source segment and affected client(s) identified.
steps.abort: If discrepancy traces to legitimate split-horizon DNS or GSLB, close as benign.

steps.title: Isolate the on-path attacking device/port
steps.desc: Administratively shut down or NAC-quarantine the switch port/device performing ARP spoofing to stop response racing.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with network operations for immediate port shutdown; capture MAC/port binding evidence first.
steps.outcome: ARP spoofing traffic ceases on the segment.

steps.title: Enable Dynamic ARP Inspection and DHCP snooping on the segment
steps.desc: Configure DAI and DHCP snooping on the affected switches to prevent future ARP-based on-path positioning.
steps.guidance: Build trusted-port/binding table from DHCP snooping before enforcing DAI to avoid outages.
steps.outcome: DAI/DHCP snooping active and verified blocking test spoofed ARP frames.

steps.title: Restore normal network operation and validate DNS integrity
steps.desc: Confirm clients resolve internal and external domains correctly and monitor the segment for renewed spoofing attempts.
steps.guidance: Run periodic ARP/DNS integrity checks for 7 days.
steps.outcome: No further spoofed responses observed.

steps.title: Review segment security posture and update baseline
steps.desc: Document the attack path, verify DAI/DHCP snooping coverage across all access-layer switches org-wide, and update the network hardening baseline.
steps.outcome: Hardening gap closed org-wide, after-action report filed.

steps.title: Determine attacker on-path position
steps.desc: Check switch CAM tables, ARP tables, and DHCP snooping logs on the affected segment to locate the on-path device performing ARP spoofing or rogue gateway/DHCP behavior enabling response racing.
steps.guidance: Compare MAC-to-IP bindings against known-good inventory; look for gratuitous ARP storms.
steps.outcome: Rogue device/port identified on the local segment.

steps.title: Flush poisoned ARP/DNS caches on affected clients
steps.desc: Force ARP cache and DNS resolver cache flush on all clients on the affected VLAN/segment to remove stale spoofed entries.
steps.guidance: Push via GPO/remote script; verify via spot-check that legitimate ARP/DNS entries are restored.
steps.outcome: Affected clients resolve the target domain correctly again.

steps.title: Deploy DNSSEC or response-authentication where supported
steps.desc: Where the affected zone/resolver supports it, enable DNSSEC validation or equivalent response-authentication to make future response-racing attempts cryptographically detectable.
steps.outcome: DNSSEC validation active and verified rejecting an unsigned forged response in testing.
steps.abort: If the zone does not support DNSSEC, document as an accepted residual risk pending broader DNSSEC rollout.

ITID-43122.def: An adversary who has gained control of a local DNS resolver, router, or DHCP configuration alters the DNS server settings or resolver responses served to victims, causing every subsequent lookup on that network to be answered maliciously.
ITID-43122.purpose: Captures DNS spoofing achieved by compromising a local resolver, home/branch router, or DHCP-assigned DNS setting rather than racing individual queries.
scopeIncludes: Router/CPE malware or credential compromise used to change configured DNS server addresses
Compromised internal recursive resolver serving forged answers to all clients
DHCP option manipulation pushing a rogue DNS server to endpoints
scopeExcludes: Per-query racing of a legitimate, uncompromised resolver (ITID-43121)
The resulting traffic-redirection outcome once the victim reaches attacker infrastructure (ITID-43123)
ITID-43122.severity: High — a compromised resolver or router affects every device relying on it, not a single session.
ITID-43122.priority: P1 for any confirmed compromise of shared DNS infrastructure (branch router, internal resolver).
ITID-43122.escalation: Escalate to network/infrastructure teams immediately to isolate the compromised device and to IR to scope the blast radius of affected clients.
indicators: Unauthorized changes to router/CPE DNS configuration
Internal resolver returning answers inconsistent with upstream authoritative records
Mass client resolution to unexpected IP ranges from a single network segment
vectors: Default/weak router admin credentials exploited to change DNS settings
Vulnerable router firmware exploited for persistent DNS hijack
Compromise of an internal recursive resolver host
rootCauses: Unpatched router/CPE firmware
Default credentials left on network infrastructure
No configuration-drift monitoring on DNS infrastructure
controls: Router/CPE credential hardening and firmware patching
Configuration-drift monitoring on DNS/DHCP infrastructure
Client-side DNS-over-HTTPS/TLS to a trusted resolver independent of local network config
ITID-43122.detection: Moderate — configuration-management and drift-detection tooling catches this reliably where deployed; otherwise surfaces only via downstream victim reports.
ITID-43122.response: Isolate and re-image or re-flash the compromised device, restore known-good DNS configuration, and audit all clients that resolved through it during the compromise window.
metrics: Router/resolver configuration-drift alerts investigated
Mean time to isolate compromised DNS infrastructure
detections: Resolver answer consistency checking against upstream authoritative sources
ITID-43122.notes: Differentiated by mechanism: this leaf is infrastructure compromise (router/resolver/DHCP), not query-racing or the redirection outcome itself.

playbook.name: DNS Spoofing via Compromised Local Resolver/Router
playbook.description: An attacker has compromised an internal DNS resolver, forwarder, or SOHO/branch router's DNS settings to serve forged responses to clients.

steps.title: Compare resolver responses against known-good authoritative answers
steps.desc: Query the suspect internal resolver directly for a set of high-value domains and compare against a trusted external/authoritative source to detect mismatched answers.
steps.guidance: Use dig/nslookup against the suspect resolver and against 1.1.1.1/8.8.8.8 or authoritative servers; flag any deviation.
steps.outcome: Confirmed forged records returned by the internal resolver/router.
steps.abort: If discrepancy is due to legitimate internal DNS overrides (split-horizon), close as benign.

steps.title: Take the compromised resolver/router out of production DNS path
steps.desc: Redirect client DNS to a known-good resolver and disable or isolate the compromised device to stop serving forged responses.
steps.guidance: Update DHCP scope options and/or client static resolver settings as an interim measure.
steps.outcome: Clients now receive correct DNS answers via the trusted resolver.

steps.title: Rebuild or factory-reset and re-harden the compromised device
steps.desc: Reset the resolver/router to a known-clean configuration or firmware image, apply latest patches, and re-apply hardened DNS forwarder configuration.
steps.guidance: Verify firmware/software integrity against vendor checksums before returning to service.
steps.outcome: Device restored to a verified clean, patched, and correctly configured state.

steps.title: Validate DNS integrity across affected segments
steps.desc: Confirm all previously affected clients now resolve correctly and monitor resolver logs for anomalies.
steps.guidance: Spot-check a sample of high-value domains from multiple client segments.
steps.outcome: No forged responses detected over a 7-day monitoring period.

steps.title: Document compromise path and harden device management practices
steps.desc: Record how admin access was obtained, update device hardening/patch cadence standards, and brief network operations.
steps.outcome: After-action report filed and hardening standard updated.

steps.title: Audit resolver/router configuration and admin access logs
steps.desc: Review the resolver's zone/forwarder configuration and the router's DNS relay settings, plus admin login history, for unauthorized changes.
steps.guidance: Check for unexpected forwarders pointing to attacker infrastructure, and for recent admin logins from unusual source IPs.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized configuration change and compromised admin credential/access path identified.

steps.title: Revoke and rotate compromised administrative credentials
steps.desc: Disable the admin account(s) used to alter the resolver/router configuration and force credential rotation for all accounts with access to that device.
steps.guidance: Check for credential reuse on other network devices.
steps.outcome: Compromised credentials invalidated org-wide.

steps.title: Enable DNSSEC validation and management-plane hardening
steps.desc: Enable DNSSEC validation on the resolver where supported and restrict device management access to an out-of-band or ACL-restricted network.
steps.guidance: Test DNSSEC validation does not break resolution for non-signed internal zones before full enforcement.
steps.outcome: DNSSEC validation active; management interface no longer reachable from general user segments.

ITID-43123.def: The end state of a successful DNS spoofing attack in which a victim resolves a legitimate domain to an attacker-controlled IP address and is transparently sent to that infrastructure, typically for phishing, malware delivery, or traffic interception.
ITID-43123.purpose: Captures DNS spoofing classified by its outcome — a victim's traffic is silently redirected to attacker-controlled infrastructure — regardless of the underlying spoofing mechanism.
scopeIncludes: Confirmed redirection of victim traffic to an attacker-hosted server following any DNS spoofing mechanism
Pharming-style mass redirection observed at the network egress or endpoint level
Cases where the spoofing mechanism itself was not captured but the redirection outcome was
scopeExcludes: The racing mechanism against an in-flight query, tracked separately when observed (ITID-43121)
The resolver/router compromise mechanism, tracked separately when observed (ITID-43122)
Persistent forged cache entries without confirmed traffic redirection (ITID-43131)
ITID-43123.severity: High — successful redirection places victims directly on attacker infrastructure, enabling credential theft or malware delivery.
ITID-43123.priority: P1 upon confirmed redirection of any production traffic.
ITID-43123.escalation: Escalate to IR immediately; treat as an active compromise vector until the destination infrastructure is assessed and blocked.
indicators: Endpoint or proxy logs showing a legitimate domain resolving to a known-bad or unexpected IP
TLS certificate mismatch warnings for a domain the user believes is legitimate
Sudden traffic shift to a newly observed IP for a long-established domain
vectors: Any successful DNS spoofing mechanism (racing, resolver compromise, cache poisoning) culminating in redirection
Malicious browser extensions or local hosts-file tampering mimicking DNS-level redirection
rootCauses: No DNS response validation at the client or resolver level
Lack of TLS certificate pinning/validation enforcement on sensitive applications
No outbound traffic monitoring correlating domain-to-IP resolution history
controls: Domain-to-IP resolution history baselining and anomaly alerting
TLS certificate validation enforcement on critical applications
DNSSEC validation and DNS-over-HTTPS/TLS to trusted resolvers
ITID-43123.detection: Moderate — strong where domain-resolution history is baselined; weak in environments without historical DNS analytics.
ITID-43123.response: Block the malicious IP/domain pairing, force re-resolution for affected clients, and assess whether credentials or data were exposed to the rogue infrastructure.
metrics: Confirmed redirection incidents per quarter
Mean time to block malicious destination IP
ITID-43123.notes: This leaf is outcome-based (redirection achieved) rather than mechanism-based, complementing the mechanism-specific siblings ITID-43121 and ITID-43122.

playbook.name: DNS Spoofing to Redirect Traffic to Attacker-Controlled Server
playbook.description: A domain resolution has been manipulated so that users are silently redirected to an attacker-controlled server, typically for credential phishing or malware delivery.

steps.title: Confirm redirection destination and scope of affected users
steps.desc: Verify the spoofed domain resolves to an attacker-controlled IP and identify which users/segments received the forged answer, via resolver query logs and user reports.
steps.guidance: Correlate helpdesk reports of certificate warnings or unexpected login pages with resolver logs for the affected domain.
steps.outcome: Confirmed attacker IP, affected time window, and list of impacted users/hosts.

steps.title: Block the attacker-controlled IP and domain at perimeter and DNS firewall
steps.desc: Immediately block egress to the attacker IP and add the spoofed domain resolution to the DNS firewall blocklist/sinkhole.
steps.outcome: Traffic to attacker infrastructure blocked.

steps.title: Remediate the DNS manipulation root cause
steps.desc: Identify and fix the mechanism enabling the spoofing (compromised resolver, cache poisoning, or on-path attacker per prior identification) and restore authoritative records.
steps.guidance: Cross-reference with related resolver/router compromise or cache poisoning playbooks if applicable.
steps.outcome: Domain resolves correctly to the legitimate destination from all affected segments.

steps.title: Notify affected users and monitor for follow-on fraud/abuse
steps.desc: Send a user advisory about the incident and monitor authentication logs for anomalous activity tied to potentially compromised credentials.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with communications/legal if customer-facing domains were involved.
steps.outcome: Users notified; no anomalous authentication activity observed post-remediation.

steps.title: Conduct after-action review and update DNS integrity monitoring
steps.desc: Document the full attack chain, notify legal/compliance if PII was exposed, and add continuous DNS-answer integrity monitoring for high-value domains.
steps.outcome: After-action report filed and monitoring control implemented.

steps.title: Assess whether credentials or data were submitted to the rogue server
steps.desc: Interview affected users and review proxy/EDR logs to determine if credentials, session tokens, or files were sent to the attacker-controlled endpoint.
steps.guidance: Check for POST requests to the malicious IP in proxy logs during the exposure window.
steps.outcome: Determination of credential/data exposure requiring downstream password resets.

steps.title: Force password reset and session revocation for exposed users
steps.desc: Reset credentials and revoke active sessions/tokens for any user confirmed or suspected to have submitted data to the rogue server.
steps.guidance: Prioritize privileged accounts first.
steps.outcome: Exposed credentials invalidated; active sessions terminated.

steps.title: Add the redirected domain to brand/phishing monitoring
steps.desc: Enroll the abused domain in continuous brand-abuse/phishing monitoring to detect any recurrence of attacker-controlled redirection infrastructure targeting it.
steps.outcome: Monitoring active and alerting verified.

ITID-43124.def: General or as-yet-unclassified DNS spoofing activity, used during initial triage before the specific mechanism or outcome is determined.
ITID-43124.purpose: Intake bucket for DNS spoofing activity that does not yet fit a specific mechanism (racing, infrastructure compromise) or outcome (confirmed redirection) leaf.
scopeIncludes: Suspected DNS spoofing reported by a user or tool without confirmed mechanism
DNS spoofing indicators found during retrospective log review with insufficient detail to classify further
scopeExcludes: Any DNS spoofing incident once the mechanism (ITID-43121, ITID-43122) or the redirection outcome (ITID-43123) has been confirmed — reclassify at that point
ITID-43124.severity: Medium pending triage; re-assess once further detail is available.
ITID-43124.escalation: Escalate to Tier 2 analysis for mechanism/outcome determination; escalate to IR if any evidence of active redirection surfaces during triage.
indicators: User report of an unexpected certificate warning or wrong-looking site
DNS answer inconsistent with expected authoritative record, mechanism unconfirmed
vectors: Any DNS spoofing technique, not yet attributed
rootCauses: Insufficient DNS logging/telemetry to determine mechanism at time of report
controls: DNS query and response logging
User reporting channel for suspected spoofing
ITID-43124.detection: Variable — dependent entirely on available logging at time of report.
ITID-43124.response: Gather additional telemetry to reclassify into a specific sibling leaf; escalate if evidence of active compromise emerges.
metrics: Count of general DNS spoofing reports pending reclassification
Mean time to reclassification
ITID-43124.notes: Catch-all triage leaf; mature incidents should be reclassified into ITID-43121, ITID-43122, or ITID-43123 once details are known.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General DNS Spoofing
playbook.description: A generic DNS spoofing event where responses to client queries are forged to point to unintended or malicious addresses, mechanism not yet classified.

steps.title: Validate reported anomalous resolution
steps.desc: Reproduce the reported resolution issue and compare the returned answer against a trusted authoritative/external resolver to confirm spoofing versus misconfiguration.
steps.guidance: Use multiple vantage points (different segments, external resolver) to triangulate scope.
steps.outcome: Spoofing confirmed or ruled out with supporting evidence.
steps.abort: If explained by legitimate caching/TTL/CDN behavior, close as benign.

steps.title: Block malicious resolution destination
steps.desc: Sinkhole or block the malicious destination IP/domain at DNS firewall and network perimeter.
steps.outcome: Client traffic no longer reaches the attacker-controlled destination.

steps.title: Remediate the underlying cause and restore correct resolution
steps.desc: Fix/rebuild the compromised component, remove any malicious hosts-file or proxy entries, and confirm accurate DNS resolution is restored.
steps.outcome: All affected clients resolve target domains correctly.

steps.title: Monitor for recurrence
steps.desc: Track resolver and endpoint logs for a defined monitoring period to confirm the spoofing does not resume.
steps.outcome: No recurrence observed over the monitoring window.

steps.title: Document findings and refine classification for future events
steps.desc: Record the confirmed vector for use in refining detection/classification, and update runbooks accordingly.
steps.outcome: After-action report filed; detection guidance updated.

steps.title: Determine spoofing vector and scope
steps.desc: Investigate whether the spoofing originates from an on-path attacker, compromised resolver, cache poisoning, or compromised endpoint hosts file/proxy settings.
steps.guidance: Check hosts files, proxy PAC settings, resolver configs, and network path for the affected clients.
steps.outcome: Vector identified and affected population scoped.

steps.title: Isolate or reconfigure the source of the spoofed answers
steps.desc: Depending on the identified vector, isolate the compromised device (resolver, router, or endpoint) from the network to stop further forged responses.
steps.outcome: Source of spoofed answers neutralized.

steps.title: Validate no residual spoofed entries remain across dependent caches
steps.desc: Sweep downstream caching resolvers, browser DNS caches, and CDN edge caches for any residual copies of the spoofed record beyond the immediate flush point.
steps.outcome: All layers confirmed serving the correct record.

ITID-43131.def: The insertion of a forged resource record into a resolver's cache so that it is served to any subsequent client querying that record, until the record's TTL expires — a persistence-oriented variant of DNS spoofing distinct from a one-off, in-flight race.
ITID-43131.purpose: Provides a protocol-level, general definition of DNS cache poisoning for use before or in place of the detailed technical breakdown maintained elsewhere in the taxonomy.
scopeIncludes: Forged records persisted in a shared recursive resolver's cache
Poisoning that affects all clients using the resolver for the TTL duration, not just the original targeted query
scopeExcludes: A single in-flight query race with no lasting cache effect (ITID-43121)
The detailed technical exploit chain and CVE-level breakdown, tracked in the Exploitation domain (ITID-32511 DNS Cache Poisoning Exploit)
ITID-43131.severity: High — persistence in a shared cache multiplies the number of affected victims over the TTL window.
ITID-43131.priority: P1 upon confirmation against any shared/production resolver.
ITID-43131.escalation: Escalate to network engineering to flush the affected cache and to IR to assess exposure of all clients served during the poisoning window.
indicators: Resolver cache entry with a TTL/value inconsistent with the authoritative source
Multiple, geographically or organizationally distinct clients redirected to the same rogue IP from a shared resolver
vectors: Exploitation of resolver software vulnerabilities to insert or overwrite cache entries
Chained on-path spoofing techniques used to seed a persistent cache entry
rootCauses: Resolver software lacking DNSSEC validation or modern cache-poisoning mitigations
Shared resolver serving both trusted and untrusted network segments
controls: DNSSEC validation
Resolver software patching and cache-poisoning mitigation features (0x20 encoding, strict source-port randomization)
Cache TTL monitoring and anomaly alerting
ITID-43131.detection: Moderate — depends on resolver-side cache monitoring, which is inconsistently deployed.
ITID-43131.response: Flush the poisoned cache entry, patch/harden the resolver, and notify all downstream consumers of the affected TTL window.
metrics: Confirmed cache-poisoning events per quarter
Resolvers hardened against known poisoning techniques
ITID-43131.notes: This is the general, network-infrastructure-level definition of cache poisoning within Protocol Exploitation. For the detailed CVE/exploit-chain analysis, see ITID-32511 (DNS Cache Poisoning Exploit) under the Exploitation domain.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General DNS Cache Poisoning (Protocol Exploitation Context)
playbook.description: An attacker has injected forged records into a caching resolver, causing it to serve malicious answers to all downstream clients until the poisoned TTL expires.

steps.title: Detect poisoned cache entries on the resolver
steps.desc: Query the affected caching resolver directly for the impacted domain(s) and compare against authoritative source records; check resolver cache-dump if supported.
steps.guidance: Look for unexpected TTL resets, unusual authority/additional-section records (classic poisoning signature), and answers pointing to non-organizational IP space.
steps.outcome: Poisoned record(s) confirmed with affected domain and resolver identified.
steps.abort: If discrepancy is explained by a legitimate DNS change propagating, close as benign.

steps.title: Flush the poisoned cache entries
steps.desc: Manually flush the affected zone/record from the resolver cache to immediately stop serving the forged answer.
steps.guidance: Flush on all resolver instances/anycast nodes serving the affected segment.
steps.outcome: Resolver returns correct authoritative answer immediately after flush.

steps.title: Patch resolver software and harden query randomization
steps.desc: Apply the latest resolver software patches and ensure source-port and transaction-ID randomization are enabled to close the poisoning weakness.
steps.guidance: Verify patch level against known CVEs for the resolver software in use.
steps.outcome: Resolver patched and randomization confirmed via test queries showing high entropy.

steps.title: Verify resolution integrity and monitor
steps.desc: Confirm the affected domain and related zones resolve correctly across all client segments and monitor for further poisoning attempts.
steps.outcome: No further poisoning detected over a 7-day monitoring window.

steps.title: Document incident and update resolver hardening baseline
steps.desc: Record the poisoning technique, patch/config gap, and update the organization's DNS resolver hardening standard to require randomization and DNSSEC validation by default.
steps.outcome: Hardening baseline updated; after-action report filed.

steps.title: Determine poisoning technique and exposure window
steps.desc: Review resolver query/response logs for signs of Kaminsky-style ID guessing, source-port predictability exploitation, or off-path packet flooding around the time the poisoned entry was cached.
steps.guidance: Check resolver source-port randomization settings and query-ID entropy configuration.
steps.outcome: Technique and time window of poisoning established, informing eradication steps.

steps.title: Notify downstream clients/services of the exposure window
steps.desc: Alert application owners and users who may have connected to the poisoned destination during the exposure window so they can assess impact.
steps.outcome: Downstream stakeholders informed and assessing their own exposure.

steps.title: Enable DNSSEC validation
steps.desc: Turn on DNSSEC validation on the resolver so forged, unsigned responses for signed zones are rejected going forward.
steps.guidance: Test against a small set of DNSSEC-signed zones before full rollout to avoid resolution failures for misconfigured zones.
steps.outcome: DNSSEC validation active and rejecting test forged responses.

ITID-43211.def: Exploitation of a wormable, unauthenticated remote-code-execution flaw in the SMBv1 protocol implementation (the class of vulnerability popularized by EternalBlue/MS17-010) to achieve remote code execution against an exposed SMB service.
ITID-43211.purpose: Provides a general, protocol-level definition of EternalBlue-class SMB exploitation for use at the network-infrastructure altitude, distinct from the detailed CVE/exploit-chain analysis maintained elsewhere.
scopeIncludes: Exploitation attempts or confirmed compromise via a wormable SMBv1 RCE vulnerability class
Self-propagating worm behavior riding this vulnerability class across a network
scopeExcludes: The detailed CVE-specific exploit-chain and payload analysis, tracked at ITID-32521 (Known-CVE SMB Remote Code Execution Exploit)
General/unattributed SMB exploitation not matching this specific wormable RCE class (ITID-32524)
ITID-43211.severity: Critical — this vulnerability class enables unauthenticated, wormable remote code execution and has historically driven large-scale ransomware outbreaks.
ITID-43211.priority: P1, immediate, regardless of confirmed compromise versus scan/attempt.
ITID-43211.escalation: Escalate to IR and network engineering immediately; treat any exposed, unpatched SMBv1 host as an active emergency requiring isolation.
indicators: SMBv1 traffic on a host that should have it disabled
Exploit-framework signatures matching the wormable SMB RCE class
Rapid lateral SMB connection fan-out consistent with worm propagation
vectors: Direct exploitation of an internet- or internally-exposed unpatched SMBv1 service
Worm propagation using this exploit class once one host is compromised
rootCauses: SMBv1 left enabled on legacy systems
Missing critical security patches (e.g. MS17-010-class updates)
No network segmentation restricting SMB traffic between hosts
controls: SMBv1 protocol disablement
Critical patch management SLAs for network-facing services
Network segmentation limiting SMB traffic to only required hosts
ITID-43211.detection: Strong — this vulnerability class is extremely well signatured by IDS/EDR and vulnerability scanners.
ITID-43211.response: Isolate affected hosts immediately, disable SMBv1 organization-wide, and patch/rebuild compromised systems; treat as a potential ransomware precursor.
metrics: Count of hosts with SMBv1 still enabled
Mean time to patch/disable SMBv1 after detection
Confirmed exploitation attempts blocked vs. successful
ITID-43211.notes: This is the general, protocol-exploitation-level definition of the EternalBlue-class threat. For the detailed CVE/exploit-chain breakdown see ITID-32521 (Known-CVE SMB Remote Code Execution Exploit) under the Exploitation domain.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General EternalBlue-Style SMB Exploit (Protocol Exploitation Context)
playbook.description: A host has been exploited via an EternalBlue-class SMBv1 remote code execution vulnerability, posing a wormable, org-wide propagation risk.

steps.title: Confirm exploitation via SMB and EDR telemetry
steps.desc: Correlate IDS/IPS alerts for EternalBlue-family exploit signatures (e.g. MS17-010) with EDR process telemetry on the target host showing anomalous lsass.exe/svchost.exe activity or unexpected SMB-spawned processes.
steps.guidance: Check for the characteristic srv.sys crash/anomaly indicators and unsigned payload injection via SMB.
steps.outcome: Confirmed exploitation host(s) and initial payload identified.
steps.abort: If IDS alert is a false positive against a patched host with no EDR corroboration, close as benign.

steps.title: Isolate all confirmed-compromised hosts
steps.desc: Network-isolate every host confirmed compromised via EDR to halt further lateral propagation.
steps.guidance: Prioritize by criticality and blast-radius (domain controllers, file servers first).
steps.outcome: All confirmed hosts isolated with no new propagation observed.

steps.title: Remove payload and persistence from compromised hosts
steps.desc: Remove the dropped payload, any implanted backdoor/worm component, and persistence mechanisms; re-image any host where clean removal cannot be assured.
steps.outcome: Hosts confirmed clean via re-scan and EDR sweep.

steps.title: Restore hosts to production and validate stability
steps.desc: Return remediated hosts to the network and monitor for exploit signature recurrence and general stability issues.
steps.outcome: No recurrence of exploit indicators over a 14-day monitoring window.

steps.title: Document incident and update patch compliance SLAs
steps.desc: Record the exposure window, patch-compliance gap that allowed exploitation, and tighten critical-patch SLA enforcement and SMBv1 deprecation policy org-wide.
steps.outcome: Updated patch SLA policy and after-action report filed.

steps.title: Scope wormable spread across the SMBv1-reachable network
steps.desc: Given the self-propagating nature of this exploit family, immediately scan the broader network segment for other hosts still running vulnerable SMBv1 and for signs of lateral spread.
steps.guidance: Use vulnerability scanner MS17-010 check plus EDR fleet-wide IOC sweep for the same payload hashes.
steps.outcome: Full list of vulnerable and/or already-compromised hosts across the environment.

steps.title: Block SMBv1/445 laterally at network segmentation points
steps.desc: Apply emergency firewall/ACL rules blocking inbound TCP 445 between workstation segments and from untrusted zones, while patching is underway.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with network team to avoid breaking legitimate file-share dependencies; use temporary allow-list for known-good server-to-server SMB.
steps.outcome: Lateral SMB exploitation traffic blocked between segments.

steps.title: Org-wide patch-verification sweep and SMBv1 disablement
steps.desc: Run an organization-wide sweep confirming MS17-010-class patches are applied on every host, and disable the SMBv1 protocol entirely where not explicitly required.
steps.guidance: Given the wormable nature of this exploit class, this sweep must cover 100% of the fleet, not just the affected segment, consistent with prior worm-domain remediation conventions.
steps.outcome: Fleet-wide patch compliance report shows 100% remediation and SMBv1 disabled except documented exceptions.

ITID-43221.def: An attacker captures an SMB authentication attempt (typically NTLM) and relays it in real time to a second target that accepts the same credentials, gaining authenticated access without ever cracking the underlying password.
ITID-43221.purpose: Provides a general, protocol-level definition of SMB relay attacks for use at the network-infrastructure altitude, cross-referencing the taxonomy's detailed exploit-chain documentation.
scopeIncludes: Real-time relay of a captured SMB/NTLM authentication handshake to a second host
Use of relay tooling (e.g. Responder/ntlmrelayx-class tools) against SMB signing-disabled targets
scopeExcludes: The detailed technique/tooling exploit-chain analysis, tracked at ITID-32522 (SMB Relay Attack Exploitation)
Passive interception without a relay/replay component (covered elsewhere as eavesdropping)
ITID-43221.severity: High — successful relay grants the attacker authenticated access equivalent to the victim account with no password cracking required.
ITID-43221.priority: P1 upon confirmed successful relay to a sensitive target.
ITID-43221.escalation: Escalate to IR immediately; force credential rotation for any account whose authentication was relayed.
indicators: Authentication events showing the same NTLM challenge/response replayed to a different host
SMB signing disabled on hosts where relay succeeded
Unusual source-to-destination authentication patterns inconsistent with normal user behavior
vectors: On-path positioning combined with a relay tool capturing and forwarding SMB authentication
Coercion techniques forcing a privileged host to authenticate to an attacker-controlled listener
rootCauses: SMB signing not enforced on servers/workstations
LLMNR/NBT-NS enabled, enabling easy credential capture on the local segment
Flat network architecture allowing broad relay reach
controls: SMB signing enforcement across all hosts
LLMNR/NBT-NS disablement
Network segmentation limiting relay reach
ITID-43221.detection: Moderate-Strong — authentication-log correlation across hosts reliably surfaces relay patterns where centralized logging exists.
ITID-43221.response: Enforce SMB signing on affected hosts, rotate credentials for relayed accounts, and identify the on-path/coercion vector used.
metrics: Percentage of hosts with SMB signing enforced
Confirmed relay incidents per quarter
ITID-43221.notes: This is the general, protocol-exploitation-level definition. For the detailed technique and tooling breakdown see ITID-32522 (SMB Relay Attack Exploitation) under the Exploitation domain.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General SMB Relay Attack (Protocol Exploitation Context)
playbook.description: An attacker captured and relayed NTLM authentication attempts over SMB to authenticate as the victim against another host, gaining unauthorized access.

steps.title: Identify NTLM relay indicators in authentication logs
steps.desc: Review domain controller and target host authentication logs for NTLM logons from unexpected source hosts/IPs relative to the authenticating user's normal workstation.
steps.guidance: Look for Event ID 4624 (Logon Type 3) NTLM authentications originating from a host acting as a relay rather than the user's own device, and correlate with Responder/ntlmrelayx-style tool signatures on IDS.
steps.outcome: Confirmed relay source host and target(s) accessed under the victim's relayed credentials.
steps.abort: If pattern matches an approved application service account proxy pattern, close as benign.

steps.title: Isolate the relaying attacker host
steps.desc: Network-isolate the host performing the relay (running Responder/ntlmrelayx or similar) to stop further credential capture and relay.
steps.outcome: Relay activity ceases.

steps.title: Enforce SMB signing across the environment
steps.desc: Enable and require SMB signing on all domain controllers, servers, and workstations to prevent relay of captured NTLM authentication, addressing the root cause.
steps.guidance: Deploy via GPO (RequireSecuritySignature) in phases, testing for legacy application compatibility issues before org-wide enforcement.
steps.outcome: SMB signing required and verified active on all critical servers and domain controllers.

steps.title: Validate signing enforcement and monitor for relay attempts
steps.desc: Confirm SMB signing rejects unsigned relay attempts via test tooling and monitor authentication logs for further relay indicators.
steps.outcome: No successful relay attempts observed over a 14-day monitoring window.

steps.title: Document incident and update Active Directory hardening baseline
steps.desc: Record the relay path, confirm SMB signing/LLMNR hardening is codified in the AD security baseline, and brief the SOC and identity team.
steps.outcome: Hardening baseline updated and after-action report filed.

steps.title: Determine scope of unauthorized access via relayed session
steps.desc: Audit what actions were performed on the target system(s) using the relayed authentication session (file access, admin share mounts, command execution).
steps.guidance: Check for use of the relayed session to add accounts, dump SAM/NTDS, or move laterally further.
steps.outcome: Full scope of unauthorized actions taken via the relay documented.

steps.title: Disable or reset the affected account(s) and target host sessions
steps.desc: Force logoff of any sessions established via the relayed credential and reset the password/Kerberos keys for the affected user account.
steps.outcome: Attacker no longer has a valid authenticated session using the victim's identity.

steps.title: Disable LLMNR/NBT-NS and restrict NTLM where possible
steps.desc: Disable LLMNR and NetBIOS Name Service (common relay-enabling name resolution poisoning vectors) and enforce Kerberos-only authentication or NTLM restriction policies where feasible.
steps.outcome: LLMNR/NBT-NS disabled fleet-wide; NTLM usage reduced per policy.

ITID-43231.def: The use of an unauthenticated (null) SMB session to enumerate shares, users, groups, or system information from a host that permits anonymous IPC$ connections, exploiting a legacy SMB protocol allowance rather than any credential weakness.
ITID-43231.purpose: Provides a general, protocol-level definition of SMB null session exploitation for use at the network-infrastructure altitude, cross-referencing the taxonomy's detailed technique documentation.
scopeIncludes: Establishing a null/anonymous SMB session against IPC$ or a share
Enumeration of usernames, group memberships, or share lists via an unauthenticated session
scopeExcludes: The detailed enumeration technique and tooling breakdown, tracked at ITID-32523 (SMB Null Session/Anonymous Access Exploitation)
Null session abuse specifically for reconnaissance/lateral movement within an already-compromised internal network, tracked at ITID-33323
ITID-43231.severity: Medium — primarily an information-disclosure and reconnaissance vector rather than direct code execution.
ITID-43231.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if enumerated information (e.g. privileged account names) is subsequently used in a follow-on attack.
ITID-43231.escalation: Escalate to the host-owning team to disable anonymous access; escalate to IR if enumeration is followed by credential-based attack attempts.
indicators: Successful anonymous logon events (null session) against a host
IPC$ connections from unauthenticated sources
Enumeration tool signatures (e.g. enum4linux-class tools) in network traffic
vectors: Direct connection to IPC$ with no credentials on a misconfigured or legacy host
Automated enumeration scripts run against a range of internal or exposed hosts
rootCauses: Legacy 'RestrictAnonymous' or equivalent setting left permissive
Unpatched or legacy operating systems retaining null session defaults
No monitoring of anonymous SMB logon events
controls: Anonymous/null session restriction hardening (RestrictAnonymous or platform equivalent)
SMB access monitoring and alerting on anonymous logons
Network segmentation limiting exposure of legacy hosts
ITID-43231.detection: Strong — anonymous logon events are reliably logged where SMB auditing is enabled.
ITID-43231.response: Disable anonymous IPC$ access on the affected host, review what was enumerated, and assess whether enumerated data was used in a subsequent attack.
metrics: Hosts hardened against anonymous SMB access
Confirmed null session enumeration events per quarter
ITID-43231.notes: This is the general, protocol-exploitation-level definition. For the detailed technique breakdown see ITID-32523; for the internal reconnaissance/lateral-movement context see ITID-33323.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General SMB Null Session Exploitation (Protocol Exploitation Context)
playbook.description: An attacker used an anonymous/null SMB session to enumerate users, groups, shares, or system information from a host without authenticating.

steps.title: Detect anonymous SMB enumeration activity
steps.desc: Review SMB/security event logs for anonymous logon sessions (Logon Type 3, ANONYMOUS LOGON) performing share enumeration, RPC calls (SAMR/LSARPC), or user/group listing.
steps.guidance: Correlate with IDS signatures for tools like enum4linux, smbclient -N, or rpcclient null-session usage.
steps.outcome: Source IP and enumerated resources (shares, users, groups) identified.
steps.abort: If activity matches an approved legacy application's null-session dependency, document and close as benign but flag for remediation.

steps.title: Block the enumerating source at the network level
steps.desc: Block the attacking source IP at the perimeter/segment firewall to stop ongoing enumeration.
steps.outcome: Enumeration traffic from the source ceases.

steps.title: Harden anonymous access restrictions fleet-wide
steps.desc: Deploy GPO settings restricting anonymous SID/name translation and anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts and shares across all domain-joined hosts.
steps.guidance: Set RestrictAnonymous=1 (or 2 where compatible), disable null session shares (NullSessionShares/NullSessionPipes empty), and verify legacy application compatibility first.
steps.outcome: Null-session enumeration blocked fleet-wide, confirmed via test enumeration attempt failing.

steps.title: Validate hardening and monitor for renewed enumeration attempts
steps.desc: Confirm the hardening policy is applied and monitor logs for further anonymous enumeration attempts.
steps.outcome: No further successful null-session enumeration observed over a 14-day window.

steps.title: Document incident and update baseline hardening standard
steps.desc: Record the exposure and codify anonymous-access restriction as a mandatory baseline control for all new and existing Windows hosts.
steps.outcome: Baseline hardening standard updated; after-action report filed.

steps.title: Assess sensitivity of information disclosed
steps.desc: Determine what user accounts, group memberships, share names, or system details were exposed via the null session, informing downstream risk (e.g. password-spray target list).
steps.outcome: Scope of information disclosure documented for risk assessment.

steps.title: Restrict anonymous access on the affected host(s) immediately
steps.desc: Apply RestrictAnonymous / RestrictAnonymousSAM registry hardening on the affected host(s) as an emergency measure pending fleet-wide rollout.
steps.outcome: Null-session enumeration attempts against the host now fail.

steps.title: Disable unnecessary SMB shares and legacy protocol versions
steps.desc: Remove any unused/legacy SMB shares discoverable via null session and disable SMBv1 where still enabled, reducing the overall enumeration attack surface.
steps.outcome: Unused shares removed; SMBv1 disabled where not required.

ITID-43311.def: An adversary gains RDP access to a host by successfully guessing or trying a small number of commonly used or weak passwords against a valid account, without needing a sustained automated brute-force campaign.
ITID-43311.purpose: Captures a single, successful RDP logon achieved because the account's password was weak or easily guessable, as distinct from a sustained brute-force campaign or a systemic policy failure.
scopeIncludes: Successful RDP logon following a small number of password guesses against a known weak password (e.g. seasonal password, common default)
Credential-stuffing-style single-attempt success using a previously breached password
scopeExcludes: A sustained, automated brute-force campaign against the account (ITID-43331/43332/43333)
Lack of an account lockout policy as the systemic root cause being tracked in its own right (ITID-43312)
Shared local administrator passwords across hosts as the specific weakness (ITID-43313)
ITID-43311.severity: High — a successful logon grants interactive access to the host.
ITID-43311.priority: P1 upon confirmed successful unauthorized logon.
ITID-43311.escalation: Escalate to IR immediately upon confirmed unauthorized interactive access; force password reset for the affected account.
indicators: Successful RDP logon (Event ID 4624 logon type 10) from an unusual source IP or at an unusual time
Logon following a small number of failed attempts from the same source
Password subsequently found in a breach-data or common-password list
vectors: Manual or lightly automated guessing of a weak password
Reuse of a credential exposed in a prior breach
rootCauses: Weak password policy not enforcing complexity/length
No multi-factor authentication on RDP
Password reuse across personal and corporate accounts
mitreTechniques: T1021.001 Remote Services: Remote Desktop Protocol
controls: Password complexity/length policy enforcement
Multi-factor authentication on RDP access
Breached-password screening against a known-compromised-password list
ITID-43311.detection: Strong — successful logon events combined with geolocation/time-of-day anomaly detection reliably surface this.
ITID-43311.response: Disable/reset the affected account, review session activity for the duration of unauthorized access, and enforce MFA before re-enabling access.
metrics: Confirmed weak-credential RDP compromises per quarter
Percentage of RDP-enabled accounts with MFA enforced
ITID-43311.notes: Differentiated from siblings by focusing on a discrete successful weak-password logon rather than the absent lockout policy or shared-password conditions that enabled it.

playbook.name: RDP Access Using Easily Guessable Password
playbook.description: An attacker successfully authenticated to RDP using a weak, dictionary-guessable password on a user or service account.

steps.title: Confirm successful RDP logon with suspicious credential pattern
steps.desc: Review Windows Security event logs (4624 Logon Type 10/RemoteInteractive) for the affected host and correlate with source IP reputation and time-of-day anomalies.
steps.guidance: Cross-check against the account's normal logon baseline (typical source IP, hours) to confirm anomalous access.
steps.outcome: Confirmed unauthorized RDP logon with account, source IP, and timestamp identified.
steps.abort: If logon matches an approved remote-work pattern, close as benign.

steps.title: Disable the compromised account and terminate active RDP sessions
steps.desc: Immediately disable the account and force-terminate any active RDP session established by the attacker.
steps.guidance: Use logoff /server or Task Manager on the host, or disable via Active Directory.
steps.outcome: Attacker session terminated and account access blocked.

steps.title: Reset credentials and enforce a strong password policy
steps.desc: Reset the compromised account's password to a strong, policy-compliant value and verify organizational password complexity/length policy is enforced for all accounts.
steps.outcome: Account secured with compliant credentials; policy gap closed.

steps.title: Restore host to service and monitor account activity
steps.desc: Return the host to normal operation and monitor the account and host for further anomalous logon attempts.
steps.outcome: No recurrence observed over a 14-day monitoring window.

steps.title: Document incident and drive org-wide password/MFA policy compliance
steps.desc: Record the incident and use it to justify accelerating MFA rollout and password policy enforcement across all RDP-accessible hosts.
steps.outcome: After-action report filed; policy enforcement roadmap updated.

steps.title: Assess password strength and reuse of the compromised account
steps.desc: Check the account's password against known-breach corpora and organizational password policy compliance to confirm the weak-password root cause.
steps.outcome: Confirmed the account password was weak/guessable and root cause established.

steps.title: Isolate the accessed host pending investigation
steps.desc: Network-isolate the host that was accessed to prevent further attacker actions or lateral movement while forensic review proceeds.
steps.outcome: Host isolated with only management access retained.
steps.abort: If host is business-critical, apply restrictive host firewall rules instead of full isolation.

steps.title: Enforce MFA and Network Level Authentication for RDP
steps.desc: Require MFA for RDP logons (via RD Gateway/Azure MFA/Duo) and enable Network Level Authentication to add a pre-authentication barrier against future credential-based attacks.
steps.outcome: MFA and NLA enforced and verified on the affected host and ideally fleet-wide.

ITID-43312.def: An RDP service reachable from the internet with no account lockout threshold configured, allowing an adversary unlimited authentication attempts against any account without triggering a lockout defense.
ITID-43312.purpose: Captures the systemic exposure created when an internet-facing RDP service has no account lockout policy, enabling unlimited password attempts regardless of any single guess's outcome.
scopeIncludes: Discovery/audit findings of internet-exposed RDP with no lockout policy configured
Incidents where an unlimited-attempt condition is identified as a contributing root cause to a successful compromise
scopeExcludes: The successful weak-password logon itself, tracked as its own leaf (ITID-43311)
The active brute-force campaign that exploits this condition, tracked under RDP Brute Force (ITID-43331–43334)
ITID-43312.severity: High — this is a systemic enabler of both weak-credential compromise and brute-force attacks, not a one-off finding.
ITID-43312.priority: P2 as a standalone exposure finding; P1 if actively being exploited.
ITID-43312.escalation: Escalate to the system-owning team to enforce lockout policy and MFA; escalate to IR if concurrent brute-force or successful logon activity is observed.
indicators: Vulnerability/configuration scan confirming no lockout threshold on RDP-facing accounts
Unlimited sequential failed-logon attempts against the same account with no lockout triggered
vectors: Direct internet exposure of RDP (port 3389 or equivalent) with default or absent lockout configuration
rootCauses: RDP exposed directly to the internet without a VPN/gateway in front of it
Group Policy account lockout settings not configured or explicitly disabled
No compensating rate-limiting at a network security appliance
mitreTechniques: T1021.001 Remote Services: Remote Desktop Protocol
controls: Account lockout policy enforcement
Removal of direct internet exposure of RDP (VPN/gateway/bastion required)
Network-level rate limiting on RDP connection attempts
ITID-43312.detection: Strong — configuration/vulnerability scanning reliably identifies this exposure.
ITID-43312.response: Configure lockout policy immediately, remove direct internet exposure, and review authentication logs for evidence of exploitation during the exposure window.
metrics: Count of internet-exposed RDP hosts without lockout policy
Mean time to remediate exposure finding
ITID-43312.notes: This is a systemic configuration-exposure leaf; it should be paired with, but not merged into, an active brute-force incident under ITID-43331–43334.

playbook.name: RDP Exposed to Internet with No Account Lockout Policy
playbook.description: An RDP endpoint directly reachable from the internet, lacking an account lockout policy, was exploited to allow unlimited authentication attempts.

steps.title: Confirm internet exposure and unrestricted authentication attempts
steps.desc: Verify via external scan/asset inventory that TCP 3389 is internet-reachable on the affected host, and review event logs for a high volume of 4625 failed logon events with no lockout triggering.
steps.guidance: Cross-reference with Shodan/Censys exposure data if available.
steps.outcome: Confirmed internet exposure and absence of lockout policy causing unmitigated attack attempts.
steps.tool: External attack surface scanner, Windows Event Viewer

steps.title: Remove RDP from direct internet exposure
steps.desc: Immediately block inbound internet access to TCP 3389 at the perimeter firewall/cloud security group and require VPN or RD Gateway for remote access.
steps.outcome: RDP no longer reachable from the internet; confirmed via external scan.

steps.title: Implement account lockout policy and enforce VPN-gated RDP access
steps.desc: Configure an account lockout threshold/duration policy domain-wide and permanently restrict RDP access to only be reachable via VPN or RD Gateway, never directly from the internet.
steps.guidance: Consistent with prior RDP-exposure remediation conventions: exposure reduction takes priority over lockout tuning alone.
steps.outcome: Lockout policy active and RDP confirmed unreachable except via VPN/gateway.

steps.title: Validate exposure closure and monitor authentication attempts
steps.desc: Re-run the external scan to confirm no direct RDP exposure remains and monitor VPN-gated authentication logs for brute-force patterns.
steps.outcome: No internet exposure detected; no unmitigated brute-force activity over 14 days.

steps.title: Document and add internet RDP exposure to continuous attack-surface monitoring
steps.desc: Record the incident and add automated recurring external scanning to catch future accidental RDP exposure quickly.
steps.outcome: Continuous monitoring control implemented; after-action report filed.

steps.title: Determine whether any authentication attempt succeeded
steps.desc: Cross-reference the failed logon flood with any subsequent successful 4624 logon from the same or related source IPs to determine if compromise occurred.
steps.outcome: Determination of whether the exposure resulted in an actual breach versus attempted-only activity.

steps.title: If compromise confirmed, disable affected accounts and isolate host
steps.desc: Disable any account confirmed compromised and isolate the host pending forensic review.
steps.outcome: Further attacker access prevented.
steps.abort: If no compromise confirmed, this step may be skipped with justification.

steps.title: Enforce NLA and MFA for remaining RDP access paths
steps.desc: Enable Network Level Authentication and require MFA on the RD Gateway/VPN for all remote desktop access going forward.
steps.outcome: MFA/NLA enforced and verified.

ITID-43313.def: The use of an identical local administrator password across multiple hosts, such that an adversary who obtains it via any one host (e.g. hash extraction, weak-credential guess) can use RDP to authenticate as local administrator on every other host sharing that password.
ITID-43313.purpose: Captures the specific weakness of a shared local administrator password reused across multiple hosts, which turns a single credential compromise into an organization-wide RDP access risk.
scopeIncludes: Confirmed use of an identical local admin password across two or more hosts, enabling RDP lateral use
Password-spray success attributable to a shared local admin password specifically
scopeExcludes: A single-host weak-password compromise with no evidence of password reuse across hosts (ITID-43311)
Lateral movement execution once inside the network using stolen domain credentials, tracked separately under Lateral Movement (ITID-33311–33314)
ITID-43313.severity: Critical — a single credential compromise cascades to every host sharing the password, dramatically expanding blast radius.
ITID-43313.priority: P1 upon confirmed exploitation; P2 as a standalone audit finding of shared local admin passwords.
ITID-43313.escalation: Escalate to IR immediately; treat as organization-wide until Local Administrator Password Solution (LAPS) or equivalent unique-password enforcement is confirmed in place.
indicators: Identical local administrator password hash found across multiple hosts during an audit
Successive RDP logons as the same local admin account across many hosts in a short window
vectors: Extraction of a local admin password/hash from one compromised host and reuse via RDP against others
Golden-image deployment practices that bake the same local admin password into every build
rootCauses: No Local Administrator Password Solution (LAPS) or equivalent unique-per-host password rotation deployed
Imaging/deployment process using a static local admin password
No monitoring for cross-host local admin authentication patterns
mitreTechniques: T1021.001 Remote Services: Remote Desktop Protocol
controls: Local Administrator Password Solution (LAPS) or equivalent per-host password rotation
Restriction of local admin RDP logon rights via Group Policy
Cross-host authentication pattern monitoring
ITID-43313.detection: Moderate — requires either a proactive password audit or correlated authentication-log analysis across hosts; not surfaced by single-host monitoring alone.
ITID-43313.response: Deploy LAPS/unique password rotation organization-wide, rotate the compromised shared password immediately, and audit for cross-host access during the exposure window.
metrics: Percentage of hosts under LAPS/unique local admin password management
Confirmed shared-password lateral RDP incidents
detections: Cross-host identical local admin logon detection
ITID-43313.notes: Differentiated from other weak-credential siblings by its systemic, cross-host cascading nature rather than a single-account, single-host weakness.

playbook.name: RDP Shared Local Administrator Password Across Multiple Hosts
playbook.description: A shared local administrator password across multiple hosts allowed an attacker who compromised one host to use RDP to laterally move across many others.

steps.title: Identify lateral RDP movement using the shared local admin account
steps.desc: Review authentication logs across hosts for the local administrator account name (or its SID) logging on via RDP from multiple internal source hosts in a short window, a classic pass-the-hash/shared-credential lateral movement pattern.
steps.guidance: Correlate 4624 Logon Type 10 events for the local admin account across many hosts in sequence.
steps.outcome: Full list of hosts accessed via the shared credential and the initial pivot host identified.

steps.title: Isolate all hosts accessed via the shared credential
steps.desc: Network-isolate every host identified in the lateral movement chain to halt further attacker activity.
steps.guidance: Prioritize domain controllers, servers, and any host with sensitive data access.
steps.outcome: All affected hosts isolated.

steps.title: Deploy unique randomized local admin passwords fleet-wide
steps.desc: Deploy Microsoft LAPS (or equivalent) to enforce a unique, randomized, automatically rotated local administrator password per host, eliminating the shared-credential root cause.
steps.outcome: LAPS confirmed active and rotating passwords on 100% of applicable hosts.

steps.title: Restore hosts to service and validate LAPS coverage
steps.desc: Return remediated hosts to production and confirm LAPS coverage extends to all domain-joined machines, monitoring for renewed lateral movement.
steps.outcome: 100% LAPS coverage confirmed; no recurrence over a 14-day window.

steps.title: Document incident and mandate LAPS as baseline control
steps.desc: Record the lateral movement chain and formally mandate unique local admin credential management as a baseline security control for all future host builds.
steps.outcome: Baseline control policy updated; after-action report filed.

steps.title: Determine attacker actions on each accessed host
steps.desc: Review EDR telemetry on each host in the lateral movement chain to identify what actions (data access, persistence, further pivoting) the attacker performed.
steps.outcome: Full scope of attacker activity across all affected hosts documented.

steps.title: Disable the shared local administrator account across the environment
steps.desc: Immediately disable or lock the shared local admin account fleet-wide to stop further use.
steps.guidance: Use a bulk script (e.g. via GPO or LAPS management) rather than manual per-host changes.
steps.outcome: Shared account can no longer authenticate anywhere in the environment.

steps.title: Remove any attacker-planted persistence on affected hosts
steps.desc: Sweep all hosts in the lateral movement chain for backdoors, new accounts, or scheduled tasks planted by the attacker, and remediate.
steps.outcome: All affected hosts confirmed clean.

ITID-43314.def: General or as-yet-unclassified RDP compromise arising from weak credential practices, used during initial triage before the specific contributing factor is determined.
ITID-43314.purpose: Intake bucket for RDP compromise attributable to weak credentials generally, before the specific weakness (single weak password, missing lockout policy, or shared admin password) has been identified.
scopeIncludes: Suspected credential-related RDP compromise pending root-cause determination
scopeExcludes: Any RDP weak-credential incident once the specific factor is confirmed — reclassify to ITID-43311, ITID-43312, or ITID-43313 at that point
ITID-43314.priority: P1 while root cause is being determined, given the interactive-access risk.
ITID-43314.escalation: Escalate to IR immediately on any confirmed unauthorized RDP access, in parallel with root-cause triage.
indicators: Unauthorized RDP logon with credential weakness suspected but not yet isolated to a specific cause
vectors: Any weak-credential RDP compromise technique, not yet attributed
rootCauses: Insufficient logging to isolate the exact credential weakness at time of detection
mitreTechniques: T1021.001 Remote Services: Remote Desktop Protocol
controls: RDP authentication logging
Incident triage workflow for credential-related access
ITID-43314.detection: Variable — dependent on logging available at time of report.
ITID-43314.response: Gather additional telemetry to reclassify into the specific sibling leaf; contain the account/host in the interim.
metrics: Count of general weak-credential RDP reports pending reclassification
ITID-43314.notes: Catch-all triage leaf; reclassify into ITID-43311, ITID-43312, or ITID-43313 once the specific weakness is known.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Weak RDP Credential Exploitation
playbook.description: A generic incident where weak RDP credentials of unspecified type (guessable, shared, or otherwise poorly managed) were exploited to gain unauthorized remote desktop access.

steps.title: Confirm unauthorized RDP access and identify the credential weakness
steps.desc: Review RDP logon events to confirm unauthorized access and determine the specific weak-credential factor involved (guessable password, no lockout, shared account, or default credential).
steps.outcome: Root credential weakness classified and affected host/account identified.
steps.abort: If logon is legitimate/approved, close as benign.

steps.title: Disable the compromised account and terminate sessions
steps.desc: Disable the affected account and terminate any active attacker RDP session.
steps.outcome: Attacker access terminated.

steps.title: Remediate the specific credential weakness identified
steps.desc: Apply the appropriate fix based on root cause: strong password reset, lockout policy configuration, unique-credential deployment (LAPS), or removal of default credentials.
steps.outcome: Credential weakness closed and verified.

steps.title: Restore service and monitor for recurrence
steps.desc: Return the host to normal operation and monitor for further weak-credential exploitation attempts.
steps.outcome: No recurrence over a 14-day monitoring window.

steps.title: Document root cause and update credential management guidance
steps.desc: Record the specific weakness for classification refinement and update credential management guidance accordingly.
steps.outcome: After-action report filed; guidance updated.

steps.title: Scope the extent of attacker activity post-access
steps.desc: Review EDR and system logs on the accessed host for attacker actions taken during the session.
steps.outcome: Scope of impact documented.

steps.title: Isolate the affected host
steps.desc: Network-isolate the accessed host pending remediation.
steps.outcome: Host isolated from further attacker access.

steps.title: Enforce NLA and MFA for RDP going forward
steps.desc: Enable Network Level Authentication and require MFA for RDP access to reduce future credential-based exploitation risk regardless of root cause.
steps.outcome: NLA/MFA enforced and verified.

ITID-43321.def: An adversary who has poisoned the local ARP cache or otherwise positioned themselves on-path between an RDP client and server intercepts and potentially manipulates the RDP session traffic in transit.
ITID-43321.purpose: Captures RDP man-in-the-middle attacks achieved by network-layer positioning (ARP spoofing or equivalent) rather than by exploiting a certificate-validation weakness in the client.
scopeIncludes: ARP cache poisoning or equivalent Layer-2 positioning used to intercept RDP traffic
On-path interception on a shared network segment (e.g. compromised switch port, rogue access point) targeting RDP sessions
scopeExcludes: Interception enabled specifically by the client accepting an invalid/unverified certificate (ITID-43322)
Post-interception credential theft classified under credential access rather than the positioning mechanism itself
