steps.outcome: Scope of device tampering documented.

steps.title: Restrict management access to the device
steps.desc: Apply an ACL restricting device management access to a controlled management network/jump host while further remediation proceeds.
steps.outcome: Device management interface no longer reachable from general network segments.

steps.title: Enable account lockout/rate-limiting on the device's management authentication
steps.desc: Where the device supports it, configure authentication rate-limiting or lockout for management access as defense-in-depth beyond credential rotation alone.
steps.outcome: Rate-limiting/lockout verified active.
steps.abort: If unsupported by the device, document as a residual-risk exception pending hardware refresh.

ITID-43733.def: General or as-yet-unclassified Telnet exploitation activity, used during initial triage before the specific mechanism is determined.
ITID-43733.purpose: Intake bucket for Telnet exploitation activity that has not yet been characterized as passive credential interception or active credential exploitation.
scopeIncludes: Suspected Telnet exploitation reported without a confirmed mechanism
scopeExcludes: Any Telnet exploitation incident once the mechanism is confirmed — reclassify to ITID-43731 or ITID-43732 at that point
ITID-43733.severity: High pending triage, given Telnet's inherent lack of transport security.
ITID-43733.priority: P1 while mechanism is being determined.
ITID-43733.escalation: Escalate to infrastructure teams immediately in parallel with triage.
indicators: Telnet-related anomaly reported without confirmed mechanism
vectors: Any Telnet exploitation technique, not yet attributed
rootCauses: Insufficient detail to determine the specific mechanism at time of detection
controls: Telnet traffic and authentication monitoring
Incident triage workflow for suspected Telnet compromise
ITID-43733.detection: Variable — dependent on available logging at time of report.
ITID-43733.response: Gather additional telemetry to reclassify into ITID-43731 or ITID-43732.
metrics: Count of general Telnet exploitation reports pending reclassification
ITID-43733.notes: Catch-all triage leaf; reclassify into ITID-43731 or ITID-43732 once the mechanism is known.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Telnet Exploitation
playbook.description: A generic Telnet exploitation event of unspecified mechanism (cleartext interception or default/weak credential access) affecting a network device.

steps.title: Confirm the exploitation and classify its mechanism
steps.desc: Review network and device logs to confirm Telnet exploitation and determine whether it was cleartext credential interception or default/weak credential-based access.
steps.outcome: Mechanism classified and affected device identified.
steps.abort: If activity matches an approved admin action, close as benign.

steps.title: Isolate the source or terminate the attacker session
steps.desc: Isolate the intercepting device (if interception) or terminate the attacker's session and reset credentials (if credential-based access).
steps.outcome: Further exploitation stopped.
steps.tool: Switch CLI/NAC or device admin console

steps.title: Replace Telnet with SSH on the affected device
steps.desc: Disable Telnet and enable SSH as the root-cause fix regardless of the specific exploitation mechanism, and audit the fleet for the same gap.
steps.outcome: SSH active and confirmed; fleet-wide audit completed.

steps.title: Validate device integrity and monitor for recurrence
steps.desc: Confirm device configuration is clean and monitor for renewed exploitation attempts.
steps.outcome: No recurrence over a 14-day monitoring window.

steps.title: Document mechanism and update Telnet deprecation policy
steps.desc: Record the confirmed mechanism and reinforce the organization's Telnet deprecation policy.
steps.outcome: After-action report filed; policy reviewed.

steps.title: Assess impact scope
steps.desc: Determine what credentials were exposed or what configuration changes were made on the affected device.
steps.outcome: Impact documented.

steps.title: Restrict management access to the affected device
steps.desc: Apply an ACL restricting management access to a controlled network segment.
steps.outcome: Management interface access restricted.

steps.title: Audit fleet-wide for remaining Telnet-enabled devices
steps.desc: Scan the network for all devices still running Telnet and prioritize migration to SSH org-wide, regardless of the specific exploitation mechanism confirmed here.
steps.outcome: Fleet-wide Telnet inventory produced with remediation plan.

ITID-43741.def: An adversary connects to an MQTT broker that requires no client authentication and freely publishes, subscribes to, or manipulates topics, exploiting a fundamental deployment misconfiguration rather than any protocol-level flaw.
ITID-43741.purpose: Captures exploitation of an MQTT broker deployed with no authentication, allowing any party network access to publish, subscribe, or administer the broker's message bus.
scopeIncludes: Direct connection to an unauthenticated MQTT broker to publish or subscribe to topics
Discovery of internet-exposed, unauthenticated MQTT brokers via scanning
scopeExcludes: Topic hijacking/spoofing against a broker that does have authentication in place (ITID-43742)
Denial-of-service flooding against the broker (ITID-43743)
ITID-43741.severity: High — no-authentication deployment is a common finding in IoT/OT environments and grants an adversary full read/write access to potentially sensitive telemetry or control messages.
ITID-43741.priority: P1 upon confirmed unauthorized broker access, particularly where the broker carries OT/control-system telemetry.
ITID-43741.escalation: Escalate to IT/OT engineering immediately to enable authentication; escalate to IR if control messages were manipulated.
indicators: Successful MQTT connection from an unexpected source with no authentication challenge
Broker configuration confirmed to have authentication disabled during audit
Unexpected publish/subscribe activity from unrecognized client identifiers
vectors: Internet scanning identifying exposed MQTT brokers with authentication disabled
Direct connection to an internal broker left unauthenticated by default configuration
rootCauses: MQTT broker deployed with default/no-authentication configuration
Broker exposed to the internet or a broader network than necessary
No security review of IoT/OT messaging infrastructure at deployment
controls: Mandatory authentication (username/password or client certificate) on all MQTT brokers
Network restriction of broker exposure to only required clients
TLS encryption for MQTT connections
ITID-43741.detection: Strong — broker access logs and network exposure scanning reliably identify this condition where reviewed.
ITID-43741.response: Enable authentication and access control on the broker immediately, review published/subscribed data for exposure or manipulation, and restrict network exposure.
metrics: MQTT brokers confirmed with authentication enabled
Confirmed unauthorized broker access incidents per quarter
ITID-43741.notes: Differentiated from siblings by root condition: complete absence of authentication, rather than topic-level abuse (ITID-43742) or availability impact (ITID-43743) against an otherwise-authenticated broker.

playbook.name: MQTT Broker with No Authentication Exploited
playbook.description: An attacker connected to an unauthenticated, internet-reachable MQTT broker and published/subscribed to topics without authorization, exposing IoT/OT data or issuing unauthorized commands.

steps.title: Confirm unauthenticated access to the MQTT broker
steps.desc: Review broker connection logs for client connections with no username/password or client-certificate presented, and check whether the broker is reachable from the internet without authentication requirements.
steps.guidance: Cross-reference with an external port scan confirming MQTT (1883/8883) reachability.
steps.outcome: Confirmed unauthenticated access with source IP(s) and accessed topics identified.
steps.abort: If broker is intentionally open for a public telemetry use case with no sensitive data, document and close as accepted risk.

steps.title: Block the unauthorized client and restrict broker network exposure
steps.desc: Disconnect the unauthorized client and immediately restrict the broker's network exposure (remove from direct internet reachability) at the firewall.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized access stopped; broker no longer reachable from arbitrary internet sources.

steps.title: Enforce broker authentication and TLS
steps.desc: Configure the MQTT broker to require username/password or client-certificate authentication and enforce TLS for all connections, closing the root cause.
steps.outcome: Broker confirmed rejecting unauthenticated/unencrypted connection attempts.

steps.title: Validate broker security posture and monitor connections
steps.desc: Confirm legitimate IoT/OT clients reconnect successfully under the new authentication scheme and monitor for further unauthorized connection attempts.
steps.outcome: No recurrence over a 14-day monitoring window; legitimate clients unaffected.

steps.title: Document and codify MQTT broker hardening as baseline standard
steps.desc: Record the incident and formalize authentication, TLS, and topic ACLs as mandatory baseline controls for all MQTT broker deployments.
steps.outcome: Baseline updated; after-action report filed.

steps.title: Assess what data was exposed or what commands were published
steps.desc: Review topic subscribe/publish activity to determine what sensor data was disclosed or what control commands were injected by the unauthorized client.
steps.guidance: Pay particular attention to any command/control topics that could affect physical processes (OT/ICS context).
steps.outcome: Scope of data exposure or command injection documented.

steps.title: Reverse any unauthorized control commands issued
steps.desc: If the attacker published control commands affecting physical devices/processes, work with OT/facilities teams to verify and reverse any unsafe state changes.
steps.outcome: Affected devices/processes confirmed in a safe, expected state.
steps.abort: If no control commands were published, skip.

steps.title: Implement topic-level ACLs
steps.desc: Configure access control lists restricting which authenticated clients may publish/subscribe to which topics, limiting blast radius even for a compromised credential.
steps.outcome: ACLs verified restricting topic access appropriately per client role.

ITID-43742.def: An adversary with access to an MQTT broker publishes forged messages to a topic that legitimate subscribers trust, or subscribes to topics to intercept data not intended for them, exploiting insufficient topic-level access control.
ITID-43742.purpose: Captures abuse of MQTT's publish/subscribe model to hijack or spoof topics, injecting false messages or intercepting data intended for legitimate subscribers.
scopeIncludes: Publishing forged/malicious messages to a topic consumed by legitimate systems (e.g. injecting false sensor readings or control commands)
Subscribing to topics beyond the client's intended scope to intercept data
scopeExcludes: Exploitation of a broker with no authentication at all as the root condition (ITID-43741)
Denial-of-service flooding of the broker (ITID-43743)
ITID-43742.severity: Critical where topics carry control-system commands (OT/ICS context); High for telemetry/data topics.
ITID-43742.priority: P1 upon confirmed topic hijacking, especially in an OT/control-system context.
ITID-43742.escalation: Escalate to IT/OT engineering and IR immediately; treat as a potential safety incident if control-topic manipulation is confirmed in an OT environment.
indicators: Messages published to a topic from an unexpected or unauthorized client identifier
Subscriber receiving unexpected/inconsistent message content
Access-control logs showing a client subscribing/publishing outside its authorized topic scope
vectors: Exploitation of overly permissive topic-level ACLs allowing any authenticated client to publish/subscribe to any topic
Client identifier spoofing to assume a trusted publisher's identity
rootCauses: No topic-level access control list (ACL) enforcement
Shared or weak client credentials across many devices
No message-integrity verification at the application layer
controls: Topic-level access control list (ACL) enforcement per client
Unique client credentials/certificates per device (no credential sharing)
Application-layer message integrity/authentication for critical topics
ITID-43742.detection: Moderate — requires topic-level access monitoring, which is inconsistently deployed in IoT/OT MQTT environments.
ITID-43742.response: Restrict topic ACLs to least-privilege, rotate compromised client credentials, and validate the integrity of any control/telemetry data affected.
metrics: Topics under enforced ACL restriction
Confirmed topic hijacking/spoofing incidents per quarter
ITID-43742.notes: Differentiated from ITID-43741 by assuming broker-level authentication exists; this leaf covers abuse of the topic-level trust model specifically.

playbook.name: MQTT Topic Hijacking/Spoofing (Publish/Subscribe Abuse)
playbook.description: An attacker with some broker access published spoofed messages on legitimate topics or subscribed to sensitive topics beyond their authorization, disrupting or spying on IoT/OT data flows.

steps.title: Identify anomalous publish/subscribe activity on sensitive topics
steps.desc: Review broker topic logs for a client publishing to a topic outside its expected role (e.g. a sensor client publishing to a command topic) or subscribing to topics beyond its authorized scope.
steps.guidance: Compare against a baseline of expected per-client topic access patterns.
steps.outcome: Anomalous client, hijacked/spoofed topic, and message content identified.
steps.abort: If activity matches an approved new integration, close as benign and update the access baseline.

steps.title: Disconnect the offending client and revoke its credentials
steps.desc: Immediately disconnect the client responsible for the topic hijacking/spoofing and revoke or reset its broker credentials.
steps.outcome: Further hijacking/spoofing from the client stopped.

steps.title: Implement or tighten topic-level ACLs per client role
steps.desc: Configure/tighten broker ACLs so each client can only publish/subscribe to the specific topics its role requires, preventing future hijacking/spoofing.
steps.outcome: ACLs verified restricting each client to its intended topic scope.

steps.title: Validate topic access controls and monitor
steps.desc: Confirm legitimate clients operate normally under the tightened ACLs and monitor for further anomalous topic activity.
steps.outcome: No recurrence over a 14-day monitoring window.

steps.title: Document and codify per-role topic ACLs as baseline standard
steps.desc: Record the incident and formalize per-role topic ACL design as a mandatory baseline for all MQTT deployments.
steps.outcome: Baseline updated; after-action report filed.

steps.title: Assess downstream impact of spoofed messages or unauthorized subscription
steps.desc: Determine whether downstream consumers acted on the spoofed message (e.g. a device changed state) or what sensitive data was disclosed via the unauthorized subscription.
steps.outcome: Impact documented.

steps.title: Reverse any unsafe state changes caused by spoofed messages
steps.desc: Work with OT/facilities/application teams to verify and reverse any incorrect device state or data caused by the spoofed messages.
steps.outcome: Affected devices/data confirmed restored to correct state.
steps.abort: If no downstream action was taken on the spoofed message, skip.

steps.title: Enforce per-client authentication and TLS if not already in place
steps.desc: Ensure all clients authenticate individually (not via a shared credential) and connect over TLS, so ACL enforcement is tied to a verifiable identity.
steps.outcome: Per-client authentication and TLS confirmed active.

ITID-43743.def: An adversary sends a high volume of connection requests or published messages to an MQTT broker, exhausting its connection, memory, or processing capacity and degrading or denying service to legitimate publishers and subscribers.
ITID-43743.purpose: Captures denial-of-service attacks against an MQTT broker via message flooding, exhausting broker or network resources and disrupting legitimate publish/subscribe traffic.
scopeIncludes: High-volume message publishing intended to exhaust broker resources
Connection flooding against the broker's listener
scopeExcludes: Exploitation of a broker with no authentication as the root condition enabling other abuse (ITID-43741)
Topic hijacking/spoofing with no volumetric/availability component (ITID-43742)
ITID-43743.severity: High — particularly in OT/IoT contexts where broker unavailability can disrupt safety-relevant telemetry or control loops.
ITID-43743.priority: P1 upon confirmed service degradation or outage.
ITID-43743.escalation: Escalate to IT/OT engineering and IR immediately upon confirmed broker unavailability, especially where control-system telemetry is affected.
indicators: Sharp spike in MQTT connection or message volume from one or more sources
Broker resource exhaustion (CPU, memory, connection limit) correlated with the volume spike
Legitimate publishers/subscribers experiencing degraded or failed connections
vectors: Automated message-flooding tooling against an exposed broker
Botnet-driven connection flooding against the broker's listener port
rootCauses: No rate limiting or connection-count restriction configured on the broker
Broker exposed to the internet or a broader network than necessary
Insufficient broker capacity headroom/monitoring
controls: Rate limiting and connection-count restriction on the broker
Network restriction of broker exposure to only required clients
Broker capacity monitoring and alerting
ITID-43743.detection: Strong — volumetric spikes and resource exhaustion are reliably surfaced by standard infrastructure monitoring where applied to MQTT infrastructure.
ITID-43743.response: Apply rate limiting/blocking against the flooding source, restore broker capacity, and assess impact to dependent telemetry/control systems.
metrics: Broker uptime during flooding events
Mean time to mitigate an active MQTT flood
ITID-43743.notes: Differentiated from siblings by impact type: availability/resource-exhaustion, rather than unauthorized access (ITID-43741) or topic-content abuse (ITID-43742).

playbook.name: MQTT Broker Denial-of-Service via Message Flooding
playbook.description: An attacker flooded an MQTT broker with a high volume of publish/connect messages, exhausting broker resources and degrading or denying service to legitimate IoT/OT clients.

steps.title: Confirm message-flood pattern via broker metrics
steps.desc: Review broker connection/message-rate metrics for an abnormal spike in publish/connect volume from one or more clients, and correlate with broker resource exhaustion (CPU, memory, connection limits).
steps.guidance: Distinguish a legitimate burst (e.g. mass device reconnect after a power event) from sustained attacker-driven flooding by checking source diversity and message content patterns.
steps.outcome: Attack confirmed with source client(s)/IP(s) and impact severity identified.
steps.abort: If the spike correlates with a known legitimate event (mass device restart), close as benign.

steps.title: Disconnect and block the flooding client(s)
steps.desc: Disconnect the identified flooding client(s) and block their source IP at the firewall/broker access control.
steps.outcome: Message flood volume drops significantly.

steps.title: Enforce authentication to prevent anonymous flooding
steps.desc: Ensure the broker requires authentication for all connections so a flooding attacker cannot reconnect anonymously after being blocked, and revoke/rotate any compromised credential used in the flood.
steps.outcome: Broker confirmed rejecting unauthenticated connection attempts.

steps.title: Restore normal broker operation and monitor resource utilization
steps.desc: Confirm broker resource utilization and legitimate client connectivity have returned to normal, and continue monitoring for renewed flooding.
steps.outcome: Normal service levels sustained over a 7-day monitoring window.

steps.title: Document and update broker capacity planning and rate-limit baseline
steps.desc: Record the attack characteristics and update broker rate-limiting configuration and capacity planning to better withstand future floods.
steps.outcome: Baseline updated; after-action report filed.

steps.title: Assess service impact on legitimate IoT/OT clients
steps.desc: Determine whether legitimate clients experienced connection drops, message delivery failures, or delayed telemetry due to the flood.
steps.outcome: Impact severity documented.

steps.title: Apply rate limiting on broker connections and message throughput
steps.desc: Configure per-client connection and message-rate limits on the broker to prevent any single client from exhausting shared resources going forward.
steps.outcome: Rate limits verified active and effective against a simulated flood.

steps.title: Deploy broker clustering/load balancing for resilience
steps.desc: Where feasible, deploy a clustered or load-balanced broker configuration so a future flood against one node does not deny service to all connected IoT/OT clients.
steps.outcome: Clustering/load balancing verified via failover test.
steps.abort: If clustering is not feasible for this deployment, document as a residual-risk exception.

ITID-43744.def: General or as-yet-unclassified MQTT exploitation activity, used during initial triage before the specific technique is determined.
ITID-43744.purpose: Intake bucket for MQTT exploitation activity that has not yet been characterized as unauthenticated broker access, topic hijacking, or message flooding.
scopeIncludes: Suspected MQTT exploitation reported without a confirmed technique
scopeExcludes: Any MQTT exploitation incident once the technique is confirmed — reclassify to ITID-43741, ITID-43742, or ITID-43743 at that point
ITID-43744.severity: High pending triage, given MQTT's common role in IoT/OT telemetry and control.
ITID-43744.priority: P1 while technique is being determined.
ITID-43744.escalation: Escalate to IT/OT engineering immediately in parallel with triage.
indicators: MQTT-related anomaly reported without a confirmed technique
vectors: Any MQTT exploitation technique, not yet attributed
rootCauses: Insufficient detail to determine the specific technique at time of detection
controls: MQTT broker access and message logging
Incident triage workflow for suspected MQTT compromise
ITID-43744.detection: Variable — dependent on available logging at time of report.
ITID-43744.response: Gather additional telemetry to reclassify into ITID-43741, ITID-43742, or ITID-43743.
metrics: Count of general MQTT exploitation reports pending reclassification
ITID-43744.notes: Catch-all triage leaf; reclassify into ITID-43741, ITID-43742, or ITID-43743 once the technique is known.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General MQTT Exploitation
playbook.description: A generic MQTT exploitation event of unspecified sub-technique (unauthenticated broker access, topic hijacking/spoofing, or broker flooding) affecting an IoT/OT deployment.

steps.title: Confirm the exploitation and classify its sub-technique
steps.desc: Review broker connection, topic, and metrics logs to confirm exploitation and determine whether it was unauthenticated access, topic hijacking/spoofing, or message flooding.
steps.outcome: Sub-technique classified and affected broker/topic/client identified.
steps.abort: If activity matches expected/approved behavior, close as benign.

steps.title: Disconnect the offending client and restrict broker exposure
steps.desc: Disconnect the malicious client, revoke its credentials if applicable, and restrict the broker's network exposure as an immediate measure.
steps.outcome: Further exploitation stopped.

steps.title: Remediate the root cause per confirmed sub-technique
steps.desc: Apply the appropriate fix: broker authentication/TLS enforcement, topic-level ACLs, or rate limiting, depending on the confirmed sub-technique.
steps.outcome: Root cause closed and verified.

steps.title: Validate remediation and monitor for recurrence
steps.desc: Confirm the fix is effective and monitor broker logs for renewed exploitation attempts.
steps.outcome: No recurrence over a 14-day monitoring window.

steps.title: Document sub-technique and refine classification/hardening baseline
steps.desc: Record the confirmed sub-technique to refine future classification and ensure the MQTT hardening baseline addresses the identified gap.
steps.outcome: After-action report filed; baseline reviewed.

steps.title: Assess impact scope
steps.desc: Determine the impact based on the confirmed sub-technique: data exposure, unauthorized command injection, or service disruption.
steps.outcome: Impact documented.

steps.title: Reverse any unsafe downstream effects
steps.desc: Work with OT/application teams to verify and reverse any unsafe device state changes or data impacts caused by the exploitation.
steps.outcome: Affected systems confirmed restored to a safe state.
steps.abort: If no downstream effect occurred, skip.

steps.title: Establish continuous broker security monitoring regardless of confirmed sub-technique
steps.desc: Set up ongoing monitoring of broker authentication failures, ACL violations, and message-rate anomalies as a standing detective control.
steps.outcome: Monitoring active and alerting verified.

ITID-44111.def: Command-and-control activity where malware computes a rotating set of pseudo-random candidate domain names (from a seed such as date, a hardcoded value, or an external input) and attempts to resolve them in sequence until one responds, with the operator registering only a small subset ahead of time.
ITID-44111.purpose: Captures C2 infrastructure that relies on a domain generation algorithm to produce large numbers of candidate domains, so the compromised host and the operator can rendezvous without hardcoding a single resolvable name.
scopeIncludes: Malware observed querying a burst of algorithmically-patterned, high-entropy domain names in a short window
Confirmed DGA family (e.g. via reverse-engineered seed/algorithm) resolving to attacker infrastructure
Time-based or date-seeded domain rotation used specifically to defeat static domain blocklisting
scopeExcludes: Fast-flux rotation of IP addresses behind a single stable domain (ITID-44112)
Use of a compromised, human-registered legitimate domain for C2 (ITID-44113)
DGA activity assessed purely for its evasion rationale rather than as an infrastructure type (ITID-44311)
ITID-44111.severity: High. DGA is a strong indicator of a capable, resilient implant that anticipated takedown and blocklisting.
ITID-44111.priority: P1 on confirmed resolution of a known-bad DGA pattern to an external IP; P2 while only the NXDOMAIN burst pattern is observed and no successful resolution is confirmed.
ITID-44111.escalation: Escalate immediately to incident response for host isolation once any DGA-pattern domain resolves successfully; loop in threat intel to fingerprint the DGA family and predict future domains for proactive blocking.
indicators: High volume of NXDOMAIN responses for algorithmically-similar domain names from a single host
High-entropy or dictionary-word-combination domain names with short TTLs
Periodic, clock-aligned bursts of DNS queries (hourly/daily) consistent with a seed rotation
A small number of the queried domains eventually resolving while most fail
vectors: Malware family with an embedded DGA module querying pre-computed candidate domains
Operator registering only the current and next period's domains ahead of the botnet's rotation
rootCauses: Endpoint compromise providing a foothold for DGA-capable malware
Absence of DNS analytics/algorithm-detection capability allowing DGA traffic to blend into normal DNS volume
mitreTechniques: T1568.002 Dynamic Resolution: Domain Generation Algorithms
controls: DNS analytics/ML-based DGA detection
Egress DNS filtering to enterprise resolvers only
Threat intel feeds of known DGA seeds/algorithms for predictive blocking
ITID-44111.detection: Strong: DGA traffic has a distinctive statistical signature (entropy, NXDOMAIN ratio, query cadence) that dedicated DNS analytics detect well even without a known malware family match.
ITID-44111.response: Isolate the host on any confirmed resolution; capture full DNS query history for the endpoint to identify the DGA family and any successfully resolved C2 domains for network-wide blocking.
metrics: Number of hosts exhibiting DGA-pattern DNS query bursts per month
Mean time to identify and block a newly-resolved DGA domain
Proportion of DGA families successfully fingerprinted vs. unattributed
ITID-44111.notes: Cross-reference ITID-44311 (Unclassified/General DGA-Based C2, Stealth/Evasion Context): this ITID documents DGA as an infrastructure-acquisition type (how the C2 rendezvous point is built and resisted takedown), while ITID-44311 covers the same underlying DGA technique framed from a stealth/evasion angle (why it defeats blocklisting). Both are legitimate, complementary framings of the same technique and should be cross-tagged rather than treated as duplicative.

playbook.name: Domain Generation Algorithm (DGA)-Based C2
playbook.description: Malware on the host is algorithmically generating and resolving large volumes of pseudo-random domains to locate a live C2 rendezvous point, evading static domain blocklists.

steps.title: Flag high-volume NXDOMAIN / pseudo-random query bursts
steps.desc: Pull DNS resolver and proxy logs for the suspect host(s) and identify bursts of queries to high-entropy, non-dictionary domains with a high NXDOMAIN ratio, characteristic of DGA probing.
steps.guidance: Score candidate domains for lexical randomness (n-gram entropy, consonant/vowel ratio) and cluster by TLD and query cadence. Cross-check against known DGA family seed/algorithm libraries (e.g., DGArchive) if available.
steps.outcome: A confirmed cluster of DGA-pattern queries is attributed to a specific host and, where possible, a named DGA family/malware strain.
steps.abort: If the burst matches a legitimate CDN/anti-tracking or ad-fraud-detection service pattern, document the false positive and close without containment.
steps.tool: DNS resolver logs / passive DNS / DGArchive

steps.title: Sinkhole or block the DGA seed space at the resolver
steps.desc: Apply DNS-layer blocking for the identified resolved domain and, where feasible, wildcard/regex blocking for the observed DGA pattern's TLD(s) to pre-empt future algorithm cycles.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with the Sinkholing (ITID-449xx) team if standing up an active sinkhole rather than a simple block, to preserve visibility into re-beaconing attempts.
steps.outcome: DGA-generated domains fail to resolve for infected hosts; outbound C2 sessions are severed.
steps.abort: If wildcard blocking risks collateral impact on legitimate traffic sharing the TLD, restrict to exact-match blocking of confirmed-resolved domains only.

steps.title: Remove the DGA malware implant
steps.desc: Identify and remove the malware binary/persistence mechanism responsible for generating DGA queries on each infected host, using EDR-driven remediation or reimaging.
steps.guidance: Reverse or sandbox-detonate the sample to extract the DGA algorithm and seed, enabling proactive future-domain prediction and blocklisting.
steps.outcome: The malware and its persistence artifacts are removed from all infected hosts, confirmed by a clean EDR scan.
steps.abort: If the implant is deeply rooted (bootkit/firmware) reimage the host rather than attempting in-place removal.

steps.title: Restore hosts to production and monitor for reinfection
steps.desc: Return remediated hosts to the network with heightened DNS monitoring for any resumption of DGA query patterns.
steps.guidance: Deploy a 14-day watchlist rule for the specific DGA signature and any predicted future domains derived from the reversed algorithm.
steps.outcome: Hosts operate normally with no recurrence of DGA queries observed during the monitoring window.

steps.title: Document DGA family and update detection content
steps.desc: Record the malware family, DGA algorithm, and indicators in the threat intelligence platform, and update DNS analytics detections to catch this DGA pattern earlier.
steps.guidance: Share the DGA seed/algorithm with threat intel partners and feed predicted future domains into the blocklist pipeline.
steps.outcome: A closed incident report with reusable detection logic for the specific DGA family.

steps.title: Identify the one live domain that actually resolved
steps.desc: Among the many algorithmically generated lookups, determine which (if any) domain successfully resolved and received a follow-up connection, since only that domain represents live attacker infrastructure.
steps.guidance: Correlate DNS answer records with subsequent outbound connection logs (firewall/proxy) to find the single resolved domain and its IP. Pivot passive DNS on that IP for sibling C2 domains.
steps.outcome: The live C2 domain and its resolved IP are identified, with any established outbound session flagged for containment.

steps.title: Isolate infected endpoints from the network
steps.desc: Quarantine all hosts identified in the scoping step via EDR or NAC isolation to prevent lateral movement and further C2 attempts while eradication is prepared.
steps.guidance: Preserve volatile memory and network state on at least one representative host before isolation completes, for malware analysis.
steps.outcome: Infected hosts can no longer reach the network while remaining available for forensic collection.

steps.title: Scope affected hosts across the environment
steps.desc: Search enterprise-wide DNS logs for the same DGA query pattern or resolved domain/IP to identify all infected endpoints, not just the one that triggered the alert.
steps.guidance: Use the entropy signature and any resolved indicators as a hunt query across SIEM DNS telemetry for the prior 30-90 days to establish dwell time and scope.
steps.outcome: A complete list of infected hosts and an initial infection timeline.

ITID-44112.def: Command-and-control activity in which a domain's DNS A/NS records are rotated across a large, frequently-changing pool of IP addresses (often compromised hosts or bulletproof-hosted nodes) on very short TTLs, so the malware always has a live resolution path even as individual endpoints are taken offline.
ITID-44112.purpose: Captures C2 infrastructure that keeps a single stable domain alive by rapidly rotating the pool of IP addresses (and often name servers) it resolves to, so takedown of any one IP does not disrupt the channel.
scopeIncludes: A single C2 domain observed resolving to dozens or hundreds of distinct IPs over a short period
Abnormally short DNS TTLs (seconds to low minutes) paired with high resolution churn
Rotating authoritative name servers (double-flux) supporting the same domain
scopeExcludes: Algorithmic generation of the domain names themselves (ITID-44111)
A one-time domain compromise with no ongoing IP rotation (ITID-44113)
Fast-flux assessed as a botnet resilience technique in the exfiltration/botnet domain (ITID-31714, a different Tier-1 framing of infrastructure resilience)
ITID-44112.severity: High. Fast-flux indicates deliberately engineered takedown resistance and frequently correlates with organized criminal or botnet infrastructure.
ITID-44112.priority: P1 once fast-flux resolution to attacker infrastructure is confirmed for an internal host.
ITID-44112.escalation: Escalate to network security to block the domain outright (IP blocking is ineffective against fast-flux) and to threat intel for tracking the flux network's scope.
indicators: Single domain with an unusually large, rapidly-changing set of A records
TTL values far below normal operational norms (e.g. under 300 seconds)
Resolved IPs spanning many unrelated ASNs/geographies inconsistent with a legitimate CDN
vectors: Botnet of compromised consumer/IoT devices used as rotating flux nodes fronting the real C2 backend
Double-flux architecture rotating both IPs and authoritative name servers
rootCauses: Reliance on IP-based blocking rather than domain/DNS-response based blocking
Lack of DNS TTL/resolution-churn monitoring
mitreTechniques: T1568.001 Dynamic Resolution: Fast Flux DNS
controls: Domain-based (not IP-based) blocking for confirmed fast-flux domains
DNS TTL/churn anomaly detection
Threat intel enrichment on flux-network ASN/geolocation diversity
ITID-44112.detection: Strong: the combination of short TTLs and abnormally high IP-rotation count for one domain is a reliable, low-false-positive signal.
ITID-44112.response: Block at the domain layer immediately; document the resolved IP set for retrospective threat hunting but do not rely on it for ongoing containment.
metrics: Number of fast-flux domains identified per quarter
Mean TTL/resolution-churn detection latency
Count of internal hosts observed resolving confirmed flux domains
ITID-44112.notes: Cross-reference ITID-44321 (Unclassified/General Fast-Flux C2, Stealth/Evasion Context): same fast-flux technique, framed here as an infrastructure-resilience type versus there as a stealth/evasion behavior. Also distinct from ITID-31714 (Fast-Flux DNS Botnet Infrastructure) which sits under a different Tier-1 domain and frames flux as a botnet-infrastructure characteristic rather than an active C2 channel property; cross-tag rather than merge.

playbook.name: Fast-Flux Domain Rotation for C2 Resilience
playbook.description: A C2 domain is resolving to a rapidly rotating pool of IP addresses (fast-flux), making IP-based blocking ineffective and complicating attribution of the true hosting infrastructure.

steps.title: Confirm fast-flux behavior via low-TTL, high-churn DNS answers
steps.desc: Analyze DNS responses for the suspect domain over time to confirm an unusually low TTL and a large, rapidly changing set of A/AAAA records, the signature of fast-flux hosting.
steps.guidance: Query passive DNS history for the domain across multiple days; a fast-flux domain typically shows dozens to hundreds of distinct IPs across diverse ASNs/geographies in a short window.
steps.outcome: Fast-flux is confirmed with a documented set of observed IPs, ASNs, and rotation interval.
steps.abort: If the IP churn is explained by a legitimate CDN/load-balancer with consistent ASN ownership, close as false positive.

steps.title: Block at the domain layer, not the IP layer
steps.desc: Apply a DNS-layer or SNI-based block for the domain name itself, since blocking individual IPs is ineffective against a rotating pool.
steps.guidance: Push the domain to the DNS firewall/RPZ and proxy category block simultaneously to close both resolution and direct-IP-with-SNI bypass paths.
steps.outcome: Outbound resolution and connection attempts to the fast-flux domain are blocked regardless of which IP it currently resolves to.

steps.title: Remove the implant and any embedded fast-flux resolver logic
steps.desc: Remove the malware from infected hosts, noting that fast-flux malware often embeds a hardcoded list of fallback domains or a DGA as backup, both of which must also be neutralized.
steps.guidance: Extract any secondary/fallback C2 domain lists from the sample via reverse engineering or sandbox analysis before wiping the host.
steps.outcome: Primary and fallback C2 mechanisms are both removed or blocked.

steps.title: Restore and monitor for fallback C2 activation
steps.desc: Return remediated hosts to production and monitor for any connections to fallback domains extracted during eradication.
steps.guidance: Maintain a watchlist for the fallback domain list for at least 30 days given fast-flux operators' tendency to rotate to backup channels.
steps.outcome: No further C2 activity observed from remediated hosts.

steps.title: Document fast-flux infrastructure pattern
steps.desc: Record the ASN diversity, rotation cadence, and any registrar response time in the incident report to improve future fast-flux detection tuning.
steps.guidance: Feed the observed ASN/IP ranges into threat intel scoring even though individual IPs will churn, as the hosting provider pattern often recurs.
steps.outcome: Updated detection logic for fast-flux behavior (TTL/IP-churn heuristics) is in place.

steps.title: Identify the authoritative name server layer (NS-level fast-flux)
steps.desc: Check whether the fast-flux extends to the authoritative name servers themselves (double fast-flux), which indicates a more resilient bulletproof-style operation requiring registrar/registry-level takedown rather than simple IP blocking.
steps.guidance: Enumerate the domain's NS records over time; frequent NS changes across unrelated ASNs indicate double fast-flux.
steps.outcome: The C2's resilience architecture (single vs. double fast-flux) is characterized to inform the correct disruption approach.

steps.title: Isolate confirmed beaconing hosts
steps.desc: Quarantine hosts confirmed to have communicated with the fast-flux domain to stop any live C2 session pending eradication.
steps.guidance: Prioritize hosts with the most recent successful connections, as fast-flux domains are typically used for high-value or resilient malware families.
steps.outcome: Active C2 sessions to the fast-flux domain are severed.

steps.title: Report the abusive domain/name servers to registrar and registry
steps.desc: File a takedown request with the domain registrar, and the hosting/NS providers backing the flux network, to disrupt the infrastructure at its source.
steps.guidance: Provide passive DNS evidence of fast-flux abuse; registrars typically act faster on fast-flux domains as they are a well-recognized abuse pattern.
steps.outcome: A takedown request is filed and tracked; the domain is suspended or its NS delegation removed.
steps.abort: If registrar cooperation is slow, proceed with internal blocking as the durable control and treat takedown as supplementary.

steps.title: Scope internal hosts beaconing to the fast-flux domain
steps.desc: Search proxy/firewall logs enterprise-wide for connections to the domain name (not just specific IPs, which are ephemeral) to find all affected hosts.
steps.guidance: Because IPs rotate, hunt on the domain/SNI/Host header rather than IP address to avoid missing infections.
steps.outcome: A complete list of hosts that resolved or connected to the fast-flux C2 domain.

ITID-44113.def: Command-and-control activity conducted through a domain that belonged to, and was compromised from, a legitimate third party (via registrar account takeover, DNS zone compromise, subdomain takeover, or a hacked website on that domain), allowing the adversary to inherit the domain's age, reputation, and categorization.
ITID-44113.purpose: Captures C2 that rides on a domain with pre-existing legitimate reputation, registration history, and often a valid TLS certificate, obtained by compromising the domain rather than generating or freshly registering it.
scopeIncludes: C2 traffic to a domain with a long legitimate registration history that a domain-age/reputation control would not normally flag
Subdomain takeover of an abandoned CNAME record pointed at attacker-controlled infrastructure
Registrar or DNS-provider account compromise used to repoint a legitimate domain's records to attacker infrastructure
scopeExcludes: A domain freshly registered by the attacker for exclusive C2 use (covered under other domain-based leaves, e.g. ITID-44111/44114)
Compromise of an entire server used as an IP-based relay without the domain layer being the compromised asset (ITID-44123)
ITID-44113.severity: High. Reputation-inherited domains defeat age/reputation-based controls and often indicate a targeted, patient adversary.
ITID-44113.priority: P1, and notify the affected third-party domain owner in parallel with internal containment.
ITID-44113.escalation: Escalate to threat intel and legal/partner-notification workflows, since a third party's infrastructure is compromised and may need coordinated remediation.
indicators: C2 traffic to a domain with reputation/category scoring inconsistent with malicious behavior
Unexplained DNS record changes on a domain not owned by the organization but observed communicating with internal hosts
Dangling CNAME later resolving to newly-provisioned attacker infrastructure
vectors: Registrar or DNS management portal account takeover
Subdomain takeover of an orphaned cloud resource record
Compromise of the legitimate domain owner's web hosting to add C2 functionality
rootCauses: Third-party domain owner's weak account security enabling registrar takeover
Abandoned DNS records left pointing at deprovisioned cloud resources
controls: Domain reputation monitoring that flags sudden behavioral change rather than relying solely on age/category
Passive DNS monitoring for record changes on partner/vendor domains
Dangling DNS record hygiene/scanning
ITID-44113.detection: Moderate: reputation and age-based controls will miss it by design; detection depends on behavioral network signals (traffic pattern, destination anomaly) rather than domain metadata.
ITID-44113.response: Contain the internal endpoint immediately; notify the legitimate domain owner and coordinate takedown/remediation of the compromised domain asset.
metrics: Number of confirmed compromised-domain C2 incidents per year
Mean time to third-party notification
Count of dangling DNS records remediated proactively
detections: Domain behavioral-anomaly scoring independent of reputation/age
ITID-44113.notes: Distinguished from ITID-44111/44112 by acquisition method: those two build new infrastructure (algorithmic or flux), this one hijacks existing trusted infrastructure. Also distinct from ITID-44123, which compromises a server for use as an IP-layer relay rather than a domain asset for naming.

playbook.name: Compromised Legitimate Domain Used for C2
playbook.description: Attackers have compromised a legitimate, previously reputable third-party domain and are using it (or a subdomain of it) to host C2 callbacks, exploiting the domain's trusted reputation to evade blocklists.

steps.title: Confirm the domain is compromised rather than attacker-registered
steps.desc: Verify domain age, registration history, and legitimate business purpose to distinguish a compromised legitimate domain from attacker-owned infrastructure, since the response and notification path differ.
steps.guidance: Check WHOIS history, certificate transparency logs, and the domain's historical content/purpose via web archives to establish it predates the malicious activity.
steps.outcome: Confirmation that the domain belongs to a legitimate third party whose infrastructure has been compromised (e.g., a hacked CMS, hijacked subdomain, or compromised DNS account).
steps.abort: If evidence instead shows attacker registration/ownership, redirect to the standard domain-based C2 (ITID-44111-44114) handling as appropriate.

steps.title: Apply narrow, path-specific blocking
steps.desc: Block only the malicious subdomain/URI path/TXT record at the proxy or DNS layer, preserving access to the legitimate parent domain for business continuity.
steps.guidance: Use full-URL or SNI+path filtering rather than domain-wide blocking where the web gateway supports it.
steps.outcome: C2 traffic to the malicious path is blocked while legitimate traffic to the rest of the domain continues uninterrupted.
steps.abort: If path-level blocking is not technically feasible and the domain has no legitimate business use internally, escalate to full domain block.

steps.title: Remove the malware implant from internal hosts
steps.desc: Remove the malicious payload and persistence mechanisms from all confirmed infected hosts.
steps.outcome: Hosts are confirmed clean via EDR scan.

steps.title: Restore hosts and confirm third-party remediation
steps.desc: Return remediated hosts to production and periodically re-check the compromised domain/path to confirm the third party has cleaned up their infrastructure.
steps.guidance: Keep the targeted block in place until the third party confirms remediation, then reassess whether it can be lifted.
steps.outcome: No further C2 traffic observed; third-party infrastructure confirmed remediated or block remains as a durable control.

steps.title: Document the abuse-of-trust pattern
steps.desc: Record the compromised domain, notification outcome, and detection gap (why a reputable domain bypassed reputation-based controls) to improve future detection.
steps.guidance: Consider whether reputation-based allowlisting policies need supplementary content-based inspection for high-reputation domains.
steps.outcome: Updated detection guidance reducing over-reliance on domain reputation alone.

steps.title: Identify the specific malicious path/subdomain and C2 protocol
steps.desc: Determine the exact URI path, subdomain, or DNS record on the legitimate domain that the malware is using for C2, distinguishing it from the domain's normal legitimate traffic.
steps.guidance: Inspect proxy logs for the specific User-Agent, URI pattern, and beacon interval; legitimate domain traffic from other business units should be preserved and not blocked wholesale.
steps.outcome: A precise indicator (subdomain, path, or TXT record) is isolated for targeted blocking without disrupting legitimate use of the parent domain.

steps.title: Isolate infected internal hosts
steps.desc: Quarantine hosts confirmed to be beaconing to the compromised domain pending eradication.
steps.outcome: Active C2 sessions are severed.

steps.title: Scope internal hosts communicating with the compromised domain
steps.desc: Search enterprise logs for all hosts that reached the malicious subdomain/path to determine infection scope.
steps.guidance: Distinguish infected hosts (hitting the malicious path) from hosts merely browsing the legitimate site normally.
steps.outcome: A confirmed list of affected internal hosts.

steps.title: Notify the third-party domain owner of the compromise
steps.desc: Contact the legitimate organization owning the compromised domain (via abuse contact, CERT, or direct relationship) to alert them so they can remediate their own infrastructure.
steps.guidance: Provide the specific compromised path/subdomain and any indicators; this both aids the wider community and may resolve the C2 vector faster than internal blocking alone.
steps.outcome: The third party is notified and, ideally, confirms remediation timeline.
steps.abort: If no abuse contact is reachable, escalate through national CERT channels.

ITID-44114.def: Command-and-control activity confirmed to rely on a domain-name layer as its resolution mechanism, where the specific acquisition/rotation technique (DGA, fast-flux, or domain compromise) has not yet been determined or does not match an existing sibling classification.
ITID-44114.purpose: Intake bucket for confirmed domain-based C2 activity that does not yet fit a more specific domain-based sibling leaf.
scopeIncludes: A domain-based C2 channel identified before triage has determined whether it is DGA-driven, fast-flux, or a compromised legitimate domain
Novel or hybrid domain-based C2 techniques not yet covered by a dedicated leaf
scopeExcludes: Any case where the specific technique has been confirmed — reclassify to ITID-44111, ITID-44112, or ITID-44113
IP-based C2 with no domain layer at all (ITID-44121-44124)
ITID-44114.severity: Medium-High pending triage; re-score once the specific technique is identified.
ITID-44114.priority: P2 during initial triage, adjusted once reclassified to a specific sibling.
ITID-44114.escalation: Escalate to the domain-based C2 sub-triage workflow; reclassify to a specific leaf as soon as evidence supports it and do not leave incidents parked here longer than the initial triage window.
indicators: Outbound DNS resolution followed by C2-pattern traffic to the resolved IP, with acquisition method undetermined
vectors: Any domain-based C2 acquisition technique, pending specific attribution
rootCauses: Insufficient DNS/network telemetry at time of detection to distinguish the specific domain-based technique
controls: General DNS/C2 traffic detection sufficient to flag the channel even before technique attribution
ITID-44114.detection: Variable, dependent on the telemetry available; sufficient to detect the channel but not to characterize it further.
ITID-44114.response: Contain the endpoint as with any confirmed C2, and drive toward reclassification to a specific sibling leaf as triage matures.
metrics: Number of incidents held in this catch-all beyond the triage SLA
Reclassification rate to specific sibling leaves
ITID-44114.notes: This is a triage/intake leaf, not a terminal classification; incidents should migrate to ITID-44111, ITID-44112, or ITID-44113 once the acquisition technique is confirmed.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Domain-Based C2
playbook.description: A host is communicating with an attacker-controlled command-and-control server addressed via a standard domain name that does not fit a more specific domain-based C2 subtype.

steps.title: Confirm the domain as malicious C2 infrastructure
steps.desc: Validate the suspicious domain against threat intelligence, WHOIS, and passive DNS to confirm it is attacker-controlled C2 rather than a benign or miscategorized destination.
steps.guidance: Check domain age, registrar reputation, hosting ASN, and any existing TI feed matches; correlate with the beacon pattern (interval, payload size, User-Agent) observed in proxy logs.
steps.outcome: The domain is confirmed as malicious C2 with supporting evidence recorded.
steps.abort: If the domain resolves to a known-benign, well-established service, close as false positive.

steps.title: Block the domain at DNS and proxy layers
steps.desc: Add the confirmed malicious domain to DNS firewall/RPZ and web proxy blocklists across the environment.
steps.outcome: Outbound resolution and connection to the domain is blocked enterprise-wide.

steps.title: Remove the malware and persistence mechanisms
steps.desc: Identify and remove the implant responsible for the C2 beaconing from each infected host.
steps.guidance: Use EDR-driven remediation where the implant is well understood; reimage where persistence is unclear or deeply embedded.
steps.outcome: Hosts confirmed clean of the implant.

steps.title: Restore hosts and monitor
steps.desc: Return remediated hosts to production with a monitoring watchlist for the domain and any related indicators.
steps.outcome: No recurrence of C2 activity within the monitoring window.

steps.title: Document indicators and close the incident
steps.desc: Record the domain, associated IOCs, and remediation actions in the incident report and threat intel platform.
steps.outcome: Closed incident with indicators available for future detection.

steps.title: Scope all hosts communicating with the domain
steps.desc: Search DNS, proxy, and firewall logs enterprise-wide for the domain and any associated indicators to determine full infection scope and timeline.
steps.guidance: Include historical logs to establish dwell time, not just current alerts.
steps.outcome: A complete list of affected hosts and an infection timeline.

steps.title: Isolate infected hosts
steps.desc: Quarantine confirmed infected endpoints via EDR/NAC to sever active C2 sessions pending eradication.
steps.outcome: Infected hosts can no longer reach the C2 domain or the wider network.

steps.title: Verify no residual persistence or scheduled re-beaconing
steps.desc: Re-scan remediated hosts and review scheduled tasks, startup items, and registry run-keys for any secondary persistence mechanism the malware may have installed.
steps.guidance: Cross-check against known TTPs for the identified malware family if attribution was possible.
steps.outcome: No residual persistence artifacts remain on any remediated host.

ITID-44121.def: Command-and-control activity where the implant connects directly to a hardcoded IP address with no intervening domain lookup, meaning the entire infrastructure hinges on that single (or small set of) IP address remaining reachable.
ITID-44121.purpose: Captures the simplest, most brittle form of C2 infrastructure: a raw IP address hardcoded into the malware with no domain name or DNS resolution step at all.
scopeIncludes: Malware configuration or static analysis revealing a hardcoded C2 IP with no associated domain
Outbound connections to a known-bad IP with no preceding DNS query for that destination
scopeExcludes: Any C2 reached via a domain name lookup, regardless of how that domain was obtained (ITID-44111-44114)

IP infrastructure specifically identified as bulletproof-hosted (ITID-44122) or as a compromised legitimate server (ITID-44123) — those describe the nature of the IP's ownership rather than its bare hardcoded use
ITID-44121.severity: Medium-High. Hardcoded IPs are operationally fragile for the attacker but offer no DNS-based detection opportunity, so they can persist undetected if network-layer monitoring is weak.
ITID-44121.priority: P1 upon confirmed successful connection to the hardcoded IP; P2 for blocked/attempted connections only.
ITID-44121.escalation: Escalate for immediate network-layer blocking of the IP and host isolation; because there is no domain to pivot on, prioritize full packet capture for protocol/behavioral analysis.
indicators: Outbound connection to a known-bad IP with no corresponding DNS query in host or network logs
Static/dynamic malware analysis revealing an embedded literal IP address
vectors: Malware shipped with a literal IP address to avoid DNS-based detection or sinkholing entirely
Fallback hardcoded IP used only if the primary domain-based channel is unreachable
rootCauses: Reliance on DNS-layer detection controls that this technique specifically bypasses
Lack of IP-reputation/threat-intel blocking at the network egress layer
controls: IP reputation/threat-intel blocking at egress
Full packet capture and network behavioral analysis to compensate for the absence of a DNS signal
ITID-44121.detection: Weak on DNS telemetry (there is none to inspect); detection depends entirely on IP reputation feeds and network-flow/behavioral analysis.
ITID-44121.response: Block the IP at the perimeter and isolate the affected host; treat the absence of DNS activity as itself a data point during host forensics.
metrics: Count of hardcoded-IP C2 incidents detected via network-flow analysis vs. DNS telemetry
Mean time to IP-block after confirmation
detections: Network flow anomaly detection absent DNS correlation
ITID-44121.notes: Differentiating axis for this Tier-4 group is infrastructure ownership/legitimacy: this leaf is agnostic to who owns the IP and focuses purely on the absence of a domain layer. ITID-44122 and ITID-44123 layer on top of this by characterizing whose IP it is.

playbook.name: Hardcoded IP Address C2 (No Domain Layer)
playbook.description: Malware connects directly to a hardcoded C2 IP address with no domain resolution step, removing DNS-layer visibility and blocking as a control point.

steps.title: Identify the hardcoded destination IP from network telemetry
steps.desc: Since there is no DNS lookup preceding the connection, identify the C2 IP directly from firewall/NetFlow logs showing outbound connections with no corresponding DNS query.
steps.guidance: Look for periodic beacon-like connections (regular interval, consistent payload size) to a raw IP with no matching DNS resolution in the same timeframe — a strong hardcoded-IP C2 indicator.
steps.outcome: The hardcoded C2 IP is identified along with the connecting host(s) and beacon cadence.
steps.abort: If the connection matches a known legitimate service that intentionally bypasses DNS (e.g., some internal appliances), close as false positive.

steps.title: Block the IP at the perimeter firewall
steps.desc: Add the C2 IP (and its immediate /29-/24 block if attribution shows dedicated malicious hosting) to perimeter firewall deny rules.
steps.guidance: Since there is no domain to block, the firewall IP block is the primary durable control; avoid over-broad CIDR blocks that could catch legitimate co-tenants on shared cloud IP space.
steps.outcome: Outbound connections to the C2 IP are blocked at the network perimeter.
steps.abort: If the IP is shared cloud infrastructure with legitimate co-tenants, scope the block as narrowly as the firewall allows (single IP, not range).

steps.title: Remove the malware implant
steps.desc: Remove the malicious binary and persistence mechanisms from infected hosts. Note that hardcoded-IP malware often has no fallback resolution mechanism, so removing the binary fully neutralizes the C2 channel.
steps.guidance: Extract any secondary hardcoded IPs from the sample via reverse engineering, since some families embed a short list of fallback IPs.
steps.outcome: Hosts confirmed clean; any fallback IPs identified and pre-emptively blocked.

steps.title: Restore hosts and monitor
steps.desc: Return remediated hosts to production with monitoring for the C2 IP and any fallback IPs.
steps.outcome: No recurrence of connections to the C2 infrastructure.

steps.title: Document IP infrastructure and update blocklists
steps.desc: Record the IP, ASN, and hosting attribution in the threat intel platform and evaluate whether NetFlow-based beacon detection needs tuning to catch non-DNS C2 earlier.
steps.outcome: Improved detection coverage for domain-less C2 beaconing.

steps.title: Attribute the IP's hosting infrastructure
steps.desc: Perform IP reputation, ASN/WHOIS, and geolocation lookups on the C2 IP to attribute it to a hosting provider and assess whether it is bulletproof/compromised/cloud infrastructure.
steps.guidance: Check for co-located known-malicious IPs in the same /24 or ASN, which often indicates a dedicated malicious hosting block.
steps.outcome: Attribution context (ASN, hosting provider, co-located indicators) recorded to support blocking and takedown decisions.

steps.title: Isolate infected hosts
steps.desc: Quarantine hosts confirmed to be beaconing to the hardcoded IP via EDR/NAC.
steps.outcome: Active C2 sessions are severed.

steps.title: Scope all hosts connecting to the hardcoded IP
steps.desc: Search firewall/NetFlow logs enterprise-wide for connections to the identified IP to determine full infection scope.
steps.outcome: A complete list of affected hosts.

ITID-44122.def: Command-and-control activity hosted on IP infrastructure leased from a hosting provider (often in a permissive jurisdiction) that is known to disregard abuse complaints, law-enforcement requests, and takedown notices, allowing malicious IPs to remain live far longer than on mainstream providers.
ITID-44122.purpose: Captures C2 infrastructure knowingly hosted with a bulletproof hosting provider that ignores abuse reports and takedown requests, giving the adversary durable IP-based infrastructure.
scopeIncludes: C2 IP addresses confirmed via threat intel to belong to an ASN with a known bulletproof-hosting reputation
Repeated abuse-report submissions to the hosting provider going unactioned over an extended period
scopeExcludes: A hardcoded IP with no attribution of hosting-provider complicity (ITID-44121)
Compromise of an otherwise-legitimate, cooperative provider's customer server (ITID-44123)
ITID-44122.severity: High. Bulletproof-hosted infrastructure typically stays live for the duration of the campaign since takedown is not a realistic containment path.
ITID-44122.priority: P1; treat abuse-report submission as a low-yield, slow-return action rather than the primary containment mechanism.
ITID-44122.escalation: Escalate to threat intel to enrich the ASN/provider and correlate with other campaigns known to use the same bulletproof host; rely on internal blocking rather than external takedown.
indicators: C2 IP resolving to an ASN flagged in threat-intel feeds as bulletproof/abuse-tolerant hosting
Long-lived malicious IP infrastructure that persists across multiple detection/reporting cycles
vectors: Adversary leasing dedicated or virtual server infrastructure directly from a bulletproof hosting provider
Reuse of the same bulletproof ASN across multiple malware families/campaigns
rootCauses: Organizational reliance on provider takedown as the primary containment strategy for externally-hosted C2
Insufficient ASN-level reputation intelligence in egress controls
controls: ASN/provider-level reputation blocking for known bulletproof hosts
Threat intel tracking of bulletproof-hosting ASNs
ITID-44122.detection: Strong at the ASN/reputation layer once the provider is known-bad; detection of a first-seen bulletproof provider relies on behavioral/traffic analysis.
ITID-44122.response: Block internally at the ASN/IP-range level rather than waiting on external abuse-report resolution; document for threat-intel campaign tracking.
metrics: Number of distinct bulletproof ASNs observed per year
Mean abuse-report response time from hosting providers (tracked to demonstrate futility/inform policy)
ITID-44122.notes: Differentiated from ITID-44121 and ITID-44123 by the ownership/cooperation axis: infrastructure here is attacker-leased and provider-shielded, rather than a bare hardcoded IP or a hijacked cooperative third-party server.

playbook.name: Bulletproof Hosting Provider C2 Infrastructure
playbook.description: C2 infrastructure is hosted with a known bulletproof hosting provider that ignores abuse complaints, meaning takedown is unlikely and internal blocking is the only reliable control.

steps.title: Confirm bulletproof hosting attribution
steps.desc: Determine the hosting provider and ASN of the C2 IP/domain and cross-check it against known bulletproof-hosting ASN watchlists and threat intelligence reporting.
steps.guidance: Bulletproof providers often show ASN-wide clusters of malicious activity, historically unresponsive abuse contacts, and offshore/lenient jurisdictions.
steps.outcome: Confirmed attribution of the C2 infrastructure to a bulletproof or abuse-tolerant hosting provider, with supporting ASN-level evidence.
steps.abort: If the provider has a normal abuse-response history, treat this as standard hosting rather than bulletproof and proceed with routine takedown reporting alongside blocking.
steps.tool: ASN/WHOIS lookups, threat intel ASN watchlists

steps.title: Apply durable internal blocking (do not rely on takedown)
steps.desc: Block the specific C2 IP/domain and consider a broader ASN-level or geo-based block for the bulletproof provider's ranges, since abuse reporting is expected to fail.
steps.guidance: Weigh business impact carefully before ASN-wide blocking; consult network/security leadership if the ASN hosts any legitimate business traffic.
steps.outcome: Internal connectivity to the bulletproof-hosted infrastructure is blocked without dependency on provider cooperation.
steps.abort: If ASN-wide blocking would impact legitimate business services, restrict to specific IP/domain blocks and rely on monitoring for related indicators instead.

steps.title: Remove the malware implant
steps.desc: Remove the malicious payload and persistence from infected hosts.
steps.outcome: Hosts confirmed clean.

steps.title: Restore hosts and sustain long-term monitoring
steps.desc: Return remediated hosts to production with sustained monitoring, since bulletproof-hosted actors often re-attempt via new infrastructure on the same provider.
steps.guidance: Maintain an ASN-level watchlist rather than closing monitoring once the specific IOC expires.
steps.outcome: No recurrence of C2 activity from the provider's infrastructure.

steps.title: Document the bulletproof provider for standing defensive posture
steps.desc: Add the ASN/provider to a standing high-risk hosting watchlist and record the incident details for future reference.
steps.guidance: Consider proposing the ASN for a standing geo/ASN-reputation block in the secure web gateway if repeated abuse is observed.
steps.outcome: Improved standing defenses against future infrastructure from the same bulletproof provider.

steps.title: Map the full scope of infrastructure on that ASN/provider
steps.desc: Since bulletproof providers are frequently reused by the same or affiliated threat actors, pivot on the ASN/IP block to identify any other C2 nodes the organization has previously seen or may be blind to.
steps.guidance: Cross-reference the ASN against historical incident data and external threat intel for a fuller picture of the actor's infrastructure footprint.
steps.outcome: A broader list of related malicious IPs/domains on the same bulletproof infrastructure is compiled for proactive blocking.

steps.title: Isolate infected hosts
steps.desc: Quarantine hosts confirmed to have communicated with the bulletproof-hosted C2.
steps.outcome: Active sessions are severed.

steps.title: File abuse report for the record despite low expectation of action
steps.desc: Submit a formal abuse complaint to the hosting provider and upstream transit providers to document due diligence, even though bulletproof providers typically do not act.
steps.guidance: Escalate to the provider's upstream transit/peering ASNs, who sometimes de-peer persistently abusive bulletproof networks even when the provider itself will not act.
steps.outcome: A documented abuse trail exists for legal/compliance purposes regardless of outcome.

steps.title: Scope internal hosts communicating with the infrastructure
steps.desc: Search logs enterprise-wide for connections to the confirmed C2 IP/domain and any related infrastructure on the same provider.
steps.outcome: A complete list of affected internal hosts.

ITID-44123.def: Command-and-control activity in which the adversary compromises a legitimate third-party server (a small business web server, an under-maintained VPS, a home router, etc.) and uses its IP address as a relay point for C2 traffic, inheriting that server's clean reputation.
ITID-44123.purpose: Captures C2 that hides behind the IP address of a legitimate, otherwise-cooperative server that has itself been compromised and repurposed as a relay.
scopeIncludes: C2 traffic terminating at or relaying through an IP address belonging to a legitimate, non-attacker-owned organization
Confirmed webshell or backdoor on a third-party server used purely to proxy/relay C2 traffic rather than as the attacker's own target
scopeExcludes: Infrastructure the attacker directly leases, even from a permissive provider (ITID-44122)
A hardcoded IP with no evidence the underlying server is a compromised legitimate asset (ITID-44121)
Compromise of a router/IoT device specifically used as a multi-hop proxy chain element for anonymization (ITID-44333, a stealth/evasion framing of a similar underlying technique)
ITID-44123.severity: High. Both the originating organization and the compromised relay's owner have exposure; the relay owner requires separate notification and remediation.
ITID-44123.priority: P1 for the victim organization; coordinate parallel P1/P2 handling with the compromised relay's owner via notification channels.
ITID-44123.escalation: Escalate to threat intel and third-party notification workflows; the relay's owner is itself a victim and needs to be informed to remediate.
indicators: C2 IP belonging to a legitimate organization with no history of malicious hosting
IP reputation clean at first sight but traffic pattern/protocol behavior consistent with C2 relay rather than legitimate service
vectors: Exploitation of an unpatched vulnerability on a third-party server to install a relay/proxy component
Compromised home router or small-office device repurposed as an unwitting relay
rootCauses: Third-party server left unpatched/unmonitored, making it an attractive relay target
Reliance on IP reputation alone, which will not flag a freshly-compromised legitimate host
controls: Behavioral/traffic-pattern analysis independent of IP reputation
Third-party/vendor compromise notification process
ITID-44123.detection: Moderate: IP reputation will not help; detection relies on traffic-pattern anomalies (protocol mismatch, timing, volume) at the compromised relay's IP.
ITID-44123.response: Contain the internal endpoint; notify the third-party relay owner promptly since they are a separate victim requiring their own remediation.
metrics: Number of confirmed compromised-relay incidents per year
Mean time to third-party relay-owner notification
detections: Traffic-pattern/protocol-mismatch anomaly detection on reputable IPs
ITID-44123.notes: Cross-reference ITID-44333 (Compromised Router/IoT Device Used as Proxy Chain Hop): closely related underlying technique, but ITID-44333 frames the compromised device as one hop in a deliberate multi-hop anonymization chain (stealth/evasion), while this leaf frames a single compromised legitimate server as the C2 infrastructure's public IP itself (infrastructure type).

playbook.name: Compromised Legitimate Server Used as IP-Based C2 Relay
playbook.description: A legitimate third-party server (not attacker-owned) has been compromised and is relaying C2 traffic by IP address, exploiting the server's clean reputation and existing trust relationships.

steps.title: Confirm the server is a compromised relay, not attacker-owned infrastructure
steps.desc: Investigate the IP's ownership, hosting context, and historical legitimate purpose to establish that a real third-party server has been compromised and repurposed as a relay.
steps.guidance: Check for a legitimate reverse DNS record, TLS certificate matching a known organization, and any known legitimate service historically running on that IP/port.
steps.outcome: Confirmation that the relay is a compromised legitimate asset, with the owning organization identified where possible.
steps.abort: If ownership cannot be established or evidence points to attacker-owned infrastructure, treat as standard IP-based C2 (ITID-44121/44124).
steps.tool: Reverse DNS / TLS certificate inspection / WHOIS

steps.title: Block the specific malicious port/service on the relay IP
steps.desc: Apply a port/service-specific firewall block for the compromised server rather than blocking the IP entirely, to preserve any legitimate business relationship with that server if one exists.
steps.guidance: If no legitimate relationship exists with the server, a full IP block is acceptable and simpler.
steps.outcome: C2 relay traffic is blocked while any legitimate service on the same host is unaffected where relevant.

steps.title: Remove the malware implant from internal hosts
steps.desc: Remove the malicious payload responsible for C2 relay communication from all confirmed internal hosts.
steps.outcome: Hosts confirmed clean.

steps.title: Restore hosts and confirm relay remediation
steps.desc: Return remediated hosts to production and monitor for confirmation that the third-party server has been cleaned up, reassessing the block once confirmed.
steps.outcome: No further C2 traffic via the relay; third party's remediation status tracked to closure.

steps.title: Document the compromised-relay pattern
steps.desc: Record findings, third-party coordination outcome, and any detection gaps in the incident report.
steps.outcome: Closed incident with lessons captured for detecting abuse of trusted third-party infrastructure.

steps.title: Identify the specific relay port/service being abused
steps.desc: Determine which service or port on the compromised server is being used for the C2 relay (e.g., a web server proxying traffic, a hijacked application port) versus the server's other legitimate services.
steps.guidance: Inspect connection metadata (destination port, protocol banner, TLS SNI/JA3) to isolate the malicious channel from legitimate traffic the server may still be serving.
steps.outcome: A precise malicious port/service is isolated for targeted blocking.

steps.title: Isolate infected internal hosts
steps.desc: Quarantine internal hosts confirmed to be using the relay for C2.
steps.outcome: Active sessions are severed.

steps.title: Scope internal hosts connecting through the relay
steps.desc: Search logs enterprise-wide for connections to the compromised server's relay port to determine internal infection scope.
steps.outcome: A confirmed list of internal hosts using the C2 relay.

steps.title: Notify the compromised server's owning organization
steps.desc: Contact the legitimate organization operating the compromised server so they can investigate and remediate their own compromise.
steps.guidance: Provide specific technical detail (port, timestamps, traffic patterns) to help their response team locate the compromise quickly.
steps.outcome: The owning organization is notified and engaged in remediation.
steps.abort: If no contact can be established, escalate via CERT/ISAC channels.

ITID-44124.def: Command-and-control activity confirmed to operate over a raw IP address with no domain resolution step, where the specific nature of the IP's ownership (hardcoded-only, bulletproof-hosted, or a compromised legitimate server) has not yet been determined.
ITID-44124.purpose: Intake bucket for confirmed IP-based C2 activity (no domain layer) that does not yet fit a more specific IP-based sibling leaf.
scopeIncludes: IP-based C2 identified before attribution work has established the hosting/ownership nature of the IP
Novel IP-based C2 arrangements not yet covered by a dedicated leaf
scopeExcludes: Any case where the IP's nature has been confirmed — reclassify to ITID-44121, ITID-44122, or ITID-44123
Any C2 reached via domain resolution (ITID-44111-44114)
ITID-44124.severity: Medium-High pending triage; re-score once IP attribution is complete.
ITID-44124.priority: P2 during initial triage, adjusted once reclassified.
ITID-44124.escalation: Escalate through the IP-based C2 sub-triage workflow and reclassify to a specific sibling leaf once attribution evidence is available.
indicators: Direct outbound connection to a raw IP with C2-pattern behavior, ownership/hosting attribution pending
vectors: Any IP-based C2 arrangement, pending specific attribution
rootCauses: Insufficient threat-intel enrichment at time of detection to attribute the IP's hosting nature
controls: General network-flow C2 detection sufficient to flag the channel before attribution
ITID-44124.detection: Variable, sufficient to detect the channel but not yet to characterize the IP's ownership.
ITID-44124.response: Contain the endpoint as with any confirmed C2 and drive toward reclassification as triage matures.
metrics: Number of incidents held in this catch-all beyond the triage SLA
Reclassification rate to specific sibling leaves
ITID-44124.notes: This is a triage/intake leaf, not a terminal classification; incidents should migrate to ITID-44121, ITID-44122, or ITID-44123 once IP attribution is confirmed.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General IP-Based C2
playbook.description: A host is communicating with an attacker-controlled command-and-control server addressed directly by IP that does not fit a more specific IP-based C2 subtype.

steps.title: Confirm the IP as malicious C2 infrastructure
steps.desc: Validate the suspicious IP against threat intelligence and connection behavior to confirm it is attacker-controlled C2.
