ITID-44441.detection: Weak-Moderate: requires specialized protocol/statistical analysis rarely deployed as a default control.
ITID-44441.response: Capture full packet data including headers for statistical analysis; isolate the host on confirmation.
metrics: Number of confirmed protocol covert-channel C2 incidents per year
Coverage of header/timing-based covert-channel detection across network monitoring
ITID-44441.notes: This is the sole leaf under its Tier-4 group and is written as a general, comprehensive treatment. Cross-reference ITID-42511 (Unclassified/General Covert Channel Exfiltration, Network Intrusion Context) elsewhere in the taxonomy, which treats the same covert-channel technique family from a data-exfiltration angle rather than command-and-control tasking; and ITID-44221 (DNS Tunneling C2), a protocol-specific covert channel already given dedicated treatment.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Covert Channel C2 (Protocol Context)
playbook.description: An implant hides C2 communication within a covert channel embedded in fields or timing of otherwise permitted network traffic, not matching a more specific sub-technique.

steps.title: Identify unused protocol fields or timing patterns carrying data
steps.desc: Review packet captures for permitted protocols (e.g. ICMP, TCP options, unused header fields) for abnormal usage patterns, unexpected field population, or timing-based signaling inconsistent with the protocol's normal function.
steps.guidance: Covert channels commonly abuse ICMP payload data, TCP/IP header reserved bits, or inter-packet timing to encode data; look for fields populated where they are normally zero/absent.
steps.outcome: A shortlist of hosts exhibiting covert-channel-consistent field/timing anomalies.
steps.abort: If the field usage matches a known legitimate diagnostic or QoS mechanism, close as false positive.

steps.title: Decide on monitoring versus immediate block
steps.desc: Weigh silent monitoring of the covert channel to scope affected hosts against immediate blocking of the abused protocol/destination.
steps.outcome: Documented containment decision.

steps.title: Remove the implant and persistence mechanism
steps.desc: Remove the implant binary/process implementing the covert channel and any associated persistence mechanism.
steps.outcome: Implant and persistence removed; no respawn observed.

steps.title: Verify no recurrence before restoring access
steps.desc: Monitor for renewed use of the covert channel technique before restoring hosts to normal network access.
steps.outcome: No recurrence observed; hosts cleared for production.
steps.abort: If activity recurs, return to containment and re-scope.

steps.title: Deploy covert-channel field/timing anomaly detection
steps.desc: Document the specific covert-channel technique observed and deploy NDR detection for the abused protocol field/timing pattern.
steps.outcome: New detection capability deployed.

steps.title: Decode and confirm covert channel content
steps.desc: Attempt to decode the suspected covert field/timing data to confirm it carries command syntax or exfiltrated data.
steps.outcome: Confirmed covert channel carrying C2 command/response content.
steps.abort: If decoding is inconclusive, escalate to specialist analysis before closing.

steps.title: Isolate affected hosts
steps.desc: Apply EDR network isolation to hosts confirmed to be using the covert channel.
steps.outcome: Confirmed hosts isolated from the network.

steps.title: Correlate destination infrastructure with threat intelligence
steps.desc: Check the destination IP against threat intel for known covert-channel C2 tooling.
steps.outcome: Attribution or campaign context established where available.

steps.title: Restrict or filter the abused protocol at the firewall
steps.desc: Apply firewall rules to strip or block the abused protocol fields (e.g. filter ICMP payload size, drop non-standard TCP options) or block the destination outright.
steps.outcome: Covert channel usage blocked network-wide.

ITID-44511.def: A C2 persistence technique in which an implant does not hardcode its C2 server address but instead periodically fetches a paste/text page controlled by the adversary, parsing it for an IP, domain, or encoded command that points to (or is) the live C2 channel. This decouples implant code from infrastructure, letting the adversary rotate real C2 endpoints without redeploying malware, and blends the lookup traffic into ordinary HTTPS traffic to a trusted, rarely-blocked site category.
ITID-44511.purpose: Captures use of a public paste/text-sharing site (Pastebin and similar) as a dead-drop resolver that malware polls to retrieve the real C2 address or next-stage commands.
scopeIncludes: Implant fetching a Pastebin/Ghostbin/similar raw-text URL on an interval to read a C2 IP/domain
Base64 or otherwise encoded C2 configuration embedded in a paste's body
Paste content used purely to redirect to the actual C2 infrastructure
scopeExcludes: Dead-drop resolution via a code-hosting platform (ITID-44512)
Dead-drop resolution via a document/spreadsheet service (ITID-44513)
Exfiltration of stolen data to a paste site (a data-exfiltration ITID, not a C2 leaf)
ITID-44511.severity: Medium-High. The technique itself signals a deliberate effort to survive domain/IP blocklisting; actual severity depends on what the C2 is being used for.
ITID-44511.priority: P2, escalating to P1 once the resolved C2 destination is confirmed active and commands have been retrieved.
ITID-44511.escalation: Escalate to IR/threat intel once a beaconing host is confirmed reaching a paste-site raw-content URL on a fixed interval; treat the paste content itself as live threat intel to pivot on.
indicators: Recurring outbound HTTPS requests to paste-site raw/API endpoints from a host with no legitimate developer use for that service
Base64-looking blobs retrieved from a public paste and stored in memory or a temp file
Paste account/page churn (content edited or replaced shortly before a new C2 IP is observed)
vectors: Implant hardcodes only the paste URL, not the C2 IP
Adversary edits the paste page to rotate C2 infrastructure post-takedown
rootCauses: Proxy/web-filtering policy allows unrestricted access to paste-site categories
No outbound traffic baselining to catch low-and-slow polling behavior
mitreTechniques: T1102.001 Web Service: Dead Drop Resolver
controls: Web/content-category filtering with logging on paste-site traffic
Outbound proxy logging retained and searchable for beacon-interval analysis
Threat-intel enrichment of paste-site URLs seen in proxy logs
ITID-44511.detection: Proxy/DNS logs give strong technical visibility into repeated requests to a small set of paste-site URLs; EDR memory/process analysis can recover the decoded C2 pointer.
ITID-44511.response: Retrieve and preserve the paste content before the adversary can edit or delete it, extract the resolved C2 destination, and pivot to blocking/sinkholing per the disruption ITIDs while continuing host-level investigation.
metrics: Count of hosts observed polling paste-site raw-content endpoints
Mean time from first detection to paste content preservation
detections: Proxy alert: recurring GET to paste-site raw/API endpoints from non-developer hosts
EDR: process reading/decoding content fetched from a browser-adjacent HTTP client library
ITID-44511.notes: Distinguish from the code-hosting and document-service variants by the hosting platform involved; the underlying dead-drop-resolver concept and MITRE mapping (T1102.001) is shared across all three sibling leaves.

playbook.name: C2 Dead-Drop Resolver via Pastebin/Text-Sharing Site
playbook.description: An implant retrieves the current C2 server address or commands by fetching a post from Pastebin or a similar public text-sharing site, allowing the operator to relocate infrastructure without updating the implant.

steps.title: Detect recurring requests to text-sharing/paste sites from non-browser processes
steps.desc: Review proxy/NGFW logs for recurring GET requests to raw paste-content URLs (e.g. pastebin.com/raw/...) originating from processes other than a browser, especially at beacon-consistent intervals.
steps.guidance: Dead-drop resolvers typically fetch the raw text endpoint directly rather than the full HTML page, and do so from a script/implant process rather than an interactive browsing session.
steps.outcome: A shortlist of hosts/processes fetching paste content in a beacon-consistent pattern.
steps.abort: If the requests map to a legitimate internal tool using the paste site's API for approved purposes, close as false positive.

steps.title: Decide on monitoring versus immediate block, noting the resolver's mobility
steps.desc: Weigh silent monitoring of paste-site fetches (since the operator can trivially edit the paste to point elsewhere) against immediate blocking, recognizing that blocking the current resolved IP does not stop the operator from posting a new address.
steps.guidance: Because the dead-drop resolver itself (the paste site access) is the more durable control point than any single resolved IP, prioritize blocking/monitoring the resolver mechanism alongside the currently resolved destination.
steps.outcome: Documented containment decision addressing both the resolver and resolved destination.

steps.title: Remove the implant and its hardcoded resolver URL
steps.desc: Remove the implant binary/script and any persistence mechanism, noting the hardcoded dead-drop resolver URL for detection tuning.
steps.outcome: Implant and persistence removed; no respawn observed.

steps.title: Verify no recurrence before restoring access
steps.desc: Monitor for renewed fetches to paste sites or the resolved C2 destination before restoring hosts to normal network access.
steps.outcome: No recurrence observed; hosts cleared for production.
steps.abort: If fetches recur to a new paste URL, return to containment and re-scope.

steps.title: Add detection for paste-site dead-drop resolver patterns
steps.desc: Document the incident and add detection for beacon-consistent, non-browser fetches to raw-content endpoints on paste/text-sharing sites.
steps.outcome: New detection rule deployed.

steps.title: Retrieve and analyze the referenced paste content
steps.desc: Retrieve the specific paste/post being fetched (via a non-attributable research method) to determine whether it currently or historically contained a C2 IP/domain or command data.
steps.guidance: Paste content may be edited or deleted by the operator; check archive/caching services for historical versions where possible.
steps.outcome: Confirmed content consistent with a dead-drop resolver (IP/domain or command payload).
steps.abort: If the paste has been deleted and no historical copy is available, proceed on traffic-pattern evidence alone.
steps.tool: Threat intel platform, web archive services

steps.title: Isolate affected hosts
steps.desc: Apply EDR network isolation to hosts confirmed to be fetching the dead-drop content.
steps.outcome: Confirmed hosts isolated from the network.

steps.title: Report the malicious paste to the hosting platform
steps.desc: Report the malicious paste content to the hosting platform's abuse team for takedown.
steps.outcome: Paste content removed at the platform level.

steps.title: Correlate the resolved C2 address with threat intelligence
steps.desc: Check the C2 IP/domain resolved from the paste content against threat intel for known infrastructure association.
steps.outcome: Attribution or campaign context established where available.

steps.title: Block the specific paste URL/site and the resolved C2 destination
steps.desc: Block the specific paste URL (or the paste site's raw-content domain if no legitimate use exists) and the currently resolved C2 IP/domain at the proxy/firewall.
steps.outcome: Both the resolver access and the resolved destination blocked network-wide.

ITID-44512.def: A C2 persistence technique in which an implant periodically fetches a file from a public (or attacker-controlled) GitHub repository, Gist, raw content URL, or release asset, parsing it for the live C2 endpoint or an encoded command set. Developer-facing infrastructure gives the traffic a plausible cover story and is rarely blocked by web filters that otherwise restrict paste sites.
ITID-44512.purpose: Captures use of a GitHub repository, Gist, or similar code-hosting artifact as a dead-drop resolver polled by malware to retrieve C2 addressing or commands.
scopeIncludes: Implant fetching raw.githubusercontent.com or a Gist raw URL to resolve C2 configuration
C2 configuration committed to a repository and updated via new commits to rotate infrastructure
Abuse of GitHub Actions artifacts or release binaries as a resolver/staging mechanism
scopeExcludes: Dead-drop resolution via a paste/text-sharing site (ITID-44511)
Dead-drop resolution via a document/spreadsheet service (ITID-44513)
Compromise of a legitimate software supply chain repository to distribute malware (a supply-chain ITID)
ITID-44512.severity: Medium-High, reflecting deliberate takedown-resistant infrastructure design; escalate based on confirmed C2 activity, not the resolver mechanism alone.
ITID-44512.priority: P2, escalating to P1 when the resolved C2 destination is live and issuing commands.
ITID-44512.escalation: Escalate to threat intel immediately so the repository/Gist can be reported to the hosting provider and monitored for further updates before the adversary deletes it.
indicators: Outbound requests to raw.githubusercontent.com or gist.githubusercontent.com from hosts with no developer/CI role
Repeated commit history on an otherwise-empty or minimal-content repository
Recently created GitHub accounts hosting the resolver content
vectors: Implant embeds only a repository/Gist URL, fetching updated content on each check-in
Adversary uses a throwaway or compromised GitHub account to host and rotate resolver content
rootCauses: Web filtering broadly allow-lists github.com/githubusercontent.com for developer productivity without granular monitoring
No baseline of which hosts have a legitimate reason to reach code-hosting infrastructure
mitreTechniques: T1102.001 Web Service: Dead Drop Resolver
controls: Egress monitoring differentiating developer/CI hosts from general endpoints for code-hosting traffic
Threat-intel reporting pipeline to code-hosting platform abuse teams
Repository/Gist content preservation before takedown requests are filed
ITID-44512.detection: Proxy and DNS logs provide good visibility into which internal hosts reach code-hosting raw-content domains; correlating against an asset inventory of legitimate developer/CI systems is the key detection lever.
ITID-44512.response: Preserve repository/Gist content and commit history, extract the resolved C2 destination, file an abuse report with the hosting provider, and pivot to endpoint containment on affected hosts.
metrics: Count of hosts observed polling code-hosting raw-content URLs outside developer/CI baseline
Time from detection to provider abuse-report filing
detections: EDR: unexpected process making outbound HTTPS calls to code-hosting domains
ITID-44512.notes: Sibling to ITID-44511 and ITID-44513; differentiator is the hosting platform (code-hosting vs. paste vs. document/spreadsheet), which drives different takedown/reporting channels.

playbook.name: C2 Dead-Drop Resolver via GitHub Repository/Gist
playbook.description: An implant retrieves the current C2 address or commands from a GitHub repository, commit, or Gist controlled by the operator, blending malicious traffic with routine developer/CI activity.

steps.title: Detect recurring requests to GitHub raw content from non-developer hosts
steps.desc: Review proxy/NGFW logs for recurring requests to raw.githubusercontent.com or gist.github.com from hosts/processes with no legitimate development or CI/CD function, particularly at beacon-consistent intervals.
steps.guidance: Correlate with asset inventory/CMDB to identify hosts that have no business reason to pull raw GitHub content (e.g. workstations outside engineering, servers with no CI role).
steps.outcome: A shortlist of hosts/processes fetching GitHub content in a beacon-consistent, non-developer pattern.
steps.abort: If the requests map to a legitimate internal automation or approved open-source dependency fetch, close as false positive.

steps.title: Decide on monitoring versus immediate block
steps.desc: Weigh silent monitoring of the repository/gist and resulting fetches (to track further commits/config changes) against immediate blocking, given the operator can push a new commit at any time to relocate the resolver.
steps.outcome: Documented containment decision addressing both the GitHub resolver and resolved destination.

steps.title: Remove the implant and its hardcoded resolver URL
steps.desc: Remove the implant binary/script and any persistence mechanism, documenting the hardcoded GitHub resolver URL for detection tuning.
steps.outcome: Implant and persistence removed; no respawn observed.

steps.title: Verify no recurrence before restoring access
steps.desc: Monitor for renewed fetches to GitHub or the resolved C2 destination before restoring hosts to normal network access.
steps.outcome: No recurrence observed; hosts cleared for production.
steps.abort: If fetches recur to a new repository, return to containment and re-scope.

steps.title: Add detection for developer-platform dead-drop resolver patterns
steps.desc: Document the incident and add detection for beacon-consistent, non-developer fetches to raw GitHub/Gist content endpoints.
steps.outcome: New detection rule deployed.

steps.title: Retrieve and analyze the referenced repository/gist content and commit history
steps.desc: Review the specific repository, gist, or commit being fetched, including its commit history, for C2 IP/domain values or command payloads, noting that content may change between commits.
steps.guidance: Public commit history often retains prior values even after the current content is edited, aiding full scope determination.
steps.outcome: Confirmed content and commit history consistent with a dead-drop resolver.
steps.tool: GitHub commit history, threat intel platform

steps.title: Isolate affected hosts
steps.desc: Apply EDR network isolation to hosts confirmed to be fetching the dead-drop content.
steps.outcome: Confirmed hosts isolated from the network.

steps.title: Report the malicious repository/gist to GitHub
steps.desc: Report the malicious repository/gist/account to GitHub's abuse team for takedown.
steps.outcome: Repository/gist/account removed at the platform level.

steps.title: Correlate the GitHub account and resolved C2 address with threat intelligence
steps.desc: Check the GitHub account/organization and any resolved C2 IP/domain against threat intel for known campaign association.
steps.outcome: Attribution or campaign context established where available.

steps.title: Block the specific repository/gist URL and resolved C2 destination
steps.desc: Block the specific repository/gist raw-content URL and the currently resolved C2 IP/domain at the proxy/firewall.
steps.outcome: Both the resolver access and resolved destination blocked network-wide.

ITID-44513.def: A C2 persistence technique in which an implant retrieves a publicly shared or link-accessible document/spreadsheet and parses its content for the live C2 endpoint, task list, or encoded configuration. The technique exploits the fact that document-collaboration domains (docs.google.com, sheets.google.com, and equivalents) are near-universally trusted and rarely subject to category-based blocking.
ITID-44513.purpose: Captures use of a publicly shared Google Docs/Sheets (or similar cloud office document) as a dead-drop resolver polled by malware for C2 addressing or commands.
scopeIncludes: Implant fetching a published/exported Google Docs or Sheets URL to parse a C2 IP/domain or command list
Use of a spreadsheet as a simple task queue that the adversary edits to issue new commands
Equivalent use of another cloud office suite's publicly shared document feature
scopeExcludes: Dead-drop resolution via a paste/text-sharing site (ITID-44511)
Dead-drop resolution via a code-hosting repository/Gist (ITID-44512)
Phishing that merely links to a malicious document for initial delivery (an initial-access ITID)
ITID-44513.severity: Medium-High; the technique's evasion value is high given how infrequently document-collaboration domains are blocked or inspected.
ITID-44513.priority: P2, escalating to P1 once the resolved C2 destination is confirmed active.
ITID-44513.escalation: Escalate to threat intel to preserve document version history (where accessible) and report the document/account to the provider before the adversary deletes evidence.
indicators: Outbound requests to docs.google.com/sheets.google.com export or publish endpoints from hosts with no interactive user session at that time
Implant behavior parsing HTML/CSV export output rather than rendering the document
Document publicly shared with link-only access and no legitimate business content
vectors: Implant embeds a published-document export URL and re-fetches it on each check-in interval
Adversary edits the shared document to push new C2 addresses or commands
rootCauses: Web filtering allow-lists cloud office suites wholesale for business productivity without content inspection
No detection logic distinguishing human document access from automated/headless fetches
mitreTechniques: T1102.001 Web Service: Dead Drop Resolver
controls: Behavioral detection distinguishing headless/automated fetches of document-export URLs from normal user browsing
Threat-intel reporting pipeline to cloud office suite abuse teams
Document/version history preservation prior to takedown request
ITID-44513.detection: Proxy logs can surface non-interactive access patterns to document-export endpoints; user-agent and timing analysis (e.g., fetch occurring without a corresponding browser session) is the strongest signal.
ITID-44513.response: Preserve the shared document and any accessible version history, extract the resolved C2 destination, file a provider abuse report, and contain the affected host.
metrics: Count of hosts observed making non-interactive fetches of document-export URLs
Time from detection to provider abuse-report filing
detections: Proxy alert: non-browser fetch of docs.google.com/sheets.google.com export endpoint
EDR: process making scripted HTTP calls that parse cloud-document export content
ITID-44513.notes: Sibling to ITID-44511 and ITID-44512; differentiator is the document/spreadsheet hosting platform, which affects both the parsing behavior observed and the takedown/reporting channel used.

playbook.name: C2 Commands Retrieved from Public Google Docs/Sheets
playbook.description: An implant retrieves C2 commands or configuration by reading a publicly shared Google Docs or Sheets document, leveraging trusted SaaS infrastructure and TLS to evade content and domain-based controls.

steps.title: Detect recurring requests to Google Docs/Sheets export endpoints from non-user processes
steps.desc: Review proxy/NGFW logs for recurring requests to Google Docs/Sheets export or publish-to-web URLs originating from processes other than a browser with an active interactive session, at beacon-consistent intervals.
steps.guidance: Implants typically fetch the document's plain-text or CSV export endpoint directly rather than rendering the full document UI, and do so without any associated Google account authentication flow.
steps.outcome: A shortlist of hosts/processes fetching Docs/Sheets content in a beacon-consistent, non-interactive pattern.
steps.abort: If the requests map to a legitimate internal reporting/automation integration, close as false positive.

steps.title: Decide on monitoring versus immediate block
steps.desc: Weigh silent monitoring of the document (to track further edits/config changes) against immediate blocking, given the operator can edit the shared document at any time to update commands.
steps.guidance: Because blocking all Google Docs/Sheets access is high-impact to normal business operations, prefer targeted blocking of the specific document URL over a blanket domain block where feasible.
steps.outcome: Documented containment decision balancing business impact against risk.

steps.title: Remove the implant and its hardcoded document URL
steps.desc: Remove the implant binary/script and any persistence mechanism, documenting the hardcoded document URL for detection tuning.
steps.outcome: Implant and persistence removed; no respawn observed.

steps.title: Verify no recurrence before restoring access
steps.desc: Monitor for renewed fetches to the document or a successor document before restoring hosts to normal network access.
steps.outcome: No recurrence observed; hosts cleared for production.
steps.abort: If fetches recur to a new document, return to containment and re-scope.

steps.title: Add detection for SaaS-document-based dead-drop patterns
steps.desc: Document the incident and add detection for beacon-consistent, non-interactive fetches to public document export endpoints.
steps.outcome: New detection rule deployed.

steps.title: Retrieve and analyze the referenced document content and revision history
steps.desc: Review the specific document/sheet being fetched, including its revision history if accessible, for command syntax or configuration values.
steps.outcome: Confirmed content and revision history consistent with a C2 command/configuration channel.

steps.title: Isolate affected hosts
steps.desc: Apply EDR network isolation to hosts confirmed to be fetching the malicious document content.
steps.outcome: Confirmed hosts isolated from the network.

steps.title: Report the malicious document to Google
steps.desc: Report the malicious document to Google's abuse/trust-and-safety team for takedown.
steps.outcome: Document removed or access revoked at the platform level.

steps.title: Correlate the document owner/account with threat intelligence
steps.desc: Check any identifiable account/organization details and resolved C2 configuration against threat intel for known campaign association.
steps.outcome: Attribution or campaign context established where available.

steps.title: Block the specific document URL at the proxy
steps.desc: Block the specific document/export URL at the proxy (using URL-path-level filtering rather than a blanket Google domain block) once scoping is complete.
steps.outcome: Access to the specific malicious document blocked without disrupting legitimate Google Workspace usage.

ITID-44514.def: A catch-all classification for C2 persistence via a legitimate web service used as a dead-drop resolver (e.g., a social media profile, forum post, cloud storage share, or messaging-platform channel used to publish C2 addressing or commands) where the specific hosting platform does not map to an existing sibling ITID, or the platform has not yet been identified at classification time.
ITID-44514.purpose: Intake bucket for a confirmed legitimate-web-service dead-drop-resolver C2 mechanism that does not fit the paste-site, code-hosting, or document-service leaves.
scopeIncludes: Dead-drop resolution via a social media post/profile bio/comment
Dead-drop resolution via a cloud storage share link (Dropbox, OneDrive, etc.) not otherwise classified
Cases pending further analysis to identify the specific legitimate web service abused
scopeExcludes: Dead-drop resolution via a paste/text-sharing site (ITID-44511)
Dead-drop resolution via a code-hosting repository/Gist (ITID-44512)
Dead-drop resolution via a document/spreadsheet service (ITID-44513)
ITID-44514.severity: Medium-High by default, consistent with the sibling leaves in this group; reassess once the specific service and C2 destination are identified.
ITID-44514.priority: P2, escalating to P1 upon confirmation of an active resolved C2 destination.
ITID-44514.escalation: Escalate to threat intel for identification and provider reporting; reclassify to a more specific sibling ITID once the hosting platform is confirmed, if a matching leaf exists.
indicators: Recurring outbound requests to a legitimate web service not typically used by the affected host/role
Content structure suggesting an encoded C2 pointer or command embedded in otherwise-benign-looking service content
vectors: Implant fetches content from an unclassified legitimate web service to resolve C2 addressing
rootCauses: Broad allow-listing of trusted-category domains without per-service behavioral monitoring
Novel or rarely-seen abuse of a legitimate platform not yet covered by a dedicated taxonomy leaf
mitreTechniques: T1102.001 Web Service: Dead Drop Resolver
controls: Egress monitoring and anomaly detection across trusted-category web traffic
Threat-intel reporting pipeline to relevant provider abuse teams
ITID-44514.detection: Coverage varies by the specific service involved; triage should aim to identify the platform quickly so the appropriate detection and reporting playbook can be applied.
ITID-44514.response: Identify the specific legitimate web service and reclassify to the matching sibling ITID where possible; otherwise handle as a generic dead-drop-resolver C2 case.
metrics: Count of incidents initially filed here later reclassified to a specific sibling ITID
detections: Proxy alert: anomalous recurring access to a trusted-category domain
ITID-44514.notes: Use sparingly; prefer the specific sibling leaf whenever the hosting platform is known. This leaf exists to avoid forcing premature/incorrect classification during initial triage.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Legitimate Web Service C2
playbook.description: An implant retrieves C2 commands or configuration from a legitimate, trusted web service not matching a more specific dead-drop-resolver sub-technique.

steps.title: Detect recurring requests to a legitimate web service from non-standard processes
steps.desc: Review proxy/NGFW logs for recurring, beacon-consistent requests to a trusted third-party web service from processes with no legitimate business need for it.
steps.outcome: A shortlist of hosts/processes exhibiting the pattern.
steps.abort: If the requests map to an approved integration, close as false positive.

steps.title: Decide on monitoring versus immediate block
steps.desc: Weigh silent monitoring against immediate targeted blocking of the specific resource, balancing business impact of blocking the broader legitimate service.
steps.outcome: Documented containment decision.

steps.title: Remove the implant and persistence mechanism
steps.desc: Remove the implant binary/script and any persistence artifacts.
steps.outcome: Implant and persistence removed.

steps.title: Verify no recurrence before restoring access
steps.desc: Monitor for renewed fetches before restoring hosts to normal network access.
steps.outcome: No recurrence observed; hosts cleared for production.
steps.abort: If fetches recur, return to containment.

steps.title: Improve detection for legitimate-service abuse patterns
steps.desc: Document the incident and add detection for beacon-consistent fetches to legitimate web services from non-standard processes.
steps.outcome: New detection rule deployed.

steps.title: Retrieve and analyze the referenced content
steps.desc: Retrieve the specific content being fetched to confirm C2 command/configuration data.
steps.outcome: Confirmed content consistent with a C2 dead-drop/configuration channel.

steps.title: Isolate affected hosts
steps.desc: Apply EDR network isolation to confirmed hosts.
steps.outcome: Hosts isolated from further C2 contact.

steps.title: Report the abused resource to the service provider
steps.desc: Report the malicious resource/account to the service provider's abuse team for takedown.
steps.outcome: Resource removed at the platform level.

steps.title: Block the specific resource URL at the proxy
steps.desc: Block the specific malicious resource URL/path at the proxy without disrupting legitimate use of the broader service.
steps.outcome: Malicious resource blocked network-wide.

ITID-44521.def: A C2 persistence technique in which an implant's check-in timing is not a fixed interval but a base interval plus a randomized jitter percentage, so consecutive beacons do not fall into the regular, easily-fingerprinted cadence that timing-based network detection relies on.
ITID-44521.purpose: Captures malware whose beacon interval is configurable and randomized (jittered) specifically to defeat fixed-interval beacon detection.
scopeIncludes: Implant configuration exposing a base beacon interval plus jitter percentage/range
Beacon timing that varies beacon-to-beacon in a way inconsistent with legitimate periodic traffic (e.g., health checks, telemetry)
Adversary tuning of jitter mid-campaign to evade a specific detection rule
scopeExcludes: Beacon check-ins disguised as a specific benign traffic type such as a software update check (ITID-44522)
Beacon timing irregularity caused by network conditions rather than deliberate jitter design
ITID-44521.severity: Medium; jitter alone is an evasion refinement, not an indicator of impact — severity should track the broader C2 campaign it supports.
ITID-44521.priority: P2 for detection/analysis purposes; priority of the underlying incident follows the associated C2 campaign's classification.
ITID-44521.escalation: Escalate to detection engineering when jittered beaconing evades an existing fixed-interval rule, so the analytic can be updated to a statistical/variance-based model.
indicators: Beacon intervals clustering around a base value with randomized variance rather than a fixed period
Network flow analysis showing session count/duration patterns consistent with beaconing despite lacking a fixed period
vectors: Off-the-shelf C2 frameworks (e.g., commercial or open-source post-exploitation kits) exposing jitter as a configuration option
rootCauses: Detection analytics relying solely on fixed-interval periodicity rather than statistical beacon modeling
Insufficient network flow retention to support long-window variance analysis
controls: Statistical/variance-based beacon detection (e.g., JA3/JA3S plus interval-distribution analysis) rather than fixed-period matching
Extended network flow log retention to support long-window analysis
ITID-44521.detection: Requires beacon-analysis tooling capable of statistical clustering rather than simple fixed-interval matching; raw flow logs alone are insufficient without such tooling.
ITID-44521.response: Treat as one facet of a broader C2 investigation; feed observed jitter parameters back into detection engineering rather than closing as a standalone finding.
metrics: Count of jittered-beacon detections requiring analytic tuning
Mean jitter percentage observed across confirmed cases
detections: Network analytics: statistical beacon-interval clustering alert
ITID-44521.notes: Differentiates from ITID-44522 by evasion axis: this leaf is about timing randomization, not disguising the beacon's content/appearance.

playbook.name: Configurable Beacon Interval with Jitter for Detection Evasion
playbook.description: An implant checks in to its C2 server at a configurable interval with randomized jitter to defeat simple fixed-interval beacon detection.

steps.title: Apply statistical beacon-interval analysis across a wide observation window
steps.desc: Run interval-distribution analysis (e.g. RITA-style jitter-tolerant beacon scoring) across proxy/NGFW logs over an extended window (days, not hours) to detect a jittered but statistically clustered check-in pattern to a given destination.
steps.guidance: Fixed-window analysis may miss jittered beacons; use a statistical scoring approach tolerant of randomized delay within a bounded range.
steps.outcome: A shortlist of hosts exhibiting statistically clustered, jittered beacon behavior.
steps.abort: If the interval distribution matches a known legitimate polling service with built-in randomized backoff, close as false positive.

steps.title: Decide on silent monitoring versus immediate block
steps.desc: Weigh continued silent monitoring (to observe the jitter range and confirm scope across all affected hosts) against immediate blocking, since abrupt cessation of check-ins may prompt the operator to suspect detection.
steps.guidance: Prefer silent monitoring/sinkholing for a defined period to fully map the jitter pattern and any additional beaconing hosts before overt disruption.
steps.outcome: Documented decision with jitter range and scope established.

steps.title: Remove the implant and persistence mechanism
steps.desc: Remove the implant binary/process and any persistence mechanism used to maintain the beacon.
steps.outcome: Implant and persistence removed; no respawn observed.

steps.title: Verify no recurrence before restoring access
steps.desc: Monitor for renewed beacon activity matching the jitter profile before restoring hosts to normal network access.
steps.outcome: No recurrence observed; hosts cleared for production.
steps.abort: If beaconing recurs, return to containment and re-scope.

steps.title: Tune jitter-tolerant beacon detection
steps.desc: Document the observed jitter range and tune SIEM/NDR beacon-detection analytics to be tolerant of randomized delay within bounded ranges.
steps.outcome: Beacon-detection analytics improved for jittered patterns.

steps.title: Correlate destination infrastructure with threat intelligence
steps.desc: Check the destination IP/domain against threat intel for known C2 infrastructure association.
steps.outcome: Confirmed or strongly suspected malicious classification.

steps.title: Isolate affected hosts
steps.desc: Apply EDR network isolation to confirmed hosts.
steps.outcome: Confirmed hosts isolated from the network.

steps.title: Correlate with EDR host telemetry
steps.desc: Correlate the network finding with EDR process telemetry to identify the implant process on the host.
steps.outcome: Implant process/binary identified on the host.

steps.title: Block the C2 destination at proxy/firewall
steps.desc: Block the confirmed C2 destination IP/domain at the proxy/firewall network-wide.
steps.outcome: C2 destination blocked network-wide.

ITID-44522.def: A C2 persistence technique in which an implant's check-in traffic mimics the request/response shape of a legitimate software update check (URL path, headers, User-Agent, response parsing logic) so that it blends with traffic generated by common applications and is less likely to be flagged as anomalous by network defenders or blocked by application allow-listing.
ITID-44522.purpose: Captures malware beacons deliberately disguised as an application software-update check to blend into expected, whitelisted traffic patterns.
scopeIncludes: Beacon requests crafted to match a known software vendor's update-check URL pattern and headers
C2 response payloads formatted to resemble a version-check JSON/XML response
Reuse of a legitimate update-checker's User-Agent string to blend into expected traffic
scopeExcludes: Beacon timing/jitter evasion without content disguise (ITID-44521)
A genuine supply-chain compromise of an actual update mechanism (a supply-chain ITID)
ITID-44522.severity: Medium; content-disguise is a detection-evasion refinement — severity should track the broader C2 campaign it supports.
ITID-44522.priority: P2 for detection/analysis purposes; priority of the underlying incident follows the associated C2 campaign's classification.
ITID-44522.escalation: Escalate to detection engineering and threat intel to identify which legitimate update mechanism is being mimicked, since this may reveal the adversary's toolkit or targeting.
indicators: Update-check-style traffic to a domain that does not match the vendor whose update format is being mimicked
Mismatch between the process making the request and the application whose update pattern is being imitated
Update-check response content that fails to parse as valid version metadata
vectors: Implant hardcodes a request template mimicking a popular application's update endpoint
Adversary registers a domain with a name similar to a legitimate vendor's update infrastructure
rootCauses: Application allow-listing/firewall rules trusting traffic shaped like known update checks without validating the destination
Insufficient TLS inspection or SNI/domain validation on outbound update-style traffic
mitreTechniques: T1071.001 Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols
controls: Domain/destination validation for traffic matching known update-check patterns
TLS inspection or SNI allow-listing tied to the actual vendor domain, not just traffic shape
ITID-44522.detection: Requires content-aware inspection (destination/domain validation, response schema checks) rather than pattern matching on request shape alone, since the shape is deliberately designed to pass.
ITID-44522.response: Identify the specific application/vendor being mimicked, validate whether other hosts running that application show the same anomaly, and treat as part of the broader C2 investigation.
metrics: Count of mimicked-update-check beacons detected
Count of distinct vendor patterns observed being disguised
detections: Network analytics: update-check pattern to non-vendor-owned destination
ITID-44522.notes: Differentiates from ITID-44521 by evasion axis: this leaf is about content/appearance disguise, not timing randomization; the two techniques are commonly combined in practice but are classified independently.

playbook.name: Beacon Check-in Disguised as Software Update Check
playbook.description: An implant's periodic check-in mimics a legitimate software update check (User-Agent, endpoint path, request structure) to blend with routine patch-management traffic.

steps.title: Validate update-check traffic against known vendor update infrastructure
steps.desc: Review proxy/NGFW logs for update-check-style requests (User-Agent and URL path resembling a software updater) directed at domains not matching the actual vendor's known update infrastructure.
steps.guidance: Cross-reference the claimed software product/vendor against its documented update endpoints; a mismatch between the claimed updater and the actual destination domain is a strong indicator.
steps.outcome: A shortlist of hosts making update-check requests to unverified/mismatched destinations.
steps.abort: If the destination matches a legitimate CDN used by the actual vendor, close as false positive.

steps.title: Decide on monitoring versus immediate block
steps.desc: Weigh silent monitoring to scope affected hosts against immediate blocking of the fake update-check destination.
steps.outcome: Documented containment decision.

steps.title: Remove the implant and persistence mechanism
steps.desc: Remove the implant binary/process disguised as the software updater, along with its persistence mechanism.
steps.outcome: Implant and persistence removed; no respawn observed.

steps.title: Verify no recurrence before restoring access
steps.desc: Monitor for renewed update-check traffic to the blocked destination before restoring hosts to normal network access.
steps.outcome: No recurrence observed; hosts cleared for production.
steps.abort: If activity recurs, return to containment and re-scope.

steps.title: Add vendor-update-endpoint validation to proxy allowlisting
steps.desc: Document the incident and add a validation rule ensuring update-check traffic to claimed vendor endpoints matches documented, verified update infrastructure.
steps.outcome: New validation/detection rule deployed.

steps.title: Correlate with EDR to confirm the requesting process
steps.desc: Confirm via EDR which process is generating the update-check traffic and whether it corresponds to the software it claims to represent.
steps.outcome: Confirmed mismatch between the claimed software and the actual requesting process/binary.

steps.title: Isolate affected hosts
steps.desc: Apply EDR network isolation to confirmed hosts.
steps.outcome: Confirmed hosts isolated from the network.

steps.title: Correlate destination infrastructure with threat intelligence
steps.desc: Check the destination domain/IP against threat intel for known C2 infrastructure association.
steps.outcome: Attribution or campaign context established where available.

steps.title: Block the fake update-check destination at proxy/firewall
steps.desc: Block the confirmed malicious destination at the proxy/firewall network-wide.
steps.outcome: Fake update-check destination blocked network-wide.

ITID-44523.def: A catch-all classification for periodic C2 beacon behavior where the specific evasion technique (timing-based jitter, content-based disguise, or another mechanism) has not been identified, or does not match an existing sibling leaf.
ITID-44523.purpose: Intake bucket for a confirmed malware beacon C2 mechanism that does not fit the jittered-interval or update-check-disguise leaves.
scopeIncludes: Confirmed beaconing behavior pending further characterization of its evasion mechanism
Beacon techniques using an evasion approach other than jitter or update-check disguise
scopeExcludes: Configurable jittered beacon interval (ITID-44521)
Beacon disguised as a software update check (ITID-44522)
ITID-44523.severity: Medium by default; reassess once the beacon's specific characteristics and associated campaign are identified.
ITID-44523.priority: P2, pending reclassification to a more specific sibling ITID once analysis completes.
ITID-44523.escalation: Escalate to the C2 beacon triage team for full characterization; reclassify once the specific technique is confirmed.
indicators: Recurring outbound connections consistent with beaconing behavior, mechanism not yet characterized
vectors: Any implant exhibiting periodic check-in behavior not yet mapped to a specific evasion technique
rootCauses: Detection captured behavior before full analysis of the beacon's evasion design was complete
controls: Beacon-analysis tooling capable of both statistical timing analysis and content inspection
ITID-44523.detection: Varies; use as an interim classification during active analysis.
ITID-44523.response: Complete beacon characterization and reclassify to a specific sibling ITID where applicable.
metrics: Count of incidents initially filed here later reclassified
ITID-44523.notes: Use only during initial triage or when the beacon evasion mechanism genuinely does not fit a sibling leaf.

ITID-44531.def: A C2 persistence technique in which an implant retrieves an ordinary-looking media file (commonly an image) from a web server, social media post, or file share, and extracts hidden C2 commands or configuration encoded within the file's pixel/bit data via steganographic techniques, so the transport payload passes casual content inspection and many automated file-type filters.
ITID-44531.purpose: Captures C2 that hides commands or configuration inside image, audio, or other media files (steganography) as a persistence and evasion mechanism.
scopeIncludes: C2 commands or configuration embedded in image least-significant-bit data and extracted by the implant
Use of a steganographic image posted to a public site as a periodic C2 check-in source
Audio or other media-file steganography used for the same purpose
scopeExcludes: Plain dead-drop resolvers using unmodified text/document content (ITID-44511 through ITID-44513)
Steganography used purely for data exfiltration rather than command retrieval (a data-exfiltration ITID)
ITID-44531.severity: Medium-High; steganographic C2 indicates a moderately sophisticated adversary investing in evasion beyond commodity techniques.
ITID-44531.priority: P2, escalating to P1 once the decoded C2 content is confirmed active.
ITID-44531.escalation: Escalate to malware analysis/reverse engineering promptly, since extracting and confirming the hidden payload typically requires specialist tooling beyond standard SOC triage.
indicators: Implant process opening and parsing image/media files fetched over HTTP(S) with no corresponding rendering/display activity
Image files with statistically anomalous pixel-data entropy compared to their apparent content
Repeated fetches of the same or similar media file from a fixed source
vectors: Implant fetches a steganographic image from a public hosting site or compromised web server on each check-in
Adversary updates the hosted image to rotate embedded C2 configuration
rootCauses: Content filtering trusts image/media MIME types without deeper payload inspection
Limited malware-analysis capacity to routinely inspect media files for steganographic payloads
mitreTechniques: T1027.003 Obfuscated Files or Information: Steganography
controls: Malware sandboxing capable of steganographic payload extraction
Entropy/statistical anomaly scanning on media files transiting the network boundary
ITID-44531.detection: Low with standard network/content filtering; meaningful coverage requires dedicated steganalysis tooling or behavioral detection of the implant's file-parsing activity on the endpoint.
ITID-44531.response: Preserve the source media file for analysis, engage reverse engineering to extract the hidden payload, and pivot to the resolved C2 destination for containment.
metrics: Count of confirmed steganographic C2 cases per year
Mean time to extract hidden payload from source media
detections: EDR: process parsing image/media file with no rendering context
Sandbox: steganalysis flag on ingested media file
ITID-44531.notes: This is currently the sole leaf in its Tier-4 sibling group at the persistence-mechanism level; no further differentiation was needed at this time.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Steganographic C2 (Persistence Mechanism Context)
playbook.description: An implant relies on steganographically embedded commands as a persistence mechanism for ongoing C2 contact, not matching a more specific sub-technique.

steps.title: Flag repeated media/file transfers with anomalous size or fetch pattern
steps.desc: Review proxy/NGFW logs for repeated downloads/uploads of media/image/document files to/from a consistent destination at beacon-consistent intervals, or files with size inconsistent with visible content.
steps.outcome: A shortlist of candidate steganographic carrier files and their transfer pattern.
steps.abort: If transfers map to a legitimate media-heavy application, close as false positive.

steps.title: Decide on monitoring versus immediate block
steps.desc: Weigh silent collection of additional carrier samples against immediate blocking of the hosting endpoint.
steps.outcome: Documented containment decision.

steps.title: Remove the implant and its steganographic component
steps.desc: Remove the implant binary/script, including the steganographic encoding/decoding component, and any persistence mechanism.
steps.outcome: Implant and steganographic components removed; no respawn observed.

steps.title: Verify no further carrier-file activity before restoring access
steps.desc: Monitor for renewed transfers matching the identified pattern before restoring hosts to normal network access.
steps.outcome: No recurrence observed; hosts cleared for production.
steps.abort: If activity recurs, return to containment and re-scope.

steps.title: Add steganalysis screening to file transfer monitoring
steps.desc: Document the incident and evaluate integrating automated steganalysis screening into proxy/DLP.
steps.outcome: New screening capability evaluated or deployed.

steps.title: Run steganalysis on sampled carrier files
steps.desc: Apply steganalysis tooling to sampled carrier files to detect and extract embedded command data.
steps.outcome: Confirmed embedded command/response data recovered.
steps.abort: If inconclusive, proceed on transfer-pattern evidence and escalate to specialist forensic support.

steps.title: Isolate affected hosts
steps.desc: Apply EDR network isolation to hosts confirmed to be exchanging steganographic carrier files.
steps.outcome: Confirmed hosts isolated from the network.

steps.title: Block the hosting endpoint at proxy/firewall
steps.desc: Block the confirmed file-hosting domain/service at the proxy/firewall network-wide.
steps.outcome: Hosting endpoint blocked for all hosts.

ITID-44541.def: A C2 persistence technique in which the adversary creates a Windows Scheduled Task that periodically launches a process (script, binary, or living-off-the-land binary) whose purpose is to check in with C2 and execute retrieved commands, ensuring the C2 channel survives reboots and user logoff without requiring a continuously running process.
ITID-44541.purpose: Captures adversary creation of a Windows Scheduled Task specifically to execute commands delivered by C2 on a recurring basis.
scopeIncludes: Scheduled Task configured to launch a C2 check-in script/binary on a timer or at logon/startup
Scheduled Task used purely for C2 command execution (as opposed to other persistence goals)
Modification of an existing legitimate scheduled task to add C2 check-in behavior
scopeExcludes: Cron-based equivalent on Linux/Unix systems (ITID-44542)
Scheduled tasks used for non-C2 persistence such as simple binary re-execution with no command-and-control channel (a persistence-only ITID outside this domain)
ITID-44541.severity: Medium-High; scheduled-task-based C2 persistence indicates the adversary intends sustained access.
ITID-44541.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if the task is actively retrieving and executing commands at time of discovery.
ITID-44541.escalation: Escalate to IR for host containment and full persistence-mechanism sweep across the environment, since scheduled-task techniques are frequently replicated across multiple compromised hosts.
indicators: Newly created scheduled task with an unusual or obfuscated action/argument string
Scheduled task triggering a script interpreter (PowerShell, wscript, etc.) with encoded command-line arguments
Task Scheduler event logs (Event ID 4698/106) showing task creation outside change-management windows
vectors: Adversary uses schtasks.exe or the Task Scheduler COM API post-compromise to register the task
C2 framework built-in persistence module automates scheduled task creation
rootCauses: Task Scheduler creation not restricted or monitored for non-administrative users/processes
Insufficient baseline of expected scheduled tasks to flag anomalous additions
controls: Scheduled task creation auditing and alerting (Event ID 4698)
Application control restricting which binaries/interpreters scheduled tasks may launch
Baseline inventory of expected scheduled tasks per host role
ITID-44541.detection: Strong via Windows Event Log auditing (Task Scheduler operational log) when enabled and monitored; EDR provides additional confirmation of the task's runtime behavior.
ITID-44541.response: Remove the malicious scheduled task, preserve its configuration for analysis, and sweep the environment for the same task name/pattern on other hosts.
metrics: Count of malicious scheduled tasks identified and removed
Mean time from task creation to detection
detections: Windows Event ID 4698/106: scheduled task creation
EDR: scheduled-task-triggered process launching script interpreter with encoded arguments
ITID-44541.notes: Differentiates from ITID-44542 by operating system/scheduler mechanism (Windows Task Scheduler vs. cron); both share the same MITRE parent technique but distinct sub-techniques.

playbook.name: Scheduled Task Created to Periodically Execute C2-Delivered Commands
playbook.description: An attacker creates a Windows Scheduled Task that periodically executes commands or scripts retrieved from a C2 server, providing durable persistence for command execution independent of an active session.

steps.title: Audit scheduled task creation events for suspicious tasks
steps.desc: Review Windows Event ID 4698 (scheduled task created) and Task Scheduler logs for tasks created outside of normal change-management processes, particularly those executing scripting engines (powershell.exe, wscript.exe, cmd.exe) with encoded or obfuscated arguments.
steps.guidance: Focus on tasks with generic or spoofed names mimicking legitimate system tasks, running with elevated privileges, and configured to run at short recurring intervals.
steps.outcome: A shortlist of suspicious scheduled tasks identified across the environment.
steps.abort: If the task matches an approved deployment/patch-management task, close as false positive after confirming with the responsible team.
steps.tool: Windows Event Logs, EDR, Task Scheduler

steps.title: Decide on disabling versus monitoring the task
steps.desc: Weigh disabling the scheduled task immediately (a low-risk containment action since the task itself is not the primary evidence source) against briefly monitoring its next execution to capture the live command retrieval.
steps.guidance: Disabling a scheduled task rarely alerts a remote operator the way a network-level block does, so prompt disabling is generally low-risk and preferred once the task is confirmed malicious.
steps.outcome: Documented decision, generally favoring prompt disabling.

steps.title: Delete the malicious scheduled task and referenced scripts/binaries
steps.desc: Delete the scheduled task definition and any referenced script/binary files, along with any other persistence mechanism used to recreate the task.
steps.outcome: Scheduled task and referenced artifacts fully removed.

steps.title: Verify no task recreation before restoring access
steps.desc: Monitor for recreation of the scheduled task (Event ID 4698) or renewed C2 contact before restoring hosts to normal network access.
steps.outcome: No recreation or renewed contact observed; hosts cleared for production.
steps.abort: If the task is recreated, return to containment and search for the underlying persistence mechanism enabling recreation.

steps.title: Add scheduled-task creation monitoring and alerting
steps.desc: Document the incident and ensure Event ID 4698 is forwarded to the SIEM with alerting rules for tasks invoking scripting engines with encoded arguments or short recurring intervals.
steps.outcome: New monitoring/alerting rule deployed for suspicious scheduled task creation.

steps.title: Analyze the task's command/script content and network correlation
steps.desc: Review the full command line, referenced script, or executable invoked by the task, and correlate its execution timestamps with outbound network connections to identify the C2 destination retrieving commands.
steps.outcome: Confirmed C2 command-retrieval behavior tied to the scheduled task.

steps.title: Disable the scheduled task across all affected hosts
steps.desc: Disable (rather than immediately delete) the malicious scheduled task on all affected hosts to halt further execution while preserving it for forensic review.
steps.outcome: Scheduled task disabled on all affected hosts; no further C2-delivered command execution.

steps.title: Block the C2 destination the task retrieved commands from
steps.desc: Block the confirmed C2 destination IP/domain at the proxy/firewall network-wide.
steps.outcome: C2 destination blocked network-wide.

steps.title: Identify all hosts with the same or similar scheduled task
steps.desc: Search across the environment via EDR/GPO reporting for the same task name, script hash, or command pattern to determine full blast radius.
steps.outcome: Complete list of affected hosts identified.

steps.title: Isolate hosts pending further investigation
steps.desc: Apply EDR network isolation to affected hosts while the underlying compromise vector is investigated.
steps.outcome: Affected hosts isolated from the network.

ITID-44542.def: A C2 persistence technique in which the adversary adds an entry to crontab (user or system) or an equivalent scheduler (systemd timer) that periodically launches a process to check in with C2 and execute retrieved commands, ensuring the C2 channel survives reboots without a continuously running foreground process.
ITID-44542.purpose: Captures adversary creation of a Linux/Unix cron job specifically to execute commands delivered by C2 on a recurring basis.
scopeIncludes: Crontab entry added to execute a C2 check-in script/binary on an interval
Systemd timer unit created for the same purpose
Modification of an existing cron entry to add C2 check-in behavior
scopeExcludes: Windows Scheduled Task equivalent (ITID-44541)
Cron entries used for non-C2 persistence with no command-and-control channel (a persistence-only ITID outside this domain)
ITID-44542.severity: Medium-High; cron-based C2 persistence indicates the adversary intends sustained access to the affected Linux/Unix host.
ITID-44542.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if the cron job is actively retrieving and executing commands at time of discovery.
ITID-44542.escalation: Escalate to IR for host containment and a persistence-mechanism sweep across the environment, since cron-based techniques are commonly scripted for mass deployment.
indicators: New or modified crontab entry referencing an unfamiliar script path or obfuscated command
Cron job invoking a shell with base64-decoded or piped remote content
Systemd timer unit files created outside change management
vectors: Adversary writes directly to /etc/crontab, a user crontab, or /etc/cron.d/ post-compromise
Worm/self-propagating malware scripts automate cron entry creation across compromised hosts
rootCauses: Crontab/systemd timer modification not monitored via file integrity or auditd rules
Insufficient baseline of expected cron jobs per host role
controls: File integrity monitoring on crontab files and cron.d directories
auditd rules alerting on crontab modification
Baseline inventory of expected cron jobs per host role
ITID-44542.detection: Strong when file integrity monitoring and auditd are deployed on Linux hosts; coverage is weak on systems without host-based logging enabled.
ITID-44542.response: Remove the malicious cron entry, preserve it for analysis, and sweep the environment for the same script/command pattern on other hosts.
metrics: Count of malicious cron entries identified and removed
Mean time from entry creation to detection
detections: auditd alert: crontab write by non-administrative process
ITID-44542.notes: Differentiates from ITID-44541 by operating system/scheduler mechanism (cron/systemd vs. Windows Task Scheduler); both share the same MITRE parent technique but distinct sub-techniques.

playbook.name: Cron Job Created for Automated C2 Check-in Execution
playbook.description: An attacker creates a cron job on a Linux/Unix host to periodically execute commands or scripts retrieved from a C2 server, providing durable persistence on network infrastructure and servers.

steps.title: Audit crontab and cron.d entries for suspicious jobs
steps.desc: Review user crontabs, /etc/cron.d, /etc/cron.daily/hourly/weekly, and systemd timers for entries invoking shell one-liners, curl/wget pipes to shell, or base64-decoded commands, particularly those added outside change-management windows.
steps.guidance: Focus on jobs referencing unfamiliar file paths (e.g. /tmp, /dev/shm), obfuscated command strings, or execution as root with no documented business purpose. On network infrastructure devices, review equivalent scheduled-job configuration (e.g. EEM applets, kron).
steps.outcome: A shortlist of suspicious cron/scheduled-job entries identified.
steps.abort: If the entry matches an approved automation/monitoring job, close as false positive after confirming with the responsible team.
steps.tool: EDR, system audit tooling, configuration management

steps.title: Decide on disabling versus monitoring the job
steps.desc: Weigh disabling the cron job immediately against briefly monitoring its next execution to capture the live command retrieval, noting that removing a cron entry is a low-risk local action unlikely to alert a remote operator.
steps.outcome: Documented decision, generally favoring prompt disabling.

steps.title: Remove the cron entry and referenced scripts/binaries
steps.desc: Permanently remove the cron entry and any referenced script/binary files, along with any other persistence mechanism used to recreate the job.
steps.outcome: Cron job and referenced artifacts fully removed.

steps.title: Verify no job recreation before restoring access
steps.desc: Monitor crontab/configuration integrity and network traffic for recreation of the job or renewed C2 contact before restoring hosts/devices to normal operation.
steps.outcome: No recreation or renewed contact observed; hosts/devices cleared for production.
steps.abort: If the job is recreated, return to containment and search for the underlying persistence mechanism enabling recreation.

steps.title: Add cron/scheduled-job integrity monitoring on network infrastructure
steps.desc: Document the incident and deploy file integrity monitoring on crontab locations and configuration-change alerting for network infrastructure devices to detect unauthorized scheduled-job creation.
steps.outcome: New monitoring/alerting rule deployed.

steps.title: Analyze the job's command content and network correlation
steps.desc: Review the full command invoked by the cron job and correlate its execution timestamps with outbound network connections to identify the C2 destination retrieving commands.
steps.outcome: Confirmed C2 command-retrieval behavior tied to the cron job.

steps.title: Disable the malicious cron job across all affected hosts/devices
steps.desc: Comment out or remove the malicious cron entry on all affected hosts/devices to halt further execution, preserving a copy for forensic review.
steps.outcome: Cron job disabled on all affected hosts; no further C2-delivered command execution.

steps.title: Block the C2 destination the job retrieved commands from
steps.desc: Block the confirmed C2 destination IP/domain at the firewall network-wide.
steps.outcome: C2 destination blocked network-wide.

steps.title: Identify all hosts/devices with the same or similar cron entry
steps.desc: Search across the environment for the same command pattern, file hash, or job name to determine full blast radius, including network infrastructure devices that may share a common compromise vector.
steps.outcome: Complete list of affected hosts/devices identified.

steps.title: Isolate affected hosts/devices pending further investigation
steps.desc: Apply network isolation/quarantine to affected hosts and, where feasible, network devices while the underlying compromise vector is investigated.
steps.outcome: Affected hosts/devices isolated from the broader network.
steps.abort: If isolating a production network device would cause unacceptable outage, coordinate a maintenance window and apply compensating firewall controls in the interim.

ITID-44543.def: A catch-all classification for C2 persistence relying on an automated task-execution mechanism other than Windows Task Scheduler or Linux/Unix cron (for example, a CI/CD pipeline trigger, a third-party job scheduler, or a platform-specific automation service), or where the specific mechanism has not yet been identified.
ITID-44543.purpose: Intake bucket for a confirmed automated-task-execution C2 persistence mechanism that does not fit the Windows Scheduled Task or cron leaves.
scopeIncludes: Automated task-execution persistence on a platform other than Windows Task Scheduler or cron
Cases pending further analysis to identify the specific scheduling mechanism abused
scopeExcludes: Windows Scheduled Task-based C2 persistence (ITID-44541)
Cron/systemd-timer-based C2 persistence (ITID-44542)
ITID-44543.severity: Medium-High by default, consistent with the sibling leaves; reassess once the specific mechanism is identified.
ITID-44543.priority: P2, escalating to P1 upon confirmation of active command execution.
ITID-44543.escalation: Escalate to IR for host/platform containment; reclassify to a more specific sibling ITID once the mechanism is confirmed, if a matching leaf exists.
indicators: Recurring automated execution of an unfamiliar task/job whose scheduling mechanism has not yet been identified
vectors: Abuse of a non-Windows/non-cron automation or scheduling service to achieve recurring C2 execution
rootCauses: Novel or platform-specific automation mechanism not yet covered by a dedicated taxonomy leaf
Insufficient monitoring of non-traditional scheduling/automation surfaces
controls: Monitoring and inventory of automation/scheduling surfaces beyond Task Scheduler and cron
ITID-44543.detection: Varies by mechanism; use as an interim classification during active analysis.
ITID-44543.response: Identify the specific automated task-execution mechanism and reclassify to the matching sibling ITID where possible.
metrics: Count of incidents initially filed here later reclassified
detections: Generic alert: unfamiliar recurring automated task execution
ITID-44543.notes: Use sparingly; prefer the specific sibling leaf whenever the scheduling mechanism is known.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Automated Task Execution for C2
playbook.description: An attacker establishes an automated task/job mechanism to periodically execute C2-delivered commands, not matching a more specific scheduled-task or cron sub-technique.

steps.title: Audit scheduled automation mechanisms for suspicious entries
steps.desc: Review all platform-appropriate scheduled-execution mechanisms (Scheduled Tasks, cron, systemd timers, CI/CD pipeline schedules, cloud function triggers) for entries created outside normal change management with suspicious command content.
steps.outcome: A shortlist of suspicious scheduled-automation entries identified.
steps.abort: If the entry matches an approved automation, close as false positive.

steps.title: Decide on disabling versus monitoring the mechanism
steps.desc: Weigh disabling the automation mechanism immediately against briefly monitoring its next execution.
steps.outcome: Documented decision.

steps.title: Remove the automation entry and referenced artifacts
steps.desc: Permanently remove the automation entry and any referenced scripts/binaries, along with related persistence mechanisms.
steps.outcome: Automation entry and referenced artifacts removed.

steps.title: Verify no recreation before restoring access
steps.desc: Monitor for recreation of the automation mechanism or renewed C2 contact before restoring hosts/systems to normal operation.
steps.outcome: No recreation or renewed contact observed; hosts/systems cleared for production.
steps.abort: If recreated, return to containment.

steps.title: Add automation-mechanism integrity monitoring
steps.desc: Document the incident and deploy monitoring/alerting for unauthorized creation of scheduled-execution mechanisms across the environment.
steps.outcome: New monitoring/alerting rule deployed.

steps.title: Analyze the job's command content and network correlation
steps.desc: Review the command/script invoked and correlate execution timing with outbound network connections to identify the C2 destination.
steps.outcome: Confirmed C2 command-retrieval behavior tied to the automation mechanism.

steps.title: Disable the malicious automation mechanism
steps.desc: Disable or remove the malicious scheduled-execution entry across all affected hosts/systems.
steps.outcome: Automation mechanism disabled; no further C2-delivered command execution.

steps.title: Isolate affected hosts/systems
steps.desc: Apply network isolation/quarantine to affected hosts/systems pending investigation.
steps.outcome: Affected hosts/systems isolated.

ITID-44611.def: A C2 technique in which the implant's command-execution logic runs without a corresponding malicious executable persisted on disk — for example, reflectively loaded into a legitimate process's memory, delivered and executed via a scripting engine directly from a network stream, or stored only in the registry/WMI repository — so that disk-based file scanning and static signature detection have little or no artifact to find.
ITID-44611.purpose: Captures C2 implants that operate entirely in memory or via legitimate OS mechanisms without writing a persistent malicious file to disk.
scopeIncludes: Reflective DLL/shellcode injection into a legitimate running process for C2 execution
PowerShell/script-based C2 payload executed directly in memory from a downloaded string with no file written
C2 configuration/payload stored in the Windows registry or WMI repository rather than on disk
scopeExcludes: C2 execution via abuse of a legitimate signed system binary that remains on disk (living-off-the-land, ITID-44621)
Traditional file-based malware that simply obfuscates its on-disk binary (an obfuscation-focused ITID outside the C2 domain)
ITID-44611.severity: High; fileless C2 typically indicates a more capable adversary and materially reduces the effectiveness of traditional file-scanning defenses.
ITID-44611.priority: P1 upon confirmation, given the detection and eradication difficulty involved.
ITID-44611.escalation: Escalate to IR and memory-forensics specialists immediately; standard disk-imaging-only response is insufficient and live memory capture is time-sensitive.
indicators: EDR alert on reflective code injection or unusual memory allocation/execution permissions in a legitimate process
PowerShell script block logging showing an in-memory download-and-execute pattern (e.g., IEX of a remote string)
Persistence artifact found only in registry/WMI with no corresponding disk file
vectors: Living-off-the-land scripting engines used to download and execute C2 payloads directly in memory
Process injection frameworks used to host C2 implant code inside a trusted process
rootCauses: Endpoint security relying primarily on file-based signature scanning without memory/behavioral analysis
Script execution policies and logging (e.g., PowerShell constrained language mode, script block logging) not enforced
controls: EDR with memory/behavioral analysis capable of detecting reflective injection
PowerShell script block and module logging enabled and monitored
Constrained language mode / application control on scripting engines
ITID-44611.detection: Requires behavioral/memory-based EDR telemetry; traditional AV/file-scanning coverage is minimal to none for this technique class.
ITID-44611.response: Prioritize live memory capture before rebooting or powering off affected hosts, since evidence may not survive a restart; proceed with full IR containment and eradication.
metrics: Count of confirmed fileless C2 incidents per year
Percentage of cases with successful live memory capture
detections: PowerShell script block log: in-memory download-and-execute pattern
ITID-44611.notes: This is currently the sole leaf in its Tier-4 sibling group at this level of the taxonomy; no further differentiation was needed at this time.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Fileless C2 (Advanced Technique Context)
playbook.description: An implant operates entirely in memory (via scripting engines, reflective DLL injection, or registry-resident code) with no persistent file artifact, complicating disk-based detection of its C2 activity.

steps.title: Detect anomalous in-memory execution via EDR behavioral telemetry
steps.desc: Review EDR for behavioral indicators of fileless execution: PowerShell/WMI/script-host processes with suspicious command lines, reflective DLL loading, unusual parent-child process relationships, or process injection into legitimate system processes generating network connections.
steps.guidance: Since no file artifact may exist on disk, prioritize process-tree, command-line, and memory-behavior telemetry over file-hash-based detection.
steps.outcome: A shortlist of hosts exhibiting fileless-execution-consistent behavior correlated with outbound network activity.
steps.abort: If the behavior matches approved administrative scripting/automation, close as false positive.

steps.title: Decide on live containment versus reboot-based disruption
steps.desc: Weigh terminating the in-memory process/injecting-host process immediately (which loses forensic evidence on reboot but halts C2 activity) against maintaining live memory capture a bit longer for full analysis before disruption.
steps.guidance: Given fileless implants do not survive a reboot, a full host reboot after adequate evidence capture is itself often an effective, low-collateral containment action; balance against the value of continued live observation.
steps.outcome: Documented containment decision balancing evidence preservation against exposure duration.

steps.title: Remove the initial-access/persistence mechanism reloading the fileless payload
steps.desc: Identify and remove whatever mechanism (registry entry, WMI subscription, scheduled task, malicious script referenced by a legitimate loader) causes the fileless payload to be reloaded into memory, since the payload itself leaves no disk artifact to remove directly.
steps.outcome: Reload/persistence mechanism removed; payload does not reappear after reboot.

steps.title: Verify no reload of the fileless payload before restoring access
steps.desc: Monitor the rebooted host for renewed suspicious process injection/behavioral indicators before restoring it to normal network access.
steps.outcome: No recurrence observed; host cleared for production.
steps.abort: If the payload reloads, return to containment and search for the remaining persistence mechanism.

steps.title: Strengthen fileless-execution behavioral detection
steps.desc: Document the incident's behavioral indicators and tune EDR detection for the specific process-injection/scripting-abuse pattern observed.
steps.outcome: New behavioral detection rule deployed.

steps.title: Capture volatile memory for forensic analysis
steps.desc: Capture a memory image of the affected host before any reboot or process termination, since the implant may leave no recoverable artifact once memory is cleared.
steps.guidance: Time-sensitive: fileless implants are lost on reboot; prioritize memory capture over other forensic steps.
steps.outcome: Memory image captured and confirmed to contain the implant's in-memory code/configuration.
steps.abort: If memory capture is not feasible before a required reboot, document all available live-response telemetry as the best available evidence.

steps.title: Isolate the host and terminate the malicious process/injected thread
steps.desc: Apply EDR network isolation and terminate the identified malicious process or injected thread.
steps.outcome: Host isolated and malicious in-memory activity halted.

steps.title: Reboot the host to clear volatile in-memory state
steps.desc: Reboot the affected host to ensure the in-memory implant is fully cleared, following completion of forensic capture.
steps.outcome: Host rebooted with no in-memory implant remaining.

steps.title: Correlate network destination with threat intelligence
steps.desc: Check the destination IP/domain identified from network correlation against threat intel for known fileless-malware-family infrastructure.
steps.outcome: Attribution or campaign context established where available.

steps.title: Block the C2 destination at proxy/firewall
steps.desc: Block the confirmed C2 destination IP/domain at the proxy/firewall network-wide.
steps.outcome: C2 destination blocked network-wide.

ITID-44621.def: A C2 technique in which the adversary drives command execution, file transfer, or data staging through legitimate, digitally-signed system utilities already present on the host (e.g., certutil, mshta, rundll32, bitsadmin, or their Unix/Linux equivalents), so that the activity blends with expected administrative behavior and evades application allow-listing and signature-based detection.
