steps.guidance: Engage digital forensics specialists given the likely extended timeframe; standard 30-90 day log retention may be insufficient, requiring extended retention sources (backups, archived logs, EDR historical telemetry).
steps.outcome: A documented timeline covering initial access through current detection, with an assessment of what data/systems the actor accessed over that period.
steps.tool: Digital forensics tooling / EDR historical telemetry

steps.title: Block the C2 infrastructure and isolate confirmed hosts
steps.desc: Once the containment plan is executed, block the C2 IP/domain and isolate all confirmed affected hosts.
steps.outcome: Active C2 communication is severed across all confirmed hosts.

steps.title: Rotate all credentials potentially exposed during the dwell period
steps.desc: Given the extended access window, rotate all credentials, tokens, and keys the actor may have harvested during their presence, not just those directly tied to the beaconing host.
steps.outcome: All potentially compromised credentials are invalidated.

steps.title: Escalate to executive and legal leadership given likely targeted-actor involvement
steps.desc: Given the sophistication implied by long-dwell stealth-optimized C2, escalate to executive leadership, legal counsel, and (where applicable) national CERT/government liaison channels for a likely nation-state or advanced persistent threat scenario.
steps.guidance: Consider engagement of specialized threat intelligence/incident response retainer resources experienced with APT-level actors.
steps.outcome: Executive and legal stakeholders are briefed and engaged; external specialist support is considered.

ITID-44722.def: A C2 pattern characteristic of espionage operations in which the adversary provisions distinct, non-overlapping C2 infrastructure (domains, servers, encryption keys) for each individual target or target set, so that discovery and attribution of one victim's C2 infrastructure yields no indicators transferable to other ongoing operations.
ITID-44722.purpose: Captures espionage-oriented C2 infrastructure deliberately segmented per target so that compromise of one victim's infrastructure does not expose the adversary's other campaigns.
scopeIncludes: Dedicated, non-reused C2 domains/servers provisioned per target organization
Distinct encryption keys or implant build configurations per target to prevent cross-victim indicator reuse
Operational security practices (e.g., no shared infrastructure across campaigns) confirmed through threat-intel analysis of multiple related intrusions
scopeExcludes: Long-term, low-volume C2 optimized primarily for stealth/dwell time rather than segmentation (ITID-44721)
Commodity C2 infrastructure reused indiscriminately across many unrelated victims (inconsistent with this leaf's defining characteristic)
ITID-44722.severity: High; deliberate per-target infrastructure segmentation indicates a sophisticated, well-resourced adversary with strong operational security discipline.
ITID-44722.escalation: Escalate to threat intelligence for cross-organization/industry-sharing coordination, since per-target segmentation limits what can be learned from a single victim's indicators alone — broader intelligence sharing is needed to build a fuller picture.
indicators: Confirmed C2 infrastructure with no overlap against known indicators from other victims of the same threat actor
Threat-intel analysis showing the adversary provisions new infrastructure per campaign/target rather than reusing prior infrastructure
Distinct implant build artifacts (compilation timestamps, embedded keys) unique to this victim
vectors: Adversary provisions dedicated infrastructure per operation as a matter of tradecraft discipline
rootCauses: Reliance on IOC-sharing/threat-intel feeds alone is insufficient against this adversary behavior, since indicators from other victims will not match
controls: Behavioral/TTP-based detection (rather than IOC-matching alone) informed by threat-intel on the actor's known tradecraft
Industry/ISAC information-sharing participation to build cross-victim pattern awareness despite infrastructure segmentation
ITID-44722.detection: Weak for IOC-based detection given the lack of cross-victim infrastructure reuse; behavioral/TTP-based detection and industry information sharing are the primary levers.
ITID-44722.response: Engage threat intelligence to characterize the actor's TTPs (not just indicators) and coordinate with industry/ISAC partners, since this victim's infrastructure will not directly help detect the same actor elsewhere.
metrics: Count of confirmed per-target-segmented espionage C2 cases
Cross-victim indicator overlap rate (expected to be low/zero for this pattern)
detections: TTP-based behavioral detection informed by threat-intel actor profile
ITID-44722.notes: Differentiates from ITID-44721 by axis: this leaf is about infrastructure segmentation/operational security discipline, not stealth-optimized check-in cadence.

playbook.name: Espionage C2 Segmented Per-Target to Limit Cross-Victim Exposure
playbook.description: The espionage actor uses dedicated, non-overlapping C2 infrastructure for this specific target, deliberately segmented to prevent indicators from this incident aiding attribution or detection of the actor's campaigns against other victims.

steps.title: Confirm target-specific (segmented) C2 infrastructure
steps.desc: Analyze the C2 infrastructure's usage pattern and any available external threat intelligence to determine whether it is uniquely dedicated to this organization, which is itself a strong indicator of a deliberate, targeted espionage operation rather than opportunistic/commodity malware.
steps.guidance: Check whether the domain/IP has zero or minimal external sightings in threat intel feeds despite apparent operational maturity — a hallmark of segmented, per-target infrastructure.
steps.outcome: Confirmation that the C2 infrastructure appears dedicated to this target, reinforcing a targeted-espionage assessment.
steps.abort: If the infrastructure shows broad reuse across many unrelated victims, treat as commodity/general espionage C2 instead (ITID-44723).

steps.title: Execute a coordinated, deliberate containment plan
steps.desc: Plan and execute containment carefully given the actor's demonstrated operational security and targeting sophistication, avoiding premature actions that could cause evidence destruction or deeper repositioning.
steps.outcome: A coordinated containment plan is executed without alerting the actor prematurely, unless active exfiltration/destruction requires immediate action.
steps.abort: If active data exfiltration or destructive action is detected, move immediately to full containment.

steps.title: Remove the implant and persistence via full reimaging
steps.desc: Reimage affected hosts from known-good images rather than in-place cleaning, given the sophistication of the actor and risk of undiscovered persistence mechanisms.
steps.outcome: Hosts are rebuilt with no residual persistence.

steps.title: Restore operations with sustained heightened monitoring
steps.desc: Return remediated hosts to production with extended heightened monitoring given the demonstrated targeted-actor sophistication.
steps.outcome: No recurrence of the segmented C2 activity during the extended monitoring window.

steps.title: Conduct full post-incident review with executive/legal stakeholders
steps.desc: Document the timeline, targeting rationale, and detection gaps, briefing executive leadership and legal on findings and any regulatory notification obligations.
steps.outcome: A comprehensive incident report with organizational-level lessons and any required regulatory follow-up identified.

steps.title: Reconstruct the intrusion timeline and assess targeting rationale
steps.desc: Perform forensic timeline reconstruction to determine initial access and identify what specifically was targeted (data, systems, individuals) to understand why this organization was selected for dedicated infrastructure.
steps.guidance: Engage digital forensics and, where available, organizational threat-modeling context (industry, geopolitical exposure, IP value) to assess likely motive.
steps.outcome: A documented timeline and an assessment of the likely targeting rationale/motive.

steps.title: Block the segmented C2 infrastructure and isolate hosts
steps.desc: Block the dedicated C2 IP/domain and isolate all confirmed affected hosts.
steps.outcome: Active C2 communication is severed.

steps.title: Rotate all potentially exposed credentials and keys
steps.desc: Rotate credentials, tokens, and keys the actor may have harvested during their dwell time, given the demonstrated targeting sophistication.
steps.outcome: All potentially compromised credentials are invalidated.

steps.title: Escalate to executive, legal, and government liaison channels
steps.desc: Given the deliberate targeting and likely nation-state or advanced-actor involvement, escalate to executive leadership, legal counsel, and relevant government/CERT liaison channels.
steps.outcome: Appropriate stakeholders are briefed and engaged, including consideration of specialist external IR support.

ITID-44723.def: A catch-all classification for espionage-motivated C2 activity where the specific characterizing pattern (stealth-optimized cadence or per-target infrastructure segmentation) has not yet been identified, or does not match an existing sibling leaf.
ITID-44723.purpose: Intake bucket for a confirmed espionage C2 mechanism that does not fit the low-and-slow-stealth or per-target-segmentation leaves.
scopeIncludes: Confirmed espionage-motivated C2 activity pending further characterization
Espionage C2 patterns other than stealth-optimized cadence or per-target segmentation
scopeExcludes: Long-term low-volume espionage C2 optimized for stealth over speed (ITID-44721)
Espionage C2 segmented per-target (ITID-44722)
ITID-44723.severity: High by default, consistent with the sibling leaves.
ITID-44723.priority: P1, pending reclassification to a more specific sibling ITID once analysis completes.
ITID-44723.escalation: Escalate to threat intelligence and executive leadership for full characterization; reclassify once the specific pattern is confirmed.
indicators: C2 activity attributed to an espionage-motivated actor, specific pattern not yet characterized
vectors: Any espionage-motivated C2 technique not yet mapped to a specific sibling leaf
rootCauses: Detection captured behavior before full analysis of the espionage C2's specific pattern was complete
controls: Threat-intel-informed behavioral detection consistent with the sibling leaves
ITID-44723.detection: Varies; use as an interim classification during active analysis.
ITID-44723.response: Complete characterization of the espionage C2 pattern and reclassify to a specific sibling ITID where applicable.
metrics: Count of incidents initially filed here later reclassified
ITID-44723.notes: Use sparingly; prefer ITID-44721 or ITID-44722 whenever the specific pattern is known.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Espionage C2
playbook.description: A host is communicating with C2 infrastructure associated with a suspected espionage operation that does not fit a more specific espionage-C2 subtype, warranting full incident-response engagement given the likely targeted nature of the activity.

steps.title: Confirm espionage characteristics of the C2 activity
steps.desc: Analyze the C2 traffic pattern, targeting, and any threat intelligence attribution to assess whether this reflects a targeted espionage operation rather than commodity malware.
steps.guidance: Look for indicators such as low-volume/stealthy beaconing, targeted data-of-interest access, or attribution to known espionage-focused threat actor groups.
steps.outcome: A documented assessment supporting an espionage classification, with any available actor attribution.
steps.abort: If evidence instead points to commodity/opportunistic malware, redirect to the appropriate general C2 playbook.

steps.title: Execute a coordinated containment plan
steps.desc: Contain the threat deliberately, balancing evidence preservation against the risk of continued actor access, in coordination with the incident commander.
steps.outcome: A coordinated containment plan is executed without unnecessarily alerting a sophisticated actor.
steps.abort: If active exfiltration or destructive action is detected, move immediately to full containment.

steps.title: Remove the implant via full reimaging
steps.desc: Reimage affected hosts from known-good images given the likely sophistication of an espionage-focused actor.
steps.outcome: Hosts are rebuilt with no residual persistence.

steps.title: Restore operations with sustained heightened monitoring
steps.desc: Return remediated hosts to production with extended heightened monitoring.
steps.outcome: No recurrence of C2 activity during the extended monitoring window.

steps.title: Conduct full post-incident review with executive/legal stakeholders
steps.desc: Document the timeline, attribution assessment, and detection gaps, briefing executive leadership and legal on findings.
steps.outcome: A comprehensive incident report with organizational-level lessons captured.

steps.title: Reconstruct the intrusion timeline via forensic analysis
steps.desc: Perform forensic timeline reconstruction to establish initial access and the scope of data/systems accessed, given the likely extended dwell time typical of espionage operations.
steps.guidance: Engage digital forensics specialists; check extended log retention sources given possible long dwell time.
steps.outcome: A documented intrusion timeline and data-exposure assessment.

steps.title: Block the C2 infrastructure and isolate affected hosts
steps.desc: Block the C2 IP/domain and isolate all confirmed affected hosts.
steps.outcome: Active C2 communication is severed.

steps.title: Rotate potentially exposed credentials
steps.desc: Rotate credentials, tokens, and keys the actor may have harvested during their dwell time.
steps.outcome: All potentially compromised credentials are invalidated.

steps.title: Escalate to executive and legal leadership
steps.desc: Escalate to executive leadership and legal counsel given the likely targeted/nation-state nature of espionage activity and potential regulatory or diplomatic implications.
steps.outcome: Executive and legal stakeholders are briefed and engaged.

ITID-44731.def: A botnet C2 component consisting of a centralized server/panel through which the botnet operator issues commands (attack instructions, module updates, targeting lists) to and receives status from a large population of compromised bot hosts, functioning as the fleet-management and command-distribution layer of the botnet.
ITID-44731.purpose: Captures the centralized C2 panel infrastructure used to manage a large population of bots as a single controllable fleet.
scopeIncludes: Centralized panel/server issuing commands to a bot population and receiving status/results
C2 protocol supporting mass command distribution to thousands or millions of bots
Panel infrastructure used to sell/lease botnet access or capacity to third parties
scopeExcludes: The bot recruitment/infection mechanism itself, classified under ITID-317xx (Malicious Software domain)
Automated bot health/check-in reporting specifically (ITID-44732), a related but distinct C2 function
Peer-to-peer botnets with no centralized C2 server (classified under ITID-31713 in the Malicious Software domain, not this domain)
ITID-44731.severity: High; a functioning centralized C2 panel indicates an operational botnet capable of being weaponized for DDoS, credential attacks, or other mass-scale abuse at the operator's discretion.
ITID-44731.priority: P1 upon confirmation of active command issuance; P2 if the panel is identified but no active campaign is underway against the organization.
ITID-44731.escalation: Escalate to threat intelligence for sinkholing/takedown coordination and to network defense to block/quarantine any internal hosts confirmed as bots.
indicators: Internal host beaconing to a known or suspected botnet C2 panel
Outbound traffic matching a known botnet C2 protocol signature
Threat-intel reporting identifying the organization's IP space in a botnet's known bot population
vectors: Compromised hosts (via malware, IoT default credentials, or vulnerability exploitation) enrolled into the botnet and directed by the centralized panel
rootCauses: Unpatched or default-credentialed internet-facing devices vulnerable to bot recruitment
Insufficient egress monitoring to detect internal hosts beaconing to botnet C2 infrastructure
controls: Egress filtering/blocklisting of known botnet C2 infrastructure
Vulnerability/default-credential management for internet-facing devices to prevent bot recruitment
Threat-intel feed integration for botnet C2 indicator matching
ITID-44731.detection: Moderate to strong when threat-intel indicator feeds are integrated with egress monitoring; coverage is weaker for newly-stood-up or previously-unseen botnet infrastructure.
ITID-44731.response: Isolate confirmed bot hosts immediately, remediate the underlying vulnerability/credential issue that allowed recruitment, and report the C2 infrastructure to threat-intel/sinkholing partners.
metrics: Count of internal hosts confirmed as bots per incident
Mean time from beacon detection to host isolation
detections: Threat intel: match against known botnet C2 panel indicators
Network: beaconing to known botnet C2 infrastructure
ITID-44731.notes: Scoped strictly to the centralized C2/communications-infrastructure angle of botnets; cross-reference ITID-317xx (Malicious Software domain) for the recruitment/infection mechanism, which is classified separately.

playbook.name: Centralized Botnet C2 Panel for Mass Bot Management
playbook.description: A host is enrolled as a bot reporting to a centralized botnet C2 panel that manages a large fleet of compromised machines, meaning the organization's asset may have been used to attack third parties, creating reputational and legal exposure beyond standard remediation.

steps.title: Confirm bot enrollment and identify the botnet family/panel
steps.desc: Analyze the host's C2 traffic pattern (check-in structure, task-polling behavior) and attribute it to a known botnet family and C2 panel via threat intelligence.
steps.guidance: Botnet check-ins often include a bot-ID registration handshake distinct from single-target C2 — look for this pattern to confirm mass-bot enrollment versus a targeted implant.
steps.outcome: The botnet family and C2 panel are identified, with the host's role (e.g., DDoS bot, spam relay, proxy/residential-proxy node, cryptomining) determined.

steps.title: Isolate the bot host immediately
steps.desc: Quarantine the host via EDR/NAC to stop any ongoing participation in botnet-directed attacks against third parties.
steps.guidance: Prioritize speed here given the ongoing third-party harm risk while the host remains an active bot.
steps.outcome: The host can no longer participate in botnet-directed attacks or receive further tasking.

steps.title: Remove the bot implant and persistence mechanisms
steps.desc: Remove the malicious payload and all persistence mechanisms from the infected host.
steps.outcome: Host confirmed clean via EDR scan.

steps.title: Restore the host and monitor for re-enrollment
steps.desc: Return the remediated host to production with monitoring for any re-enrollment attempt to the same or a successor botnet panel.
steps.outcome: No recurrence of botnet check-in activity.

steps.title: Document the incident including reputational/legal outcome
steps.desc: Record the botnet family, third-party impact assessment, and any legal/communications actions taken in the incident report.
steps.outcome: Closed incident with lessons captured, including any process improvements for faster bot-enrollment detection.

steps.title: Determine whether the host has been used to attack third parties
steps.desc: Review outbound traffic logs for evidence that the host has participated in attacks against external targets (DDoS traffic, spam sending, credential-stuffing, proxying malicious traffic) rather than only receiving inbound tasking.
steps.guidance: This determination directly affects legal/reputational exposure — check outbound connection volume/pattern spikes and any external abuse complaints received by the organization referencing this host's IP.
steps.outcome: A documented assessment of whether and how the host was used against third parties, with supporting evidence.

steps.title: Block the botnet C2 panel infrastructure
steps.desc: Block the C2 panel's IP/domain at the perimeter and scope for any other internal hosts checking in to the same panel.
steps.outcome: No further internal hosts can enroll in or receive tasking from the botnet.

steps.title: Report the botnet panel to relevant takedown coordination bodies
steps.desc: Report the identified C2 panel to law enforcement, industry ISAC, or takedown coordination groups given the mass-victim nature of botnet infrastructure.
steps.outcome: The report contributes to broader botnet disruption efforts.

steps.title: Escalate to legal for reputational/liability assessment if outbound attack activity is confirmed
steps.desc: If evidence shows the host attacked or was used against third parties, escalate to legal counsel and communications/PR to assess liability exposure and any obligation to notify affected third parties or authorities.
steps.outcome: Legal and communications stakeholders are briefed and any external notification obligations are identified.
steps.abort: If no third-party attack activity is found, this step can be skipped and standard remediation followed.

ITID-44732.def: A botnet C2 component in which infected bots periodically report health/status telemetry (uptime, resource availability, network conditions) back to the C2 infrastructure, allowing the operator to maintain an accurate real-time inventory of available bot capacity distinct from the general command-distribution function of the centralized panel.
ITID-44732.purpose: Captures the C2 sub-mechanism by which a botnet automatically monitors bot health and check-in status to maintain an accurate, actionable fleet inventory.
scopeIncludes: Bot check-in traffic reporting host status/health metrics used to maintain fleet inventory
Automated culling/re-enrollment logic that removes non-responsive bots or attempts re-infection
Dashboard/reporting layer within the C2 panel summarizing live bot population health
scopeExcludes: The centralized command-issuance/panel infrastructure generally (ITID-44731)
The bot recruitment/infection mechanism itself, classified under ITID-317xx (Malicious Software domain)
ITID-44732.severity: High; consistent with the broader botnet C2 sibling group, since this function directly supports the operator's ability to reliably weaponize the botnet.
ITID-44732.priority: P1 upon confirmation of active check-in reporting from internal hosts.
ITID-44732.escalation: Escalate to network defense for host isolation and to threat intelligence for sinkholing/takedown coordination.
indicators: Recurring low-content health/status beacon traffic distinct from command-retrieval traffic, from the same host
Beacon payload structure consistent with telemetry reporting (uptime, resource metrics) rather than command execution
vectors: Bot client software includes a built-in health-check-in routine separate from its command-polling routine
rootCauses: Insufficient egress monitoring to distinguish low-volume health-check-in beacons from normal background traffic
controls: Egress filtering/blocklisting of known botnet C2 infrastructure
Behavioral analytics distinguishing health-check-in beacon patterns from normal traffic
ITID-44732.detection: Moderate; health-check-in beacons are typically low-volume and can blend with background traffic without dedicated behavioral analytics.
ITID-44732.response: Isolate confirmed bot hosts and remediate the underlying infection consistent with standard botnet remediation; the health-check-in mechanism itself does not require separate handling beyond confirming host compromise.
metrics: Count of internal hosts confirmed reporting health/check-in telemetry to botnet C2
detections: Behavioral analytics: low-content periodic beacon consistent with health/status reporting
ITID-44732.notes: Distinguishes from ITID-44731 by function: this leaf is specifically about health/check-in telemetry, not general command issuance.

playbook.name: Botnet C2 with Automated Bot Health/Check-in Reporting
playbook.description: The host performs regular automated health/check-in reports to a botnet C2 (uptime, resource availability, capability metadata) used by the operator to maintain and monetize the bot fleet, indicating the host has been an active, sustained participant in someone else's botnet.

steps.title: Confirm the check-in protocol and botnet family
steps.desc: Analyze the structured check-in traffic (fields such as uptime, bandwidth, OS/hardware metadata) to confirm it matches a known botnet health-reporting protocol and attribute it to a family via threat intelligence.
steps.outcome: The botnet family and check-in protocol are identified, along with how long this host has been reporting (via consistent check-in history in logs).

steps.title: Isolate the bot host
steps.desc: Quarantine the host via EDR/NAC to stop further check-ins and any pending tasking.
steps.outcome: The host can no longer report to or receive instructions from the botnet C2.

steps.title: Remove the bot implant and persistence mechanisms
steps.desc: Remove the malicious payload and persistence from all confirmed bot hosts.
steps.outcome: Hosts confirmed clean via EDR scan.

steps.title: Restore hosts and monitor for re-enrollment
steps.desc: Return remediated hosts to production with monitoring for renewed check-in attempts.
steps.outcome: No recurrence of check-in activity.

steps.title: Document the incident and any legal/reputational outcome
steps.desc: Record the botnet family, dwell time, and impact assessment; evaluate detection gaps that allowed sustained undetected check-in activity.
steps.outcome: Closed incident with lessons captured for earlier detection of sustained bot check-in patterns.

steps.title: Determine the sustained dwell time and role in the botnet
steps.desc: Use the check-in history to establish how long the host has been part of the botnet and what capability/role it has been reporting (e.g., available for DDoS, proxy relay, resource for rent), since sustained participation increases the likelihood of third-party harm.
steps.outcome: A documented dwell-time timeline and role assessment.

steps.title: Block the botnet C2 infrastructure and scope other internal bots
steps.desc: Block the C2 IP/domain and search enterprise-wide for other hosts exhibiting the same check-in pattern.
steps.outcome: The full internal botnet footprint is contained.

steps.title: Assess third-party attack/reputational exposure
steps.desc: Review outbound traffic for evidence the host was actually tasked to attack or serve third parties (versus merely reporting availability without being used), to scope legal/reputational exposure.
steps.outcome: A documented assessment of third-party impact, escalated to legal if confirmed.

ITID-44733.def: A catch-all classification for botnet C2/communications-infrastructure activity where the specific mechanism (centralized command panel or automated health/check-in reporting) has not been identified, or does not match an existing sibling leaf.
ITID-44733.purpose: Intake bucket for a confirmed botnet C2 mechanism that does not fit the centralized-panel or health-check-in leaves.
scopeIncludes: Botnet C2 mechanisms pending further characterization
Botnet C2 patterns other than centralized-panel command issuance or health/check-in reporting
scopeExcludes: Centralized botnet C2 panel for mass bot management (ITID-44731)
Botnet C2 with automated bot health/check-in reporting (ITID-44732)
Peer-to-peer botnets with no centralized C2 (ITID-31713, Malicious Software domain)
ITID-44733.severity: High by default, consistent with the sibling leaves.
ITID-44733.priority: P1 upon confirmation of active bot C2 communication.
ITID-44733.escalation: Escalate to network defense and threat intelligence per standard botnet handling.
indicators: Confirmed bot C2 communication, specific mechanism not yet characterized
vectors: Any botnet C2 mechanism not yet mapped to a specific sibling leaf
rootCauses: Insufficient egress monitoring, consistent with the broader botnet C2 sibling group
controls: Egress filtering/blocklisting of known botnet C2 infrastructure
ITID-44733.detection: Varies by mechanism; use as an interim classification during active analysis.
ITID-44733.response: Identify the specific C2 mechanism and reclassify to a specific sibling ITID where possible; otherwise isolate and remediate per standard botnet handling.
metrics: Count of incidents initially filed here later reclassified
detections: Generic alert: botnet C2 communication detected
ITID-44733.notes: Use sparingly; prefer ITID-44731 or ITID-44732 whenever the specific mechanism is known.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Botnet C2
playbook.description: A host is enrolled in a botnet reporting to C2 infrastructure that does not fit a more specific botnet-C2 subtype, meaning the host may have been used against third parties in addition to requiring standard remediation.

steps.title: Confirm bot enrollment and botnet attribution
steps.desc: Analyze the host's C2 traffic to confirm botnet enrollment and attribute it to a known family via threat intelligence where possible.
steps.outcome: Botnet enrollment is confirmed with any available family attribution.
steps.abort: If the traffic does not match a mass-bot pattern, treat as standard targeted C2 instead.

steps.title: Isolate the bot host
steps.desc: Quarantine the host via EDR/NAC to stop participation in the botnet.
steps.outcome: The host can no longer receive tasking or attack third parties.

steps.title: Remove the bot implant
steps.desc: Remove the malicious payload and persistence mechanisms from the infected host.
steps.outcome: Host confirmed clean via EDR scan.

steps.title: Restore the host and monitor
steps.desc: Return the remediated host to production with monitoring for re-enrollment attempts.
steps.outcome: No recurrence of botnet check-in activity.

steps.title: Document the incident
steps.desc: Record the botnet indicators and any legal/reputational outcome in the incident report.
steps.outcome: Closed incident with indicators available for future detection.

steps.title: Assess whether the host was used to attack third parties
steps.desc: Review outbound traffic for evidence of participation in attacks against external targets, to scope reputational/legal exposure alongside standard remediation.
steps.outcome: A documented assessment of third-party impact, escalated to legal if confirmed.

steps.title: Block the botnet C2 infrastructure
steps.desc: Block the C2 IP/domain and scope for other internal hosts checking in.
steps.outcome: No further internal hosts can enroll or receive tasking.

steps.title: Verify no residual persistence remains
steps.desc: Re-scan the host for scheduled tasks, startup items, or registry run-keys the bot malware may have used for persistence.
steps.outcome: No residual persistence artifacts remain.

ITID-44741.def: A C2 technique in which a trusted internal party (employee, contractor) knowingly establishes or repurposes internal network infrastructure — a rogue access point, unauthorized VPN tunnel, or dual-homed device — to give an external adversary a relay point for C2 traffic that would otherwise be blocked at the perimeter, trading the insider's legitimate access for the adversary's benefit.
ITID-44741.purpose: Captures a malicious insider deliberately provisioning an internal network access point that an external adversary uses to relay C2 traffic into or out of the environment.
scopeIncludes: Insider standing up a rogue wireless access point or unauthorized VPN/tunnel bridging external C2 infrastructure to the internal network
Insider connecting a dual-homed device to bridge an isolated/segmented network segment for adversary C2 relay
Insider knowingly relaying C2 commands manually on the adversary's behalf using their own authorized access
scopeExcludes: Insider disabling security controls (e.g., firewall rules, EDR) to permit C2 traffic without providing a physical/network relay point (ITID-44742)
Unwitting insider action (e.g., falling for phishing) that incidentally enables C2 — that is an initial-access ITID, not insider-assisted C2
ITID-44741.severity: Critical; a knowing insider actively bridging network access for an external adversary represents one of the most severe C2 enablement scenarios, combining technical and trust-based compromise.
ITID-44741.priority: P1 immediately upon confirmation or credible suspicion.
ITID-44741.escalation: Escalate immediately to HR, legal, and executive leadership in parallel with technical IR, given the personnel/insider-threat dimension; involve law enforcement where criminal intent is suspected.
indicators: Unauthorized wireless access point or network bridge device discovered on the internal network
Network traffic showing an internal device relaying C2 sessions between an external destination and internal hosts with no legitimate business function
Insider's access/badge/VPN logs showing physical or remote presence correlated with the relay device's activation
vectors: Insider physically installs a rogue AP or bridge device in a facility
Insider establishes an unauthorized outbound VPN/tunnel from an authorized workstation
rootCauses: Insufficient network access control (802.1X/NAC) allowing unauthorized devices to join internal segments
Inadequate insider-threat monitoring/behavioral analytics on privileged or trusted personnel
controls: Network access control (802.1X/NAC) restricting device onboarding to authorized hardware
Rogue AP/wireless intrusion detection system
Insider-threat behavioral monitoring program
ITID-44741.detection: Moderate; wireless IDS and NAC provide strong technical detection of rogue devices, but detecting the insider's intent typically requires correlation with HR/behavioral indicators beyond network telemetry alone.
ITID-44741.response: Physically locate and remove the rogue relay infrastructure, suspend the insider's access pending investigation, and coordinate with HR/legal/law enforcement before any confrontation.
metrics: Count of confirmed insider-provisioned C2 relay incidents
Mean time from rogue-device detection to removal
detections: Wireless IDS: rogue access point detected
ITID-44741.notes: Differentiates from ITID-44742 by mechanism: this leaf is about the insider providing a physical/network relay point, not disabling existing controls.

playbook.name: Insider Provisioning Internal Network Access Point for External C2 Relay
playbook.description: An insider has knowingly provisioned an internal network access point (e.g., a rogue device, exposed port, or VPN credential) that an external actor is using as an internal C2 relay, requiring HR/Legal-coordinated handling and evidence preservation before any account action.

steps.title: Confirm the internal relay and preserve evidence before any visible action
steps.desc: Identify the specific internal access point (device, port, VPN account) serving as the C2 relay, and preserve forensic evidence (logs, device state, access records) before taking any action that could alert the insider.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with HR and Legal before any account or device action per the organization's insider-threat playbook; premature action can compromise both the investigation and any subsequent employment/legal process.
steps.outcome: The relay point is identified and evidence is preserved in a forensically sound manner without tipping off the insider.

steps.title: Coordinate simultaneous access revocation and evidence capture
steps.desc: Once evidence is preserved and HR/Legal has approved action, simultaneously revoke the insider's relevant access and disable the rogue device/relay to prevent further external actor access while minimizing risk of evidence destruction.
steps.guidance: Timing coordination with HR/Legal/Security is critical — a delay risks continued external access, while premature action risks alerting the insider before evidence capture is complete.
steps.outcome: The external actor's access via the relay is cut off, and the insider's ability to interfere with the investigation is minimized.

steps.title: Remove the rogue access point and any external implants
steps.desc: Physically/logically remove the rogue device or access configuration, and remove any malware/implants the external actor deployed via the relay.
steps.outcome: The relay mechanism and any associated implants are fully removed.

steps.title: Restore normal operations and complete the HR/Legal process
steps.desc: Restore affected systems to normal operation and complete the HR/Legal disciplinary or legal process regarding the insider, with security monitoring confirming no residual external access.
steps.outcome: Normal operations resume with the insider matter resolved through the appropriate HR/Legal channel.

steps.title: Document the incident and review access provisioning controls
steps.desc: Record the incident timeline, insider-threat handling outcome, and evaluate whether access provisioning/monitoring controls need strengthening to prevent recurrence.
steps.outcome: Closed incident with process improvements identified for both technical controls and insider-threat handling procedures.

steps.title: Identify the insider and assess intent versus negligence
steps.desc: Determine the identity of the individual who provisioned the access point and gather evidence on whether the action was knowing/malicious versus negligent (e.g., misconfigured personal device, social-engineered into installing remote access), which affects both response and disciplinary/legal path.
steps.guidance: Work with HR/Legal to review access logs, communications (where legally permissible), and interview planning; do not conduct interviews without HR/Legal involvement.
steps.outcome: An evidence-based assessment of insider intent is documented for the HR/Legal-led process.

steps.title: Block the external C2 infrastructure
steps.desc: Block the external actor's C2 IP/domain at the perimeter.
steps.outcome: The external actor can no longer reach the internal relay point.

steps.title: Scope the external C2 infrastructure and extent of access gained
steps.desc: Determine what the external actor accessed via the insider-provisioned relay and identify the associated C2 infrastructure.
steps.outcome: A documented scope of external actor access and the associated C2 indicators.

ITID-44742.def: A C2 technique in which a trusted internal party with legitimate administrative access knowingly modifies, disables, or creates exceptions in firewall rules, EDR/AV configuration, proxy policy, or logging so that an external adversary's C2 traffic passes through existing security infrastructure undetected or unblocked.
ITID-44742.purpose: Captures a malicious insider deliberately disabling or weakening existing security controls to permit C2 traffic that would otherwise be blocked or detected.
scopeIncludes: Insider adding a firewall/proxy allow-rule or exception specifically enabling C2 traffic to a known adversary destination
Insider disabling or uninstalling EDR/AV on specific hosts to prevent C2 implant detection
Insider disabling or truncating logging on relevant network/security devices to reduce C2 traffic visibility
scopeExcludes: Insider providing a physical/network relay point without directly disabling existing controls (ITID-44741)
Unintentional misconfiguration by an administrator with no malicious intent (a configuration-error ITID outside the insider-threat context)
ITID-44742.severity: Critical; deliberate control disablement by a privileged insider removes the organization's primary detection/prevention layer for the associated C2 activity.
ITID-44742.priority: P1 immediately upon confirmation or credible suspicion.
ITID-44742.escalation: Escalate immediately to HR, legal, and executive leadership in parallel with technical IR; involve law enforcement where criminal intent is suspected; treat all changes made by the insider's credentials as untrusted pending full audit.
indicators: Firewall/proxy rule change logs showing an undocumented allow-rule or exception created outside change management
EDR/AV service stopped, uninstalled, or tampered with on specific hosts by an administrative account
Logging configuration change reducing retention/verbosity on security infrastructure, correlated with a specific administrator's session
vectors: Insider with firewall/proxy administrative access creates a covert allow-rule
Insider with endpoint administrative rights disables or uninstalls EDR/AV on targeted hosts
rootCauses: Insufficient change-management controls (peer review, approval workflow) on security-control configuration changes
Lack of tamper-protection or out-of-band monitoring on EDR/AV and logging infrastructure itself
controls: Change-management approval workflow for security-control configuration changes, with peer review
Tamper-protection on EDR/AV agents preventing local disablement even by administrative accounts
Out-of-band/immutable logging independent of the primary security infrastructure
ITID-44742.detection: Moderate to strong when configuration-change auditing and EDR tamper-protection alerting are in place; weak where administrative changes are not independently reviewed or alerted on.
ITID-44742.response: Revert the unauthorized control changes immediately, audit all other changes made under the same credentials, suspend the insider's access pending investigation, and coordinate with HR/legal/law enforcement.
metrics: Count of confirmed insider control-disablement incidents
Mean time from unauthorized change to detection/reversion
detections: Firewall/proxy change-audit alert: undocumented rule modification
ITID-44742.notes: Differentiates from ITID-44741 by mechanism: this leaf is about disabling/weakening existing controls, not standing up a new relay point.

playbook.name: Insider Disabling Security Controls to Enable C2 Traffic
playbook.description: An insider with legitimate administrative access has knowingly disabled or weakened security controls (firewall rules, EDR agents, logging) to allow an external actor's C2 traffic through undetected, requiring HR/Legal-coordinated handling and evidence preservation before any account action.

steps.title: Identify the disabled/weakened control and preserve evidence before visible action
steps.desc: Determine exactly which security control was disabled or modified (firewall rule, EDR agent, logging pipeline) and when, preserving configuration-change logs and audit trails before taking any action that could alert the insider.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with HR and Legal before any account or configuration action per the insider-threat playbook; capture change-management/administrative audit logs showing who made the change and when.
steps.outcome: The specific control change is identified and evidence is preserved in a forensically sound manner.

steps.title: Restore the disabled security control immediately
steps.desc: Re-enable or restore the disabled/weakened security control to its correct configuration, closing the gap the insider created.
steps.guidance: Verify the restored configuration against a known-good baseline rather than trusting the insider's own historical configuration, in case other changes were also made.
steps.outcome: The security control gap is closed and future C2 traffic through this path is blocked.

steps.title: Remove any implants deployed during the exposure window
steps.desc: Identify and remove any malware or unauthorized access mechanisms the external actor deployed while the security control was disabled.
steps.outcome: All implants deployed during the exposure window are removed.

steps.title: Restore normal operations and complete the HR/Legal process
steps.desc: Confirm all security controls are fully restored and verified against baseline, and complete the HR/Legal disciplinary or legal process regarding the insider.
steps.outcome: Normal security posture is confirmed restored and the insider matter is resolved through the appropriate HR/Legal channel.

steps.title: Document the incident and strengthen change-control safeguards
steps.desc: Record the incident timeline and evaluate whether change-management controls (e.g., dual-approval for security control changes, tamper alerting) need strengthening to prevent recurrence.
steps.outcome: Closed incident with process improvements identified for both technical change controls and insider-threat handling procedures.

steps.title: Identify the insider and assess intent versus error
steps.desc: Determine the administrator responsible for the change and gather evidence on whether it was a knowing, malicious act versus an operational error or social-engineered action, working with HR/Legal on the investigative approach.
steps.guidance: Do not conduct interviews or confront the individual without HR/Legal involvement and approval.
steps.outcome: An evidence-based assessment of insider intent is documented for the HR/Legal-led process.

steps.title: Coordinate access revocation with HR/Legal timing
steps.desc: Once evidence is preserved and HR/Legal has approved action, revoke the insider's administrative access to prevent further control tampering or evidence interference.
steps.guidance: Time this precisely with HR/Legal to avoid tipping off the insider before evidence capture is complete.
steps.outcome: The insider can no longer modify security controls or interfere with the investigation.

steps.title: Scope the external C2 activity enabled by the control gap
steps.desc: Determine what C2 traffic and external actor access was enabled during the window the control was disabled, and identify associated C2 infrastructure and affected hosts.
steps.guidance: Reconstruct the exposure window precisely using the configuration-change timestamp as the starting point for the hunt.
steps.outcome: A documented scope of external actor access and affected systems during the exposure window.

steps.title: Block the external C2 infrastructure
steps.desc: Block the external actor's C2 IP/domain at the perimeter now that visibility/controls are restored.
steps.outcome: The external actor's C2 channel is severed.

ITID-44743.def: A catch-all classification for insider-assisted C2 activity where the specific mechanism (provisioning a network relay point or disabling existing security controls) has not been identified, or does not match an existing sibling leaf.
ITID-44743.purpose: Intake bucket for a confirmed insider-assisted C2 mechanism that does not fit the relay-provisioning or control-disablement leaves.
scopeIncludes: Insider-assisted C2 mechanisms pending further characterization
Insider-assisted C2 patterns other than relay provisioning or control disablement
scopeExcludes: Insider provisioning internal network access point for external C2 relay (ITID-44741)
Insider disabling security controls to enable C2 traffic (ITID-44742)
ITID-44743.severity: Critical by default, consistent with the sibling leaves.
ITID-44743.priority: P1 immediately upon confirmation or credible suspicion.
ITID-44743.escalation: Escalate immediately to HR, legal, and executive leadership per standard insider-threat handling.
indicators: Confirmed or suspected insider involvement in enabling C2 activity, specific mechanism not yet characterized
vectors: Any insider-assisted C2 mechanism not yet mapped to a specific sibling leaf
rootCauses: Insufficient insider-threat monitoring, consistent with the broader sibling group
controls: Insider-threat behavioral monitoring program consistent with the sibling leaves
ITID-44743.detection: Varies by mechanism; use as an interim classification during active analysis.
ITID-44743.response: Identify the specific insider-assisted mechanism and reclassify to a specific sibling ITID where possible.
metrics: Count of incidents initially filed here later reclassified
detections: Generic alert: suspected insider-assisted C2 activity
ITID-44743.notes: Use sparingly; prefer ITID-44741 or ITID-44742 whenever the specific mechanism is known.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Insider-Assisted C2
playbook.description: An insider has provided some form of assistance (access, information, or action) enabling an external actor's C2 channel that does not fit a more specific insider-assisted C2 subtype, requiring HR/Legal-coordinated handling and evidence preservation before any account action.

steps.title: Identify the nature of insider assistance and preserve evidence
steps.desc: Determine what form of insider assistance enabled the C2 channel (information disclosure, access provisioning, control tampering, or other) and preserve relevant logs/records before taking any visible action.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with HR and Legal before any account or system action; document findings in a forensically sound manner.
steps.outcome: The nature and mechanism of insider assistance is documented with preserved evidence.

steps.title: Coordinate access revocation and control restoration with HR/Legal timing
steps.desc: Once evidence is preserved and HR/Legal approves, revoke relevant insider access and restore/close whatever mechanism enabled the C2 channel.
steps.guidance: Time actions carefully to avoid alerting the insider prematurely while minimizing continued external exposure.
steps.outcome: The insider-enabled pathway is closed and further external actor access is prevented.

steps.title: Remove any implants or unauthorized access mechanisms
steps.desc: Identify and remove any malware or unauthorized access the external actor established via the insider-enabled pathway.
steps.outcome: All external actor footholds are removed.

steps.title: Restore operations and complete the HR/Legal process
steps.desc: Restore affected systems to normal operation and complete the HR/Legal disciplinary or legal process regarding the insider.
steps.outcome: Normal operations resume with the insider matter resolved through the appropriate channel.

steps.title: Document the incident and review relevant controls
steps.desc: Record the incident timeline and evaluate whether access, monitoring, or change-control processes need strengthening to prevent recurrence.
steps.outcome: Closed incident with process improvements identified.

steps.title: Identify the insider and assess intent
steps.desc: Determine the individual involved and assess, with HR/Legal, whether the assistance was knowing/malicious versus negligent or coerced.
steps.guidance: Do not interview or confront the individual without HR/Legal approval and involvement.
steps.outcome: An evidence-based assessment of insider intent is documented for the HR/Legal-led process.

steps.title: Block the external C2 infrastructure
steps.desc: Block the external actor's C2 IP/domain at the perimeter.
steps.outcome: The external actor's C2 channel is severed.

steps.title: Scope the external C2 activity and access gained
steps.desc: Determine the C2 infrastructure involved and what access/data the external actor obtained as a result of the insider assistance.
steps.outcome: A documented scope of external actor access and associated indicators.

ITID-44811.def: A cloud-hosted C2 technique in which the adversary provisions short-lived virtual machine instances from a public cloud provider, using each instance for only a brief operational window before terminating it and standing up a replacement with a new IP address, so that IP-based blocklisting and reputation systems cannot keep pace with the rotation cadence.
ITID-44811.purpose: Captures C2 infrastructure hosted on cloud virtual machines that are deliberately and frequently rotated/re-provisioned to defeat IP-reputation and blocklisting defenses.
scopeIncludes: C2 traffic to a cloud-provider IP range that changes association with the same implant family on a frequent (hours-to-days) cadence
Automated infrastructure-as-code tooling used by the adversary to stand up and tear down C2 VMs on a schedule
Use of multiple cloud regions/providers in rotation to further defeat blocklisting
scopeExcludes: C2 hosted on an auto-scaling group specifically to blend with legitimate application instances rather than primarily to rotate IPs (ITID-44812)
Traditional bulletproof-hosting C2 infrastructure with no cloud-specific ephemeral-instance rotation
ITID-44811.severity: Medium-High; the technique reflects deliberate infrastructure agility and materially reduces the shelf-life of IP-based blocklisting.
ITID-44811.priority: P2, escalating to P1 once active command execution against the organization is confirmed.
ITID-44811.escalation: Escalate to threat intelligence to shift from IP-blocklisting to domain/certificate/behavioral-indicator-based detection, since IP indicators will have a very short useful life against this technique.
indicators: C2 destination IP changing every check-in cycle while other implant behavioral characteristics remain constant
Cloud-provider ASN/IP-range churn associated with the same C2 domain or certificate fingerprint
Threat-intel reporting a high rate of infrastructure turnover for the associated campaign
vectors: Adversary uses cloud provider APIs/CLI or infrastructure-as-code templates to automate rapid VM provisioning and teardown for C2 hosting
rootCauses: Detection relies primarily on IP-reputation/blocklisting with insufficient domain- or certificate-based correlation
Cloud egress traffic broadly allow-listed by IP range/ASN rather than validated by destination behavior
controls: Domain/certificate-fingerprint-based detection layered over IP-reputation blocklisting
Cloud-provider abuse reporting pipeline for rapid takedown requests
Behavioral (protocol/traffic-pattern) detection independent of destination IP
ITID-44811.detection: Weak for IP-based blocklisting alone given the rotation cadence; moderate to strong when domain/certificate-fingerprint or behavioral detection is layered in.
ITID-44811.response: Pivot detection to domain/certificate/behavioral indicators rather than relying on the specific IP observed; file abuse reports with the cloud provider promptly, understanding the instance will likely already be terminated.
metrics: Mean IP-rotation interval observed per confirmed campaign
Count of cloud-provider abuse reports filed
detections: Behavioral C2 detection independent of destination IP reputation
ITID-44811.notes: Differentiates from ITID-44812 by primary purpose: this leaf is about IP-rotation cadence to defeat blocklisting, not blending with legitimate auto-scaled application traffic.

playbook.name: Ephemeral Cloud VM Rotated Frequently to Evade IP-Based Blocklisting
playbook.description: Attacker C2 infrastructure runs on short-lived cloud VM instances that are spun up, used briefly, and torn down or replaced with a new IP, defeating traditional IP-reputation-based blocking and requiring cloud-native audit log analysis to track.

steps.title: Correlate beaconing against cloud provider IP churn via CloudTrail-equivalent logs
steps.desc: Analyze internal connection logs alongside cloud provider audit/billing logs (CloudTrail, Azure Activity Log, GCP Audit Logs — either the org's own if the attacker used the org's cloud account, or external cloud IP range attribution) to identify the pattern of short-lived VM instances serving as C2.
steps.guidance: If the ephemeral VM is in the organization's own cloud tenant (attacker pivoted internally), pull CloudTrail/Activity Log records for instance launch/termination events correlated with the malicious IP's active window; if externally hosted, rely on passive DNS/IP-lifecycle threat intel instead.
steps.outcome: The ephemeral VM pattern is confirmed and, where the resource is in the org's own cloud account, the specific instance launch event and launching identity are identified.
steps.abort: If the churn is explained by legitimate auto-scaling of a known business service, close as false positive.
steps.tool: CloudTrail / Azure Activity Log / GCP Audit Logs

steps.title: Block on the stable indicator, not the rotating IP
steps.desc: Apply blocking based on the stable domain/TLS fingerprint/behavioral indicator identified during identification, since IP-only blocking will lag behind the rotation.
steps.outcome: C2 traffic is blocked regardless of which ephemeral IP is currently active.
steps.tool: Secure web gateway / IDS with fingerprint matching

steps.title: Redeploy any affected cloud resources from known-good images
steps.desc: Rather than attempting in-place cleanup of any organization-owned cloud compute that was compromised or used to launch the ephemeral VMs, redeploy from a known-good image/IaC template.
steps.guidance: Standard cloud-native IR practice favors redeployment over in-place remediation given the difficulty of fully verifying a compromised cloud resource's integrity.
steps.outcome: Affected cloud resources are running from clean, verified images.

steps.title: Restore operations and monitor for new ephemeral infrastructure
steps.desc: Return remediated hosts/cloud resources to production with monitoring for the stable indicator across any newly spun-up ephemeral VMs.
steps.outcome: No recurrence of C2 activity within the monitoring window.

steps.title: Document the ephemeral-VM evasion technique
steps.desc: Record the technique, stable indicators identified, and any cloud credential compromise details in the threat intel platform, and evaluate whether cloud IAM least-privilege controls need tightening.
steps.outcome: Updated detection guidance and, where relevant, cloud security posture improvements.

steps.title: Identify the beacon/domain pattern independent of the rotating IP
steps.desc: Since IPs rotate quickly, identify a stable indicator (domain name, JA3/TLS fingerprint, URI pattern, or malware check-in structure) that persists across VM rotations for more durable detection and blocking.
steps.outcome: A stable, rotation-independent indicator is identified for blocking and hunting.

steps.title: Revoke any compromised cloud credentials and isolate the compute resource
steps.desc: If the ephemeral VM runs in the organization's own cloud account, immediately revoke the credentials/access key that launched it and isolate or terminate the instance's network access (security group/NSG lockdown) rather than waiting for it to be torn down naturally.
steps.outcome: The compromised cloud account access is revoked and the instance is network-isolated.

steps.title: Remove the malware implant from internal hosts
steps.desc: Remove the malicious payload responsible for communicating with the ephemeral C2 infrastructure from all confirmed internal hosts.
steps.outcome: Hosts confirmed clean.

steps.title: Scope internal hosts and, if applicable, the compromised cloud account
steps.desc: Determine all internal hosts communicating with the ephemeral C2 infrastructure, and if the VMs are running in the organization's own cloud account, determine how that account/credential was obtained.
steps.outcome: Full scope of affected hosts and, where relevant, the compromised cloud credential/account is identified.

steps.title: Isolate infected internal hosts
steps.desc: Quarantine internal hosts confirmed to be communicating with the ephemeral C2 infrastructure.
steps.outcome: Active C2 sessions are severed.

ITID-44812.def: A cloud-hosted C2 technique in which the adversary places a malicious instance inside (or mimics the configuration of) an auto-scaling group belonging to a compromised cloud account, so that the malicious instance shares the IP range, tagging, security-group membership, and traffic patterns of legitimate application instances, making it difficult to distinguish from normal infrastructure scaling activity.
ITID-44812.purpose: Captures C2 infrastructure deliberately hosted within a legitimate auto-scaling group so that malicious instances blend administratively and network-wise with the organization's own or a partner's legitimate application instances.
scopeIncludes: Malicious instance launched within a compromised account's existing auto-scaling group configuration
C2 traffic blending with legitimate application traffic due to shared security-group/network placement
Adversary tagging/naming the malicious instance to match the legitimate fleet's naming convention
scopeExcludes: Ephemeral standalone VM rotation primarily to defeat IP blocklisting, without blending into an existing legitimate fleet (ITID-44811)
Compromise of the auto-scaling/orchestration control plane itself for purposes other than C2 hosting (an infrastructure-compromise ITID outside this domain)
ITID-44812.severity: High; blending within a legitimate fleet indicates cloud-account-level compromise and significantly increases the difficulty of instance-level detection.
ITID-44812.priority: P1 upon confirmation, given the implication of underlying cloud account/control-plane compromise.
ITID-44812.escalation: Escalate to cloud security and IR immediately; treat the entire auto-scaling group and its associated cloud account credentials as potentially compromised, not just the identified malicious instance.
indicators: An instance within a known auto-scaling group exhibiting network behavior inconsistent with the application's expected function
Instance launch outside the auto-scaling group's normal scaling trigger/schedule
Cloud API audit logs showing manual instance launch or scaling-policy modification inconsistent with legitimate operations
vectors: Adversary compromises cloud account credentials with permissions to launch instances into an existing auto-scaling group
Adversary modifies a launch template/configuration to include malicious startup logic
rootCauses: Overly permissive cloud IAM roles allowing instance launch/configuration changes without sufficient approval controls
Insufficient per-instance behavioral baselining within auto-scaling groups
controls: Cloud IAM least-privilege enforcement on instance launch/scaling-policy permissions
Cloud API audit logging (e.g., CloudTrail) with alerting on scaling-policy or launch-template modification
Per-instance behavioral baselining within auto-scaling groups to flag outliers
ITID-44812.detection: Moderate; cloud API audit logs provide strong evidence once reviewed, but per-instance behavioral anomaly detection within a large auto-scaling fleet requires dedicated cloud-security tooling.
ITID-44812.response: Treat as a cloud account compromise: rotate all associated credentials, audit the full auto-scaling group and launch configuration history, and isolate/terminate the malicious instance while preserving forensic evidence.
metrics: Count of confirmed auto-scaling-group C2 blending incidents
Mean time from anomalous instance detection to cloud credential rotation
detections: Cloud audit log: launch-template/scaling-policy modification alert
Cloud-native behavioral anomaly: outlier instance within an auto-scaling group
ITID-44812.notes: Differentiates from ITID-44811 by primary purpose: this leaf is about blending with a legitimate fleet, not rapid IP rotation across standalone instances.

playbook.name: C2 Hosted on Auto-Scaling Group Blending with Legitimate Application Instances
playbook.description: C2 infrastructure is deployed within a cloud auto-scaling group alongside (or disguised as) the organization's own legitimate application instances, exploiting shared IP ranges and trust to evade detection.

steps.title: Identify the rogue instance within the auto-scaling group via cloud audit logs
steps.desc: Review CloudTrail/Activity Log/Audit Log records for the auto-scaling group to identify an instance launched outside the expected IaC/deployment pipeline or with anomalous configuration (unexpected AMI/image, unusual launch identity, off-schedule launch time).
steps.guidance: Compare launch template/configuration hashes of all instances in the group against the approved baseline to spot the anomalous one.
steps.outcome: The specific rogue instance is identified and distinguished from legitimate application instances in the same group.
steps.abort: If all instances match the approved baseline, the C2 activity may be occurring via a compromised legitimate instance rather than a rogue one — pivot to investigating application-level compromise instead.
steps.tool: CloudTrail / Azure Activity Log / GCP Audit Logs

steps.title: Isolate the rogue instance without disrupting the legitimate scaling group
steps.desc: Remove the specific rogue instance from the auto-scaling group and quarantine it (security group lockdown) for forensic analysis, while leaving legitimate instances in service.
steps.guidance: Use targeted instance-level isolation rather than pausing or destroying the entire auto-scaling group, to preserve application availability.
steps.outcome: The rogue instance is isolated without impacting the legitimate application's availability.

steps.title: Redeploy the auto-scaling group from a verified known-good image/template
steps.desc: Update the launch template/IaC definition to a verified known-good baseline and force a rolling redeployment of all instances in the group, rather than attempting to individually verify each existing instance.
steps.guidance: Standard cloud-native IR practice favors full redeployment from a trusted baseline over in-place verification of a potentially tampered fleet.
steps.outcome: All instances in the auto-scaling group are running from a verified clean baseline.

steps.title: Restore normal scaling operations and monitor
steps.desc: Confirm the auto-scaling group is operating normally with only verified instances, and monitor for any further anomalous launch events.
steps.outcome: The auto-scaling group operates normally with no recurrence of rogue instance launches.

steps.title: Document the technique and strengthen pipeline/IaC controls
steps.desc: Record the introduction vector and recommend controls such as launch template drift detection, signed AMIs, or stricter CI/CD credential scoping to prevent recurrence.
steps.outcome: Improved cloud deployment security posture and updated detection for launch-template drift.

steps.title: Determine how the rogue instance was introduced
steps.desc: Investigate the launch event's originating identity/credential and the CI/CD or IaC pipeline to determine how the rogue instance was introduced into the trusted auto-scaling group (compromised pipeline credentials, direct API access via stolen keys, or a vulnerable application allowing self-scaling abuse).
steps.outcome: The introduction vector is identified, informing which credentials/pipeline stages require remediation.
steps.tool: CI/CD pipeline logs / cloud IAM logs

steps.title: Revoke the compromised credential/pipeline access used to introduce the instance
steps.desc: Revoke or rotate the specific credential, API key, or CI/CD access that was used to launch the rogue instance.
steps.outcome: The attacker can no longer introduce additional rogue instances via the same access path.

steps.title: Rotate any secrets/keys the rogue instance may have accessed
steps.desc: Since the rogue instance shared network/IAM context with legitimate application instances, rotate any secrets, database credentials, or service tokens it may have had access to.
steps.outcome: All potentially exposed secrets are invalidated and replaced.

steps.title: Scope internal hosts communicating with the rogue instance
steps.desc: Determine which internal hosts have communicated with the rogue instance's IP/endpoint within the auto-scaling group's shared load balancer or IP range.
steps.outcome: A complete list of affected internal hosts.

ITID-44813.def: A catch-all classification for C2 hosted on cloud virtual machine infrastructure where the specific technique (rapid ephemeral rotation or auto-scaling-group blending) has not been identified, or does not match an existing sibling leaf.
ITID-44813.purpose: Intake bucket for a confirmed cloud VM-based C2 mechanism that does not fit the rapid-rotation or auto-scaling-blending leaves.
scopeIncludes: Cloud VM-based C2 mechanisms pending further characterization
Cloud VM-based C2 patterns other than rapid rotation or auto-scaling blending
scopeExcludes: Ephemeral cloud VM rotated frequently to evade IP-based blocklisting (ITID-44811)
C2 hosted on auto-scaling group blending with legitimate instances (ITID-44812)
ITID-44813.severity: Medium-High by default, consistent with the sibling leaves.
ITID-44813.priority: P2, pending reclassification to a more specific sibling ITID once analysis completes.
ITID-44813.escalation: Escalate to cloud security and threat intelligence for full characterization; reclassify once the specific technique is confirmed.
indicators: Confirmed cloud VM-hosted C2 activity, specific technique not yet characterized
vectors: Any cloud VM-based C2 technique not yet mapped to a specific sibling leaf
rootCauses: Insufficient cloud-native detection tooling, consistent with the broader sibling group
controls: Cloud-native detection and IAM controls consistent with the sibling leaves
ITID-44813.detection: Varies by mechanism; use as an interim classification during active analysis.
ITID-44813.response: Complete characterization of the cloud VM-based C2 mechanism and reclassify to a specific sibling ITID where applicable.
metrics: Count of incidents initially filed here later reclassified
detections: Generic alert: cloud VM-hosted C2 activity detected
ITID-44813.notes: Use sparingly; prefer ITID-44811 or ITID-44812 whenever the specific technique is known.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Cloud VM-Based C2
playbook.description: A host is communicating with C2 infrastructure hosted on a cloud virtual machine that does not fit a more specific cloud-VM-based C2 subtype.

steps.title: Confirm the cloud VM endpoint as malicious C2
steps.desc: Validate the suspicious cloud VM endpoint against threat intelligence and traffic behavior to confirm it is attacker-controlled C2.
steps.guidance: Where the VM is in the organization's own cloud account, check CloudTrail/Activity Log/Audit Log records for its launch context; where external, use IP/ASN attribution.
steps.outcome: The cloud VM endpoint is confirmed as malicious C2 with supporting evidence recorded.
steps.abort: If the endpoint matches approved business cloud usage, close as false positive.
steps.tool: Cloud audit logs / threat intel platform

steps.title: Block the specific cloud VM endpoint
steps.desc: Add the confirmed malicious cloud VM IP/hostname to proxy and firewall blocklists.
steps.outcome: Outbound connection to the C2 endpoint is blocked enterprise-wide.

steps.title: Redeploy any affected organization-owned cloud resources from known-good images
steps.desc: Where organization-owned cloud compute was compromised, redeploy from a verified known-good image rather than in-place cleaning.
steps.outcome: Affected cloud resources run from a clean, verified baseline.

steps.title: Restore hosts and monitor
steps.desc: Return remediated hosts/cloud resources to production with a monitoring watchlist for the endpoint and related indicators.
steps.outcome: No recurrence of C2 activity within the monitoring window.

steps.title: Document indicators and close the incident
steps.desc: Record the cloud VM endpoint, associated IOCs, and remediation actions in the incident report and threat intel platform.
steps.outcome: Closed incident with indicators available for future detection.

steps.title: Scope all hosts communicating with the cloud VM C2
steps.desc: Search logs enterprise-wide for the specific endpoint to determine full infection scope and timeline.
steps.outcome: A complete list of affected hosts and an infection timeline.

steps.title: Revoke any exposed cloud credentials and isolate compute resources
steps.desc: If the VM is in the organization's own cloud account, revoke the credentials that launched or accessed it and isolate the instance via security group lockdown.
steps.outcome: The compromised cloud resource is isolated and its access path revoked.
steps.abort: If the VM is external attacker-owned infrastructure with no organizational cloud account involvement, skip this step.

steps.title: Remove the malware implant from internal hosts
steps.desc: Remove the malicious payload responsible for the C2 beaconing from each infected internal host.
steps.outcome: Hosts confirmed clean.

steps.title: Isolate infected internal hosts
steps.desc: Quarantine confirmed infected endpoints via EDR/NAC to sever active C2 sessions.
steps.outcome: Infected hosts can no longer reach the C2 endpoint.

ITID-44821.def: A C2 technique in which the adversary deploys command relay logic as a serverless function (e.g., AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, Google Cloud Functions) invoked via its platform-provided HTTPS endpoint, so implant traffic terminates at a trusted cloud-provider domain with no persistent server to seize, block by IP, or forensically image in the traditional sense.
ITID-44821.purpose: Captures C2 relayed through a serverless (Function-as-a-Service) endpoint rather than a persistent VM, leveraging the platform's trusted domain and ephemeral execution model.
scopeIncludes: Implant check-in traffic to a serverless function's HTTPS invocation endpoint that relays commands to/from the true C2 backend
Serverless function used to proxy/obfuscate the true C2 destination behind a trusted platform domain
Adversary-controlled cloud account hosting the malicious function
scopeExcludes: C2 command queuing via a managed message queue/event bus service specifically (ITID-44822), a related but architecturally distinct mechanism
Traditional VM-hosted C2, including ephemeral/rotated instances (ITID-44811/44812)
ITID-44821.severity: High; serverless C2 is architecturally resistant to IP-based blocking and traditional server seizure, reflecting a sophisticated adversary.
ITID-44821.priority: P1 upon confirmation of active command relay.
ITID-44821.escalation: Escalate to threat intelligence and the cloud provider's abuse/trust-and-safety team promptly, since function-level takedown (not IP blocking) is the effective disruption path.
indicators: Implant traffic terminating at a serverless platform's function-invocation domain (e.g., *.lambda-url.*.on.aws, *.azurewebsites.net/api/*) with no corresponding legitimate application use
Function invocation logs (where accessible via threat intel or provider cooperation) showing a pattern consistent with C2 relay rather than a normal application workload
vectors: Adversary provisions a free-tier or low-cost cloud account specifically to host a relay function
Adversary compromises an existing cloud account and adds a malicious function alongside legitimate workloads
rootCauses: Egress filtering allow-lists entire cloud-provider domains/IP ranges for productivity reasons without per-endpoint validation
Limited security tooling visibility into serverless-specific traffic patterns
controls: Egress monitoring capable of distinguishing specific serverless-endpoint destinations rather than allow-listing entire provider domains
Threat-intel reporting pipeline to cloud provider trust-and-safety teams for function-level takedown
ITID-44821.detection: Weak with coarse domain-level allow-listing; moderate with granular URL/endpoint-level egress inspection and threat-intel indicator matching.
ITID-44821.response: Report the specific function endpoint to the cloud provider for takedown (IP blocking is ineffective against the shared serverless IP space), and pivot to endpoint containment on affected hosts.
metrics: Count of confirmed serverless-endpoint C2 incidents
Mean time from detection to provider takedown of the malicious function
detections: Egress inspection: serverless function-invocation endpoint with no legitimate application mapping
ITID-44821.notes: Differentiates from ITID-44822 by mechanism: this leaf is about direct HTTP invocation of a relay function, not asynchronous command queuing via a message/event service.

playbook.name: C2 Relay via Serverless Function Endpoint
playbook.description: Attackers are using a serverless function (e.g., a Lambda, Azure Function, or Cloud Function endpoint) as a C2 relay/proxy, exploiting the function's legitimate cloud-provider domain and pay-per-use ephemeral execution model to blend in and evade blocking.

steps.title: Identify the serverless function endpoint acting as a relay
steps.desc: Analyze proxy/firewall logs for connections to a cloud-provider-owned serverless function invocation URL, then check whether the function belongs to the organization's own cloud account (via CloudTrail/Activity Log/Audit Log) or is externally attacker-owned.
steps.guidance: Serverless C2 relays often show a distinctive URL pattern (e.g., *.lambda-url.*.on.aws, *.azurewebsites.net/api/*, *.cloudfunctions.net) — use this to distinguish from ordinary web traffic.
steps.outcome: The specific function endpoint is identified and its ownership (internal vs. external) is determined.
steps.abort: If the function matches an approved internal integration, close as false positive.

steps.title: Block the specific function endpoint
steps.desc: Apply a targeted block for the specific function invocation URL rather than the broader cloud provider domain, which hosts many unrelated legitimate functions.
steps.outcome: C2 traffic to the specific serverless relay is blocked while other legitimate serverless traffic is unaffected.

steps.title: Redeploy any affected serverless functions and rotate exposed keys
steps.desc: For any organization-owned serverless functions found to be compromised or abused, redeploy the function from source-controlled, verified code and rotate any API keys/secrets the function had access to, rather than attempting in-place remediation.
steps.guidance: Standard cloud-native IR practice for serverless compromise favors full redeployment and credential rotation over patching in place.
steps.outcome: Affected serverless resources are running clean code with rotated credentials.

steps.title: Restore operations and monitor for new serverless relays
steps.desc: Return remediated hosts/functions to production with monitoring for new serverless-endpoint C2 patterns.
steps.outcome: No recurrence of C2 activity within the monitoring window.

steps.title: Document the serverless relay technique
steps.desc: Record the technique and any cloud account compromise details in the threat intel platform, and evaluate whether serverless deployment permissions need tightening.
steps.outcome: Improved cloud security posture and detection guidance for serverless-relay C2.

steps.title: Review function invocation and execution logs for the relay pattern
steps.desc: If the function is in the organization's own account, pull its execution/invocation logs (CloudWatch Logs equivalent) to understand the relay's request/response pattern and what backend C2 it forwards to.
steps.outcome: The relay's forwarding destination (the true backend C2) is identified where the function is org-owned.
steps.abort: If the function is externally owned, rely on network-level indicators instead.
