steps.title: Disable or delete the organization-owned function and revoke its invocation permissions
steps.desc: If the function resides in the organization's own cloud account, immediately disable/delete it and revoke the IAM role/permissions it uses, and revoke the credential that deployed it.
steps.outcome: The malicious function can no longer be invoked or used as a relay.
steps.abort: If the function is externally owned, skip this step and rely on network blocking.

steps.title: Remove the malware implant from internal hosts
steps.desc: Remove the malicious payload responsible for using the serverless relay from all confirmed internal hosts.
steps.outcome: Hosts confirmed clean.

steps.title: Scope internal hosts communicating with the serverless relay
steps.desc: Search logs enterprise-wide for connections to the function endpoint to determine infection scope.
steps.outcome: A complete list of affected internal hosts.

steps.title: Isolate infected internal hosts
steps.desc: Quarantine internal hosts confirmed to be using the serverless relay for C2.
steps.outcome: Active C2 sessions are severed.

ITID-44822.def: A C2 technique in which the adversary uses a managed cloud messaging service (e.g., AWS SQS/SNS, Azure Service Bus/Event Grid, Google Pub/Sub) as an asynchronous command-and-control channel: the implant polls or subscribes to a queue/topic for commands and publishes results back, so that C2 traffic is indistinguishable in transport from legitimate use of the same managed service and inherits the service's trusted domain and TLS certificate.
ITID-44822.purpose: Captures C2 command distribution via a managed cloud message queue or event bus service, using the platform as an asynchronous, trusted-domain command channel.
scopeIncludes: Implant polling a cloud message queue/topic for commands published by the adversary
Implant publishing exfiltrated data or command results to a queue/topic monitored by the adversary
Adversary-controlled or compromised cloud account hosting the queue/topic infrastructure
scopeExcludes: Direct HTTP invocation of a serverless function endpoint for command relay (ITID-44821), an architecturally distinct mechanism
Legitimate application use of the same messaging services with no C2 relationship
ITID-44822.severity: High; use of a managed message queue for C2 reflects deliberate abuse of a trusted, asynchronous, and typically well-monitored-by-reputation cloud service.
ITID-44822.priority: P1 upon confirmation of active command exchange via the queue/topic.
ITID-44822.escalation: Escalate to threat intelligence and the cloud provider promptly for account-level investigation and takedown, since the underlying queue/topic may span multiple compromised victims.
indicators: Implant traffic authenticating to and polling a cloud messaging service endpoint with no corresponding legitimate application
Cloud account audit logs showing queue/topic creation and message publish/consume activity inconsistent with normal application use
Credentials for the messaging service embedded in implant configuration
vectors: Adversary provisions a cloud account with a message queue/topic and embeds its access credentials in the implant
Adversary compromises an existing cloud account's messaging infrastructure to add a covert C2 channel alongside legitimate traffic
rootCauses: Egress filtering allow-lists entire cloud-provider messaging-service domains without per-resource validation
Overly permissive cloud IAM credentials embedded in implants, when stolen from a legitimate source, are not rotated or scoped narrowly
controls: Cloud IAM least-privilege scoping and rotation for messaging-service credentials
Egress monitoring capable of distinguishing specific queue/topic-resource destinations
Cloud API audit logging with alerting on anomalous queue/topic creation and access patterns
ITID-44822.detection: Weak with coarse domain-level allow-listing; moderate to strong with cloud API audit-log review and credential-usage anomaly detection.
ITID-44822.response: Revoke the implicated cloud credentials, report the account/resource to the provider, and pivot to endpoint containment on affected hosts; investigate whether the same queue/topic infrastructure spans other victims.
metrics: Count of confirmed message-queue-based C2 incidents
Mean time from detection to credential revocation
detections: Cloud audit log: anomalous message queue/topic creation and access
Credential-usage anomaly: implant-embedded cloud credential authenticating to messaging service
ITID-44822.notes: Differentiates from ITID-44821 by mechanism: this leaf is about asynchronous queue/topic-based command exchange, not direct synchronous function invocation.

playbook.name: C2 Command Queue via Cloud Message Queue/Event Bus Service
playbook.description: Attackers are using a cloud-native message queue or event bus service (e.g., SQS/SNS, Azure Service Bus/Event Grid, Google Pub/Sub) as an asynchronous C2 command-and-control channel, exploiting the service's trusted status within cloud environments.

steps.title: Identify the abused queue/topic via cloud audit logs
steps.desc: Review cloud audit logs (CloudTrail, Azure Activity Log, GCP Audit Logs) for anomalous queue/topic creation, subscription, or message publish/consume activity, particularly from unexpected identities or at unusual volumes/patterns.
steps.guidance: Look for a queue/topic not defined in the organization's IaC baseline, or legitimate queues receiving messages from unauthorized publishers.
steps.outcome: The specific abused queue/topic and the identity publishing/consuming malicious messages are identified.
steps.abort: If activity matches an approved application's normal use of the queue, close as false positive.
steps.tool: CloudTrail / Azure Activity Log / GCP Audit Logs

steps.title: Revoke access to the abused queue/topic and remove unauthorized subscriptions
steps.desc: Remove any unauthorized publisher/subscriber permissions on the queue/topic and revoke the IAM credentials used to establish them.
steps.outcome: The attacker can no longer publish or consume messages via the queue.

steps.title: Delete the abused queue/topic or restore it to its verified baseline configuration
steps.desc: Remove the rogue queue/topic entirely, or if it is a legitimate resource that was abused, restore its access policy to the verified baseline.
steps.outcome: The queue/topic configuration matches the approved, secure baseline.

steps.title: Restore operations and monitor queue activity
steps.desc: Return remediated resources to production and monitor queue/topic activity for any recurrence of unauthorized publish/subscribe patterns.
steps.outcome: No recurrence of abusive queue activity within the monitoring window.

steps.title: Document the message-queue C2 technique
steps.desc: Record the technique and evaluate whether queue/topic access policies and monitoring need strengthening to detect similar abuse earlier.
steps.outcome: Improved cloud messaging security posture and detection guidance.

steps.title: Inspect message content and consumer to understand the C2 mechanism
steps.desc: Where message content is retrievable (not fully encrypted or accessible via provider console/logs), inspect it to understand the command structure and identify the consuming compute resource (host/container/function) that acts on the C2 commands.
steps.outcome: The C2 command structure and the consuming resource are identified.

steps.title: Isolate the consuming compute resource
steps.desc: Isolate the host/container/function that was consuming and acting on malicious queue messages, via security group lockdown, container network policy, or EDR isolation as appropriate.
steps.outcome: The compute resource acting on C2 commands is isolated from further tasking.
steps.tool: EDR / cloud security groups / network policy

steps.title: Redeploy the affected consuming resource from a known-good image and rotate credentials
steps.desc: Redeploy the compromised consuming compute resource from a verified known-good image/template and rotate any credentials/keys it had access to, rather than attempting in-place cleaning.
steps.outcome: The consuming resource runs clean code with rotated credentials.

steps.title: Scope all resources publishing to or consuming from the abused queue
steps.desc: Determine all internal hosts, containers, or functions that are publishing to or consuming from the compromised queue/topic.
steps.outcome: A complete list of affected resources.

ITID-44823.def: A catch-all classification for C2 activity confirmed to use serverless/managed cloud service infrastructure where the specific mechanism (direct function-endpoint invocation or message-queue/event-bus command exchange) has not been identified, or does not match an existing sibling leaf.
ITID-44823.purpose: Intake bucket for a confirmed serverless C2 mechanism that does not fit the function-endpoint or message-queue leaves.
scopeIncludes: Serverless C2 mechanisms pending further characterization
Serverless C2 patterns other than function-endpoint invocation or message-queue exchange
scopeExcludes: C2 relay via serverless function endpoint (ITID-44821)
C2 command queue via cloud message queue/event bus service (ITID-44822)
ITID-44823.severity: High by default, consistent with the sibling leaves.
ITID-44823.priority: P1, pending reclassification to a more specific sibling ITID once analysis completes.
ITID-44823.escalation: Escalate to cloud security and threat intelligence for full characterization; reclassify once the specific mechanism is confirmed.
indicators: Confirmed serverless/managed-cloud-service C2 activity, specific mechanism not yet characterized
vectors: Any serverless C2 mechanism not yet mapped to a specific sibling leaf
rootCauses: Insufficient egress/resource-level monitoring, consistent with the broader sibling group
controls: Egress monitoring and cloud API audit logging consistent with the sibling leaves
ITID-44823.detection: Varies by mechanism; use as an interim classification during active analysis.
ITID-44823.response: Complete characterization of the serverless C2 mechanism and reclassify to a specific sibling ITID where applicable.
metrics: Count of incidents initially filed here later reclassified
detections: Generic alert: serverless-hosted C2 activity detected
ITID-44823.notes: Use sparingly; prefer ITID-44821 or ITID-44822 whenever the specific mechanism is known.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Serverless C2
playbook.description: A host is communicating with C2 infrastructure implemented via a serverless/cloud-managed service that does not fit a more specific serverless-C2 subtype.

steps.title: Confirm the serverless C2 endpoint via cloud audit logs
steps.desc: Validate the suspicious serverless endpoint against cloud audit logs and threat intelligence to confirm it is being used as C2, and determine whether it is organization-owned or externally attacker-controlled.
steps.outcome: The serverless C2 endpoint is confirmed with ownership determined.
steps.abort: If it matches approved business use, close as false positive.
steps.tool: Cloud audit logs / threat intel platform

steps.title: Block the specific serverless endpoint
steps.desc: Apply a targeted block for the specific endpoint at the proxy/firewall layer.
steps.outcome: Outbound connection to the endpoint is blocked.

steps.title: Redeploy affected serverless resources from known-good code and rotate keys
steps.desc: Redeploy any compromised organization-owned serverless resources from verified source and rotate exposed keys, rather than in-place remediation.
steps.outcome: Affected resources run clean code with rotated credentials.

steps.title: Restore operations and monitor
steps.desc: Return remediated hosts/resources to production with a monitoring watchlist.
steps.outcome: No recurrence of C2 activity within the monitoring window.

steps.title: Document indicators and close the incident
steps.desc: Record the endpoint, associated IOCs, and remediation actions in the incident report and threat intel platform.
steps.outcome: Closed incident with indicators available for future detection.

steps.title: Scope all hosts/resources communicating with the endpoint
steps.desc: Search logs enterprise-wide for the specific endpoint to determine full infection/exposure scope.
steps.outcome: A complete list of affected hosts/resources.

steps.title: Disable the organization-owned serverless resource and revoke associated credentials
steps.desc: If the resource is organization-owned, disable/delete it and revoke the credentials used to deploy or invoke it.
steps.outcome: The malicious serverless resource can no longer be used.
steps.abort: If externally owned, skip this step.

steps.title: Remove the malware implant from internal hosts
steps.desc: Remove the malicious payload from all confirmed internal hosts.
steps.outcome: Hosts confirmed clean.

steps.title: Isolate infected internal hosts
steps.desc: Quarantine confirmed infected endpoints to sever active C2 sessions.
steps.outcome: Infected hosts can no longer reach the C2 endpoint.

ITID-44831.def: A C2 technique in which the adversary deploys a malicious workload (pod/container) into a compromised Kubernetes cluster to host or run an implant, blending it among the cluster's many legitimate workloads and leveraging Kubernetes' orchestration to survive individual node restarts.
ITID-44831.purpose: Captures a C2 implant deployed as a malicious pod or container running within a compromised Kubernetes cluster.
scopeIncludes: Malicious pod deployed via a Deployment/ReplicaSet or directly via the API to run a C2 implant or relay
Container image (from a public or private registry) containing embedded C2 implant logic, deployed into the cluster
Adversary using a compromised namespace/service account to deploy the malicious workload
scopeExcludes: C2 achieved via direct abuse of a compromised Kubernetes API server credential without deploying a workload (ITID-44832)
Persistence specifically via a CronJob or DaemonSet resource type (ITID-44833), a related but architecturally distinct mechanism
ITID-44831.severity: High; a malicious workload running inside a Kubernetes cluster typically has network reach to other cluster workloads and potentially to cloud metadata services, expanding blast radius beyond a single host.
ITID-44831.escalation: Escalate to cloud/container security and IR immediately; assess whether the malicious pod had access to the cluster's service account tokens or cloud metadata endpoint, which could indicate broader compromise.
indicators: Unexpected pod/deployment in a namespace with no corresponding legitimate application change record
Container image pulled from an unrecognized registry or with a name mimicking a legitimate system component
Pod exhibiting outbound network connections inconsistent with its apparent application function
vectors: Adversary exploits a vulnerable/misconfigured Kubernetes API server or compromised CI/CD credentials to deploy the malicious workload
Adversary uses a compromised container registry or supply-chain foothold to inject a malicious image into the deployment pipeline
rootCauses: Kubernetes API server exposed without adequate authentication/authorization controls
Insufficient admission-control policy (e.g., no image-provenance/signature verification) allowing arbitrary images to run
controls: Kubernetes admission control enforcing image provenance/signature verification
Network policies restricting pod-to-pod and pod-to-metadata-service traffic by default
Kubernetes audit logging with alerting on unexpected workload deployment
ITID-44831.detection: Moderate to strong with Kubernetes audit logging and runtime container security tooling; weak in environments without cluster-level audit logging enabled.
ITID-44831.response: Isolate and terminate the malicious workload, audit the deployment pipeline/API access path used to introduce it, and rotate any service account tokens the pod may have accessed.
metrics: Count of confirmed malicious-pod C2 incidents
Mean time from deployment to detection
detections: Kubernetes audit log: unexpected workload deployment
Runtime container security: anomalous outbound network connection from pod
ITID-44831.notes: Differentiates from ITID-44832 (API-server-access-only abuse without a workload) and ITID-44833 (CronJob/DaemonSet-specific persistence).

playbook.name: C2 Implant Deployed as Malicious Kubernetes Pod/Container
playbook.description: Attackers have deployed a malicious pod/container within the organization's Kubernetes cluster that serves as a C2 implant, exploiting cluster access or a vulnerable workload to establish a foothold inside the containerized environment.

steps.title: Identify the malicious pod via Kubernetes audit logs
steps.desc: Review Kubernetes audit logs for pod creation events that deviate from the expected deployment pipeline (unexpected namespace, image registry, service account, or creating identity).
steps.guidance: Compare the pod's image against the organization's approved image registry/allowlist and check for privileged security context settings, which are common in malicious pods seeking to escape container isolation.
steps.outcome: The malicious pod, its namespace, and its creation context (who/what created it) are identified.
steps.abort: If the pod matches an approved deployment, close as false positive.

steps.title: Isolate the malicious pod's namespace
steps.desc: Apply a restrictive Kubernetes network policy to the affected namespace (or the specific pod) to cut off its network communication while preserving it for forensic analysis, rather than immediately deleting it.
steps.guidance: Capture pod logs, environment variables, and a memory/filesystem snapshot before deletion where the cluster tooling supports it.
steps.outcome: The malicious pod's network access is severed while forensic evidence is preserved.
steps.abort: If immediate risk requires it, delete the pod immediately and rely on any centralized logging already captured.

steps.title: Delete the malicious pod and any associated resources
steps.desc: Delete the malicious pod, its associated service account (if attacker-created), and any persistent volumes or config maps it introduced.
steps.outcome: The malicious workload and its supporting resources are fully removed from the cluster.

steps.title: Restore normal cluster operations and monitor
steps.desc: Confirm the cluster is operating normally with only verified workloads, and monitor Kubernetes audit logs for any further anomalous pod creation events.
steps.outcome: The cluster operates normally with no recurrence of malicious pod deployment.

steps.title: Document the technique and strengthen cluster security controls
steps.desc: Record the initial access vector and recommend controls such as admission controllers/image signing enforcement, tighter RBAC, or network policy hardening to prevent recurrence.
steps.outcome: Improved Kubernetes security posture and updated detection for anomalous pod creation.

steps.title: Determine the initial access vector into the cluster
steps.desc: Investigate how the attacker gained the ability to create the malicious pod — compromised CI/CD credentials, an exposed/misconfigured Kubernetes API server, a vulnerable application allowing container escape, or a compromised service account token.
steps.outcome: The initial access vector is identified, informing which credentials/configurations require remediation.

steps.title: Revoke the compromised credential/service account used for initial access
steps.desc: Revoke or rotate the specific credential, API token, or service account that enabled the attacker to create the malicious pod.
steps.outcome: The attacker can no longer deploy additional malicious pods via the same access path.

steps.title: Redeploy affected legitimate workloads from known-good images and rotate cluster secrets
steps.desc: Redeploy any legitimate workloads that shared the compromised namespace/node from verified known-good images, and rotate any Kubernetes secrets, service account tokens, or cloud credentials the malicious pod may have accessed.
steps.guidance: Standard cloud-native/Kubernetes IR practice favors redeployment from a trusted baseline over attempting to verify a potentially tampered node or workload in place.
steps.outcome: The cluster's legitimate workloads run from a clean baseline with rotated secrets.

steps.title: Scope the extent of cluster and network access the pod obtained
steps.desc: Determine what network access, service accounts, secrets, or other pods/namespaces the malicious pod could reach given its assigned permissions and network policy context.
steps.outcome: A documented scope of potential lateral movement and data exposure within the cluster.
steps.tool: Kubernetes RBAC review / network policy review

ITID-44832.def: A C2 technique in which the adversary retains and abuses a compromised Kubernetes API server credential (service account token, kubeconfig, or exposed dashboard access) to issue commands directly against the cluster's control plane — executing commands in existing pods (e.g., via exec), reading secrets, or modifying resources — using the legitimate API as the command-and-control interface itself.
ITID-44832.purpose: Captures C2 achieved through direct abuse of a compromised Kubernetes API server credential, using the API itself as the command channel rather than deploying a dedicated malicious workload.
scopeIncludes: Adversary using `kubectl exec`-equivalent API calls against an existing legitimate pod to run commands
Adversary using compromised API server access to read/exfiltrate secrets or ConfigMaps as part of an ongoing C2 relationship with the cluster
Repeated, periodic API server access consistent with C2-style check-in/command-issuance behavior
scopeExcludes: Deployment of a dedicated malicious pod/container as the C2 implant (ITID-44831)
Persistence via a CronJob/DaemonSet resource (ITID-44833)
ITID-44832.severity: High; direct control-plane access represents a severe compromise with the potential for cluster-wide impact.
ITID-44832.escalation: Escalate to cloud/container security and IR immediately; treat the compromised credential as fully burned and rotate all cluster credentials it could have accessed, not just the one directly observed.
indicators: Kubernetes audit log showing exec/API calls from an unfamiliar source IP or user-agent using a legitimate service account/kubeconfig
API access pattern showing periodic, C2-like check-in behavior against the control plane rather than a single one-off action
Secret/ConfigMap read access inconsistent with the credential's normal usage pattern
vectors: Adversary obtains a leaked kubeconfig or service account token (e.g., from a compromised CI/CD pipeline, exposed repository, or SSRF against the cloud metadata service)
Exposed, unauthenticated Kubernetes dashboard or API server directly accessible from the internet
rootCauses: Kubernetes API server exposed to the internet or overly broad network without adequate authentication
Service account tokens/kubeconfigs not rotated or scoped to least privilege, and not monitored for anomalous use location/pattern
controls: Kubernetes API server network restriction (no unauthenticated internet exposure)
Service account token rotation and least-privilege RBAC scoping
Kubernetes audit logging with anomaly detection on API access source/pattern
ITID-44832.detection: Moderate to strong with Kubernetes audit logging and RBAC-usage anomaly detection; weak in clusters without audit logging enabled or with overly broad service account permissions masking anomalies.
ITID-44832.response: Revoke and rotate the compromised credential and all credentials it could have accessed, audit the full history of its API usage, and assess cluster-wide impact before considering the incident contained.
metrics: Count of confirmed API-server-credential-abuse C2 incidents
Mean time from credential compromise to detection
detections: Kubernetes audit log: anomalous API access source/pattern using existing service account
RBAC anomaly detection: unusual resource access pattern for a given credential
ITID-44832.notes: Differentiates from ITID-44831 and ITID-44833 by mechanism: this leaf is about abusing existing control-plane access directly, not deploying new workloads or scheduling resources.

playbook.name: C2 via Compromised Kubernetes API Server Access
playbook.description: An attacker has obtained direct access to the Kubernetes API server (via a stolen kubeconfig, exposed unauthenticated endpoint, or compromised service account token) and is using that access channel itself as a command-and-control mechanism to manipulate the cluster.

steps.title: Identify unauthorized API server access via Kubernetes audit logs
steps.desc: Review Kubernetes API server audit logs for authentication/authorization events from unexpected source IPs, unusual user identities, or API calls inconsistent with the calling identity's normal behavior pattern.
steps.guidance: Pay particular attention to calls from outside the expected network perimeter (if the API server is meant to be internal-only) and to high-privilege verbs (create, delete, exec) from anomalous sources.
steps.outcome: The unauthorized access pattern, source, and identity/credential used are identified.
steps.abort: If the access matches an approved administrative session, close as false positive.

steps.title: Revoke the compromised credential/token immediately
steps.desc: Revoke the specific kubeconfig, service account token, or cloud IAM credential the attacker used to access the API server.
steps.guidance: Rotate the cluster's CA-signed certificates or token signing keys if the compromise suggests broader credential material was exposed.
steps.outcome: The attacker's access to the API server is immediately cut off.

steps.title: Remove all attacker-created resources and revert unauthorized changes
steps.desc: Using the scoped activity record, delete any attacker-created pods, service accounts, RBAC bindings, or config maps, and revert any unauthorized changes to legitimate resources.
steps.outcome: The cluster state is restored to reflect only legitimate, authorized configuration.

steps.title: Restore normal cluster administration and monitor
steps.desc: Confirm normal administrative access is restored through verified channels only, and monitor API server audit logs closely for any recurrence of anomalous access.
steps.outcome: Normal cluster operations resume with no recurrence of unauthorized API access.

steps.title: Document the compromise and strengthen API server security posture
steps.desc: Record the root cause and recommend controls such as API server network restriction, credential rotation policy, and audit log alerting improvements.
steps.outcome: Improved Kubernetes API server security posture and updated detection guidance.

steps.title: Determine how API server access was exposed or the credential obtained
steps.desc: Investigate whether the API server itself was unintentionally exposed to the internet, or whether a kubeconfig/service account token/cloud IAM credential with cluster-admin-equivalent access was stolen.
steps.outcome: The root cause (exposure vs. credential theft) is identified, informing the correct remediation path.
steps.tool: Network configuration review / cloud IAM logs

steps.title: Restrict API server network exposure
steps.desc: If the API server was unintentionally exposed, immediately restrict its network access to only authorized administrative sources (VPN, bastion, or private network).
steps.outcome: The API server is no longer reachable from unauthorized network sources.
steps.tool: Network security groups / firewall / API server configuration

steps.title: Rotate all cluster secrets and redeploy affected workloads from known-good images
steps.desc: Rotate all secrets, service account tokens, and credentials the attacker may have accessed given cluster-admin-level exposure, and redeploy affected workloads from verified known-good images.
steps.guidance: Given the severity of API-server-level compromise, treat the entire cluster's secret material as potentially exposed.
steps.outcome: All cluster secrets are rotated and workloads run from a clean baseline.

steps.title: Scope all actions taken via the compromised API access
steps.desc: Review the audit log for the full session of attacker activity — what pods, secrets, config maps, RBAC bindings, or namespaces were created, read, or modified.
steps.outcome: A complete record of attacker actions taken via the compromised API access.

ITID-44833.def: A C2 persistence technique in which the adversary creates a Kubernetes CronJob (for recurring, scheduled execution) or DaemonSet (for ensuring a pod runs on every/every-matching node) specifically to sustain C2 implant execution across the cluster's normal pod lifecycle, node scaling, and restarts, functioning as the Kubernetes-native analog of a Windows Scheduled Task or Linux cron entry.
ITID-44833.purpose: Captures C2 persistence established via a malicious Kubernetes CronJob or DaemonSet, ensuring recurring or cluster-wide execution that survives pod restarts and scheduling churn.
scopeIncludes: CronJob resource created to periodically execute a C2 check-in/command script
DaemonSet resource created to ensure a C2 implant pod runs on every node (or a targeted subset) in the cluster
Modification of an existing legitimate CronJob/DaemonSet to add C2 behavior
scopeExcludes: A one-off malicious pod/deployment without a scheduling/persistence resource (ITID-44831)
Direct API-server credential abuse without deploying a scheduling resource (ITID-44832)
ITID-44833.severity: High; DaemonSet-based persistence in particular can achieve near-cluster-wide implant presence, materially increasing blast radius and eradication difficulty.
ITID-44833.priority: P1 upon confirmation, especially for DaemonSet-based persistence given its cluster-wide reach.
ITID-44833.escalation: Escalate to cloud/container security and IR immediately; a DaemonSet finding in particular should trigger a cluster-wide sweep before declaring containment complete.
indicators: CronJob or DaemonSet resource with an unfamiliar name/image not tied to a known legitimate deployment
Kubernetes audit log showing CronJob/DaemonSet creation outside change-management/CI-CD-driven deployment activity
DaemonSet pods present on an unexpectedly large fraction of cluster nodes
vectors: Adversary with API server or CI/CD pipeline access creates the malicious CronJob/DaemonSet directly
Adversary modifies an existing legitimate scheduling resource's container image/command to add C2 behavior
rootCauses: Insufficient admission control / policy-as-code restricting who can create CronJob/DaemonSet resources or with what image sources
Lack of drift detection comparing deployed cluster resources against source-controlled infrastructure-as-code definitions
controls: Admission control/policy-as-code restricting CronJob/DaemonSet creation and image sources
Infrastructure-as-code drift detection comparing live cluster state against source of truth
Kubernetes audit logging with alerting on CronJob/DaemonSet creation or modification
ITID-44833.detection: Moderate to strong with Kubernetes audit logging and drift-detection tooling; weak in clusters managed without infrastructure-as-code discipline or audit logging.
ITID-44833.response: Remove the malicious CronJob/DaemonSet, sweep all cluster nodes for remaining implant pods (particularly for DaemonSet-based persistence), and audit the deployment path used to introduce the resource.
metrics: Count of confirmed CronJob/DaemonSet-based C2 persistence incidents
Fraction of cluster nodes affected in DaemonSet-based cases
detections: Kubernetes audit log: CronJob/DaemonSet creation or modification alert
IaC drift detection: unmanaged cluster resource identified
ITID-44833.notes: Differentiates from ITID-44831 and ITID-44832 by mechanism: this leaf is specifically about scheduling/orchestration-resource-based persistence, the Kubernetes analog of the Windows Scheduled Task and cron leaves (ITID-44541/44542).

playbook.name: C2 Persistence via Malicious Kubernetes CronJob/DaemonSet
playbook.description: An attacker has established persistence in the Kubernetes cluster using a malicious CronJob or DaemonSet that periodically re-establishes C2 connectivity, ensuring the implant survives pod restarts and simple pod deletion.

steps.title: Identify the malicious CronJob/DaemonSet via Kubernetes audit logs
steps.desc: Review Kubernetes audit logs and current cluster object inventory for CronJob or DaemonSet resources that deviate from the approved IaC baseline (unexpected schedule, image, namespace, or creating identity).
steps.guidance: DaemonSets are especially notable since they run on every node — check for one running outside the standard monitoring/logging DaemonSets the cluster is expected to have.
steps.outcome: The malicious CronJob/DaemonSet, its schedule/node coverage, and creation context are identified.
steps.abort: If the resource matches an approved deployment, close as false positive.
steps.tool: Kubernetes audit logs / kubectl get cronjobs,daemonsets

steps.title: Suspend the CronJob/DaemonSet without deleting it, pending forensic capture
steps.desc: Suspend the CronJob schedule or apply a node-selector/taint to prevent the DaemonSet from scheduling new pods, while preserving the resource definition and any running pods for forensic capture.
steps.guidance: Capture the full resource YAML, associated pod logs, and container image details before deletion.
steps.outcome: The persistence mechanism can no longer trigger new C2 pods while evidence is preserved.
steps.abort: If immediate risk requires it, delete the resource immediately and rely on already-captured logs.

steps.title: Delete the malicious CronJob/DaemonSet and any spawned pods
steps.desc: Remove the persistence mechanism and all pods it has spawned across affected nodes.
steps.outcome: The persistence mechanism is fully removed from the cluster.

steps.title: Restore normal cluster operations and monitor
steps.desc: Confirm normal scheduled workloads are running as expected, and monitor audit logs for any recurrence of unauthorized CronJob/DaemonSet creation.
steps.outcome: The cluster operates normally with no recurrence of the persistence mechanism.

steps.title: Document the persistence technique and strengthen admission controls
steps.desc: Record the access vector and recommend controls such as admission controllers restricting CronJob/DaemonSet creation to approved pipelines, and tighter RBAC scoping.
steps.outcome: Improved Kubernetes security posture and updated detection for unauthorized scheduling resources.

steps.title: Determine the access path used to create the persistence mechanism
steps.desc: Investigate how the attacker obtained sufficient privilege to create a CronJob/DaemonSet — compromised CI/CD credentials, an over-privileged service account, or direct API server access.
steps.outcome: The access vector is identified for remediation.

steps.title: Block the C2 infrastructure the persistence mechanism connects to
steps.desc: Block the associated C2 IP/domain at the network layer and revoke the compromised credential/access path used to create the resource.
steps.outcome: Any remaining active pods from the persistence mechanism cannot reach their C2 destination.

steps.title: Redeploy affected nodes/workloads from known-good baselines and rotate secrets
steps.desc: Given DaemonSet-level persistence runs on every node, consider node-level compromise; redeploy affected nodes from a known-good image where node-level tampering is suspected, and rotate all cluster secrets and service account tokens the persistence mechanism could access.
steps.outcome: Cluster nodes and workloads run from a clean baseline with rotated credentials.
steps.tool: Cluster node management / Kubernetes secrets management

steps.title: Scope the extent of cluster/node coverage and C2 reach
steps.desc: Determine which nodes/namespaces are affected (all nodes if a DaemonSet, or just the schedule's target namespace for a CronJob) and what C2 infrastructure the persistence mechanism connects to.
steps.outcome: A documented scope of affected nodes and the associated C2 indicator.

ITID-44834.def: A catch-all classification for C2 activity confirmed to involve a compromised Kubernetes cluster where the specific mechanism (malicious pod deployment, direct API-server credential abuse, or CronJob/DaemonSet persistence) has not been identified, or does not match an existing sibling leaf.
ITID-44834.purpose: Intake bucket for a confirmed Kubernetes-based C2 mechanism that does not fit the malicious-pod, API-credential-abuse, or CronJob/DaemonSet-persistence leaves.
scopeIncludes: Kubernetes-based C2 mechanisms pending further characterization
Kubernetes-based C2 patterns other than the three specific sibling mechanisms
scopeExcludes: C2 implant deployed as a malicious Kubernetes pod/container (ITID-44831)
C2 via compromised Kubernetes API server access (ITID-44832)
C2 persistence via malicious Kubernetes CronJob/DaemonSet (ITID-44833)
ITID-44834.severity: High by default, consistent with the sibling leaves.
ITID-44834.priority: P1, pending reclassification to a more specific sibling ITID once analysis completes.
ITID-44834.escalation: Escalate to cloud/container security and IR for full characterization; reclassify once the specific mechanism is confirmed.
indicators: Confirmed Kubernetes-cluster-related C2 activity, specific mechanism not yet characterized
vectors: Any Kubernetes-based C2 mechanism not yet mapped to a specific sibling leaf
rootCauses: Insufficient Kubernetes audit logging/admission control, consistent with the broader sibling group
controls: Kubernetes audit logging and admission control consistent with the sibling leaves
ITID-44834.detection: Varies by mechanism; use as an interim classification during active analysis.
ITID-44834.response: Complete characterization of the Kubernetes-based C2 mechanism and reclassify to a specific sibling ITID where applicable.
metrics: Count of incidents initially filed here later reclassified
detections: Generic alert: Kubernetes cluster C2 activity detected
ITID-44834.notes: Use sparingly; prefer the specific sibling leaf whenever the mechanism is known.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Kubernetes-Based C2
playbook.description: A Kubernetes cluster resource is communicating with C2 infrastructure in a manner that does not fit a more specific Kubernetes-based C2 subtype.

steps.title: Confirm the Kubernetes-based C2 activity via audit logs
steps.desc: Review Kubernetes audit logs and network telemetry to confirm which cluster resource (pod, service account, or API access) is involved in the C2 activity.
steps.outcome: The specific cluster resource and its role in the C2 activity are identified.
steps.abort: If the activity matches approved cluster operations, close as false positive.

steps.title: Isolate the affected resource
steps.desc: Apply network policy or namespace-level isolation to the affected resource, preserving it for forensic capture where feasible.
steps.outcome: The resource's C2 communication is severed.

steps.title: Remove the malicious resource and associated artifacts
steps.desc: Delete the malicious pod/resource and any associated persistence artifacts from the cluster.
steps.outcome: The malicious workload is fully removed.

steps.title: Restore normal cluster operations and monitor
steps.desc: Confirm the cluster is operating normally and monitor for recurrence of the C2 pattern.
steps.outcome: No recurrence of C2 activity within the monitoring window.

steps.title: Document indicators and close the incident
steps.desc: Record the indicators and remediation actions in the incident report and threat intel platform.
steps.outcome: Closed incident with indicators available for future detection.

steps.title: Scope the extent of cluster access and affected resources
steps.desc: Determine what other cluster resources, namespaces, or secrets may have been affected or accessed.
steps.outcome: A documented scope of affected cluster resources.

steps.title: Revoke the compromised credential/access path
steps.desc: Revoke or rotate the credential/service account that enabled the malicious activity.
steps.outcome: The attacker can no longer leverage the same access path.

steps.title: Redeploy affected workloads and rotate cluster secrets
steps.desc: Redeploy affected legitimate workloads from known-good images and rotate any secrets/tokens potentially exposed.
steps.outcome: Cluster workloads run from a clean baseline with rotated credentials.

ITID-44841.def: A C2 technique in which the adversary uses a legitimate SaaS platform's documented REST API (via a compromised or adversary-created API key/OAuth token) to relay commands and exfiltrate results — treating the SaaS platform's own automation/integration surface as a covert C2 channel that inherits the platform's trusted domain and typically permissive API-access policies.
ITID-44841.purpose: Captures C2 conducted through abuse of a legitimate SaaS platform's own REST API, using the platform's normal integration surface as the command channel.
scopeIncludes: Implant using a stolen or attacker-created API key/OAuth token to read command data from a SaaS platform resource (e.g., a CRM record, ticketing item) and post results back
Abuse of a SaaS platform's webhook/integration feature to relay commands
C2 traffic authenticated as a legitimate (compromised) API consumer of the platform
scopeExcludes: GraphQL-specific API abuse for command exchange (ITID-44842), a related but architecturally distinct mechanism
Legitimate SaaS platform use with no C2 relationship
ITID-44841.severity: High; API-based C2 through a legitimate SaaS platform is difficult to distinguish from normal automation/integration traffic and often indicates a targeted, well-planned operation.
ITID-44841.priority: P1 upon confirmation of active command exchange via the API.
ITID-44841.escalation: Escalate to the SaaS platform's security/trust team and to identity/access management to revoke the abused API key or OAuth token immediately, and audit all actions taken under that credential.
indicators: API activity logs (from the SaaS platform or a CASB) showing anomalous access patterns, volume, or timing inconsistent with the credential's normal usage
API key/OAuth token usage from an unexpected source IP or geography
REST API calls reading/writing data in a pattern consistent with command polling and result posting rather than normal business use
vectors: Adversary steals an API key/OAuth token via phishing, credential stuffing, or a prior compromise, then uses it for C2 relay
Adversary registers a new, seemingly legitimate API integration/app within a compromised SaaS tenant
rootCauses: Insufficient API key/OAuth token scoping, rotation, and monitoring for SaaS integrations
No CASB or SaaS-security-posture tooling providing visibility into API-level activity patterns
mitreTechniques: T1071.001 Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols
controls: API key/OAuth token least-privilege scoping and regular rotation
CASB or SaaS-security-posture management (SSPM) monitoring API-level activity for anomalies
SaaS platform audit-log review integrated into the SOC's detection pipeline
ITID-44841.detection: Weak without dedicated CASB/SSPM tooling, since API traffic to the SaaS platform's legitimate domain otherwise looks like normal integration activity; moderate to strong with such tooling in place.
ITID-44841.response: Revoke the abused API key/OAuth token immediately, audit all actions taken under that credential during the compromise window, and coordinate with the SaaS platform's security team.
metrics: Count of confirmed SaaS-API-based C2 incidents
Mean time from detection to credential revocation
detections: CASB/SSPM: anomalous API access pattern for a given credential
SaaS audit log: unusual integration/app activity
ITID-44841.notes: Differentiates from ITID-44842 by API paradigm: this leaf covers REST API abuse; the sibling leaf covers GraphQL-specific abuse.

playbook.name: C2 Using Legitimate SaaS Platform's Own REST API as Command Channel
playbook.description: Malware issues commands and receives responses through a legitimate SaaS platform's own documented REST API (e.g., using an attacker-controlled account's API token), exploiting the platform's trusted API domain and standard authentication flow as a C2 channel.

steps.title: Identify the API endpoint and account/token used for C2
steps.desc: Analyze proxy/API gateway logs for calls to the SaaS platform's REST API from the suspect host, identifying the specific endpoint(s), API token, and account driving the traffic.
steps.guidance: Look for API call patterns (polling cadence, resource type accessed) inconsistent with the platform's normal client application usage — e.g., an API call pattern resembling command polling rather than typical business workflow use.
steps.outcome: The specific API endpoint, account, and token used for C2 are identified.
steps.abort: If the API usage matches an approved integration, close as false positive.

steps.title: Revoke the malicious API token/account
steps.desc: Revoke the specific API token and, if the account is organization-owned, reset its credentials/MFA to cut off attacker use of the API channel.
steps.outcome: The malicious API token can no longer authenticate to the platform's API.

steps.title: Remove the malware implant from internal hosts
steps.desc: Remove the malicious payload responsible for driving the API-based C2 communication from all confirmed internal hosts.
steps.outcome: Hosts confirmed clean.

steps.title: Restore hosts/accounts and monitor for token reuse
steps.desc: Return remediated hosts and re-enabled accounts to production with monitoring for any attempt to reuse the revoked token or create a replacement.
steps.outcome: No recurrence of C2 activity within the monitoring window.

steps.title: Document the API-based C2 technique
steps.desc: Record the platform, API pattern, and account compromise details (if applicable) in the threat intel platform, and evaluate whether API-usage anomaly detection needs improvement.
steps.outcome: Updated detection guidance for API-based C2 abuse of trusted SaaS platforms.

steps.title: Determine if the API token belongs to a compromised legitimate account
steps.desc: Check whether the API token/account is a legitimate organizational or partner account that has been compromised, versus an attacker-created account on the platform.
steps.guidance: Review the account's creation date and prior legitimate usage history via the SaaS platform's admin console if organizationally owned.
steps.outcome: Clarity on whether a legitimate account requires separate credential-reset/compromise handling.

steps.title: Block the specific API endpoint pattern where feasible
steps.desc: Apply proxy-layer blocking for the specific malicious API call pattern/endpoint if the platform's broader API domain must remain accessible for legitimate use.
steps.outcome: C2 traffic to the specific API endpoint is blocked while legitimate platform API use continues.
steps.abort: If path-level blocking isn't feasible and no legitimate business use exists, block the platform domain for affected hosts.

steps.title: Scope internal hosts using the API-based C2 channel
steps.desc: Search logs enterprise-wide for the specific API endpoint/token usage pattern to determine infection scope.
steps.outcome: A complete list of affected internal hosts.

steps.title: Isolate infected internal hosts
steps.desc: Quarantine hosts confirmed to be using the API-based C2 channel.
steps.outcome: Active C2 sessions are severed.

ITID-44842.def: A C2 technique in which the adversary uses a compromised or adversary-created GraphQL API credential against a SaaS or web application's GraphQL endpoint, exploiting GraphQL's flexible query/mutation structure — often a single endpoint handling many logical operations — to relay commands and exfiltrate results in a way that is harder to enumerate and log at the same granularity as traditional REST endpoints.
ITID-44842.purpose: Captures C2 conducted through abuse of a GraphQL API's query/mutation flexibility to exchange commands and results within a single, often under-logged, request pattern.
scopeIncludes: Implant issuing GraphQL queries/mutations against a compromised tenant's GraphQL endpoint to retrieve commands or post results
Abuse of GraphQL introspection or batching features to consolidate C2 command exchange into fewer, less-distinguishable requests
C2 traffic authenticated as a legitimate (compromised) GraphQL API consumer
scopeExcludes: REST API abuse for command exchange (ITID-44841), a related but architecturally distinct mechanism
Legitimate GraphQL API use with no C2 relationship
ITID-44842.severity: High; GraphQL's single-endpoint, flexible-query nature makes command-level logging and anomaly detection materially harder than for equivalent REST API abuse.
ITID-44842.priority: P1 upon confirmation of active command exchange via the GraphQL API.
ITID-44842.escalation: Escalate to the platform's security/trust team and to identity/access management to revoke the abused credential immediately; note that standard REST-endpoint-based logging/alerting may not have captured the activity, requiring GraphQL-specific log review.
indicators: GraphQL query/mutation logs (where available) showing anomalous field-selection patterns or volume inconsistent with the credential's normal usage
A single GraphQL endpoint receiving traffic volume/pattern inconsistent with the small number of legitimate client applications expected to use it
Credential usage from an unexpected source IP or geography against the GraphQL endpoint
vectors: Adversary steals a GraphQL API credential/token via phishing or prior compromise, then crafts queries/mutations to relay C2 commands
Adversary abuses an overly permissive GraphQL schema (e.g., no field-level authorization) to access broader functionality than intended
rootCauses: GraphQL endpoints deployed without field-level authorization or query-complexity/rate limiting
Logging infrastructure built for REST-style endpoint enumeration, providing poor visibility into GraphQL query/mutation-level activity
mitreTechniques: T1071.001 Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols
controls: Field-level authorization and query-complexity/rate limiting on GraphQL endpoints
GraphQL-specific logging capturing query/mutation content, not just endpoint hit counts
API credential least-privilege scoping and rotation
ITID-44842.detection: Weak with standard endpoint-hit-count logging alone; requires GraphQL-aware logging/monitoring tooling capturing query and field-level detail for meaningful coverage.
ITID-44842.response: Revoke the abused credential immediately, review available GraphQL query/mutation logs for the compromise window, and coordinate with the platform's security team on schema/authorization hardening.
metrics: Count of confirmed GraphQL-API-based C2 incidents
Mean time from detection to credential revocation
detections: GraphQL-aware logging: anomalous query/mutation pattern for a given credential
ITID-44842.notes: Differentiates from ITID-44841 by API paradigm: this leaf covers GraphQL-specific abuse, exploiting its single-endpoint/flexible-query characteristics; the sibling leaf covers REST API abuse.

playbook.name: C2 Using GraphQL API Abuse for Command Exchange
playbook.description: Malware uses a GraphQL API endpoint (either a legitimate platform's own GraphQL service or an attacker-hosted one designed to look like normal application traffic) to exchange C2 commands, exploiting GraphQL's flexible query structure to encode commands and data within seemingly ordinary API queries.

steps.title: Identify the GraphQL endpoint and analyze query/mutation structure for command encoding
steps.desc: Analyze proxy/API gateway logs for POST requests to a GraphQL endpoint (typically a single URL path such as /graphql) and inspect the query/mutation payloads for encoded command data disguised within field names, variables, or arguments.
steps.guidance: GraphQL's single-endpoint model means traditional URL-path-based detection is ineffective — inspect POST body content and query structure/complexity instead; look for unusual field names or nested query patterns not matching the platform's published schema.
steps.outcome: The GraphQL endpoint and the command-encoding pattern within its queries are identified.
steps.abort: If the queries match legitimate application schema usage, close as false positive.
steps.tool: Proxy logs / API gateway logs with payload inspection

steps.title: Block the GraphQL endpoint or revoke the abused account/token
steps.desc: If attacker-hosted, block the endpoint at the proxy/DNS layer; if hosted on a legitimate platform via a compromised account, revoke the token/account credentials instead.
steps.outcome: The C2 channel via the GraphQL endpoint is severed.
steps.tool: Secure web gateway / SaaS admin console

steps.title: Remove the malware implant from internal hosts
steps.desc: Remove the malicious payload responsible for driving the GraphQL-based C2 communication from all confirmed internal hosts.
steps.outcome: Hosts confirmed clean.

steps.title: Restore hosts and monitor for schema/endpoint changes
steps.desc: Return remediated hosts to production with monitoring for any resumed or shifted GraphQL-based command traffic.
steps.outcome: No recurrence of C2 activity within the monitoring window.

steps.title: Document the GraphQL abuse technique
steps.desc: Record the endpoint, query encoding pattern, and any account compromise details in the threat intel platform, and evaluate whether API gateway inspection needs GraphQL-aware payload analysis.
steps.outcome: Updated detection guidance for GraphQL-based C2 abuse.

steps.title: Determine if the GraphQL service is legitimate-platform-hosted or attacker-owned
steps.desc: Determine whether the GraphQL endpoint belongs to a legitimate SaaS platform (being abused via a compromised account/token) or is entirely attacker-hosted infrastructure designed to mimic legitimate API traffic.
steps.outcome: Clarity on infrastructure ownership informs whether account-compromise handling or standard C2 blocking is the correct response path.

steps.title: Isolate infected internal hosts
steps.desc: Quarantine hosts confirmed to be using the GraphQL C2 channel.
steps.outcome: Active C2 sessions are severed.

steps.title: Scope internal hosts communicating with the GraphQL C2 channel
steps.desc: Search logs enterprise-wide for the specific GraphQL endpoint and query pattern to determine infection scope.
steps.outcome: A complete list of affected internal hosts.

ITID-44843.def: A catch-all classification for C2 activity confirmed to abuse a legitimate cloud/SaaS platform's API surface where the specific API paradigm (REST or GraphQL) has not been identified, or does not match an existing sibling leaf — for example, gRPC or SOAP-based API abuse.
ITID-44843.purpose: Intake bucket for a confirmed API-based C2 mechanism that does not fit the REST-API or GraphQL-API abuse leaves.
scopeIncludes: API-based C2 mechanisms pending further characterization
API-based C2 patterns using a paradigm other than REST or GraphQL
scopeExcludes: C2 using a legitimate SaaS platform's REST API as command channel (ITID-44841)
C2 using GraphQL API abuse for command exchange (ITID-44842)
ITID-44843.severity: High by default, consistent with the sibling leaves.
ITID-44843.priority: P1, pending reclassification to a more specific sibling ITID once analysis completes.
ITID-44843.escalation: Escalate to identity/access management and the platform's security team for full characterization; reclassify once the specific API paradigm is confirmed.
indicators: Confirmed API-based C2 activity, specific paradigm not yet characterized
vectors: Any API-based C2 mechanism not yet mapped to a specific sibling leaf
rootCauses: Insufficient API credential scoping/monitoring, consistent with the broader sibling group
controls: API credential least-privilege scoping and monitoring consistent with the sibling leaves
ITID-44843.detection: Varies by paradigm; use as an interim classification during active analysis.
ITID-44843.response: Complete characterization of the API-based C2 mechanism and reclassify to a specific sibling ITID where applicable.
metrics: Count of incidents initially filed here later reclassified
detections: Generic alert: API-based C2 activity detected
ITID-44843.notes: Use sparingly; prefer ITID-44841 or ITID-44842 whenever the specific API paradigm is known.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General API-Based C2
playbook.description: A host is exchanging C2 commands via an API channel that does not fit a more specific API-based C2 subtype.

steps.title: Identify the API endpoint and confirm malicious use
steps.desc: Analyze proxy/API gateway logs to identify the specific API endpoint and confirm it is being used for C2 rather than legitimate application integration.
steps.outcome: The API endpoint is confirmed as malicious C2 with supporting evidence.
steps.abort: If it matches approved integration usage, close as false positive.

steps.title: Block the API endpoint or revoke the associated credential/token
steps.desc: Depending on infrastructure ownership, block the endpoint at the proxy/DNS layer or revoke the compromised API token/account.
steps.outcome: The API-based C2 channel is severed.

steps.title: Remove the malware and persistence mechanisms
steps.desc: Identify and remove the implant responsible for the API-based C2 communication from each infected host.
steps.outcome: Hosts confirmed clean of the implant.

steps.title: Restore hosts and monitor
steps.desc: Return remediated hosts to production with a monitoring watchlist for the endpoint and related indicators.
steps.outcome: No recurrence of C2 activity within the monitoring window.

steps.title: Document indicators and close the incident
steps.desc: Record the endpoint, associated IOCs, and remediation actions in the incident report and threat intel platform.
steps.outcome: Closed incident with indicators available for future detection.

steps.title: Scope all hosts communicating via the API channel
steps.desc: Search logs enterprise-wide for the specific endpoint/pattern to determine full infection scope and timeline.
steps.outcome: A complete list of affected hosts and an infection timeline.

steps.title: Isolate infected hosts
steps.desc: Quarantine confirmed infected endpoints via EDR/NAC to sever active C2 sessions.
steps.outcome: Infected hosts can no longer reach the API-based C2 channel.

steps.title: Verify no residual persistence remains
steps.desc: Re-scan remediated hosts for scheduled tasks, startup items, or registry run-keys the malware may have used for persistence.
steps.outcome: No residual persistence artifacts remain.

ITID-44911.def: A defensive/response action classification (not an adversary technique) in which the SOC, its DNS provider, or a threat-intel/law-enforcement partner reconfigures DNS resolution for a confirmed C2 domain so that queries resolve to a controlled sinkhole IP instead of the adversary's real infrastructure, cutting off the C2 channel while capturing telemetry on which internal hosts continue attempting to reach it.
ITID-44911.purpose: Captures the organization's own or a partner's deliberate DNS sinkholing of an identified malicious C2 domain during active incident response, redirecting the domain to a controlled, non-functional destination.
scopeIncludes: Organization-initiated DNS sinkhole entry added for a confirmed malicious C2 domain via internal DNS/RPZ
Partner or upstream DNS provider sinkholing a domain that also affects the organization's resolution of it
Sinkhole deployment used to identify additional infected hosts by monitoring resolution attempts
scopeExcludes: An internal, analyst-controlled redirect used specifically to capture and analyze live malware callback traffic for research purposes (ITID-44912)
IP/domain blocking performed at the firewall/proxy layer rather than via DNS resolution redirection (ITID-44921/44922)
ITID-44911.severity: Not applicable in the traditional threat-severity sense — this leaf classifies the organization's own disruption action; document the severity of the underlying C2 incident being responded to separately.
ITID-44911.priority: P1 for IR-process purposes: sinkholing is typically a time-sensitive action taken as soon as a C2 domain is confirmed, to immediately cut adversary access while investigation continues.
ITID-44911.escalation: Coordinate with legal/threat intel before any external-facing blocklist or sinkhole action that could tip off the adversary or affect third parties (e.g., if the domain is shared infrastructure); notify network operations before deployment to avoid unintended resolution impact on legitimate services.
indicators: N/A — this leaf logs a defender action rather than an indicator of adversary activity; the associated evidence is the sinkhole configuration change and the resulting resolution-attempt telemetry
Post-sinkhole DNS query logs showing continued internal resolution attempts against the sinkholed domain, identifying additional infected hosts
vectors: N/A — not an attack vector; this leaf documents a defensive action taken in response to an identified C2 domain
rootCauses: N/A — not a root-cause-bearing leaf; document root causes under the originating C2 incident's own ITID classification
mitreTechniques: T1568.002 Dynamic Resolution: Domain Generation Algorithms
controls: Internal DNS RPZ (Response Policy Zone) or equivalent sinkholing capability
Coordination process with DNS/network operations for sinkhole deployment
Sinkhole resolution-attempt logging integrated into the SOC's host-identification workflow
ITID-44911.detection: N/A for detecting adversary activity; the sinkhole itself becomes a detection source for identifying additional infected hosts via their continued resolution attempts.
ITID-44911.response: Validate the sinkhole redirect is functioning correctly (test resolution), monitor sinkhole logs for infected-host identification, and monitor for the adversary's fallback C2 mechanism (e.g., a backup domain or IP-direct fallback) that the malware may switch to once the primary domain stops resolving.
metrics: Count of C2 domains sinkholed per year
Count of additional infected hosts identified via post-sinkhole resolution telemetry
Mean time from C2 domain confirmation to sinkhole deployment
detections: Sinkhole DNS query log monitoring for infected-host identification
ITID-44911.notes: ATT&CK documents attacker behavior, not defensive takedown actions, so mapped_mitre_tactics/techniques are intentionally left empty for this leaf and its siblings in the C2 Disruption and Takedown Methods branch. This leaf logs the org's/partner's own counter-C2 action, not something the org suffers.

playbook.name: DNS Sinkhole Deployed Against Identified C2 Domain
playbook.description: The organization needs to stand up and validate a DNS sinkhole to redirect a confirmed malicious C2 domain to a controlled server, both to sever attacker access and to gain visibility into which internal hosts continue attempting to reach it, without breaking any legitimate traffic that might share infrastructure.

steps.title: Confirm the domain is safe to sinkhole without collateral impact
steps.desc: Verify the domain is exclusively malicious with no legitimate shared use (e.g., not a compromised legitimate domain still serving real content) before committing to a sinkhole rather than a simple block.
steps.guidance: Check the domain's current content, any legitimate subdomains sharing the parent zone, and confirm via threat intelligence that sinkholing (versus notification-based takedown) is the appropriate response.
steps.outcome: Confirmation that sinkholing the domain will not disrupt legitimate services.
steps.abort: If the domain has legitimate shared use, use path/subdomain-specific handling (see ITID-44113/44133) instead of a full sinkhole.

steps.title: Deploy the sinkhole DNS record and validate resolution
steps.desc: Configure the DNS firewall/RPZ or internal authoritative override to resolve the target domain to the designated sinkhole IP, then validate resolution from a test host within the environment.
steps.guidance: Stage the change in a test/limited scope first if the DNS infrastructure supports phased rollout, to catch configuration errors before full deployment.
steps.outcome: The domain resolves to the sinkhole IP for all internal DNS clients, confirmed via test resolution.
steps.abort: If resolution testing reveals unexpected behavior (e.g., the domain still resolving externally for some clients, or DNS server errors), roll back and troubleshoot before proceeding.

steps.title: Use sinkhole telemetry to identify and remediate infected internal hosts
steps.desc: Analyze which internal hosts are hitting the sinkhole and treat each as infected, driving standard malware removal (EDR remediation/reimaging) for each.
steps.outcome: All internal hosts identified via sinkhole telemetry are remediated.

steps.title: Maintain the sinkhole as a standing control and monitor for decline in hits
steps.desc: Keep the sinkhole in place as a durable control, monitoring hit volume over time to confirm successful remediation across the estate (declining then zero internal hits).
steps.outcome: Internal sinkhole hits decline to zero, confirming full remediation.

steps.title: Document the sinkhole deployment and outcomes
steps.desc: Record the domain, sinkhole configuration, hosts identified/remediated, and any legal review outcome for future reference and process improvement.
steps.outcome: A documented sinkhole deployment record supporting future similar actions.

steps.title: Determine sinkhole objectives: disruption only, or intelligence collection
steps.desc: Decide whether the sinkhole's primary purpose is purely defensive disruption (redirect to a null/blackhole server) or active intelligence collection (redirect to a controlled listener capturing check-in metadata from any infected hosts, internal or external).
steps.guidance: Intelligence-collection sinkholes require legal/privacy review if external (non-organizational) traffic may be captured; coordinate with legal counsel before standing up a collection-capable sinkhole with any external reach.
steps.outcome: A documented decision on sinkhole type and, if collection-capable, legal sign-off obtained.

steps.title: Verify no legitimate traffic is being redirected/broken
steps.desc: Monitor the sinkhole listener and any application error reports for signs that legitimate business traffic was inadvertently captured or broken by the redirect.
steps.outcome: Confirmation that only malicious/infected-host traffic is landing on the sinkhole, with no legitimate service disruption.
steps.abort: If legitimate traffic is found landing on the sinkhole, immediately narrow the sinkhole scope (specific subdomain/record type) or roll it back.

steps.title: Verify no residual persistence remains on remediated hosts
steps.desc: Re-scan remediated hosts for scheduled tasks, startup items, or registry run-keys the malware may have used for persistence.
steps.outcome: No residual persistence artifacts remain on any remediated host.

ITID-44912.def: A defensive/response action classification (not an adversary technique) in which the SOC or malware-analysis team redirects a confirmed C2 domain/IP to an internally-controlled, instrumented listener designed to interact with the implant's callback protocol, capturing command requests, beacon structure, and configuration data for analysis rather than simply dropping the traffic.
ITID-44912.purpose: Captures the organization's use of an internal, analyst-controlled sinkhole redirect specifically to capture and analyze live malware callback traffic rather than merely to cut off the channel.
scopeIncludes: Internal redirect of a C2 domain/IP to an analyst-controlled listener that logs or interacts with beacon traffic
Use of the redirected traffic to extract implant configuration, campaign identifiers, or additional C2 infrastructure
Controlled interaction (e.g., responding to beacon requests) to elicit further implant behavior for analysis, within authorized scope
scopeExcludes: Simple DNS sinkholing intended primarily to block resolution and identify infected hosts, without active analytical interaction (ITID-44911)
IP/domain blocking with no redirection or capture component (ITID-44921/44922)
ITID-44912.severity: Not applicable in the traditional threat-severity sense — this leaf classifies the organization's own analysis action; document the severity of the underlying C2 incident separately.
ITID-44912.priority: P2 for IR-process purposes: typically performed once initial containment (e.g., sinkholing or blocking) is already in place and time allows for deeper analysis.
ITID-44912.escalation: Coordinate with legal before any active interaction with the implant beyond passive capture, since active response can raise authorization and jurisdictional questions; ensure analysis activity is documented and scoped to an approved authority.
indicators: N/A — this leaf logs a defender action; associated evidence is the captured beacon/callback traffic and any extracted implant configuration
Analysis findings (implant version, campaign ID, additional C2 infrastructure) derived from the captured traffic
vectors: N/A — not an attack vector; this leaf documents a defensive analysis action taken in response to an identified C2 channel
rootCauses: N/A — not a root-cause-bearing leaf; document root causes under the originating C2 incident's own ITID classification
controls: Isolated analysis environment/listener infrastructure separate from production
Documented authorization process for active response/analysis interaction with adversary infrastructure
Chain-of-custody handling for captured beacon traffic and extracted configuration
ITID-44912.detection: N/A for detecting adversary activity; this action itself is a source of deep technical intelligence once deployed.
ITID-44912.response: Validate the redirect/listener is functioning as intended, extract and disseminate any actionable intelligence (additional infrastructure, campaign attribution) promptly, and monitor for the adversary noticing the redirect and adapting.
metrics: Count of analyst-controlled sinkhole captures performed per year
Count of additional C2 infrastructure indicators derived from captured traffic
detections: N/A — this leaf documents an analysis action rather than a detection
ITID-44912.notes: ATT&CK documents attacker behavior, not defensive takedown/analysis actions, so mapped_mitre_tactics/techniques are intentionally left empty. Differentiates from ITID-44911 by purpose: this leaf is about active analytical capture, not primarily blocking/host-identification.

playbook.name: Internal Sinkhole Redirect for Malware Callback Analysis
playbook.description: The organization needs to redirect a suspected malware's C2 callback to an internal controlled sinkhole purely for analysis purposes — to observe malware behavior, capture beacon content, and confirm scope — without alerting the actor or breaking legitimate traffic.

steps.title: Confirm the callback target and assess analysis value
steps.desc: Confirm the specific C2 callback destination and determine what analytical value an internal sinkhole redirect would provide (e.g., capturing beacon protocol details, confirming additional infected hosts, or observing malware behavior when it believes it has reached its C2).
steps.outcome: A documented rationale for pursuing an internal analysis sinkhole rather than immediate blocking.
steps.abort: If immediate containment outweighs analysis value (e.g., active data exfiltration risk), skip to direct blocking instead.

steps.title: Deploy the internal sinkhole redirect scoped only to affected hosts
steps.desc: Configure internal DNS/routing to redirect only the affected/suspected hosts' resolution of the C2 domain to the internal sinkhole listener, avoiding a broader environment-wide change that could tip off a sophisticated actor.
steps.guidance: Scope narrowly using host-specific DNS views or routing rules rather than a global DNS firewall entry, to limit detection risk and blast radius if the redirect configuration has issues.
steps.outcome: Only the intended hosts are redirected to the internal sinkhole, with the wider environment's resolution of the domain unaffected.

steps.title: Use captured analysis to drive full remediation
steps.desc: Use the beacon/callback data captured by the sinkhole to inform full removal of the malware from the affected host(s) and any additional hosts identified through the analysis.
steps.outcome: All hosts identified through sinkhole analysis are remediated.

steps.title: Decommission the analysis sinkhole and restore normal resolution
steps.desc: Once analysis and remediation are complete, remove the scoped sinkhole redirect and confirm normal DNS resolution/blocking (via standard blocklist) is in place going forward.
steps.outcome: The temporary analysis sinkhole is cleanly decommissioned with standard blocking controls left in place.

steps.title: Document the malware behavior and analysis findings
steps.desc: Record the captured beacon protocol details, malware behavior observations, and any new indicators discovered in the threat intel platform.
steps.outcome: Enriched threat intelligence supporting future detection of the same malware family.

steps.title: Design the sinkhole to convincingly emulate expected C2 responses
steps.desc: Determine what response behavior the malware expects from its C2 (specific HTTP headers, response codes, or protocol handshake) so the internal sinkhole listener can be configured to elicit maximum behavioral information from the malware without it detecting the redirect.
steps.guidance: Where possible, sandbox-detonate a sample first to understand expected C2 response formats.
steps.outcome: A sinkhole listener configuration designed to convincingly interact with the malware for analysis purposes.

steps.title: Validate the sinkhole is capturing traffic without disrupting the host's normal operation
steps.desc: Confirm the sinkhole listener is receiving and logging the malware's callback traffic, and that the redirect has not broken any legitimate application function on the affected host.
steps.outcome: Confirmed callback capture with no unintended side effects on the host.
steps.abort: If legitimate application traffic is being broken by the scoped redirect, narrow further or roll back.

steps.title: Verify no residual persistence remains
steps.desc: Re-scan remediated hosts for scheduled tasks, startup items, or registry run-keys the malware may have used for persistence.
steps.outcome: No residual persistence artifacts remain.

ITID-44913.def: A catch-all classification for the organization's/partner's own DNS sinkholing action against a C2 domain where the specific purpose (primarily blocking/host-identification, or primarily analytical capture) has not been characterized, or does not match an existing sibling leaf.
ITID-44913.purpose: Intake bucket for a confirmed C2 sinkholing action that does not fit the blocking-focused or analysis-focused sinkhole leaves.
scopeIncludes: Sinkholing actions pending further characterization of primary purpose
Sinkholing actions serving a purpose other than blocking/host-identification or analytical capture
scopeExcludes: DNS sinkhole deployed against identified C2 domain, primarily for blocking/host-identification (ITID-44911)
Internal sinkhole redirect for malware callback analysis (ITID-44912)
ITID-44913.severity: Not applicable — this leaf classifies the organization's own response action.
ITID-44913.priority: P1-P2 for IR-process purposes, consistent with the sibling leaves.
ITID-44913.escalation: Coordinate with legal/threat intel per standard sinkholing action handling; reclassify once the specific purpose is confirmed.
indicators: N/A — this leaf logs a defender action
vectors: N/A — not an attack vector
rootCauses: N/A — not a root-cause-bearing leaf
controls: Internal DNS RPZ/sinkholing capability consistent with the sibling leaves
ITID-44913.response: Identify the primary purpose of the sinkholing action and reclassify to a specific sibling ITID where possible.
metrics: Count of incidents initially filed here later reclassified
detections: N/A — this leaf documents a response action
ITID-44913.notes: ATT&CK documents attacker behavior, not defensive takedown actions, so mapped_mitre_tactics/techniques are intentionally left empty. Use sparingly; prefer ITID-44911 or ITID-44912 whenever the purpose is known.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General C2 Sinkholing Action
playbook.description: The organization needs to execute a sinkholing action against C2 infrastructure that does not fit a more specific sinkholing subtype, safely disrupting the malicious channel without breaking legitimate traffic.

steps.title: Confirm the target is appropriate for sinkholing
steps.desc: Verify the C2 indicator is malicious and confirm sinkholing (versus simple blocking) is the appropriate response, checking for any legitimate shared use of the infrastructure.
steps.outcome: Confirmation that sinkholing will not disrupt legitimate services.
steps.abort: If legitimate shared use exists, use targeted path/account-specific handling instead.

steps.title: Deploy and validate the sinkhole
steps.desc: Configure the sinkhole redirect and validate correct resolution/routing behavior via test traffic.
steps.outcome: The sinkhole is functioning as intended with validated redirect behavior.
steps.abort: If validation reveals configuration issues, roll back and troubleshoot.

steps.title: Remediate hosts identified via sinkhole telemetry
steps.desc: Treat hosts hitting the sinkhole as infected and drive standard malware removal.
steps.outcome: All identified hosts are remediated.

steps.title: Maintain or decommission the sinkhole as appropriate
steps.desc: Keep the sinkhole as a standing control or decommission it once its purpose is served, confirming normal operations continue.
steps.outcome: The sinkhole's disposition is resolved appropriately with confirmed remediation.

steps.title: Document the sinkhole action and outcomes
steps.desc: Record the action taken, hosts identified/remediated, and any legal review outcome.
steps.outcome: A documented record supporting future similar actions.

steps.title: Determine sinkhole scope and objective
steps.desc: Decide whether the sinkhole is for disruption only or intelligence collection, and obtain legal review if external traffic capture is possible.
steps.outcome: A documented decision on sinkhole type and any required legal sign-off.

steps.title: Verify no legitimate traffic disruption
steps.desc: Monitor for signs that legitimate traffic was inadvertently captured or broken by the sinkhole.
steps.outcome: Confirmation of no legitimate service disruption.
steps.abort: If disruption is found, narrow scope or roll back.

steps.title: Verify no residual persistence remains
steps.desc: Re-scan remediated hosts for scheduled tasks, startup items, or registry run-keys the malware may have used for persistence.
steps.outcome: No residual persistence artifacts remain.
